11500119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11500119.value: A substantial amount of research has been devoted to covariance estimators, which play an indispensable and critical role in economic, financial and statistical studies (Newey and West, 1987; Fan, Liu, Wang, et al., 2018). It is also crucial for practical applications like risk management, portfolio allocation, and regression analysis (Jagannathan and Ma, 2003; Fan, Zhang, and Yu, 2012). However, high-dimensional and high-frequency data, which are contaminated by microstructure noise and asynchronous trading, pose new challenges to covariance estimations. Kim, Wang, and Zou (2016) further documents an economically significant trade-off, in the current available approaches, among positive definiteness, unbiasedness, consistency and rate of convergence, which decreases its applicability in areas like vast portfolio selections and evaluations. This proposal intends to push current theoretical boundaries by proposing a novel covariance estimator via a machine learning (ML) approach. Assuming that the large covariance can be decomposed into a low-rank matrix and a sparse one, our proposed method aims to provide unbiased, consistent and positive definite estimates of these two components in a one-step procedure. Our new method is fully nonparametric. We avoid the imposition of linear factor models, but let the data directly determine the low-rank component, which avoids potential misspecification errors in the construction of the data generating process of a low-rank matrix and possible contractions in the number of factors. Moreover, unlike current approaches, which require the stock constituents of a large portfolio to be well-diversified among different industries with prior knowledge of their classifications, our method will overcome this limitation by allowing for valid investigations on vast portfolios that have constituents with unobserved connections and from concentrated industries. Traditional ML methodologies are widely applied on i.i.d. data, therefore this proposal will bridge ML technologies with serially dependent financial data by developing a novel efficient ML algorithm. Moreover, we will design the algorithm so that the initial bias-adjusted volatility is not required to be positive semi-definite, which will enable the optimal rate of statistical convergence. Moreover, we will derive a data-driven algorithm to select the optimal tuning parameters for ease of practical use. As an application, we plan to apply our new ML approach to a large panel of asynchronously traded assets. We aim to consistently identify and estimate the systemic and idiosyncratic risk components for vast portfolios and conduct out-of-sample portfolio evaluations. The success of our novel ML approach will help justify the role machine learning techniques play in modern financial practices. 大量的研究致力于协方差估计，它在经济，金融和统计研究中发挥着不可或缺的关键作用。它对于风险管理，投资组合分配和回归分析等实际应用也至关重要。然而，被微结构噪声和异步交易污染的高维和高频数据对协方差估计提出了新的挑战。Kim (2016)进一步证明了在当前可用的方法中，在正确性，无偏见性，一致性和收敛率之间进行经济上显着的权衡，这严重恶化了大量投资组合选择和评估的有效性。 该提议旨在通过机器学习（ML）方法提出新的协方差估计来推动当前的理论界限。假设大协方差可以分解为低秩矩阵和稀疏矩阵，我们提出的方法旨在通过一步过程提供这两个分量的无偏，一致和正定估计。我们的新方法完全是非参数的。我们避免强加线性因子模型，但让数据直接确定低秩分量，这避免了低秩矩阵的数据生成过程的构造中潜在的错误指定误差以及因子数量的可能收缩。此外，与目前的方法不同，现有方法要求大型投资组合的股票成分在不同行业之间进行多样化，并且事先了解其分类，我们的方法将通过允许对未被观察到的成分构成的投资组合进行有效调查来克服这一局限性。连接和集中的行业。 传统的ML方法被广泛应用于i.i.d.因此，该提议旨在通过开发新的有效ML算法将ML技术与依赖于串行的金融数据联系起来。此外，我们将设计算法，使初始偏差调整的波动率不需要是正半正定，这将实现统计收敛的最佳速率。此外，我们将推导出一种数据驱动算法，以选择最佳的调整参数，以便于实际使用。作为一种应用，我们计划在一大批异步交易的高频资产上采用我们的新ML方法。我们的目标是始终如一地识别和估计大型投资组合的系统性和特殊风险成分，并进行样本外的投资组合评估。我们新颖的ML方法的成功将有助于证明机器学习技术在现代金融实践中的作用。

11500119.label: Realisation of objectives
11500119.value: This is a completion report for my general research fund, entitled “A mixed Convex penalized Machine Learning Approach for High-Dimensional Financial Data with its Application on Vast Portfolio Selections (11500119)”. My original project objectives involve five dimensions and I shall elaborate each corresponding realization in details here. 1. The first objective was to provide a novel machine learning approach to achieve a positive definite, bias-adjusted and consistent large covariance estimate on high-dimensional and high-frequency data. Due to technological advancements, high-frequency intraday data for a high-dimensional cross-sectional assets is becoming more readily available, offering a new and valuable source of detailed information for analyzing essential statistics at finer intervals that are not present in low-frequency data. High-dimensional covariance estimation plays a crucial role in various applications such as constructing extensive optimal portfolios, comprehending leverage effects, pricing financial instruments, managing tail risks, and estimating risk premia of risk factors. Conventional approaches to analyze high-dimensional and high-frequency datasets are often through factor models, particularly through the principal component analysis (PCA) techniques. It leverages the concept of dimension reduction to identify latent factors and model high-dimensional asset returns. Traditionally, factor models assume that common factors exhibit strong signals compared to idiosyncratic errors. However, empirical studies encounter challenges in recovering covariance structures and identifying latent factors due to the presence of weak factors, microstructure noises, and non-synchronized trading activities associated with high-frequency data. Furthermore, based on extensive simulation results and empirical validations, this study initially establishes that the PCA method encounters challenges when dealing with high-frequency sampled asset returns, such as at 1-minute intervals or even more frequently. The presence of microstructure noises can lead to biased covariance estimators in existing methods, where noise signals significantly impact the estimation accuracy. Prior studies often resort to a noise-robust positive semi-definite sample covariance estimator to avoid bias correction, albeit at the cost of slower convergence rates for the integrated covariance estimator. While the truncation of negative eigenvalues can enforce PSD, this approach risks altering the fundamental covariance structure. Existing literature explores a Cholesky decomposition-based PSD integrated covariance estimator for a limited set of assets, sacrificing the factor model structure. I Hence, given the current scenario, this project underscores the critical need to develop a novel machine learning-based high-dimensional covariance estimator. This advancement is essential for empirical practitioners to effectively analyze the relationships among a large number of high-frequency sampled asset returns. Following the clarification of the objectives of our novel estimation approach, this study effectively integrates machine learning methods with high-frequency continuous stochastic modeling. Inspired by the practical achievements of a comprehensive factor model, we utilize a low-rank plus sparse matrix decomposition technique to capture the interdependence among asset returns. Instead of relying on a rigid factor model with consistent factor loadings, as typically seen in traditional PCA-based approaches, we apply nuclear norm regularization to the low-rank matrix driven by common factors and an off-diagonal penalty to the sparse matrix induced by idiosyncratic risks. Our newly devised estimator guarantees finite-sample positive-semi definiteness (PSD) by utilizing a PSD-constrained covariance estimator, thereby preserving the authentic covariance matrix structure while upholding convergence rates. Hence, the first objective has been successfully completed. 2. This method will enable the investigation of vast portfolios with constituent stocks from concentrated industries and with unobserved connections. Our secondary aim was to apply the recently introduced method to high-dimensional portfolio management, a goal that has been effectively achieved. In an empirical study, we utilize data from the trade and quote (TAQ) database spanning from 2008 to 2016 to estimate monthly high-frequency statistical factors for the stock components of the S&P 500 indexes based on a 5-minute sampling frequency. We include all stocks traded on NYSE, AMEX, and NASDAQ to create two sets of high-frequency economic factors, incorporating both the momentum-augmented Fama-French four factors and extended eleven factors. Our analysis reveals dynamic relationships between the statistical factors derived from our regularized covariance estimator and the economic factors, offering empirical support for a time-varying factor model as discussed in Kong et al. (2021). Furthermore, to evaluate the out-of-sample performance of our proposed estimator, we conduct extensive portfolio selections with varying levels of short-sales constraints. We compare the performance against other covariance estimators, including those accommodating latent statistical factors using our regularized estimator and PCA-based estimators. Additionally, we consider a time-series regression-based covariance estimator utilizing two sets of observable economic high-frequency factors. 3. We will re-study vast portfolio selection and allocation issues. This project has also examined how large-dimensional covariance estimation for high-frequency observations affects the performance of out-of-sample portfolio allocation. Particularly, unlike existing studies that focus on an ideal scenario that only long positions are allowed, our project enables both long and short strategies on portfolio allocation decisions. We construct optimal portfolios using various covariance estimators. Specifically, we explore two approaches for estimating the systematic risk-driven low-rank component: one based on latent factors and the other on economic high-frequency factors. For the first category of covariance estimators involving latent statistical factors, we utilize our machine learning driven method and PCA-based methods. In the second category, we employ a time-series regression-based covariance estimator to estimate the low-rank matrix. This includes the market factor, the momentum-augmented FF4 factors, and the extended 11 factors. Our regularized covariance estimator demonstrates superior efficiency and robustness in portfolio selection, yielding higher out-of-sample Sharpe ratios compared to existing methodologies. 4. This proposal will bridge machine learning techniques with financial practices and help verify the promising role machine learning methodologies can play in modern financial applications. This project makes a significant contribution by effectively integrating machine learning techniques into financial studies. Specifically, we detail the incorporation of machine learning regularizations into continuous-time modeling. Additionally, we introduce a novel machine learning algorithm tailored to our high-dimensional and high-frequency data. Furthermore, we establish a compelling relationship between machine learning advancements and empirical interpretations, showcasing the equivalence of our regularized covariance estimator to a penalized least-squares estimator. Our research demonstrates that our regularized covariance estimator can be derived by augmenting the loss function with a weighted group-LASSO penalty. Our approach applies diverse penalties to statistical factors based on their strengths, ensuring the recovery of the correct set of latent factors—both strong and weak—that account for the majority of asset return variation. By heavily penalizing redundant factors associated with idiosyncratic errors that evolve at a slower pace than common factors, we effectively eliminate unnecessary factors. These advancements render our method especially valuable in contemporary financial applications. Recent empirical findings have highlighted the presence of weak factors in financial markets. Our approach is adept at identifying and selecting both strong and weak factors while distinguishing idiosyncratic ones. 5. After we obtain our theoretical results and empirical findings, we will submit them to top tier finance and economic journals. This project has also attained this goal satisfactorily. This project has produced one research paper, entitled “A Regularized High-Dimensional Positive Definite Covariance Estimator with High-Frequency Data”. This paper has been accepted and published in the top A+ journal, Management Sciences. The full paper can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.04138.

11500119.label: Major findings and research outcome
11500119.value: This paper introduces a novel regularized covariance estimator within a general factor framework to model the covariance structure and latent factors among high-dimensional returns with high sampling frequencies. We investigate the varying roles of different factor strengths in accurately estimating the integrated covariance matrix. An intriguing connection is established between our regularized covariance estimator and a weighted group-LASSO least-squares estimator, which applies diverse penalties to factors based on their signal strengths. This enables the recovery of the latent factor structure, encompassing both strong and weak factors, and identification of different strength patterns without prior knowledge of factor types. Through extensive simulation studies encompassing strong, weak, mixed, and time-varying factor models, we demonstrate the satisfactory finite sample performance of our method. Our approach excels in extensive portfolio allocations, leading to significantly reduced out-of-sample portfolio risk and improved Sharpe ratios. The broad applicability, attractive asymptotic properties, and straightforward implementation of our proposed method make it particularly valuable in financial settings. A key outcome of this project is the publication of a research paper in a prestigious Economics and Finance journal, Management Science.

11500119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11500119.value: Here are the potential extensions for the project: 1. Dynamic Covariance Matrices in Multivariate GARCH Models: The methodology can be extended to estimate dynamic covariance matrices in high-dimensional multivariate GARCH models, enhancing the modeling of time-varying dependencies among multiple assets. 2. Nonparametric Conditional Covariance Estimator: Development of a nonparametric conditional large-dimensional covariance estimator can capture the evolving systematic and idiosyncratic co-movements in financial data, providing a more nuanced understanding of the changing relationships among assets. 3. Consistent Covariance Estimator for Nonstationary Data: Considering the increasing evidence of structural changes in time-series financial data, a consistent covariance estimator for nonstationary large-dimensional financial data with time-varying variance-covariance matrices can be explored. This would enable better adaptation to changing market conditions and trends. These avenues represent promising directions for future research, offering opportunities to enhance the methodology's applicability and effectiveness in capturing the complexities of financial data dynamics.

11500119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11500119.value: This project introduces a novel way to estimate covariance (how assets move together) for high-frequency data in a complex financial model. We integrate machine learning regularization techniques with continuous modeling. We improve on traditional methods by considering weak factors that have less influence compared to other factors. Our method ensures that the estimates are positive and realistic even in noisy trading environments. To make our approach practical, we develop an efficient algorithm to solve the problem. This project offers user-friendly algorithms and computer codes, accessible on the Management Science website. These tools are designed to assist practitioners in analyzing high-dimensional and high-frequency asset data effectively.

11500419.label: Project Objectives
11500419.value: Derive the asymptotic distributions of frequentist model average estimators under a general parametric model assuming fixed parameters without invoking the local misspecification framework. Compare analytically and numerically the interval estimates and confidence interval coverage probabilities obtained based on our approach with those obtained by the ad-hoc method of Buckland et al. (1997) and under the local misspecification framework of Hjort and Claeskens (2003) and Liu (2015). Conduct real data analysis based on the proposed approach.

11500419.label: Realisation of objectives
11500419.value: 1. We have successfully obtained the asymptotic distributions of the smoothed-AIC (S-AIC) and smoothed-BIC (S-BIC) weights and averaging estimators under the fixed parameter setup. This departure from the commonly assumed local misspecification assumption used in previous studies in the literature is a notable advancement. In our investigation, we have gone a step further by deriving the asymptotic distributions of the "scaled" versions of the S-AIC and S-BIC weights, denoted as SS-AIC and SS-BIC, respectively. These scaled counterparts address a major limitation of the S-AIC and S-BIC methods, which assign weights to all models without considering the presence of the parameter of interest. Specifically, we have discovered that the asymptotic distribution of SS-AIC is a non-linear function of a normal random vector, while that of SS-BIC follows a normal distribution. 2. We have devised a techniuqe for computing the confidence intervals under the fixed parameter setup, utilising the asymptotic distributions we derived. We have applied our theoretical findings to evaluate the accuracy of the confidence intervals proposed by Burham and Anderson (2002). Their method for constructing confidence intervals lacked a comprehensive investigation of its properties, which we have now addressed. To further assess the performance of different methods, including those obtained under the local misspecification framework, we conducted a simulation study. This study allowed us to examine the properties of confidence intervals based on various approaches and compare their effectiveness. 3. We put our methods into practice by applying them to two distinct datasets: one related to growth economics and another focused on the songbird species Troglodytes invisibilis. Through our analysis of real-world data, we found that the SS-AIC and SS-BIC methods exhibited the highest level of precision. These findings indicate that the SS-AIC and SS-BIC methods are particularly reliable and accurate when applied to real data. Overall, our real data analysis supports and speaks favorably of the SS-AIC and SS-BIC methods.

11500419.label: Major findings and research outcome
11500419.value: The research outcomes of this project have been summarized in ten papers published in reputable journals such as the Journal of the American Statistical Association, Biometrics, Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, Statistica Sinica, Statistics and Computing, Journal of Multivariate Analysis, Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference, Annals of the Institute of Statistical Mathematics, Statistical Analysis and Data Mining, European Journal of Operational Research, and one paper currently under review. While the focus of these papers remains centered on model averaging, the project has extended beyond its original scope by exploring more complex models. These include the semi-parametric additive model, treatment effect models, quantile regression, the zero-inflated Poisson model, models with inequality constraints, support vector machines and averaging bandwidths in kernel regression. By considering these diverse models, the project has devised a range of methodologies for model averaging that can be applied in various contexts. Significantly, the project has developed a comprehensive set of theoretical results pertaining to the properties of model averaging estimators across different model scenarios. This research effort has successfully filled a substantial gap in the existing literature while expanding our understanding of the theoretical properties of model averaging estimators. Overall, the project's contributions have not only advanced the field of model averaging but have also broadened our knowledge about its applicability and theoretical foundations.

11500419.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11500419.value: There are several important areas that require further investigation in our research. Currently, our limit theory assumes that both the parameter dimension (the number of unknown factors we are studying) and the number of candidate models are fixed. However, it would be intriguing to explore the asymptotic distributions of the S-AIC and S-BIC weights and averaging estimators when the dimensionality of the candidate models increases with the sample size, or when the number of candidate models becomes very large. Furthermore, in the past decade, optimal model averaging theory has seen significant development. Various criteria for choosing weights, such as those based on optimal mean squared error, Kullback-Leibler Divergence score, and leave-subject-out cross-validation, have been proposed. Investigating the asymptotic distributions of the corresponding model averaging estimators under the fixed parameter setup would be a meaningful and challenging topic for future research. By delving into these areas, we can enhance our understanding of how model averaging performs in more complex scenarios and broaden the range of applications where it can be effectively used.

11500419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11500419.value: For a long time, statisticians have focused on selecting a single statistical model based on specific criteria and ignoring the information contained in other models. In recent years, a new approach called model averaging has gained popularity. Instead of picking just one model, model averaging combines multiple relevant models to make decisions based on the collective information they provide. Previous studies have mainly looked at the properties of the estimated point values resulting from model averaging. However, this project goes a step further by investigating how confident we can be in making conclusions based on this approach. While some previous work has touched on this topic, it made unrealistic assumptions that all models become very similar to the smallest model in the pool as the amount of data decreases. In this project, we relax these assumptions to make our analysis more realistic. We develop techniques to compute model averaging-based confidence intervals, which provide a range within which we can be reasonably confident the true values lie, for the unknown factors we are studying. This project fills an important gap in the existing research on model averaging, making it more practical and accessible for researchers to use in their work.

11500519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11500519.value: 本项目旨在研究在线信息（包括社交媒体和大众媒体信息）如何影响定价。在我们之前的研究中，我们发现在线产品评论的增加会影响价格。该研究计划推进文本挖掘技术，进一步研究在线文本信息中的哪些信号会影响价格。 该研究计划解决两个主要问题。首先，我们要检查在线信息是否提供额外的定价信号。为了解决这个问题，我们需要进行严格的计量经济学分析，考虑在线信息不同方面之间的相互作用，分析他它们可能作为价格变化的前提。 另外，我们要研究从在线文本信息中检测信号的方法。尽管在主题检测和情感分类方面存在一些文本挖掘的研究，但这些研究与定价的目的不太一致。该研究旨在研究可供用于定价的文本挖掘方法。 研究中要研究的两个问题是相互关联的。无效的文本信号提取，会影响对其定价效果的准确衡量。可能需要反复努力来解决本研究中的两个问题。 这项研究具有理论和实践价值。从理论上讲，它有可能加深我们对在线信息在不断变化的商业环境中对定价的影响的理解。在实际上，本研究中的文本挖掘技术可供管理者用于日常定价决策，包括更广泛的业务问题，如资产定价。

11500519.value: The project mainly examines textual mining algorithms to extract (relational and non-relational) signals from various sources and assess these signals’ impact on the market. This project conducts a series of studies on two types of markets: stock market and crowdfunding market. Through the studies, this project has accomplished all designed objectives. 1. Aligning with the first objective, this project examined how the readability (or complexity) of user-generated content (UGC) (by fundraisers) in crowdfunding affects the perception of the backers and their support of projects. This project took a machine-learning approach to assess text readability. Built on the dual processing theory, this project examined whether the effect of UGC readability varies in different stages of fundraising projects. In other words, the effect of textual elements of UGC depends on the maturity of the project (product) being evaluated by customers. 2. Furthermore, aligning with the first objective, this project examined the firm-generated content on social media by leading P2P firms. This project extracted two signals on risk management and operations management from these social media posts. Then, this project examined if these signals reflect the operational status of the firms and their success in the market. This project argued that the management signals extracted from firm-generated content could mitigate information asymmetry and support investors’ judgment on the firms, especially when disclosure is not required by regulation. 3. Aligning with the second objective, this project built a text mining algorithm that extracts firm relations from online news. The algorithm first extracts entity (firm) names and identifies related firms in the same argument. The algorithm then conducts sentiment classification to label if the firms have co-benefit or counter-benefit relations as reflected by the news. This project considers that the relationship signal reflects the external relations of firms. Built on the attention theory, this project considers it will attract investors and influence the pricing and valuation of firms on the stock market. 4. Furthermore, aligning with the second objective, this project explored deep learning and large language models to extract signals from patent text that will affect the market. This study’s concentration is on the novelty of patents. This study investigated two groups of textual novelty measures: similarity-based and predictability-based measures. These measures use sentence-BERT, variational autoencoder, and GPT technologies, respectively, to capture if a patent is similar to or can be predicted by prior patents. Experiments show the measures have different abilities in distinguishing novel vs non-novel text. Built on the technology evolution theory, this project examined their impact on high-tech startup’s valuation on the stock market. 5. As we mentioned, this project conducts studies on two types of markets: stock market and crowdfunding market. We conduct rigorous assessments of the text signal’s impact on these markets. For example, for the crowdfunding disclosure readability measure, we investigate its time-vary impact on fundraising success using a Heckman + Instrument variable approach. For the studies of firms' co/counter-benefit relation and patent novelty study, we examine their impact on the stock market abnormal return through a VAR model. Overall, this project has accomplished all designed objectives.

11500519.label: Major findings and research outcome
11500519.value: The project makes both methodological and empirical contributions to the literature that lead to several papers (accepted/under review/in preparation), as shown in part C. From a methodological perspective, we propose several textual signal measures that can be used in practice, including manage signals from social media, firm relation signals from news, and textual novelty signals from patents. In particular, the firm relation signal is developed based on comparative linguistic analysis; the patent novelty signals are developed based on deep learning and large language models. These measures are shown to be significant in influencing firms’ valuation on the stock market after factoring in other (established) textual signals, including signals on news and patent novelty, respectively. This study provides new insights into investor perception of news and patents and suggests new research directions for text mining, which could have an impact on practices. From an empirical perspective, we derive several findings related to different application contexts. In a crowdfunding market, this project demonstrates that both project updates amount and readability can have a time-varying effect on project pledging. Specifically, more updates and difficult-to-read updates will have a more pronounced impact on fundraising in the later project stage. This implies that backers’ information processing of each project becomes more effective when project updates are properly managed throughout the project lifecycle. Such findings deepen our theoretical understanding of backer engagement via information processing toward better project success. In a financial market, this project shows that patent novelty positively affects the firm’s equity. Additionally, predictability-based novelty outperforms similarity-based novelty in predicting firms’ abnormal returns. This project provides evidence that the effect can be attributed to investors’ digestion of patent content and their assessments of technological development trends. This effect is more pronounced for younger firms and those with fewer patents, where investors have fewer signals to gauge the firm’s innovation capabilities. This study underscores the potential of advanced language models to enhance the understanding of investors’ assessment of firms’ innovations. Overall, we believe the findings summarized in the outputs of the project would bring significant impacts on our understanding of textual signals in market valuation.

11500519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11500519.value: Our research shows the effectiveness of textual signals extracted from various texts in affecting the market. In particular, our later studies draw attention to the effectiveness of deep learning and large language models in this problem. When the proposal was crafted in 2018, BERT was not yet published. (BERT was published in Oct 2018.) However in this 6 years, significant advantages have been made in NLP and textual analysis. We are happy to catch up this trend and switch from some classic approaches to large language models in the progress of the project. Obviously, future studies should explore more on deep learning and large language models in this direction.

11500519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11500519.value: In our daily lives, many products/services/financial assets are described using text. We, as humans, often can capture hidden signals from these textual descriptions in assessing the value of these objects. However, this cognition process is subtle, and we do not fully understand it yet. This project takes a build-and-compare approach to develop measures from textual descriptions and compare them with human reactions (in the market) to judge (or speculate) if humans take a similar way of thinking. We show people care about the novelty of text, the relations of firms embedded in text, and the difficulty/complexity of text (depending on the maturity of items to assess).

11501219.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11501219.value: 集團附屬企業，內部組織結構，和投資效率：一項跨國研究

11501219.label: Project Objectives
11501219.value: To investigate whether group-affiliated firms (“affiliates”) are able to make investment decisions more efficiently than stand-alone, independent firms (“stand-alones”). This will involve an across-group, firm-level comparison of investment efficiency between affiliates and stand-alones. To examine whether the role of business group affiliation in enhancing investment efficiency (or, equivalently, ameliorating investment inefficiency) is more prominent in emerging market countries with less developed external (capital and product) markets than in developed market countries with better developed external markets. To investigate whether and how the influence of business group affiliation on investment efficiency differs systematically across different within-group organizational structures. To this end, I plan to use subsamples to compare between affiliates in a pyramidal structure and those in a horizontal structure. To examine whether an affiliate’s position within a pyramidal group (upper versus lower layer) influences its investment efficiency. More specifically, I plan to investigate whether an affiliate’s within-pyramid position shapes its investment efficiency by splitting the subsample of pyramidal group firms into three subgroups: apex, bottom, and middle. I will then examine whether investment efficiency is higher for bottom-layer firms than for apex-layer firms.

11501219.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11501219.value: The business group is a prevalent and popular organizational form in many countries outside the U.S. It comprises a set of legally independent firms that are closely linked to one another via a complex ownership structure and social interactions. Prior research on business groups has investigated both the benefits (value-adding perspective) and drawbacks (value-destroying perspective) of this form of ownership structure. The value-adding perspective typically argues that, when external markets are not well developed, the business group provides member firms with internal capital markets and financing advantages, as well as providing co-insurance in the form of bailouts (during financial crises) and risk sharing. Under this perspective, business group affiliation helps member firms to undertake profitable investment projects. In contrast, the value-destroying perspective emphasizes potential agency problems inherent in separating ownership (cash flow rights) from control (voting rights). This wedge is an important source of agency problems, especially in emerging market economies with weak legal regimes, ineffective governance mechanisms, and low-quality reporting. In this situation, the business group provides the incentives and means for the ultimate controlling owner to pursue inefficient investments for private gain. Given these two competing perspectives, the impact of business group affiliation on investment efficiency is ultimately an empirical issue. Prior studies have examined the impact of business group affiliation on earnings management or information environments, firm valuation, and corporation innovation. To my knowledge, however, the impact of business group affiliation on firm-level investment efficiency has received little attention. Consequently, little is known about: (i) whether group-affiliated firms are more efficient in their investment decisions, compared with stand-alone, independent firms; (ii) if so, whether the former is better than the latter in constraining over-investment, under-investment, or both; and (iii) the conditions under which group-affiliated firms better allocate their investment resources at firm level. I propose to investigate these important, unexplored issues using a large international sample of group-affiliated firms and comparable stand-alone, independent firms. With this sample, I will first analyze the impact of business group affiliation on firm-level investment efficiency, and then explore whether this relation is differentially affected by within-group organizational structure (pyramidal versus horizontal) and within-pyramid position (apex-layer versus bottom-layer). 在美國以外的很多國家，企業集團是一種非常普遍流行的組織形式。它由一組公司組成，這些公司通過複雜的股權結構和社會關係而緊密聯係在一起。以往的文獻研究了這種特殊的股權結構的好處（價值增加視角）和壞處（價值破壞視角）。價值增加視角認為，當外部市場發展不完善時，企業集團不但為其成員企業提供內部資本市場和融資優勢，而且以救助（在金融危機中）和風險分擔的形式提供互相擔保。從這個視角來說，附屬於集團有助於企業進行有收益的投資活動。相反，價值破壞視角認為所有權（現金流量權）和控制權（投票權）的分離可能會導致潛在的代理問題。這種分離是導致代理問題的一個重要因素，特別是在新興市場中，因為新興市場的法律制度較弱，治理機制有效性較低，財務報告質量較差。在這種情況下，企業集團給最終控制人提供了動機和方式去進行缺乏效率的投資，以獲得私利。考慮到這兩種對立的假說，公司附屬於企業集團與其投資效率的關係仍然是一個實證問題。以往的研究探討了附屬於企業集團對其盈餘管理，信息環境，企業價值和公司創新的影響。但據我所知，學者很少關注附屬於企業集團對其公司層面的投資效率的影響。因此我們並不了解：（1）集團附屬企業相對於非集團的獨立企業是否有更有效的投資決策；（2）如果是，前者相較於後者是否有更少的過度投資，更少的投資不足，或者兩者皆有；（3）在什麼情況下集團附屬企業能夠更好地進行公司層面的投資資源配置。基於集團附屬企業和相似的非集團獨立企業的跨國大樣本，我準備研究這些尚未被探討的重要的問題。利用這些樣本，我先分析附屬於企業集團對其公司層面投資效率的影響，然後探討集團內部組織結構（金字塔結構VS平行結構）和金字塔層級（頂層VS底層）是否會影響它們之間的關係

11501219.label: Realisation of objectives
11501219.value: With respect to our first objective, our analyses using 29,954 firm-years from 48 countries (or jurisdictions) reveal that relative to stand-alone firms, group-affiliated firms are more efficient in their investment decisions. This finding suggests that with group-wide financial resources under its control, the business group provides member firms with sufficient internal funding, thus helping them overcome financial difficulty and undertake positive NPV (net present value) projects with sufficient cash flows. This could mitigate the under-investment problems. Moreover, knowledge spillover within the group alliance network helps member firms identify potentially profitable business opportunities, allocate funds to more profitable projects, and constrain firms from taking on negative NPV projects, which can reduce excessive investment. Taken together, our results indicate that the group affiliates are more efficient in investment decisions by constraining both over-investment and under-investment. With respect to the second objectives, our results show that the financing advantage that affiliated firms have over non-affiliated firms is more prominent when the firms have difficulties in gaining access to external financing. This finding suggests that the internal capital markets created via business group affiliation play a more important role in countries with less-developed capital markets, given that external financing is costlier in such countries. To provide systematic evidence on the third objective stated in 5.1., we further test whether the discovered relations differ systematically across different within-group organizational structures and across upper- and lower-layer affiliates. On the one hand, the pyramidal structure (e.g., when a manufacturer owns its supplier or distributor) may facilitate the transfer of corporate funds between different layers within the pyramid to finance affiliates’ investment opportunities. . On the other hand, the pyramidal structure may also provide the ultimate owner with more incentives and opportunities to extract private control benefits or tunnel corporate resources for private gain. Our results show that the affiliates in a group with pyramidal structure are more efficient in the investment decisions than those in a group with horizontal structure. Regarding the fourth objected stated in 5.1., we conjecture that, within a business group, lower-layer firms are typically high-growth businesses, with high product market competition, more disclosure transparency, and thus lower agency costs than higher-layer firms. We further conjecture that upper-layer firms are more likely to extract private control benefits via asset diversion or tunneling, they tend to be less transparent and thus have higher agency costs. We provide evidence in support of the above conjectures. In particular, we find that affiliates at the lower layer are more (less) likely to undertake positive (negative) NPV projects than upper-layer firms. Collectively, our evidence on cross-sectional variations in the role of group affiliates could provide managers of group-affiliated firms with useful insights into the choice of business group structure (e.g., horizontal versus vertical integration).

11501219.label: Major findings and research outcome
11501219.value: Our research documents the positive effect of business group affiliation on firm-level investment efficiency using a large international sample. Prior research on business groups has investigated both the benefits (value-adding perspective) and drawbacks (value-destroying perspective) of this form of ownership structure. We first document that group-affiliated firms are more efficient in their investment decisions than stand-alone firms, supporting the value-adding perspective. Further, this effect arises because the former is better than the latter in constraining both over-investment and under-investment. Moreover, this internal capital allocation matters more in countries with high external financing restrictions. Analysis at the business group level reveals that this relation is more pronounced for member firms in a pyramidal structure group and located in the lower layer.

11501219.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11501219.value: My former Ph.D. student, Dr. Siwen Fu (Assistant Professor at USTC, University of Science and Technology of China) have developed another project in which we examine whether common auditors who audit group-affiliated firms the audit quality of common auditors are further developing a project are of higher audit quality than stand-alone auditors. Our results generally indicate that common auditors are able to provide higher quality audit assurance service than stand-alone auditors. This finding is novel in that it confirms the presence of auditor knowledge spillover effect within the business group.

11501219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11501219.value: Using an international sample of firms from 48 economies, we find that group affiliation status positively relates to the efficiency of investment decisions. The results of our conditional analysis reveal that the more efficient investment decisions by group affiliates are associated with group-affiliated firms’ tendency to engage less in both over-investment and under-investment, compared to stand-alone firms. Taken together, our results support the value-adding perspective of group affiliation. We further document that the positive impact of group affiliation on investment efficiency is more pronounced for firms in countries where external financing is restricted or costly, and thus, the internal capital market is important. Our within-group, firm-level analysis provides further evidence that the benefit sides of group affiliation are more prominent for firms in a group with pyramidal structure rather than those in a group with horizontal structure. Moreover, for affiliates within a pyramid, the same benefits are greater for affiliates located in the lower layer of a pyramid than those located in its upper layer. Our findings enrich the literature examining group affiliates’ investment decisions. In particular, this study highlights the role of organizational structure in shaping firms’ investment decisions, and the results complement those of previous studies.

11502319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11502319.value: With the surge of data analytics and machine learning usage in business, data has become a critical asset for firms. Owing to the abundance of diverse data that firms can collect and use, how firms interact with the data has significant strategic implications. Such changes have brought new competitive landscapes in which data can be collected and shared at unprecedented speed and scale. At the heart of the development, data brokers play an essential role in facilitating the sharing of competitive business intelligence amongst firms. Furthermore, individual firms can also rely on technologies to gather the relevant data and make an adjustment to the competition strategies based on the knowledge generated from the data. Hence, the emergence of the new data-centric era has created profound impact on firms’ data collection and competitive strategies. In prior studies, information between competitive firms may have been shared through a third party (such as a supplier), but not in the form facilitated by a data broker. In this study, we focus on the strategic interactions amongst two competitive firms and a data broker, where we examine a host of data-related strategies by the data broker. It includes how to set the data sharing price and what is the degree to which the data broker chooses to improve the information quality when they are provided to the firms. As far as the firm is concerned, the availability of data and market intelligence will have implications to its strategies on pricing and product quality. Thus, the collective strategic actions considered in this study are novel and have not been discussed before. In recent years, there have been increased scrutinization regarding how firms utilize consumer data to advance their interests which may turn out to be detrimental to the consumers. A typical concern is related to the violations of privacy concerns of the consumers. In this study, we aim at another issue which may also have a negative consequence to the consumers whereby the presence of data broker can potentially steer the market competition towards some kind of collusive outcomes. Indeed, there has been much debate on whether data-driven pricing models (e.g., algorithmic pricing) facilitate tacit collusion among firms. Therefore, in addition to understanding the competitive interactions amongst the focal firms, our study will provide insights on the consumer welfare implications, which may provide critical insights to policy-makers in this new data-centric era. 隨著數據分析和機器學習在業務中使用的激增，數據已成為企業的重要資產。由於公司可以收集和使用大量不同的數據，公司如何使用數據具有重大的戰略意義。這些變化帶來了新的競爭格局，在以前所未有的速度和規模收集和共享數據。作為開發的核心，數據經紀人在促進公司間競爭性商業智能的共享方面發揮著至關重要的作用。此外，各個公司還可以依靠技術收集相關數據，並根據數據生成的知識對競爭策略進行調整。因此，新數據中心時代的出現對企業的數據收集和競爭戰略產生了深遠的影響。 在先前的研究中，競爭公司之間的信息可能通過第三方（例如供應商）共享，但不是以數據代理促成的形式共享。在這研究，我們專注於兩個競爭公司和數據經紀人之間的戰略互動，我們在那裡檢查數據經紀人的相關策略。它包括如何設置數據共享價格以及選擇在提供給公司時的數據與信息質量。就公司而言，數據和市場情報的可用性將具有對其定價和產品質量策略的影響。因此，本研究中考慮的集體戰略行動是新穎的，以前沒有討論過。 近年來，越來越多審查關於企業如何利用消費者的數據中產生不利影響。一個典型的問題是與侵犯隱私問題有關消費者。在這項研究中，我們討論另一個可能對消費者的負面影響。數據經紀人的存在可能會引導市場競爭對某種合謀結果產生影響。確實，有過關於數據驅動的定價模型（例如算法定價）是否鼓勵企業之間默契合謀。因此，除了了解競爭,我們的研究將專注於公司之間進行的互動，消費者的福利，以及為決策者提供新的見解

11502319.label: Major findings and research outcome
11502319.value: We find several interesting and novel insights from the two studies. For the first study, first, we show that the data broker may strategically sell collective insights exclusively to one publisher (exclusive selling) instead of selling to both publishers (non-exclusive selling). This result implies that adopting an exclusive strategy and making data insights scarcer for some firms may be better for the data broker. Second, we illustrate that the data broker can facilitate or inhibit publisher competition, depending on its interests in setting the data insights selling strategies. Finally, the data broker may induce both competition-mitigation and value-enhancing effects that affect the outcome of social welfare. Interestingly, while the data broker’s decision (i.e., exclusive selling) may lead to less competition in the market, social welfare can still improve. It improves because the collective insights generated by data brokers allow publishers to increase their targeting value to advertisers more efficiently. For the second study, our results show that high-value firms with competitive advantages in product or service value often sell less data than low-value firms, implying that high-value firms rely less on direct data monetization than low-value firms. Surprisingly, as direct data monetization prevails, high-value firms further dominate the market for selling products or services, suggesting that data brokers may actually hinder, rather than facilitate, market competition. Finally, direct data monetization may benefit both consumer surplus and social welfare because it facilitates data-sharing between firms, allowing firms to obtain additional insights to improve their product or service offerings.

11502319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11502319.value: We are currently focusing on publishing the two studies. There are various extensions one can think of, including the strategic interactions between the data broker and major platform (which also possesses a significant data repository) and how that would affect downstream firms.

11502319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11502319.value: Data broker plays an important role in affecting marketing competition. In the first study, we show that a data broker may strategically choose to sell data exclusively to one firm. This strategy is chosen based on the downstream competition conditions, and therefore the data broker may indirectly interfere with the market competition outcome of its clients. In our analysis, we find situations where the presence of a data broker can increase or decrease social welfare. The second study takes the firms' perspective where firms may choose to sell data and insights from the data broker. This is related to the data monetization strategy commonly considered by firms these days. We also find conditions where the data broker may hurt instead of help market competition. Both studies have policy implications.

11502419.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11502419.value: Information technology (IT) has been deeply embedded in firm operations in modern corporations. Researchers and practitioners have established that IT investment leads to a better firm performance by giving firm better competitive advantage (Melville, Kraemer, and Gurbaxani 2004; Wade and Hulland 2004; Piccoli and Ives 2005; Mithas, Ramasubbu, and Sambamurthy 2011; Lim, Stratopoulos, and Wirjanto 2011). However, given the central role of IT systems in firm information gathering, recording, compiling, analyzing, and reporting, it is somewhat surprising that the empirical evidence is scant on how the IT system affects the firm information disclosure practice. In this study, we want to advance this line of research by focusing on how IT resource base can affect firm reporting quality and risk. Accounting information is summarized and populated through IT modules in most firms. Conceptually, firm IT characteristics should be among the underlying factors in determining firm reporting quality, e.g., reliability, relevancy, and timeliness, and reporting risk. In this study, we focus on two dimensions of firm IT resources, IT extensiveness and IT standardization, and examine how reporting quality and risk are affected. To the extent that IT systems could reduce errors and save labor efforts in the information collection and financial reporting process, we argue that more coverage of IT tools and systems can yield more accurate financial reporting, fewer estimation errors, shorter reporting lags, and reduce the overall reporting risk. Also, holding the firm IT coverage constant, the more standardized the IT implementation is, the lower integration costs are required, and better reporting quality and lower reporting risk are expected. We employ IT extensiveness to capture the functional and organizational scope of IT tools and systems used in a firm to support its business activities and IT standardization to capture the extent to which common IT tools and systems are implemented in different business units of a firm to support common organizational activities (Du, 2015). This research makes several contributions. First, it adds to the literature on reporting quality and risk by identifying the effects of IT and helps to further our knowledge for the underlying drivers behind reporting quality and risk, which have a central role in the financial accounting literature. Second, our work helps to understand the potential mechanism of IT value creation. Third, this study has implications for practitioners and managers on how firms may improve their reporting activities through firm IT investment. 信息技术是现代企业运营的重要基础。信息系统在企业信息收集，记录，编制方面具有核心作用。研究人员和从业人员已经确定信息技术投资会通过提供更好的竞争优势以帮助公司实现更好的业绩。 在这项研究中，我们关注信息系统如何影响公司信息披露实践，进而影响公司报告质量和风险。

11502419.label: Realisation of objectives
11502419.value: Following our research agenda, we have developed testable empirical predictions to address our objectives. Using the data provided by the Harte & Hanks database, we measure firm ES extensiveness and ES standardization following the literature (Du 2015). In our recent revision, we switch the terms from IT extensiveness/standardization to ES extensiveness/standardization. First, we test the relation between ES extensiveness and firm reporting and disclosure quality. Using both univariate and multivariate regression methods, we find no relation between ES extensiveness and firm reporting and disclosure quality. Further investigation using cross-sectional tests yields no supporting evidence as well. We attribute this lacking of results to the lack of variation in our ES extensiveness variable, given the fact that most of firms in our sample have ERP in place during the sample period and many of the ERP systems have similar modules. Then we turn to the impact of IT standardization on firm reporting and disclosure quality. Our baseline tests show that a higher degree of ES standardization is associated with more accurate and precise management forecasts, i.e., fewer forecast errors and narrower forecast range. This baseline finding suggests that ES standardization, on average, improves firm disclosure quality, and its synergy value created across different business units outweighs local business unit optimization. The results using only accounting module ES standardization yields similar results. Next, we conduct several robustness tests to strengthen the baseline findings on the relation between ES standardization and management forecasts. Specifically, we examine how the baseline relation between the two is conditioned upon or moderated by operating uncertainty, firm external information environment, and external financing dependence. Our empirical tests are consistent with the cross-sectional predictions, supporting our baseline results and the underlying mechanism. In additional tests, we examine the impact of ES standardization on firm mandatory reporting quality. Firm ES generates informational inputs for both voluntary disclosure and mandatory reporting and could potentially impact both in a similar way. However, ES standardization is arguably less related to a firm’s reporting quality. This is because ES is part of firm infrastructure and it is not designed to directly constrain managerial reporting opportunism. Using several empirical proxies for reporting quality, we find that ES standardization reduces error-related restatements significantly but has no significant impact on fraud-related restatements or accruals-based earnings management. These contrasting results extend our understanding of the consequences of firm ES standardization and help confirm that our findings regarding firm voluntary disclosure are less likely driven by correlated omitted variables or reserve causality. We also examine the relation between ES standardization and audit fees. Other things being equal, more standardized ES requires less complex skill set and less audit efforts from external auditors, thereby lowering audit fees. We find results consistent with this prediction. This audit fee result, coupled with the mandatory reporting results mentioned above, suggests that ES standardization helps simplify firm operation activities and increase internal information quality, which in turn improves firm reporting quality in a cost-effective way. Lastly, we provide some preliminary evidence to shed some light on the mechanisms through which ES could affect firm information provision. Our hypotheses are built on the premise that higher ES standardization brings about an increase in the efficiency of firm operation and information processing. To validate this premise, we examine whether the impact of ES standardization is more pronounced for firms that are less efficient. Using the length of the operating cycle as a proxy for firm business efficiency (Omer, Shelley, and Tice 2014), we find that firms with longer operating cycle benefit more from more standardized ES.

11502419.label: Major findings and research outcome
11502419.value: This study investigates how enterprise system standardization affects corporate information provision. We find that firms with more standardized enterprise systems provide more accurate and precise management earnings forecasts. This finding is more pronounced when (i) firms face higher operating uncertainty; (ii) firms are more opaque; and (iii) firms are more dependent on external financing. Our baseline findings are robust to using the instrumental variable approach, suggesting that our results are unlikely to be driven by potential endogeneity. In addition, we find that enterprise system standardization improves a firm’s mandatory reporting quality as it reduces the likelihood of error-related restatements, but has little effect on constraining managerial reporting opportunism. Furthermore, we find that enterprise system standardization results in lower audit fees. Finally, we provide some initial evidence indicating that the observed improvements in the qualities of voluntary disclosure and mandatory reporting are a result of the standardization enhancing firm operating efficiency. Currently, we have polished our paper and submitted it to a top-tier peer review accounting journal, the Accounting Reivew, for publication consideration. We have not presented the paper much as during the past three years, many conferences were affected by Covid.

11502419.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11502419.value: We provide evidence that ES standardization improves the quality of voluntary disclosure and mandatory reporting, but does not constrain managerial reporting opportunism, i.e., fraudulent reporting or accruals-based earnings management. Our study extends existing literature by focusing on one key attribute of ES, and provide evidence suggesting that firm-wide operational consistency and informational integration improve a firm’s internal information environment. Our results indicate that ES standardization may contribute to the ES business value, and are relevant to both researchers and practitioners. In addition, our study contributes to the literature by exploring the effects of ES on a firm’s internal information production process. Existing literature provides some initial, yet mixed, evidence on the average effect of ES implementation on firm disclosure and reporting practices. Our study furthers the line of study by unpacking the general relation and specifically focusing on the level of firm ES standardization (e.g., Masli, Peters, Richardson, and Sanchez 2010; Dorantes et al. 2013; Pincus et al. 2017). The findings of this study help to resolve the conflicting evidence in the literature by focusing on an important ES feature, i.e., ES standardization, that could enhance firm information quality and therefore increase firm value.

11502419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11502419.value: This study examines whether and, if so, how a firm’s enterprise system (ES) influences its information provision. Corporate information provision plays a central role in financial markets and has long been at the center of mainstream accounting and finance research. Prior accounting literature documents a variety of firm-level factors determining corporate information production, including firm operating characteristics, reporting practices, corporate governance, external monitoring forces, and contractual incentives. Meanwhile, with the ever-growing digital reach, a firm’s information technology (IT) has become an inextricable part of its information provision. IT has penetrated to the core of business operations and strategies given its role in the connectivity with business partners, data collection, marketing, and automation of business processes. Among all IT investments, ES is especially crucial in a firm’s information provision. However, current literature provides limited and inconclusive evidence on how IT, especially ES, affects corporate information environment. Against the above backdrop, our study aims to provide large-sample, systematic evidence on this under-explored issue by investigating how firm ES standardization influences a firm’s information provision via its disclosure activities, and some insights on how ES could affect firm business value.

11502919.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11502919.value: The recent Nobel laureate, Paul Romer, proposes that technology is the key input to a firm’s production function and key source of economic growth (Romer 1986; Romer 1990). His models explain how innovative technologies in the early 1990s such as computer code for word processor or the internet have given rise to increasing returns to scale in production and sustained exponential growth in the economy. Nowadays firms interact with each other to inspire innovations and knowledge spillovers, technology affinities have become increasingly important in firm growth and productivity (Jaffe, Trajtenberg, and Henderson 1993; Bloom, Schankerman, and Van Reenen 2013). In this innovation- and technology-based economy, it is crucially important for auditors to understand their clients’ technological position to make better auditing decisions and professional judgments. Furthermore, technology spillovers could occur beyond the traditional industry boundaries; client firms are therefore less likely to be concerned about potential leakage of proprietary information when they hire the same auditor as their close technology peers, compared to the situation where they appoint the same auditor as their product market competitors. Therefore, auditor expertise developed from client technological closeness should constitute a critical type of auditor specialization in addition to industry specialization. There is already a long series of literature showing that industry specialist auditors provide better audit quality and earn audit fee premia due to their greater knowledge of industry, business and accounting practices compared to non-specialists (Dopuch and Simunic 1982; Craswell, Francis, and Taylor 1995; Balsam, Krishnan, and Yang 2003; Ferguson, Francis, and Stokes 2003; Krishnan 2003; Mayhew and Wilkins 2003; Francis, Reichelt, and Wang 2005; Carson 2009; Reichelt and Wang 2010; Fung, Gul, and Krishnan 2012; Goodwin and Wu 2014). To the best of our knowledge, however, the literature has paid little attention to how client technological links could influence auditor specialization, which could accordingly affect audit quality and fee premiums. To fill this void in the literature, we examine whether auditors derive expertise from client technological proximity while controlling for the within-industry client product closeness. Such evidence will help to shed lights on whether auditors develop expertise from their client technological links beyond industry borders. We also intend to investigate whether auditors develop greater technological expertise when their client firms have a more intense and specific technology focus, when their client firms belong to a more concentrated industry, when these client firms are more opaque or less transparent.

11502919.label: Realisation of objectives
11502919.value: I have achieved all the research objectives in a paper, “Auditors’ Technological Proximity Knowledge”, accepted for publication in The Accounting Review in December 2022. In that paper, we show that auditors develop technology knowledge in addition to industry specialization. We include client-specific product similarity measure (instead of client-specific product-market proximity proxy as proposed in the original proposal) following the editor’s and reviewers’ suggestions. We conduct a more refined audit office fixed effects (instead of audit firm fixed effects as proposed in the original proposal) model for testing auditor knowledge accumulation (we followed the eidtor’s and reviewers’ comments to avoid terming it as “specialization” or “expertise” in the published paper) on both the technology space and product space. We perform a bunch of additional tests as mentioned in the original proposal to substantiate our inferences. Below I more clearly explain how my co-author and I achieved the project objectives in more detail. As technological affinity could be distinct from product similarity, we investigate whether auditors develop incremental knowledge from clients’ technological affinity over and above product-market similarity. Following Bloom et al. (2013), we construct a technology proximity measure to capture firms’ technology affinity with other firms audited by the same audit office/other offices of the same audit firm. We control for product similarity, auditors’ overall technological expertise, and market share-based auditor industry specialization when assessing the incremental effect of client technological proximity on audit quality and audit fees. We test our main hypotheses using a panel dataset that we construct for the period of 2000_2017 by merging two databases, Audit Analytics and Compustat. We find that audit quality increases and audit fees decrease when a client firm has a greater technological affinity with other clients of its audit office. We also find evidence of such technological knowledge spillovers at other audit offices of the same audit firm. Our findings indicate that auditors develop technological proximity knowledge at both the audit firm and audit office levels. Consistent with Zhang (2018), Bills et al. (2020), and Chang, Hsu, and Ma (2022), we also find some weak evidence that a company exhibits higher audit quality and lower audit fees when its product market is more similar to that of other clients of its audit office/audit firm. Overall, this evidence lends support to the intuition that auditors develop technology-specific knowledge on top of product-market knowledge from their clients. We undertake two cross-sectional tests to further validate our main results. First, we show that the impact of an auditor’s accumulated technological proximity knowledge is more salient when the auditor’s clients are technology intensive. Second, we find that the effects of client technological links on audit quality and audit fees are stronger for Big N auditors, which have more resources and a larger client base to accumulate technological proximity knowledge than non-Big N auditors. Lastly, we perform two additional tests to further distinguish between the technological proximity effect and the product similarity effect. We first show that our main findings hold in both high and low product similarity subsamples, suggesting that technological proximity has an independent impact on audit quality and audit fees, even when the product closeness is weak. In another test, we find that both the within- and across-industry technological proximity are significantly related to audit quality and audit fees measures, indicating that technological proximity has an incremental impact on audit outcomes beyond the traditional industry boundary where product linkage is mainly concentrated.

11502919.label: Major findings and research outcome
11502919.value: We exploit the technological proximity between a focal firm and the other clients of the focal firm’s auditor to examine whether auditors develop technological proximity knowledge over and above clients’ product-market similarity. We find that audit quality improves when auditors provide audit services to clients with a high degree of technological proximity after controlling for product-market similarity, auditors’ overall technological expertise, and industry specialization effects. We also find that auditors offer audit fee discounts for their efficiency gains from auditing multiple clients with technological affinity. We further show that the benefit of the technological knowledge spillover holds at both the audit office and audit firm levels. In cross-sectional tests, we find that the effects of client technological proximity on audit quality and audit fees are more pronounced when the clients are technology-intensive firms and appoint Big N auditors. We also perform two additional tests to further distinguish between the technological proximity and product similarity effects. We find that technological proximity has an independent impact on audit quality and audit fees, even when the product closeness is low, and that auditors develop technological proximity knowledge from clients in both the same industry and different industries. Collectively, our findings can be viewed as an indication that technological proximity has an incremental impact on audit quality and audit fees on top of the product-market similarity, auditors’ overall technology- and industry-specific expertise. Our analysis broadens the scope of auditor knowledge from the traditional product-market space to the technology space. We provide novel evidence that auditors deliver better audit quality and offer an audit fee discount when auditing clients with relatively high technological proximity. We find that the benefit of the technological proximity knowledge spillover not only resides within specific offices, but also spreads to other offices of the same audit firm. Our study also extends the literature on technological information spillover to auditing research. We show that auditors benefit from technological information spillover when their clients are linked in technological fields, which is distinct from other economic links, including the industry and supply chain links.

11502919.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11502919.value: The technological closeness measure investigated in this project could be used for other future potential projects examining the auditors' technological proximity knowledge.

11502919.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11502919.value: In a world of increasingly monopolistic accountancy firms, our study looks at the way in which technology knowledge spillovers are affecting the audit process, potentially to the benefit of both auditing companies and their clients. We argue that auditor technological knowledge and experience developed from clients’ technological proximity constitutes a critical type of auditor expertise in distinction to auditor industry specialization. They show that auditors develop knowledge from clients with technology affinity, resulting in higher audit quality and lower audit fees. Interestingly, auditors accumulate knowledge and experience from their clients’ technological proximity at both the audit office and audit firm levels.

11503619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11503619.value: Digital download, digital rental, and subscription-based streaming are the three digital distribution channels for video contents in the home entertainment industry. Despite their growing importance in revenue generation relative to traditional physical channels, how these digital channels interact with each other is not well studied, because of the lack of good data about these digital channels and the difficulty of inferring causality. This research proposes to utilize a unique dataset provided by NPD VideoWatch on consumers’ viewing behavior and a natural experiment that offers an exogenous shock to the streaming availability of video contents featured by Epix to investigate the inter-relationships among these digital distribution channels. This study will make an important empirical contribution to the multi-channel management literature and also provide managerial implications for both content owners and streaming service providers on how to better manage these channels together. 數字下載、數字租賃和基於訂閱的流媒體是家庭娛樂行業中電影与電視節目等視頻內容的三個數字分發渠道。儘管它們相對於傳統渠道在創收方面的重要性日益增加，但由於缺乏關於這些數字渠道的良好數據來源以及推斷因果關係的難度，這些數字渠道如何相互作用尚未得到很好的研究。這項研究提出利用NPD提供的關於消費者觀看行為的獨特數據集和一個為Epix所擁有視頻內容在流媒體渠道的覆蓋提供外部衝擊的自然實驗以研究這些數字分發頻道之間的相互關係。本研究將對多渠道管理文獻做出重要的實證貢獻，並為視頻內容所有者和流媒體服務提供商提供如何更好地管理這些渠道的管理意義。

11503619.label: Realisation of objectives
11503619.value: The project aims to investigate the interaction relationships between subscription-based streaming, digital downloads, and digital rentals. The interaction between two channels is often determined by evaluating how the demand of one channel responds to a change in the other channel. In our context, we are interested in how digital downloads and digital rentals may vary when the availability of video content on subscription-based streaming sites changes. One such change in streaming availability occurred when Epix changed its streaming partner from Netflix to Hulu in 2015. However, due to the limited number of Epix movies available in digital download or digital rental channels, we examine another change: when a title is newly added to the leading streaming site, Netflix. The advantage of this approach is that the number of movies available on both Netflix and digital download/rental channels is sufficiently large for our empirical analyses. Therefore, we first study how the demand in digital download and digital rental channels changes around such events to achieve the three project objectives outlined in the proposal. Additionally, the number of Epix movies sold on physical DVDs is much larger. We consider this a new opportunity to investigate how subscription-based video streaming affects DVD sales. This way, we can continue to leverage the natural experiment that occurred in 2015 when content owner Epix switched its streaming partner from Netflix to Hulu. This event created an exogenous shock that significantly reduced the streaming availability of Epix's content due to the difference in market shares of the two streaming service providers at the time. This occurrence allows us to investigate the causal effect of subscription streaming on physical DVD sales. In summary, this project has examined how the change in streaming availability of movies affects demand in three other channels, including digital downloads, digital rentals, and physical DVDs.

11503619.label: Major findings and research outcome
11503619.value: Using a panel dataset of 114 movie titles from July 2014 to December 2016, we find that the number of digital downloads or digital rentals increases by 17% to 18% on average after a movie title becomes available for streaming on Netflix. These results suggest that subscription-based streaming complements both digital download and digital rental channels. This research study was published in the International Conference on Information Systems in 2020. Our second research study shows that the decline in streaming availability of Epix’s content led to a 36.07% increase in its monthly DVD sales over the 15 months following the event. We also find that the cannibalization between subscription-based streaming and physical DVD channels is much stronger for movies with higher levels of content stickiness (e.g., more recent titles, titles with a general audience (G) or parental guidance (PG) rating, or those belonging to the children/family genre). This research study was published in the journal Decision Support Systems in 2022.

11503619.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11503619.value: There is significant potential for further development of this research by exploring the impact of subscription-based streaming on other media channels and consumer behavior. Future research could investigate the following aspects: 1. Analyze the effect of streaming platforms’ original content on digital downloads, rentals, and physical DVD sales. As platforms like Netflix and Amazon Prime produce more exclusive content, it is essential to understand how this impacts other distribution channels. 2. Investigate consumer preferences and behaviors across various media channels, including the influence of factors such as user demographics, taste, and accessibility on channel choice. 3. Explore the implications of emerging technologies, such as virtual reality and augmented reality, on the consumption of media content and the potential for integration with subscription-based streaming platforms. The proposed course of action for these further developments would include conducting comprehensive literature reviews, collecting relevant data from multiple sources, employing advanced statistical techniques, and collaborating with industry experts and stakeholders to ensure practical relevance and applicability.

11503619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11503619.value: This research project examines the relationship between subscription-based video on demand (SVOD) services, like Netflix and Hulu, and transactional video on demand (TVOD) options, such as digital downloads and rentals from iTunes, Amazon Prime Video, and YouTube. The study aims to understand how consumers choose between these different options and how these choices impact the home entertainment industry. The findings reveal that when a movie title becomes available on a subscription-based streaming service like Netflix, the demand for digital downloads and rentals also increases. This suggests that SVOD services actually complement TVOD channels, rather than competing with or replacing them, as some might assume. Understanding this complementary relationship between SVOD and TVOD channels is valuable for content owners and streaming service providers. It implies that a positive relationship exists between these types of channels, where an increase in demand for one can lead to an increase in demand for the other. This knowledge can help content owners and streaming platforms better manage their offerings and design marketing strategies that take advantage of the synergy between subscription-based streaming, digital downloads, and digital rentals, ultimately leading to increased revenue in the home entertainment industry.
