11601419.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11601419.value: This project seeks to explore how the right to religious freedom of Protestant house churches has been restricted under the existing repressive legal framework from a socio-legal perspective given that China has established an instrumentalist legal system. The recent dissolution of a large number of Protestant house churches in China has been widely reported in the international press, which indicates a significant change of approach to Protestant house churches under the newly revised Regulation of Religious Affairs (RRA). Through analyzing the RRA, it was found that it has taken an integrated legalistic-political approach to Protestant house churches. On the one hand, the RRA upholds the principles of legality according to which it is unlawful for a Protestant house church to operate in practice unless it registers and obtains approval from the state-sanctioned religious bodies and/or religious affairs authorities. In addition, given the tension between Protestant house churches and state-sanctioned churches, the RRA has adopted an interim legalistic approach towards them, that is, a Protestant house church may submit an application to the government to be designated a temporary site. In this way, it can bypass the state-sanctioned religious bodies, although it still needs to register with the government temporarily. On the other hand, the RRA integrates a grassroots-level political approach to Protestant house churches in that local government has the task of managing religious affairs within its own administrative area, with the help of villagers’ committees and residents’ committees, although no details are provided about the specific legal role of the grassroots-level organizations. The existing literature has focused on Protestant house churches largely from religious and sociological perspectives. The integrated legalistic-political approach to Protestant house churches in the RRA and the extent to which such an approach to restricting the religious freedom of Protestant house churches is effective in practice has not yet been studied. Through a mix of analytical literature review, in-depth fieldwork in China including ethnographic observations and interviews with church leaders, officials, etc., as well as contextual analysis of relevant judgments and documentations concerning the right to religious freedom of Protestant house churches, this project will produce and disseminate fundamental knowledge about the conditions and ways of restricting the right to religious freedom of Protestant house churches under the newly-integrated legalistic-political approach as provided for by Chinese law. 该研究主要从社会实证的角度来探讨中国家庭教会在目前的法律框架下行使宗教自由权的限度。自改革开放以来，中国在一定程度上已经建立一个符合其政权体制的法律制度，由此，宪法上所确认的宗教自由权可以在多大程度上实现是法律与社会领域绕不开的研究命题。该课题主要探讨中国家庭教会的宗教自由权在目前的法律结构中可以在多大程度上得到行使，或者说，政府在实践中究竟采取了何种方法来限制中国家庭教会的宗教自由权的行使，以及这些方法的实际效果究竟如何，从而可以更深入地理解中国家庭教会宗教自由权在中国法律与社会中所具有的独特形态。

11601419.label: Realisation of objectives
11601419.value: This project employs empirical methods to explore the right to religious freedom of Protestant house churches (PHCs) in China. It has now achieved the specific objectives as listed in the research plan. In order to understand the conditions under which PHCs may exercise their right to religious freedom in China’s context, the analysis of the issues involved draws primarily upon participant observation, in-depth interviews and online ethnography. It was found that, due to the government’s great tolerance for politically reciprocal collusion with house churches, it is possible for some PHCs to operate with non-government-sanctioned clergy, in a non-government-sanctioned venue, and right “under the nose” of the government itself. In this regard, in a politically liberal environment, it is possible that the boundary between those government-sanctioned Protestant churches operating within the framework of the Regulation of Religious Affairs (RRA) and those PHCes operating outside of it may sometimes be blurred, as the former also often do not need to strictly follow the government rules in practice. In this vein, it is also possible that registered Protestant churches, like those that are unregistered, will cooperate with the government in some way for their own good. However, if the environment is particularly politically repressive (most commonly due to specific political movements), the differences between the two will be made visible. A PHC, despite being registered with the government, may have to contingently operate in as underground a way as possible to hide from the sight of the government and the public. In contrast, an official government-sanctioned church will usually be required—albeit perhaps reluctantly, and using various strategies—to persist, accommodate repression, and embrace (at least on the surface) the imposed political demands or even indoctrination in order to adapt themselves to the changing political situation within the restrictive framework of the RRA. Moreover, the local authority in charge, if not under pressure from the superior authority, usually does not choose to adopt confrontational measures in the first instance; instead, it often takes a more tolerant approach toward these unregistered churches if no concerns regarding “social stability” have been raised. It may however be the case that certain church services (particularly those of a relatively large size) may annoy some neighbors with different beliefs, who may file complaints to the authority. If this occurs, the authority in charge may subsequently experience some pressure to respond and implement some follow-up measures, such as prohibiting the church service being conducted at least in that specific location; if it did not do so, it may risk being criticized for “dereliction of duty” given these religious activities being conducted on unregistered sites. Of course, the house church usually understands the government’s position on the matter and will often choose to move to another place without confronting it. Strategically, in practice, an urban house church usually selects a worship location in an industrial building, where there are no residential tenants and almost nobody around on Sundays (the rent is also likely to be relatively cheap). Of course, this situation is often different in rural areas. Residents of a village community are usually very familiar with their neighborhoods; accordingly, it is often very difficult for the house church to find a relatively hidden but convenient place, and worship services are therefore often conducted in the home of some resident. In practice, the grassroots authorities often employ a political approach to mobilizing and encouraging neighbors (particularly the Party members, usually considered as “vanguards” of the community) to report any “illegal” activity in their neighborhood. This certainly exerts huge pressure on house church leaders living in rural communities, as there is no way to remove the “curse” of “illegality” imposed by the RRA. It was also found that due to the regional diversity across the country, the government’s attitude may vary from one place to another. Undoubtedly, in a less tolerant (or even much more confrontational and repressive) environment, the government may strategically interfere with the operations of house churches in various ways: these may include periodically talking to and pressuring the leaders of house churches, going to the scene to warn believers of the “illegality” of their activities during the church service, etc. This kind of interference can demonstrate the satisfactory, or sometimes ingratiating, commitment among law enforcement to its superior authority, provided that this does not raise concerns of “social stability” that may affect performance. In this situation, a house church usually chooses to operate in a semi-underground way in order to escape from the possible intervention or even repressive measures of the government. In a less tolerant environment of this kind, the government and house church enter into a kind of “cat-and-mouse” relationship, where the latter, which is ultimately subject to contingent political whim, typically makes the bulk of the accommodations in order to provide its regular church service to believers as far as possible with minimal government interference. Normally, these churches can only operate with small congregations. Moreover, the legislative framework for governing religions as prescribed by the RRA was further improved in the 2017 amendment. It finds that the revised RRA has actually taken an integrated legalistic-political approach to PHCs that is more restrictive than before. First, it has strengthened the ‘illegality’ approach, according to which it is ‘unlawful’ for a PHC to operate in practice unless it registers and obtains approval from the state-sanctioned religious organizations (i.e. Three-Self Patriotic Movement (TSPM) / China Christian Council (CCC)) and/or religious affairs authorities. Legally speaking, the house church making the application, if approved, becomes a legal state-sanctioned entity. At the same time, such registration will cause religious adherents to be affiliated with the state-sanctioned church. Accordingly, pastors of the state-sanctioned church will also be those sanctioned by the government, rather than those that may have otherwise or previously been in charge of these unregistered PHCs. In practice, this is hardly practicable for a PHC, since a primary reason why a PHC insists on its independence from the government is that it largely disagrees with the patriotic religious organisations supervised by the government and its churches from a theological perspective, and views these government-monitored registered churches as unsuitable places to worship God according to their supreme evangelical or some other religious mission. Furthermore, the newly revised RRA integrates a grassroots-level political approach to PHCs, whereby the local government has the task of managing religious affairs within its own administrative area, with help from villagers’ committees and residents’ committees (article 6). The underlying political approach can be gleaned by considering Chinese Communist Party (CCP)’s latest institutional reform to unify the function of administering religious affairs, transferring it to CCP’s United Front Work Departments from the State Council. Given that the CCP has ultimate authority over organizations, such a move reveals the CCP’s attempts to strengthen its comprehensive leadership over religious affairs, with the goal of ensuring that it is able to efficiently unify and mobilize the different authorities involved (such as national security, public security, building authorities, etc.) to manage religious affairs. Moreover, this has cleared the way for CCP to employ its ‘mass line’ method to mobilize people to become involved in political movements.

11601419.label: Major findings and research outcome
11601419.value: It was found that the house church, being without manifest legal status, operates in a guerrilla-like fashion, capable of adapting to the varying degrees of government tolerance from one place to another. In such a guerrilla model, it is possible that governments with a more tolerant attitude may act in collusion with the house church; this is particularly true when enforcing the dismantling of these unregistered house churches may raise concerns of “social stability”, which has been prioritized in the political agenda, particularly in a strong culture of respecting religions. Meanwhile, a house church may be cooperative with the government’s pro forma commitment to the enforcement of laws and policies, to the extent that its operation of the guerrilla model will not affect the government’s performance, in both normal politics and the repressive environment during the political movements, and occasionally with the fieldwork investigation of the “undercover investigation team” (anfang zu) dispatched by the superior authority. Such collusion is conditional, and may be broken when a house church with a high profile enters into the public sphere and challenges – even if only potentially – the ideological dominance of the CCP’s Marxist atheism. Although international connections and support may be factors temporarily considered by the government when opting not to take compulsory measures to dismantle it, the church is ultimately subject to law enforcement by the government under CCP’s leadership. Although, on the surface, the RRA provides channels enabling a house church to obtain legal status through the registration system, this system by no means works to accord them a meaningful legal status. The deliberate vacuum of manifest legal status for these unregistered house churches has enabled the government, with an authoritarian resilience, to restrain the religious freedom of unregistered religions in line with the politically contingent nature of authoritarian atheistic politics, in order to maintain the dominance of CCP’s militant atheism. In addition, the CCP’s integrated legalistic–political approach to PHCs, as adopted in the revised RRA in 2017, has further reinforced the ideological dominance of Marxist atheism for the purpose of maintaining the CCP’s monopoly on power and the stability of the regime. In summary, the house church, being deliberately afforded no manifest legal status, operates in a variety of adaptive ways under an authoritarian regime that upholds the CCP’s militant atheism.

11601419.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11601419.value: With the development of religions and the establishment of an instrumental legal system in China over the past decades, law and religion has been an increasingly important topic in the scholarship. The factors that influence religious freedom may change further. This largely depends on the changing landscape of the Party-state-religion relations in the context. Given that China has been attempting to build up an enterprise of authoritarian legality that fits with the leadership of the CCP and practices a certain degree of religious freedom, more interdisciplinary research will be needed in order to address the relevant law and religious freedom issues in the context.

11601419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11601419.value: This project seeks to explore how the right to religious freedom of Protestant house churches (PHCs) has been restricted under the existing legal framework from a socio-legal perspective given that China has established an instrumentalist legal system. It was found that the varying degrees of religious freedom practiced by these churches are subject to the tolerance of the government. At one end of the spectrum, this tolerance may lead to a politically reciprocal collusion between law enforcement officials and the house church, while at the other end, this arrangement may be broken by subsequent repressive measures that work to dismantle the church; this is particularly likely when a church’s high-profile engagement in the public sphere challenges the ideological dominance of the Party’s Marxist atheism. Moreover, it was found that the newly revised Regulation of Religious Affairs (RRA) has taken an integrated legalistic-political approach to PHCs. On the one hand, it is possible for the government to categorize a PHC as “unlawful” in practice according to the RRA. On the other hand, the RRA integrates a grassroots-level political approach to engaging villagers’ committees and residents’ committees in the political movements against these PHCs.

11602119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11602119.value: 文化研究，博物館研究和物質文化的學者認為，博物館不僅是收集和展示歷史文物的地方（Wright 1984），也是一個與政府同謀的文化社會機構（Bennett 1995：23）。博物館與國族建構有著錯綜複雜的關係。博物館展覽可以改變社會價值觀（Luke 2002：xiv），包括我們對香港是一個甚麼社會及我們是誰的看法。如果我們將博物館視為政治空間，那麼博物館的展品，設置及展覽就是在各方（包括現有政權，博物館資助者，博物館歷史，藏品和策展專業知識與日常工作）之間進行權力對話而成的結果。 本研究將探討香港主權回歸後，1997年至2017年這20年間，香港公立博物館講述了香港和中港關係的哪些故事？回歸後香港政府同時推廣香港作為「亞洲國際城市」，這些故事是怎樣被講述的？沉浸式和互動媒體技術的發展又如何改變展覽展示的方式？ 我們將收集和分析康樂文化署的政策文件，博物館展覽政策文件，博物館報告，以及訪問博物館從業員，從而理解香港博物館發展，博物館在香港社會所扮演的角色，及日常運作模式。我們亦會使用敘說分析及參與觀察研究，分析展覽觀眾如何欣賞及參與互動展覽，過程中如何建構身份及中國與香港，以及香港與國際社會關係。

11602119.label: Realisation of objectives
11602119.value: Objective 1: To critically survey Hong Kong’s major public museum exhibitions between 1997 and 2017 We use content analysis to examine all 351 special exhibitions hosted by the six museums: 1. Hong Kong Museum of History, 2. Hong Kong Heritage Museum, 3. Hong Kong Science Museum, 4. Hong Kong Museum of Coastal Defence, 5. Hong Kong Museum of Art, and 6. Hong Kong Film Archive. We investigated how many exhibitions were organized per year since each institution has been established to date; we also looked into the geographical, temporal scopes the exhibition covered and the subjects of the shows. Between 1997 and 2020, there are huge variations of the number of the exhibitions these six museums presented, from 16 (held by Museum of Coastal Defence the least) to 126 special exhibitions (held by Heritage Museum). The geographical scopes of these surveyed exhibitions are: 49.1% of these exhibitions showcase subjects in relation to Hong Kong, 14.1% about China, 13.5% about Hong Kong and China, and 11.5% about the world. In terms of the temporal scheme, there are 59.8% of the exhibition presenting subjects in contemporary period, with 17.3% modern period and 8.7% ancient period. We defined the modern period in Western history as after the Middle Ages (around 16 century) till the end of the Second World War (1945); while the modern period in Hong Kong from the British colonization to the end of the Second World War (1841 - 1945); and China from the first Opium War to the establishment of the PRC (1840 - 1949). Before that is deemed as ancient and after that as contemporary. Lastly, we found that the subjects of art (including visual arts, performing arts, and music) stand out in the surveyed exhibition (41.1%), while 27% about social and economic development, as well as folk cultures and customs; 17% about pop culture, fashion and design; 17% about technological invention and appliance; 14.4% about humanities and also 14.4% about political, military history and sovereign; 12.4% about traditional craft and architecture; 10.6% about traditional folk culture and mores (chart 4): Objective 2: To collect and analyse Leisure and Cultural Services Department (LCSD) policy documents, museum exhibition policies, museum reports, etc. to determine the roles that museums play in the past, present and future We collected all the policy documents of LCSD and did some summaries and analyses. We also find that Audit Commission Hong Kong made some important questions and criticisms on the nature of HK public museums, its aims, etc. The existing legislation (a) does not include the definition of a museum and does not define the fundamental aims, objectives and functions of museums; (b) does not include any provisions on the system of governance for museums; and (c) is silent on issues relating to the obligations of museums to manage and preserve their cultural and historical collections for the benefits of current and future generations. (Audit Commission Hong Kong 2006, p11) In our previous report, we drafted questions and invited senior administrator for interviews. We invited them for interview but we recevied no reply. Nevertheless, we did attend different seminars government officials gave speech. For example, in 2022 HK Art Scene: Global Opportunities and Challenges held on 18 September 2022 at Shouson Theatre, HK Arts Centre, we find speakers have diverse ideas on HK arts and cultural development and the relationship between Hong Kong, China and the international. In response to the 14th Five Year Plan of the Chinese government in 2021, the present Hong Kong SAR government officials emphasize on developing overseas exchange and creative industries based on the employment of digital technologies. Raistlin Lau, Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism, states “the newly-established Culture, Sports, and Tourism Bureau consolidates the culture, sports, and tourism portfolios, with a view to realizing HK’s new positioning as a hub for arts and cultural exchanges between China and the rest of the world promulgated in the 14th Five Year Plan, reinforcing HK’s leading position in the international arts market, and facilitating the development of arts, cultural and creative industries.” Besides, Lau mentions that the SAR Government is working in four directions to promote work in this area: a. the government will gradually establish world-class cultural facilities and multicultural spaces to provide soil for artists, art groups and practitioners to jointly nurture cultural and artistic creations. b. the government will strengthen exchanges and cooperation with mainland and overseas art and cultural institutions to further establish Hong Kong's status in the international art scene. c. the government will grasp international trends and allocate additional resources to encourage the cultural and creative industries to embrace digital technology. d. the government should strengthen Hong Kong's cultural and artistic talent pool. Chairman of Arts Development Council, Fok Kai-kong, emphasized institutionalization of overseas exchanges in respond to regional competition. He mentioned South Korea uses legal forms to encourage corporates to participate in building infrastructure for arts and culture, and Singapore vigorously attracts cultural and art talents. Indeed, in a discussion panel moderated by Dr. Tang Shu-wing, the panelists do not have consensus of the status of Hong Kong museums in the globe and the relationship of Hong Kong and the world. While Louis Ng (Museum Director, Hong Kong Palace Museum) comments that the three museums in Hong Kong (M+, MOA, and Forbidden City) already have the best curatorial standards in Asia, Eve Tam Mei Yee (Deputy Director (Culture) in the Leisure and Cultural Services Department) disagrees and comments that evaluating Hong Kong art on a global scale, it is not considered to be at the top of the heap, nor is it at the forefront of China. To Tam, Hong Kong needs to enhance its soft power and cultural confidence. Prof. Lo King-man (Founder, HKAC), who is expert of drama, gave a harsh comment on HK drama development, that Hong Kong is below world class, and creative development is less than satisfactory. There are many dramas, but most are translated and adapted ones. Hong Kong does not have an opera house, and there is no policy support. After 25 years of Handover, Hong Kong has built mega infrastructural arts and cultural museums, but the discussion is still about raising the local cultural quality, building up overseas exchange and developing digital technologies. Objective 3: To analyse how Hong Kong public museums narrate Hong Kong history, culture and identity, and Hong Kong-China relationship We focus on Bruce Lee exhibitions because of three reasons. First, it is one of the most popular exhibitions in the previous five years. Between 20 July 2013 and 31 December 2020, the "Bruce Lee: Kung Fu · Art · Life" exhibition has enjoyed continuous popularity, attracting a total attendance of about 3.7 million. Second, the original exhibition was revamped and we find the revamped exhibition “A man beyond the ordinary: Bruce Lee” (exhibition starts from 28 November 2021) narrates a different story about Bruce Lee, bringing out different emphasis on identity issues. Third, the redesign of the exhibition introduces (immersive) multimedia experiences, and we would like to examine how multimedia afford audience engagement in issues of Hong Kong identity. Research outcome will be discussed in section 6.1.

11602119.label: Major findings and research outcome
11602119.value: We submitted one manuscript titled ‘Museumising Bruce Lee: (De)political imagination and the culture of disappearance’ for consideration for publication in the International Journal of Heritage Studies in October 2023 and is now under review for the resubmitted version. This manuscript explores the complex dynamics surrounding the representation of Bruce Lee in two exhibitions in one Hong Kong public museum, focusing on the (de)political imagination and the culture of disappearance that shape his legacy. It delves into the ways in which Bruce Lee’s image and narrative have been manipulated, concealed, and commodified within museum contexts, obstructing a critical examination of the self in relation to nationalism and nation-building. Another research manuscript examines the differing perceptions of the revamped “A Man Beyond the Ordinary: Bruce Lee” exhibition, which opened on November 28, 2021. The study argues that university students from varying sociocultural backgrounds interpret the same exhibition differently. The findings indicate that mainland Chinese students tend to view Bruce Lee as a Chinese nationalist figure who promoted Chinese nationalism and martial arts globally. In contrast, Hong Kong-grown university students do not consider Bruce Lee to be inherently Chinese or Hongkonger, but rather perceive him as an American-born Hongkonger. The Hong Kong-grown students exhibit a more skeptical attitude toward the exhibition. Even though the exhibition features interactive installations and gamified display items, a few Hong Kong-grown students still find the exhibition uninteresting and question the narrative presented.

11602119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11602119.value: Regarding potential further development of this research, we consider several avenues to expand the scope and depth of the investigation. One promising direction would be to consider broadening the participant pool to include a more diverse range of stakeholders, such as museum curators, policymakers, and community members. By incorporating these diverse perspectives, the study could uncover the nuanced power dynamics, institutional constraints, and sociocultural factors that underpin the museumification of Bruce Lee's legacy. Furthermore, a longitudinal approach, tracking the evolution of representation in museum exhibitions over time, could reveal the shifting narratives, curatorial decisions, and audience responses that reflect the changing sociopolitical and cultural landscapes. This diachronic perspective could offer valuable insights into the dynamic and contested nature of cultural heritage and its interpretation.

11602119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11602119.value: Scholars have long recognized the significant role of museums in establishing and maintaining national legitimacy, as well as shaping collective identity. In the context of Hong Kong, the transfer of sovereignty from the United Kingdom to the People’s Republic of China in 1997 has given rise to tensions between Chinese national identity and local Hong Kong identity. The research team conducted a comparative analysis of two Bruce Lee exhibitions hosted at the Hong Kong Heritage Museum, delving into the complex dynamics surrounding the representation of this iconic figure. The distinct approaches taken by the two exhibitions in appropriating Lee’s legacy draw attention to the changes in associated narratives, reflecting the broader shifts in the cultural and political climate. Importantly, the audience research on the revamped “A Man Beyond the Ordinary: Bruce Lee” exhibition reveals diverse perspectives from university students with varying sociocultural backgrounds. These findings shed light on the complex interplay between museums, nationalism, and the public's interpretation of cultural icons like Bruce Lee. By unpacking these dynamics, the research offers valuable insights into the contested nature of cultural heritage representation and its sociopolitical implications.

11602719.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11602719.value: The project assesses the efficacy of China’s legal process in protecting employees against unfair dismissal. It investigates judicial decisions, asking how effectively judges protect employees who challenge the fairness of their dismissal. The central components of the research are a comprehensive national survey of all adjudications over a 9 year period of an important category of unfair dismissal cases -- the “serious breach” dismissals --, an evaluation of the change in the judicial approach to this type of cases before and after the implementation of the relevant employee-protection regulations and a qualitative study based on interviews with judges. Serious breach dismissal cases are particularly important to understanding the efficacy of China’s employee protection regime because the right of an employer to terminate immediately an employee who commits a “serious breach” of its internal regulations is prone to manipulation. Article 39(2) of China’s Labour Contract Law provides that an employer who exercises the right incorrectly must compensate the employee for unfair dismissal but nowhere does Chinese law provide a test for unfair dismissal. It is therefore up to the courts to decide whether a dismissal that the employee contests is unfair or not. One key issue in making that decision is whether a court has an obligation to review the reasons that the employer cites as grounds for a “serious breach”. If the court considers that it has no obligation to review those reasons then it in effect simply confirms whatever decision the employer has made, no matter how unfair and wrongful that decision is. Since judges’ understanding of whether their courts are bound to review the “fairness” of the dismissal is crucial to the outcome of serious breach dismissal cases, it is important to know how judges decide this question but no comprehensive empirical study of this type of cases in China has been conducted to date. This project seeks to fill that gap by conducting an empirical analysis of a representative sample of all available “documents of adjudication decisions” on serious breach dismissal cases in every Chinese court from 2010 to 2018, coupled with in-depth fieldwork at the basic-level courts in a major Chinese city. 此項目評估了在中國法律程序對受到不公平解雇的員工保護的有效性。此項目通過對法官在保護不服解雇結果的員工的有效性提出疑問並調查研究有關判決結果。本次研究的中心部分是調查不公正解雇案件中一種重要類別 – "嚴重違規" 解雇。 嚴重違規解雇的案件對理解中國的員工保護政策十分重要，因為用人單位以嚴重違反用人單位的規章制度為由而立即解雇雇員的權利趨於人為操作。《中華人民共和國勞動合同法》第39條第二款規定用人單位違反規定不公正解除勞動合時應賠償勞動者損失，然而中國法律並未有對不公正解雇進一步規定。因此決定解雇是否公正取決於法院態度。在作出決定時，關鍵問題在於法庭是否有責任考慮用人單位提出的嚴重違規的情形。若法庭認為其並無此責任，則實際上法庭即已認定用人單位作出的任何決定而無關該決定是否不公正、錯誤。正因法官對於法庭是否應考慮解雇的公正性的理解不同，其判斷對這類“嚴重違規”解雇案件結果十分關鍵。因此了解法官如何判斷以上問題尤為重要。然而目前在中國尚未有關於這類案件比較全面的實証研究。通過對所有“嚴重違規”結果案件在2010年至2018年期間可獲取的裁判性文件的代表性樣本採取實証研究，並通過在中國重要城市的基層法院開展的深度實地考察，本項目意在填補這一空缺。

11602719.label: Realisation of objectives
11602719.value: The PI conducted a thorough quantitative study to, among other things, assess the effectiveness of the civil process in protecting employees’ rights in Serious Breach Dismissal Cases in China (Objective 1). The PI and the RA have coded a representative sample of “documents of adjudication decisions” (DADs) of Serious Breach Dismissal Cases during the period between 2010-2018. The final number for the DADs analysis was 2054. The information from the DADs was hand-coded into a computer. Four independent coders were trained for content analysis. The average inter-coder reliability, measured by Cohen’s Kappa, was 0.876789. To supplement the quantitative study, the author collected data from 34 informants who are all judges. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with nine of the informants, all of whom are experienced in adjudicating labour disputes. All 34 informants responded to a questionnaire on issues relating to labour disputes in general and Serious Breach Dismissal Cases specifically. The research reveals that the civil process is not particularly effective in protecting employees’ rights in Serious Breach Dismissal Cases in China (Objective 1). The data shows (n=2054) the employers have come out ahead by a substantial margin. The employers’ winning rate is 66.89 percent. The employee’s winning rate is only 14.95 percent. This is a whooping difference of 51.94 percent in terms of winning rate comparison. The partial wining rate for both sides is 18.16 percent. Courts in most cases only conducted a simple factual review to see if the employer’s internal regulations have been violated by the employee. Courts in most cases did not conduct a substantive assessment of whether the dismissal was fair or unfair (“fairness review”). The data reveals that the fairness review is pivotal in the determination of litigation outcome. Had the court conducted a fairness review in every case, the employees would have prevailed. The failure of the court to conduct a fairness review is solid proof that courts favour employers. It is submitted that the project has fully achieved Objective 1. The research also assessed how different independent variables (e.g. geography, socio-economic circumstances, policy factors, local regulations, whether the court reviews the fairness of the dismissal) affect the success rate of the employee litigants (Objective 2). This study coded a number of independent variables about the employee that directly or indirectly affect the outcome of the case. For instance, the gender of the employee has been coded to assess whether gender played a role in the outcome of the case. The average earned income of the employee was coded to test whether financial resources of the employee affected the chance of winning. The study also coded a number of independent variables about the employer. The capacity of the employer can be critical in determining outcome. As shown in some studies, government agencies and government-related firms commanded overwhelming advantage against all other entities. The location of the parties vis-a-vis the location of the court was also recorded to assess whether there is pattern of local protectionism. A key variable of party capability, legal representation, has also been coded. Temporal and regional variations are recorded to assess the variations in local judicial policies (and local economic development) on labour disputes and changes in the litigation of labour disputes through time. Based on the above, it is submitted that Objective 2 has been fully achieved. Objective 4 calls for the evaluation of the change in the judicial approach to Serious Breach Dismissal Cases before and after the implementation of the key employee-protection regulations (i.e. the SPC 2008 Interpretation and the Suzhou Regulations). As mentioned in the Midterm Report, it was difficult to obtain DADs prior to 2010 in Suzhou (these DADs are not accessible by the public and courts are unlikely to grant access), the research focus have been modified to assess the divergences of judicial practice between Suzhou courts (which implemented key employee-protection regulations) and courts of neighbouring cities in Jiangsu Province (where local employee-protection regulations are absent)(modifying Objective 4). Ultimately, Wuxi was chosen (where employee-protection regulations are absent) to compare with Suzhou. Data was collected to assess the impact of local labour regulations on labour disputes adjudication in the context of unfair dismissal (Objective 3). An empirical study (accepted for publication) investigates the judicial practice of Suzhou and Wuxi. Suzhou employers are required under the relevant local regulations to give employees the opportunity to be heard prior to dismissal, while Wuxi does not. After analyzing and discussing 140 cases from Suzhou and 234 cases from Wuxi, the study concludes that giving employees the opportunity to be heard is essential for protecting their rights, as evidenced by the higher success rates for employees in Suzhou compared to those in Wuxi. The analysis highlights the significance of local regulations in ensuring labour protection in China and determining the success rate of the employee in labour disputes. For details, see third output in Part C. Based on the above, the project has fully achieved Objectives 3 and 4. The interviews and questionnaires in the first output (see Part C) revealed factors that affected the willingness of the judge to review both the procedural and substantive fairness of the dismissal in the adjudication of Serious Breach Dismissal Cases (Objective 5). For instance, informants have consistently expressed the importance of honouring “corporate autonomy” in adjudication to avoid upsetting the employers’ commercial decisions, including dismissal decisions. Due to this consideration, many judges are unwilling to assess the substantive fairness of the dismissal. The employees’ greater success rates in Suzhou (see third output in Part C) revealed that due process considerations played a role in Suzhou judges’ determination of cases. As required by local regulations, Suzhou employers are required to give employees an opportunity to be heard before dismissal. Based on the above, it is submitted that Objective 5 is fully achieved. The PI has distributed the first output (see Part C) to most of his contacts in the Chinese judiciary. The PI has an extensive network of judges and most of his contacts are members of the court leadership (deputy division heads, division heads, vice presidents and presidents). It is believed that this will help raise awareness and may indirectly influence judicial practice in the handling of Serious Breach Dismissal Cases in a way that will enhance procedural and substantive safeguards for employee litigants (Objective 6). The output would also provide useful information and data on Serious Breach Dismissal Cases to labour rights NGOs in China on the subject of unfair dismissal (Objective 7). The PI has close contacts with activist lawyers in China who specialize in labour disputes. The outputs will provide useful information to these lawyers and assist them in their court work. Based on the above, it is submitted that Objectives 6 and 7 have been partially achieved. Due to Covid, it was not possible for the PI to attend international conferences. However, the PI has given a number of internal talks about this subject and distributed the outputs to various leading scholars around the world. This helps to keep the academic dialogue going in the area of labour rights protection in China.

11602719.label: Major findings and research outcome
11602719.value: This project investigates how courts handle labour disputes in China using empirical methods focusing on serious breach dismissal cases. Serious breach dismissals are dismissals that result from employees breaching internal regulations of the employer to a serious degree. The first round of major findings came with the publication of the PI’s article with the University of Pennsylvania Journal of International Law titled, “Are Chinese Courts Pro-Labor or Pro-Employer?” (see first output in Part C). The study found that (a) despite the established view that Chinese courts are pro-labour, it was discovered through data analysis of 2,054 sampled cases that courts are in fact pro-employer; (b) the employers have won by a substantial margin. The employers’ winning rate is 66.89% while the employee’s winning rate is only 14.95%. This is a whooping difference of 51.94% in terms of winning rate comparison. The partial wining rate for both sides is 18.16%; (c) courts in most cases only conducted a simple factual review to see if the employer’s internal regulations have been violated by the employee; (d) Courts in most cases did not conduct a substantive assessment of whether the dismissal was fair or unfair (“fairness review”); (e) the data reveals that the fairness review is pivotal in the determination of litigation outcome. Had the court conducted a fairness review in every case, the employees would have prevailed; (f) The failure of the court to conduct a fairness review is solid proof that courts favour employers. The second round of major findings came with the publication (accepted for publication) of the PI’s article with Washington International Law Journal titled, “Does Black-Letter Law Matter in Labor Rights Protection in China? – A Tale of Two Cities” (see third output in Part C). This article presents an empirical analysis of the judicial practice of Suzhou and Wuxi. Suzhou employers are required under the relevant regulations to give employees the opportunity to be heard prior to dismissal, while Wuxi does not. After analyzing 140 cases from Suzhou and 234 cases from Wuxi, this article concludes that giving employees the opportunity to be heard is essential for protecting their rights, as evidenced by the higher success rates for employees in Suzhou compared to those in Wuxi. The analysis highlights the significance of black-letter law in ensuring labour protection in China.

11602719.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11602719.value: This project can be further developed through expanding the scope of investigation beyond serious breach dismissals. After all, there are many types of labour disputes in China. The position of courts in relation to serious breach dismissals may not be representative of their position in relation to other types of labour disputes. For instance, Article 40(3) of the Labour Contract Law, under which the employer may revoke an employment contract (with one month’s notice or payment in lieu) if “the objective conditions taken as the basis for conclusion of the contract have significantly changed, so that the original employment contract cannot be performed”. One possibility is to compare the court decisions in Beijing with the decisions in Shanghai. The hypothesis is that as Beijing is the political centre, courts are more likely to favour employees, while Shanghai courts, being more commercially minded, may find for the employers. Another possible study based on the existing project is to look into how labour dispute arbitration committees deal with serious breach dismissals. As the committees are the first instance forum for labour disputes, it would be interesting to see how their decisions defer from courts.

11602719.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11602719.value: This project investigates how courts handle labour disputes in China using empirical methods focusing on serious breach dismissal cases. Serious breach dismissals are dismissals that result from employees breaching (or allegedly breaching) internal regulations of the employer to a serious degree. The established view is that, as a socialist nation, the courts in China favour employees. This project tested this established view. It found that, contrary to conventional understanding, Chinese courts are in fact pro-employer as evidenced by the substantial margin of victory of employers over employees. This project also tested whether black-letter law matters in the protection of labour rights in China. An empirical analysis of the judicial practice of two of China’s economically developed cities, Suzhou and Wuxi was carried out. Suzhou employers are required under the relevant regulations to give employees the opportunity to be heard prior to dismissal, while Wuxi does not. Through analysing the relevant cases, this project concludes that giving employees the opportunity to be heard is essential for protecting their rights, as evidenced by the higher success rates for employees in Suzhou compared to those in Wuxi. It highlights the significance of black-letter law in ensuring labour protection in China.

11602919.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11602919.value: “擴展立體視覺”（Expanded Stereoscopy）打破立體（3D）藝術中感知現實主義（perceptual realism）的霸權，旨在探索廣闊而尚未被開發的交替3D視覺領域。人們亟需廣泛的立體沉浸式技術，這一意識是本研究誕生的動機。 1849年立體攝影術（Brewster Stereoscope布儒斯特立體鏡）誕生後，立體視覺一直是邊緣的——唯希治閣（Alfred Hitchcock）的《電話謀殺案》（Dial M for Murder，1954）及安迪華荷（Andy Warhol）和莫里西（Paul Morrissey）的《慾望科學怪人》 （Flesh for Frankenstein，1973）是少數例外。然而，自占士金馬倫（James Cameron）的《阿凡達》（Avatar，2009）以來，立體電影已成為電影發行的事實標準。與此同時，虛擬現實（VR）和增強現實（AR）技術已經發展成熟，相關應用也激烈增加（Google Cardboard，2014；Oculus Rift，HTC Vive，Playstation VR，2016；Microsoft HoloLens，2017）。就未來的使用而言，3D技術有望進一步發展。2017年10月，Facebook的首席執行官馬克·朱克伯格（Mark Zuckerberg）承諾將讓10億人用上VR（Manthorpe 2017）。 立體視覺雖然是新興的，但它現時仍在使用此技術肇始時設立的運作原則。在物理層面，立體視覺通過左右圖像的立體融合產生3D深度感知。然而，除了標準地模仿人類視覺，立體視覺還可以用來提供新的感知和美學。 雖然雙眼競爭（Binocular rivalry）等現像已在認知神經科學和心理物理學中得到了很好的研究（Levelt 1965; Walker 1978; Alais＆Blake 2005; Zou 2017），但它們的藝術潛力仍未得到充分發掘。 Salvador Dali，Memo Akten和Sebastian Buerkner等藝術家是探索這個領域的少數人之一。我們提出“擴展立體視覺”（Expanded Stereoscopy）這一術語來描述這種實現“立體”的過程，它創造了一個空間——在這一空間中，或許深度的關係相互脫節和矛盾，或許雙眼競爭被用於創造獨特的視覺效果或引導觀眾注意力，或許新的維度和視覺強度從平面的源材料中被挖掘出來。這種對立體視覺擴展性、科技輔助性的應用開拓了在現實世界中無法“看”到的新方式，可以被視為感官的真正擴展。 本研究將涉及民族誌研究部分（採訪立體視覺的藝術家）和研究創作部分（基於實踐的擴展立體視覺研究）。體現此調查研究的創意作品，將探索“擴展立體視覺“的不同策略，基於紮根理論（Grounded theory，Strauss ＆ Glaser 1967）對觀眾評估，以確定擴展立體視覺對觀眾的影響。評估結果將通過會議報告和期刊文章傳播。創意作品將在香港及海外展出。

11603119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11603119.value: The anticorruption campaign of “hunting the tigers and sweeping the flies” at the auspices of President Xi Jinping since his ascension to power in 2012 has garnered tremendous public support in China. Public opinion and academic research have so far largely centered on how to make anticorruption more effective and less selective so as to round up more “tigers and flies”. Little attention has been paid to the possibility of aiming at the wrong targets, i.e. wrongfully charging, prosecuting and convicting an innocent official in the pursuit of anticorruption. This gap is surprising, given the unique political and legal systems established under the CCP ruling since 1980 and the history of miscarriages of justice during successive political purges prior to 1980. This study aims to fill the gap by investigating miscarriages of justice in anticorruption in China since 1980. Based on a review of the institutional flaws contributing to corruption and ineffective anticorruption in the literature, this study draws on the institutional theory to identify institutional factors for wrongful corruption convictions: the possible abuse of party leadership in anticorruption, the prevailing culture of rule of man regardless of the political slogan of “ruling the country by law”, the long tradition of violation of human rights and presumption of guilty in the criminal justice system, and the overarching application of the performance evaluation system in the bureaucracy. It plans to achieve three objectives: a) to examine the characteristics of such cases, and identify the direct contributing factors and underlying political factors for the wrongful convictions, drawing on the literature on wrongful convictions of violent offenders; b) to analyze the channels for the exoneration of wronged officials; and c) to explore the mechanisms for the prevention of miscarriages of justice in anticorruption. It is based on a triangulation of research methods: an aggregated case study of 51 ascertained wrongful corruption cases and field research including observations of court hearings in four cities in China and in-depth interviews with legal professionals and victims of wrongful corruption convictions. The implications of the proposed study are two-fold: 1) it extends the literature on wrongful convictions to examine a different group of non-violent offenders and explores the extent to which findings from the two groups converge, and 2) it contributes to anticorruption in China by calling our attention to the possibility of miscarriages of justice and remedies for such grave errors of justice.

11603119.value: This project investigates wrongful convictions in the context of anti-corruption in China. Thus, future course of action is two-fold: On wrongful convictions: 1) Add the cases into the Registry of Wrongful Convictions in China which is scheduled to roll out in late 2023 (with internal funding from City University of Hong Kong); 2) Develop an integrated approach on preventing wrongful convictions in China; 3) Continue to explore the salient topics under wrongful convictions in China, e.g. use of torture in police interrogations, admissibility of evidence collected through unlawful means, the role of media and advocacy groups, remedial assistance to victims of wrongful convictions and their families. On anti-corruption: 1) Apply Institutional Theory to the fight of corruption in different spheres of the political hierarchy.

11603119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11603119.value: Miscarriages of justice are a grave violation of human rights and undermine the integrity and legitimacy of the criminal justice system. Nevertheless, any possible miscarriage of justice in anti-corruption is overshadowed by the public enthusiasm to reign in rampant corruption. Thus, it is even more compelling for us to recognize its existence, understand its characteristics, examine the channels for exoneration and ultimately establish an effective preventive mechanism. Wrongful corruption convictions should not be mistakenly treated as a countercurrent of or antithesis to rigorous anti-corruption. Proactive prevention of wrongful convictions should be built into any anticorruption campaign, so as to render the latter more accountable and effective. This project is a first attempt to investigate wrongful convictions of non-violent defendants, in contrast to the focus on violent defendants in the literature. It has both theoretical and empirical implications.

11603219.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11603219.value: It is commonly assumed that the success of anti-corruption agencies (ACAs) is partially dependent on institutional trust and positive perceptions of their effectiveness. The relationship between trust and effectiveness is seen to be direct, causal and mutually reinforcing, forming a virtuous circle: perceived effectiveness generates institutional trust and institutional trust enhances effectiveness. Conversely, a perceived lack of effectiveness will impact negatively on public trust in an institution, while a loss of institutional trust can jeopardise its performance. However, our previous research on Hong Kong’s Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) (GRF 9042104, 2015) suggests that the relationship between trust and the perception of effectiveness is more complex, a finding which, if proven, has important implications for the work of ACAs and possibly other government institutions. We argue that institutional trust in an ACA is multi-faceted. It is composed of two major elements: 1) evaluations based on different kinds of public perceptions including the effectiveness, powers and integrity of the ACA and (2) combinations of past and present perceptions which may interact to produce a nuanced view of trust in the ACA. Perceived effectiveness in combatting corruption may generate what we term "generalised trust", but there is no necessary positive linear relationship between effectiveness and institutional trust because positive perceptions may be based on factors other than effectiveness. For example, the institutionalisation of an ACA’s structures and processes over time may mitigate the impact of negative beliefs about its effectiveness. Even if an ACA is currently perceived to be ineffective, the overall level of trust, based on its previous performance, may still remain high. We will investigate the puzzling relationship between institutional trust and perceptions of effectiveness in corruption prevention. We will use a mixed methods research approach. A survey will be conducted to measure institutional trust and perceptions of effectiveness and we will also analyse longitudinal raw data from the ICAC’s annual surveys (1977-2017). The quantitative research will be supplemented by a qualitative analysis of selected corruption-related cases and their perceptual impacts on institutional trust and effectiveness in this research. This research will provide ground-breaking material for the academic analysis of trust and effectiveness in ACAs and, more broadly, in government institutions. It will also have practical implications in providing a more nuanced picture of public perceptions of the ICAC and a better understanding of the factors contributing to Hong Kong's success in preventing corruption. 腐敗預防中的信任度和效能感 通常認為，反貪機構的成功有賴于公眾對其信任和對其效能的正面感知。公眾信任和效能感之間的關係被認為是直接關聯的、有因果機制的，且可以互相強化。因此它們之間可以形成一種良性循環，即：公眾有效能感便會產生信任，而信任反過來又會增強效能感。反之，公眾缺乏效能感會降低其信任度，而信任的喪失可能會危及效能感。然而，我們之前對香港廉政公署的研究項目（GRF 9042104, 2015）表明，信任度和效能感知之間的關係要比想象中複雜的多，如果是這樣的話，那麼我們的研究將會對廉署乃至其它政府機構的工作有所啟發。 我們認為，對反貪機構的信任是多層面的。它由兩個主要因素構成：1）公眾對反貪機構的效能、權力和誠信等各方面的感知；2）基於過去和現在的感知之互動而產生的對反貪機構的信任。對打擊腐敗效能的認可會帶來某種信任，我們稱其為“產出的信任”。但效能和信任之間並不一定存在正相關，因為對反貪工作的正面看法可能來自其它因素，而非反貪效能。例如，反貪機構的組織架構和工作流程隨時間的推移而制度化，就有可能消除公眾對其效能的負面看法。即便一個反貪機構目前被認為效能不高，公眾基於其以往的表現，對它的整體信任水平可能還是很高。在本研究中，我們將分析對反貪機構的信任度和預防腐敗的效能感之間的這種複雜關係。 我們將同時使用定性方法和定量方法。我們會開展一項問卷調查，測量信任度和效能感這兩個變量，並結合來自廉政公署年度問卷調查（1977-2017）的縱向原始數據進行分析。我們還會選取相關的腐敗案例以及它們對本研究所關注的信任度和效能感的影響進行定性分析，作為定量研究的補充。 本研究將為關於反貪機構（以及其它政府機構）的信任和效能的學術研究帶來突破性的資料。本研究亦會有實際意義，它將更加細緻地呈現公眾對廉政公署的看法，並有助於更深入地了解促成香港成功反腐的各項因素。

11603219.label: Realisation of objectives
11603219.value: The research team worked diligently to fully realize the four objectives of the project. In what follows, we report what we did and how we achieved each of these objectives. Objective 1: To conduct a longitudinal analysis of institutional trust and perceptions of effectiveness with reference to the ICAC, drawing on its survey data between 1977 and 2017 and on our previous and proposed research. We began with extensive desk-based collection and analysis of government documents, media reports, and relevant scholarly works on issues concerning institutional trust and the perceived effectiveness of corruption prevention. In the process, we paid special attention to the material about Hong Kong and especially the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC). The broad and detailed documentary analysis and literature review served two purposes. The first was to get a general picture of where things stood in the existing research on the issue of trust and effectiveness in corruption prevention. Secondly, the extensive literature review enabled us to develop measurements and hypotheses about the two broad variables (trust and effectiveness) of this project and their relationships. Having done the document analysis, we proceeded with data collection. We gathered and consolidated the raw data and/or reports of the ICAC’s annual surveys from 1977 to 2022. The database, which covers 45 years of survey results, provided us with important information about the fight against corruption in Hong Kong and its achievements and perceived shortcomings. It allowed us to conduct a longitudinal study of public perceptions of corruption prevention in Hong Kong, including citizens’ understandings and interpretations of what corruption was and its levels, their satisfaction with and trust in the government and the ICAC’s efforts, and their expectations for future development in controlling corruption. Objective 2: To conduct a survey specifically designed to ascertain levels of institutional trust and perceptions of effectiveness in the ICAC and possible congruities and disparities between the two. Our plan to conduct a survey for data collection was successfully executed. The survey was administered with the help of the Social Sciences Research Centre at The University of Hong Kong in May and June 2020. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, we conducted the survey by phone (via both domestic fixed and mobile lines). For fixed lines, seed numbers were obtained from the online White Pages residential directory by dropping the last digital number. Then, all ten possible numbers (0 through 9) were added to the seed numbers, yielding the sampling frame for the fixed-line respondents. Within each household, the survey candidate was selected using the “Modified Next Birthday” rule. The sampling frame for the cellphone survey was obtained from blocks allocated by the Office of the Communications Authority (OFCA) for mobile use, and telephone numbers were randomly selected and used for contacting respondents. Eligible candidates were individuals aged 18 or above who spoke Cantonese, Putonghua, or English. Cantonese is the major language in Hong Kong, but the research team prepared the questionnaire in various languages. In the end, a total of 2,009 questionnaires were completed. In the survey, we measured institutional trust by asking respondents about the extent to which they trust the ICAC and other government institutions. A 5-point Likert-type scale was used, with options ranging from “not at all” to “very much”. Assessing the perceived effectiveness appeared to be somewhat more complex. We identified six specific areas of fighting corruption in Hong Kong (i.e., controlling illegal business transactions, cross-border collusion, government-business collusion, bribery, nepotism, and abuse of public power). Respondents were invited to evaluate the effectiveness of the ICAC’s anticorruption work in these areas, with answers ranging from “least effective” to “very effective”. The average value of the answers to these questions was taken as the measure of a respondent’s perception of the effectiveness of the ICAC. In case some respondents did not fully understand the meaning of some questions, a brief example would be provided to help them understand the specific question. Objective 3: To analyze findings relevant to building social intolerance of corruption, particularly, public willingness to report corruption and effective resource allocation for ACAs Although there is no single or simple recipe for effective control of corruption, scholars and practitioners consider Hong Kong as a model of success. However, other than a powerful and independent anticorruption agency, the ICAC, and its three-pronged strategy — law enforcement, corruption prevention, and community education, little was known about how the general public in Hong Kong perceived and responded to corruption and corruption control. Our third objective attempted to fill this gap. We began with the assumption that the public’s intolerance of corruption and willingness to report suspected cases were attributable to the fact that they held strong trust in the ICAC’s anti-corruption determination and effort and were confident in its effectiveness. Our findings confirmed the relevant hypotheses. On that basis, we further explored what variables might influence the level of trust and the perception of institutional effectiveness and how and to what extent the two might interact with each other. We concluded that the two can form a virtuous circle to lower social tolerance for corruption and to encourage citizens to support and engage in the fight against corruption. Objective 4: To explore the implications of the Hong Kong experience for other regions Hong Kong’s experience in fighting corruption is believed to be influential in the world, and, as estimated, somewhere between thirty to forty national-level anti-corruption agencies worldwide were established based on the idea of a single, powerful, and centralized institution like the ICAC. Our research focused on Hong Kong but was not limited to it. We went beyond the city itself to explore the implications of the Hong Kong experience for other regions. For example, we conducted a comparative study of three Chinese cities—Hong Kong, Taipei, and Changsha. Drawing on empirical data collected in the three places, we were able to identify two important factors that would help explain the variations in the level of confidence in anti-corruption efforts among the public: citizens’ perceived level of existing corruption and the degree of their satisfaction with the government’s anti-corruption endeavor. We also explored the implications of Hong Kong’s anti-corruption strategies for Mainland China where local innovations were strongly encouraged in order to seek more effective ways and more substantial achievements in controlling corruption. A comparative analysis of the propensities toward bribery between Hong Kong and a mainland city was conducted and yielded interesting findings. In these studies and others, we suggested that the ICAC’s organizational structure was more a reference to best practice than a model to be copied. The most important was to change social attitudes toward corruption. The ICAC’s experiences in discovering what the public was really thinking about corruption and its prevention, building trust and promoting positive perceptions of effectiveness, and using various means to raise public awareness and form consensus may be particularly relevant for Mainland China and for some anti-corruption agencies in developing countries.

11603219.label: Major findings and research outcome
11603219.value: This GRF project has yielded in total nine peer-reviewed publications, including five in English and four in Chinese. The main findings are summarized below. To begin with, based on the longitudinal analysis of the ICAC surveys and on a large-scale survey conducted by ourselves, this project uncovers the novel and complicated relationships between institutional trust and the perceived effectiveness of anti-corruption agencies (ACAs). We find, firstly, that citizens’ trust impacts the perception of institutional effectiveness more than the reverse. This may indicate that trust is not only performance-based but also character-based, with the latter lasting longer and exerting a greater impact on perceptions of institutional performance (Xiao, Gong and Tu, 2024). Secondly, when public trust in an ACA is low, especially in the early years of its creation, the agency’s highly effective performance in curbing corruption may allow it to earn trust from citizens. The earned trust will then enable the ACA to suffer less loss in social support at times when it is considered not as effective as before. Building such a virtuous circle is a long and difficult process, which may be interrupted by exogenous factors that cause disjunctions between trust and perceived effectiveness. However, the virtuous circle, once established, can alleviate the negative impact of perceived institutional ineffectiveness on trust (Xiao, Scott and Gong, 2022). Second, this project reveals the significant factors contributing to institutional trust, public confidence, and institutional effectiveness, which are all crucial for anti-corruption governance. Citizens’ confidence in government control of corruption is affected by their perceptions of the level of existing corruption and by the extent to which they are satisfied with their government’s anti-corruption efforts (Xiao, Gong, Yu, Juang and Yuan, 2020). When public trust in an ACA is low, the agency’s high performance in curbing corruption may allow it to enhance its trust from citizens (Xiao, Scott and Gong, 2022). Moreover, the ACA’s capacities, including 1) the organizational capacity reflecting public perceptions of its structure, functions, procedures, and the integrity of personnel, and 2) the environmental capacity focusing on its ability to deal effectively with the changing social environment, significantly contribute to citizens’ perceived effectiveness of the ACA (Gong, Scott, and Xiao, 2023). Last but not least, while innovations in combatting corruption may enhance institutional effectiveness, whether they can succeed or not depends on to what extent they are able to gain public trust and support (Gong and Yang, 2022). Finally, this project provides solid evidence and theoretical insights supporting a bottom-up anti-corruption strategy in enhancing governance. By drawing on the rich empirical evidence of the ICAC, this project finds that co-creation of public values, such as trust and zero-tolerance of corruption, in society is crucial for anti-corruption success in Hong Kong (Gong, 2023, 2022; Yang and Gong, 2020). A supportive social environment and citizens’ trust in the ACA’s capacity in fighting corruption can significantly reduce bribery propensities, as revealed in a comparative study of Hong Kong and city A in the Greater Bay Area (Xiao, Gong and Lao, 2020). Note: All the citations in the 6.1 sub-section can be found in the publications listed in Part C.

11603219.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11603219.value: Two directions for future research are identified during the implementation of this GRF project. To begin with, we recognize the importance of successful anti-corruption reforms for good governance. Surprisingly, success factors in fighting corruption have been understudied and, consequently, we know little about how and why anti-corruption reforms can succeed. Drawing on the successful experience of the ICAC in Hong Kong, the PI developed and submitted a new GRF proposal titled “Paths to Success: A Qualitative Comparative Analysis of Anticorruption Reforms” in 2023. This proposed study will employ qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) methods (fsQCA and mvQCA) to empirically investigate the theoretical propositions concerning the necessity of successful anti-corruption reform. Second, through this project, we also find that innovation in anti-corruption measures, if successful, can greatly enhance the effectiveness of anti-corruption. The project team has worked with the ICAC to identify about 40 innovative anti-corruption measures adopted by the ICAC. We will employ the QCA approaches to analyze the conditions that contribute to a high level of innovation in combating corruption and lessons to be drawn from these innovative measures.

11603219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11603219.value: This research is a detailed examination of institutional trust and the perceived effectiveness of anti-corruption agencies (ACAs). It also explores the interconnection between the two and sheds light on broader government institutions. Drawing on a case study of the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) in Hong Kong, the research provides insights into public perceptions of corruption prevention and identifies key success factors in combating corruption. While there may be a perceived virtuous circle between perceived effectiveness and trust in an institution, our findings reveal a more intricate relationship between the two. Institutional trust in ACAs encompasses multiple dimensions, including evaluations of their effectiveness, authority, and integrity, as well as a blend of past and present perceptions of their performance. Perceived effectiveness in addressing corruption may foster what we term "generalized trust," yet this does not necessarily entail a linear relationship with institutional trust, as positive perceptions may stem from other factors beyond effective performance. Notably, even in cases where an ACA is deemed ineffective at a certain time, trust levels may remain high due to its past performance. The exploration of this puzzling phenomenon holds both theoretical and practical significance and provides valuable insights for policy making and implementation.

11603319.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11603319.value: 哈利特·门罗在中国：现代主义、旅行及跨国诗学

11603319.label: Project Objectives
11603319.value: To assess and historically contextualize Monroe's unpublished journals and letters that document her travels in China during her first and second journeys (1911 and 1934). I will examine Monroe's travel accounts in terms of her awakening to non-Western aesthetics, which resulted in a reformulation of her own poetic praxis, to interpret how this literary reformation, as a crucial inflection in her editorial position, contributed to evolving political and social discourses on China in the first half of the twentieth century. To illuminate Monroe's connections with influential Americans resident in China and to explore the implications of these contacts in terms of Monroe's editorial interests and her views of poetry as progressive, economically viable, and socially constructive. As it engages with scholarship on America's historically evolving economic and political role in East Asia, this study will respond to a research lacuna by investigating how the context of U.S.-China relations subtly yet surely influenced domestic literary publishing. To foreground Monroe as an intermediary and overlooked figure in the modernist movement whose engagement with contemporaneous poetry was inter/trans-national, cosmopolitan, and pragmatic. Monroe's positions on poetry, her authority in the publication of poetry and later in poetry as a professional activity, and her status as an independent woman in the literary marketplace from the 1910s to the 1930s provide a substantial new encounter with modernism as a movement. To document new historical knowledge about Monroe and her interactions in China and East Asia that will affect the currently prevailing reading and interpretation of modern U.S. and world poetry. The examination of historical records, including correspondence between Monroe and various relevant writers in the U.S. and China, will underpin the narration of this history to nuance and complicate our reception of the literary aesthetics and texts of this period.

11603319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11603319.value: This project situates the works of the American writer and editor Harriet Monroe within the historical context of early twentieth-century U.S.-China relations. Monroe is known primarily as the founder and editor of "Poetry: A Magazine of Verse", a publication founded in 1912 that became an important forum for modern Anglo-American poetry. Monroe was the editor of "Poetry" for twenty-four years, from the magazine's founding until her death in 1936, and was instrumental in defining the magazine's scope, selecting works for publication, and securing financial backing. Monroe went on two journeys to China (first in 1911, shortly before the founding of "Poetry", and then again in 1934). As I explore the journals and correspondence that document these journeys (archived in the Harriet Monroe Papers at the University of Chicago), I will show that Monroe's travels to China, her reception of Chinese civilizational and cultural values, and her insights into contemporary social life powerfully influenced her aesthetics. In showing how China provoked Monroe's aesthetic awakening, and indeed had a pervasive effect on other poetry of this period, this research will reveal that Monroe's interest in China was pivotal to challenging twentieth-century nationalist paradigms and promoting a transnational and cosmopolitan position on modern literature. While illuminating the extent to which Monroe's literary interests emerged out of this context of travel and cross-cultural experimentation, this project will pay close attention to the specific ways in which American publishers and writers were influenced by East-West geopolitical events. As Monroe interacted and corresponded with well-known diplomats and financiers who were based in China during this period, she gained an intimate perspective on the ways in which China's historical transitions were conceptualized by Americans and in relation to Western political and economic interventions. Clarifying this historical context will nuance, and even change, our reading of literary texts produced during this period and will shape our theories of literary cultures to emphasize their emergence in relation to specific political and economic contexts. In assessing the social implications of Monroe's China journeys, the research project will plumb Monroe's importance as a writer and editor to underline the broad historical significance of her developing interest in China. The outcomes of this project will be disseminated through scholarly publications: two journal articles, three conference papers, and eventually a monograph about Monroe, her China journeys, and her influence on literary modernism. 本项目将美国作家兼编辑哈利特·门罗的作品置于二十世纪早期的中美关系这一历史背景中进行讨论。1912年，门罗创立《诗刊》杂志，并使其成为现代英美诗歌的一大阵地。自创刊至1936年去世，她负责编纂工作长达二十四年之久，并在杂志议题范围的确立、作品选登、及获得资金支持方面发挥了重要作用。她曾于1911年和1934年两次前往中国。那些经历在各种刊物及信件往来中都有记载。不难看出，她的中国之行，她对中华文明和文化价值的接纳，以及她对当代社会生活的洞见极大程度地影响了她的美学理念。中国激发了她的审美觉醒，也对同时期其他的诗歌作品产生了普遍影响。在对上述内容进行探讨的过程中，本研究将揭示，门罗对中国的浓厚兴趣对于挑战二十世纪的民族主义范式、促进现代文学的跨国及世界性地位至关重要。 在阐明门罗的文学兴趣是如何在旅行与跨文化实验的背景下产生的同时，本项目将密切关注 美国出版商和作家受东西方地缘政治事件影响的具体方式。在此期间，门罗通过书信与驻中国的著名外交官与金融家频繁互动交流，由此，她对美国人如何概念化中国的历史转型及西方政治经济干预与该转型的关系有了深刻理解。阐明这一历史背景，将影响我们对这一时期诞生的文学文本的理解，将塑造我们的文学文化理论，将强调文学文化的诞生与特定的政治经济背景的紧密关联。在评估门罗中国之旅的社会意义的同时，本项目将突出其作为一名作家和编辑的重要性，并强调她对中国的极大兴趣具有怎样的广泛历史意义。最终的研究结果将通过学术出版物进行传播，涵盖两篇期刊论文，三篇会议论文及一部阐述门罗、其中国之行及其对现代主义文学的影响的专著。

11603319.label: Realisation of objectives
11603319.value: The first objective of this project was realized through my research into Monroe’s writings and interest in Asian cultures and aesthetics, which I examined in relation to a wider historical and political context. A key point that I discuss in my book is how Monroe viewed her publication strategy as an ‘Open Door Policy,” a phrase that resonates with the American political position on China and Asia generally. Here I make the case that the geopolitical context of America in Asia -- one that valued the free flow of capital and commodities -- informed her editorial position and the way that she viewed the circulation of literature and poetry. Monroe’s travels to China provide insights into America’s evolving interest in Asian aesthetics, one that has consequences on the development of literary publishing, but it also reveals how the wider political context of China’s historical changes after 1912 converge with Progressive-era notions of cultural and social reform that were reliant on ideas of competition and open markets. The project has also been largely successful in terms of achieving the second main objective which involves investigating how Monroe’s contacts and connections with American residents in China informed her editorial praxis. For example, in my book I describe Monroe’s correspondence with Oriental art collector and industrialist Charles Freer, someone she had met in Beijing and with whom she developed a friendship. By referring to this relationship, and the letters exchanged between Monroe and Freer, I show that it was through individuals like Freer that Monroe was able to establish Poetry Magazine, as the business elite – especially those based in Chicago - recognized the value of promoting globally-orientated and distinctly cosmopolitan cultural work. In terms of the third main objective, the project facilitated my research on Monroe’s influence and status as an author and editor. By describing Monroe’s editorial work the project reveals how she viewed literature and poetry as ‘built’ through collaborations and networks rather than through the creative work of individuals in isolation. While the focus of this research project was on Monroe’s connections with Asian cultures and aesthetics, the work that I have published also reveals how her interests in literary publishing were economically grounded and based on ideas of ‘audience’ as a formative influence. This aspect of Monroe's editorial work is described in the article that I wrote for the journal 'English Studies'. The research that I have conducted helps to further establish and illustrate Monroe’s influential role as a literary editor and how she played a key intermediary role. In terms of the fourth main object, the project provided some insights into a larger context of modern poetry during the period. For example, as I discuss Monroe’s role as an editor of 'Poetry', I show that her interest in translations of modern Chinese contrasts with the more fashionable Western interest in ‘ideographic’ Chinese aesthetics during the period. This research shows that Monroe recognized the changing cultural landscape of China and did not fixate on classical Chinese poetry and the visual aesthetics of Imagism (or what Western poets and sinologists believed to be essentially Chinese); instead, she chose to publish translated works of a less formal and more loquacious vernacular style. Furthermore, her descriptions of historical change in China contributes to a worldview that acknowledges the transmission of artistic influences across national and political borders. In this sense, the project has revealed an aspect of literary history that has previously been unrecognized.

11603319.label: Major findings and research outcome
11603319.value: While the initial aim of the project was to publish a book that outlines Monroe’s professional contributions to modernism and her interactions with China, the result was a book with a wider scope that focuses on other authors and travellers of the period who also visited or chose to reside in China during the early 20th century. In this book I dedicate a chapter to Monroe's writings on China where I describe her journeys to Asia and how her impressions of China informed her poetics and worldview. As I conducted further research on Monroe I published one article on her travels to China in the journal English Studies. The outcome of this research, therefore, can be viewed in terms of how the project sheds light on Monroe’s status in literary history, but also in terms of a wider scope of British and American authors who developed connections with China during the period. Through a detailed examination of Monroe’s writings, the project reveals how literary cultures emerged as a result of Monroe’s business-minded entrepreneurship, her knowledge of a changing print media landscape, and her interest in the ethics of progressive-era social reform. This view of Monroe’s pragmatism and sensitivity to changing social trends and demographics challenges the view that twentieth-century literature was driven by the experimentation of the avant-garde, and shows that as writers and poets struggled to innovate and subvert the cultural norms, the literary editor played a key intermediary role. Monroe’s travels to China were formative in terms of developing her worldview and her conception of poetry as always ‘in the world’, multifaceted, and capable of crossing linguistic and national boundaries.

11603319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11603319.value: I plan to continue my research on Monroe and hope to write an extended biography of her one day. I am particularly interested in how Monroe’s understanding of poetry and literary publishing was informed by modern notions of audience and media, a view that contrasts sharply with the 19th century Romantic notion of individual authorship and creative genius. At the same time, there are strands of research that I hope to continue working on and developing that are more generally focused on America’s evolving interest in Asia during the early twentieth century.
