11603819.label: Realisation of objectives
11603819.value: The three objectives for this project have been fully achieved. This project aimed to investigate anxiety in learning English as a foreign language (EFL) among Chinese Children and its links with parental literacy beliefs and practices. Concerning objectives one and two, our team developed a battery of tests and scales to assess EFL anxiety and ability, and parental literacy beliefs and practices. Test items of EFL anxiety and ability and related linguistic and cognitive skills with difficulty level suitable to primary school children were constructed. They assessed word reading, vocabulary knowledge, reading comprehension, phonological awareness, and nonverbal cognitive ability. They differentiated children with higher or lower ability/level in these variables. These tests were administered on 257 primary school second graders in Hong Kong. The results showed great individual variations of EFL anxiety levels among the children, with some children having noticeably low anxiety while some children having considerably high anxiety. Also, EFL anxiety was negatively linked to English language ability in children. In addition, parental literacy practices were negatively linked to and parental language anxiety was positively correlated with children’s EFL anxiety. Concerning objective three, our team devised a parent-child reading intervention supporting parents to engage in English shared book reading with their children. We designed the shared reading materials which supported the parents to engage in dialogic reading with their children, promoting a supportive environment for English language acquisition in children. This intervention was designed with an awareness of the varying English proficiency levels among parents. The use of storybooks with audio-recordings of the stories, and the training which encouraged the parents to use their language repertoire when reading with their children, supported the engagement of parents with different English proficiency levels. Our team produced tailor-made training materials and held training workshops for parents. There were 168 families recruited. The participating families were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions (dialogic reading, typical parent-child reading, and control). We administered pre-test and post-test of EFL anxiety and ability to the participating children. We evaluated the dialogic reading and parent-child reading effects by comparing children’s EFL anxiety and ability across the three conditions. The results showed the potential of dialogic reading on reducing EFL anxiety in children. The research experience of this study has provided important insights into developing effective family intervention for enhancing children’s learning in English as a foreign language. Overall, this project has advanced our knowledge of the anxiety in learning English as a foreign language among Chinese Children and the underlying factors contributing to it.

11603819.label: Major findings and research outcome
11603819.value: A number of important findings, leading to several journal publications and conference papers, have been obtained from this project. Major findings and research outcomes are summarized below. Firstly, this project developed a set of tests and scales assessing language anxiety and ability in Chinese children, and indicated the individual variations of English language anxiety and ability levels in these children (Chow, 2021; Chow 2023). Secondly, it identified factors fundamental to EFL anxiety (Chow, 2023; Chow, Mo & Dong, 2021). Specifically, parental literacy practices were negatively linked to and parental EFL anxiety was positively correlated with children’s EFL anxiety (Chow, 2023). Thirdly, this project showed the important roles of home literacy environment, including parent-child reading, on children’s acquisition of English as a second language (Dong & Chow, 2022). Overall, the findings of this project have provided prominent insights into the ways to enhance effective foreign language learning through reducing EFL anxiety in children.

11603819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11603819.value: The findings and the outcomes of this project have laid an important ground for development of future research on children’s development in English as a foreign language. This project has provided empirical evidence on the important roles of home literacy environment in EFL anxiety in Chinese children. While more is known about adolescents’ and adults’ foreign language anxiety, there have been limited studies on children’s foreign language anxiety and its underlying factors. The extent to which various home literacy environment factors influencing children’s foreign language anxiety is unclear. Our findings support the development of future research which compares language anxiety of children with different linguistic backgrounds. Also, the project produced a set of parent-child reading materials supporting foreign language learning in children. These materials can be adapted to different language combinations in further research. In addition, the intervention will be refined based on the findings and the experience of this project for future large-scale randomised controlled trial, involving a wider community of families with children learning English as a foreign language.

11603819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11603819.value: Foreign language acquisition is increasingly a key milestone for children in many countries. As foreign language learners are acquiring a language that they rarely use in daily conversation, they often perform less competently in it than in their native language, which can cause foreign language anxiety. This study addressed important issues regarding children’s anxiety in learning English as a foreign language (EFL) and its underlying factors. In this study, we indicated individual variations in EFL anxiety in Chinese children and the extent to which parental literacy beliefs and practices played a role in these variations. Also, we showed that parent-child reading contributed to reducing EFL anxiety in Chinese children. The findings have offered important insights into the development of accurate assessments of children’s anxiety in foreign language learning and effective interventions. They will also inform education policy on how schools could work with parents to ease children’s foreign language anxiety. Overall, the findings from this study can potentially help parents, educators and practitioners better understand the affective aspects of foreign language learning in children, and the ways to enhance effective foreign language learning through reducing foreign language anxiety in children.

11604419.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11604419.value: This research explores the role of the Public Works Department (PWD), the official agency responsible for the design of governmental buildings, in shaping architectural modernism in colonial Hong Kong. Since its establishment in the 1870s, the PWD, led by architects from Britain, had built many impressive public buildings in the idiom of classical architecture. Notably, in the 1930s the PWD abandoned the classical style prevailing in not only governmental but also private buildings sponsored by Western businesspeople at that time. Instead, the PWD experimented with new design ideas in public buildings such as markets and schools, making them the earliest examples of modernist architecture in Hong Kong. What prompted the PWD to shift its architectural thinking? After World War II, civilian construction in Hong Kong ground to a halt due to a shortage of private funding. The PWD, the major patron of architecture during the postwar rehabilitation period, decided to embrace modernist design in almost all governmental buildings. How did this decision change the architectural culture of Hong Kong? Through the study of the buildings undertaken by the PWD, this research attempts to dismantle the two mainstream discourses that have prevented us from creating a critical historiography of modernist architecture in colonial Hong Kong. The “alien discourse” suggests that architectural modernism was not indigenous to non-Western societies, so modernist architecture in Hong Kong and other European colonies was simply the dissemination or mimicry of the colonizers’ architectural inventions. This discourse ignores the fact that the PWD started designing modernist buildings in Hong Kong in the 1930s, when architectural modernism was still a matter of significant debate among architects in Britain. On the other hand, the “progressive discourse” considers modernist architecture, with a philosophy based on rationality, efficiency, and functionality, as the natural choice for contemporary lives. Every city with a vigorous economy would eventually adopt modernist architecture, and Hong Kong was no exception. In fact, the rehabilitation of Hong Kong after the war imposed an enormous financial burden on the colonial government. The PWD’s decision to construct modernist buildings, which required modest capital expenditures, was a thoughtful response to postwar social conditions and financial realities. The significance of this research is that it will provide the historical contexts that explain the advent and rapid dominance of architectural modernism in Hong Kong and acknowledge the PWD’s contributions to this process.

11604419.label: Realisation of objectives
11604419.value: All project objectives have been successfully met. Regarding objective 1, the project team undertook comprehensive historical research to understand the historical context, socio-political conditions, and financial realities in Hong Kong that precipitated the emergence and swift ascendancy of architectural modernism. This involved examining government reports and publications, archival documents, colonial office records, and correspondence among government departments. Furthermore, historical newspaper articles and architectural journals provided invaluable insights. Through these sources, the project team was able to chart the socio-economic development of Hong Kong during the 20th century. Our findings indicate that the introduction of modern architecture to Hong Kong was a direct consequence of the city’s economic crisis during the interwar period. The aftermath of the First World War (WWI) severely disrupted international trade, leading to an unstable supply of food and consumer goods in Hong Kong and a marked increase in the cost of living. The combination of elevated living costs and stagnant wages brought about economic hardship for the residents of Hong Kong. Their grievances, fuelled by the growing anti-imperialism sentiment in China, culminated in strikes and boycotts during the 1920s. Economic difficulties continued into the 1930s, exacerbated by the global Great Depression and political unrest in China. During this interwar period, the PWD constructed most public buildings within stringent budgets. Extensive use of reinforced concrete became a hallmark of this era, reducing construction costs and significantly altering building design. Elaborate embellishments common in traditional government buildings were impractical with this material. The neutral appearance of modern architecture, devoid of associations with Western classical styles, additionally helped to avoid triggering anti-imperialist sentiments amongst the population of Hong Kong. This shift in the PWD’s architectural preferences signalled a transition from traditional to modern design. Regarding objective 2, the project team conducted extensive research to explore the debates, ideas, and discourses that underlie architectural modernism in Hong Kong. We analysed architectural journals specific to Hong Kong, such as the Hong Kong and South China Builder, the Hong Kong and Far East Builder, and the Far East Architect & Builder. Additionally, we scrutinised historic newspaper reports published in both Chinese and English. Our findings unveil an intriguing trend concerning the architectural exchange between Hong Kong and Shanghai. Local newspapers, such as the South China Morning Post (SCMP), started to cover the design and construction of new and modern architecture in foreign countries during the late 1920s and 1930s. Interestingly, the SCMP reported more frequently on modern-styled buildings constructed in Shanghai than in Europe, the birthplace of the Modern Movement in architecture. The development of modern architecture in Shanghai captured the attention of architects and government officials in Hong Kong. M. H. Logan, a senior partner of the architectural firm Palmer and Turner, conveyed his admiration for the architectural booms and modernisation in Shanghai during an interview with the SCMP, and called for Hong Kong to reform its architectural practices. The Chair of the Urban Council, R. R. Todd, directed PWD architects to use the modern Shanghai markets as references when designing the Central Market in Hong Kong. However, modern architecture did not gain acceptance in Hong Kong without criticism. In 1930, PWD architect C. E. Moore delivered a series of six public lectures on the topic of ‘modern architecture’ for the University Engineering Society of the University of Hong Kong. Moore observed that new and modern architecture seemed to be heading in the wrong direction as it had lost all connection with the masterpieces of the past. He criticised the modern era, arguing that ‘utility’ had become the essential factor in building design, often at the expense of the finest principles of beauty. Regarding objective 3, the project team undertook a thorough analysis to investigate the organisation and personnel of the PWD, as well as the governmental policies and procedures pertaining to the creation of public buildings. Our study included annual departmental reports from the Director of Public Works, official PWD publications, records of the Legislative Council proceedings, and documents from other governmental bodies—such as the Urban Council and the Education Department—who were clients and users of the public buildings in focus. In 1844, the government reformed the role of Land Officer to Surveyor General, tasked with overseeing the construction of basic infrastructure and managing land registration and auctions. The Surveyor General headed the Surveyor General’s Department, which was transformed into the PWD in 1892. Since all public works necessitated the use of public funds, a Public Works Committee was established under the Legislative Council in 1884 to vet any plans for constructing new government buildings. By 1915, the PWD was organised into seven subdepartments, with the Architectural and Maintenance of Buildings branch (AMB) specifically created to design and construct new government buildings, as well as to refurbish and maintain existing ones. Over the next two decades, the number of PWD subdepartments gradually increased to between 10 and 14, with the AMB being renamed the Architectural Office (AO) in 1924. The AO continued to be the subdepartment responsible for building design until it was reorganised into the Architectural Services Department in 1986. Regarding objective 4, the project team has gathered and scrutinised numerous architectural drawings of modern government buildings designed by the PWD. These drawings are presently archived at the Public Records Office and the Architectural Services Department. Additionally, the project team has produced cartographic records for the selected buildings to facilitate design analysis. Our research reveals that the PWD began experimenting with modern building designs in the 1930s. A select number of government buildings, many of which were public markets, adopted the styles of Striped Classicism or Streamline Moderne. However, following the Second World War, there was a profound shift in the design ethos. The PWD moved away from the streamlined appearance of buildings and instead adopted a modernist design philosophy, characterised by rectangular building shapes with asymmetrical planning and façade designs. This shift towards modernist forms was significantly influenced by functional planning considerations.

11604419.label: Major findings and research outcome
11604419.value: The project unveils three main findings that illuminate the emergence and dominance of architectural modernism in Hong Kong, attributing this transformation to technological, economic, and cultural shifts. Firstly, the introduction of reinforced concrete in the 1880s for the construction of floor and roof slabs signified a departure from the neoclassical and Edwardian styles traditionally employed by the PWD. By 1910, the PWD had erected two piers entirely from reinforced concrete, fostering a minimalist aesthetic that diverged from earlier ornamental designs. This transition, detailed in the PI’s book ‘Everyday Architecture in Context’, was epitomised by the construction of the Western Market (South Block) in 1913, after which classical idioms were largely forsaken. Secondly, the economic recessions following the First World War significantly influenced the PWD’s direction, steering it towards minimalist design and the use of concrete for its economic and practical benefits. Financial constraints in the aftermath of the Second World War (WWII) further limited budget allocations for new government buildings. Consequently, the PWD adopted modernist designs for nearly all governmental structures in Hong Kong. This pragmatic approach, which prioritised functionality and cost-effectiveness over elaborate embellishments, reflected the social conditions and financial realities of the post-war rehabilitation period. The PI explores this evolution in the article ‘Too New, Too Ugly, and Too Unimportant?’, emphasising the utilitarian and minimalist yet heritage-rich nature of modern buildings. This viewpoint was also shared in a column in the Hong Kong Economic Journal, advocating for a deeper appreciation of Hong Kong’s modern architectural legacy. Lastly, the influence of global architectural trends, especially the Streamline Moderne movement from 1930s Shanghai, significantly impacted the design of Hong Kong’s public buildings. The Central Market, completed in 1939, serve as a notable example of this influence, as discussed in ‘Everyday Architecture in Context’. Following WWII, the Public Works Department (PWD) wholeheartedly embraced modernist principles, favouring simple, cuboid building forms with asymmetrical façades dominated by horizontal lines and functional layouts. These designs deliberately eschewed connections with Western classical motifs, thereby sidestepping any anti-imperialist criticisms. The City Hall, completed in 1962, stands as a pivotal example of the modern architectural aesthetic and the civicness it embodied. This transition, marked by the PWD’s responsiveness to both economic and cultural shifts, will be explored further by the PI in an upcoming presentation at the North American Conference on British Studies in November 2024.

11604419.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11604419.value: The research holds significant potential for further development along three distinct pathways. A comparative analysis with other British colonies could offer insights into both global and local factors that have shaped the modernisation of colonial architecture. By examining various colonial contexts, this approach may uncover unique adaptations and innovations in architectural strategies, potentially providing a broader understanding of how modernism evolved within colonial settings. Moreover, exploring the architectural dialogue between Hong Kong and Shanghai unveils another rich avenue for investigation. This inquiry could reveal the extent of mutual influences and shared innovations, offering a deeper comprehension of the regional dynamics that contributed to the development of architectural modernism. Furthermore, a focused exploration of the adoption and impact of reinforced concrete in Hong Kong promises to shed light on a pivotal moment in the city’s architectural history. This research could elucidate how reinforced concrete not only revolutionised building practices and aesthetics but also came to symbolise modernity in construction, significantly shaping the architectural landscape. Each of these pathways offers a distinct yet interconnected route to enhance our understanding of Hong Kong’s architectural transformation, contributing significantly to the broader field of architectural studies.

11604419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11604419.value: This research illuminates the crucial role played by the Public Works Department (PWD) in steering the architectural evolution of colonial Hong Kong towards modernism. Motivated by technological advancements, economic constraints, and cultural shifts, the PWD transitioned from the neoclassical styles that had been prevalent since the 1840s to modernist architecture in the 1930s, a move that was notably progressive even by British standards. The widespread adoption of reinforced concrete from the 1910s, the economic challenges following the wars, and the influence of global architectural trends prompted the PWD to embrace minimalist, functional, and cost-effective designs for government buildings. This shift from ornate traditional styles to pragmatic modernist ones was in line with contemporary needs and financial realities. Following the Second World War, the PWD’s wholehearted commitment to modern design cemented its status as the dominant architectural style in Hong Kong for the ensuing decades. Contrary to the perception of mere Western imitation, this research underscores how local conditions and influences uniquely moulded Hong Kong’s architectural modernism. Beyond the minimalist facades of modern buildings lay thoughtful considerations of post-war social conditions and fiscal realities.

11605519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11605519.value: For decades, economists have debated the proper role of government in the economy. The helping-hand model of government considers government intervention an effective way to cure market failures while the grabbing hand model holds a skeptical view of government intervention in economic development. Corporations operate in an institutional environment determined by the political, social and economic conditions of a country. Political interference over corporate decision-making can significantly affect corporate governance and firm performance. The helping-hand hypothesis posits that shareholders benefit from close ties with the government by receiving tax subsidies, borrowing from state-owned banks at a preferential term and/or being bailed out by the government during financial difficulty. In contrast, the grabbing-hand hypothesis argues that strong government ties hurt shareholders because government officials and politicians influence firms to allocate resources not to benefit shareholders, but to reward their political supporters. This project plans to examine which model best explains Chinese firms, which operate under state capitalism, where the state influences the resource allocation of economic activities and the decision-making of major corporations. To test the models, we intend to make use of the recent Dangjian (party building) reform—a major measure undertaken by the Chinese Communist Party since 2016 to solidify its leadership position in state-owned enterprises (SOEs). By utilizing this exogenous event, we have the chance that rarely available in the past to examine the causal inference of political control over corporate governance and firm performance. In addition to SOEs, our project also examines the impact of party building reform to privately owned enterprises (POEs) who voluntarily incorporated party organizations into their internal governance system. Furthermore, the subject of research covers not only Chinese A-share listed companies but also Chinese companies that listed on overseas stock exchanges, such as those in the U.S., Hong Kong and Singapore. The research result will further the understanding of the extent to which and the channels through which the state intervenes in the business decision of Chinese firms and how political intervention impacts firm performance. Finally, we seek to provide policy suggestions to regulators and stock exchanges as to the governance and investor protection of Chinese firms. 長期以來，經濟學家們都在爭論政府在經濟中的作用。政府的援助之手假說認為政府干預是解決市場失靈的有效途徑，而掠奪之手假說卻對政府干預經濟發展持懷疑態度。而對於公司，由於其所處的制度環境是由一個國家的政治、社會和經濟條件共同決定的，政府對公司決策的政治干預會顯著影響其治理以及績效表現。援助之手假說認為股東通過接受稅收補貼、從國有銀行以優惠條件借貸以及在財政困難時接受政府救助等手段而受益於他們與政府的密切關係。相反，掠奪之手假說認為公司與政府的緊密關聯損害了股東的利益。政府官員和政治家在影響公司的資源配置時更有動機獎勵他們的政治支持者，而不是使股東受益。在中國大陸，政府所推行的國家資本主義制度使得國家能夠影響經濟活動中的資源配置以及大型（主要是國有）企業的決策。本研究計畫旨在探討何種假說更能合理解釋中國企業的現狀。 我們計畫以近期的黨的建設改革為背景來驗證兩個假說。此一改革措施是中國共產黨自2016年以來為鞏固其在國有企業中的領導地位而採取的一項重要舉措。通過利用此一外生事件來驗證政治控制與公司治理以及企業績效之間的因果推論。除了國有企業，我們的研究還考察了黨的建設改革對那些自願將黨組織納入其內部治理體系的民營企業的影響。此外，我們的研究對象不僅包括中國的A股上市公司，還包括在海外證券交易所如美國、香港和新加坡上市的中國公司。本研究並將進一步瞭解國家干預企業經營決策的程度和途徑，以及政治干預對企業績效的影響。最後，我們將試圖就中國企業的公司治理和投資者保護議題，向監管機構和證券交易所提供政策性建議。

11605519.label: Realisation of objectives
11605519.value: We have achieved all five goals set out in the proposal through a series of empirical research. The team has published four journal papers and created a complete dataset on the level of political control of all 3,446 Chinese listed companies. To ascertain the level of political control over Chinese firms (Objective 1), we make use of the Dangjian (party building) reform—a major measure undertaken by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to solidify its leadership position in state-owned enterprises (SOEs). The reform requires SOEs to amend their corporate charters to formally adopt party committees as part of the corporate internal governance system. We collected data on firms that adopted the amendments and relevant charter provisions and assessed the effect of the overall reform and the specific impact of different governance provisions. The following four papers are our major research output: 1. Christopher Chen, Re-Jin Guo, and Lauren Yu-Hsin Lin*, The Effect of Political Influence on Corporate Valuation: Evidence from Party-Building Reform in China, 73 International Review of Law and Economics 106120 (2023). 2. Lauren Yu-Hsin Lin and Curtis Milhaupt*, Party Building or Noisy Signaling? The Contours of Political Conformity in Chinese Corporate Governance, 50(1) Journal of Legal Studies 187-217 (2021). 3. Lauren Yu-Hsin Lin*, Institutionalizing Political Influence in Business: Party-Building and Insider Control in Chinese State-Owned Enterprises, 45 Vermont Law Review 441-480 (2021). 4. Christopher Chen and Lauren Yu-Hsin Lin, Foreign Political Interference in the Governance of Listed Companies: A Market and Behavioral Analysis, 31 Duke Journal of Comparative and International Law 301-349 (2021). To identify firms that amended their articles of association in response to the dangjian policy, we searched the disclosure documents of all 3,446 non-financial A-share listed Chinese companies. During the four-year period, we found that 1,046 non-financial A-share listed firms formally wrote party organizations into their articles. We manually collected and hand-coded corporate charter provisions relating to party-building according to the model provisions published by SASAC on January 7, 2017. We built a database of corporate charter amendments including the date of amendment and specific party-building provisions adopted by each firm (Objective 4). In Paper 1, PI and Co-I Prof. Chris Chen estimate the market response to the party-building charter amendments and compare the effect on SOEs vs non-SOEs (Objective 3). Recognizing that ownership might not be a perfect proxy for party-state influence, we refine the analysis by using firms’ response to the amendment request as a proxy for the level of political influence on firms. In the hazard analysis, we explore the channels through which state exercises control and influence over firms (Objective 2). In Paper 2, PI and Co-I Prof. Curtis Milhaupt investigate the differences in political influence between state-owned enterprises and privately-owned enterprises and examine the characteristics of firms that adopted different sets of provisions. This paper empirically ascertains the level of political control over different types of firms and portrays the landscape of political control in Chinese corporate governance (Objective 1, 2, and 3). In Paper 3, PI explores the shareholders’ voting response to the amendment and develops an account of political renegotiation during the power struggle process by presenting the evidence of multiple amendments in several SOEs. This paper also helps to delineate the path towards amendments and relevant stakeholders’ response to such a widespread governance change. Through this exercise, this paper fulfils Objective 1, 2 and 3. In Paper 4, we discovered the channels through which the state exercises control over firms (Objective 2) and estimate the level of political control over Chinese firms listing on overseas stock exchanges, including those in Hong Kong (Objective 5).

11605519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11605519.value: Close observation of the party-building campaign provides insights into the complex terrain the Chinese party-state must navigate to achieve its policy objectives via corporations it ostensibly controls. Chinese state capitalism is a distinctive species of corporate capitalism. But our research reveals that the corporate form embeds a system of organizational governance norms that are in considerable tension with control by a political party. Particularly because many of China’s most important SOEs are publicly listed companies with substantial non-state shareholdings, the party-state’s demand for political conformity is constrained not only by agency problems but also by market discipline and the dictates of the corporate law. Our research on responses to the dangjian policy raises a number of important legal and policy questions for China’s domestic economy and external economic relations. Domestically, it remains to be seen whether mandated political involvement in corporate governance will affect firm performance and economic dynamism. This will depend on how assiduously the party-building charter amendments are complied with and enforced. Externally, the question is whether this effort to formalize the role of the Chinese Communist Party in corporate governance will exacerbate suspicions of Chinese foreign direct investment around the world.

11605919.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11605919.value: The recent discourse of Confucian constitutionalism in the context of modern East Asia has several interesting features if we approach it in comparison with the ongoing theoretical debate among Western political and constitutional theorists. First, Western liberal theorists are mainly concerned with the normative status of judicial review (and the constitutional court) in relation to democracy, whereas Confucians pay special attention to the constitutional reform of the legislature or establishment of the Constitutional Academy that is independent of, or superior to, the three main branches of government. Second, Western theorists are divided roughly into two camps, one defending legal (rights-based) constitutionalism and the other championing (republican) political constitutionalism, whereas Confucian theorists appear nearly unified in their emphasis on the constraint of popular sovereignty and the democratic authority of the legislature. Third, despite their shared interest in counter-majoritarianism and similar valorization of the substantive outcomes of the democratic process, legal constitutionalists are concerned about the substance of liberal rights enshrined in the constitution (or moral principles such as the ideal of human dignity), whereas Confucian constitutionalists are interested in goods thought to be vital for the people’s well-being. Finally, in securing the substances they valorize, although legal constitutionalists consider the court to be the core institution for this constitutional task, Confucian constitutionalists working in political philosophy pay virtually no attention to the court, leaving law completely displaced in their constitutional theories. This project explores the Confucian theory of political constitutionalism, which follows the emphasis of the existing proposals of Confucian constitutionalism—in general, Confucian meritocratic constitutionalism—on the people’s well-being, while securing this fundamental good in such a way as to achieve both procedural and substantive justice under the circumstances of modern politics marked by pluralism and disagreement. More specifically, this project aims to construct Confucian democratic constitutionalism as a mode of constitutionalism that is best suited for Confucian democracy and pragmatically justified under modern political circumstances in East Asia. It has two central aims: first, to provide a firm moral foundation for constitutional democracy in East Asia with reference to Confucianism, and second, to determine the constitutional institutions and practices that are best suited for the Confucian and democratic contexts. 如果与西方政治和宪法理论家中现有的讨论相比较，最近有关现代东亚语境下的儒家宪政讨论有几个有趣的特征。首先，西方自由派学者主要关注司法审查（和宪法法院）在民主政体中的规范地位，而儒家则特别关注立法机构的宪法改革或如何建立独立于政府三个主要分支之外的宪法学院。其次，西方理论家大致分为两个阵营，一个是捍卫法律（基于权利的）宪政主义，另一个是支持共和主义的政治宪政主义，而儒家宪政学者几乎一致强调对于人民主权和民主权力的宪法约束。第三，尽管他们都反多数主义并希望保证民主进程中的实质结果，法律宪政主义者主要关注的实质结果是基于宪法中所载的自由权利（或是道德中所载的基本原则，比如人权），而儒家宪政主义者则非常在意对人民福祉至关重要的事物。最后，在保护他们所追求的权益时，法律宪政主义者认为法院是执行这项宪法任务的核心机构，但是从事政治哲学工作的儒家宪政主义者几乎从不关注法院，以致他们的宪法理论中有关司法的讨论基本不存在。这个课题目的在于探讨儒家的政治宪政理论。它遵循儒家宪政主义现有提案（广义的儒家贤能宪政主义）中对于人民福祉的重视，同时它确保这一基本利益的实现路径在多元且充满分歧的现代政治环境中也符合程序与实质正义。具体地说，本课题旨在将儒家民主宪政主义重构为一种最适合儒家民主且适应东亚现代政治环境的宪政模式。它有两个核心目标：第一，为东亚宪政民主提供系于儒家思想的道德基础;第二，确立最适合儒家和民主语境的宪法制度和实践。

11605919.label: Realisation of objectives
11605919.value: This research has produced one single-authored monograph titled Confucian Constitutionalism: Dignity, Rights, and Democracy (OUP 2023) and three research papers (please see the publications attached). All four key aims of this research have been fully achieved through the publication of my book, which consists of six main chapters. In Chapter 1, I trace the recent bifurcation of Confucian political and constitutional theorists into two competing camps to their differing accounts of human dignity in Confucianism: human dignity as achievement, which is unequally distributed based on one’s virtue, and human dignity as moral potential, which is equally possessed by all humans. Though Confucian meritocrats have strong classical support for the inegalitarian ideal of dignity from both Mencius and especially Xunzi, two ancient Confucian masters with contrasting accounts of human nature, I argue that the inegalitarian ideal of dignity is fundamentally incompatible with the principle of “equal protection of rights before law,” which virtually all Confucian meritocrats take for granted. After showing how Xunzi’s political theory can also support egalitarian human dignity, I then establish two foundational rights of Confucian democratic constitutionalism—the equal right to political participation and the equal right to protection of constitutional rights—and present them as the underlying normative values of the dignity of legislation and the authority of the court, respectively. Chapter 2 turns to the recent liberal critics’ challenge to the moral legitimacy of Confucian democracy from a pluralist standpoint. According to liberal critics, any attempt to justify Confucian democracy in mediation of Confucian perfectionism inevitably confronts a dilemma—the pluralism dilemma as I call it—between its embrace of pluralism and its perfectionist promotion of Confucianism. In this chapter, I defend Confucian democracy against this pluralist challenge. While appreciating the challenge’s call to take pluralism seriously, I argue that rejecting the argument for Confucian democracy based on a liberal analytic philosophical formula does serious injustice to the political purpose of Confucian democracy as has been pursued by scholars in East Asia (and beyond) during and after the third wave of democratization. The chapter proceeds by pointing out how the liberal critics’ Rawls-inspired understanding of “comprehensive doctrine” fails to note the important practical distinction between partial and full comprehensive doctrines, how their formal distinction between “Confucian citizens” and “non-Confucians” with regard to the justifiability of Confucian democracy is misguided, and why their charge of oppression of or discrimination against non-Confucians is overstated. In Chapter 3, I defend and rearticulate what I call in my earlier work public reason Confucianism, a mode of Confucian democratic perfectionism in which a special style of public reason is affiliated with partially comprehensive Confucianism (i.e., civic Confucianism), as best suited to deal with moral disagreement. Central to public reason Confucianism is that while encouraging citizens to cultivate public reasons with reference to Confucian mores, rituals, civilities, and moral sentiments in which they are still embedded, despite holding diverse moral and religious doctrines as private individuals, it promotes active public participation and deliberation in making important public decisions that affect all in a way consistent with the principle of egalitarian dignity. The result is what I call “democratic pluralism,” pluralism accommodated by democratic public reasons, and public reason Confucianism defends democratic pluralism as the most desirable way to come to terms with pluralism and disagreement in an East Asian constitutional democracy. In short, Chapter 3 addresses the political implications of the “vertical” interaction between partially comprehensive civic Confucianism and democratic values, principles, and institutions under the condition of moral disagreement. In Chapter 4, I argue that the argument for the meritocratic house renders lawmaking a mere instrument for the regime’s performance legitimacy or mainly in service of the goods external to the moral value of lawmaking itself. After highlighting the pivotal importance of the people’s political right to participate in the most authoritative public decisions, which are concerned with the legitimate coordination of their complex social, economic, and political interactions, I contend that one can begin to talk about the dignity of legislation in a Confucian polity only if the polity in question is a constitutional democracy that acknowledges the independent moral worth of political equality and the right to political participation. My central claim in this chapter is twofold: first, that the politics of public reason Confucianism makes legislation dignified and centrally important in a Confucian constitutional democracy, and second, that in Confucian constitutional democracy, the dignity of legislation is expressed in terms of (1) respect of human dignity and plurality, (2) trust-building political relationship, (3) protection of minorities, and (4) the constitutional power to impeach high-level public officials including the head of the state. The central aim of Chapter 5 is to illuminate the general nature of Confucian democratic constitutionalism as a normative political theory predicated on what I call weak well-being consequentialism. First, Confucian democratic constitutionalism is distinguished from Confucian meritocratic constitutionalism. Resting on strong well-being consequentialism, Confucian meritocratic constitutionalism acknowledges no meaningful distinction between matters concerning rights and moral principles and matters pertaining to well-being and public policy. Second, Confucian democratic constitutionalism is also distinguished from legal constitutionalism that is wary of the democratic legislature that operates on majoritarianism and, for this reason, prizes judicial review as the soul of constitutionalism. Confucian democratic constitutionalism understands the citizenry’s democratic self-government as its core and takes the democratic legislature as its driving engine, the venue where constitutional norms, values, and rights are deliberated and vetted in accordance with the procedures guided by the principle of egalitarian dignity. Finally, unlike political constitutionalism, however, Confucian democratic constitutionalism does not regard judicial review as anti-democratic and rather finds it conducive to the perfectionist side of Confucian democracy. In Chapter 6, I argue that Confucian democratic constitutionalism promotes active constitutional dialogue between the branches of the government, especially between the legislature and the court. The chapter consists of several core arguments. First, even though the equal right to political participation and the equal right to constitutional protection of other civil and political rights combine to constitute the normative foundation of Confucian democratic constitutionalism, it is important to note that the latter is derived from the former, giving the dignity of legislation more normative weight than the authority of the court. Second, the equal right to constitutional protection of rights gives the court the power of judicial review but this power is not absolute. Confucian democratic constitutionalism understands the court as a constitutional institution devoted to a cooperative search for the culturally relevant conception of rights through dialogue with the legislature who is more institutionally and effectively connected with the people, the ultimate source of political authority. Lastly, Confucian democratic constitutionalism promotes a weak-form judicial review not only in the sense that it actively promotes inter-institutional interactions between the legislature and the court toward a cooperative search for so-called “Confucian democratic rights,” but more importantly, because such interactions take a dialogic form in mediation of the Confucian public reasons of the people, which encourages both the legislature and the court to be in a constant and open-ended dialogue with civil society.

11605919.label: Major findings and research outcome
11605919.value: This research presents a constitutional theory of democratic self-government that is normatively appealing and politically practicable in East Asia’s historically Confucian societies that are increasingly pluralist, multicultural, and rights sensitive—namely, Confucian democratic constitutionalism. Inspired by early twentieth-century Confucian constitutionalists such as Liang Qichao and Liang Shuming who explored the self-government of the people in the Confucian soil, this book constructs a political theory in which democratic self-government and constitutional protection of rights are mutually constitutive and reinforcing. First, it presents egalitarian human dignity as the underlying moral value of Confucian constitutionalism. Then, it derives two foundational rights from the Confucian account of egalitarian human dignity—the equal right to political participation and the equal right to constitutional protection of civil and political rights—and shows how each of these rights justifies the establishment of the legislature and the judiciary respectively as two independent constitutional institutions equally committed to the protection and promotion of the people’s moral and material well-being, now reformulated in terms of rights. Special attention is paid to how regular and institutionalized dialogues between the legislature and the constitutional court in mediation of Confucian public reason can be conducive to an effective determination of rights and their legitimate protection, actualizing the people’s constitutional self-government under the circumstances of value pluralism and moral disagreement. Thus constructed, Confucian democratic constitutionalism is distinguished not only from Confucian meritocratic constitutionalism that rejects the ideal of democratic self-government but also from two dominant Western models of constitutionalism—liberal legal constitutionalism and political constitutionalism.

11605919.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11605919.value: This research has produced the first book-length research that integrates normative Confucian political theory and comparative constitutionalism into a coherent philosophical thesis. My book, the major output of this research, provides an important theoretical framework against which the normative argument for Confucian democracy and Confucian meritocracy can be critically evaluated with a view to building an institutional structure that can best enhance and protect the well-being of the people. This research will also offer a new set of future research projects, including the question of "power" in Confucian political theory, why Confucian meritocrats must be democrats, and Neo-Confucian constitutionalism. In fact, I've recently proposed a new book project (entitled "Power: A Confucian Theory") to Manchester University Press and I also have agreed with Oxford University Press to work on a sequel of "Confucian Constitutionalism" by focusing on how Confucian meritocrats can improve their normative argument by learning from Confucian democrats.

11605919.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11605919.value: This research aims to present a constitutional theory of democratic self-government that is normatively appealing and politically practicable in East Asia’s historically Confucian societies that are increasingly pluralist, multicultural, and rights sensitive—namely, Confucian democratic constitutionalism. Rather than pitting democratic self-government again constitutionalism, Confucian democratic constitutionalism offers an overarching and coherent normative perspective on the foundational moral worth or dignity of human being, as conceived by Confucianism, the rights it generates as the legally-entrenched moral entitlements by which people can protect their basic interests, and the legal and political institutions that safeguard such rights in a way that is consistent with Confucian values and moral reasoning.

11606719.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11606719.value: Using the case of transitioning Myanmar and its decades-old legacy of military involvement in politics, this project seeks to understand how nascent civilian institutions establish and consolidate mechanisms for the oversight of the armed forces under conditions of entrenched praetorianism – a situation where the military holds decisive influence over the political process. Have civilian agencies and elected representatives been able to effectively challenge the continuing dominance of the military in post-junta Myanmar? How have the resolutely interventionist armed forces responded to initial steps taken towards civilian control? What does it tell us about Myanmar’s trajectory of democratization, and the role of civilians in overseeing powerful militaries in Southeast Asia, and beyond? Capitalizing on the PI’s ongoing field research on military intervention and the resurgence of parliament in post-junta Myanmar, this GRF project focuses on the national legislature, crafted by the 2008 Constitution and tasked with the scrutiny of other government branches. It interrogates the legitimacy, viability, and achievements of the legislative organs in designing and employing procedures of oversight of the military since parliament reconvened in 2011. It will probe into the proposition that Myanmar’s nascent parliament and its members have attempted to challenge the dominance of the military whilst scrutinizing its activities, expenditures and behaviours. The study is guided by four interrelated research questions: (1) how effective has the annual legislative scrutiny of the defence budget proven to be; (2) has the ritual of parliamentary questions in the Union legislature offered a meaningful opportunity for backbenchers to expose military misconduct and forced the army into (re)action; (3) have legislative investigations been effectively carried out on matters related to military (mis)conduct – particularly land seizures – and if so, have these parliamentary inquiries yielded positive results; and (4) how have Myanmar’s armed forces responded to these above attempts at contesting its autonomy and reserved domains? The planned contribution of this project is twofold. First, informed by the political science literature on civilian control, the study hopes to enhance our theoretical grasp of the patterns of civil-military relations under uncertain army-driven transitions. Second, the PI will mine unexplored Myanmar-language material – i.e. proceedings of the first two “post-junta” legislatures (2011-16 and 2016-21) – to unearth empirical evidence of civilian control and assess the initial steps taken towards parliamentary oversight of the military. The analysis of legislative records will be refined through in-depth interviews with parliamentary and military officials in Yangon and Naypyidaw. 本研究以緬甸政權過渡及其數十年來軍人干政的歴史，探討在軍隊掌左右政治進程之影響力，根深蒂固的普力奪主義條件下，新生文官機構如何成立，並加強對武裝部隊的監管。文官機關及民選代表是否能有效地應向後緬甸軍政府的持續支配地位作出挑戰？強硬干預的武裝部隊怎樣回應文官政府？緬甸的民主進程，以及文官對東南亞及其他地區強大軍隊的監察角色又如何？ 充分利用首席研究員正進行有關軍方干政及後緬甸軍政府在議會復辟的研究，本項目著眼於2008年新憲法制定及自2011年重召的國會立法機關所設計及運用的軍事監督程序的合法性﹑可行性及績效作出審視。另亦探討緬甸新成立國會與其議員一方面試圖挑戰軍方統治，另一方面又仔細審查軍方的活動﹑開支及行為。 本文研究問題有四﹔〔一〕 如何有效地立法審議通過年度國防預算；〔二〕在例行的聯邦議會質詢有否提供真正的機會讓後座的議員揭露軍事人員的不當行為及強迫行動；〔三〕可否能透過立法有效調查有關涉及軍方﹙不當﹚行為，特別是徵用土地。如有，這些議會質詢都能取得正面效果；〔四〕 緬甸武裝部隊如何就他們的自主權和保留領土的企圖作出回應。 本研究預期會作出雙重貢獻：首先，從政治學文官掌控理論文獻基礎上，提升掌握有關軍方主導的不明朗過渡期軍民關係的模式。其次，首席研究員會拆解緬甸專用語『後軍政府』，發掘文官掌控的實證數據及評估國會監察軍隊的初步措施。透過與仰光和內比都的議會和軍方官員的深入訪談來完善立法記錄的分析。

11607319.label: Realisation of objectives
11607319.value: Objective 1: A total of 84 criminal cases were identified from China Judgements Online. The crimes committed in these cases took place between 2003 and 2018. A descriptive analysis of these cases was conducted to provide a background for ghost bride-induced crimes in China. Crimes committed. Among the 84 cases, some involved the commission of multiple crimes. More than 60% (66.7% and 61.9%) of these cases involved the stealing and trading of corpses. About one-tenth (9.5%) involved murder, attempted murder, or bodily harm. Five cases (6%) were related to tomb robbery. It is worth mentioning that two cases (2.4%) involved the kidnap of women and four cases (4.8%) involved the abuse of power or bribery of office-bearers working in institutions concerned (e.g. hospitals). The fact that only 84 cases were convicted in court over a 15-year period suggests this crime is either a very rare phenomenon or the chances of being arrested and prosecuted are extremely low. Number of criminals involved. In 29 cases (34.5%), only one criminal was involved, and two criminals were involved in about one-quarter (27.4%) of the cases. Another one-fifth of cases involved three to four criminals (10.7% each). Some criminal gangs were quite large, involving five people or more (16.8%). The average number of criminals per case was 2.7. Number of recidivists. About half of the 84 cases (48.8%) were committed by recidivists who had previously committed similar or multiple crimes related to ghost marriages. If a crime was committed by a group of criminals in any single case, we considered the case as committed by a “recidivist” when at least one of the criminals was recidivist. Corpses and victims. The 84 criminal cases involved 250 corpses (98.4%) and four living persons (1.6%) who were victims of the crime. Corpses are defined in the present study as the body of the dead, regardless of whether they are intact, including the remaining bones and bone ashes of the dead if they have been buried for a long time. Victims are defined as those living persons who are victimised for ghost marriages but exclude those victimised because of other causes. Gender. In terms of gender, the majority of the corpses were female (90.6%), and all four victims (100%) were female. To a certain extent, this reflects that the crimes committed were gender-specific, indicating the existence of a ghost bride market. Characteristics of corpses and victims. It is extremely difficult to determine the characteristics of corpses because these individuals are dead. However, in a limited number of cases, we were able to identify some characteristics of 37 corpses and 4 victims. Close to half (48.6%) were newly buried corpses, which were buried within a period of 6 months before the crime was committed. About a quarter of the corpses’ (27%) graves or residences were in the same neighbourhood as the criminal’s residence. For instance, they lived in the same or the next village. Seven corpses (18.9%) were relatives of criminals. All four living persons who were victimised lacked the ability to protect themselves, such as children or the mentally retarded. Locations of demand and supply. Of the 84 cases, 83 mentioned the provinces where the crimes were committed, and 67 cases mentioned where the corpses were required for ghost marriages. Based on this information, we can construct the demand and supply sides for the corpses or victims for the arrangement of ghost marriages. On the demand side, the provinces with the highest demand for corpses were Shanxi and Shaanxi (40% and 31.4%, respectively). Situated in the region between Central and Northern China, these provinces are neighbouring each other, suggesting that a culture of ghost marriage has been established in this region. On the supply side, the provinces with the highest supply of corpses were also Shanxi and Shaanxi (32.6% and 24.4%, respectively), followed by Henan (18.6%). Locations of buyers. When we investigated the specific locations of buyers, we found that approximately two-thirds came from villages (62.5%). Prices of corpses and victims. Matching for the dead used to be free, but it costs more now than matching the living, ranging from several thousand to ten thousand RMB due to the lack of supply. Overall, our data reveal that the prices differ greatly among the corpses, ranging from RMB1,125 to RMB135,000, with an average price of RMB23,913. For living persons, the prices ranged from RMB14,000 to RMB70,000, with an average price of RMB 26,333. Objective 2: To demonstrate the criminal business processes of the ghost bride market, a detailed analysis of two widely reported cases was conducted to illustrate the processes involved in ghost marriages. The two cases found the operation of the ghost bride market is created as a result of market forces, with element of human connections. Within the networks, there is no restriction in membership, and economic relations precede social relations. Members’ participation is more likely to be opportunistic and financially driven who may not share similar criminal attributes and skills as shown in the two case studies. The criminals are entrepreneurs aiming at maximizing their financial benefit but not seeking other influences. Consisting of both legal and criminal operators, the network is facilitated by brokers, or ghost matchmakers, with market information and entrepreneurship. On the demand side, the information suppliers can be any ordinary person, such as the clients themselves, their relatives, neighbours, or hospital workers who pass on the supply information to the matchmakers. On the supply side, however, they are criminals who are engaged in kidnapping, murder, or tomb robbery. It is interesting to know that the local hospitals’ morgues have become a supply platform for the trading of ghost brides. A weird phenomenon at the funeral homes occurred, where most of the bodies that were cremated were males. Since women’s corpses can be sold, few were brought in for cremation. Based on the data collected, we suggest that the structure for a “one-stop service” may be available for ghost marriage --- the service begins from the second the death is pronounced, the information flows from hospital support workers, to the unit managing the funeral, to the brokers or ghost matchmakers, and then to the family in need. There are no fixed boundaries for business networks that can cross cities and provinces. A female victim may be kidnapped and murdered or a female corpse may be dug out from a tomb in one province and transferred to a buyer in another province. Within the networks, ghost matchmakers usually have abundant knowledge of the males and females within the villages nearby, and they match both the dead and the alive. By acting as brokers, they fill the structural holes, connecting otherwise disconnected networks. They connect criminals and clients. Situated at the central node of the network, they have the greatest connectivity to other partners and thus have access to most information on supply, demand, and pricing.

11607319.label: Major findings and research outcome
11607319.value: Chinese criminals are exceptional in developing entrepreneurship using guanxi. The present study demonstrates how a ghost bride market is created as a result of established historical culture and takes place in specific geographical regions of China. Ghost marriages have existed for a long time and have a direct relationship with folk sorcery, which is not uncommon among rural people who believe in the existence of ghosts and spirits. The sorcery is promoted by ghost matchmakers, who use feng shui and other fortune-telling methods to settle the occurrence of disasters and indirectly maintain and spread the mysterious and spiritual culture. When they discover the death of a male in a household, they bring together and promote ghost matching, profiting from the ghost bride business. The existence of these brokers and their numbers depend on the demands of the rural market. The present study confirms previous research that considers geography and history in the establishment of trading networks in rural China. It also supports previous research that culture can shape economic behaviour and institutions, and that a market is an interaction between economic and cultural factors. In addition, the ghost bride market can explain the actual social and economic lives in China’s rural areas. The present study shows that ghost bride-induced crimes often occur in poorer provinces, as reflected by their relatively lower GDP. Most importantly, the majority of those used in ghost bride marriages were women. While ghost marriages create a market of supply and demand in booming rural China, the market also indicates income and gender inequality behind the crime. In traditional Chinese beliefs, the problem of malign wandering spirits is attributed to both males and females, but the study found that gender distinction exists. Considering the continuing patriarchal systems in rural China, ghost marriages favour males. Death of an unmarried and childless male cuts off his family tree, resulting in the loss of his family’s property. After his ghost marriage, his family can adopt a child to become their new heir, continuing the family line. Therefore, the ancestral tribute and property inheritance system of the village community is the root of the custom of ghost marriage favouring male, which sparks a market of ghost brides.

11607319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11607319.value: Rural criminology is a global topic and there are research groups in the American Society of Criminology and the European Society of Criminology that investigate crime in rural area. However, rural criminology is underdeveloped in mainland China, and thus there is great potential to develop this topic in the Chinese academic world. However, since the PI will retire at the end of December 2022, no further action can be pursued further under GRF scheme.

11607319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11607319.value: The custom of ghost marriages has been passed down since the ancient times in China. Adults who died before marriage could not be buried with their ancestors. Their families did not want to leave bodies outside, as they believed that the spirits would become lonely. Instead, they wished to find husbands or wives for their dead relatives to continue the family tree. The custom has spawned a large ghost bride market, resulting in the trading of female corpses. This industry and its profits have driven criminals to kidnap and murder women, raid tombs and morgues, steal and traffic corpses. The study demonstrates that while in the folklore the stigma of being unmarried should apply to both men and women, the corpses trafficked are mainly women and in poorer provinces. While ghost marriages create a market of supply and demand in booming rural China, the market also indicates income and gender inequality behind the crime. The study supports previous research that culture can shape economic behaviour and institutions, and that a criminal market is an interaction between economic and cultural factors. The findings can give insight to criminologists in developing crime prevention strategies.

11607419.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11607419.value: Background. Close relationships are vital to our physical and mental well-being. The presence and quality of close relationships are among the most reliable and robust predictors of health and longevity (Holt-Lunstad, Robles, & Sbarra, 2017). Forgiveness and self-regulation play important roles in building and maintaining close relationships (Fincham & Beach, 2002; Baumeister, 2005). However, the investigation of the association between self-regulation and forgiveness in close relationships is scant. Forgiveness is crucial for interpersonal relationships, and possibly involves self-regulation processes (Burnette et al., 2014). For instance, forgiveness requires regulation of one’s emotions and motivations towards the transgressor (McCullough, Worthington, & Rachal, 1997). Nevertheless, the causal relationship between self-regulation and forgiveness in close relationships has not been thoroughly examined in previous literature. Purpose. To fill the gap in the literature, this research aims to understand the associations between self-regulation and forgiveness in close relationships. In particular, this research aims to examine the stability of the self-regulatory model of forgiveness among individuals who are involved in romantic relationships over time (Study 1), and the causal connection between self-regulation and forgiveness in experimental vignettes (Study 2). Methodology. Two studies will be conducted to test the link between self-regulation and forgiveness. Study 1 is a longitudinal design study where participants who are involved in romantic relationships will complete online survey concerns with regarding self-regulation, forgiveness and relationship outcomes at two-time points. Study 2 is an experimental design study, a priming procedure will be used to manipulate self-regulatory strength and assess participants’ levels of forgiveness in hypothetical transgression scenarios, and relationship outcomes. Contributions. Close relationships and of the continual social interactions involved ultimately influence a person’s health in a multitude of ways. The findings from this research program will shed light on the theoretical and practical implications of relationship flourishing. Particularly, this research provides a unique theoretical contribution to understanding the causal effect of self-regulation on forgiveness by proposing the self-regulatory model of forgiveness. On the practical side, this research might provide important implications to relationship building and maintenance through developing self-regulatory strength that facilitates forgiveness. 親密的人際關係對個人的身心健康至關重要。這種關係的存在和質量是一個人健康和長壽的最可靠和最強大的預測因素（Holt-Lunstad, Robles, & Sbarra, 2017）。寬恕和自我調節在建立和維持親密的人際關係中發揮著重要作用（Fincham＆Beach，2002; Baumeister, 2005），然而，對這些關係中自我調節和寬恕之間關係的研究很少。寬恕不僅對人際關係至關重要，而且可能涉及自我調節過程（Burnette et al., 2014）。例如，寬恕需要有意識地調節一個人對侵越者的情緒和動機（McCullough, Worthington, & Rachal, 1997）。此外，在以前的現存文獻中，沒有經驗性地徹底檢查自我調節與緊密人際關係中的寬恕之間的因果關係。為填補文獻中的這一空白，本研究評估親密關係中自我調節與寬恕之間的互惠關聯。 特別是，這個研究提案的目的是：i）檢測親密關係中的自我調節模式之穩定性（研究1）; ii）通過使用實驗情景評估自我調節與寬恕之間的因果關係（研究2）。

11607419.label: Major findings and research outcome
11607419.value: Across two studies, we sought to explore the possible mediating role of forgiveness in the linkage between self-control and relationship outcomes, employing both cross-sectional (Study 1; n = 205) and longitudinal (Study 2; n = 600) designs. Participants in heterosexual romantic relationships completed online survey(s) assessing their levels of self-control, forgiveness, and the quality of their relationship. Results provide support for the self-regulatory model of forgiveness, in which higher level of self-control is associated with higher level of forgiveness, which in turn, are associated with better relationship outcomes in Study 1. These results confirm that trait self-control is associated with forgiveness and relationship satisfaction, commitment, and closeness, and show that forgiveness plays a mediating role in the associations between trait self-control and relationship satisfaction, commitment, and closeness In Study 2, we evaluated whether self-control predicts greater future forgiveness using a longitudinal design. The results of Study 2 offer support for our hypothesized models in which forgiveness mediated the links between trait self-control and relationship satisfaction, commitment and closeness in a two-wave longitudinal study. Specifically, greater trait self-control at the initial assessment predicted a stronger tendency to forgive the offending partner after four weeks, which was associated with a more satisfying, committed, and a closer relationship, over a four-week period. The proposed mediation models were confirmed in both cross-sectional data (Study 1) and two-waves longitudinal data (Study 2). The findings revealed that trait self-control was positively associated with state forgiveness, which in turn positively affected relationship satisfaction, commitment and closeness. The present study advances our theoretical understanding of the mechanisms underlying the association between self-control and relationship outcomes.

11607419.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11607419.value: Future research should consider replicating this mediating relationships by collecting one or two more wave(s) of data (longitudinal design) and with different time intervals (e.g., two-month, six-month or twelve-month). Finally, Hong Kong is a vibrant metropolis where East meets West and highly value relational harmony. It would be interesting to explore if the self-regulatory model of forgiveness in the context of romantic relationships could be replicated in other non-Western cultures. A possible plan open to scale up the current research is to: (1) replicate the findings of this study with samples across cultures (in both individualistic and collectivistic cultures); (2) collecting one more wave of data (longitudinal design) and incorporate behavioural intentional measures by using validated hypothetical scenarios.

11607419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11607419.value: Forgiveness is important for romantic relationships. This research provides insight to healthy and thriving relationships. The findings of this research indicate that people with higher self-control and more forgiving seem to be more satisfied, committed and perceived closeness in their relationships. In particular, people with higher self-control are more likely to have level of forgiveness, and they are the ones have better overall relationship outcomes.

11608219.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11608219.value: 机制设计关注制定（制度性）规则。通常，参与一项机制的主体可能具有隐藏信息并采取无法验证的隐藏操作。因此，在潜在的利益冲突下，需要一个精心设计的机制来识别这种信息不对称。许多机制设计问题中一个固有的因素是风险。从一个组织的激励结构，到影响消费者福利、企业竞争甚至国家安全的政府政策，一种机制的结果可能是高度不确定的。尽管在过去的半个世纪中，机制设计理论取得了重大进展，但对于实践中涉及到高风险、高回报的重要机制，现有理论没有给出令人满意的指导：最先进的机制设计文献通常假设规划者和参与者都具有拟线性（即风险中性）的效用。尽管这一假设促进了对各种复杂问题的分析，当风险对于参与个体具有重要影响时，这一假设可能过于严格。 在本项研究中，我们的目标是建立一个综合的理论框架，将风险和经济主体的异质性风险偏好纳入考虑范围。在设计超越拟线性效用环境的机制时，一个众所周知的困难是建立合适的均衡解。考虑到任何非平凡、具有风险性机制的结果通常会对某些主体产生有利影响而对其他主体不利，且每个主体的风险偏好可能取决于这些结果，我们将创新性地采用一种二分法的方法来处理。通过使用对数超模块工具（log supermodularity）来表征异质性风险偏好，而不是传统的阿罗-普拉特（Arrow-Pratt）测量，本研究将为处理机制设计理论中的风险问题提供一种易处理的新方法。 理论分析之外，我们也将对一些高风险、高回报的机制进行实证研究。我们选择在实践中经常采用的两种机制，资产配置和创新激励机制，来进行结构估计。这两种机制通常都涉及高风险和高回报。为了克服在非拟线性效用环境下的模型非识别特征，我们将创造性地通过组合同一组个体的两种不同行为数据来构建识别源。 这项理论与实证的综合研究将深入分析风险和异质性风险偏好如何影响高风险机制的结果，以及最佳风险分担如何使规划者和参与者都获得更高的效用。我们的预期结果将对现实世界中的机制设计问题产生新的重要政策影响。

11608219.label: Realisation of objectives
11608219.value: Regarding objectives 1 and 2, we have completed two theoretical papers addressing these questions. The first paper (see also Section 6.1) examines optimal multi-unit auctions where bidders exhibit heterogeneous risk aversion. We find that when the auctioned items are risky and both winning and losing have significant consequences for the bidders, the first-price sequential Dutch auction Pareto dominates all other formats in the class of first-come second-price (FCSP) auctions. The second paper complements the discussion on optimal mechanisms by focusing on optimal information disclosure rules for aftermarket participants. In this context, bidders have private information about their production costs. After the auction, the winning bidder competes with a third party under differentiated Cournot competition. Our analysis shows that full disclosure of the winner’s marginal cost is the uniquely optimal information policy, positively impacting both the designer’s revenue and ex-post efficiency. As for the empirical part of the project (objectives 3 and 4), we encountered significant challenges due to the Covid-19 pandemic. Although we successfully acquired a dataset on flower auctions, the process took much longer than anticipated. The widespread lockdowns from 2020 to 2022 hindered travel and data collection efforts, and the institutions with which we had negotiated data acquisition either shut down or scaled back their operations during the pandemic. Consequently, instead of focusing on firm behavior, we shifted our attention partially to dynamic public behavioral patterns during the pandemic—another high-risk context for which U.S. data was more readily available. A novel structural estimation method and associated counterfactual analysis reveals that public behavior during the early pandemic exhibited a polarized distribution. This finding has important implications for optimal mechanisms in combating pandemics and other public health crises (see the final paper in Section 6.1 for more details).

11608219.label: Major findings and research outcome
11608219.value: The main research outputs of this project include two theoretical papers and one empirical study: 1. “Sequential Multi-Unit Auction with Independent Risk” by Audrey Hu, Jingfeng Lu, and Wenbo Zhao This paper examines sequential auctions for multiple identical objects conducted for bidders with unit demand. Bidders exhibit risk-independent preferences, meaning their preferences over income risk do not depend on their private types. Each round is modeled as a first cum second-price (FCSP) auction, where the winner’s payment is an arbitrary increasing function of the highest two bids from active bidders, allowing the auction format to vary across rounds. We show that a pure strategy monotone equilibrium exists for bidders with any income risk preference (including DARA). If bidders are averse to income risk, the equilibrium price sequences necessarily drift downward. While all FCSP auctions are ex post efficient, we conclude that the first-price (or Dutch) sequential auction is Pareto optimal when both sellers and bidders are risk averse. 2. “Optimal Auction Design with Aftermarket Cournot Competition” by Yanlin Chen, Audrey Hu, and Jun Zhang This paper studies optimal information and mechanism design for selling an object to asymmetric, privately informed bidders, where the winning bidder competes with a third party under differentiated Cournot competition afterward. We decompose the problem into two sub-problems: Bayesian persuasion and standard mechanism design. Full disclosure of the winner’s marginal cost emerges as the unique optimal information policy, combined with allocating the auctioned object to the bidder with the highest “virtual surplus.” Bidders’ signaling incentives increase the seller’s expected revenue and lower discriminatory reserve prices in the optimal mechanism, improving ex post efficiency, measured by the probability of no sale. 3. “Polarized Public Responses to a Pandemic: Theory and Evidence” by Xu Han, Audrey Hu, and Joyce Liu This paper explores a sequential pandemic game with heterogeneous, risk-averse agents. Engaging in more activities yields a higher flow payoff but also induces greater infection risk. We first construct a theoretical model characterizing public behavior during a pandemic. Our findings indicate that a polarized distribution of public responses arises when the hazard rate of risk exposure is constant and sufficiently high. Empirical findings align with this polarized equilibrium; using data from the American Time Use Survey, our counterfactual analysis reveals that the proportion of individuals who did not socialize during the pandemic significantly increased, while the distribution of social time spent among those who did socialize remains unchanged.

11608219.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11608219.value: We have successfully acquired a dataset on flower auctions. With the flower auction dataset, we can further develop our findings by analyzing real-world auction dynamics and bidder behaviors in this context. Proposed actions include: 1. Data Analysis: Validate and refine our auction models with the dataset, exploring how risk preferences and auction formats affect bidding behavior and outcomes. 2. Mechanism Testing: Experiment with different auction designs based on our theoretical work in the flower auction setting to identify which formats yield the highest revenues. 3. Collaboration: Partner with auction houses to implement our theoretical findings, providing tailored auction designs to optimize their operations. Additionally, Audrey has invited Yating Yuan, who’s currently based in the UK, to work on optimal contract design for a high-risk pandemic scenario.

11608219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11608219.value: This research project has produced significant findings in auction theory and public response during crises. The first paper explores the revenue-maximising sequential auction when bidders are averse to income risk. The second paper investigates how to optimally design the auction and disclose information to a third-party participant who interacts with the winner in the aftermarket. The third paper examines how people react during a pandemic, revealing that individuals’ responses can become polarized, with some choosing to avoid socializing altogether while others maintain their social activities. Overall, this research enhances our understanding of auction strategies and public behavior in critical situations, offering insights that can be applied in both economic and public health contexts.

11608619.label: Project Objectives
11608619.value: 釐清道德重整會的國際源起，探究它如何由基督教的靈修活動進入國際政治場域、如何被美國中央情報局收編的來龍去脈、前經後過，並分析它的含混性與暖昧性。 研究道德重整會香港分會如何進入香港及其在地化的過程，特別審視它與在港一眾美國基金會、英國政府、港英政府、國民黨政府、日本政教界的關係，進而展開它針對香港文教界發起的道德重整運動的探討。 究查分會在香港的創辦宗旨、經費來源、組織架構、核心成員的軍政商學背景，進而探究它的社群脈絡以及籌辦活動的內容。當中，尤將集中觀察它與香港大學、各私立專上院校以及1963年成立的香港中文大學之間的互動往來。 研究該會如何因應冷戰香港本土局勢、環球政局的發展，從而策劃香港境外及在地相關文化活動，實踐其社會關懷；由此而觀察在地知識社群、報刊媒體等等對道德重整運動的觀感、報導與評議。 歸納道德重整運動透過怎樣的一套「知識論述」以進入香港文教界，並將特別着眼於儒學思想、傳統文化精神價值是如何與道德重整運動的「絕對道德標準」結合，從而發揮其改造社會、圍堵共產主義的力量。透過相關研究，希望有助深入地窺探冷戰香港複雜、多元的社會思想面貌與文化氛圍。

11608619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11608619.value: 「道德重整運動」從一場發源於英國牛津團契的靈修活動，在戰後迅速發展為溝通各國文化差異、追求和平共處乃至環球抗共的國際化運動。作為冷戰亞洲的政治、經濟、情報中心的香港，道德重整運動迅速由一批活躍於商界、文教界乃至政界的反共社群興起，進入香港社區，吸引不少專上院校學生參與。本計劃將對這一不無含混性、暖昧性的運動進入冷戰期間香港後的在地化過程──諸如組織架構之建立、實施活動的策略、思想方針之釐定乃至「知識化」論述等作出深入探究。分析它如何在美國情治機構主導及台灣方面的影響下、透過與境外其他國家特別是日本道德重整協會的互動，從而展開這一運動關於青年學生的思想工作。透過相關研究，本計劃將估量這一運動在港可能發揮的反共影響力以及它在香港高校發展過程中扮演的角色，特別是它對高校與國際文教機構來往及走向國際化時所發揮的作用。藉着這些成果，希望能夠有助於我們了解香港的不同文化社群在冷戰局勢下的人文活動、政治關懷以及對中國何去何從的思考問題，進而深入窺探冷戰香港複雜、多元的社會思想面貌與文化氛圍。

11608619.label: Realisation of objectives
11608619.value: 本計劃的研究目標只曾作數個字眼的小修改(如第四點目標，主要是使之更簡潔)，總體上與2018年呈交申請計劃時沒有什麼區別。 本計劃自2020年1月開展以來，曾參加三次學術研討會，並於會上發表研究成果，與海內外學術界有廣泛交流。建基於這些初步研究成果，PI再將之發展成嚴謹的學術論文，已有兩篇論文得以成功發表於擁有國際聲譽的優秀學術期刊。這兩篇論文都屬於長篇論文，PI 在此基礎上將之發展成為一本專門論述文化冷戰的書──《無遠弗屆：美國的文化冷戰與香港 (1949-1979)》。PI於2023年10月寄呈北京三聯書店，目前仍處於審查階段。可以說，藉着上述研究，本計劃擬定的五項研究目標已是完全達至了。 另外，PI有四篇論文及相關訪問稿將可望於2024年出版。其中一篇名為『冷戦期東アジアの内的関連―香港における道徳再武装運動の視点から』的論文，將刊於《東洋文庫：戦後日中関係史論文集》 ，這篇論文是由PI的中文稿〈冷戰東亞的政治聯繫：道德重整運動在香港的視域〉譯成，翻譯者為東京大學的年輕學者。 至於一篇研究唐君毅的論文及一篇訪問稿，表面上來看與道德重整運動(MRA)在香港發展的關係不深，但它們對於了解MRA在香港興起的時代背景、MRA所寄身的機構或組織的人事脈絡、香港社會的文化氛圍等等都會有所裨益。MRA與唐君毅管理的新亞書院乃至中文大學成立後的多名同事有極為密切的關係。MRA這場運動的核心人物如李毓田、凌道揚、蔡貞人等是新亞書院與中文大學的教員。凌道揚更曾多年身居中文大學的領導層，MRA的訪問團也曾在新亞書院與中文大學表演及交流。但正如本文提及的，唐君毅卻不欲對此一運動多談論。此外，1960年代在新亞書院讀書的陳志誠教授，對此場運動亦有耳聞，但在訪談中亦未有詳述。 PI於2023年7月終於有機會前往日本拜訪日本的道德重整運動總部，與現今的日本MRA領袖兼澀澤榮一家族當家──澀澤千鶴子聯繫。在她的幫助下，PI在MRA總部與三位負責具體事務的高層人員訪談，並獲送贈若干研究材料。於2023年12月，PI亦有機會在香港接觸到一位曾參與數次MRA活動的人士，目前於其幫助下，可望與已移民加拿大的一些當年在港參與MRA的年長成員聯繫。隨着時間發展/沉澱、聯繫渠道的建立，相信有助於進一步拓展本計劃的研究範疇，使本計劃在未來繼續獲深廣的研究。

11608619.label: Major findings and research outcome
11608619.value: PI在台灣中央研究院《新史學》發表了一篇體現本研究成果的長文──〈文化冷戰 ──道德重整運動在香港的發展〉 (本文原長六萬字，後與刊物編輯多次往來刪削後，以逾四萬多字的版本發表)，在總結裏曾經提及：MRA在香港的身影既然絕非曇花一現，那麼，它的發展過程與人事網絡便尤有值得注意之處。畢竟，MRA在香港自1950至1970年代的近三十年的活動足跡，正好讓我們可以了解好像MRA這樣一種政教糾纏的國際性運動的時代意義。特別是它在香港發展的興衰，讓我們多了一個不同的視角，觀察曾經活躍在香港的南來知識群體的在地參與及改造社會的嘗試，這對我們進深了解戰後香港的人際網絡、國際交流及社會發展等等的問題，相信都會有一定的裨益的。透過本計劃的研究，我們已可以清晰看到這場席卷全球、並在香港發展的宗教政治運動，是與主導全球冷戰的美國當局息息相關。至於它在香港的發展，則與第三勢力與香港在地文教界人士共同發起的。在MRA進入香港社會的過程中，我們已可以認識它的宗旨、核心人員、組織架構、經費以及活動的目的。MRA在香港的發展往往借助於與傳統中國文化、儒家哲學的結合，再藉着與基督教的教義的宣傳、教會學校的推動，從而發揮其改造社會的力量。透過相關研究，希望有助深入地窺探冷戰香港複雜、多元的社會思想面貌與文化氛圍。

11608619.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11608619.value: 長遠而言，本研究可以再作進一步的擴展，研究MRA在日本興衰的課題，將可以新的角度揭示戰後美國藉着MRA而在日本策動的東亞冷戰戰略，並展示日本舉國上下如何藉着參與MRA的活動而重返國際舞臺的經過。有關研究對於研究日本在戰後的國家政治發展與港臺的互動關係也會是大有裨益的。PI於2023年6月有機會在日本的MRA總部訪談負責人，目前也已陸續聯絡上曾經在香港參與MRA活動的當事人。PI於2023年11月呈交的最新一份GRF計劃書，便是以MRA在日本的興衰為題的新研究計劃，預計相關訪談可以讓本計劃在獲得持續的努力下獲得更多成果。

11608619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11608619.value: 本研究透過在美國、英國及香港本地的歷史檔案與報刊文獻，成功解讀及揭示了MRA這場運動在香港發展的前經後過。同時，本研究也發現，MRA在香港的發展與戰後日本有極為緊密的關係，而美國於戰後對日本國家定位的不斷調整，也直接影響MRA的壯大與發展，進而影響香港及台灣的MRA發展，從而構成了MRA在東亞冷戰發揮了重要的文化冷戰功能。香港的第三勢力集團參與MRA運動，與他們的政治目的是有千絲萬縷的關係的，但不論是第三勢力在香港的活動還是MRA在香港的興衰，都是與東亞的冷戰格局變化有很密切的關係的。
