12608719.label: Major findings and research outcome
12608719.value: The major findings were presented in the exhibition 'Dropped' at Osage gallery. During space flight humans have accidentally dropped or deliberately placed a wide variety of objects into space. These broadly fall into 4 categories: a. Tools - b. Clothing- c. Human waste and food.- d. objects of specific scientific or personal and cultural significance. There has often been a casual disregard for the consequences of debris and littering in space. The environment in near earth space has been dramatically effected by human presence and there are many new ways being developed to address the problems of how to clear up the mess. Nearly every orbiting object is tracked and data is available for monitoring purposes. Many objects (Hammers, Golf Balls, Javelins) have been thrown on the surface of the moon just to see how far they would travel yet none were subsequently collected or picked up. On the surface of the moon there is a plethora of objects and materials at landing sites which have now required the status of Archeological sites and there is considerable interest in the effects the space environment has had on the materials and the objects left there. Space Archeology is an emerging field. Attitudes to pollution in space have changed significantly as a result of the proliferation and direct threat they present to Space Exploration and damage to satellite systems on earth. The whole project was featured in a news.TVB programme on the 2nd February 2022. The project was also reviewed in Ming Pau on the 14.11.2022 in the culture section.

I will hope to further present the film 'Off- Earth' at talks and exhibitions internationally once travel becomes possible again.

12608719.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12608719.value: The project identifies, examines and explores a series of hand held objects directly tied to the exploration of space travel and voyages to the moon, which have either been accidentally dropped or deliberately placed in space by the 533 individuals who have travelled there. The web platform www.Dropped.Space is a comprehensive collection of these objects bought together for the first time as an archive in the form of photographs, films and 3d scans. The significance is in the value of this collection as a visual, material and cultural study of space flight through these objects and the value is in what insights these objects provide about the development of space technologies, clothing and tools and the specific cultural and scientific significance humans attach to objects in space. The project draws attention to the growing problem of space pollution and human neglect for the environment off earth.

12608919.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12608919.value: The research project investigates the licit and illicit commerce in opium and its derivatives between Turkey and East Asia in the early twentieth century. The research aims to reveal the complex networks that brought Turkish opium to China at a time when previously dominant British-Indian sources of opium were withdrawn and new national laws and international treaties increasingly restricted the legal marketplace for the drug. The research project will uncover the formation, composition, and extent of these commercial networks, paying particular attention to their transcommunal and transnational reach. It will further examine the measures carried out by state authorities and shipping companies to combat smuggling and establish control over the maritime traffic that connected the ports of the Mediterranean and South and East China Seas. Finally, it will assess the diplomatic impact of the opium trade and efforts at its suppression on relations between Turkey, Japan, and China, in terms of both their bilateral ties and the three countries’ joint participation in new forms of international organisation such as represented by the League of Nations. The research project will excavate these subversive networks through the collection and analysis of Turkish and Greek government documents, Hong Kong and Shanghai municipal and police records, the archives of the China Customs Service, the reports of the opium control board of the League of Nations, international newspaper collections, and the observations of American, British, and French diplomatic representatives and colonial officials. This research will lead to the publication of a peer reviewed journal article which will examine the attempt of private and state bodies in Turkey to penetrate the east Asian opium market in the 1920s and 1930s and the competition and local and international political opposition they faced. The research will further contribute to the completion of what will be the first monograph length study on the traffic in narcotics in the early twentieth century eastern Mediterranean, with the role of Asian markets forming one chapter of the manuscript, with the research prepared for other chapters already complete N/A

12609119.label: Project Objectives
12609119.value: To establish a theoretical framework on the relationship between technology and popular music creativity. While the framework is valid to examine similar cases elsewhere, it is established to be applied to Hong Kong’s Cantopop music scene by mapping various prior studies on technology and music creativity to local musicians’ practices in song production. To examine the use of music technology in Cantopop production after 2000s through detailed analyses of a selected repertoire of songs, in-depth interviews with composers, arrangers, singers, producers, and sound engineers, so as to understand the use of technology in their creative process. To relate the above findings to Hong Kong’s socio-political cultural contexts so as to see how technology and technological development affect music’s potential to embody socio-political issues. To present the project findings at one international conference. To produce one academic journal article to appear in an international refereed journal. To produce an anthology that captures the essence of this project, entailing songs that embodied the technological and creative experience of the actors involved with annotations about their unique musical features as well as their creators.

12609319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12609319.value: This project examines the extent to which social media use contributes to an informed, tolerant, and active citizenship in a media-saturated but politically polarized and fragmenting society. While the “logic of connective action” (Bennett & Segerberg 2012, p. 739) states the political implications of social media, several disconnective actions have emerged when people experience political disagreement, such as cutting off political discussion, masking their political viewpoints, or even terminating relationships (Wells et al., 2017). While digital media technologies enable people to select an information repertoire, i.e., online sources or connections from which they communicate political information (Wolfsfeld, Yarchi, & Samuel-Azran, 2016), they also create echo chambers, where like-minded people are clustering and non-like-minded people are detached. It jeopardizes a cornerstone of societal well-being and the civic culture (Almond & Verba, 1963), undermining the ability of people to communicate with people holding different viewpoints and to be aware of the rationales and arguments of others (Habermas, 1989). This project will explain how people respond to political disagreement, such as by remaining silent, or by filtering their connections on social media, and how these online behaviors facilitate or undermine political engagement. The project starts from reviewing literature on reactions to political disagreement (Barnidge, 2017; Mutz, 2002), namely, the spiral of silence and political homophily. Then it elaborates two types of politically motivated online behaviors, namely, 1) opinion expression avoidance strategies (Hayes, 2007) and 2) information repertoire filtration (John & Dvir-Gvirsman, 2015). The project will investigate the outcomes of these processes through indicators of an informed, tolerant, and active citizenship: 1) political knowledge, 2) political polarization, and 3) political participation. The project focuses on Hong Kong, a society with a high digital media penetration rate, which has also witnessed several controversial political events over the last two decades. Using a mixed-methods approach, the project will conduct focus group interviews to understand why and how disagreement-evoked expression avoidance strategies and information repertoire manipulation are taking place. A two-wave panel survey based on representative samples will be implemented before and after a milestone political event, i.e., the 2020 Legislative Council election. It will explore causal relationships between reactions to political disagreement and their consequences. The project aims to understand how digital media nurture a diverse public sphere, with a more open, egalitarian, reasoned, and rational discourse of deliberation (Habermas, 1989). It aims to make conceptual generalizations to other media-saturated and politically polarizing and fragmenting societies.

12609319.label: Realisation of objectives
12609319.value: The project team reviewed and updated related theories on political disagreement, affective polarization, social media communication, and political participation. Guided by the theoretical frameworks, the project team implemented a population-based two-wave online panel survey and a virtual focus-group interview. The online survey was based on a stratified sample implemented in Hong Kong from 8 July to 22 July 2020 (wave 1, n = 1208) and from 8 September to 22 September 2020 (wave 2, n = 791). Participants were local Hong Kong citizens aged between 18 to 65 years, recruited by Dynata, an online survey firm. The online focus group interview was conducted on 22 – 25 March 2021. We recruited 26 Hong Kong residents aged from 20 to 33 and implemented the discussion on Slack, an encrypted online platform asynchronously and anonymously within the study period. Results from the mixed-methods approach are informative and meaningful to address all five research objectives. Objective 1. To examine the interplay between political disagreement on social media and different dimensions of political engagement in a politically-divided city-state; To address our research objectives, we distinguished two types of political participation to better examine the relationships between political disagreement and political engagement. We termed the actions “activist participation” if the participants need to reach a decision with a fixed political standpoint, such as joining a rally or demonstration, signing a petition, or boycotting a business for political reasons; we termed those actions as “deliberative participation” when a mutual understanding of different political views among participants is important to achieve the desired political goals, and opinion diversity contributes to the continuance of these activities, such as volunteering, contributing to a community project, contacting media to share political views, or attending meetings of a community group. We also focused on people’s information repertoire filtration, such as unfriending, blocking, untagging photos, as well as stopping the receipt of information from disconnected sources, such as unsubscribing from a news forum or opting out of virtual communities. We found that exposure to political disagreement would lead to both types of political participation via the mediation of information repertoire filtration. Our study provides a nuanced understanding of how people use social media to curate their sources and connections in responding to political conflicts in a high-choice and highly politically polarized environment. Objective 2. To elaborate and explain people’s disagreement-evoked communication practices on social media, i.e., adopting opinion expression avoidance strategies and filtering information repertoires. From the survey study, we found that people would conceal their political opinion from withdrawal behaviors, i.e., removing previously published contents, such as (1) deleting or editing the posts; (2) asking people to untag themselves from a post, and (3) untagging themselves from a photo published on social media. The levels of these withdrawal behaviors were moderate (wave 1: M = 2.19, SD = 1.03; wave 2: M = 2.22, SD = 0.98). We also identified the extent to which people filtered their information repertoire, such as (1) hiding or blocking someone’s comments or posts on social media because of his/her political viewpoints; (2) unfriending or unfollowing some friends because of political viewpoints; (3) leaving or opting out from an online group for political reasons; (4) unsubscribing from public social media pages because of their political viewpoints; and (5) reporting someone because of their political viewpoints. The mean values of these items showed that the levels of such behaviors are moderate (wave 1: M = 2.30, SD = 0.95; wave 2: M = 2.31, SD = 0.93). We found that encountering political disagreement is the major predictor of withdrawal behaviors and information repertoire filtration. The focus-group interview revealed more nuanced disagreement-evoked communication practices on social media. We found that most discussants regarded maintaining interpersonal harmony as more important than solving political disagreement, especially for their socially close connections; therefore, they would stop discussing politics to maintain social relations. Discussants were aware of the potentially negative consequences of expressing viewpoints on politically sensitive topics. They adopted several strategies to conceal their viewpoints, such as nonengaging, diverting to other topics, and pretending to agree. Discussants also used sophisticated privacy management tactics on social media to manipulate the visibility of their communicative behaviors. Objective 3. To illuminate whether these disagreement-evoked communication practices influence political knowledge, political polarization, and political participation; We found that disagreement-evoked communication practices would lead to political participation. However, we did not identify a statistically significant effect of political disagreement on political knowledge. In the exploration of political polarization, after reviewing the latest literature, we found that while several studies addressed the antecedents of polarization or its consequences on nonpolitical issues, “little has been written on [the political consequences of affective polarization]” (Iyengar et al., 2019, p. 139). Therefore, we investigated the consequences of affective polarization to fill this research gap. We found that affective polarization plays an important role in Hong Kong people's political life, making the political consequences of disagreement-evoked communication practices vary. We found that the indirect effect of exposure to disagreement on both types of participation via information repertoire filtration was stronger when the affective polarization was low. In other words, the “disagreement --> information repertoire filtration --> political participation” linkage is more salient when people are less polarized. Objective 4. To advance knowledge on the framework of the spiral of silence and political homophily, and to validate and clarify the contradictory findings of the political implications of digital media technologies; The present study advances theoretical frameworks of the spiral of silence, political homophily, affective polarization, and political engagement in the social media setting and in a highly politically polarized context. We found that the (non-)communication affordances of social media would group likely-minded people together to achieve their political goals. Undoubtedly, such a highly personalized online connection makes organizing and mobilizing political activities easier. However, such a homogenous information repertoire might lessen the ability of people to comprehend the other side of an argument and thereby undermine deliberation. Objective 5. To offer a better understanding of the extent to which using social media may or may not lead to an informed, tolerant, and active citizenship in the context of Hong Kong and make conceptual generalizations to other societies in the world, which are media-saturated but politically polarized and fragmenting. Our project has advanced prevailing beliefs and research on the role of social media in supporting deliberation and an active public sphere. It contributes to a nascent research agenda that examines disagreement-evoked (dis-)communication in online settings and the consequent political outcomes. It contributes to research on the connective logic of social media by offering countervailing evidence and debunking a technologically deterministic view of the political potential of social media. When the connectedness of social media grants people the liberty to manage their online connection, it also enables people to opt out of the marketplace of ideas. Polarization may be shaped by user choices rather than merely technical determinants. The current study offers an empirical analysis of how social media may be a double-edged sword in both facilitating or jeopardizing a society's well-being and civic culture. References Iyengar, S., Lelkes, Y., Levendusky, M., Malhotra, N., & Westwood, S. J. (2019). The origins and consequences of affective polarization in the United States. Annual Review of Political Science, 22, 129-146.

12609319.label: Major findings and research outcome
12609319.value: We conducted a population-based two-wave online panel survey and a virtual focus-group interview. In the survey study, we found that exposure to disagreement would lead to using opinion expression avoidance strategies, such as removing previously published content on social media. Disagreement would also trigger people to filter their information repertoire, such as unfriending others or opting out from online communities. Disagreement leads to political participation via the mediation of information repertoire filtration. That is, exposure to disagreement leads people to filter their information repertoire by disconnecting from those with whom they disagree, and information repertoire filtration could facilitate political engagement. Meanwhile, we found that affective polarization would vary the political consequences of disagreement-evoked communication practices. The indirect effect of disagreement on participation via information repertoire filtration was more substantial when polarization was low. The focus-group interview revealed nuanced disagreement-evoked (non-)communication practices on social media. We found that most discussants regarded maintaining interpersonal harmony as more important than solving political disagreement, especially for their socially close connections; therefore, they would stop discussing politics to maintain social relations. Disagreement would increase political knowledge if meaningful dialogues were conducted afterward. Discussants were aware of the potentially negative consequences of expressing viewpoints on politically sensitive topics. They adopted several strategies to conceal their views, such as nonengaging, diverting to other topics, and pretending to agree. Discussants also used sophisticated privacy management tactics on social media to manipulate the visibility of their communicative behaviors. The above findings are reported in several research outcomes. We presented a paper from the two-wave online panel survey at the 72nd Annual Conference of the International Communication Association (ICA), Paris, France, on the effects of political disagreement on political participation. An updated version of the paper has been published in Social Media + Society, a leading journal in the field (Q1 in SSCI-Communication). Another paper derived from the virtual focus-group interview was presented at the 105th Annual Conference of the Association for Education in Journalism and Mass Communication (AEJMC), Detroit, the US. The manuscript is now under revision and will be resubmitted to Telematics & Informatics, a Q1-ranked SSCI interdisciplinary journal on digital media and society. We have also submitted two papers to two flagship communication journals, investigating people’s responses to political disagreement in a networked public and its social and political implications.

12609319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12609319.value: 1. The current study is based on self-reported data. Future studies may use users' behavioral data, such as their online digital traces, to validate the results obtained from the present study. 2. The current study relies on an opt-in online panel, and those who are younger, with higher educational levels, and have more digital skills are inevitably overrepresented. Future studies may consider using a stricter probability sample to enhance the generalizability. Future studies may also consider focusing on the political engagement of under-represented populations. 3. Future studies may examine the role of social media algorithms, such that whether the algorithm-empowered platforms would capture users' unfriending behaviors and follow their preferences, thereby enlarging political polarization. 4. Political attitudes may spill over into non-political domains such as social relations, economic behaviors, and job recruitment. Future studies should consider whether political disagreement or other political attitudes will lead to actions in non-political fields. 5. Further studies may consider using a cross-polity comparative approach to compare Hong Kong with other societies.

12609319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12609319.value: Social media has enabled individuals to actively select their tastes by following or subscribing to specific accounts or joining discussion groups. It may also insulate people's own beliefs from the rebuttal of opposing views by unfriending or blocking others or using social media's privacy settings to manipulate their visibility to different people. When such non-communicative behaviors grant liberty for people to manage their online connection, in the long run, such disconnection would inevitably make people opt out of the marketplace of ideas. We conducted a virtual focus-group interview and a two-wave online survey. We found that disagreement makes people hide their true opinion or unfriend others, and such non-communicative behaviors help people join political activities with those with similar political views. We found that social media makes it easier for people in the political middle-ground to select their political information sources, becoming the victims of social media disconnection. Our project offers a systematic empirical analysis of how social media may be a double-edged sword in both facilitating or jeopardizing deliberative and respectful communication and, thereby, a polity's well-being and civic culture.

12609919.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12609919.value: Physical activity (PA) is related to decreased risks for morbidities and mortality. Among working populations, PA may also be a risk factor for absenteeism and presenteeism. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended at least 150 min/week moderate-to-vigorous intensity PA (MVPA) for adults for health. However, more than half of adults in Hong Kong did not meet the recommended level. Compared to great efforts made for promoting PA for children, few attentions have been paid to those at work. Web-based interventions have been growing rapidly in the past decade. Existing evidence has suggested this type of interventions an effective means to improve PA and health. However, several challenges limit application of the web-based interventions, in particular smaller long-term effects and lower participant engagement and retention rates compared to traditional workplace-based approach, where face-to-face workshops or counselling, posters or other intervention format adopted. A blended approach combining web-based and traditional workplace-based forms might lead to more effective. However, research on this topic is scarce. Following the intervention mapping (IM), we developed a 3-armed cluster randomized controlled trial (cluster-RCT) to improve PA, health, and work productivity among a randomly selected sample of office employees in Hong Kong. The three arms are: a purely web-based intervention arm, a blended intervention arm combining the web-based components with face-to-face workshops and posters, and a control arm. The intervention is personally tailored based on social psychological theories. It will last for three months and then participants will be followed up for nine months to examine long-term effects of the intervention. The primary outcome will be objectively measured MVPA using an accelerometer. Secondary outcomes will consist of health-related variables (including adiposity, blood pressure, blood sugar, blood lipids, self-reported depression, anxiety, stress, and health-related quality of life) and work-related variables (including absenteeism and presenteeism). We will primarily aim to compare between-group differences in the abovementioned outcomes, with a hypothesis in favor of the blended intervention. Secondly, we will examine between-group differences in participant engagement and retention, as well as mediation and moderation effects of theoretical determinants of MVPA change (such as motivation, self-efficacy, and intention) and socio-demographic factors. If effective, the intervention can be promoted to all office employees in Hong Kong to promote their PA, health and work productivity. In addition, our findings, if effectiveness is more favorable in the blended intervention arm, will implicate a new direction for similar interventions in the world. 適當的身體活動（Physical activity，PA）可以降低患病和死亡的風險。在工作人群中，PA也可能與缺勤和假性出勤（presenteeism）有關係。世界衛生組織（WHO）建議成年人每週從事至少150分鐘中高強度的身體活動（moderate-to-vigorous intensity PA，MVPA）對健康有益。但是，香港超過一半的成年人沒有達到WHO建議的水平。與為提高兒童身體活動量所做的巨大努力相比，很少有人關注工作人群。在過去十年中，基於網絡的干預研究迅速發展。現有證據表明，這種干預措施是改善身體活動和健康的有效手段。然而，與傳統的基於工作場所的方法相比，網絡干預的某些局限性限制了該方法的應用，特別是網絡干預的長期效果比較小、參與者的參與率和保留率比較低。而結合網絡和傳統工作場所形式的混合干預可以互相取長補短，有可能產生更大的干預效果。但是，相關研究甚少。以干預映射法（intervention mapping，IM）做為理論框架，我們設計了一項包含三組的集群隨機對照試驗（cluster randomized controlled trial，cluster-RCT），旨在提高香港辦公室員工的身體活動量、健康和工作效率。我們將在香港隨機選取有代表性的辦公室員工，以工作場所為單位把他們隨機分配到純粹的網絡干預組、結合網絡干預和傳統工作場所干預措施的混合干預組、以及對照組。所採用的干預措施則根據社會心理學理論為個體量身定制。本干預為期三個月，然後參與者將被跟踪九個月，以評估干預的長期效果。本研究的主要結果變量是用加速度計客觀測量的MVPA。次要結果包括與健康相關的變量（肥胖指標、血壓、血糖、血脂、自我報告的抑鬱、焦慮和壓力，以及與健康相關的生活質量）和與工作相關的變量（缺勤和假性出勤）。本研究的主要目的是比較上述結果的組間差異，並假設混合干預組的干預措施更效果。其次，我們將研究各組參加者參與性和保留性的差異，以及健康行為理論決定因素（如動機、自我效能和意圖）和社會人口學因素的中介效果和調和效果。如果有效，本干預可以向香港所有辦公室員工進行推廣，以提高他們的身體活動、健康和工作效率。此外，如果混合干預組的干預效果更大，本研究結果亦將為世界上類似的干預研究提供新的方向。

12610119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12610119.value: Resilience is the process of adapting well in the face of adversity, trauma, tragedy, threats or significant sources of stress (American Psychological Association, 2004). There is sufficient evidence showing strong association between resilience and self-rated successful aging (Jeste et al., 2013; Wagnild, 2003). Resilience plays a critical role when older adults face the daily stress that comes from physical and mental loss with advancing age (e.g., changes in cognitive functioning, aging-related degradations in physical fitness), dysfunctional relationships with family members, increased isolation from society, and even the impact of extreme weather conditions (Yeung & Fung, 2007). Considering the significant meaning of resilience to older adults’ daily life, promotion of resilience among older adults is certainly worthy of lucubration. The promotion is even more urgent to Hong Kong given that one in three people will be 65 years old or above by 2036 (Census and Statistics Department, 2017). Among the various influential factors on resilience, health-related lifestyles and higher functionality of individuals are identified as having strong associations with high resilience (Hardy et al., 2004). Moreover, regular exercise and/or physical activity (PA) has been found to be the key mediator within these associations (Silverman & Deuster, 2014). Strength training was found to increase muscle strength by increasing muscle mass, and by improving the recruitment of motor units as well as increasing their firing rate in older adults. It was recommended that healthy old people should train 3 or 4 times weekly for the best results (Mayer et al, 2011). In a preliminary review, Windle (2012) found a lack of publications that had adopted an intervention design in the studies of resilience in older adults. He further recommended that studies employing randomized controlled trial (RCT) design with specific intervention strategies as well as less robust evaluation using controlled trials should be conducted. MacLeod and colleagues (2016) also found that the resilience interventions targeting older adults generally were not exist. They also found no tested interventions incorporating physical activity to build resilience among older adults, despite research suggesting that PA is an important factor of resilience. Based on the above comments of Windle (2012) and MacLeod and colleagues (2016), as well as the potential benefits of strength training contributes to the older people as indicated by Mayer and colleagues (2011), the current study aims to examine the effectiveness of resistance training on resilience among Chinese older adults in Hong Kong adopting a RCT design. 心理韌性是指在面對逆境、創傷、悲劇、威脅或重大壓力時做出的適應過程（美國心理學會，2004）。大量研究表明，心理韌性和自評的健康老齡化有密切的關係（Jeste等，2013；Wagnild，2003）。當長者面臨日常生活的壓力時，心理韌性起了重要作用。這些壓力來自隨著年齡增長而產生的生理和心理方面的落差（如認知功能的改變，身體素質的下降、失調的家庭關係、與日俱增的社會孤立感，甚至是極端天氣情況的影響（Yeung & Fung，2007。鑒於心理韌性對長者日常生活具有重要意義, 針對促進長者心理韌性的研究值得大家的支持。尤其是對香港長者來說更為迫切需要，因為到2036年，香港將有三分之一的長者達到65歲或以上（政府統計處，2017）。在眾多影響心理韌性的因素中，健康生活方式以及個體的身體機能與心理韌性有密切的關係（Hardy等，2004）。規律的鍛煉或體能活動也被證實在這些關係中起到了關鍵的中介作用（Silverman & Deuster，2014）。研究指出力量訓練可以通過提高肌肉體積和運動單位的募集能力和觸發率來提高長者的肌肉力量。對於身體健康的長者，建議每週鍛煉3到4次以達到最佳效果（Mayer等，2011）。Windle（2012）發現在目前已發表關於長者心理韌性的文章中，很少有研究者採用干預的研究設計。他建議未來可以採用有具體干預方案的隨機對照試驗 (RCT) 設計來進行研究。基於上述建議, 本研究採用了隨機對照試驗設計來檢驗力量訓練干預對於提高香港長者心理韌性的效果。

12610119.label: Realisation of objectives
12610119.value: Objective 1 was achieved. The effectiveness of resistance training was examined among 58 older adults using the functional fitness test, using the Senior Fitness Test Battery (Rikli & Jones, 2013), The Chinese version of the Resilience Scale (CRS) (Wagnild & Young, 1993), and The Chinese Short From -36 (C-SF-36) (Zhao & Chung, 2017). At first, 203 older adults were recruited, then 141 of them were involved in the eligibility screen test. After randomization, there were 58 older adults included in the resistance training group for the pre-test. There were 53 older adults who remained to participate in post-test and follow-up tests. From June 1 to September 26 2021, the intervention took place over 4 months (16 weeks), with 3 sessions per week and 60 minutes per session. Each session included 10min for warm-ups, 40min for the main exercise, and 10min for cool-down (Chung et al., 2021). The intensity was light to somewhat hard (RPE 11 to 13; using the Cantonese version of RPE) (Chung et al., 2013). The intervention content of the resistance training group was adapted from Seguin et al. (2002)’s “Growing Stronger: Strength Training for Older Adults”, and incorporate with some minor modifications under the professional advice from the Physical Fitness Association of Hong Kong, China. Other than bodyweight training, resistance training had utilized dumbbell weights and adjustable ankle weights ranging from 1kg to 3kg. The intensity of each exercise was 3-4 sets with 10-12 repetitions per set, using the circuit training approach. Adjustments were made according to the individual’s level of fitness, as well as adaptability and progression of the training. To enhance participants’ awareness of one’s progression and for better evaluation, a log sheet was provided for recording the intensity and achievement of each lesson. All the data were analysed using SPSS 27.0 Version (IBM, Chicago, IL), with the significance level at p<0.05. In regard to the intervention effect and intervention group differences, the one-way repeated measure analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted to determine the changes of each outcome parameter among the three-time points (i.e., pre-test, post-test, and follow-up test) within each group. Furthermore, the one-way analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) with the baseline value as a covariate was conducted with the outcomes at the post-test and follow-test to examine the group effect on each outcome parameter. For the primary outcome, the level of resilience among Hong Kong older adults was measured before, after, and three months after the intervention using ANOVA. It is important to note that the level of resilience showed no significant outcomes in ANOVA analysis, indicating a somewhat stable level of resilience before and after the intervention. For the secondary outcomes, including functional fitness and health-related quality of life, they were assessed using the same analytical method. Body Composition within the group effect showed significant results in the main factor ‘Time” with F(1.916,99.62)=17.70, p<0.001. Similarly, the fat percentage change of the within-subject effect only indicated a significant reduction in the Resistance Training group, with F(1.722,86.10)=9.704, p<0.001. For muscular strength and ability, the lower limb muscular strength and endurance using the 30s chair stand test did not show significant within-group differences in the “Time” factor in Resistance training. For Muscular Strength, the pairwise comparison revealed a significant reduction from pre-test to both post-test (difference = 2.327) and follow-up test (1.66). It showed a significant effect in the ‘Time x Group” interaction effect, with F(2,230)=6.66, p<0.001, as well. For endurance, however, no significant interaction effect was detected. For Flexibility and Dynamic Balance, both sides of the chair sit-and-reach test demonstrated significant differences within the Resistance Training Group, with F(2,102)=3.78, p=0.06 and F(2,70)=7.80,p=0.001, respectively. It showed a significant within-subject difference at both the left and right-hand side of the backstretch test, with F(1.85,92.58)=4.04,p=0.023 and F(2,100)=5.58, p=0.005, respectively. Among the variables within the quality of life scale, participants showed significant within-subject differences in bodily pain and social functioning. According to previous research, resistance training has mainly been compared with aerobic exercise in older adults' strength and fitness conditioning. This comparison demonstrates differences in muscle strength and aerobic ability between the two types of training. Concerning the relationship between resistance training and older adults' psychological outcomes, the effect and relationship between resistance training and cognitive function in older adults has tended to be examined (Chelho-Junior et al., 2022; Marvros et al., 2017). Despite resilience being considered an influential element in facilitating positive and active aging, there is a lack of resilience interventions focused on older adults in both the fields of psychology and health. Therefore, even though there is no significant difference in resilience to resistance training before and after the intervention, the current study provided updated evidence on the effectiveness of resistance training on older adults’ psychological status. Moreover, the study documented the high level of resistance and quality of life among Hong Kong older adults, so as the functional fitness level. Objective 2 was achieved. In the primary outcome, the ANCOVA showed no significant between-group differences in the level of resilience after the intervention. Nevertheless, based on the descriptive statistics, participants of the Tai Chi Group have a slightly higher resilience score than that of the Resistance Training Group. For secondary outcomes, the differences between the intervention groups and control groups were demonstrated using the planned contrast and ANCOVA analysis at different time points. For muscle strength, Planned contrast revealed that there was a significant difference in the arm curl test among the intervention groups and control group, t(125)=-2.596, p=0.01, after the intervention. The ANCOVA outcomes have also demonstrated a significant between-group effect in the post- and follow-up time point. For aerobic ability, the planned contrast also revealed a significant difference among the intervention groups and control group in the post-test, with t(123)=-2.82, p=0.006. It has also shown a significant between-group effect in both post-and follow-up test. For flexibility and dynamic balance, planned contrast revealed that there was a significant difference in the left-hand side of the backstretch test among the Tai Chi Group and Resistant Training Group in the post-test, t(123)=-2.29, p=0.02, and a significant difference in the 8ft up-and-go test among Tai Chi Group and Resistant Training Group in the post-test, t(124)=-2.95, p=0.004. In the follow-up test, the planned contrast mainly focused on the results of the body compositions, including BMI and fat percentages. They showed significant differences between the intervention groups and control group yet not between the Tai Chi and resistance training groups. Among the variables within the quality of life scale, participants in all groups showed significant within-subject differences in bodily pain and social functioning while the Tai Chi group showed significant differences in physical functioning, with F(1.98, 67.3)=3.28, p=0.04. However, the ANCOVA showed no significant between-group differences in all aspects of quality of life, so as the planned contrast. Based on the between-group effect, it has been found that Tai Chi can increase muscle strength and endurance in older adults rather than only psychological and physical balance outcomes. In summary, the research found that Tai Chi is more effective in enhancing older adults' psychological status, and resilience, especially. While both intervention groups have improved older adults’ overall functional fitness compared with the control group, yet to a smaller extent in terms of statistical significance.

12610119.label: Major findings and research outcome
12610119.value: In terms of resilience and quality of life, according to descriptive statistics, the Tai Chi group participants appeared to have a significantly higher level of improvement than the Resistance Training group based on descriptive statistics. In resilience, all groups showed no significant differences in the within-subject effect and the "Time x Group" interaction effect. On the quality of life scale, participants in all groups showed significant within-subject differences in bodily pain and social functioning while the Tai Chi group displayed significant differences in physical functioning, with F(1.98, 67.3)=3.28, p=0.04. In terms of the functional fitness level, the analysis indicated that resistance training participants showed significant improvements in upper limb muscular strength and endurance as well as flexibility. In addition, they showed significant reductions in fat percentage. Tai Chi participants demonstrated significant improvement in lower limb muscles and aerobic ability. Nonetheless, both groups demonstrated a significant reduction in BMI. Significant differences were seen between the intervention and control groups in the arm curl and aerobic ability tests compared to the control group. However, significant differences were only seen between the intervention groups (Tai Chi and Resistance Training) in the flexibility and dynamic balance test. In general, Hong Kong older adults have a relatively high level of resilience and quality of life. Also, they have a medium level of functional fitness compared to the functional fitness norm published in 2016 (Chung et al., 2016). Despite the differences in the psychological outcomes being not notable, there were significant differences in some of the major functional fitness items when comparing both within-group and between-group effects.

12610119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12610119.value: To extend our existing work, further studies may consider: 1. Investigate and examine the potential moderating and mediating factors within the association between resistance training and psychological outcomes, such as personality traits, social interaction, and other self-actualisation elements. 2. Study the goal-related moderators or elements that may influence the effectiveness of the interventions, such as self-efficacy, self-regulation, goal setting effect and the coaching style of the instructor that might have affected participants’ goal setting strategies. 3. To develop and examine the effectiveness of resistance training plus interventions (e.g., resistance training plus stretching or yoga training), which aim to improve the effectiveness of the intervention program, especially psychological outcomes. 4. To explore participants' perceptions and feelings about the intervention program, identify facilitators and barriers to the intervention, and evaluate the quality of the intervention. This facilitates the improvement and sustainability of future intervention studies.

12610119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12610119.value: Resilience is being seen as a psychological variable that facilitates successful and positive ageing. Combined with active ageing, mind-body intervention and aerobic exercises were commonly examined for their effects on self-related successful ageing, yet the effect of resistance training remained inconsistent in this study. According to the results of the study, both intervention groups experienced significant reductions in BMI as well as significant improvements in overall fitness when compared with the control group. Despite this, there were no significant differences between groups in terms of resilience and quality of life after the intervention. Tai Chi group participants showed a higher level of improvement than that of resistance training group participants. In future studies, the moderator and mediating factors that affect the effectiveness of resistance training on psychological outcomes should be examined, or more directly, mind-body exercises should be incorporated into resistance training in order to enhance the psychological benefits that resistance training brings, while simultaneously promoting active ageing.

13100019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13100019.value: 時至今日，全球共發現356種龜。由於部份己鑑定的物種可能為多於一個單一物種的種群，實際上龜類的物種數目可能更多。現時大部分龜類均為受威脅物種，準確辨認每一個物種以及其分佈是保育它們的基礎，加深對它們的認知有助策劃有效的保育措施。 本計劃的目的為了解兩種亞洲龜類 – 大頭龜(Platysternon megacephalum) 以及眼斑水龜(Sacalia bealei) 的生態及其演化歷程，並將研究所得用於未來的保育計劃上。根據國際自然保護聯盟瀕危物種紅色名錄，以上兩種龜己被列入瀕危 (EN) 級別。現時對這兩種龜的生態和種群上的認知不多，促使我們進行此研究。再者，上述龜類在香港尚有穩定族群，增加此研究的可行性。直至此刻，在親緣地理學及族群遺傳學方面，尚未有關於這兩種龜的研究在進行中。本研究將使用受廣泛認可的雙限制酶切位點標定法(double digest restriction site-associated DNA sequencing [ddRADseq]) 闡明兩個龜種的生態以及其演化歷程。相比其他方法，ddRADseq在採集大量個體的基因組數據時比較便宜。初步研究的結果證實ddRADseq能有效採集這兩種龜的基因數據：在大頭龜發現最少1467個基因座；在眼斑水龜發現最少3307個基因座 (共10%數據遺失)。在電腦運算及分析下，採集到的數據有助了解它們族群之間的關係﹑幫助估計有效族群大小﹑了解基因流動的情況以及其繁殖生物學。最終，研究所得將會引領臨場棲息地及族群保育，亦有助於龜類人工繁殖計劃。 保育工作的成效取決於研究人員﹑政府及非政府組織之間的互相合作。本計畫以進化生物學及生態學的角度為保育瀕危的大頭龜及眼斑水龜定下根基。本研究將會： 1. 闡明大頭龜及眼斑水龜的演化歷程；2. 提供它們生態學及繁殖生物學上的見解；3. 協助香港龜類保育計劃，並將與政府部門 (漁農自然護理署) ﹑非政府組織 (嘉道理農場暨植物園﹑香港海洋公園保育基金﹑香港兩棲及爬行動物保育基金 – 香港兩棲及爬蟲協會) 合作。通過實行研究及一系列的保育計劃，大頭龜及眼斑水龜將免於絕種，有望成為亞洲龜類保育的典範。

In this study, we included samples collected by ourselves, along with samples from seven international institutions. We believe that we were successful in this objective, and we will soon publish several papers on the subject. We believe our work will encourage future researchers to use the ddRADseq method for genetic studies of turtles. (b) Clarify the genetic relationships between populations of P. megacephalum and S. bealei across Asia and in Hong Kong (100% COMPLETE) THIS OBJECTIVE HAS BEEN COMLETELY ACHIEVED. • Outcome 1a: Evaluate the validity of named subspecies. Currently, there are three recognised subspecies of P. megacephalum: P. m. megacephalum (Vietnam and China [Anhui, Fujian, Guangdong Guangxi, Hong Kong, Hunan, Jiangxi, Zhejiang], P. m. peguense (China [Hainan], Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam), and P. m shiui (Vietnam and China [Guangxi, Hainan]). These results are based on a morphological analysis (Ernst & Laemmerzahl 2002). We provide support of the three subspecies with genetic data. Also, our results point towards the presence of only one subspecies in Hainan Province, China. This will need to be further investigated with additional samples. We also have new findings for to regions—Myanmar and Hong Kong. For Myanmar, we include specimens from two wildlife seizures. These samples separate into three distinct clusters; although we do not know the origin of these samples, this provides a working hypothesis that populations in Myanmar have genetic structure and are genetically distinct. This will need to be tested with known-locality samples. Lastly, for Hong Kong, populations in different stream drainages are genetically distinct. This result highlights the importance of geographic barriers—instead of mountains, which are usually barriers, lowland valleys seem to separate populations of this high-elevation species. • Outcome 2a: Evaluate the higher-level relationships between populations across its geographic range. Sacalia bealei is found in southern China (Guangdong, Fujian, Jiangxi Provinces, and Hong Kong). Previous studies of S. bealei found that this species has low genetic variation (Lin et al. 2022). In contrast, using a genetic technique with more resolution, we found that S. bealei is more genetically diverse and has more geographic structure than previously believed. Each of our three geographic localities were genetically distinct. What was surprising is that the two populations in Hong Kong are genetically distinct, despite a short geographic distance. This again highlights the importance of geographic barriers in Hong Kong keeping populations separated. Additionally, our work provides a roadmap for future research, emphasises the need for sampling from Guangdong and Jiangxi Provinces. (c) Provide insight on the ecology and reproductive biology of P. megacephalum and S. bealei. (60% COMPLETE) WE UNDER-ACHIEVED IN THIS OBJECTIVE BECAUSE OF DIFFICULTY DISTINGUISHING BETWEEN NATURAL AND ANTHROPOGENIC FACTORS. ATTEMPTING TO OVERCOME THIS PROBLEM, WE RAN DIFFERENT ANALYSES. RESULTS ARE PROMISING, BUT OTHER LABORATORY AND ANALYTICAL METHODS ARE NEEDED (NOT IN THE SCOPE OF BUDGET). TO COMPENSATE, WE PUT MORE EFFORT INTO THE PHYLOGENETIC ANALYSES (OBJECTIVE “B”) WHERE THE RESULTS WERE MORE RELIABLE. • Outcome 1b, 2b: Understand the population genetics (population substructure, population size), ecology (effective population size, gene flow), and reproductive biology (parentage, mating system) of S. bealei and P. megacephalum and populations of Hong Kong. SACALIA BEALEI We successfully ran analyses to infer the population substructure (Structure) and gene flow (FineRADstructure), while other analyses (Migrate-N, Colony, Related) produced inconclusive results. Introgression and gene flow were inferred between the three groups. This was supported by the relatively close co-ancestry of individuals between the different groups; the “all” group contains individuals from all three groups. However, this result is confounded by the wildlife trade, since this pattern can be produced artificially through human transport of individuals. These results are promising, but more work needs to be done to differentiate between natural and artificial causes. PLATYSTERNON MEGACEPHALUM The same analyses were run for P. megacephalum, and the results were similar—detection of introgression and gene flow between groups. These results are promising, but more work needs to be done to differentiate between natural and artificial causes. In our submitted manuscript (Fong et al., under review), which was made possible through sampling of faces during this project, we found that wild populations in Hong Kong have distinct faecal microbiotas. Additionally, P. megacephalum and S. bealei from the same site have distinct faecal microbiotas. This implies that geography and species identity are important factors in shaping the gut microbiota, with diet (preference, availability) being important. (d) Apply results to advise the conservation of these two species by working with NGOs (Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden, Ocean Park Conservation Foundation, Hong Kong Society of Herpetology Foundation) and a governmental department (Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department). (90% COMPLETE) CONSERVATION IS AN ONGOING PROCESS, WHICH IS WHY WE SET THE COMPLETION OF THIS GOAL TO 90%. WE HAVE ALREADY MADE TREMENDOUS PROGRESS IN APPLYING OUR WORK TO THE CONSERVATION OF THESE SPECIES, BUT MORE WORK CAN BE DONE. WE WILL CONTINUE WORKING WITH GOVERNMENTS AND NGOS TO CONSERVE THESE SPECIES. • Outcome 3a: Provide genetics-based recommendations to improve ex situ breeding. PLATYSTERNON MEGACEPHALUM Our work has provided genetic data supporting the population structure across Asia, as well as in Hong Kong. We have worked with AFCD to draft a species action plan (using these data as evidence) for P. megacephalum. This document will guide conservation management of this species in Hong Kong. Additionally, we have shared these data with Wildlife Conservation Society-Myanmar to aid in their breeding of their trade seized animals, and they have provided emails thanking us. SACALIA BEALEI This species is currently the focus of a breeding programme in Hong Kong (Ocean Park, HKHERP, Lingnan University). These data are currently being used to guide how to combine breeding pairs to preserve natural genetic structure, as well as maintain diversity. In particular, we identified the genetic origin of the individuals, with one individual from Hong Kong. • Outcome 3b: Provide ecological data to aid in the proper management of habitats and populations. The finding that is most important for proper management in Hong Kong is that both species have genetically distinct populations across Hong Kong. This means that care needs to be taken when translocating individuals. For example, when there is a wildlife conservation in Hong Kong, AFCD needs to determine its geographic origin before releasing it to the wild. If released to the incorrect population, it may cause unnatural introgression. These findings have been included in the species action plan of P. megacephalum.

13100019.label: Major findings and research outcome
13100019.value: Through genomic analysis, we have a better understanding of the phylogeographic pattern in two endangered turtle species: Platysternon megacephalum and Sacalia bealei. Both species exhibit genetic structure in relation to geography. For P. megacephalum, our data to supports the validity of the three morphological/geographic subspecies, while for S. bealei, we discovered it to be genetically different across its range. These are both new discoveries. These findings are foundational in guiding conservation management. We discuss two issues here. First, both species are in conservation breeding programmes to ensure their survival. These findings guide how to select breeding pairs to preserve diversity and the natural, evolutionary patterns. For S. bealei, we identified the geographic origin of the 33 individuals in the breeding colony: 17 from Fujian, 1 from Hong Kong, and 15 uncertain. In this case, we need to identify and obtain more native Hong Kong individuals to preserve the local population. Second, these species are often involved in the wildlife trade, and problems arise during trade seizures because the origin of individuals is unknown. Our work provides a case study on using DNA to identify the origin of trade seizure individuals. Several years ago, the Hong Kong government seized some P. megacephalum, and released them back to the wild at an isolated site. We identify these individuals to, luckily, be native to a nearby site in Hong Kong. Future conservation action of these two species can now be properly planned by being grounded in scientific data. We have shared these data and are working with the Hong Kong government (AFCD) and local NGOs (Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden, Ocean Park, Hong Kong Society of Herpetology Foundation). These partnerships will continue beyond the completion of this project, to develop science-based conservation plans for these two Hong Kong species. Additionally, this work has made impact through research output: 1 MPhil student, 2 presentations at international conferences, and 3 publications in peer-reviewed journals. The MPhil student will graduate in 2024 and pursue a career in wildlife conservation. The presentations provided exposure for our work and helped initiate future collaborations. For the publications, two are under review (BMC Microbiology [IF=4.465], Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution [IF=5.019]) and one under preparation (target Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution [IF=5.019]). One publication on the faecal microbiota of these two species, seemingly unrelated, was possible by leveraging sample collection (simultaneously collected blood samples for DNA and faecal samples for microbiota).

13100019.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13100019.value: We lay groundwork for future studies. The completed genetic work has advanced our knowledge, but is incomplete; due to limitations in availability, not all geographic locations were included. We have identified the important regions for future fieldwork to collect new samples. These species are found in different countries/regions, so we will strengthen and develop international collaborations to pursue this work. Additionally, with the growth of the field of molecular ecology (using molecular techniques to address questions in ecology, evolution, behaviour, and conservation) through newly developed methods, we will explore ways to leverage the data we have collected to further understand these species. Also, with the utility of the ddRADseq method being demonstrated, we will explore using this approach to study other species in Hong Kong. We have already leveraged our experience to obtain funding (Ocean Park Conservation Fund) to study another endangered turtle species in Hong Kong—the Wattle-necked Softshell Turtle (Palea steindachneri). Lastly, one important result of this project is the close collaboration with the Hong Kong government and NGOs. We will continue communicating with these parties to identify the urgent research needs for conservation. This approach is important to ensure the usefulness and impact of our research.

13100019.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13100019.value: Turtles worldwide are endangered. To protect them, we should first evaluate the similarity/difference of populations by comparing their DNA. In this study, we compare the DNA of populations of two endangered Hong Kong species: Big-headed Turtle (Platysternon megacephalum) and Beale’s-eyed Turtle (Sacalia bealei). For the Big-headed Turtle, we found that DNA can separate the three subspecies, and even different Hong Kong locations. The results were similar for the Beale’s-eyed Turtle, with DNA distinguishing populations in Hong Kong and Mainland China. These results contribute to our theoretical understanding of how new species form—geographic barriers (oceans, unsuitable habitat) separate the species and allow populations to become different. Practical application of this work is with conservation management. Identifying the origin of individuals helps in captive breeding and wildlife trade seizures. We work with Ocean Park and HKHERP to breed the Beale’s-eyed Turtle, ensuring only Hong Kong males and females are paired for breeding. Also, we work with the HK government to identify the origin of trade seizures so they can be released back to the wild. We will continue working with these partners to develop science-based conservation plans for these valuable Hong Kong species.

13500119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13500119.value: Servant leadership is unique among leadership approaches because of its prioritization of serving the needs of all followers and helping them achieve their full potential. This leadership approach has positive effects on followers, groups, and organizations. Now that these positive results have been consistently supported, even when controlling other approaches to leadership (Hoch, Bommer, Dulebohn, & Wu, 2018), it is time to explore another key tenet of servant leadership theory—that group members reciprocally affect servant leaders, resulting in an upward spiral of servant leadership development. This project focuses on the leadership transition period in which leaders are newly promoted. During this transition period, which involves new leader-member and leader-group relationships, we investigate the dynamics of the development of servant leadership and exchange relationships. We first theorize the reciprocal associations of servant leadership with the two types of exchange relationships influenced by the new leaders: leader-member exchange (LMX) and team-member exchange (TMX). The reciprocal associations suggest that servant leadership nurtures high-quality, serving relationships not only between leader-member dyads but also among group members. Furthermore, they depict the co-development of servant leadership and exchange relationships within new leader-member dyads and between new leaders and their groups. Second, we examine the broader relational context as a contingent factor for the co-development process of servant leadership and exchange relationships. Group members in the leadership transition period tend to interpret their relationships with the new leader based on their relationships with the former leader (i.e., the transference effect). In particular, the literature highlights the salient effect of the former leader’s abusive supervision. We thus examine its moderating role in the influence of new leader servant leadership on LMX and TMX. Third, we examine the dynamics of how servant leadership affects the performance and well-being of leaders through LMX and TMX during leadership transition. This knowledge will advance servant leadership theory and address practical concerns on how to retain and develop servant leaders who are assets to organizations and who contribute positively to the work climate and organizational bottom line. We will test our hypotheses in two longitudinal field studies covering the leadership transition period. One involves “seasoned” leaders, and the other involves junior leaders who are leading for the first time. The leadership transition context, which involves new leader-member and leader-group exchange relationships, provides a unique opportunity to examine our theoretical model regarding the co-development of servant leadership and exchange relationships. 服務型領導力是一種獨特的領導力方式。這種領導力方式關注下屬，強調服務所有下屬的需求及幫助下屬充分地發揮潛能。它對下屬，工作團隊，乃至企業都有正面的作用。即使控制了其他領導力方式，實證研究仍然一致地證明了這些正面作用的顯著性。在現有文獻的基礎上，本研究擬探索服務型領導力的另一主旨：團隊成員能夠反向地影響領導，從而呈現出一種持續的服務型領導力的發展的良性循環。 本研究聚焦于領導更替時期。在這個時期，團隊領導剛獲晉升，替代舊的領導；工作團隊中需要發展新的領導-成員和領導-團隊交換關係。我們研究服務型領導和這些人際交換關係如何在這個時期發展。首先，我們探索服務型領導力和工作情景下的兩種主要的人際交換關係（即：領導-成員交換和團隊-成員交換）之前的互惠關係。服務型領導力不僅有利於發展高質量的領導-成員交換關係，還有利於成員與其團隊發展高質量的交換關係。這兩種交換關係能夠進一步地推動服務型領導力的提高。因此，在領導更替時期，服務型領導力與人際交換關係能夠協同發展。 其次，我們從人際關係的角度探索上述關係的邊界條件。在領導更替期間，團隊成員如何看待他們與新領導的關係受到他們與舊領導的關係的影響。尤其地，文獻強調了舊領導的辱虐型領導力的作用。因此，本研究探索舊領導的辱虐型領導力對上述關係的調節作用。 第三，我們研究服務型領導如何通過人際交換關係的中介作用，對領導自身的工作績效和身心健康產生影響。此研究對於如何保留和發展服務型領導具有重大的現實意義。 本研究涉及兩個涵蓋了整個領導更替時期的縱向實地研究。第一個研究涉及有領導經驗的領導的更替，第二個研究涉及無領導經驗的領導（即首次從基層員工晉升到領導職級）的更替。這兩個縱向研究為探索服務型領導力與人際交換關係的協同發展提供了獨特和有價值的實證基礎。

13500119.label: Realisation of objectives
13500119.value: Our research team has successfully met the three project objectives (PO) based on two major projects, underpinned by three large-scale, independent longitudinal field studies. In Project 1, we collected five-wave, multisource longitudinal field data from a large manufacturing company, involving 3,712 employees, 474 team leaders, and 97 executive leaders. Project 2 included two separate studies in the new leader onboarding context. The first study collected five-wave field data from 1,103 employees undergoing leadership transitions within a large manufacturing company. The second study involved six-wave, multisource longitudinal field data collection from 1,087 employees and 319 new leaders at a large retail company. In Project 1, based on the demands-resources theory, we propose and test a dual-path model that explores how servant leadership influences leader job performance and psychological strain through two psychological pathways: the energizing pathway through leader need satisfaction and the draining pathway through leader role conflict. Additionally, we introduce leader-leader exchange (LLX) as a pivotal moderating resource that not only enhances the positive impacts of servant leadership but also mitigates its potential negative consequences. This research framework is crucial for elucidating the impact of servant leadership on new leaders’ performance and well-being (PO #3) and the moderators of these relationships (PO #2). Servant leadership is renowned for its emphasis on prioritizing the needs of followers and other stakeholders, contributing significantly to various organizational, team, and individual outcomes. However, critiques of this model suggest a potential downside: leaders may prioritize others at the expense of their own well-being, potentially leading to strain and diminished performance, thus questioning the sustainability of such leadership practices. Nevertheless, this perspective may overlook the inherently prosocial nature of servant leadership, which can also energize leaders. Existing research provides mixed views on these dual impacts of servant leadership on leaders, lacking detailed insights into the mechanisms and conditions under which servant leadership is more beneficial. Our project addresses these gaps by developing a nuanced understanding of the underlying processes and the circumstances that optimize the balance between personal benefits and costs. This has significant implications for practicing sustainable leadership that effectively serves and benefits others. This research has been published in Journal of Applied Psychology. In the initial submission, the field study used a multi-wave, multi-source design, involving matched cases of 123 managers and 1,372 employees. The review team suggested that we should explore the dynamics of servant leadership and therefore we conducted a new longitudinal field study. In Project 2, we ground our theoretical model and empirical research within the context of new leader onboarding to address the three key Project Objectives. This project is completed and under friendly review and will be submitted to Academy of Management Journal for publication consideration. The success of new leaders during onboarding periods has become a focal point for both researchers and practitioners due to the prevalence of such transitions and their inherent challenges. Statistics indicate that about one-third of leaders are transitioning at any given time, with nearly half of internally promoted leaders failing to meet expectations. Securing follower support is crucial for new leaders, as appointment alone does not guarantee this backing. Servant leadership has been shown to effectively build relationships and garner support. Nevertheless, new leaders often encounter a dilemma with servant leadership. While building relationships is essential, the sustainability of this demanding approach and its actual impact on team performance during onboarding remain concerns. On the one hand, servant leadership demands a significant investment in meeting followers' needs, potentially depleting leaders' resources. This calls for further exploration into how new leaders can sustainably adopt servant leadership practices. On the other hand, the onboarding process typically stresses the importance of demonstrating immediate high performance and results, which might conflict with the servant leadership’s emphasis on addressing followers’ personal goals over organizational objectives. The intensive focus required to invest in followers and build relationships during the tumultuous onboarding period raises questions about its efficacy in improving team performance. To address these complexities, we utilize the central tenets of social exchange theory—focusing on direct, indirect, and generalized reciprocity—and integrate the leader- and follower-centric perspectives to propose a dynamic reciprocal relationship between servant leadership and leader-member exchange (LMX) and team-member exchange (TMX) during the onboarding of new leaders. We hypothesize and test the self-reinforcing spirals between servant leadership and these two types of exchange relationships (PO #1), which are crucial for the sustainable practice of servant leadership during challenging onboarding periods. Moreover, we explore whether increases in LMX and TMX can clarify the mechanisms through which servant leadership influences team performance during new leader onboarding (PO #3). The dynamic nature of this period, a critical phase of transition and development for teams, makes improvements in team performance particularly significant. Our research provides vital insights into the factors driving these performance gains and examines how increases in LMX and TMX differentially contribute to team performance improvement. Existing research primarily at the individual level, employing cross-sectional designs, has shown that LMX plays a more significant role than TMX in predicting individual job performance. However, our study expands on this by using a longitudinal approach to rigorously test the lagged effects of changes in both LMX and TMX in an integrated model. Our findings reveal that TMX, rather than LMX, holds stronger predictive power for team performance. The increase in LMX might lead to an over-investment in individual follower relationships and solicit closer scrutiny of how economic resources are allocated among team members. This focus could shift attention away from team performance achievement. Our research underscores that the dynamics of social exchanges at the team level exhibit unique characteristics and impacts that differ significantly from those at the individual level. Third, we identify and analyze unique boundary conditions that affect the impact of servant leadership and the development of social exchange relationships during new leader onboarding (PO #2). Incorporating both relational and leadership succession perspectives, we explore how negative social exchanges from former leaders’ abusive supervision can hinder the development of LMX and TMX by new servant leaders. Our study thus sheds light on the lasting effects of previous leadership behaviors and the potential for servant leadership to overcome these challenges. Our findings illustrate how servant leadership can enable new leaders to win over followers previously abused by their former leaders. Notably, the field studies for our research projects were conducted in companies listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. These studies facilitated us to develop productive research and consultancy relationships with these companies, allowing us to effectively transfer our findings into the managerial policies, practices, standards, and behaviors of these companies. In a project with a large manufacturing company, which faces significant challenges in attracting, managing, and retaining staff due to the nature of the work (low skill requirements and long working hours), our research led to significant enhancements in managerial and leadership practices. These improvements increased employee satisfaction and reduced turnover. In another project, conducted with a large retail company, we provided insights into leadership and store management that substantially improved store sales performance. Our initiatives, which promote people-oriented leadership and relationship-building, have been instrumental in creating a more inclusive and cohesive workplace, contributing to overall performance and wellbeing.

13500119.label: Major findings and research outcome
13500119.value: In Project 1, we investigated how servant leadership impacts leader wellbeing and performance, revealing nuanced relationships moderated by LLX. 1. Servant leadership boosted psychological need satisfaction, reducing leader psychological strain. However, this effect did not extend to improving leader job performance. Additionally, the positive effects of servant leadership on reducing psychological strain were more pronounced when LLX was high. When LLX was low, high levels of servant leadership resulted in decreased need satisfaction and then increased psychological strain. 2. While no direct relationship was found between servant leadership and leader role conflict, LLX moderated this relationship. When LLX was low, high levels of servant leadership increased role conflict, resulting in higher psychological strain and poorer job performance. When LLX was high, high levels of servant leadership helped reduce role conflict, leading to lower psychological strain and enhanced job performance. We contribute to the servant leadership theory and practices by unpacking its energizing and draining mechanisms. The moderating role of LLX sheds light on when this demanding leadership is beneficial to leaders’ well-being and performance. In Project 2, we focused on the new leader onboarding context and explored (1) the reciprocal relationships between new leader servant leadership and LMX/TMX; (2) the mediating effects of increase in LMX/TMX on the relationships between new leader servant leadership and increase in team performance; and (3) the moderating effects of former leader abusive supervision. 1. Across the two longitudinal studies, we consistently found that servant leadership and LMX/TMX positively influenced each other in a reciprocal manner. These reciprocal relationships created an upward spiral where servant leadership facilitated new leaders to enhance exchange relationships with followers and among followers; Increased social exchanges further promoted the development of servant leadership in new leaders. 2. Increase in TMX, but not increase in LMX, contributed to improved team performance. Increase in TMX, but not LMX, also mediated the positive effect of new leader servant leadership on team performance improvement. 3. The abusive supervision of former leaders weakens the positive associations between new leader servant leadership and LMX/TMX in the team for new leaders with relatively shorter leadership tenure. This weakening moderating effect does not apply to new leaders with longer leadership tenure. Our findings provide crucial insights into the sustainability of servant leadership practices. The distinctive effects of the two types of social exchange underscore building strong team relationships to enhance performance under new leadership.

13500119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13500119.value: 1. Exploring the differential impact of LMX and TMX on Team Performance. Future research should explore the nuances and dynamics of these exchanges at the team level. It is valuable to examine whether increase in LMX leads to an over-investment in redundant follower relationships and solicit closer scrutiny of how economic resources are allocated among team members, which shift attention away from team performance achievement. 2. Developing and testing a more time-sensitive model for leadership transition. Future research should also focus on developing and testing a time-sensitive model and conducting longitudinal field studies that cover the actual leadership transition. Such a model would facilitate a comprehensive examination of the joint effects of new leaders’ leadership approaches and the historical context of their teams, including the influence of former leaders leadership approaches. This approach will provide a deeper understanding of how these factors jointly influence the development of relationships and, ultimately, performance outcomes. 3. Investigate gender differences. Given that servant leadership is often viewed as a communal-oriented approach, its effects might vary by gender. This research conjecture provides crucial insights into the gender (dis)advantages for new leaders adopting servant leadership during onboarding.

13500119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13500119.value: Servant leadership is valued because it helps build relationships and enhance work outcomes. But there’s a catch: servant leaders may lean too far into serving others to the detriment of oneself. While it focuses on serving others, leaders must be cautious not to neglect their own well-being and performance. Our research shows that servant leaders thrive when they have supportive bosses. Without that support, engaging in servant leadership can become exhausting. For new leaders, practicing servant leadership is beneficial during their onboarding periods. It allows them to establish strong relationships with followers and nurture strong relationships among followers in the team. This cultivation of strong interpersonal relationships creates a self-reinforcing cycle, making servant leadership a sustainable practice during challenging onboarding periods. Importantly, it’s the improvement of interpersonal relationships among team members, rather than just between the leader and the team, that really boosts team performance. Moreover, consistently practicing servant leadership can be a powerful strategy for new leaders to win over followers who have experienced poor treatment from previous leaders. By putting their team’s needs first, leaders can transform a challenging start into a strong foundation for collective success.

13500619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13500619.value: 在很多情況下，消費者需要通過搜索從而獲得產品信息。現有的文獻注重搜索環境帶來的影響而忽略了購買后賠償（例如產品責任）影響消費者搜索以及福利。最近，平臺對銷售產品的責任引起了廣汎的社會關注。 產品責任應該如何在平臺与銷售者之間分配？為了回答這個問題，我們構建一個消費者搜索模型。在模型里，消費者在購買產品之前不能分辨產品質量的好壞。但如果產品造成消費者損失后，銷售者和平臺可能需要作出賠償。初步的分析顯示越高的銷售者產品責任會導致越高的產品價格，所以消費者福利不一定提高。例外，如果平臺對消費者損失負一定對責任時，整體消費者福利會提高。這個研究計劃為現有的文獻帶來新的研究分析，對平臺与銷售者產品責任的分配有政策意義。

13500619.label: Realisation of objectives
13500619.value: In order to accomplish objective 1, we have developed a theoretical model of consumer search that builds upon Stahl's work (1989) while incorporating the fact that experts can be held accountable for the services they provide. Our model focuses on an expert market where each consumer faces either a major or minor problem. A major treatment can address both types of problems, but it is up to the expert to identify the problem and offer the consumer a recommended treatment at a certain price. The consumer is unable to directly observe the type of problem they have, and they can choose to accept the expert's offer or continue searching for other experts and their offers sequentially. If the consumer accepts an expert's offer, the expert is obligated to solve the problem, and the consumer can verify the treatment performed. However, experts may have higher profits from major treatments compared to minor ones, creating an incentive for them to recommend major treatments even for minor problems. Regarding objective 2, we conduct an analysis of equilibrium and comparative statics. Specifically, we establish a symmetric perfect Bayesian equilibrium, where searchers determine an optimal reservation price for each recommended treatment, while experts choose treatment prices using mixed strategies. In this equilibrium, experts always recommend a major treatment for a major problem. However, they may engage in deceit by recommending a major treatment even for a minor problem. We verify the existence of this equilibrium and then analyze how it is affected by variations in search friction, market competition, and expert liability. To achieve objective 3, we examine various scenarios in which experts may or may not be held liable for treatment outcomes, treatments may or may not be verifiable by consumers, and the presence or absence of marketplace organization. We compare the welfare outcomes under these different situations and draw conclusions regarding the policies that should be implemented to address the issue of asymmetric information in expert markets.
