14306519.label: Major findings and research outcome
14306519.value: (1) Development of selective cage C functionalization of o-carboranes via photolysis of cage C-I bond (Pub. #2 and #13) Photoalkynylation and photocyclization of iodocarboranes with a wide variety of alkynes have been developed for the first time, which is a very promising approach for clean, efficient, transition-metal-free and cheap synthesis of a large class of 1-alkynyl-o-carboranes and o-carborane-fused cyclics. As this reaction does not require strong bases, photocatalysts and high temperatures, it has a broad substrate scope. The mechanistic studies indicate that the reaction proceeds via the radical process. The isolation of carborane-fused spiro product suggests that the reaction involves the formation of a spiro radical species, which is responsible for the generation of regioisomers of the cyclization products. This work represents significant advances over the known methods for the synthesis of 1-alkynyl-o-carboranes, and also sets a very good example for the functionalization of boron clusters using photochemistry. On the other hand, a synthetic method to alkenylated-o-carboranes via photoalkenylation of iodocarboranes with unactivated alkenes has been achieved. This reaction features a transition-metal-free protocol, light-promoted reaction with mild reaction conditions, broad substrate scope and good functional group tolerance. (2) Development of selective cage C functionalization of o-carboranes via merging photochemistry with base metal catalysis (Pub. #5). A light-promoted Cu catalyzed cage C-arylation of non-prefunctionalized o-carboranes with a variety of aryl iodides at room temperature has been developed, leading to the preparation of a variety of 1-aryl-o-carboranes and o-carborane-fused cyclics. Employment of earth abundant copper as catalyst, this method also demonstrates the advantages of using simple o-carboranes as starting material, not prefunctionalized iodocarboranes, and mild reaction condition under room temperature. (3) Development of selective cage C functionalization of o-carboranes via carboryne intermediates (Pub. #1, #8 and #9). Using 1-Li-2-OTf-o-C2B10H10 as precursor, o-carboryne undergoes an efficient [2 + 2] cycloaddition with a large variety of vinyl ethers at room temperature to give a series of carborane-fused cyclobutanes in very good to high isolated yields. On the other hand, o-carboryne undergoes an efficient [4 + 2] cycloaddition with various conjugated enynes, followed by a subsequent [2 + 2] cycloaddition at room temperature, generating a series of carborane-fused tricyclo[6.4.0.02,7]dodeca-2,12-dienes in moderate to high isolated yields. Furthermore, o-carboryne reacts at room temperature with a large variety of alkynes and alkenes possessing α-CH proton to give a series of o-carboranyl allenes and alkenes in good to high isolated yields. These reactions have a broad substrate scope from alkyl, aryl to silyl substituents. This protocol provides a facile synthetic method to access cage C-substituted carboranyl derivatives. (4) Understanding the reaction mechanisms (Pub. #2, #8 and #15) On the basis of control experiments and DFT calculations, reaction mechanisms involving cage carbon-centered carboranyl radicals have been proposed to account for the formation of the products. (5) Development of other methods for cage C functionalization of o-carboranes (Pub. #6, #11, and #14) New methods for cage C functionalization of o-carboranes via the insertion of unsaturated molecules into the cage C-B bond(s) have also been developed. In summary, this original work has resulted in 15 peer-reviewed articles published in international chemistry journals including J. Am. Chem. Soc. (x 1), Nat. Commun. (x 1), Chem. Soc. Rev. (x 1), Chem. Sci. (x 2), Org. Lett. (x 1), Dalton Trans. (x 2), Organometallics (x 2), New J. Chem. (x1), and J. Mater. Chem C (x1). PI was invited to give one plenary, two keynote and one invited lectures at international conferences. Two PhD students have been trained, of which one has been graduated.

14306519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14306519.value: Functionalization of o-carboranes via transition metal catalysis and photochemistry has been achieved. We wonder if electrochemistry could be another approach for selective functionalization of o-carboranes.

14306519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14306519.value: Carboranes, a class of carbon-boron molecular clusters, can be viewed as three-dimensional analogues of benzene. They are finding many applications in coordination/ organometallic chemistry as versatile ligands, in medicine as boron neutron capture therapy agents and in supramolecular design/nanomaterials as useful building blocks. All this has recently drawn considerable attention to carborane chemistry. However, the exceptional thermal and chemical stable 3D structures of carboranes make their derivatization difficult, limiting their application scope. The development of an efficient and general technique to functionalize carboranes will be one of the main issues in this field. In this project, we have developed several reactions for the functionalization of carboranes, leading to the invention of several methods for the efficient synthesis of a large class of cage C-functionalized o-carboranes under mild conditions with high yields. These functionalized o-carboranes may find applications in materials and medicine.

14306719.value: Helmholtz型微分方程的數值方法及分析

14306719.label: Project Objectives
14306719.value: We formulate scalable iterative methods with effective preconditioners for general Helmholtz-type systems, and formulate a general analytical framework that ensures the stable and efficient convergence of these iterative methods. We apply our proposed analytical framework to various Helmholtz-type systems with different boundary conditions to demonstrate if the iterative methods are stable and efficient. Based on the results, we improve the general analytical framework to achieve better stability and higher efficiency. We conduct a series of numerical experiments to check the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed iterative methods in terms of all critical problem-related parameters. Based on these results, we further improve the iterative methods and the general analytical framework for optimal convergence.

14306719.value: 這個RGC項目的主題是構造一類求解Helmholtz型微分方程的有效預處理方法以及分析應用這些預處理方法後的離散Helmholtz系統的穩定性和適定性. 這類預處理方法可同普通的迭代法相結合應用於離散Helmholtz系統，每次迭代只需要在一些小的子區域上求解小型的離散Helmholtz系統，附上某些適當的吸收邊界條件. 這些預處理方法的另外一個主要特徵是可應用於高頻波問題，所以分析時要利用高波速加權以後的能量範數來估計預處理方法後的離散Helmholtz系統相應的離散算子的範數以及預值的下界. 我們知道通常的區域分解法都要加上適當的粗網空間以便可適用於大規模問題的求解，但我們的新方法不需要加上任何粗網空間都可以有效地用於求解大規模的離散Helmholtz問題, 並且新方法的實現比現有的大部分預處理方法簡單.

14306719.label: Realisation of objectives
14306719.value: We have made a very successful effort and realized the original objectives in the project, achieved also a series of very encouraging and exciting theoretical and numerical results in several aspects that are closely related to the project but were not expected in our proposal. In the work [1], we studied a generalized Helmholtz equation, the H(curl) interface equation which are much more challenging to solve numerically than the non-interface problems due to their global low regularity. It has remained challenging how to design stable and accurate schemes for these interface equations so that the resulting large-scale discrete systems can be solved efficiently. Unfitted meshes are highly attractive in 3D computation as they can avoid generating complex interface-fitted meshes. Most existing unfitted mesh methods rely on nonconforming approximations and often cause an obvious loss of numerical accuracy. We proposed an effective a Petrov-Galerkin scheme by developing a comprehensive study of some new edge immersed finite element (IFE) spaces, and showed optimal convergence without loss of accuracy. We developed a systematic framework based on H1, H(curl), and H(div) IFE spaces, and the new method can generate large-scale discrete systems of the H(curl) interface equations that can be solved by the existing optimal fast solvers such as Hiptmair-Xu preconditioners. This is the first numerical work to deal with high-contrast Maxwell-type interface problems with unfitted meshes. It has been still extremely challenging to solve efficiently linear Helmholtz equations with high wave number, while it is much more difficult to solve the nonlinear Helmholtz (NLH) equations. In our recent work [9], we were the first to propose an adaptive finite element method (AFEM) for solving a general NLH equation with both high frequencies and corner singularities, and the impedance boundary conditions. We first established some crucial wave-number-explicit stability estimates and the singularity decomposition for the NLH solutions, then a priori stability and error estimates for the FEM system over general meshes. The crucial reliability and effectiveness of the AFEM were established. The convergence and quasi-optimality of our AFEM were also proved the first time for the NLH problem. The important nonlinear phenomenon of optical bistability with Gaussian incident waves was clearly recovered by the adaptive method. In the work [7], we proposed another efficient AFEM for solving a quasilinear saddle point magnetostatic Maxwell system, a generalization of the Helmholtz equation. The solution to this nonlinear system presents some mathematical singularities that bring a great difficulty for most existing methods to provide numerical approximations with acceptable accuracy. We proposed a new AFEM based on a residual-type a posteriori error estimator consisting of element and face residuals. To overcome the technical difficulties due to the special saddle point structure and nonlinear curl-curl form of the system, we introduced three crucial and delicate analytical strategies that enable us to realize both the reliability and efficiency of the proposed estimator for this nonlinear system. Surprisingly, we can demonstrate the convergence of the AFEM solutions in the energy-norm as well as prove the convergence of the sequence of error estimators. This adaptive method provides a new strategy to solve the large-scale finite element system arising from both the Helmholtz and Maxwell system stably and efficiently. In our work [8], we proposed a computationally cheap AFEM for solving a H(curl)-elliptic constrained optimal control problem that is a generalization of the Helmholtz optimal control problem. Even though we used a computationally much cheaper finite element pair to approximate the state and control of the optimal system, we proved the resulting AFEM can achieve the same accuracy as those much more expensive higher order finite elements. We proposed an error estimator that involves both the residual-type error estimators and lower-order data oscillations. We were able to derive a posteriori error estimates for the newly proposed error estimators and the strong convergence of the discrete states and controls from the AFEM in both the energy-norm and L2-norm. In the work [5], we studied the time-harmonic Maxwell system with generalized impedance conditions, which is a generalization of the Helmholtz system. The impedance parameter can be very general. We first analysed the vanishing order of the solutions to the Maxwell system, and developed the strong unique continuation of the Maxwell system. Our new unique continuation results were then applied to understand a long-standing and highly challenging ill-posed inverse electromagnetic scattering problem, and enables us to derive several novel unique identifiability results in solving some physically challenging inverse problems. These new results and analysis are crucial to help us understand and construct efficient and effective solvers for the large-scale systems arising from the Helmholtz and Maxwell systems. In the work [6], we considered two general inhomogeneous time-dependent wave equations with Sommerfeld radiation condition. We made a systematic investigation of the inverse wave problem to recover the shape and coefficients associated with these time-dependent wave equations. We studied also in depth the ill-posed inverse problems of determining a convex polygonal obstacle and the coefficient appearing in the wave and Schrödinger equations from a single dynamical data. When the near-field data is available through measurement, we are able to show that the sound speed of the wave equation along with its contrast support of the convex-polygon type can be uniquely determined mathematically. We further derived a unique identifiability for recovering both an electric potential and its support appearing in the Schrödinger equation. In the work [3], we comprehensively studied the electromagnetic scattering by arbitrarily shaped non-magnetic nanoparticles with high refractive indices, and impedance and radiation conditions included. It was physically observed that when illuminated by visible light, these particles can exhibit a very strong isotropic magnetic response. We provided a rigorous mathematical justification of this important physical phenomenon, and built up a priori estimates for the subwavelength resonances and the associated resonant modes, which enabled us to gain the existence of resonances and obtain their asymptotic behaviors in terms of the particle size and high contrast in model parameters. We then developed a creative multipole radiation framework that helps us find the exact orders of magnitude and blow-up rates when the resonances occur. In our work [4], we developed a systematic framework to provide a mathematical justification of the important physically observed phenomenon, the Minnaert resonance. This has wide applications, e.g., in the effective realization of acoustic metamaterials using bubbly media. The governing model is a coupled system of the acoustic and elastic wave equations with general boundary conditions, involving the interface, Neumann and radiation conditions. We then focused on the low-frequency resonance for acoustic bubbles embedded in soft elastic materials, involving two wave propagations. We demonstrated that Minnaert resonance could indeed occur under very general conditions. Our mathematical results provide direct and insightful guidance as well as the great potential for the effective realization of negative elastic materials by using bubbly elastic media. For all the numerical methods we proposed and nearly all typical PDE models discussed in this project, especially the Helmholtz and Maxwell equations, we have carried out a large number of numerical simulations to show their stability, efficiency and convergence for various PDE models as well as to verify our theoretical predictions and analysis; more details can be found in all the publications listed in this completion report.

14306719.label: Major findings and research outcome
14306719.value: We will list the major findings and research outcome below, while more detailed theories and and boundary conditions can be found in section 5.3 for realisation of objectives. In [1], we proposed an effective Petrov-Galerkin scheme by developing a comprehensive study of some new edge immersed finite element (IFE) spaces, and showed optimal convergence without any loss of accuracy. We developed a systematic framework based on the H1, H(curl), and H(div) IFE spaces, and proved the new method can generate large-scale discrete systems of the H(curl) interface equations, which can be solved by the existing optimal fast solvers such as Hiptmair-Xu preconditioners. In [9], we were the first to propose an adaptive finite element method (AFEM) for solving a general NLH equation with both high frequencies and corner singularities, and the impedance boundary conditions, We established some crucial wave-number-explicit stability estimates and the singularity decomposition for the NLH solutions, and a priori stability and error estimates for the FEM system over general meshes. The reliability and effectiveness of the AFEM were established. The convergence and quasi-optimality of our AFEM were proved the first time for the NLH problem. The nonlinear phenomenon of optical bistability with Gaussian incident waves was recovered by the AFEM. In [7], we proposed an efficient and robust AFEM for solving the quasilinear saddle point magnetostatic Maxwell system. The new AFEM is based on a residual-type a posteriori error estimator consisting of element and face residuals. We demonstrated the convergence of the AFEM solutions and the error estimators. In [5], we studied the time-harmonic Maxwell system with generalized impedance conditions. We first analysed the vanishing order of the solutions to the Maxwell system and derived the strong unique continuation of the Maxwell system. Our new unique continuation results were then applied to understand a long-standing and highly challenging ill-posed inverse electromagnetic scattering problem, to derive several novel unique identifiability results in solving a physically challenging inverse problem. In [4], we developed a systematic framework to provide a mathematical justification of an important physically observed phenomenon, the Minnaert resonance. By focusing on the low-frequency resonance for acoustic bubbles embedded in soft elastic materials, we demonstrated that Minnaert resonance indeed occurs under very general conditions. For all our proposed numerical methods, we have carried out a large number of numerical simulations to show their stability, efficiency and convergence as well as to verify our theoretical predictions and analysis.

14306719.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14306719.value: This project has developed a series of efficient numerical solutions of large-scale discretized systems arising from Helmholtz-type equations, and developed several systematic frameworks to help analyse the convergence and stability of the numerical methods. It will be practically important to construct and analyse more efficient preconditioning-type solvers for these large-scale systems. We have studied the Minnaert resonances for bubble elastic structures, and shown the Minnaert resonance can occur under general constructions. But we considered only the case that a single bubble is embedded in a soft elastic material and the resonance is mainly generated by the p-wave, it would be important to study the case with multiple bubbles and more general bubbly elastic structures. Adaptive methods are good choices for efficiently and stably solving the Helmholtz type models. But the development and justifications of adaptive methods, especially their quasi-optimal complexity are challenging. We presented some mathematical theories to help understand the stability and convergence of these adaptive methods. But for practical applications, it is also extremely important to understand if the adaptive methods can really reduce stable and accurate numerical solutions with least degrees of freedom in comparison with other non-adaptive methods.

14306719.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14306719.value: In this project we proposed a series of efficient numerical methods for solving large-scale discrete systems arising from Helmholtz type models of partial differential equations, with various boundary conditions, including the impedance type conditions. These Helmholtz type models have wide applications, such as acoustic, elastic and electromagnetic wave propagations as well as their inverse wave scattering problems that are encountered in seismic, radar and radio imaging, and non-destructive techniques for recovering various inhomogeneous medium inclusions. These Helmholtz type models of partial differential equations are generally very challenging to solve numerically and stably. The major challenge comes from the fact that the solutions to the models are often highly oscillatory, and singularities may occur at boundary corners and material interface, therefore sufficiently fine mesh is often needed to maintain numerical accuracy at high wavenumbers, leading to the large-scale discretized systems that are possibly complex-valued, non-symmetric and indefinite. Most existing numerical methods are unstable or ineffective for solving these large-scale systems. We also developed several general mathematical frameworks and theories to analyse the convergence, accuracies, stability and efficiencies of our proposed numerical methods. A series of key mathematical tools and strategies are proposed to handle various technical difficulties in both the numerical methods and numerical analysis. Most importantly, all the analyses are carried out under special Helmholtz-energy inner product and norms weighted appropriately with the wave number. Some of the numerical methods do not include coarse solvers but still possess high effectiveness and robustness, unlike most existing methods. This unique and special feature makes the methods easy to implement in real applications.

14306819.label: Project Objectives
14306819.value: Mapping out the free energy landscape of loop conformational transition. Our preliminary work indicates that the conformational transition of AAAD catalytic loops occurs beyond the sub-microsecond timescale accessible by plain MD simulations. In the work proposed here, we plan to employ enhanced sampling methods such as the string method with swarms of trajectories, to determine the path of loop conformational transition as well as the corresponding free energy landscape. Key residues and interactions identified along the transition path will be further examined experimentally by our collaborator. Analyzing solvent and O2 accessibility and their role in AAAD reaction type specificity. The reactions catalyzed by canonical AAADs (TDCs and TyDCs) and aldehyde synthase AAADs (PAASs and 4HPAASs) diverge after the carbanion generation step. In the latter type of AAADs, an O2 molecule attacks the resulting quinonoid intermediate whereas in the former no such attack takes place and the quinonoid is instead protonated. We plan to determine the O2 diffusion pathway and water occupancy map within both types of AAADs, in order to understand how these enzymes control solvent and oxygen accessibility as well as the role of such control in their reaction type specificity. Exploring the impact of non-catalytic structural elements on loop dynamics and AAAD activity. In one isoform (GAD65) of the mammal glutamic acid decarboxylase, residues not directly involved in catalysis can affect the enzyme's activity by rendering its large catalytic loop in a disordered state. As a result, GAD65 exists primarily in an inactivated form. Our MD simulations on CrTDC have shown that the dynamics of its large catalytic loop may be affected by the folded vs. unfolded states of a short helix. Along with our collaborator, we plan to further explore the impact of such non-catalytic structural elements on the activity of plant AAADs.

14306819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14306819.value: Aromatic amino acid decarboxylases (AAADs) in plants are involved in the biosynthesis of a wide variety of valuable pharmaceutical alkaloids. However, their structure-function relationship remained unclear as no crystal structure was available. In a recent joint study, our collaborator resolved the first set of plant AAAD structures, including both canonical and aldehyde synthase AAADs from four different plant species. These structures revealed a large conformational transition of two catalytic loops in the enzymes --- upon reaction, the loops switched from an open to a closed state to seal the active site entrance. We performed altogether 9.5-us molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on one of the AAADs, CrTDC, to examine the dynamics of its catalytic loops. Building upon this preliminary work, here, we plan to adopt a variety of enhanced sampling methods to thoroughly investigate the structure and dynamics of plant AAADs' catalytic loops. Specifically, Hamiltonian replica exchange simulations will first be performed to refine AAAD models with missing loop residues. Applying the string method with swarms of trajectories, we will then determine the most probable transition path of loop closure as well as the corresponding free energy landscape. Key residues and interactions identified along the transition path will be further probed by our collaborator with mutagenesis and kinetics experiments. Through calculating water occupancy and O2 diffusion pathway, we will further examine how plant AAADs control solvent and oxygen accessibility to their active sites as well as the role of such control in their reaction type specificity. 14306819.label: Realisation of objectives
14306819.value: We have largely followed the proposed objectives to investigate 1) the loop conformational dynamics, 2) solvent and O2 accessibility as well as 3) the impact of non-catalytic loop residues of plant AAADs. Specifically, towards objective 1, we began by utilizing several approaches, including Modeller, Rosetta and Alphafold2 (AF2) to predict the complete loop structures of all four proposed AAADs, namely, CrTDC, PsTyDC, AtPAAS and Rr4HPAAS. The enhanced sampling method HREX (Hamiltonian replica exchange) was then employed to refine the predicted structures. However, despite seemingly reasonable performance of HREX evaluated initially via metrics such as root mean square deviation (RMSD), further and more extensive tests on the PsTyDC system did not yield significantly improved agreement between the HREX-optimized structure and the crystal structure. In light of this result and the decent agreement between the original AF2 prediction and the crystal structure, we chose to utilize AF2 and crystal structures in our subsequent MD simulations. Next, we conducted multiple copies of microsecond simulations on the representative CrTDC to investigate loop conformational transition between the open and closed state. In the original objective 1, free energy calculation and enhanced sampling were proposed to recover the loop conformational transition. However, as our multi-microsecond plain MD simulations already captured the transition events, no enhanced sampling method originally proposed was employed and the transition dynamics and the loop conformations was instead analyzed directly from microsecond plain MD simulations. For this reason, we consider objective 1 to be largely achieved despite the difference in the methods employed from those proposed. Towards objective 2, we conducted multiple 100-ns MD simulations on all four AAADs, and, as proposed, employed the implicit ligand sampling method to determine the oxygen accessibility via computing its 3D potential of mean force (PMF) profiles with the single-step free energy perturbation approach. The solvent (water) accessibility is analyzed through 3D occupancy maps computed from these simulation trajectories. In addition to the wild type enzymes, we also performed the above calculations and analysis on their single-point mutants, where a key catalytic residue was replaced by its counterpart in other AAADs. This objective is 100% achieved. Towards objective 3, we have constructed in silico CrTDC mutant with certain non-catalytic residues removed. Simulations and analysis of these systems are currently on-going. The underachievement (60%) of this objective is largely due to the delay caused by multiple rounds of refining HREX protocols and checking its performance against experimental reference as mentioned earlier. We expect the on-going simulations and analysis to be completed within the next few months.

14306819.label: Major findings and research outcome
14306819.value: Through multi-microsecond MD simulations, we uncovered the transition of CrTDC's large catalytic loop between its open and close states. Transition intermediate states, secondary structures and the dynamics of loop conformations have been revealed. Our results indicated that the open/closed transition of the large catalytic loop could readily occur on the multi-microsecond timescale, while the secondary structure of the loop did not exhibit strong correlation to its open vs closed conformation. Implicit ligand sampling on four plant AAADs produced 3D free energy profiles of oxygen molecules within these proteins. By mutating a key catalytic tyrosine in canonical AAADs (CrTDC and PsTyDC) to the corresponding phenylalanine in AAASs (AtPAAS and Rr4HPAAS) and vice versa, we further showed that this single-point mutation did not affect oxygen diffusion pathways and free energy profiles significantly. Along with the 3D water occupancy maps of both wild-type and mutant AAADs, these results enabled detailed comparison of active-site O2 and solvent accessibility across the plant AAAD family. A manuscript summarizing the above results is in preparation and a draft is attached to this report. Building upon our work on plant AAADs and again joining forces with our experimental collaborator, we also investigated EPS1, a neofunctionailzed member of the plant BAHD acyltransferase family. Through microsecond MD simulations on both wild-type and mutant EPS1, we characterized the unique pericyclic rearrangement lyase mechanism employed by the enzyme and unveiled the critical protective function of a threonine residue transiently involved in substrate binding. These simulations provided detailed insights into the catalytic mechanism employed by EPS1 and the intricate control of plant salicylic acid biosynthesis. Following an earlier unsuccessful submission, the manuscript resulting from this work has been revised and is expected to be re-submitted soon, which is also attached to this report.

14306819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14306819.value: Along the line of studies reported here, we plan to further examine loop dynamics of plant AAADs with modification on non-catalytic loop residues. Our work on these proteins has also set the stage for future investigation of other plant enzymes, especially those with potentially large conformational changes in their flexible loop regions. The combination of microsecond plain MD simulations and in silico mutation have proven valuable in the assessment of structural and dynamic details of plant AAADs. Supplementing these approaches with free energy calculations, we plan to continue and expand our investigation on the conformation and dynamics of various plant enzymes.

14306819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14306819.value: In this work, we performed computer modeling and simulations of plant AAADs, a family of enzymes involved in the aromatic amino acid metabolism. Through multi-microsecond molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we revealed how a large catalytic loop in these enzymes switched between its open and closed states. A key residue residing on this loop is a tyrosine in two proteins investigated here (canonical AAADs) whereas in the other two proteins (AAASs) the residue at the corresponding position is a phenylalanine. Employing the implicit ligand sampling method and in silico single-point mutation, we computed the free energy profiles of oxygen diffusion in all four wild-type AAADs as well as their mutants with the aforementioned tyrosine replaced by a phenylalanine (or vice versa). Our calculations enabled detailed comparison of active-site oxygen and solvent accessibility among different AAAD family members. Furthermore, we investigated EPS1, a plant enzyme involved in the biosynthesis of salicylic acid. Through a combination of modeling approaches, we refined the bound poses of the substrate and products of EPS1. Using microsecond MD simulations on both wild-type and mutant EPS1, we further characterized the catalytic mechanism of the enzyme and identified critical active-site residues essential for its lyase activity and stability.

14307019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14307019.value: Observations of interstellar media (ISM) have improved considerably during the past decade. Traditional surveys have collected extensive information about ISM densities, temperature and mean/dispersion of gas motions. This type of information is usually treated isotropically, e.g. the total mass, mean density and velocity dispersion of molecular clouds, the nursery of stars. In recent years it has gradually become apparent that ISM are permeated with ordered magnetic-fields (B-fields; Li et al. 2009, 2011, 2014, 2015) and thus the specific field direction should break the symmetry and isotropy of the aforementioned cloud properties. Indeed, our team has discovered that gas velocities (Li et al. 2011; Otto, Ji & Li 2017; Liu & Li 2018), cloud shapes (Li et al. 2013), cloud fragmentation (Law, Li & Leung 2018) and even star formation efficiencies (Li et al. 2017) are all affected by B-field orientations. Here the gas velocities involve two types, turbulence and gravitational contraction, and the anisotropies of both are observed. Furthermore, given the ordered B-field, the turbulence must be trans- to sub-Alfvénic, and ion/neutral motions can potentially be decoupled based on the induction equation. We have also pioneered the observation of the decoupling of the turbulent motions of ions and neutrals (Li & Houde 2008; Li et al. 2010; Tang, Li & Lee 2018). The ordered B-fields are only dynamically effective to the ISM if neutrals and ions (thus also B-fields) are well coupled. The decoupling environment therefore appears to be a critical stage for cloud fragmentation and thus star formation. This proposal combines our strengths in both anisotropy and decoupling studies by crosschecking the observations of the two phenomena. If turbulence is anisotropic and ion/neutral motions are indeed decoupled, we should observe that the anisotropies of ion and neutral turbulence are systematically different. We will check this through both observational and numerical simulation approaches. Also, if gravitational contraction is anisotropic, the ambipolar diffusion during this process should result in a stronger contraction anisotropy for ions. The study’s results may provide an important new tool for resolving the contested notion of contraction ambipolar diffusion. Starting from the 1980s, this was hypothesised as a critical process in star formation, but proof of its existence has long been disputed. 傳統的星際物質覌測，諸如質量, 密度, 溫度等, 均為各向同性. 近年越來越多的證據顯示磁場充斥於星際空間, 而其方向當破壞前述的各項同性. 的確, 中大恆星生成組發現分子雲形狀, 碎裂, 甚或恆星生成率都跟磁場方向有關. 本計劃的目的是研究氣體速度和磁場的關係. 除了湍流速度當因磁場顯示出各向異性, 中性分子和帶電分子也當顯示不同的各向異性. 中性分子和帶電分子運動的分離對恆星生成有決定性的影響. 本組在中/帶電粒子的運動分離 （雙極性擴散）以及氣體運動的各向異性都有領先的研究. 本計劃, 雙極性擴散的各向異性, 結合本組強項, 期能進步了解恆星生成的機制.

14307019.label: Major findings and research outcome
14307019.value: 1. The view on velocity structures in molecular clouds and their relationship with magnetic fields (B field) has evolved during the past decade from almost no correlation to highly parallel. Our numerical simulations suggest a more nuanced picture: Depending on whether the self-gravity is dynamically dominant, the velocity field can be governed by either contraction (at high densities) or turbulence (at low densities), and their anisotropies will tend to be either perpendicular or parallel, respectively, to the B fields. High-density regions are always embedded in the low-density fore/background, so the velocity behaviors from lines of sight (LOSs) with high column densities will be a mixture of orthogonal anisotropies, which can be hard to interpret and necessitates zooming in onto certain LOS scales to better characterize localized behaviors. We tested and confirmed the above prediction with CO observations of the Taurus molecular cloud. 2. Magnetized turbulence plays a significant role in star formation, but it is difficult to observe. Only the line-of-sight velocity distribution can possibly be probed by emission/absorption line observations, which constitute so-called position-position-velocity (PPV) data. Using magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations, we demonstrated two simple and rapid methods to probe, respectively, turbulent velocity spectra and probability density functions (PDFs) of volume density from PPV data cubes. A comparison between the proposed methods and those in the literature was then performed using both simulations and observational data. 3. The relation between the magnetic field strength and density (B-n relation) of molecular clouds tells how significantly magnetic fields (B-fields) can regulate star formation. So far, most observations of B-n relations are compared with the "textbook model”, which assumes an isolated gas sphere collapsing under the “flux-freezing” condition, i.e., a perfect coupling between gas and B-fields. In reality, however, cloud cores may continuously accrete from the envelopes, and the validity of the flux-freezing assumption decreases with increasing density. Here we present the first 3D two-fluid (neutrals and ions) magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of gas cores embedded in a uniform background cloud density to study the effects of ambipolar diffusion (AD, the ion-neutral decoupling) on B-n relations. Compared to the control group assuming flux-freezing, the AD cases started with shallower B-n relations, due to the decoupling between neutral contraction and B-fields. The later development, however, diverged from this intuitive expectation: the drag force between ions and neutrals allowed the ions to concentrate the B-fields more efficiently than the flux-freezing cases and resulted in a steeper B-n relation. Our findings require previous interpretations of the observed B-n relations be fundamentally rethought.

14307019.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14307019.value: By comparing the B-field orientation dispersions from observations and from MHD simulations at various scales, we realized that molecular cloud turbulence is sub-Alfvénic at cloud scales and turns slightly super-Alfvénic within sub-pc cloud cores. Sub-Alfvénic turbulence must be anisotropic, so should be magnetically trans-critical contraction, as illustrated by MHD simulations and TMC observations. However, the two types of anisotropy dominate at different densities and are orthogonal to each other. The slightly super-Alfvénic turbulence in cloud cores is not enough to twist the B-field and form protostellar disks, which is the so-called magnetic braking catastrophe. However, our study indicated that this may be an overconcern, as flux-freezing is not a good approximation in cloud cores where the magnetic Reynolds number is not very high. We found that turbulence-induced ambipolar diffusion (TAD)—the decoupling between neutral eddies and B-field—may be as high as 0.5 pc, which indicates that ideal MHD is not ideal for cloud core simulations. In the future, we will perform observation surveys to statistically pin down the TAD scale.

14307019.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14307019.value: Why does aurora only happen in the polar regions? Because solar winds are "guided" by the Earth magnetic fields. The same guiding mechanism also happens in molecular clouds, where the solar wind in the above example is replaced by turbulence. That is, turbulence in molecular clouds should be anisotropic due to the magnetic fields that permeate clouds. This magnetic-field regulation in molecular clouds, however, is not as sufficient as in solar winds. This is because solar winds are almost fully ionized, while molecular clouds are mostly neutral, which means that cloud gas can decouple from cloud fields. This decoupling is called ambipolar diffusion (AD). We tried to understand anisotropy and AD of molecular cloud turbulence using both observation and numerical simulation data. The result can help us understand the formation of protostallar disks and thus star formation, as molecular clouds are the birth place of stars.

14307219.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14307219.value: The aim of this project is to investigate the electron counting model, the edge stability, and equilibrium shape of quasi 2D materials under various growth conditions. Quasi 2D materials have attracted vast research interest due to their superior electron, optic, and spintronic properties. One of the major challenges for the development of quasi 2D applications is the limited crystal quality and poor morphology control during the growth. Despite the experimental results on the morphology and shape of various nanosheets of MoS2, MoSe2, and Bi2Te3, the theoretical understanding of their edge stability and equilibrium shape is limited because there lacks proper electron counting model that match the 6 fold coordinate systems and the current algorithm on the edge stability is problematic because of the strong charge transfer and coupling between edges. Density functional theory is a well-established technique that can accurately calculate defects, surface and interface properties. By applying this approach, we have proposed new algorithms on the stability analysis of polar surfaces and edges of 2D materials. Still, quasi 2D materials is much more challenging due to the complicated nature of the crystal structure and the high coordination numbers. In this proposal, we plan to. (1) propose new guidelines on electron counting model for quasi 2D materials and investigate the edge stability based on the model. (2) perform equilibrium shape constructions as functions of chemical potential and temperature, and propose new strategies to modify the growth conditions and passivation schemes on the edge. Our proposed research will make accurate predictions of edge stability and equilibrium shape possible. Such predictive power is not only important in the engineering problems in the growth of quasi 2D materials, but also may provide important insights on 3D crystals. The new guidelines in electron counting model will also benefit fundamental scientific understanding in surface and defect physics. 這個項目的目的是研究電子計數模型，邊緣穩定性，以及在各種生長條件下准二維材料的平衡形狀。 准2D材料由於其優越的電子，光學和自旋性質而引起了廣泛的研究興趣。其發展的主要挑戰是不佳的晶體質量和不良的生長形態控制。盡管有一些各種形態和形狀的實驗結果，但是對於MoS2，MoSe2和Bi2Te3穩定性和平衡形狀的理論理解是有限的，這一方面也是因為缺乏適當的電子計數模型來匹配6重近鄰系統和以及缺乏邊緣穩定性算法。 密度泛函理論是一種可以精確計算缺陷，表面和界面特性的方法。通過應用這種方法，我們提出了二維材料極面和邊緣穩定性分析的新算法。然而，准2D材料由於其復雜的晶體結構和高配位數而及富挑戰性。在這個提案中，我們計劃。 （1）提出准二維材料和電子計數模型的新指南，並基於該模型研究邊緣穩定性。 （2）進行平衡形狀結構的計算，並提出新的在邊緣生長調整策略和鈍化方案。 我們的方案將幫助我們准確預測邊緣穩定性和平衡形狀。這種預測能力不僅對准2D材料的生長很重要，也可能為3D晶體生長提供重要的指導。電子計數模型的新指南也將從根本上加深對表面和缺陷物理學的科學理解。

14307219.label: Realisation of objectives
14307219.value: To fulfil the objective one, a new algorithm has been developed and published on the edge of MoS2 with a systematical investigation on the electron distribution and electron counting model with different edge reconstructions. A general principle based on the local geometry of the edge passivation has been obtained and numerically proved to be critical to match with experimental observations. Based on the edge passivation scheme an absolute formation energy algorithm was developed tested under various chemical potential ranges. Based on the energy, equilibrium shapes were calculated and found to match with experimental results in the S rich region. In the S poor region, we found that a reconstruction assisted by O yields stable configuration. With proper growth temperature included, we eventually solved the most challenging problem of equilibrium shape as a function of S chemical potential and our results match with experimental results very well. This is the only research work that matches with experimental works and also illustrate for the first time on the important role of O in the role of passivation of edge. The work has been published at Journal of Physical Chemistry C. Based on the algorithm and insights developed in the first objective, a gap sealing problem near the zigzag edge of BN was identified and a solution based on the H passivation was confirmed to be effective to produce smooth row by row growth. The physical origin of the sealing problem is the large edge atom distortion during the growth and dimer formation of SP1 hybridization leads to a large barrier for the final atom to incorporate and form ideal edge by edge growth. Therefore, we name this effect as a "sealing problem". The paper was published at journal of applied physics. Along the research pathway, we also discovered an intriguing quantum mechanical oscillatory interaction between isovalent centers in semiconductors through the metallization process with the lattice. Our works shed light on the precise control of defects in semiconductors. The related work was published at European physics letter. Next, a decoration of transition metal near the zigzag edge of MoS2 was found to introduce a novel topological order of magnetism in the spin chain by magnetizing the edge state of Mo d orbitals. An intercell vs. intracell tuning strategy was proposed to tune the magnetic order. The related works was published at Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics. Inspired by the edge and surface investigation of the electron counting model developed and the interesting magnetization scheme on the edge of the MoS2, we applied this strategy to other transition metal oxides and discovered an Artificially controlled nanoscale chemical reduction in VO2 through electron beam illumination. This work illustrate important facet dependence and surface defect incorporation mechanism introduced by e beam illumination that trigger different behaviors of phase changes. This work was published at Nature Communications. Also, the surfactant strategies of H was tested on ScCoO2.5 surface and inner surfaces. We discovered a very interesting abnormal stability of hydrogenic defects and magnetism near the HSrCoO2. 5 (0 0 1) surface. In this work, we discovered a strange preference for H defects on sub-surface and internal surface, different from traditional semiconductors. The work was published at journal of Applied Surface Science. Finally, we published one systematical review articles on the edge reconstructions of MoS2, which demonstrate our leading roles on the reconstructions of MoS2. The article was published at journal of applied physics.

14307219.label: Major findings and research outcome
14307219.value: 1, We invented a new algorithm on the edge stability of quasi-2d material system, which is critical in the understanding of phase stability, crystal growth and device fabrications. We also developed important insights on the geometrical properties of the edge and surface reconstructions that serve as critical guidelines in the algorithm design and also edge passivation strategies. 2, We propose and illustrate a one dimensional spin chain model with a decoration of transition metal elements on the zigzag edge of MoS2. The edge reconstruction strongly favors a three-fold symmetry that is critical to realize the topological magnetic order. 3, We discovered a hidden quantum oscillation between isovalent dopants in semiconductors that is long missed in the field of semiconductor physics. In the research, we also illustrate the possible theoretical approach combining a Green's function's approach with tight binding theory in both direct and reciprocal space. Also, the bond orbital coupling with the lattice is the key physical origin for the oscillation to occur. 4, We discovered a long missed gap filling difficulty problem during the growth of 2D edges and found out a solution to solve this problem. 5, Based on the insights of electron counting model developed, we discovered a chemical reduction strategy based on surface e-beam irradiation and illustrate the unique surface orientation dependence for the chemical reaction to occur. The interface reconstruction and stability were also found to be important in the dynamical process. 6, An abnormal preferences of H attachment on the surface and inner surface was discovered in the thin film ScCoO2.5, inspired by the electron counting analysis and local geometrical analysis. Also, we developed a new theoretical method combining crystal field splitting and bond orbital coupling approaches. The related research results were published at good journals, such as nature communication, applied surface science, journal of physical chemistry, etc. With our insights developed, we experimental collaborators discovered and understood that the defects near the surface and interface reconstructions are critical in a lot of important physical processes. The related research results were presented in 9 conferences, include APS March meeting and CPS fall meeting. In addition, two MPHIL students and one PHD student performed related research works graduated in the period. Several undergraduate students also learned fundamentals of the techniques and conducted related research.

14307219.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14307219.value: Inspired by the research activities supported by this research fund, in the future, it is important to set up a new focus and understanding on the defect and defect complex near the interface of phase change materials. Molecular dynamical simulation with quantum mechanical accuracies can be important frontier to explore with the help of machine intelligence. More fruitful research results are expected to see on the surfaces and near the edge or interfaces with hidden dynamical properties illustrated by the simulation and experimental collaboration.

14307219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14307219.value: We discovered an important algorithm to analyze the edge stability of quasi-2D materials and realized that the geometry of edge reconstruction is key to realize successful passivation and surfactant effects that are critical in a lot of scientific and engineering applications. With the insights developed, we discovered a lot of novel phenomena near the edge and interfaces with proper attachment of elements. An array of crystal growth problem, topological magnetic ordering chain, chemical reaction problem, and surface science problem were solved with the insights developed. Throughout the practices, we want to address the importance of surface stability of polar and nonpolar edges and surfaces and innovative computational physical algorithm are the key to fully understand all the important technical problems in the future. At the same, several graduate students conducted the related research graduated in the funding period and several undergraduate students are also involved in the research and gathered valuable experience.

14307719.label: Project Objectives
14307719.value: To design and synthesize a series of beta-cyclodextrin-conjugated phthalocyanines and boron dipyrromethene derivatives, and study their host-guest interactions with a range of ferrocene-based quenchers in aqueous media. The binding constants and quenching efficiencies in terms of fluorescence emission and singlet oxygen generation will be determined. To investigate the displacement processes of these host-guest complexes with adamantane-modified ligands that can target the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) overexpressed in a variety of human cancer cells. The restoration of fluorescence emission and singlet oxygen generation will be monitored using UV-Vis and fluorescence spectroscopic methods, and the efficiencies will be optimized through systematic variation of the host and guest species. To study the in vitro properties of these supramolecular complexes using both EGFR-positive and negative cancer cell lines. The activation in intracellular fluorescence and photocytotoxicity will be examined in adamantane-tagged cells, and the results will be compared with those for non-labeled cells. To extend the study to tumor-bearing nude mice in which the tumor will first be tagged with adamantane through tail intravenous injection of the adamantane-modified tumor-targeting ligands, followed by intravenous injection of the deactivated host-guest complexes. The in vivo activation will be examined by monitoring the increase in fluorescence intensity in the tumor. Ex vivo imaging will also be performed to determine the specificity of the photosensitizers toward the tumor compared with other major organs. Various controls will be used for comparison.

14307719.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14307719.value: Light has long been used for medical applications. By utilizing its action on a photosensitive drug and oxygen which results in the generation of cytotoxic reactive oxygen species (ROS), a promising therapeutic modality, namely photodynamic therapy (PDT), has been developed over the last few decades for treatment of some localized and superficial cancers, as well as certain non-cancerous conditions. The therapeutic efficacy depends on several interdependent factors, among which the photosensitizers play an extremely vital role. As a result, considerable effort has been put into the development of advanced photosensitizers which have superior photophysical properties, high tumor specificity, and good pharmacokinetic profiles. With a view to confining the photodynamic action at the tumor site, several approaches have been explored, which include conjugation of photosensitizers with tumor-targeting ligands, encapsulation of photosensitizers into nanocarriers that can accumulate in tumor through the enhanced permeability and retention effect, and incorporation of control units that can regulate their photosensitizing ability through interactions with tumor-associated stimuli. Although these strategies have been found to be effective, they usually involve a tedious synthetic procedure, particularly for multifunctional molecular systems, or elusive therapeutic action and mechanism. To circumvent these problems and develop more advanced photosensitizers, we propose herein a facile supramolecular approach to assemble highly efficient and multifunctional photosensitizing systems in a bioorthogonal manner. We will first design and prepare a series of beta-cyclodextrin-conjugated photosensitizers based on phthalocyanines or boron dipyrromethenes, as well as a series of ferrocene-based quenchers. It is envisaged that the two components will form host-guest complexes in aqueous media, and by careful matching the photo-activities of the hosts could be quenched by the guest species. Upon interactions with adamantane groups preferentially localized in cancer cells through conjugation to tumor-targeting ligands, the guest quenchers will be displaced due to the stronger binding between the beta-cyclodextrin and adamantane moieties, thereby restoring the fluorescence and ROS generated by the photosensitizers. Apart from solution and cellular studies, we will also examine the above effect in tumor-bearing nude mice through a “tag, displace, and activate” process. This two-step non-covalent bioorthogonal approach enables site-specific activation of photosensitizers, which can greatly reduce the photo-damage to normal cells and tissues, and is therefore highly promising for further development of advanced photosensitizing systems toward targeted PDT. 長期以來，光學技術在醫學領域得到了廣泛的應用。光動力治療（PDT）作為一種很有發展前景的治療方法，在過去幾十年裡已經得到快速發展，特別是用於治療一些局部、淺表的癌症，同時亦用於一些非癌症疾病的治療。光動力治療通過利用光敏藥物和氧氣之間的作用而產生具有細胞毒性的活性氧（ROS），其治療效果取決於多個相互關聯的因素，其中光敏劑發揮著極其重要的作用。因此，大量的工作已經投入到開發具有優良光物理性質、強腫瘤靶向性和良好藥物代謝動力學特性的先進光敏劑。到目前為止，研究者們已經探索了很多方法可以將光動力作用精准的應用於腫瘤部位，從而避免對正常組織的損傷，其中最常見的方法包括將光敏劑和腫瘤靶向配體直接結合的主動靶向法；將光敏劑封裝到納米載體中，通過增強滲透滯留效應使其在腫瘤中累積的被動靶向法；以及引入控制單元，通過與腫瘤微環境的響應機制來調節光敏劑光敏活性的方法。這些方法雖然有效，但通常都會涉及到一個冗長的合成過程，或者不明確的治療機制，特別是對於多功能分子的系統。因此，為了克服這些問題，開發更先進的光敏劑，我們提出了一種簡易的超分子方法，以生物正交的方式組裝成高效以及多功能的光敏系統。首先，我們會設計及製備一系列環糊精修飾的酞菁或硼二吡咯烷酮類的光敏劑，以及一系列基於二茂鐵的猝滅劑。我們設想這兩種物質在水介質中會形成主-客體複合物，通過仔細匹配主-客體的光學活性，主體光敏劑可以完全被客體化合物猝滅。另一方面，通過與腫瘤靶向配體的結合，金剛烷可以預先被靶向傳遞到腫瘤細胞中，當被客體分子猝滅的光敏劑複合物遇到腫瘤細胞中的金剛烷時，由於環糊精對金剛烷分子具有更高的親和力，客體猝滅劑將會被替換出來，從而光敏劑的螢光和ROS可以得到恢復。我們會在溶液和細胞中對這個光敏系統進行研究，此外，我們還將通過一個“標記、置換和啟動”的過程來研究上述光敏系統對荷瘤裸鼠的影響。這種兩步的非共價生物正交方法可以特定的在某個位置啟動光敏劑，從而大大的降低了光敏劑對正常細胞和組織的光損害，對進一步開發針對靶向PDT的先進光敏系統具有很好的前景。

14307719.label: Realisation of objectives
14307719.value: This project aims to develop a facile supramolecular approach to assemble highly efficient and multifunctional photosensitizing systems for photodynamic therapy against cancer. To initiate this project, we first prepared an aza boron dipyrromethene substituted with four β-cyclodextrin units (ADP-CD4) and its meso-brominated analogue (BrADP-CD4) (J. Med. Chem. 2021, 64, 15461-15476). While the former was a highly fluoresced species, having two heavy bromo groups that could promote the intersystem crossing, the latter served as an efficient photosensitizer. With four hydrophilic β-cyclodextrin moieties, both compounds exhibited excellent water solubility. In addition, we also synthesized a β-cyclodextrin-conjugated zinc(II) phthalocyanine (Pc-CD) (ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2022, 14, 14903-14915). Similarly, the conjugation with a hydrophilic and bulky β-cyclodextrin substituent could promote the dispersion of the phthalocyanine molecules and enhance their fluorescence emission and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation in water. For binding with the above host compounds, a series of guest species were also prepared, including two ferrocenes substituted with a black-hole quencher (Fc-Q) or a polyethylene glycol chain (Fc-PEG) and two adamantanes conjugated with the peptide sequence YHWYGYTPQNVI (labeled as GE11) or QRHKPRE (labeled as QRH*), namely Ad-GE11 and Ad-QRH*, respectively. Both peptide sequences have been reported to exhibit high affinity toward the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), which is overexpressed in a wide range of cancer cells. All the compounds were characterized with various spectroscopic methods. Their purify was confirmed by reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography. The supramolecular interactions of these host and guest species in water were then studied with electronic absorption and steady-state fluorescence spectroscopic methods. For the host-guest interactions between ADP-CD4 and Fc-Q or Ad-QRH*, the 1:4 binding stoichiometry was confirmed by Job’s plot analysis. The binding constants were estimated to be (2.5 ± 0.1) x 10e19 M-4 and (2.9 ± 0.2) x 10e19 M-4, respectively. With a BHQ-3 quenching unit, Fc-Q could greatly reduce the fluorescence intensity of ADP-CD4 upon complexation. The host-guest interactions of Pc-CD and Fc-PEG led to the formation of an amphiphilic complex that underwent self-assembly in aqueous media to form the nanosystem Pc-CD@Fc-PEG with a hydrodynamic diameter of 124−147 nm. Owing to the self-quenching effect and the ferrocene-based quencher, this nanosystem was completely quenched in terms of fluorescence emission and ROS generation. By performing all these studies, the first objective was fully achieved. With all these host-guest complexes, we then examined their activation through displacement of the encapsulated ferrocene quenchers with adamantanes as the binding of β-cyclodextrin with adamantane is generally stronger than that with ferrocene. Upon addition of Ad-QRH*, the fluorescence of ADP-CD4@Fc-Q and ROS generation of BrADP-CD4@Fc-Q were gradually recovered as shown spectroscopically. By using free QRH* as negative control, it confirmed that the recovery was due to a competitive displacement process. Similarly, Ad-QRH* could also displace the guest species in the nanosystem Pc-CD@Fc-PEG and consequently disrupt the nanostructure, as confirmed by dynamic light scattering, thereby restoring the fluorescence emission and ROS generation in water. Hence, the second objective was also accomplished. After performing these studies in aqueous media, we further demonstrated the targeted delivery and site-specific activation of the theranostic agents at the cellular level. Ad-GE11 was first used to tag the EGFR-positive A431 and A549 cells through incubation for 1 h, which ensured that the adamantane moieties were mainly anchored on the cell membrane instead of entering into the cell cytoplasm. Subsequent incubation of these cells with ADP-CD4 (for 10 min) led to the occurrence of strong fluorescence mainly on the cell membrane. Without the pre-treatment with Ad-GE11 or by using the EGFR-negative HepG2 cells, the fluorescence signal was almost invisible. Further studies showed that the cellular uptake of ADP-CD4 was mediated by the host-guest interactions through receptor-mediated endocytosis. Similar in vitro results were obtained for the brominated BrADP-CD4, though the extent of restoration in fluorescence emission was smaller due to its weaker fluorescence compared with that of ADP-CD4. This compound, however, could serve as a photosensitizer. Its cell-selective photocytotoxicity was demonstrated using various controls with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) as low as 1 μM. The activation of ADP-CD4@Fc-Q in fluorescence emission by Ad-QRH* in EGFR-positive cells was also demonstrated. Without the pre-treatment with Ad-QRH*, using the free QRH* peptide for pre-incubation, or using the EGFR-negative HepG2 cells, the change in fluorescence intensity was negligible. The active targeting effect of Ad-QRH* followed by activation through displacement resulted in targeted delivery and site-specific activation of ADP-CD4. Similarly, the intracellular restoration effects were also studied for BrADP-CD4, both in terms of fluorescence emission and photocytotoxicity. Upon pre-incubation with Ad-QRH* followed by light irradiation, the initially quenched host-guest complex BrADP-CD4@Fc-Q became highly cytotoxic toward the EGFR-positive HT29 and A431 cells. For the nanosystem Pc-CD@Fc-PEG, it could also be activated similarly using Ad-QRH* in the two target cell lines (HT29 and A431), but not the EGFR-negative HEK-293 cells, through displacement-induced disassembly of the nanosystem. With these in vitro results, the third objective was also fully achieved. Finally, in vivo studies were performed for some of these host-guest complexes. To study the biodistribution of ADP-CD4, A431 tumor-bearing nude mice were first injected intravenously with ADP-CD4 with or without post intratumoral injection with Ad-GE11 immediately. The fluorescence image of the mice was monitored continuously over 96 h. The mice were then sacrificed to harvest the tumor and some major organs for measuring their fluorescence intensities. It was found that the intratumoral fluorescence intensity was increased along with time for the mice being post-treated with Ad-GE11. In contrast, the intensity remained essentially unchanged for the mice without the post-treatment. After 96 h, the intensity in tumor was about 3-fold higher for the former compared with the latter, while the fluorescence intensities in the organs were similar for the two groups of mice. These results demonstrated that the adamantane units localized in the tumor could promote the accumulation of the β-cyclodextrin-conjugated fluorescent probe through host-guest interactions. Using the complex ADP-CD4@Fc-Q instead of ADP-CD4, the fluorescence intensity in the body of the mice was diminished due to the quenching effect of Fc-Q. However, for the mice with post-treatment with Ad-QRH*, the fluorescence signal at the tumor site appeared as early as 2 h after the intravenous injection of ADP-CD4@Fc-Q, while the signal could hardly be observed for the mice without the post-treatment throughout the whole period of time. Ex vivo study showed that the fluorescence intensity in tumor was about 4-fold higher for the mice being post-treated with Ad-QRH* compared with the untreated control. The activation was clearly due to the displacement of Fc-Q with Ad-QRH* at the tumor site. The in vivo site-specific activation was also demonstrated using Pc-CD@Fc-PEG and Ad-QRH* in HT29 tumor-bearing nude mice. Apart from the activation in fluorescence emission, the activation in PDT efficacy was also evaluated using different controls. For the mice being sequentially treated with Pc-CD@Fc-PEG intravenously, Ad-QRH* intratumorally, and light irradiation (675 nm, 0.1 W, 60 J cm-2), the tumor could be completely eradicated. Hematoxylin and eosin staining of the tumor slides also showed more necrotic and apoptotic cells for the positive treatment group compared with the controls. For the stained organ slides, noticeable abnormality was not observed, showing that all these treatments did not cause systemic toxicity. These in vivo results showed that last objective was also achieved.

14307719.label: Major findings and research outcome
14307719.value: Targeted delivery of photosensitizers using hydrophilic and tumor-directing carriers and site-specific activation of their photocytotoxicity are two promising strategies for enhancing the specificity of photodynamic therapy against cancer. With this funding, we have developed a novel supramolecular bioorthogonal approach to integrate these two functions. We first prepared a β-cyclodextrin-substituted aza-boron-dipyrromethene-based photosensitizer and used a ferrocene-substituted black-hole quencher to inhibit its photosensitizing ability through host-guest interactions. Upon encountering the adamantane moieties that had been delivered to the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-overexpressed cancer cells through specific binding of the conjugated peptide to this receptor, the ferrocene-based guest species were displaced due to the stronger binding interactions between β-cyclodextrin and adamantane, thereby restoring the photodynamic activity of the photosensitizer. Hence, this two-step process enabled targeted delivery and site-specific activation of the photosensitizer, as demonstrated through a series of experiments in aqueous media, in a range of EGFR-positive and negative cancer cell lines, and in tumor-bearing nude mice using various controls. This work was published in J. Med. Chem. 2021, 64, 15461-15476. This study was then extended to the self-assembled nanosystem of a β-cyclodextrin-conjugated phthalocyanine-based photosensitizer and a ferrocene-substituted poly(ethylene glycol) (Mn = 2000). Owing to the self-quenching effect and the ferrocene-based quencher, the nanosystm could not emit fluorescence and generate reactive oxygen species. Similarly, upon interactions with molecules of an adamantane substituted with an EGFR-targeting peptide in water and in EGFR-positive HT29 and A431 cells, the ferrocene guest species were displaced, resulting in disassembly of the nanoparticles and restoration of their photoactivities. The half-maximal inhibitory concentrations were as low as 1.24 μM (for HT29 cells). The nanosystem could also be activated in the tumor of HT29 tumor-bearing nude mice being intratumorally injected with the peptide-conjugated adamantane, leading to increased intratumoral fluorescence intensity and effective eradication of the tumor upon laser irradiation. The results further demonstrated that this two-step supramolecular approach could actualize site-specific photosensitization and minimize nonspecific phototoxicity in a general photodynamic treatment. This work was published in ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2022, 14, 14903-14915.

14307719.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14307719.value: This research project involves the design and synthesis of a series of β-cyclodextrin-conjugated photosensitizers and guest species conjugated with a quencher or tumor-targeting ligand, as well as the use of their host-guest complexes to achieve targeted delivery and site-specific activation of the photosensitizers for precise photodynamic therapy against cancer. Although a large number of host-guest photosensitizing systems have been reported, the use of this supramolecular bioorthogonal approach for achieving both of these targeting functions is still in its infancy. It is expected that this facile and versatile approach can be developed further to achieve better outcomes. For example, the use of more tumor-specific ligands, such as monoclonal antibodies instead of the EGFR-targeting peptides could further enhance the tumor specificity. The use of cucurbit[n]urils instead of β-cyclodextrin as the host species could strengthen the binding with the guest species that might facilitate the biological studies, particularly in animal models. For the self-assembled nanosystem, the study could also be extended by encapsulating a theranostic agent so that it could also be released during the displacement-triggered disassembly of the nanoparticles for promoting the antitumor efficacy and widening the scope of the applications.

14307719.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14307719.value: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a promising treatment modality for cancer. It utilizes light to activate a photosensitive drug followed by the interaction with the endogenous oxygen to generate cytotoxic reactive oxygen species. With a view to confining the photodynamic action at the tumor site, various approaches have been explored, such as conjugation of the photosensitizers with a tumor-targeting ligand and the use of activatable photosensitizers that are responsive toward the tumor-associated stimuli. Although these strategies are effective, they usually involve a tedious synthetic procedure and an elusive therapeutic mechanism. In this research project, we have developed a facile supramolecular bioorthogonal approach to achieve both targeted delivery and site-specific activation of photosensitizers for precise PDT. To achieve these goals, we have synthesized a series of β-cyclodextrin-conjugated photosensitizers and ferrocene or adamantane-modified quenchers and peptides that can target the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) overexpressed in cancer cells. Through the host-guest interactions, the photosensitizers can be delivered selectively to the EGFR-positive cells and specifically activated therein through a competitive displacement process. The binding interactions between the host and guest species in aqueous media have been studied with various spectroscopic methods, while the targeting effect has also been demonstrated in tumor-bearing nude mice.

14307819.label: Project Objectives
14307819.value: To develop spontaneous formation and template-guided formation methods to create size-controllable OHP micro- or submicro-structures, thus enabling manipulation of optical out-coupling in OHP based light-emitting devices; to compare the controllability, reproducibility, crystal quality and luminescent properties provided by the different methods and identify the key processing parameters to control the structure formation process. To establish the design or selection principles of molecular additives by investigating their roles in the crystal growth and defect passivation of the OHP structures and their modification effect to the substrate surface. To develop a hybrid passivation approach, where molecular additives are combined with small-sized metal cations, halide anions and/or their reaction products with the surface OHP layer to achieve robust surface defect passivation. To systematically characterize the morphology and light-emitting property of the structured OHP films and the opto-electrical properties of the corresponding OHP devices; in particular, to explore the use of (i) quantitative phase microscopy in studying the dynamic formation processes of the OHP structures and (ii) electroabsorption microspectroscopy in studying the device physics and degradation mechanisms in the structured devices. To demonstrate enhanced light extraction efficiency of LEDs in near-infrared emission ranges. After device optimization, we target to achieve OHP LEDs with > 20 % external quantum efficiency and improved stability (e.g., a lifetime of more than 1000 hours under 20 mA/cm^2 stress).
