14607919.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14607919.value: 本研究目的是了解和評估聽障遊人在香港濕地公園的多感官體驗。本研究將了解聽障遊人如何通過其受限制的感官能力來感知、應對和理解周圍的景觀環境。 公共空間(例如：公園)的全面可達性和無障礙體驗，正處於社會可持續性和殘疾研究的前沿。多感官體驗的概念可以深化這些方面的理論和方法學的發展，尤其這些知識存在著兩方面的缺口。第一，從多元感官功能的角度了解香港公共城市公園的設施及景觀，尚未得到充份檢視。第二，公園內的感官障礙遊人，尤其是聽障人士，其感官換置或適應性並未得到充分了解。 透過香港濕地公園的個案，本研究旨在從聽障遊人的體驗中全面研究五種人類感官，並了解參與研究的聽障人士，如何描繪其感官體驗和認知。通過一系列的免費導賞和遊覽，闡釋參與者自行報告的感官刺激、公園環境和感官因素。主要研究方法包括對參與者的觀察、問卷調查和小組討論。研究期望包括240名參與者。 本研究通過整合多元感官旅遊目的地管理與營銷、無障礙旅遊與休閒，以及景觀評估的研究領域，更新這些方面的理論和知識。研究成果可促進這些知識領域的融合，改善和加強不同程度的感官障礙和殘疾人士，在面對分割和老年化的社會上的感官體驗。研究亦會帶來一些政策和實際環境上的貢獻，包括為優化公園環境的感官質量和感官刺激，提出實際且有效的建議，以改善感官障礙人士的體驗。

14607919.label: Realisation of objectives
14607919.value: This research investigates the multi-sensory experience of visitors with hearing impairment in the Hong Kong Wetland Park through spatial mapping of their self-reported positive and negative sensory stimuli, and expression of the overall experience. This study combines sensory mapping and textual analysis of participants’ experiences and contributes to the understanding of sensory impairment and experience in a multi-functional landscape of a public park. As sensory impairment is a relatively untapped area of tourism research, the results of this study enrich the domains of knowledge and theoretical development of accessibility in recreation and tourism, sensory experience and landscape assessment. The four research objectives have been achieved: 1. A series of field visits for a total of 104 sampled voluntary participants with hearing impairment were set up. The results show the geographical distribution of sensory features and their spatial pattern across different zones and areas in the Wetland Park. A combination of different stimuli can be found in the park, although visual, auditory and tactile elements seem to be more prominent. In connection, 279 general visitors in the Wetland Park were also surveyed for comparison of their sensory experiences with visitors with hearing impairment. Geographical distribution of sensory stimuli and their spatial pattern of magnitude are clearly observed. Some locations have demonstrated stronger and more positive sensory experience reported by the study participants, which were stimulated by some features providing sensorial opportunities and functions. Natural features provide more than visual stimuli to the park visitors with hearing impairment, which is the primary sense for them to experience the surrounding environment. The Wetland Park shows a combination of stimuli although visual, auditory and tactile elements are more prominent. These sensory stimuli are distributed and diversified across different areas in the park and they also combine to provide a multi-sensory experience to the visitors. Tactile experience of the participants with hearing impairment is relatively rich compared with other non-visual senses. This finding is supported by mapping and participants observations. 2. This comparative research examined the sensory experience creation process between visitors with hearing impairment and general visitors in Hong Kong Wetland Park. The findings suggest three variables with significant differences: the experienced tactile sense, interactions with other visitors, and the feeling of attachment to the park. First, tactile sense is found to be prominent and stronger among visitors with hearing impairment with severe and mild hearing difficulty than general visitors. Such observation concurs with some earlier studies, for example, where general visitors received the least attention from tactile images online across the five basic senses, and that non-visual senses did determine richness of the overall visitor experience and impression of the destination. Although the current study suggests that a combination of sensory stimuli with visual and acoustic senses is the most pertinent to the overall sensory experience, only tactile stimuli in the Wetland Park show an inter-group difference. Second, both sub-groups with mild and severe hearing difficulty possess a significantly stronger experience in terms of interactions with other visitors, than that of general visitors. In many attractions and public spaces, it was observed that visitors with hearing impairment tended to be reliant on social interactions for enhancement of their experience. Third, both sub-groups with mild and severe hearing difficulty possess a significantly stronger experience in terms of feelings of attachment to the Wetland Park after their visit. Similar to some studies on general visitors, visitors with hearing impairment tend to express their satisfaction with the site of visit and develop some positive behavioural intention to revisit or recommend the place to others. 3. Self-reported experiences in the park also indicate barriers and solutions of the park environment by the participants. The requested experiential enhancement is related to physical environmental features and services, which were regarded as interpersonal and structural barriers of visitors with disabilities. These two forms of barriers are also regarded as the functional capacity of access to the site of visit, which included internal and external physical access at site level, sensory access with the provision of assistive devices for users with disabilities, and communication access for information and interactions with different people. These barriers were found in the travel experience of people with visual impairment, but seemed to be less relevant for visitors with hearing impairment in the current study. Sensory barriers are not observed in the current study, where participants with hearing impairment still apparently rely on visual stimuli for enhancing their park experience. However, the finding that visitors with hearing impairment have a stronger tactile sense than general visitors diverges from previous research findings. Furthermore, non-visual senses are not incorporated in the reported model of sensation process, but most of the significant coefficients are the same between the two groups of respondents. Content analysis of recommendations to park improvement provided by participants with hearing impairment after their visits is presented in the research outcomes. Based on the presence of frequent words mentioned by participants with hearing impairment, different aspects of recommendations were coded into categories. Experience-based recommendations mainly surround park features and environment, and programming and experience enhancement. Two overwhelming categories of improvement are facility improvement and guided service. 4. Two research reports were shared with the Hong Kong Wetland Park, Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD), The HKSAR Government, and The Hong Kong Society for the Deaf (HKSOD) respectively with the following key suggestions: - First, apart from physical mobility, more consideration should be taken to provide a universal design improving accessibility for park users and tourist destinations with various types of sensory needs. The readily available facilities for visitors with hearing impairment in the Wetland Park include an induction loop system installed at the information counter and ticket office. Whereas this may facilitate individual aspects of disabled users’ experience at the park, implementing a cluster of compatible features like colourful plants with pleasant smells and special textures in certain locations may foster a more enhanced and holistic visitor experience in the environmental setting. Positive sensory stimuli can be introduced to the areas currently marked by negative sensory experiences. Unwelcoming sensory conditions such as washrooms odour and construction noise should be eliminated wherever possible to prevent accumulation and exaggeration into an overall negative sensory experience. - Second, removing barriers and restrictions is key to improving the sensory experience of visitors with hearing impairment. This, however, has been difficult because of the diversified needs and impairment conditions across different groups. Nevertheless, the wise use of multi-sensory stimuli and protection and management of relevant resources, for example, in nature-based destinations and natural features, tend to enhance both the sensory potential and user experience, and ultimately remove the barriers to long-term accessibility and enjoyment in public spaces and parks. The park and other destination management authorities should optimize the sensory environment and maximize the potential of sensory stimuli that leverage high-quality sensory experiences of visitors with different disabilities. Some features that stimulate visitor senses, such as more “touchable” plants, natural surfaces, models and sculptures, may be introduced and shared among all users through the design of multi-sensory dimensions of the destination environment.

14607919.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14607919.value: Future studies may dissect the underlying process of the sensation creation process through, for example, focus group discussions with visitors with hearing impairment. Geographically, it would be interesting to examine the sensory experiences in various spaces and locations, such as public parks, other parts of the city or other cities. Further research should also be conducted to identify similarities and differences between visitors with hearing impairment and general visitors, sub-groups of visitors with varying degrees of hearing difficulty, who are deaf from birth, who use sign language, and those who lost their hearing later in life, after the age of 3. Inter-group statistical comparison in this study carries a sampling bias due to a difference in sample size between participants with hearing impairment and general visitors. The results recognize a need to better understand an under-researched minority group – visitors with hearing impairment – in the domains of accessible tourism, barrier removal and sensory experience. Another constraint is caused by the inability to provide an in-depth investigation into the underlying spatial-temporal pattern of sensory experience attributed to hearing impairment. Therefore, future studies may examine the spatial pattern of sensory stimuli experienced by visitor groups with different types of impairment.

14607919.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14607919.value: This study investigates the multi-sensory experience of visitors with hearing impairment in Hong Kong Wetland Park through participant mapping of their self-reported positive and negative features, and expression of the overall experience. A series of field visits for a total of 104 sampled voluntary participants with hearing impairment were set up. The results show the geographical distribution of sensory features and their spatial pattern across different zones and areas in the Wetland Park. A combination of different stimuli can be found in the park, although visual, auditory and tactile elements seem to be more prominent. In connection, general visitors in the Wetland Park were also surveyed for comparison of their sensory experiences with visitors with hearing impairment. The research is of novel theoretical significance by integrating the research areas of multi-sensory tourist destination management and marketing, accessible tourism and recreation, and landscape assessment. The research outcomes strengthen the discussion of improving and enhancing the sensory experiences of varied degrees of sensory impairment and disability in an increasingly disenabled and aging society. With respect to its policy and practical contributions, the findings furnish park authorities with some recommendations on how to provide better sensory quality and park environments for sensory-impaired visitors.

14608519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14608519.value: The birth of Daoxue 道學 during the Song dynasty (960–1279) is a key topic in Chinese intellectual history. Considering the influence of Daoxue thought on the East Asian world since the thirteenth century, the proposed research explores the origin of Daoxue by re-thinking the narrative of one of the most influential writings in Chinese intellectual history, the Song Yuan xue'an 宋元學案 (Case Studies of the Learning of Song and Yuan Scholars), compiled by Huang Zongxi黃宗羲 (1610–1695) and Quan Zuwang 全祖望 (1707–1755) in the early Qing. Specifically, my research explores the formation of the intellectual tradition found by Cheng Yi 程頤 (1033–1107) and Cheng Hao 程顥 (1032–1085), i.e., the “Cheng School” (Chengmen 程門), in the transition period from the Northern Song to the Southern Song, and how the oversimplified portrait of this tradition in the Song Yuan xue'an influenced the modern conception of the early history of Daoxue. Through an in-depth analysis of various Song sources, this research examines how the construction of the Cheng School took different approaches in the late Northern Song. The main thesis of the proposed research not only aims to challenge the conventional conception of the “Cheng School” as the academic lineage of the Cheng brothers in the Song Yuan xue'an, but it also attempts to reconstruct the Chinese intellectual landscape in the early twelfth-century. By scrutinizing the writings of the friends, students, and self-proclaimed followers of the Cheng brothers, this research demonstrates how these scholars with different intellectual backgrounds actively participated in the formation and consolidation of the Cheng School. By demonstrating that these traditionally-defined “minor” scholars were actually major contributors to the intellectual tradition of Daoxue, I will supplement the portraits of the Cheng School in the Song Yuan xue'an with a more objective evaluation of the early history of Daoxue. Additionally, the proposed research demonstrates how the students of the Cheng brothers promoted the status of the Chengs and also took advantage of their masters’ reputation to enhance their own intellectual and political status in the early twelfth century. Therefore, the role played by personal interests in the development of the “Cheng School” should not be underestimated. An examination of these interests will enhance the existing study of Daoxue history by emphasizing the role played by human factor in shaping Chinese intellectual traditions. In this light, it reveals the mentality and patterns of behavior of Chinese scholar-officials in a more nuanced way. 宋代道學運動允稱中國思想史上之關鍵問題。考慮到十三世紀以後道學思想對東亞世界的整體影響，本研究嘗試溯源道學運動萌發時的歷史動態，探究程顥、程頤兩位先生所創立之「程門」及其發展經過。這一溯源工作之出發點，乃由反思黃宗羲、全祖望兩位大儒所編《宋元學案》開始。通過梳理、分析不同類別的宋代材料， 本研究試圖指出，《宋元學案》過份簡單化了早期道學史的發展，尤其是「程門」的建構過程。據此而言，本研究不僅旨在挑戰《宋元學案》的既定論述，更力求（局部）重建十二世紀中國的思想版圖。透過細讀二程乃至二程門人、講友的相關材料，包括私人書信、回憶錄、學術作品等等，我希望能夠彰顯二程門人在建構「程門」過程中的重要性。事實上，這些採取不同手段發揚「程學」的二程門人，才是「程門」得以形成的主要原因。沒有他們，道學思想恐怕無法流傳後世，甚至等不到朱熹橫空出世的年代。以《宋元學案》為代表的傳統學案體著作在描繪學派之時，時將作為學派核心的「傳主」與作為學派支流的門人劃為兩截。從學術史角度來看，這種劃分有其合理性。但是，從思想傳播的角度來看，門人所起的作用更甚於老師。他們是否能被簡單歸類為「次級」學者？另外，在「程門」這一個案中，除了宣揚老師學說外，二程門人同時也在利用老師名聲為自己創造更好的政治和思想環境。個人利益因素在學派建構過程中起的作用不可輕視。從這一點來說，研究「程門」形成的過程，也有助於我們理解中國傳統知識份子思維、心性乃至行為模式中的複雜與糾結。

14608519.label: Realisation of objectives
14608519.value: In the past research phase of my GRF project (Jan. 1, 2020 to June 30, 2023, 42 months), the PI has achieved all of the five proposed objectives through the production of the following research outputs, including eight articles, one book manuscript, as well as some papers for future publication projects. In the first phase from 2020 to 2021, the PI published two articles (Part C, 8, RO 1&2) that cover Objective 2, 3, 4 and one book chapter (Part C, 8, RO 3) that deals with Objective 5 mostly. My midterm report has already discussed the details of these articles. In the second phrase from the mid 2021 to 2023, the PI published a series of articles and papers that address research questions revolving around the formation of early Daoxue community and its impact on traditional teacher-student relationship (Objective 1 & 5). The article “The “Black Sheep” of Early Daoxue Community: The Making of Xing Shu’s Historical Image” touches upon the formation of Daoxue through a careful investigation of one so-called disloyal member of Daoxue community. It also serves as a pioneering study of Song historiographical operations through which the historical image of Daoxue mentorship was shaped (Objective 1, 4, &5). The two articles on Cheng Yi’s and mostly his students’ conception of “realization” (cheng 誠) and the editions of Cheng Yi’s collected sayings (yulu 語錄, mostly collected by Cheng’s students) (Part C, 8, RO 6 & 8) adopt philosophical and bibliographical approaches in responding to the research questions the PI mentioned in Objective 3 and 4. These two articles call for a multi-faceted understanding of Song Daoxue history from a cross-disciplinary perspective, which received positive comments from colleagues of relevant fields. The article on the editions of Cheng Yi’s collected sayings has been selected by the committee of the China Association for Song Dynasty Studies (宋史研究會) as one of the representative articles published by the annual publication of the Association. The article concerning Yu Yingshi’s 余英時 eminent work on Song intellectual history (Part C, 8, RO 5) echoes my book chapter (Part C, 8, RO3) on Qian Mu’s 錢穆 study of early Daoxue community. Revisiting Professors Yu and Qian’s classic studies, the two articles reveal various strategies used by Daoxue and pro-Daoxue scholars to promote private scholarship and argue for a more comprehensive understanding of the integration between private and official scholarship in Song China (Objective 3,4 & 5). In this light, my last article produced during the research phrase (Part C, 8, RO7) explores the complexity of Song scholar-officials’ mentality and cast doubt on various Daoxue narrative that obscured our understanding of their intellectual identity and self-identification (Objective 5). In the second phase of the current research project, the PI also prepared a book manuscript that summarizes his research findings in the past three years (Part C, 8, RO9). The book manuscript, temporarily named Anxiety of Making Influence: Development of Early Daoxue Community, covers all the five Objectives of the project by offering a comprehensive examination of the formation of early Daoxue in the transition period from the late eleventh to the early twelfth centuries. As the pioneering work in Western language that thoroughly investigates early Daoxue history beyond the “master-oriented” scope coined by conventional narrative like the Song Yuan xue’an 宋元學案, this book examines the Cheng brothers’ students and their contribution to the formation of Daoxue from three perspectives: their competition for state recognition and political authority, the representation and self-representation of these students in relevant textual records, and their invention of new interpretations on particular Classics. From these perspectives, those conventionally perceived “minor” scholars could be deemed as major contributors to the consolidation and even construction of Daoxue and the more renowned neo-Confucian movement spreading over East Asian in later centuries. The PI has completed most of the chapters of the book and plans to submit it to an acclaimed press for review in the coming year.

14608519.label: Major findings and research outcome
14608519.value: First developed from a rather “revisionist” review on the narrative in the Song Yuan xue’an, this three-years project turned out to be some broader aspirations to revisit the general intellectual landscape of Song China in the transitional period from the late eleventh to the early twelfth centuries. With its focus on a group of thinkers in related to the conventionally categorized Daoxue community during this period, this project demonstrates how these scholars profoundly contributed to the scholarship founded by the Daoxue pioneers in the early-twelfth century and developed the scholarship into a real “tradition”. The project complicates our understanding of Song intellectual landscape through an in-depth analysis of textual sources in related to Daoxue community, especially the genre of collected sayings, which represents a special form of aural records in between oral and written ones. Based on my research findings, I calls for a methodological reflection on the deconstruction of the meta-narrative of Song intellectual history represented by Song Yuan xue’an in my most recent research outcomes (e.g. Part C, 8, RO7). After 42 months of intense research, conference trips, and library tours, the PI completed this project with more research outputs than he proposed before. Current research outputs include six journal articles, one book chapter, one article in edited volume, and a nearly finished (80-85%) book manuscript. Out of the six journal articles, four have already been published or accepted by top-tier English and Chinese journals (Part C, 8, RO1, 2, 4, 7). The other articles have been published in reputable journals (Part C, 8, RO6 & 8). The English book manuscript, with its summary attached here (Part C, 8, RO9), will be completed in the coming year during my sabbatical leave. The PI aims at an international university press to publish it.

14608519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14608519.value: Based on the research outputs, the PI is also considering publishing another Chinese monograph in future, consisting of case studies of early Daoxue history. It may also worth noting that in the past two years the PI has contributed to the formation of a circle of researchers who shared interests in the twelfth century Chinese intellectual history within and outside his own research institution. The first product of this circle of scholarship was an international workshop in China in March, 2024, in which the PI served as one of the keynote speakers. The PI will continue cultivating these scholarly connections to broaden his research scope on relevant fields.

14608519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14608519.value: This project tells a story about how some scholars in Song China (960-1279) whom have been overlook by previous studies actually contributed to the formation of one of the great, if not the greatest, intellectual traditions in East Asia. It tells the story of the birth of Daoxue/neo-Confucianism in the transition period from the late eleventh to the early twelfth centuries with a focus on not the Daoxue “masters” like the Cheng brothers but the masters’ students. Previously, these students have received much less attention from both traditional and modern scholars and have been categorized as “minor” scholars by historians. This project argues that the Song “minor” scholars could be deemed as major contributors to the consolidation and even construction of the renowned neo-Confucian movement spreading over East Asia in later centuries. By probing into these “minor” scholars’ intellectual and political efforts in promoting their teachers’ scholarship, the project rewrites early Daoxue history that has still been largely shaped by the “master-oriented” narrative represented by the Song Yuan xue’an.

14609119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14609119.value: The Belt and Road Initiative, a key recent policy initiative of the Chinese central government and a core element of China’s growing importance in global politics, is foremost an economic initiative with a major focus on infrastructure development. However, the revival of the old Silk Road connotes not only the idea of economic exchange but also the exchange of people, of knowledge, and not least of religious beliefs. The proposed research examines the role of Chinese cross-cultural foreign missions in order to investigate how far this more active role of China on the world stage is reflected in religious communication and paralleled by Christian missionary movements. The background of this research is the observation that China’s past four decades of economic growth have been accompanied by an equally astonishing growth of Christianity. This is part of a wider shift within global Christianity, with the center of gravity moving towards the global South and the influence of Christians in the Global South on global mission increasing. Believers from South Korea have assumed a particularly prominent role within the world mission movement. Whether Chinese Christians follow the path of South Korean mission is one of the interests of this research. The research plan is to collect evidence on common practices, strategies, missionary agents, main challenges, common narratives and mission-theological paradigms now emerging from China, where mission is still in the early stages of development. It will do so by gathering publicly available information about Chinese missionary activities, by qualitative research with missionaries in the field, mission trainers, and people in charge of mission organizations, and by integrating the results in a discussion of the contexts in which Chinese mission endeavor takes place. The focus of the research will be on Chinese mission within Asia, particularly in Southeast and Central Asia. The study tries to consider the roles and potential impacts of the emerging Chinese mission movement within China’s increasingly assertive role in international politics. 靈巧如蛇，馴良如鴿子？ 一帶一路處境中的中國海外宣教 「一帶一路」倡議是中國中央政府近年推出的一個重要政策倡議，也是中國在全球政治中日益重要的一個核心元素，最重要的是它是一項經濟倡議，主要聚焦于基礎設施建設的發展。 然而，舊絲綢之路的復興，不僅意味著經濟的交流，也包括人與人的交流、知識的交流，尤其是宗教信仰的交流。 該研究方案考察中國跨文化外國宣教的影響，目的是為了調查中國在世界舞臺上發揮的積極深遠影響如何通過宗教交流層面反映出來，同時伴隨著基督徒的宣教運動。 這項研究背景是基於中國過去四十年經濟增長同步伴隨著驚人的基督教增長的觀察。 這是全球基督教內部更廣泛轉變的一部分，隨著基督教中心向全球南方轉移，全球南方基督徒對全球宣教的影響日益增長。 韓國信徒在全球宣教運動中已經扮演了突出卓越的角色。 中國基督徒是否會遵循韓國的宣教路徑是本研究的興趣點之一。 此研究計畫旨在收集有關共同實踐、戰略、宣教機構、主要挑戰、共同敘事和目前在中國出現的宣教-神學范式的證據，在此，宣教仍然處於早期發展階段。 研究通過收集有關中國宣教士活動的公開能獲得的資訊，通過對在此領域的宣教士，宣教培訓員，和負責宣教機構的人員進行定性研究，並整合中國宣教在這些領域所做的貢獻的討論結果。 該研究聚焦在亞洲範圍內的中國宣教，尤其是在東南亞和中亞。 該研究試圖從中國在國際政治中越來越佔據重要地位的內部來考量新興的中國宣教運動扮演的角色和潛在影響。 關鍵字 中國宣教—世界宣教—全球基督教——絲綢之路復興—海外中國基督教

14609119.label: Realisation of objectives
14609119.value: The objectives spelled out in the project application have mostly been achieved. See below a short summary of each objective: 1. Objective 1: To gather qualitative data on the extent of Chinese missionary activities overseas While a scientifically accurate number of missionaries is, due to reasons explained in the application, impossible to establish, this research has established a credible estimation regarding the global extent of missionary activities of Chinese overseas missionaries. The research used a snowball sampling system based on interviews with Chinese missionaries in different geographical contexts. The details of how the insights have been gained and the methodological difficulties that had to be overcome are described in the article that will be published in Theology and Mission in World Christianity. 2. Objective 2: To analyze strategies of Chinese missionary activities The research successfully analyzed various strategies for Chinese missionary activities. A particular focus was on analyzing how missionaries responded to linguistic and cross-cultural challenges and how their communicative aspects mitigated the difficulties arising from them. An important discovery was the strong connection between missionary activities and overseas Chinese Christian congregations, an aspect discussed in the article to be published in Theology and Mission in World Christianity. 3. Objective 3: To analyze geographical preferences and preferred people-groups The quantitative findings (objective 1) were gained by collecting evidence through interviews from several countries. This method allowed an assessment of geographical preferences and people groups. Additionally, a comparison with preference patterns in Hong Kong, which shares many theological and missionary visions with mainland Chinese Christians, supported the findings gained through interviews. The interest behind this objective was the intention of verifying an oft-mentioned trend toward mission among Muslims. The findings partly confirm such a connection, yet they show that pragmatic factors such as accessibility of a mission field still play a more important role. 4. Objective 4: To identify core values and theological visions of Chinese missionary activities The interviews revealed several motifs that frequently occurred in missionaries’ narratives, important among them a burden for spreading the Christian faith among Muslims, a willingness to endure hardship, a sense of a ‘gospel debt,’ and a divine calling, as discussed in the article published in the International Bulletin of Missionary Research. The Back to Jerusalem Movement, a missionary vision that has received substantial criticism in the past, is still regarded as a popular overall framework integrating many of the individual motifs of Chinese missionaries. 5. Objective 5a: To analyze social, cultural, political, economic, and other factors affecting Chinese missionaries and to understand the interaction between social, political, and economical expansion and the shifting missionary role of ethnically Chinese Christians The interviews paid considerable attention to the various factors that affected Chinese missionaries. An important factor among those identified was the ecclesial background of missionaries. The results of the interviews suggest categorizing the different missionaries into five groups – missionaries from rural house church networks, from Wenzhou, from urban house churches, from ethnic minorities, and overseas Chinese who returned to China and were sent out as missionaries from there. Another important factor was a broadly shared ambiguity between the benefits that the increased economic and political power brings to Chinese overseas missions and the more repressive religious policies, which affect Christians inside and missionaries outside of mainland China. As a result, many overseas Chinese missionaries stand in critical tension to China’s growing international economic and political presence. The growth of overseas Chinese Christian congregations, which is a direct result of increased Chinese economic activity overseas, builds an important financial and spiritual support base. 6. Objective 5b: To consider the roles and potential impacts of Chinese mission on Chinese foreign relations The insights gained from interviews and the analysis of other resources revealed that the growing presence of Chinese missionaries does not directly impact Chinese foreign relations. Yet, the presence of missionaries may be an obstacle to smooth relations with economic partners and may disturb economic interests of Chinese overseas activities, as seen in a tragic incident in Pakistan’s Baluchistan province, near the Gwadar harbor, a core part of the China –Pakistan Economic Corridor and of China’s Maritime Silk Road. On the other side, the presence of Chinese missionaries offers another face of Chinese presence around the world and a counter-narrative to the presence of Chinese corporations engaged in trade or in infrastructure, which in some contexts are perceived as a threat to the local economy and local cultures. 7. Objective 6: To examine the dynamics between Chinese missionaries and locals, that is, to collect information about how Chinese missionaries are received and what challenges they experience The covid pandemic and the related travel restrictions made the interaction with recipients of Chinese missionaries’ outreach activities impossible. The RGC thus accepted a revision of this objective, instead evaluating the dynamics between Chinese missionaries and locals based on the self-assessment of missionaries. Many interviewees admitted significant difficulties immersing in local contexts and developing cross-cultural expertise. They self-critically found that Chinese mission was too often too introverted and drawn back into the orbit of Chinese overseas Christian churches, thus serving their own rather than the local population. 8. Objective 7: To publish at least two articles and to present insights at a major mission conference. The findings of the research not only offered material for two articles and one conference presentation (see Part C) but led to two further conference presentations and provided support for a book chapter in the book "Christians in the City of Hong Kong: Chinese Christianity in Asia’s World City," to be published in autumn 2023 by Bloomsbury Academics. The topic created considerable public interest, as it offered an alternative view of China’s international impact, one that focused on impacts beyond the common economic and political realm. A full-page interview in the internationally most recognized Swiss newspaper brought some of the early findings to a public outside of the academic world. While the conference and knowledge transfer output may exceed the planned objective, the publication of an article in a peer-reviewed series rather than in a regional peer-reviewed journal (besides the one in an international peer-reviewed journal) needs an explanation: 1. The PI decided that the visibility and accessibility of an article in a book of the series Theology and Mission in World Christianity surpass the one of a publication in a regional journal, even more so, as the volume is specifically dedicated to Chinese mission. 2. The series is peer-reviewed and is well-received by the scholarly community. 3. Within the said volume, the PI’s article is the only one that specifically addresses the present state of Chinese overseas mission. 4. The PI regards the claim of the RGC, in its negative response to an application for amendment of the objective, that the peer-review process of an edited volume is less rigorous than in a peer-reviewed journal, as not necessarily true or, if true, only gradually so. A claimed less rigorous peer review is compensated by higher visibility and accessibility, as this PI’s article appears in a volume that relates more closely to the topic of his research. Taking into account the RGC’s rejection of an application to amend objective 7, the PI sees this objective as achieved to 95%.

14609119.label: Major findings and research outcome
14609119.value: a) The research successfully established evidence for the extent of Chinese overseas mission. The resulting assessment is significantly lower than the claim of many promoters of Chinese mission. Estimates based on interviews of Chinese missionaries in various countries lead to a more exact assessment of numerical realities. b) The research revealed patterns of geographical and ethnic preferences that partly confirm but also significantly deviate from the often-expressed ‘burden’ of Chinese missionaries for Muslims. c) The research identified major types of Chinese missionaries, depending on their ecclesial, spiritual, and theological background. It distinguishes five types: missionaries from rural house churches, from urban house churches, from ethnic minorities, from Wenzhou, and from overseas Chinese returnees’ communities. d) The research made different trajectories of the extension of Chinese Christianity visible. Some missionaries support China’s economic expansion and use the presence of Chinese businesspeople to reach out to the local population. They support a narrative popular among many Asian mission promoters that Western missionaries, due to their colonial past, are disqualified for mission. Others stand at a critical distance to China’s rise and recognize that the hardships caused by restrictive religious policies inside China parallel those caused by the behavior of large Chinese corporations outside China. Yet, indirectly, and unintentionally, they also serve the advancement of Chinese interests because they establish people-to-people relations that appear to soften the negative impacts of China’s economic activities. e) The study diagnosed a network of partners supporting the emerging Chinese mission movement. Of particular importance are Korean missionaries who play an important role inspiring, guiding, and educating Chinese missionaries. Equally important are overseas Chinese congregations who build a financial, spiritual, psychological, and manpower support base. The danger of Chinese missionaries’ entanglement with overseas Chinese congregations is that they may be reabsorbed in the Chinese orbit. They support the creation of a transnational ethnoreligious space that, in fact, keeps both Chinese migrants and Chinese missionaries from integrating into their host societies. f) The study describes core ideas in the self-understanding of Chinese missionaries, among them the idea of a divine calling to reach the people in South, Central, and West Asia, in the geographical area between China and Israel, and the idea that Chinese Christians are now paying back a ‘gospel debt,’ that is, the idea that after having received thousands of missionaries in China, today’s Chinese church repays this debt by sending an equal number of missionaries abroad.

14609119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14609119.value: Research on the Chinese cross-cultural overseas mission movement has the potential of being conducted on a long-term basis, as this is a movement very much in the process of development. It shows similarities with the development of the Korean mission movement, which, within only 3 decades, has become a major factor in global Christian mission. While the Korean mission is well documented by the Korean Research Institute for Mission (KRIM), nothing of this kind of research exists for the emerging Chinese mission movement. While Chinese religious policies would make a continuous and open research institute difficult, the Chinese overseas mission movement deserves continuous attention, as it adds another important layer to China’s growing presence around the world. What makes the presence of Chinese missionaries particularly interesting is that they are, in contrast to large parts of China’s overseas presence, not state-based or driven by economic interests, but a grassroots movement. Further funding would allow • to understand how Chinese overseas mission activities are affected by changing religious policies both at home and overseas, • to keep the understanding of the numerical extent and geographical preferences of Chinese missionaries updated, and • to further analyze the impacts of Chinese missionaries in their local contexts.

14609119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14609119.value: The starting point of this research project was the question of how far the growing international economic and political clout of China finds reflection in the religious field, more particularly in Chinese Christians’ overseas mission activities. After decades of significant Christian growth in China, the investigator studied how far this religious growth would spill over into cross-cultural overseas missions. The study was mainly based on interviews with Chinese missionaries in the field and with people supporting these missionaries. While there have been articles on Chinese overseas missions before, this study is the first to investigate this emerging mission movement more systematically. The findings confirmed a growing presence of Chinese cross-cultural overseas missionaries but disproved reports by some promoters of Chinese missions who offer much higher estimates of Chinese overseas missionaries. It identified core motifs that inspire Chinese missionaries, most importantly a passion for mission among Muslims. While these missionaries benefitted from the growing wealth of Chinese Christians at home and Chinese expatriate Christians abroad, many of them showed a critical distance to Chinese economic activities overseas. Their missionary work stands in contrast to those Chinese economic activities that are perceived critically by local people, and it creates an important counter-narrative.

14609219.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14609219.value: This study will examine how urbanization has reshaped property structures in rural China from a gender perspective. Rather than seeing rural residents as homogeneously dispossessed or as the new rich under the property boom, this study will examine people’s different property holding positions in the process of urbanization. As the rural property regimes of family-based land tenures and self-built housing are transformed into the urban property registration system, urbanization often undermines women’s property rights given their contested citizenship and the difficulty to distinguish individual rights from collective and joint ownership structures. But to some extent, urbanization may also empower women and free women from the rural constraints. However, little is known about how women and men fare differently in top-down and bottom-up urbanization pathways. The proposed project builds upon a previous GRF project on “rehousing villagers in China’s urban sprawl.” The previous project focused on land development and housing relocation in the urbanizing northwestern China. This proposed project takes up the next discussion thread with a new research focus on property restructuring from a gender perspective, based on field sites in northwestern and southeastern China (Ningxia and Zhejiang respectively). The top-down massive demolition and relocation processes are more dominant in the field site in Ningxia, whereas the bottom-up forces of self-development are more influential in the field site in Zhejiang. The previous project examined different rehousing projects and their consequences in property development and community rebuilding in Ningxia, whereas the proposed project incorporates gender as an important lens to comprehend contested citizenship and inequality patterns across regions. This study will shed light on how the rural property structure is urbanized differently in top-down and bottom-up urbanization pathways and whether it leads to more equal access to resources or reinforces inequalities between genders and generations. The changing property structures evolve together with gender roles and family relations in the urbanizing China. This study not only focuses on property holding positions but also explores the related agency and status of men and women, including how people negotiate, access, make decisions about and make sense of the changing property structures. This study will use both quantitative survey data and qualitative interviews from the two research sites to examine formal registration and informal customary use of properties, and explore subjective meanings of property structures. Both instrumental and emotional implications of property structures will be studied to evaluate gender equality in the urbanizing China.

14609219.label: Realisation of objectives
14609219.value: The project involves a three-fold analysis of property restructuring and social life in urbanization based on extensive fieldwork in 2020-2023 in Western and Eastern China. The first part of the project focuses on the mechanisms of property restructuring, as described in Objective 1. From a top-down perspective, governments have loosened compensation criteria to facilitate land development and address grassroots discontent. From a bottom-up perspective, villagers have drawn on multiple principles when dividing the newly acquired properties. Quantitative survey results and qualitative case analysis illustrate how people weighed and negotiated principles of exchange, entitlement, altruism, male privilege, and need in distributing housing properties. The project demonstrates how these principles interacted in three dimensions: between parents and children, between elder and younger children, and between sons and daughters. The multi-dimensional processes of property restructuring show the persisting gender effect and the ambiguous generation and parity effects when rural families were relocated or enclosed into urban areas. The second part of the project, corresponding to Objective 2, examines the outcomes of property restructuring concerning entitlement and access to resources for men and women. In general, housing relocation led to accelerated downstream transfers from parents and the persisting disadvantages of daughters in accessing the newly acquired urban wealth. However, when housing replaced farming as a primary source of economic security, there were rising desires to care for entitlement for each child and secure elderly care for parents. The outcomes of property restructuring vary by family resources and family structures, especially between big and small families, and between families with sons only, daughters only, or with both sons and daughters. As local governments minimized the intervention in redistributing properties at the grassroots level, the government discourses of social stability and family harmony have pushed for internal affairs related to the newly acquired urban wealth to be solved by families and communities themselves. The third part of the project, as shown in Objective 3, explores the implications of property restructuring for household dynamics and individual agency. Although governments have framed urban exposure and rural transformation as part of the national modernization campaign, the property boom for communities of relocated villagers does not necessarily lead to ideational changes as predicted by modernization theories. People have strived for economic security and wealth by negotiating their positions in families and communities, and the power dynamics that define who are insiders continue to be gendered. Nevertheless, property restructuring has allowed some women to mobilize family resources and grasp economic opportunities in a market of increasing uncertainties. Depending on individual aspirations, family support, and access to local resources and connections, many young women have exerted different forms of agency in conducting migration and return migration and seeking economic achievements and self-realization. The project finds how female entrepreneurship is facilitated by their access to family resources and how their mobility is shaped by family property structures. Although not all women can overcome the structural and ideological constraints in accessing the new urban wealth, these findings point to the limited chance of disadvantaged groups to strive for family decision-making power and improve their socioeconomic status in an era of urban expansion and rural transformation.

14609219.label: Major findings and research outcome
14609219.value: The first part of the project reports on the multiple mechanisms of property restructuring when villagers were relocated into the expanding cities. Rural households have drawn on multiple principles to prioritize the housing needs of sons, care for the entitlement of each child, compensate less privileged children, and secure elderly care for parents. Parents and elder siblings did not have apparent advantages in property structures, but gender inequality persisted along with the increasing awareness of individual interests (Song and Li, 2024). As compensation and relocation policies have loosened and left resource redistribution to grassroots communities and families, relocated households have negotiated the division of properties based on the availability of resources and the needs and contributions of individual family members (Sun and Song, 2024). Meanwhile, intrahousehold inequalities in access to properties are no longer taken for granted but have become an issue that needs to be justified. The second part of the project illustrates the mixed outcomes of property restructuring in urbanization. The consequent property structures vary by family resources and family structures. The male privilege is more persistent in big families and in families with both sons and daughters. Compared with their male counterparts, women commonly do not express a sense of entitlement, and female entitlement remains frequently represented by their male family members. However, some women have gained greater access to family resources in relocation, especially when they have fewer siblings, when the family has daughters only, or when their families have sufficient resources to care for the needs and contributions of women (Sun and Song, 2024; Song and Li, 2024). The third part of the project finds the far-reaching implications of property restructuring regarding household dynamics and individual agency. Depending on their property positions, some women managed to mobilize family resources in pursuing market success and embracing entrepreneurship (Song, 2024; Han et al., 2024), such as running family hotels (Song and Zhou, 2021, conference presentation). Another finding concerning the gendered status and empowerment is about their migration patterns: women deliberate on their access to family resources and local connections when conducting return migration to their hometowns, not only to serve family utility but also to seek economic achievements and self-realization (Li and Song, 2024; Song and Jackson, 2024).

14609219.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14609219.value: Urbanization in China has led to a property boom, but the wealth is not evenly distributed among affected villagers. The present project lays a foundation for understanding the shifting property structures from a gender perspective. The project can be extended to examine how women and men manage their economic positionalities and negotiate their career and family life in urban neighborhoods and workplaces to seek autonomy and respect. Another field of future research is to explore grassroots reaction to economic insecurity and injustice after villagers were relocated in urbanization, especially concerning the rise of married-out women disputes. Given the governmental emphasis on social stability and family harmony, it is important to examine how grassroots discontent is channeled via litigation or mediation. Although governments and developers can adopt quick and convenient solutions by providing more generous compensation deals, it is to be examined if more fundamental social institutions of marriage, family, and property can be challenged or reformed in response to community disputes, family conflicts, and grassroots appeals.

14609219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14609219.value: Under the national development goals of urban expansion and rural transformation in China, this project examines how property structures have evolved among relocated villagers from a gender perspective. The project examines the property restructuring mechanisms and finds multiple principles for dividing resources across generations, siblings, and genders, given the desire to have individual urban homes among youth and the need to seek support in an urban setting for older people. As an outcome, property restructuring has reinforced gender and social inequality and created some limited space to negotiate access to the new urban wealth among disadvantaged groups. In big families and in families with both sons and daughters, patriarchal traditions are more persistent. In small families and in daughter-only families, women have a better chance to strive for a greater share in relocation properties. The shifting property structures in massive urbanization and rural transformation have far-reaching implications for gendered opportunities to strive for market success and embrace entrepreneurship. Given their gendered access to family resources, young women have negotiated migration and return migration trajectories accordingly. The evolving opportunity structures and gendered constraints point to uneven economic insecurity for relocated villagers and unequal chances of adventuring in the market of increasing uncertainties.

14609519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14609519.value: Despite constraining political context, environmental non-government organizations (eNGOs) have carved out a field of existence in China. They have become important institutional players in environmental politics. Studies on eNGOs have examined how they navigate the complex political and institutional environments to advocate for policy change, yet these studies confront major problems. Much research relies on temporally-limited case studies, which, despite major virtues in terms of depth and insight, often lack analytic controls. In addition, limited research has examined in a systematic way the effects of various institutional forces, i.e., government, foundations, and the nonprofit sector, on eNGO policy advocacy and its impact on environmental governance. We address these issues by proposing a longitudinal and comparative study of eNGO policy advocacy in China. Here, advocacy is broadly defined as any attempt to influence public policy on behalf of a collective interest. Specifically, the project will address the following four research questions: (1) How do institutional factors affect eNGOs’ advocacy investment and tactics? (2) Given the evolving political environment and the changing eNGO sector, has there been systematic change in eNGOs’ advocacy investment and tactics? What led to this change? (3) Given the fragmented nature of authoritarianism in China, are there regional variations in eNGOs’ advocacy investment and tactics? How do they relate to differences in regulatory and political contexts across jurisdictions? (4) Ultimately, what are the outcomes of eNGO policy advocacy? Building on our prior research on eNGOs and environmental governance, we will collect data from two sources--nationwide surveys and semi-structured interviews—and combine them with data collected in 2014-2015 to build a two-wave panel data set. We will use multiple analytic techniques, including quantitative and qualitative analyses, to examine the antecedents and outcomes of eNGO policy advocacy. The proposed research represents the first attempt at developing a longitudinal and comparative study of Chinese eNGOs and will improve estimations of causal effects. It will contribute to the literature on public management and environmental governance by expanding the scope of existing theories to a different institutional setting. It will also unfold the complex interactions between eNGOs and the government and suggest ways in which various institutional actors may help enhance eNGOs’ capacity in policy advocacy. 儘管政治環境受到限制，中國的民間環保組織已經逐漸開拓出一片領域。他們日漸成為環境政治過程中的重要參與者。既有的對環保組織的研究已經研究了它們如何駕馭複雜的政治和制度環境來倡導政策變革，但是這些研究存在一些主要問題。大部分研究運用單個時間點的案例；儘管這些案例加深了我們對政策倡導的深度理解，它們通常缺乏分析控制。此外，有一些研究已經系統的研究了各種制度力量，包括政府，基金會和非營利部門對環保組織政策倡導及環境治理的影響。 在本研究中，我們通過對環保組織政策倡導的縱向和比較研究來彌補既有研究的不足。在此，倡導被廣泛的定義為任何代表集體利益影響公共政策的嘗試。具體而言，我們試圖回答四個研究問題： 1）制度因素如何影響環保組織政策倡導的投入和戰略選擇？ 2）針對不斷變化的政治環境和環保組織行業，環保組織的倡導投入和戰略有何變化？是什麼因素導致了這些變化？ 3）針對中國威權主義的碎片化特性，環保組織的倡導投入和戰略選擇是否存在地區差異？這些差異跟不同地區的監管和政治環境背景相關嗎？ 4）最終，環保組織政策倡導的結果是什麼？ 在我們對環保組織和環境治理的既有研究的基礎上，我們將收集兩方面的數據：關於環保組織的全國性的調查和針對領導人的半結構化訪談。我們將新收集的數據和既有的在2014-2015年收集的數據合並起來構建雙波面板數據集。我們將使用多種分析技術，包括定量和定性分析，來研究環保組織政策倡導的原因和結果。這項研究是開展中國環保組織縱向和比較研究的第一次嘗試，它將改進對因果效應的估計。本研究主要有兩大貢獻。第一，它將對現有的公共行政和環境治理理論擴展到一個不同的制度環境。第二，它將揭示環保組織和政府之間的複雜互動，並在各個參與者如何能協力提高環保組織政策倡導的能力方面提出建議。

14609519.label: Realisation of objectives
14609519.value: This research project aimed to examine the longitudinal and comparative change of environmental NGOs' policy advocacy in authoritarian China, looking specifically at the changing landscape for ENGO development and how ENGOs have adapted to the changes in their advocacy strategies and organizational development. However, the project implementation was laden with unforeseen obstacles that tested the resilience of the project team. Specifically, the obstacles consisted of four aspects. First, the social protests in Hong Kong in 2019 and the stigma surrounding Hong Kong made fieldwork difficult. The intricate web of socio-political tensions further complicated the landscape, demanding innovative approaches to navigate the barriers to progress. Second, the three-year COVID-19 pandemic in mainland and Hong Kong restricted the team's ability to conduct fieldwork, underscoring the importance of adaptability and remote methodologies in research endeavors. Third, one of the key project members took maternity leave in 2022. In addition, the departure of a liaison person from the Tsinghua University-affiliated think tank necessitated a strategic shift in collaboration to Prof. Tan at the University of Mining and Technology-Beijing (CUMT-BJ) for survey administration. This transition required time to adjust contract specifications and survey data collection details. Despite the trials and tribulations encountered along the way, the project team was able to achieve the majority of their objectives successfully. Below, we detail how each project objective was successfully met. 1. Identify patterns of variations in advocacy investment and tactics across eNGOs 2. Identify major political and organizational factors affecting eNGOs' advocacy investment and tactics 3. Perform longitudinal analysis as to how institutional and organizational factors affect eNGOs' advocacy investment and tactics across time We examined the landscape of ENGOs through a nationwide survey. Data was collected from 120 ENGOs, with 58 organizations participating in the recent survey and the initial round conducted during 2014-2015. Furthermore, we conducted 65 interviews with ENGO leaders, encompassing both domestic NGOs and international NGOs working with domestic ENGOs. These data help capture a nuanced understanding of the evolving advocacy strategies and organizational dynamics within the ENGO sector. Currently, with the findings and analyses derived from the survey data and interviews, we are working on three papers, which are slated for submission to top-tier peer-reviewed journals in the coming months. - Given the data we have from 58 ENGOs in the two rounds of data collection, we are conducting a qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) to illuminate the shifts in advocacy strategies employed by ENGOs over time. This analysis can uncover the complex interplay of political and organizational factors influencing advocacy approaches and the varied policy outcomes. - During the fieldwork, we noticed that many ENGOs are facing serious operational difficulties, and some have even closed down. We are examining the survival and demise of ENGOs in the past ten years and testing how organizational ecology, institutional linkages, and resource dependencies influence ENGOs' survival. We have presented this paper in two conferences and are ready to submit the refined paper in two months. - We zoomed into ENGOs' use of social media, focusing on how changes in the political environment influenced the social media discourse and strategies adopted by ENGOs on digital platforms. We have presented this paper in a workshop and a conference, and are now finalizing the paper for submission in a month. 4. Examine whether eNGOs' policy advocacy varies across jurisdictions and identify institutional and political factors relating to the variations Our survey and interviews cover ENGOs across diverse regions, including Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Chongqing, and Kunming. We have developed a framework to delineate the nuances in the institutional and regulatory landscapes influencing ENGO operations and have collected preliminary data to map out these variations. For the next step, we will establish connections between the intricacies of the institutional and regulatory environments on one spectrum and the advocacy strategies employed by ENGOs on the other. This analytical approach can help shed light on how the fragmented governance structure prevalent in China manifests in ENGO advocacy. The analysis for this qualitative paper will be completed in the first half of 2025 and will be presented in major conferences. 5. Identify strategies that can help both NGOs and policymakers to facilitate sustained NGO development and to promote effective cross-sector collaboration in environmental governance. This objective focuses on building effective dialogue between NGO practitioners, policymakers, and academics. This is an ongoing process. Invited by the Oxford Bibliographies project, we developed a comprehensive bibliography on civil society in China, encompassing a repository of over 100 studies on NGOs in China, of which many are on ENGOs. This compilation serves as a pivotal resource for practitioners and policymakers interested in China’s NGO landscape, facilitating informed discussions and nurturing mutual understanding. We hosted a delegation from the China Association for NGOs (CANGO), a government-organized NGO collaborating with foreign and domestic NGOs to bolster fundraising, technical support, and capacity-building initiatives for grassroots NGOs in China. We also meet with representatives from the Gates Foundation, engaging in knowledge exchange sessions to share research insights and bridge the gap between academia and practices. These collaborative efforts stand as instrumental efforts toward enhancing cooperation and efficacy within the NGO ecosystem.

14609519.label: Major findings and research outcome
14609519.value: The development of ENGOs in China is intricately shaped by a nuanced interplay between contrasting green-light and red-light policies and regulations. Greenlight policies, such as the Belt and Road Initiative and the Two Mountains Theory, create a conducive environment and legitimizing framework for ENGO engagement and impact within the environmental governance. Conversely, red light policies pose hurdles to ENGO development, exerting constraints on their operational scope and outreach. Regulations such as the National Security Law of 2015, the INGO Law of 2017, the Data Security Law of 2021, and the Guarding State Secrets Law of 2024 collectively impose restrictions on ENGO development to varying degrees. The interplay between these green and red-light policies underscores the complex terrain in which ENGOs navigate, oscillating between opportunities for growth and challenges stemming from regulatory constraints. Given the intricate environment, we found that - Overall, 71.5 percent of ENGOs have survived since 2014, translating to an estimated 3.5 percent mortality rate yearly. - We found that the survival rate for government-organized NGOs is 85%. In contrast, for grassroots civic NGOs, it is 55%, suggesting that the playing field is uneven. - Our analysis shows that NGO density in a region is positively associated with ENGO survival, GONGOs are more likely to survive than grassroots NGOs, ENGOs engaging in more administrative advocacy are more likely to survive, and ENGOs with higher dependencies on foundation funding are more likely to survive. These results show how organizational ecology, institutional linkages, and resource dependencies shape ENGO survival in different ways. - We collected ENGOs' social media posts (N=163,369) from 2013 to 2019 and used structural topic modelling to examine changes in ENGOs' social media engagement strategies. Our findings show that the trend of ENGOs' social media posting was marked by a consistent decline from 2013 to 2017, followed by a slight resurgence in post numbers after that, suggesting that ENGOs are using social media platforms more cautiously. Certain topics, such as climate change, ecosystem, and river protection, saw a decline, whereas wildlife, habitat, and documentary saw a significant rise, suggesting that ENGOs are gearing more toward environmental education and shying away from policy advocacy online. They are also refraining from discussing specific issues and topics but focus more on broader and more general discussions, which are less risky.

14609519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14609519.value: Moving forward, we will finalize the three working papers and submit them to top journals in the next few months. In parallel, we will start working on two additional papers: 1) examine how regional disparities influence ENGO operations, strategies, and impact in a fragmented governance system, and 2) examine the evolution of funding mechanisms adopted by NGOs over the past decade, shedding light on the adaptive strategies these organizations employ to navigate financial challenges and sustain their missions effectively. This project has helped strengthen our collaboration with the Center for Environmental Education and Communications of the Ministry of Ecology and Environment. We will leverage their expertise with ENGOs and local environmental bureaus and launch a survey experiment to examine how ENGOs engage with corporations of different ownerships (such as state-owned enterprises, public ownership, and private enterprises) in sustainability. Building upon our current investigations into ENGO development within China, we submitted a new grant proposal on ENGO internationalization in the 2024/2025 General Research Fund (GRF). We propose to unravel the diverse pathways through which ENGOs engage beyond national borders and participate in global civil society and international affairs.

14609519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14609519.value: Environmental nongovernmental organizations (ENGOs) have emerged as pivotal actors in China's environmental governance, championing causes like species conservation, sustainable development, and renewable energy. While these organizations often operate with limited resources and staff, their impact on policymaking is significant. However, existing research has paid insufficient attention to how institutional factors shape ENGO advocacy and how different strategies lead to varying advocacy outcomes longitudinally. Our research project examines ENGOs' policy advocacy in authoritarian China from a longitudinal and comparative perspective. Using data from surveys and interviews conducted in 2014-15 and 2022-2023 respectively, we analyzed the survival and demise of ENGOs in the past decade, their advocacy strategies, and engagement with social media. Findings show that 1) the mortality rate for ENGOs is approximately 3.5 percent in the past decade, 2) ENGOs adopt politically safer approaches to policy influence, 3) ENGOs are decoupling from international networks in domestic activities, while actively participating in China's international development initiatives. This research sheds light on the adaptive strategies and evolving dynamics of ENGOs within China's changing political landscapes.

14611019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14611019.value: While previous studies and policies have largely focused on the rural children affected by parental migration, this study argues that urban left-behind children also deserves scholarly and public policy attention, as they might also face challenges resulted from absence of parents due to migration. Based on the first nationally representative survey on adolescents in junior high school, while 29% of the rural children are left-behind (with 15.8% completely left-behind with both parents having migrated and 13.4% left-behind with one migrant parent respectively), 20% of the urban children are also left-behind (with 9.8% completely left-behind with both parents having migrated and 10% left-behind with one migrant parent respectively). The share of migrant children is even slightly higher among urban children than that among rural children, with the share of migrants being 9% and 8 % among urban children and rural children respectively. Building on the literature of migration, intergenerational transfer of inequality, sociology of education, this project plans to the first two waves of the first nationally representative education survey-China Education Panel Survey and aims to examine the following research questions: 1) How does migration (both parental migration and children’s own migration) affect adolescents’ cognitive development and school enrollment? 2) Does the effect of parental and child migration on children’s developmental outcomes vary by urban/rural origin of the children? In particular, I investigate whether children benefit from being brought along rather than being left-behind, and whether the potential impact of migration varies by the hukou origin of students, and how parental capital and school-context factors contribute to shaping educational inequalities between migrant and non-migrant students and also by rural and urban origin. This study is unique in several aspects. First, it utilizes longitudinal data from the first nationally representative education survey that collects information from both children, parents and schools, which helps to depict the complex process how migration affects children’s cognitive development and educational outcomes through varied access to family and school capital. Second, it is the first study to bring attention to urban migrant children and urban left-behind children who have been increasingly affected by migration but are still absent in previous literature on migration and children in China. Third, this study compares the impact of parental migration and child migration by rural/urban status, contributing to the limited understanding of how the impact of migration on education might vary by urban/rural status of origin and selectivity of migrant parents. 14612019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14612019.value: Family carers of people with first-episode psychosis (FEP) often face high levels of physical, emotional and financial demands/burdens. This can adversely affect their caregiving experiences and general well-being, and are associated with high psychological distress and family conflicts and consequently contributed to patients’ relapses and/or re-hospitalizations. While family psychoeducation and other supportive group programs are effective in enhancing carers’ knowledge of psychosis and stress management, these interventions require face-to-face education sessions over a long interval and high engagement and trusting relationships with both group therapist/facilitator and peer members and often result in low attendance, fear/inability of openly feeling expressions and high withdrawals/drop-outs. In views of the above difficulties/challenges, a manual-guided self-learning program facilitating self-help and flexible self-decided learning paces, with a guided reading (on a validated self-help manual) and caregiving practice schedule with stress management skills training facilitated by a psychiatric nurse, has shown significant benefits in controlled trials for family carers in schizophrenia and depression by the research team. This multi-center randomized controlled trial adopts a repeated-measures, three-arm design to examine and compare the effects between two alternative interventions (Family-facilitated Self-Learning for Caregiving program, FSLCP and Professional-led Psychoeducation Group program, FGP, in addition to routine care) and routine outpatient and family support service only for family carers of Chinese people with FEP over a 18-month follow-up. Both outcome and process evaluation will be conducted for 198 randomly selected family carers of outpatients with FEP. There are two primary outcomes, including caregiving burden and family functioning, and several secondary outcomes for both carers and patients. They will be measured at recruitment, and 2-week, 9-month and 18-month post-intervention. Mixed-model multivariate/repeated-measures analysis of variance tests will be used to compare mean-value changes in these outcomes, and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis performed to analyze the relative risks of re-hospitalizations, between three groups over 18-month follow-up. It is primarily hypothesized that the FSLCP participants will produce significantly greater improvements in carers’ perceived burden and family functioning than those in PPGP and treatment-as-usual group over the 18-month follow-up. Clinical significant changes in the primary outcomes will also be assessed within and between groups according to Jacobson and Traux’s criteria to examine the actual clinical benefits to carers and patients. With significant positive outcomes found in the FSLCP, this family intervention can be adopted by community mental healthcare services in Hong Kong, and replicated in other countries, to improve family-oriented care in early psychosis.

14612019.label: Realisation of objectives
14612019.value: This multi-center randomized controlled trial adopted a repeated-measures, three-arm design to examine and compare the effects between two alternative interventions (Family-facilitated Self-Learning for Caregiving program, FSLCP and Professional-led Psychoeducation Group program, FPG, in addition to routine care) and routine outpatient and family support service only for family carers of Chinese people with FEP over an 18-month follow-up. The study materials were prepared in January 2020 and the subject recruitment was conducted between February - December 2020 in the four Integrated Community Centers for Mental Wellness (ICCMWs) run by the Caritas Hong Kong and Yang Memorial Methodist Social Service (i.e., two in the New Territories and one in each of Kowloon and H.K. Island regions), serving about 30% (>3,000) of patients with early psychosis. Equal number of eligible families from each center were randomly selected from the member lists of six ICCMWs and randomly assigned into one of the study groups by the full-time research assistant, using computer-generated random numbers provided an independent statistician. A total of 198 families of people with first-episode psychosis were recruited (49-50 participants per center); and after the research assistant had obtained written consents from individual participants and completed the pre-test questionnaires, the participants were randomly assigned by a part-time research assistant to one of the three study arms (FSLCP, family psychoeducation group or FPG, or routine care only; 66 participants per group). Those in FSLCP or family psycho-education group were then allocated into six subgroups (10-13 members) according to their preference/time convenience, which allowed the participants to be more engaged in self-care/problem-solving discussion and practices. After completed the baseline measurements, all 198 participants were randomized by the full-time research assistant to receive one of the three study interventions over five months according to their group assignments. Ethical approval and permission to access patients’ clinical information were obtained from the CUHK-NTEC joint Clinical Research Ethics Committee (CRE_2019_052) and the governing boards of the ICCMWs under study. There were two primary outcomes, including caregiving burden and family functioning, and several secondary outcomes for both carers and patients. They were measured at recruitment, and 1-week, 6-/9-month and 18-month post-intervention. All of the study objectives and hypotheses as per original application were achieved and the study has been completed in line with the proposed time schedule.
