14612019.label: Major findings and research outcome
14612019.value: This multi-center randomized controlled trial adopted a repeated-measures, three-arm design to examine and compare the effects between two alternative interventions (Family-facilitated Self-Learning for Caregiving program, FSLCP and Professional-led Psychoeducation Group program, FPG, in addition to routine care) and routine outpatient and family support service (TAU) only for family carers of Chinese people with FEP over an 18-month follow-up. Overall, 188 (94.9%) participants completed the assigned intervention and ≥1 post-test. Average attendances to FSLCP and psychoeducation group sessions were 3.1 and 9.2 (SD=0.7 and 1.3; median=2.5 and 8.0, range 1-4 and 6-12, respectively); and average module completion of the FSLCP was 4.0 (SD=1.0; median=4.0, range=2-5). There were also four, four and six dropped out or loss to contact (totally 14 participants) over the intervention period in FSLCP, psychoeducation and usual care group, accordingly. There were also two, three and two participants withdrew (totally 7 participants) from the study in FSLCP, psychoeducation and usual care group, accordingly. The results of GEE test indicated significant interaction (Group x Time) treatment effects on six study outcomes (FBIS, FAD, SPSI-R:S, duration of re-hospitalizations, PANSS, and QPR) between three groups over 18-month follow-up, Wald χ2= 8.01-20.61, p= 0.02-0.001), with moderate to large effect sizes (η2) between 0.10 and 0.35 using repeated-measures ANOVA test. Pairwise contrast tests following the GEE indicated that comparing with the TAU and/or FPGP, the FSLCP reported significant greater improvements in: - Caregiving burden (FBIS) and family functioning (FAD) at Times 1 - 3 than the TAU, and at Time 3 than the FPGP. - Problem-solving ability (SPSI-R:S) at Times 2 and 3 than the TAU, as well as at Time 3 than the FPGP. - Psychotic symptoms (PANSS) and subjective recovery (QPR) at Times 2 and 3 than the TAU; and subjective recovery (QPR) at Time 3 than the FPGP. - Average length or duration (days of hospital-stay) of re-hospitalizations at Time 3 than both the TAU and FPGP. The FSLCP participants reported significantly less number of patients re-hospitalized over past six months than other two study groups over the 18-month follow-up (Krukal-Wallis test=6.17, p=0.005), in which the FSLCP had significantly less patients re-hospitalized at Time 3 [8 (12%) than both psycho-education group [13(19%)] and TAU [18(27%)], Mann-Whitney test=7.90 and 17.9, p=0.05 and 0.005, respectively. Clinically significant changes of the functional state of the FSLCP participants mainly occurred at T3 in the FBIS, FAD and PANSS (i.e., 43-50% indicated clinically significant improvements in these psychosocial functions).

14612019.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14612019.value: The positive findings of this RCT suggest further multi-centre, across-country RCT to test the FSLCP for family caregivers of psychotic patients in recent onset of illness (≤3 years) with diverse socio-demographic and clinical characteristics, as well as having comorbidities of other mental disorders in Chinese/Asian countries, and over a longer period of follow-up (e.g., >1 year). An in-depth qualitative investigation of the FSLCP about the experiences and views of the participants, and/or prospective predictive study with a larger sample of FSLCP participants, are also recommended to identify the therapeutic components and mechanism of actions of the intervention.

14612019.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14612019.value: This multi-center randomized controlled trial adopted a repeated-measures, three-arm design to examine and compare the effects between two alternative interventions (Family-facilitated Self-Learning for Caregiving program, FSLCP and Professional-led Psychoeducation Group program, in addition to routine care) and routine outpatient/family support service only for family caregivers of adult patients with first-episode psychosis over an 18-month follow-up. Around 95% of the study participants completed the assigned intervention and at least one post-test. There were totally 7.4% and 3.7% dropped-out/loss-to-contact and study withdrawal, respectively. No adverse effect was reported. The FSLCP was found effective in improving carers’ caregiving burden, family functioning, and problem-solving ability, and patients’ psychotic symptoms, subjective recovery, and duration of psychiatric hospitalizations over 9 and/or 18 months follow-ups, in comparison to usual care only. The FSLCP participants also statistically significant greater improved in carers’ caregiving burden, family functioning and problem-solving ability, and their patients’ subjective recovery at 18 months follow-up, when compared with family psychoeducation group. The FSLCP participants also reported a smaller number of patients re-hospitalized than the other study groups over the 18-month follow-up. In addition, the FSLCP participants (43%-50%) had clinically significant improvements (becoming 'normal') in caregiving burden, family functioning and psychotic symptoms over the 18-month follow-up.

14612119.label: Realisation of objectives
14612119.value: The 4 project objectives were achieved. To carry out this project, we employed a design-based research (DBR) methodological approach consisting of 2 research cycles (Cycle 1 and Cycle 2) with iterative phases of Design, Enactment, Analysis, and Refinement; 1 cycle per school year). As per the original research plan, this DBR was carried out in the context of formal senior secondary geography education in Hong Kong. There were 9 participating schools at the 3 different academic bands (upper, average and lower), involving a total of 9 geography teachers and 504 secondary-4 students. >> Design LIVIE is a pedagogical framework that we proposed to leverage SVVR to enable students to conduct inquiry fieldwork-based learning in the form of virtual expeditions, with a combination of (i) in-lesson face-to-face teacher-facilitated “classwork” and (ii) off-lesson individual SVVR-supported inquiry fieldwork-based “homework” (Jong et al., 2019). EduVenture-VR is an integrated SVVR learning system that we developed to actualise the implementation of LIVIE (Jong et al., 2020a). At the outset of Cycle 1, we provided training for the teachers on LIVIE and EduVenture-VR, as well as the LIVIE materials developed for a curricular module in the formal geography curriculum in senior secondary geography education in Hong Kong. Prior to the Enactment phase of Cycle 1, to better acquaint themselves with the pedagogical operation of LIVIE, the teachers piloted experimenting on the implementation of LIVIE in their own secondary-3 classes (Jong et al., 2020a). >> Enactment X 2 In Cycle 1’s Enactment phase, in each school, the teacher implemented LIVIE to facilitate a secondary-4 class to study the curricular module. In this cycle, there were a total of 253 student participants from the 9 schools (Jong et al., 2020b). In Cycle 2’s Enactment phase, in each school, the teacher implemented LIVIE with the incorporation of the new teacher facilitation practices formulated in the Refinement phase (see below) to facilitate another secondary-4 class to study the same module. In this cycle, there were a total of 253 student participants from the 9 schools (Jong et al., 2022). In Cycle 2, in each school, we deliberately requested the teacher to select a class that was comparable with the participating class in Cycle 1, in terms of academic performance. We cross-checked that there was no significant difference (p > 0.05) between the school-based geography examination mean scores of the 2 classes respectively prior to their participation in the Enactment phases in Cycles 1 and 2. During the Enactment phases in both cycles, apart from in-class observation in each school, we conducted additional research data collection work, including teacher reflective think-aloud gathering, just-in-time and purposive student/ teacher interviews, and collection of the students’ virtual inquiry artefacts. >> Analysis X 2 In the Analysis phases in Cycles 1 and 2, in each school, we administered the knowledge test to the students. The test questions were developed in accordance with the recent public geography examination questions pertaining to the curricular module. Every test paper collected in each cycle was individually marked by 2 senior geography teachers from 2 non-participating schools; the Kappa values: 0.88 (Cycle 1) and 0.92 (Cycle 2). Moreover, in each school, in Cycles 1 and 2, we conducted in-depth, semi-structured student interviews to probe into their learning experience with LIVIE. We employed layering and interrelating approaches to analysing the collected interview data to triangulate and explain the knowledge test results. In the Analysis phase of Cycle 1, we revealed a number of problems arising from the implementation of LIVIE, impeding the students’ learning process. Some of the problems generically happened in all schools across the 3 academic bands, while the others uniquely happened in the schools at a particular academic band (Jong et al., 2022). >> Refinement Three teacher groups were formed to work on the optimisation of LIVIE by addressing the problems revealed in Cycle 1 (Jong et al., 2022). The 3 teachers at the same schools’ academic band were grouped together. We discussed the findings in Cycle 1 with each teacher group and collaborated with them to formulate possible interventions for improving/ enhancing the implementation of LIVIE in their own schools. Specifically, we aimed to derive new teacher facilitation practices for tackling the identified problems. All these newly derived practices were enacted by the teachers in the Band-1, Band-2, and Band-3 schools during the Enactment phase of Cycle 2 (Jong et al., under-review). DIFFICULTY & SOLUTION: There were a total of 9 schools participating in this project. According to the original plan, the data collection work in the second research cycle (September 2020 to July 2021) would have been conducted in 4 schools during the fall semester of 2020 and in the remaining 5 schools during the spring semester of 2021. However, due to the context of COVID-19 in Hong Kong, face-to-face teaching was suspended in September 2020, and the 4th COVID-19 wave hit in the 4th quarter of 2020. As a result, the 4 schools involved in the fall semester had to revise their entire secondary-4 geography teaching plan. Therefore, we were unable to conduct the research work in these 4 schools from September 2020 to December 2020 as planned. Consequently, we postponed the research work in these 4 schools to the fall semester of 2021. This is the reason why we applied to postpone the project completion date for 6 months, and we appreciate the approval from the RGC panel. 14612119.label: Major findings and research outcome
14612119.value: In the Design phase of the DBR (Jong et al., 2019), in the experiment on the 9 teachers’ pilot implementation of LIVIE and the comparison with the conventional textbook-based learning approach, it was shown that LIVIE had significantly positive pedagogical effects on the upper-, average-, and lower-academic students, with small to medium effect sizes (Jong et al., 2020a). After the Enactment and Analysis phases in Cycle 1, it was revealed that a number of problems arose from the implementation of LIVIE, impeding the students’ virtual inquiry fieldwork-based learning process. Some of the problems generically happened in all schools across the 3 academic bands, while the others uniquely happened in the schools at a particular academic band. All these problems are summarised in Table 1 in the conference paper of ICCE 2020 (Jong et al., 2020b) and recapped in Appendix A in the CAE journal paper (Jong et al., under-review). Fourteen specific new teacher facilitation practices [see Table 2 in the CAE journal paper (Jong et al., under-review)] for tackling these “generic” and “unique” problems were developed in the Refinement phase in Cycle 2 and enacted by the teachers in the Band-1, Band-2, and Band-3 schools in the Enactment phase in Cycle 2. According to the quantitative analysis (and the qualitative triangulation) of comparing the students’ performance across the 3 academic bands at the Enactment phases in Cycles 1 and 2, the new teacher facilitation practices which were respectively enacted in different schools in Cycle 2 functioned to mitigate the “generic” and “unique” problems and significantly advance the pedagogical effectiveness of LIVIE, with medium to large effects (Jong et al., 2022, Jong et al., under-review). Grounded on the results of this DBR work, 5 teacher facilitation principles for optimising the process of students’ SVVR-supported virtual inquiry fieldwork-based learning were developed [as delineated in the CAE journal paper (Jong et al., under-review). Additionally, in the course this DBR study, we have gained a more thorough understanding of what and how other researchers in the same field have done. Hence, at the completion stage of this project, we further conducted a systematic critical review on the current educational use of SVVR (Jiang, Jong et al., under-review), aiming to shed light on future research directions for the field from more comprehensive and broader perspectives. 14612119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14612119.value: This research underlines the crucial role of teacher facilitation in SVVR-supported learning, which has been largely neglected in the field. It offers researchers and educational practitioners both scholarly and practical insights into exploiting the educational use of SVVR in formal schooling and advancing its pedagogical effectiveness through teacher-facilitating support. Although this DBR focused on secondary geography education, the developed principles and practices of teacher facilitation have broader implications for the future application of SVVR in other subject domains across K-12 and higher education. These principles and practices provide insights into how SVVR can be further adopted in subjects like language, geology, biology, history, natural science, social work, medicine, construction management, and more, where immersive learning is deemed vital. Further research is needed to enhance our understanding of the effective integration of SVVR-supported learning in various formal educational settings of different discipline fields.

14612119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14612119.value: The use of technology in education has become increasingly important since the 21st century, with a focus on constructivist approaches that emphasise active student learning and the supportive role of teachers. However, research on the use of spherical video-based virtual reality (SVVR) in formal K-12 education has been limited, particularly in regard to the facilitating role of teachers. This study aimed to fill this gap by developing teacher-facilitating tactics for SVVR-supported virtual inquiry fieldwork-based learning through a design-based research approach. It resulted in the construction of a pedagogical framework and teacher-facilitating principles and practices for harnessing SVVR in inquiry learning. This research offers insights for researchers on leveraging SVVR in education and for practitioners seeking to implement SVVR-supported learning in their classrooms. The principles and practices developed in the study have broad implications for the use of SVVR in other subject domains and educational contexts, where immersive and interactive pedagogies are valued. In a nutshell, the work provides the field with both scholarly and practical insights into exploiting the educational use of SVVR in formal schooling and advancing its pedagogical effectiveness through teacher-facilitating support.

14612519.label: Project Objectives
14612519.value: To offer a novel conceptual framework to understand the commonality of feeling empathically toward other people and toward the self. To demonstrate the cognitive underpinning (i.e., flexibly shifting between self- and other-perspective) in the process of simulating an emotional experience incompatible with the egocentric stance. To investigate the roles of two situational factors, mood state and availability of somatosensory representation, in relating perspective shifting flexibility to empathic responses.

14612519.label: Realisation of objectives
14612519.value: We have accomplished the research project as planned. Below please find details regarding how the project objectives were achieved. 1. Two research ethics approvals were obtained for 1) pilot correlational research (SBRE-19-226) and 2) experimental study in which participants’ would be manipulated to get exposed to other people’s distress and to retrieve shameful personal experiences (CREC No.: 2018.599). 2. Self-report instruments for assessing key constructs including 1) Self-directed empathy, 2) Other-directed empathy (vicarious sharing of emotions), and 3) dispositional susceptibility to other- and self-emotion were developed and validated. 3. Behavioural batteries assessing socio-cognitive functioning have been developed and validated as planned, including the 1) Visuospatial Perspective Shifting (VPS) Task, and 2) Multifaceted Empathy Test. 4. We designed the paradigms manipulating the formation of somatosensory or propositional representations as well as a mood induction procedure for other- and self-empathy. We conducted multiple pilot studies to optimize study parameters and experimental details. The paradigms were validated before we formally launched the experiments. 5. Acknowledging reviewers’ comments on the clinical potential of the project, we further explored factors which interact with VPS propensity. An individual experiment was designed during the height of the pandemic when interactive experiments such that we could continue data collection and maintain project progress despite the unstable pandemic situation. Addressing a clinically pertinent factor, we investigated negatively biased self-referential learning and empathic emotions such as guilt and shame in individuals vulnerable to dysfunctional interpersonal relationships and self-directed aggression. 6. Despite challenges faced during the COVID-19 pandemic for data collection, by the end of the project 150 participants were recruited to test our two hypotheses regarding VPS flexibility and self-oriented and other-oriented empathy respectively. This was accomplished by hiring an additional research assistant to speed up data collection once social distancing measures were lifted, as well as recruiting the help of our undergraduate and postgraduate students in recruitment and data collection. 7. Data-entry (self-report measures) and data cleaning (computerized tasks) were performed collaboratively by the research assistants and student helpers. Preliminary analysis was conducted to detect erroneous information and outliers. 8. The PI (Chui-De Chiu) performed the data analysis and interpreted the results with the Co-Is of the project (Prof. Chang Jen-Ho, Prof. Mak Wing-Sze Winnie, and Prof. Marieke Tollenaar). 9. In addition to successfully demonstrating flexible VPS as the foundation of simulating an emotional experience incompatible with the egocentric stance (i.e., altercentric experience), the specific link between control processes involved in egocentric perspective-resumption and both other- and self-empathy was established through conducting an experimental causal chain analysis, showing that availability of embodied somatosensory representation impacts the generation of self- and other- oriented empathy through reliving an altercentric experience egocentrically. 10. To further investigate the novel inclusion of autonomic arousal in the framework of VPS propensity and self- and other-directed empathy, a meta-analysis was conducted to dissect the specific linkage between heart-rate variability and components of empathy. 11. In a recent peer review of on our submitted manuscript on the subject, we were requested to recruit another sample to replicate our findings. We have successfully re-run the experiment with 90 participants and secured a consistent result. 12. Regarding output, 1) eight publications have been published under the grant and two are under review; 2) twelve workshops, research seminars and guest lectures were held in non-governmental organizations, universities, and hospitals both locally and overseas; 3) fifteen undergraduate and postgraduate students received research trainings through their direct involvement in the project, and fifteen research theses were generated. Our work paves way for the designing of novel interventions to help those disadvantaged in perspective-shifting and empathically responding to themselves and others. We look forward to future publications and projects integrating and sharing these findings with the community. To what extent were the objectives realized: 100%

14612519.label: Major findings and research outcome
14612519.value: 1. We began with the question about the involvement of somatosensory representation in visuospatial perspective shifting (VPS). We manipulated time pressure, working memory load, and posture remapping and examined how they impacted upon the controlled and autonomic processing of VPS. We showed that posture remapping but not time pressure and working memory load influenced the automatic processing of VPS. This finding provides initial evidence for the involvement of somatosensory representation in the early stage of VPS [1]. 2. We further investigated factors that would intervene in linking VPS to empathy. While as predicted emotional arousal had a null effect, negative schematic self-association was a factor which moderated the prosocial effect of VPS. In a social context of wrongdoing, flexible perspective shifting correlated with dispositional guilt, an empathetic emotion which prompted repair. However, for participants additional with heightened negative schematic self-association, they endorsed intensified dispositional shame which related to aggression and self-attack [4]. Heightened negative schematic self-association, a comparative strength of pairing self with social rejection opposite to social acceptance, was a cognitive feature of individuals with unresolved traumatic stress, such as early interpersonal maltreatment [2,7]. 3. Two experiments offered further quasi-experimental evidence for the importance of somato-sensory representation in the exercise of empathy. In the other-empathy experiment, participants hearing an audiotaped narrative of life hassles were instructed to either imagine the person’s feeling, remember the narrative, or formulate solutions. We replicated again the link between flexible perspective shifting and empathetic feeling. Importantly, this link appeared solely in the imagination condition, in which the somatosensory representation of the person’s experience was available [9]. A similar result was evident for self-empathy, when participants recalled a shameful experience. Individuals with flexible perspective shifting endorsed heightened empathetic feeling if they were instructed to reconstruct the moment. No empathic feelings in quicker perspective shifters if they engaged in solution planning in which their attention was diverted to propositional representation (manuscript in preparation). 4. In response to reviewers’ suggestion, we explored in a meta-analysis the link between concurrent physiological reactivity and empathy. We targeted the competing hypotheses between whether it is heightened physiological arousal (a consequence of emotion contagion) or lowered physiological arousal (a prerequisite as emotion regulation) that should characterize empathy. Our result showed a trend in support of the emotional regulation hypothesis, though more studies should be conducted to settle down the methodological inconsistency in the existing literature [10].

14612519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14612519.value: Our immediate plan is to complete the publication plan for the last few papers. The review process offers precious communication with international experts about our work. We look forward to inputs about three specific topics we would love to further pursue. First, we get interested in the translational work which creates clinical impact. Our research demonstrates flexible perspective shifting is a pivotal dispositional factor which determines whether individuals can generate an intersubjective understanding toward another’ inner world. We also show the success of this exercise depend upon the deliberate construction of somatosensory representation. It is vital to develop a training program which cultivates this essential interpersonal skill. Second, we would like to address the empathetic distress newly identified from the project----shame. Our result indicates that unresolved traumatic stress can turn the prosocial guilt into maladaptive shame through negative schematic self-association. While shame prevails in trauma-spectrum disorders, we would like to verify this new formulation of trauma-spectrum disorders. Finally, we would like to investigate the unclear association of physiological activity and empathetic feeling. We get interested in the emotion regulation hypothesis, considering how to use physiological feedback to train the empathetic sensitivity for people with low perspective shifting.

14612519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14612519.value: Humans are wired to connect, but in an ever-changing, diverse world, we are constantly tasked with overcoming internal and external conflicts to reach our full potential. Empathy, the ability to simulate an emotional experience incompatible with one’s egocentric stance, is thus vital. Noting neural and phenomenological resemblances between sharing the feelings of others (i.e., other-directed empathy) and mindfully accepting one’s own emotions in response to failures (i.e., self-directed empathy), the current study aimed to establish a novel framework addressing the commonality of self- and other-directed empathy by investigating a cognitive process integral to the simulative process – flexible switch between of self- and other-perspective. While shifting from the self- to other-perspective allows one to see from another point of view, it should be the resumption of a self-perspective, by which the understanding can be considered from an experiential, first-person perspective, that is vital to engender empathic feelings towards another or a disadvantaged self. Through multiple experiments, we found evidence supporting our hypothesis. Most importantly, even for those with the social advantages of flexible perspective-shifting, it is the ability to relive the experience of the incompatible other, beyond an analytical understanding, that is key to empathic connection.

14613219.label: Project Objectives
14613219.value: to analyze how China has attempted to establish the regulatory regime for Fintech; to ascertain the way in which the regulation of Fintech is enforced in practice; to identify and analyze factors the interaction of which has contributed to the constitution of the institutional environment in which China’s regulation of Fintech has been made and enforced; and to draw implications from the Chinese experience for the international discourse and debate on the regulation of Fintech.
rows: to analyze how China has attempted to establish the regulatory regime for Fintech;
to ascertain the way in which the regulation of Fintech is enforced in practice;
to identify and analyze factors the interaction of which has contributed to the constitution of the institutional environment in which China’s regulation of Fintech has been made and enforced; and
to draw implications from the Chinese experience for the international discourse and debate on the regulation of Fintech.

14613219.label: Realisation of objectives
14613219.value: With the funding support of the grant, the project objectives have been successfully achieved. Overall, the project has carried out an authoritative, comprehensive and contextualized examination of the development and regulation of Fintech in China. It has produced a rich body of research outputs both in terms of quality and quantity (see Part C), which are of both theoretical and practical significance. To start with, the project has fulfilled the first objective of analyzing how China has attempted to establish the regulatory regime for Fintech. The project traces the historical development of the Chinese Fintech regulation. For instance, the project examines the evolution of the regulation during the whole period of the rise and fall of the online P2P lending industry in China. The project also discusses how China decided to ban the initial coin offerings (ICO). To achieve this objective, the project provides a doctrinal and systematic analysis of the relevant rules under the regulatory regime. Secondly, the project analyzes the way in which the regulation of Fintech is enforced in practice. This is done by looking at relevant cases and collecting market data as to the context in which the law operates. After the doctrinal analysis of black-letter law under the first objective, the project goes on to provide insights into how the law is put into practice. For instance, the project examines the enforcement of the data privacy regime in mobile payment, thereby discovering practical issues associated with the protection of privacy in practice. The third objective is fulfilled with the identification of relevant factors that have contributed to the constitution of the institutional environment for the making and enforcement of China’s regulation of Fintech. Based on the examination of law and practice as required under the first two objectives, the project has tried to identify the contributing factors, so as to help readers understand not only what the law is but also why the law is the way that it is. For instance, it identifies the factors behind the heightened privacy risk in mobile payment, and shows how the law is designed to respond to these factors. It also explains the need for regulation of Fintech sectors, such as cryptoassets and robo-advisors, by discussing the benefits and risks they bring to the market and society. Finally, the project critically evaluates the regulation of Fintech in China from a comparative perspective, discovering the strengths and weaknesses of the Chinese experience. In doing so, the project fulfills the fourth objective of drawing implications from the Chinese experience for the international discourse and debate on the regulation of Fintech. Indeed, as the world’s leader in Fintech, China’s experience is valuable, and China has both stories of success and lessons of failure. The comparative insights can be useful for China to further improve its regulation, but also have important implications for other jurisdictions.

14613219.label: Major findings and research outcome
14613219.value: First, the goal of Fintech regulation is to achieve two main objectives, namely facilitating financial innovation and market development on the one hand, while ensuring risk control and investor protection on the other. These two objectives may usually be consistent with each other, but in some circumstances, they may be diametrically opposed. Hence, the regulatory task is to strike a balance between the two regulatory objectives. Second, the regulatory balance is a delicate one and needs to be adjusted according to the local conditions. As such, the point of balance is static, but dynamic, which means that it is necessary to review and reform the regulatory regime when the market situation evolves. It should also be noted that the importance of local considerations does not mean that it is meaningless for jurisdictions to learn from each other. Different jurisdictions may face the same problems and it is always useful to look at them from a comparative perspective. The point is that foreign experiences should not be taken at face value but rather need to be considered in light of the local conditions. Third, the regulatory regime for the Fintech markets is a work-in-progress, which is not surprising given the fast-changing pace of the underlying Fintech markets. In China, this is also generally in line with the gradualist approach that China has taken towards its economic reform. Indeed, the current regulatory regimes for most Fintech sectors have evolved in an accretive way in response to problems without any real focus on overall mission in the long term. As a result, the relevant rules are scattered around many different laws and regulations, which makes the regime very complex with many internal conflicts. Hence, it is advisable to streamline the regulation to reduce discrepancy and improve coherence. At a more fundamental level, given the novel and disruptive nature of Fintech, it is important to consider whether we can still use the traditional regulatory framework for Fintech, or we need to think outside the box and introduce a new one specifically for Fintech. Fourth, the efficacy of the Fintech regulation is a function of the substantive rules and the enforcement strategies. For many Fintech sectors in China, such as mobile payment, there are multiple enforcement agencies, which has caused confusion and inconsistency in practice. This is essentially an issue of how to design an efficient institutional structure of financial regulation.

14613219.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14613219.value: There is great potential for further development of the research, and two main courses of action can be pursued. On the one hand, the Fintech market continues to develop with the emergence of new sectors and the regulatory landscape continue to evolve with the promulgation of new rules, and thus there is a need for more research to be conducted on them. For instance, China has recently promulgated several important new laws and regulations in relation to privacy and data protection, which will have a significant impact on the development of the Fintech market. To stimulate the post-covid economic development, China has also adjusted its policy on big Fintech companies. Another important development is the recent push for more trial use of the Chinese central bank digital currency. On the other hand, the project is geographically focused on Mainland China, and it can extend to cover other jurisdictions, particularly those included in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, namely Hong Kong and Macao. In this connection, there is also a need to examine the regulatory cooperation amongst the different jurisdictions. The research findings of this project can provide a solid foundation for the further research.

14613219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14613219.value: Financial technology (Fintech) brings about paradigmatic changes to the traditional financial system and society at large, presenting both challenges and opportunities. This project provides a comprehensive, contextualized and empirical examination of the development and regulation of Fintech in China. Besides examining the key elements of the regulatory regime, the project also looks at the making and implementing of the regulatory regime and evaluate the extent to which the regulation is appropriate and effective in striking a balance between fostering innovation and protecting consumers. Given China’s leadership in some Fintech areas, such as mobile payment, the project traces the successes and shortcomings of China’s regulatory regime for Fintech. It has produced significant research outputs both in terms of quality and quantity, which are of both theoretical and practical value. Theoretically, by examining the Chinese experience, the project makes an important contribution to the international discourse and debate on the regulation of Fintech. On the practical side, it can assist the international community, including lawyers, regulators, policymakers and market players, to better understand the Fintech market and its regulation in China.

14613619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14613619.value: Value-added tax (VAT) is the most widely used indirect tax in the contemporary world. The tax was designed half a century ago, when it applied to sales of goods and the provision of traditional services. Applying the law to modern digital services such as telecommunications, media streaming, gaming, and cloud storage has proved challenging. The research project will investigate how a robust and administrable VAT can be designed to apply effectively to the digital economy. The study will focus on two aspects of VAT design. The first is the application of VAT to cross-border digital supplies. Consumers of digital supplies can be located in places other than a supplier’s location and receive services that do not pass through physical border controls. This poses a fundamental challenge to the VAT, threatening revenue losses and imposing significantly unequal treatment on domestic and international services providers. This first focus of the study will examine how China’s VAT regime can be modernised to address the challenges of cross-border trade in services. Despite the success of China’s technology sector - Tencent and Alibaba are now among the world’s top 10 most valuable and biggest companies, the country has made almost no progress on modernising its VAT system to accommodate the new commerce. In contrast, other jurisdictions, most notably Australia and the European Union, have introduced new systems designed to impose VAT on cross-border digital services. The revenue implications of the failure to amend China’s VAT system are significant, as are the disadvantages imposed on would be service exporters. The second focus of the research is domestic VAT issues within China. The study will investigate the challenges and implications of domestic trade in digital services on tax collection and distribution of VAT revenue between provinces within China. Currently, provinces are entitled to 50 percent of VAT revenue, allocated to the province in which a supplier is registered. The expansion of the digital economy raises many questions about VAT collection and the viability of the current allocation regime. Domestic and international implications for the VAT of the growth of the digital economy make this research an imperative. Research findings will fill in a gap in VAT scholarship and provide a blueprint for reform in China. The research will contribute to the understanding of the impact of changes in China’s VAT rules on Hong Kong’s growing trade in digital services with China. N/A

14614719.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14614719.value: 在社會科學研究領域，交互效應分析被廣泛應用於邊界條件之確認。實證研究基本上亦驗證了雙重和三重交互效應之作用。現存文獻中，已有大量研究報告提出對雙重交互效應之相關檢驗，但涉及三重交互效應的研究則相對有限。然而，在近20年，有關三重交互效應之研究卻有增長之趨勢，並逐漸形成一個以三重交互效應為基礎的分析框架，從而闡釋和理解多樣化的心理和社會現象。在三重交互效應分析中，已知一些方法學的因素，例如信度，會影響研究結果的一致性或準確性。同時，對於如何進行三重交互效應的潛分析，到現在還沒有一個具體的指導方針。理論上，某些適用於雙重交互效應潛分析的方法或可直接運用於三重交互分析之上，但從實踐角度來看，這些傳統方法在處理三重交互模型中多個交互作用項時，其可行性確實存疑。即使是一些看似可行的方法，由於一些實踐上的障礙，它們的具體表現亦存在不確定性。這些方法學上的問題，大大限制了研究者對心理和社會現象的理解及其理論的建立，並嚴重地阻礙了社會科學研究的發展與進步。 本研究項目提出了四種不同的三重交互效應潛分析方法，從而為社會科學研究提供實效性、理論性和方法學三方面的啟示。這些方法主要以無約束乘積指標技術和因子分值技術為基礎，並針對每一項技術提出兩種具體方案。因此，我們界定了四種分析方法，即（1）最佳匹配項目無約束分析法（best items in matching in unconstrained approach），（2）打包匹配無約束分析法（parceling for matching in unconstrained approach），（3）偏差迴避因子分值法（bias-avoiding factor score），（4）最佳項目因子分值法（best-item factor score）。上述四種方法皆具備極佳之可行性及操作性。每種方法均可在一般的結構方程模型軟件上運行。本項目將進行模擬數據實驗，以評估這些方法的具體表現。同時，通過界定合適的數據分析條件，模擬實驗亦會協助研究者選擇最佳的統計分析方法。最後，本項目還將開發一個R程式，供研究者進行三重交互效應潛分析及效力檢驗，從而促進三重交互分析在社會科學研究中的運用。

14614719.label: Realisation of objectives
14614719.value: Objective 1: As an extension to constrained product indicator approach, unconstrained product indicator approach (UPI) with a matched-pair strategy has been proposed to reduce the complexity of a latent interaction model since a smaller number of constraints is generally needed in UPI. Yet, when there are uneven number of indicators in latent factors, the use of UPI with the matched-pair strategy can be problematic since some indicators will be left unused in creating a latent interaction term. To minimize the loss of information, two variants in UPI, namely 1) matching by best items and 2) matching by parceling, were studied in latent two-way and three-way interaction analyses. For both methods, we proposed a two-step procedure. In Step 1, among the target exogenous factors (with uneven number of indicators) from which latent interaction is to be examined, indicators of each factor are selected by 1) making reference to the indicator reliability, or 2) combining multiple items into item parcels. In Step 2, indicators prepared in Step 1 are multiplied to create product indicators. Then, the conventional UPI is performed to model the latent interaction effect. Hence, with the aforementioned two-step procedure, Objective 1 was achieved. Objectives 2-3: In factor score approach (FS), we computed the predicted factor score of each individual factor based on the information from the estimated factor loadings and the factor variance-covariance matrix in a factor analytic model. These factor scores are then treated as the observed manifestations of those latent variables. Due to the problem of factor indeterminacy, different sets of factor scores can be predicted with different prediction methods and may show different degrees of prediction bias. In this project, we studied two methods in FS, namely 1) bias-avoiding method and 2) best-item method in latent two-way and three-way interaction analyses. For both methods, we proposed a two-step procedure. In Step 1, for the bias-avoiding method, the predicted factor scores of latent exogenous factors are computed by regression method, while the predicted factor scores of latent endogenous factors are computed by Bartlett method. For the best-item method, a factor analytic model is fitted by replacing one of the indicators in a latent factor with an average of all the indicators (i.e., the best item). By specifying the error covariance to model the possible indicator dependencies, the resulted factor loading matrix and factor variance-covariance matrix are used to predict the factor score. In Step 2, the factor scores of two to three latent exogenous factors are multiplied to create the product of factor scores and then, conventional two-way and three-way interaction analyses can be performed with the factor scores of lower-order and higher-order latent factors. Hence, with the aforementioned two-step procedure, Objectives 2 and 3 were achieved. Objective 4: A series of simulation studies was conducted to examine the performance of the four methods in latent two-way and three-way interaction analyses. Model conditions of sample size, number of items in latent factor, reliability, size of the interaction effect, and distribution of latent factor were systematically manipulated. Based on the results of the simulation studies, the key findings can be summarized as below: 1. The performance of the four methods was comparable in both latent two-way and three-way interaction analyses. 2. The performance of the four methods was generally better along with the increase of sample size, size of interaction effect, and reliability, as well as the decrease of skewness in latent factor. a. Given a moderate size of interaction effect, the performance of the two UPI methods and the bias-avoiding FS method yielded an acceptable performance when 1) reliability was larger than 0.70 and 2) sample size was larger than 360. b. The best-item FS method failed to yield an acceptable performance in most of the model conditions. 3. When the number of items was even across latent factors, the two UPI methods and the bias-avoiding FS method showed a comparable performance. 4. When the number of items was uneven across latent factors, the two UPI methods failed to perform well and the bias-avoiding FS method still maintained an acceptable performance. Hence, Objective 4 was achieved. Objective 5: Over a wide range of model conditions, the bias-avoiding FS method showed a better performance over the other three methods in latent two-way and three-way interaction analyses. To facilitate the convenient use of the bias-avoiding FS method, a R program was developed to help researchers in performing the two-step procedure in this method. Hence, Objective 5 was achieved.

14614719.label: Major findings and research outcome
14614719.value: In this project, we proposed four methods (two UPI methods and two FS methods) in latent two-way and three-way interaction analyses. Our findings helped to accomplish various research outcomes methodologically, practically, and educationally. Methodologically, first, we showed that the bias-avoiding FS method is the best among the four methods. Throughout a series of simulation studies, the bias-avoiding FS method is the only method that shows satisfactory performance under different model conditions. Furthermore, this method has additional advantages over others: 1) it is simple to implement with common statistical software programs, 2) it allows the test of higher-order interaction models and interaction-as-outcome models easily without a complicated and error-prone model specification, and 3) it utilizes all indicators and avoids arbitrary pairing of indicators. Based on these findings, a manuscript titled “Latent moderation analysis: A factor score approach” was prepared and published in Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal (see publication #1, Section 8, Part C). Second, we came up with some new findings during our investigation of the problem. Specifically, we discovered that when a specific non-linear relationship exists between the two moderators, the implied three-way interaction could in fact be spurious. A simple index was proposed to examine whether such a relationship exists empirically. Based on this finding, a manuscript titled “A note on evaluating the moderated mediation effect” was prepared and published (online) in Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal (see publication #3, Section 8, Part C). Practically, an R program was developed to facilitate the application of the bias-avoiding FS method. Users only need to specify the indictors for each latent factor and the program will compute the regression-based FS and Bartlett FS accordingly. The program can be downloaded at https://www.dropbox.com/s/mua8djgxjt63rca/FS_program.R?dl=0. Educationally, to promote the integration of research and education as stated in the education plan, two postgraduate students were recruited in this project (see Section 10, Part C). We provided training to them on the basic concepts in latent interaction analysis and R programming. One student formulated an interaction hypothesis in social psychology and used empirical data to examine a model that focused on the interaction dynamics between self-control and fear of negative evaluation on psychological well-being. Based on her findings, a manuscript titled “The role of fear of negative evaluation on the effects of self‑control on affective states and life satisfaction: A moderated mediation analysis” was prepared and published (online) in Current Psychology (see publication #2, Section 8, Part C).

14614719.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14614719.value: There are two potential ways to further develop the research. First, we can extend the bias-avoiding FS method to the analysis of latent conditional process models. Currently, the method requires a clear identification of the independent and dependent variables because different methods are being used for computing their factor scores. However, in a latent conditional process model, the latent mediator serves as an intervening variable, and thus it is not straightforward to determine the optimal method for computing its factor score. Further research is needed to modify the method for these models. Second, we can apply the bias-avoiding FS method to test the latent interaction hypotheses in a multilevel context. Given the clustered data, it is common to examine the cross-level latent interaction effect, which typically involves differentiating the latent variables into between- and within-level components. As the current method is based on the traditional factor analytic model from which the factor scores are derived, a similar bias-avoiding procedure using the multilevel factor analytic model can therefore be developed in a multilevel context accordingly. Systematic simulation studies can be conducted in the future to examine the empirical performance of this method.

14614719.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14614719.value: This project proposed and compared four different methods for testing a latent three-way interaction effect. In contrast to a two-way interaction, testing a three-way interaction is more complicated and vulnerable to measurements’ unreliability. In the literature, there are no clear guidelines on how to test a latent three-way interaction that account for variables’ unreliability. Moreover, the methods for testing a two-way interaction might not be directly applicable to analyzing the latent three-way interaction, because a larger number of latent product terms and a larger number of latent factors with uneven items are typically involved in a latent three-way interaction model. Through a series of simulation studies, we evaluated the empirical performance of these four methods, and found that the bias-avoiding factor-score method generally works the best. Furthermore, we discovered that when a specific non-linear relationship exists between the two moderators, the implied three-way interaction could in fact be spurious. A simple index that examines if such a non-linear relationship exists empirically was proposed. Overall, the significance of this project is that we successfully identified the conditions for the method to work, and the project also provides new insights into how to analyze complex latent interactions in social science research.

14615819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14615819.value: This design research proposal investigates the feasibility to build an alternative timber house typology for the Dong Minority community in Hunan, China. The goal is to create a design template for a self-build dwelling from prefabricated timber components addressing two critical issues currently facing the Dong community, i.e.: preventing their rich architectural culture from moving ever closer towards extension and, to propose a new commercial model to inject a financial stimulus into an area that has witnessed a huge exodus of working adults who seek employment in the city. For centuries the Dong communities have been almost entirely self-sufficient, with the environment in which they lived being a measure of their standard of living. The “Ganlan” style wooden house “hanging building”, built on the slopes and supported by pillars on the lower sides, embodies the natural relationship between the interior and exterior worlds, connected to the core values of their culture: family and land – the archetype sustainable house. Although the Ganlan house constitutes the basic unit of community life, as Dong villages are rendered devoid of working age youth, traditional Dong architecture has lost ground and meaning. The unfortunate ramifications resulting in the traditional house rapidly being replaced by either brick and wood dwellings or most recently by the self-build concrete framed structures. There is no denying that Dong culture is changing. Villages and houses are rapidly adapting to a higher standard of living; warmer, safer from the perils of fire and equipped with modern plumbing. However, what we are witnessing today is nothing short of a catastrophic demise, with the advent of concrete frame structures literally eradicating an entire architectural heritage. With the notion of prefabrication, self-build and community participation all engraved into Dong’s architectural DNA, this research proposes an alternative modernization strategy that reconnects the house to its original cultural identity and in parallel prevents Dong’s traditional architectural heritage from becoming a mere aesthetic maquillage instead of something profoundly rooted in its material being. Traditional Dong timber houses will soon no longer be built, replaced by a hybrid concrete pastiche, completely foreign to the territory. Rather than yield to this trend, this research seeks to propose an alternative solution, in the form of a pilot prototype house, where material technology and self-build initiatives could become the catalyst for both regenerating their house typology and simultaneously create an alternative industry as a source of income to the community. 本研究提出在中國湖南侗族聚居區建造適應性木構住宅原型的可能性。研究的目標成果是建立侗族農村自建住宅的模板以改善侗族社會當前面臨的問題，例如侗族豐富的建築文化流失和農村空心化的現象。 侗族人民已經在侗族聚居區裏自給自足地生活了幾個世紀。侗族住宅是傳統的幹欄式住宅：它們建在山腰上，連接著侗族人的家與土地，實現了室內和室外空間的自然過渡。雖然侗族幹欄式住宅構成了社會生活的基本單元，但由於青壯年人口的缺失，住宅的底層已經不再用於飼養牲畜。因此，傳統的磚木結構正在快速地被自建混凝土結構取代。 沒有人可以否認侗族的文化正在改變。村落和建築正在快速地適應人們對生活的更高要求：保暖、防火、管道的安裝以使用現代設備等等。然而，我們今天看到的破壞是災難性的：混凝土框架結構對侗族建築遺產造成了巨大的威脅。自建和社區參與存在於侗族人的基因裏。本研究將提出靈活的現代化策略，既能將侗族的原始文化認同與住宅結合在壹起，也能防止紮根於侗族聚落的建築遺產變成沒有靈魂的裝飾品。 很快，人們將不會再建造傳統的侗族木構住宅，取而代之的是與這片土地維和的混凝土和木結構混合的模仿。本研究致力於提出靈活的解決方法而不是向這種現象頭像。我們希望在住宅試點項目中保留傳統材料和自建的模式而改造侗族村民的住宅，同時，創造新的產業來豐富村民的收入來源。

14615819.label: Realisation of objectives
14615819.value: The completion of the project has yielded numerous discoveries, significantly impacting social development and fostering valuable research insights. It has made a difference to the Dong minority village of Gaobu, paving the way for an alternative approach to preservation and rural heritage development, developing a design and construction language that adapts rather than starts from scratch. From an academic perspective, it has established the prototype as a paradigm for Participatory Action Research, allowing architectural researchers to contribute, participate and lead this developing field of research. Through their implementation, we have also been able to directly contribute to the local economy of the village, providing a much-needed livelihood for several local carpenters. Despite facing challenges, notably the constraints imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic preventing travel to the village for nearly two years, our team managed to successfully implement all aspects of the project. Objective 01 - Completion 100% 1. For nearly three years, we engaged in comprehensive research on various Dong dwellings, analysing both their environmental impact and their patterns of habitation. 2. The majority of our discoveries were documented in the midterm report, which outlined structural, material, and performance-related findings. 3. After the midterm report, our team has maintained supervision on multiple residences, utilizing our findings for a recent journal publication and as foundational material for a PhD thesis under the guidance of the principal investigator. 4. The survey played a direct role in shaping the design evolution and ultimate realization of the Mutation House Project. 5. Throughout this investigative process, we identified the family with whom we later collaborated to develop the definitive prototype for the "Mutation House." Objective 02 - Completion 100% 1. The majority of the tectonic and engineering investigation occurred during the initial phase of the project, as detailed in the midterm report. 2. These findings were then deciphered and integrated during the subsequent phase. The fundamental elements of Dong Architectural Language—such as Joints, Carpentry tools, Prefabrication system, and Material properties—were analysed and adapted into modern design solutions. 3. Innovations in systems and materials were implemented in the initial "Abstract" prototype. 4. The "Abstract" prototype for the Mutation House was entered into the Architectural Review "Future Projects Award" 2021, a prestigious professional competition, and secured first place in the "Future Residential Project of the Year" category, surpassing over 50 other submissions. 5. To gain first-hand knowledge from local carpenters, our team of research assistants shadowed a specific "Ink Master" across various construction sites. 6. We surveyed approximately a dozen medium to large-scale timber merchants operating in the Tongdau region. 7. For the realization of the final "hybrid" Mutation House, we collaborated closely with a specialized CLT company, Zhizhong Building Technology (Shanghai), which provided engineered timber at a competitive price point. 8. All of the above insights were directly applied in the construction of the final Mutation House prototype. Objective 03 - (16 months) Completion 100% 1. Two prototypes were developed: one named "Abstract" served as a conceptual model for a potential all-timber dwelling, while the other, named "Built," was realized based on a hybrid timber/concrete concept. 2. As detailed in the grant proposal, the principal investigator successfully secured a 500,000 HKD donation from the Chan Cheung Mun Chung Charitable Fund in Hong Kong, which exclusively financed the construction of the final prototype, covering both materials and labour costs. 3. At the date of writing this report, the final Mutation House stands at 70% completion, with a projected finish date set for 2024, coinciding with the occupancy by residents and the inauguration of the research centre. 4. In collaboration with the resident family and representatives from the village of Gaobu, the Mutation House will serve a dual purpose: functioning as both a residential dwelling and a community research Centre. Scholars, researchers, and students will have the opportunity to visit and engage in participatory action research aimed at enhancing the local housing infrastructure. 5. The Centre will actively involve local artisans, carpenters, and community members from Gaobu and beyond, promoting the advantages and possibilities of a contemporary Dong house design that minimizes the use of concrete. 6. Design serves as a channel for preserving heritage, as the traditional Dong timber framework evolves into a concrete grid, creating new models of habitation while simultaneously enhancing the structural and fire safety of the dwelling. 7. Through the prototype, we have cultivated a network of craftsmen and carpenters, contributing to the preservation of a craft that is rapidly disappearing. 8. The Heritage Officials of Tongdau have closely monitored and participated in the evolution of the project, expressing interest in its future development. Objective 04 - Completion 75% Building and Environmental Performance • Structure: the structural stability of the reinforced concrete frame has been assessed and approved by a structural engineer. Structurally Mutation House offers a considerable improvement of the traditional vernacular timber house. • Fire: From a fire safety standpoint, the hybrid design complies with the national code, vernacular houses struggle in this respect. • Noise: a major concern for residents is the complete lack of noise insulation in traditional houses, mutation house aids this problem. • Light: Dong traditional house interiors are dark. Mutation House has been designed to maximize natural light through the orientation and size of openings. • Circulation: the central stair design has improved the interior vertical circulation of the dwelling providing a central staircase that complies with building codes and allows for social interaction. • Ventilation: New Concrete Dong dwellings fall short of providing adequate natural ventilation compared to traditional houses. Mutation house in this respect incorporated timber for floor, wall and ceiling materials improving the performance. • Sustainability: a major factor in the design has been that all materials should be sourced locally. Except for concrete and steel reinforcement that have to come from nearby factories, all materials have been sourced from a 20 km radius.

14615819.label: Major findings and research outcome
14615819.value: This action research project started with the question “How can we improve the living conditions of a Dong Minority traditional timber dwelling without losing its cultural DNA?”. Over three years, the project has diagnosed problems associated with the Dong “Ganlan” house, through direct engagement with the remote rural village of Gaobu, Hunan Province. Reflective of broader trends in rural China, the advent of modernisation and alternative construction methods has profoundly altered the architectural landscape, contributing to the reshaping of the social fabric of Gaobu. Through direct engagement with the community, including university workshops, comprehensive fieldwork, oversight of the construction process by an RA residing in the village, and the dedication of three PhD students focusing their theses on Dong architecture and Gaobu-related issues, we crafted a design strategy in partnership with the local community. We aimed to devise a "hybrid" dwelling utilizing both concrete and timber elements, tailored to local requirements, feasible to be built by local carpenters and builders, offering adaptability, and importantly serving as a prototype for future residences that could organically spread by “osmosis” throughout the village and its surroundings. We designed two Mutation House prototypes, an “abstract” and a “built” version. The abstract version was conceived as an exercise to study the potential of the Dong timber frame system and was presented to the “Architectural Review Future Projects Awards”, (2021) where it was awarded Residential Project of the Year, helping the Dong house typology become recognised international as a paradigm for potential sustainable rural living. The final built prototype; conceived, designed and built with a local Gaobu family, was realized thanks to a donation by the Chan Cheung Mun Chung Charitable Fund and was entirely built by local carpenters and labour. Social and Academic Impact: • Helped a local Dong family build a new residential building, • Generated a new house typology from which locals can learn, • Created a Research Centre within the house to study Dong architecture and craftsmanship. • Given employment to more than 20 local villagers • Contributed to a safer, (fire, circulation, codes) Dong traditional dwelling. • Contributed to two academic papers, one published and one currently under review. • The Mutation House project was presented at numerous international institutions including Stanford University, UN-Habitat in Nairobi and the Architectural Association in London.

14615819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14615819.value: The future trajectory of the project has been carefully integrated into its design. In partnership with the residents of the final "Mutation House," we have reached an agreement for the prototype to evolve into a Research Center for "Dong Minority Living Heritage." This centre will serve as a hub for connecting villagers, researchers, and students from across China, fostering the preservation of Dong heritage. The CUHK School of Architecture has already committed to organizing several summer workshops and undergraduate elective classes at the centre. Additionally, the Heritage Committee of Tongdao has approached the principal investigator (PI) to explore the application of the hybrid typology in other villages. Furthermore, discussions are underway with several local schools in the Pingtan Valley interested in constructing hybrid Dong houses for their campuses. Crucially, the project has established "Participatory Action Research" as an alternative approach to architectural practice, emphasizing close collaboration with the community in shaping normative research. As rural communities undergo inevitable transformations, our role as active researchers is to facilitate this transition in a manner that respects and preserves the values and heritage integral to Dong society's rich cultural tapestry.

14615819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14615819.value: The Dong minority villages in Hunan are grappling with a fundamental question of how to navigate the complexities of modernization without sacrificing their deep-rooted cultural heritage. The Dong house, known as the "Ganlan" (干欄), a traditional timber-framed dwelling, has served as the cornerstone of their community for centuries, embodying the essence of communal life. However, with the advent of concrete construction methods, traditions passed down through generations of carpenters are vanishing rapidly. This research-by-design project has devised a framework to challenge the pervasive trend of "concrete migration" that is occurring in rural China. By engaging and collaborating with local participants, we have developed a house that aims to translate the latent potential of the traditional Dong house into a contemporary dwelling. Through interactive engagement, the "Mutation House" has revitalized the village of Gaobu and is now regarded as an alternative blueprint for future rural residential development. Its significance lies in its ability to be copied by neighbours and spread organically by osmosis to neighbouring villages. Beyond its social impact, the project has also contributed to the advancement of a nascent field of architectural research, Participatory Action Research, where the Mutation House Prototype catalyzes inquiry and knowledge generation.

14616119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14616119.value: This research aims to elucidate the impact of British governance on the cultural concepts and daily life of the Hong Kong Chinese people from 1842 to 1941 through the lens of human-animal relationships. British attitudes towards animals were strongly influenced by two different and seemingly contradictory ideas that were taking shape in 19th- century Britain, namely public health and animal protection. The concept of public health regarded animals as a potential threat to sanitation and called for a proper distance between animals and humans physically, if not emotionally. Animal protection, however, rested on the idea that animals are capable of feeling pain and that the best possible actions should be taken to reduce animal suffering. These concepts of public health and animal protection were embodied in the Hong Kong government's policies towards the Chinese population. For example, in an 1874 report, colonial surgeon B. C. Ayres expressed dismay that “pigs were kept in houses all over the town, by hundreds, and that pigsties were to be found under the beds and in the kitchen … every bed in these houses had from five to seven large pigs in a sty constructed underneath it." Ayres called for a more stringent pig licensing system to ensure a proper distance between men and pigs. In 1924, English newspaper China Mail published an article to support legislating against animal cruelty, stating that “[t]he Chinese have handled animals in their own way ... Domination has taught them nothing. If gentle persuasion and teaching are of no avail, then by all means apply the rigora [sic] of the new Bill to the uttermost.” This author saw punishment as a necessary means of teaching the Chinese people the proper way to handle animals. Animals therefore played a significant role in British colonists’ visions of the civic and moral order and served as catalysts that facilitated the growing intrusion of colonial governance into Hong Kong Chinese people's everyday lives. Nonetheless, how to strike a balance between social stability and the desire to “civilize” the colonized people created constant dilemmas that the British colonists had to grapple with. This interdisciplinary project weaves together colonial studies, public health and animal studies. It analyzes the extent to which the dissemination of such colonial knowledge as public health and animal welfare instigated changes in Chinese people's attitudes towards animals and created a new mode of culture among the Hong Kong Chinese population. 本研究旨在通過人與動物的關係，闡明英國殖民統治自1842年至1941年對香港華人的文化觀念和日常生活的影響。十九世紀英國出現的「公共衛生」和「動物保護」兩種看似互相矛盾的新觀念，對英國人對待動物的態度影響深遠。公共衛生概念將動物視為對衛生的潛在威脅，並要求民眾與動物保持適當距離。而動物保護概念則主張由於動物能夠感受疼痛，因而人類應仁慈對待動物，盡可能減少動物的痛苦。 公共衛生和動物保護概念亦體現於政府對香港華人的政策中。1874年的一份報告書中，殖民地醫官艾爾斯（Philip B. C. Ayres）懊惱地表示，「數以百計的豬隻被畜養在市區的房屋中，牠們有的在床底下，有的在廚房......這些房子的每張床底下都可找到五至七頭豬。」他建議政府建立更嚴格的發牌制度，規管市民在城市內養豬，以確保人與豬保持適當距離。 另外，1924年英文報章《德臣西報》刊登文章支持政府立法禁止虐待動物，文章指出，「中國人一直以自己的方式對待動物...... 過去的管治並沒有令他們學懂什麼。若溫和的勸說和教導無濟於事，便需要嚴格推行新法例。」這位作者認為懲罰是教導中國人仁慈對待動物的必要手段。 可見，在英國殖民者的文明及道德秩序觀念中，動物佔有重要地位，並為殖民統治介入華人日常生活提供合理依據。儘管如此，如何在維持社會穩定與「教化」華人之間取得平衡，往往是殖民者不得不面對的兩難困境。 此研究結合殖民研究、公共衛生和動物研究等方法學，分析公共衛生和動物福利等「殖民知識」，如何影響香港華人對待動物的態度，以及如何在香港華人社會塑造一種新的文化模式。

14616119.label: Realisation of objectives
14616119.value: 1. How did the notions of public health and animal welfare co-exist and contradict each other in Hong Kong's colonial policies from 1842 to 1941? The research is able to use pigs as an example to illustrate how the notions of public health and animal welfare shaped the situation and well-being of pigs in colonial Hong Kong. Pigs were regarded as a nuisance in public health ordinances. Yet, the animal welfare ordinances and news reports always highlighted pigs as victims of people's lack of sensibilities about their sufferings. Pig crates were reformed to avoid bamboo splits cutting into animal flesh. The size of pig crates' holes needed to be reduced to prevent their legs from protruding. Animal activists did not see these measures as contradictory. From their perspectives, so long as animals, no matter pets or pests, are capable of feeling pain, they were entitled to the right to not suffer from pain. 2. How did the public health ordinances passed at different times between 1842 and 1941 define animals (pigs in particular) and influence British colonial governance over the Chinese population in Hong Kong? This research examines Colonial Surgeon Ayer's 1874 report, as well as various public health ordinances passed in 1887, 1903, and 1935, to explain how pigs were removed from houses where people lived, and then relocated from urban areas to remote regions. Yet, the colonial government faced a delicate balancing act to reconcile its "civilizing" project with the imperative of maintaining political stability. The Chinese pig farm owners in New Kowloon staged strong protests in 1939. As a result, the colonial government put its rezoning project on hold for a decade. 3. What were the pig-keeping practices of the urban Chinese people in early colonial Hong Kong? What accounts for the difficulties the Hong Kong government faced in enforcing the prohibition on pig-keeping in urban Hong Kong? The existing historical sources do not fully address this question. Ayer's report provides a detailed description of the location of pigsties in Chinese people's residences. Osbert Chadwick's 1882 report noted that city dwellers kept kitchen slops and vegetable refuse to feed their pigs. Some Chinese people kept their pigs on the outskirts of the city. Pig keepers would collect pig wash from urban dwellings and in return, carry away dry rubbish and ashes. Fragmentary newspaper sources report that some Chinese were arrested for keeping more pigs than allowed by their licenses. I will closely read the newspapers to uncover additional sources to address this question. 4. What role did the HKSPCA play in disseminating ideas on animal welfare to the Chinese people in Hong Kong? To what extent did the HKSPCA enjoy the support of the Hong Kong government? This research demonstrates that the HKSPCA maintained a close relationship with the colonial government and played a crucial role in developing animal welfare legislation. Yet, Eurasian and Chinese elites, such as Chow Shouson and the Ho-tung couple, proved indispensable in shaping the development and application of these animal protection laws. They served as vital intermediaries, helping to bridge the gap between the colonial authorities, the HKSPCA, and the broader Chinese community. The 1935 animal protection ordinance was passed without strong opposition because the HKSPCA's publicity efforts, combined with increased coverage in prominent Chinese newspapers, helped familiarize Hong Kong's Chinese population with the legal consequences of cruelty to animals. 5. What were the similarities and differences between the animal welfare ordinances in Hong Kong and the Straits Settlements? What gave rise to these similarities and differences? From the National Library in Singapore, I collected materials from the Government Gazette and Legislative Council proceedings. They explained that Singapore's 1930 Ordinance, on which Hong Kong's 1935 ordinance was modelled, was influenced by Britain's 1911 Animal Welfare Act and related ordinances passed in the Federated Malay States in 1910 and 1915. Further research is needed to fully explain the interconnections between these animal welfare acts. Additionally, unlike the HKSPCA, the SPCA in Singapore did not enjoy government support. This difference in local power dynamics makes a comparison between the animal protection efforts in Hong Kong and Singapore challenging, but potentially worthwhile for understanding how unique local contexts influenced the reception of the animal protection concept. 6. To what extent did the new knowledge about animals disseminated by the British colonists (including government officials and HKSPCA) influence the Hong Kong Chinese people's understanding of animals? The government disseminated new knowledge about animal welfare through the enactment and implementation of ordinances, as well as coverage in Chinese newspapers and radio broadcasts. However, it is important to note that this was not a unilateral process. Rather, it involved opposition, negotiation, and compromises on the part of the government and HKSPCA. Collaborative work with Chinese and Eurasian elites proved crucial in bridging the gap between the colonial authorities, the HKSPCA, and the broader Chinese community. I have reviewed materials from the Kung Sheung Daily News and Tien-kwong Po newspapers, and will conduct a closer reading of these sources to more thoroughly address this question. The COVID-19 pandemic from 2020 to 2022 regrettably had some adverse impacts on my research activities. Due to travel restrictions and public health measures implemented during that period, I was unable to attend academic conferences overseas. This prevented me from presenting my research findings and engaging in idea exchanges with fellow scholars. As a result, the budget allocation earmarked for conference participation and travel remained unspent.
