15501119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15501119.value: Meetings, incentives, conventions, and exhibitions (MICE) tourism is considered high value-added business tourism. In particular, exhibitions exert considerable impact on the local economy. The 2016 economic impact study of the Hong Kong Exhibition and Convention Industry Association (HKECIA, 2017) reported that the Hong Kong (HK) exhibition industry contributes HKD52.9 billion (2.1% of GDP) to the local economy, a fiscal impact of HKD1.9 billion, and the creation of 77,000 full-time equivalent jobs. Furthermore, exhibition visitors and exhibitors spend 66% and 75%, respectively, more than overnight tourists. Given the significant economic contribution of the exhibition industry, destinations compete with one another for exhibitions to boost local tourism and trading business. To stay ahead of its competitors, the HK exhibition industry should continue to provide unique offerings through innovations to appeal to various international markets (SCMP, 2017), thereby maintaining destination competitiveness in exhibition tourism. Service-dominant (S-D) logic elaborates on how service innovation occurs by offering value propositions to customers (Grőnroos & Voima, 2013; Michel et al., 2008). S-D logic emphasizes the role of value propositions in service innovation and shifts the understanding of innovation “from the production of innovative products to resource integration and value propositions” (Michel et al., 2008, p. 65). Thus, developing existing or creating new value propositions is regarded as a service innovation in S-D logic (Vargo & Lusch, 2008). Nevertheless, qualitative and quantitative studies on the process of developing existing or creating new value propositions remain scarce. This study aims to identify the process by which practices and/or resources or practices of integrating resources result in value propositions in the exhibition industry based on the logic that service innovation is identified with the creation of new value propositions. To achieve this aim, Study 1 qualitatively explores four research objectives based on big data analytics, exhibition service innovation project analysis, in-depth interviews, and expert panel reviews. Thereafter, Study 2 validates the qualitative data through a survey. This study elucidates the manner in which value propositions are developed and created for service innovation, thereby contributing to the literature on value proposition formation and facilitators and barriers to value propositions for service innovation. Consequently, this study can assist HK exhibition organizers in offering unique value propositions for service innovation and thus, solidify the competitiveness of HK as an exhibition destination. 會展（會議、獎勵、大會和展覽）旅遊被認為是高附加值的商業旅遊形式。尤其值得一提的是會展對當地經濟產生了相當大的影響。2016年香港展覽及會議業協會發布的經濟影響研究報告 (HKECIA，2017年) 稱：香港會展業為本地經濟貢獻了529億港元(占本地生產總值的2.1%)，財政影響達19億港元,並且創造了相當於77,000個全職工作崗位。此外，會展參觀者和參展商的花費分別比過夜遊客多66%和75%。鑒於會展業對經濟的重大貢獻，目的地相互競爭以推廣會展，從而促進本地旅遊業和貿易業務。為了保持領先于競爭對手，香港會展業應繼續透過創新提供獨特的產品，吸引各個國際市場(《南華早報》，2017年)，從而維持會展旅遊目的地的競爭力。 服務為主導的邏輯詳細闡述如何通過為客戶提供價值定位來進行服務創新(Grónroos & Voima，2013；Michel et al., 2008)。服務為主導的邏輯強調價值定位在服務創新中之作用，並且將對創新的理解“從生產創新產品向資源整合及價值定位轉變” (Michel et al., 2008, p. 65)。因此，開發現有或創造新的價值定位被視為服務為主導的邏輯中之服務創新（Vargo & Lusch，2008)。 然而，關於開發現有或創造新的價值定位過程之定性及定量研究還很少。本研究根據服務創新與創造新價值定位相一致的邏輯，旨在確定會展行業中做法及/或資源提供價值定位以及把資源整合於價值定位做法之過程。為了達到此目標，研究一根據大數據分析、會展服務創新項目分析、深度訪談和專家小組審核，對四個研究目標進行了定性探索。然後，研究二通過調查驗來證定性數據。本研究闡述了為服務創新而開發和創造價值定位之方式，從而對關於服務創新中價值定位之形成、輔助因素以及障礙的文獻作出貢獻。因此，本研究有助於香港會展組織商為服務創新提供獨特的價值定位，從而鞏固香港作為會展目的地之競爭力。

15501119.label: Realisation of objectives
15501119.value: To achieve research objectives below, Study 1 (qualitative research) conducted an extensive literature review to generate an initial pool of qualitative data, after which in-depth interviews with 15 industry professionals were led to analyze 15 innovation projects in enriching the qualitative data. The qualitative data were finalized with a panel review of 15 experts. To validate the qualitative data from Study 1, Study 2 (quantitative research) conducted a survey with 327 employees of the Hong Kong Exhibition & Convention industry Association (HKECIA) member firms. 1. To identify the types of practices and resources that offer value proposition In Study 1, this study conducted in-depth interviews with 15 exhibition industry professionals and analysed 15 exhibition innovation projects with the support of the HKECIA. The findings suggested the following six practices engaged in offering value proposition. (1) Operating practice is designed to create and deliver value proposition to customers using resources; (2) Value proposition-finding practice identifies (a) value propositions with customer value creation and (b) customer needs for new forms of creating value; (3) Interaction practice enables the communication of value propositions to customers or the co-creation of value propositions with customers; (4) Organizing and staffing practices organize the work and allocate staff responsibility involved in providing and representing value propositions: (5) Networking practice refers to how firms involve members of their network to create, deliver, or negotiate value propositions; and (6) Teambuilding and knowledge-sharing practices are used to build teamwork and share knowledge and skills to realize the value propositions. For resources involved in the creation of value propositions, typical operand resources in the exhibition industry include digital platforms, computers, software, and related IT systems because many show organizers have relied on virtual exhibitions and online marketing platforms during the pandemic. Commonly found operant resources include networking with customers and external stakeholders (e.g., service contractors, industry associations, business partners, governments); number, knowledge, and skill of staff; customer database; adaptive company culture for new ideas and change; and intelligence in the target market and competitors. For more details, please refer to our research publication. 2; To examine the process of developing existing or creating new practices and resources To achieve objective 2, this study analyzed 15 service innovation projects in the Hong Kong exhibition industry with the support of the HKECIA. According to the analysis of innovation projects, firms in the Hong Kong exhibition industry are likely to rely on existing (aforementioned) practices and resources, rather than new practices and resources, involved in the creation of value propositions. According to the findings, firms that actively engage in innovation aggressively utilized existing practices and resource to identify potential business threats and opportunities in dealing with constantly changing business environment. The findings suggest that the key to the process of developing practices and resources is senior management leadership in innovation and company support for innovation, given that many of the innovation projects analyzed from this study were developed from senior management’s idea and support. For more details, please refer to our research publication. 3. To identify facilitators and barriers to the development of existing or the creation of new practices and resources In-depth interviews and innovation project analysis reflect the following facilitators and barriers. Typical facilitators refer to effective and transparent communication, teamwork, senior management leadership, staff passion and motivation, awareness of market potential, active communication and interaction with customers, adaptive company culture, risk management, and competitor analysis. Many of firms in the Hong Kong exhibition industry are small to mid-sized companies. Therefore, common barriers include a lack of labor and professional knowledge, limited general resource, inability to implement PR, a lack of contents for new value proposition, less coordinating work with business partners, and reluctance to accept changes. For more details, please refer to our research publication. 4.To explore how practices integrate resources into value propositions Throughout Study 1, this study identified 7 sub-practices with 43 attributes that integrate resources into value propositions: (1) senior management leadership in innovation, (2) company support for innovation, (3) project teamwork, (4) employee proactive attitude, (5) collaboration with customers, (6) collaboration with business partners, and (7) competitor management. To validate the qualitative findings from Study 1, Study 2 (quantitative research) conducted a survey with the employees of the HKECIA member firms, consequently turning qualitative findings into 5 sub-practices with 40 attributes that integrate resources into value propositions: (1) company innovation culture, (2) project teamwork, (3) collaboration with customers and business partners, (4) competitor management, and (5) employee proactive attitude. Those sub-practices and attributes reflect how practices integrate resources into value propositions. For more details, please refer to our research publication.

15501119.label: Major findings and research outcome
15501119.value: Drawing on a mixed-methods approach, this study identifies and elucidates the practices involved in creating value propositions for service innovation, thereby extending the S-D logic literature to a conceptual understanding of developing value propositions. This study also published research findings in Tourism Management, a top journal with Impact Factor of 12.879. In addition, this study shared research findings with the HKECIA and generated managerial implications for the HK exhibition industry practitioners to design strategic plans and decisions to implement service innovation through the offering of new value propositions and to maintain the competitive edge of their exhibitions, thereby bringing more business visitors to an exhibition destination and fostering business tourism. Specifically saying, many of the HKECIA member firms are small local companies and do not generally maintain a well-established system of developing service innovation. Cultivating and embedding innovation culture in their organization would be difficult for them. The findings for the practices involved in creating value propositions indicate to the industry professionals the dimensions and attributes that underlie the practices. Thus, the study findings can act as a blueprint for service innovation project management to offer new value propositions. In other words, when HKECIA member firms aim to establish service innovation culture by offering new value propositions to their customers but do not know where to start and what to do, the findings of the present study can serve as a useful reference that allows firms to understand each dimension and its measures involved in the creation of value propositions. Thus, the firms can strategically develop and maintain service innovation culture. In addition, regular check-up of innovation competency is critical to even those firms equipped with established innovation culture due to the dynamic nature of the industry that requires the firms to keep abreast of constantly changing business and competitor environment. For instance, some of the HKECIA member firms developed service innovation by creating new value propositions (e.g., virtual shows, virtual business matching, hybrid of virtual and physical shows) to survive during the pandemic. This finding suggests to the firms the importance of rapidly adjusting to an unforeseen industry environment by exercising innovation competency. By utilizing the findings from this study as a checklist survey, exhibition firms periodically assess their innovation competency to understand their capability of developing and managing service innovation and to identify the areas of concern for further improvement.

15501119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15501119.value: This study suggests the development of service innovation index for future research. For example, the HKECIA can further develop the current findings into service innovation index in collaboration with academic researchers. The service innovation index can be created by assigning a suitable rating and weight to the findings developed from this paper. The index can be annually updated and reported by HKECIA as a service innovation rating and certification scheme for firms to monitor and understand their innovation performance score relative to other firms, thereby allowing firms to understand their current position in innovation performance and to make strategic actions accordingly. The service innovation index can be instrumental in aiding the HK exhibition firms in maintaining competitive innovation performance, consequently allowing the HK exhibition industry to stay ahead of its competitors from other countries.

15501119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15501119.value: Examining value propositions is a compelling research agenda, given that (1) developing existing or creating new value propositions is regarded as a service innovation in S-D logic and (2) value propositions (a prerequisite for customers’ value creation) are instrumental in customers’ cocreation. However, empirical research on the process and practice of creating value propositions has been neglected in the extant literature. Study 1 qualitatively identifies the types of practices and the resources (operant and operand), facilitators, and barriers involved in the development of value propositions in the exhibition industry. Thereafter, Study 2 conducts a survey to statistically validate findings derived from the qualitative data. Throughout Study 1 and 2, this research identifies and elucidates the practices involved in creating value propositions for service innovation, thereby extending the S-D logic literature to a conceptual understanding of developing value propositions. Furthermore, the research findings generate managerial implications for exhibition industry practitioners to design strategic plans and decisions to implement service innovation through the offering of new value propositions and maintain the competitive edge of their exhibitions, thereby bringing more business visitors to an exhibition destination and fostering business tourism.

15501319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15501319.value: This project is motivated by the booming (pedal-assist) electric bike-sharing systems, which, along with electric vehicle and e-scooter sharing, form the basis for so-called "electrified shared-mobility systems". For example, Jump Bikes runs dock-free electric bike-sharing systems in the U.S. (e.g., San Francisco, New York City) and Europe (e.g., Berlin); Limebike has electric bikes in Seattle; Chinese vendors OFO and MoBike are planning similar projects; etc. Electrified shared-mobility systems largely deviate from existing non-electrified ones (e.g., ride-sharing, bike-sharing) mainly due to two special features: (1) high investment cost and (2) complex recharging operations. Among such systems, pedal-assist electric bikes have their own unique features: (1) unlike electric vehicles, they can serve customers even without electricity but at a low service level; (2) compared to regular bikes and e-scooters, they enable a wider range of mobility and attract a larger group of customers; and (3) they can be very flexible in the case of dock-free systems. Due to these features, many urgent questions arise at both the electric bike-sharing firm level (in terms of planning and operations) and the policymaker level (in terms of government regulations). Therefore, in this project, we will use an electric bike-sharing system as a representative of electrified shared-mobility systems and investigate several critical issues arising from the former that also broadly exist in the latter. We will primarily tackle the following challenging questions: First, given the high investment cost, charging-level-dependent demand, and initially limited demand information, how can a firm (she) choose a robust capacity supply and continuously improve her decision making? Second, given the wide range of mobility and diverse customer groups, how can the firm design a joint recharging and redistribution policy enabling high profitability and robust service quality? How can she unlock the crowdsourcing potential (e.g., incentivized customers or volunteers) to improve system operations? Third, what should a policymaker (he) do in response to the new booming shared-mobility, which may complement or compete with existing transportation modes? Should he encourage its development via a completely hands-off approach, or should he set restrictive regulations to limit its development? By answering these questions, we will analyze both data-driven optimization and game-theoretic models. We will obtain insightful implications for managing electrified shared-mobility systems, ensuring effective business interactions between the policymaker and the firm, and developing implementable solutions for capacity design and recharging/redistribution operations. Our results will also contribute to the management of non-electrified and future autonomous electric vehicle sharing systems. 該項目受目前蓬勃發展的電動自行車共享系統所啟發。該系統與電動車和電動踏板車共享系統一起構成了所謂的“電氣化共享交通系統”。與傳統的非電氣化系統相比，電氣化共享交通系統具有如下兩個特徵：（1）高投資成本和（2）複雜的充放電操作。其中，具有踏板輔助的電動自行車更具有其獨特的特徵：（1）與電動汽車不同，它們可以在沒有電力的情況下為客戶服務（儘管服務水平更低）; （2）與普通自行車和電動滑板車相比，它們可以實現更廣泛的移動性並吸引更多的客戶; （3）在無樁的情況下，它們可以非常靈活。由於這些特點的存在，在電動自行車共享公司層面（比如規劃和運營方面）和決策制定者層面（比如政府法規方面）都出現了許多急迫問題有待解決。因此，在這個項目中，我們將使用電動自行車共享系統作為電氣化共享交通系統的代表，並調查由前者所產生且廣泛存在於後者的幾個關鍵問題。 我們將主要解決以下具有挑戰性的問題。首先，面對高投資成本、受充電水平影響的隨機需求以及公司運營初期有限的需求信息，企業應如何選擇產能供應並不斷改進其決策？其次，鑑於廣泛的移動性和多樣化的客戶群體，公司應如何設計集成充電與調度的合理運行計劃，且實現高盈利能力和優秀的服務質量？第三，面對這些新興發展但可能會與現有的交通方式競爭的共享交通系統，決策制定者應該如何應對？是應該通過完全不干涉的方式鼓勵其發展，還是應該制定限制性規定來限制其發展？ 通過回答這些問題，我們將分析數據驅動的優化和博弈論理論模型。我們將獲得有關管理電氣化共享交通系統的深刻啟示，確保決策制定者與公司之間的有效業務交互，並為產能設計和集成充電與調度提供可實施的解決方案。我們的結果還將有助於管理非電氣化和未來的自動電動汽車共享系統。

15501319.label: Realisation of objectives
15501319.value: All five objectives have been achieved. Electrified shared-mobility systems have been booming recently due to their significant sustainability for society and excellent accessibility to the public. In this project, our research unfolds in two steps. First, we study a traditional shared-mobility system as the starting point. Specifically, we consider a shared micromobility system that consists of lightweight vehicles (e.g., bikes). It offers an eco-friendly form of short-distance travel and helps alleviate city traffic congestion, achieving a sustainable urban transportation system. The operator of a shared micromobility system often bears the cost of physical assets: micromobility vehicles. Thus, it is crucial to properly set the initial vehicle allocation (i.e., capacity design) for different service regions to satisfy customer demands. In addition, as customers can pick up and drop off vehicles in any region, the system may experience a severe mismatch between vehicle supply and demand under uncertain customer arrivals. To better match supply with demand, the operator needs to constantly relocate the micromobility vehicles across the regions. When the operator plans for the initial vehicle allocation, he needs to take future relocation decisions into consideration. Thus, it is critical to integrate the initial vehicle allocation and subsequent relocation decisions to maximize the operator's profitability. Currently, many shared micromobility operators outsource vehicle relocation to third-party logistics providers (3PLs). Due to the high setup cost incurred in each 3PL request, it is too costly to frequently engage the 3PL for vehicle relocation across the service regions to rebalance the supply and demand. To overcome this challenge, some firms adopt a crowdsourcing strategy to hire individual riders to relocate vehicles. The integrated vehicle allocation and relocation problem becomes incredibly complex when the operator employs both rider crowdsourcing and 3PL for vehicle relocation. We formulate the integrated vehicle allocation and relocation problem under demand uncertainty as a two-stage stochastic integer program on a time-space network. The operator's objective is to maximize his expected profit. In the first stage, the operator decides the initial vehicle allocation before the demands are realized. In the second stage where demand realizations are observed, the operator decides the relocation of vehicles across the regions to match supply with demand over multiple time periods. For a special case with two service regions, we find that under the optimal relocation strategy, rider crowdsourcing and the 3PL are not used simultaneously in any region and period. Instead, the optimal relocation strategy will choose a method with a lower relocation cost per vehicle. For a more general case with multiple service regions, we first approximate the rider incentive function using a piecewise-linear function. The approximation introduces some binary variables, which can be relaxed to continuous variables without affecting the optimal objective value of the second-stage relocation problem. We show that the approximation is asymptotically tight. We then propose an algorithmic approach incorporating scenario-based and time-based (temporal) decomposition ideas to efficiently solve the two-stage problem. Numerical experiments using real data in the industry suggest that our approach significantly outperforms the CPLEX solver in both solution quality and computational time. We further explore many managerial insights by answering a series of research questions: Given a limited budget for acquiring vehicles (due to the policymaker's regulations or financial constraints), how does the budget affect the initial vehicle allocation? How does this initial allocation affect the subsequent vehicle relocation across the regions? How does a budget for crowdsourcing individual riders affect vehicle allocation and relocation? What is the best strategy for vehicle relocation (i.e., rider crowdsourcing only, 3PL only, both of them or none of them)? Under each relocation strategy, are there any interesting temporal or spatial features of the shared micromobility system? How can the significant crowdsourcing potential be explored in other similar systems (like last-mile delivery)? Second, we proceed to incorporate electric vehicles (EVs) into the shared mobility systems. Note that EVs can only be charged/discharged at specific locations equipped with specific facilities, and the charging/discharging process is time-consuming. During this period, EVs are idle and unusable for consumer trips. This means introducing EVs and potential vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology affects vehicle accessibility. Adjusting allocation can offset the impacts of changes in vehicle accessibility. However, dynamically adjusting the number of EVs across different periods is prohibitively expensive, given the high cost associated with EV ownership. This highlights the importance of optimizing the initial vehicle allocation (i.e., capacity design concerning the number of EVs) in the starting period for the EV-sharing mobility system with V2G. Since the initial allocation significantly influences subsequent operations, it is crucial to consider EV operations when optimizing allocation decisions. This ensures that both allocation and operation decisions are well-decided. Thus, we integrate EV allocation and operations into one model. In addition, the uncertain nature of consumer trips adds great complexity to the problem. These trips also exhibit correlations across all regions and time periods. Nevertheless, obtaining perfect knowledge of consumer trip correlations is impractical. Thus, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization (DRO) approach, which effectively uses historical data to accommodate interrelated uncertainties in consumer trips without requiring perfect information. Therefore, the system operator can obtain a robust capacity allocation by capturing limited demand information and unknown demand distribution. We formulate an integrated vehicle initial allocation and operation problem under correlated uncertainties as a two-stage DRO problem on a time-space-SoC network, where SoC indicates the state-of-charge of each EV. The operator aims to minimize its expected cost under the worst-case joint distribution within an ambiguity set. Such an ambiguity set is constructed based on the support and first- and second-moment information of uncertain demands, which can be collected from historical data. In the first stage, the operator decides the initial vehicle allocation before demands are realized. In the second stage, where correlated demands are observed, the operator manages vehicles across regions to meet demands over multiple time periods. We reformulate the two-stage DRO problem as a semi-definite programming (SDP) model. To deal with the significant computational difficulty of the SDP reformulation, we introduce principal component analysis (PCA)-based outer and inner approximations to reduce the size of positive semi-definite (PSD) matrices in the SDP model. We also propose an algorithmic approach incorporating time-based decomposition to further strengthen the solving process. Through numerical experiments using real data, we show that our proposed approaches can obtain high-quality solutions in a significantly short computational time. We further explore many managerial insights by answering a series of research questions: How can we implement DRO in the integrated allocation and operation problem under correlated uncertainty while keeping computational tractability? How does uncertainty correlation affect the solution quality How can the operator’s decisions improve as more demand data becomes available? Are there any interesting features in charging/discharging during operations? How can we incorporate the crowdsourcing potential for jointly recharging and redistributing EVs? How do the charging and discharging activities of EVs affect the electric grid operations? In addition to charging/discharging, what other activities in EVs' operations have exciting features? As all the above managerial insights in the two-step studies are well explored, we achieve all five objectives.

15501319.label: Major findings and research outcome
15501319.value: From Paper 3 and Paper 4 in Part C, we can summarize our findings and insights as follows: (i) If the vehicle allocation budget (due to financial constraints or policymaker’s regulations) is tight, the number of relocated vehicles in the second stage increases as the initial vehicle allocation increases. In contrast, if the vehicle allocation budget is sufficiently large, the number of relocated vehicles decreases as the initial vehicle allocation becomes larger. (ii) The 3PL satisfies mostly mass relocation needs, while rider crowdsourcing mainly serves sporadic relocation needs. Investing in rider crowdsourcing can increase profit, reduce demand loss, and improve the vehicle utilization rate of the system with an existing 3PL relocation method. (iii) The rider crowdsourcing complements (benefits) the 3PL when the crowdsourcing budget is low but substitutes the 3PL when the budget is high. (iv) To increase the supply in high-demand pick-up regions, the 3PL may relocate vehicles in batches from faraway, low-demand regions, while rider crowdsourcing tends to relocate a few vehicles each time from neighboring regions. (v) The crowdsourcing potential can also help improve the efficiency of last-mile delivery significantly. We apply the DRO methodology innovation in Paper 2 in Part C to solve the model in our second-step study, where more data increases the solution's effectiveness. Meanwhile, we can summarize our findings and insights (see details in Paper 1 and Paper 5 in Part C) as follows: (i) Most EVs charge electricity during the early hours of the day when electricity prices and trip demands are low. Conversely, EVs discharge electricity during periods of high electricity prices. (ii) An increased charging speed contributes to a reduction in the number of allocated vehicles, an enhancement in the vehicle utilization rate, and a drop in total costs. (iii) EVs process charging and discharging more frequently under the time-based pricing scheme than the electricity-based pricing scheme. (iv) Relocation peaks occur when consumer trips significantly rise. Vehicles are relocated from regions with a positive net flow to regions with a negative net flow. (v) The crowdsourcing potential can also be applied to improve the efficiency of joint charging and relocation of EVs, while the charging and discharging activities of EVs affect the electric grid operations significantly.

15501319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15501319.value: This project studies an important problem in the operations management of electrified shared mobility. There are several potential directions for future research. In the first-step study, we have the following potential studies to conduct. (i) The 3PL uses only one truck to perform its service, while we may consider multiple trucks. (ii) We simplify the cost structure of the shared micromobility system because of the limited information available. The results may be improved with more information provided. (iii) Besides the two temporal demand patterns studied (i.e., bimodal and unimodal patterns), we can explore other demand distributions and customer behaviors to enrich the insights. In the second-step study, we have the following potential studies to conduct. (i) We consider only the correlated uncertainties of the customer demands, while other potential correlated uncertainties can be incorporated, such as vehicle failures. (ii) We consider moment-based ambiguity sets in the paper while we may explore alternative ones. For example, as the amount of available data increases, potentially yielding a more reliable empirical distribution, we may consider a discrepancy-based Wasserstein ambiguity set. (iii) As the EVs should interact with the power grid, we may integrate the operations of the EVs and the power grid.

15501319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15501319.value: Electrified shared-mobility systems have been booming recently due to their significant sustainability for society and excellent accessibility to the public. The operator of such a system often bears the cost of physical assets (i.e., mobility vehicles). Meanwhile, the operator should carefully consider the charging and relocation activities of the mobility vehicles. Therefore, it is crucial to properly set the initial vehicle allocation (system capacity design) for different service regions to satisfy customer demands while operating the system to charge and relocate electric vehicles. We utilize historical data to help characterize the demand profile, by which we further build up data-driven stochastic optimization models to help decide the number of allocated vehicles at the beginning of each day and determine the charging and relocation operations within the day. With real data, our models provide shared mobility firms with robust decisions when facing limited demand information and unknown distribution. We observe that crowdsourcing the firm’s decision-making can be continuously improved when more data is incorporated. In addition, by introducing crowdsourcing potential into the system, we can more efficiently relocate the vehicles. The government’s regulations significantly impact the firm’s decisions in allocating and relocating vehicles.

15501419.label: Project Title(Chinese)
15501419.value: 旅遊業中的消費者抵制: 道德觸發器、目的地形象及緩解策略

15501419.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15501419.value: An increasing number of consumers seeks to act beyond their immediate interests and consider the effect of their consumption choices on the wider society, either nationally or globally. In this type of consumption, individual interests are positioned as secondary to other concerns, such as the welfare of workers, the environment, animals, or political issues. When these dominant concerns are not addressed, the consumers may engage in various overt (brand avoidance, product boycott) and covert (downshifting, voluntary simplicity) anti-consumption practices. Accordingly, there has been an increasing number of destination boycotts worldwide. Hong Kong became a boycotted destination in 2014 as a result of the “Occupy Central” events when the Mainland Chinese took the calls for boycott to the social network Weibo. China itself was the object of boycott following the Tiananmen Square protest, which negatively affected its tourist image. Despite the growing number of consumer resistance cases in tourism, existing research has barely tackled this issue either theoretically or practically. The aim of this research is to understand consumer in tourism by focusing on the link between destination avoidance triggers, destination brand image, and remedial strategies. The proposed research investigates the context of China’s country and brand image, a suitable setting given its controversial reputation on the global marketplace. Besides extending currently very limited research on non-consumption in tourism, in the long-term, results of this study will point to important practical implications. Destination marketing organizations (DMOs) have little or no control over a tourism destination’s political system, the state of human and animal rights, cultural discourses, and social problems, which inevitably influence the reputation of the destination in the global marketplace, including tourism. This is especially problematic at the country-level marketing since image of a place as a country influences its image as a tourist destination. The findings are expected to equip destination marketers with knowledge of common triggers for destination avoidance and help devise marketing strategies to help alleviate its effects on destination image. The findings can inform the crisis marketing communication. Second, consumers who engage in political consumerism, or “voting with dollar” to influence societal changes, tend to be well educated, high earners with good political and societal awareness, and to reside in affluent countries. Individuals with such a profile also happened to be the most sought-after tourism market segment, and thus understanding what triggers these consumers not to travel to certain destinations can help better connect with them long-term. 越來越多的消費者尋求超越其眼前利益之行動，並且考慮其消費選擇對全國或全球廣大社會之影響。在此類消費中，個人利益的定位不如其它問題重要，如工人福利、環保、動物或政治問題。當這些主要問題得不到解決時，消費者可能會採取各種公開(品牌回避、產品抵制)和隱蔽(降檔、自願簡單)的反消費做法。因此，世界各地有越來越多的人抵制目的地。2014年，由於“佔領中環”事件，香港成為被抵制的目的地，當時中國內地人也在社交網絡微博上呼籲抵制。在六四事件之後，中國內地本身亦成為被抵制的對象。六四事件負面影響了中國的旅遊形象。儘管旅遊業中的消費者抵制案件越來越多，但無論是理論上還是在實踐上，現有研究幾乎沒有解決這個問題。本研究旨在通過關注避免目的地的觸發因素、目的地品牌形象和補救策略之間的聯繫，瞭解旅遊消費者。本研究調查了中國的國家背景和品牌形象，鑒於其聲譽在全球市場上的爭議性，這是一個合適的環境。本研究除了能夠延伸目前關於旅遊中非消費方面非常有限的研究以外，研究結果將具有長遠而重要的實際意義。 目的地行銷組織對旅遊目的地的政治制度、人與動物權利狀況、文化話語和社會問題的控制很小或缺乏，這不可避免地影響到目的地在全球市場(包括旅遊業)的聲譽。這個問題在國家級行銷中尤為明顯，因為某地作為國家的形象影響到其作為旅遊目的地的形象。研究結果預計會使目的地行銷人員瞭解避免目的地的常見觸發因素，並且有助於制定行銷策略，有助於減輕其對目的地形象之影響。研究結果可以為危機行銷溝通提供資訊。其次,參與政治消費主義或“用美元投票”來影響社會變化的消費者，往往受過良好教育、收入者、具有良好的政治及社會意識、居住在富裕的國家。此類型個人亦恰好是最受追捧的旅遊市場細分；因此瞭解是什麼觸發這些消費者不前往某些目的地，將有助於更好地與他們長期保持聯繫。

15501619.label: Project Objectives

15501619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15501619.value: Upselling refers to a salesperson’s effort to persuade a consumer to choose a superior and more expensive product or service option instead of the originally chosen one. In upselling, the message and its timing matter. In this study, we will examine upselling in the context of hotel room upselling. The aim is to examine consumers’ attitudes toward upselling promotions and intention to purchase the upselling option at the time of booking, between booking and arrival, and during check-in, depending on the framing of the upselling message (difference in price versus quality). The conceptual framework of the study is based on the construal-level theory and reactance theory. Given the typical temporal delay between booking and actual stay, it is important to understand how consumers react when upselling options are presented to them at different points in time. We argue that psychological distance has an impact on consumer preferences. We further suggest that consumers might perceive upselling negatively, and show reactance to such promotions. In the proposed study, we aim to examine the joint impact of the timing and framing of the upselling message on consumer perceptions. 追加銷售是指銷售人員試圖說服消費者選擇更高級、更昂貴的產品或服務選項，而不是最初選擇的產品或服務選項。在追加銷售中，訊息及其時機十分重要。本項研究中，我們將研究酒店房間的追加銷售。目的在於檢查消費者預訂時、預訂與到達之間以及入住期間對追加銷售促銷的態度，以及購買追加銷售選項的意向，具體取決於追加銷售資訊(價格差異與相應品質之間關係)的框架。本研究之概念框架是以識解理論及反應理論為基礎。鑒於預訂和實際入住之間的典型時間延遲，有必要瞭解消費者對不同時間點向其提供追加銷售選項時的反應。我們認為心理距離對消費者的偏好有影響。我們進一步提出消費者可能會對追加銷售持負面看法，並且對此類促銷表現出抵觸。我們提出的研究旨在研究追加銷售訊息的時機及框架對消費者認知的共同影響。

15501619.label: Major findings and research outcome
15501619.value: The main findings of the study are the following: When the framing of upselling message involves specific room attributes, consumers show more favorable attitudes when receiving the promotion one week prior to arrival (vs immediately after the booking). However, when the framing of upselling message involves price, consumer attitudes do not differ across the time of receiving the promotion. Reactance mediates the effect of message timing on consumer attitudes when the message framing involves specific room attributes.

15501619.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15501619.value: In this study we manipulated temporal distance by hypothetical scenarios. Experiencing an actual psychological temporal distance may result in different perceptions. Future studies should recruit participants who have an actual hotel room booking and offer them an upselling promotion at different time points between booking and arrival.In addition, the scenarios in our study used a fixed time frame (one week prior to arrival) to represent proximity to the stay. In reality, hotels typically upsell three to five days prior to arrival. The timing also depends on numerous factors, such as the lead time, consumer type and the number of available upselling options. A closer examination of the optimal upselling time between booking and arrival that considers these influential factors would be valuable.

15501619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15501619.value: The purpose of this study is to investigate the interactive effect of timing and framing of hotel’s upselling message on consumer attitudes toward the message. The mediating role of reactance between the timing of upselling message and consumer attitudes is also explored. A 2 (timing: immediately after the booking vs one week prior to arrival) by 2 (framing: concrete vs abstract) experimental design was used. A total of 250 Chinese consumers were recruited and were randomly exposed to a hotel online upselling scenario. The consumer attitudes and reactance were measured. This research suggests that hotel managers should offer concrete message framing that includes specific room attributes at the time proximal to consumers’ arrival to increase acceptance of online room upselling. In addition, it is important for hotel managers to take consumers’ reactance into consideration when developing an online upselling strategy. Research on online hotel room upselling is scant. This study adds to the upselling literature by examining the joint influence of timing and framing of upselling promotions on consumer attitudes toward such messages. Furthermore, this study extends our understanding of the role of reactance in the online upselling process.

To gauge the attributes and dimensionality of experiential luxury consumption in high-end hotels among Chinese consumers. 15502019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15502019.value: Studies of luxury consumption have focused on tangible products without referring to experiential services, the popularity of which is increasing among Chinese consumers. China now leads the world in luxury consumption, and Chinese consumers’ growing interest in experiential services carries significant implications for the service sector, including hospitality. However, most studies have focused on defining conspicuous consumption and explaining the motives behind consuming tangible luxury products without identifying the key attributes, determinants, and outcomes of experiential luxury consumption. Taking luxury hotels as an example, this study will use the Zaltman metaphor elicitation technique to explore experiential luxury consumption among Chinese consumers. Results are expected to advance our understanding of why and how consumers engage in experiential luxury consumption, particularly in Chinese society, and to identify corresponding implications for the luxury industry. 关于奢侈品消费的研究主要集中在有形产品上，没有涉及体验式服务，而后者在中国消费者中越来越受欢迎。目前，中国在奢侈品消费方面领先世界。中国消费者对体验式服务日益增长的兴趣，对包括酒店业在内的服务业具有重要意义。然而，大多数研究专注于定义炫耀性消费和解释消费有形奢侈品的动机，而没有揭示体验式奢侈品消费的关键属性、决定因素和结果。本研究将以奢华酒店为例，运用萨尔特曼隐喻诱引技术(Zaltman metaphor elicitation)探索中国消费者的体验式奢侈品消费。研究结果将有助于我们理解消费者，特别是中国的消费者，为什么以及如何参与体验式奢侈品消费，并给奢侈品行业以相应的启示。

15502019.label: Realisation of objectives
15502019.value: This project encountered pandemic-related challenges. The study was originally intended to describe mainland Chinese consumers’ luxury hospitality experiences in Hong Kong; it was scheduled to be a 2-year project beginning in January 2020. However, the COVID-19 outbreak prevented the research team from contacting mainland travelers as planned. The project was accordingly delayed. The team requested an extension from the funding agent on December 1, 2020. As recommended by the RGC panel, a contingency plan was created to avoid additional delays given that cross-border leisure travel was minimal due to the pandemic. The study’s focus shifted from mainland travelers to local Hong Kong residents with RGC approval. Qualified local hotel members who used luxury hotel services in Hong Kong were invited for ZMET interviews. The research team pilot-tested the ZMET protocol with Hong Kong residents who had had a luxury hotel consumption experience in this territory within 12 months prior to the interview date. The protocol was subsequently modified to suit the research objectives and to prepare for data collection as circumstances would allow. ZMET was used to understand Chinese individuals’ experiential consumption in luxury hotels. Qualified participants were recruited through multiple sources using snowball sampling. Interviews were held with 16 consumers until data saturation was reached. Eligible interviewees had either stayed at or engaged in a consumption experience at an upscale hotel within the previous 12 months. Interviews lasted roughly 84 minutes on average; all were audio recorded and transcribed verbatim with participants’ consent. Regarding age, interviewees ranged from their 20s to their 50s. Their rich recall offered valuable insights into luxury experiences. The ZMET protocol entailed several steps. First, prior to interviews, participants were asked to choose 8–10 photos depicting their most memorable luxury experiences and reactions at a luxury hotel. Second, during interviews, participants described the content of and their feelings about each image as it related to their experiences. Third, participants’ sensory experiences at luxury hotels were examined by deconstructing their encounters based on taste, touch, smell, sound, color, and feelings. Fourth, participants were invited to construct a summary image that best represented their experiences and to create a visual story about an ideal stay; these steps were intended to inspire participants to envision their ideal experience. Lastly, participants were invited to draw a mental map with key constructs and elements that captured their experiences at high-end hotels. In total, 134 photos, 16 summary images, and 16 mental maps were collected for analysis. Most interviews were conducted in Chinese; two were in English based on participants’ preference. Verbal information was processed using the qualitative data analysis software Quirkos. The luxury consumption experience structure in Figure 1 was derived from participants’ mental maps, visual storytelling, and sensory images from verbal and nonverbal data. Results yielded three layers of experiences, namely supportive experiences, personal/social experiences, and affective experiences. Interpretations of these dimensions of luxury hospitality consumption addressed the three objectives stated in the proposal. Findings demonstrated Chinese individuals’ motivations to engage in luxury hotel consumption. The results also revealed experience-based dimensions and attributes along with how hotel offerings contributed to such experiences. In the first layer, tangible and intangible hotel offerings served as experiential stimuli (e.g., exclusive services, spectacular views, dining experiences, artistic décor, hotel ambience, large spaces, and facilities). These experiences in turn prompted personal/social encounters involving social connections, social symbolism, and enjoyment in settings such as family gatherings. Affective experiences manifested from personal/social experiences; participants reported feeling comfortable, relaxed, happy, peaceful, and healed. Supportive experiences, personal/social experiences, and affective experiences totaled 491, 141, and 198 instances, respectively. Supportive experiences encompassed hotel guests’ direct experiences drawn from sensory interactions amid exclusive services, spectacular views, dining experiences, artistic décor, hotel ambience, large spaces, and facilities. These experiences were sparked by hotel offerings’ multisensory stimuli throughout consumption. Personal/social experiences and affective experiences arose from supportive experiences with such offerings. These results reflected strong connections among hotel offerings, luxury consumption motives, participants’ affective consumption feelings, and the construction of overall experiential luxury consumption in high-end hotels. Although the proposed study objectives were realized through ZMET, the researchers opted to reach out to mainland Chinese participants via a follow-up survey (i.e., using funds that were initially reserved for travel to mainland China for ZMET during the pandemic). Again with RGC approval, an online survey was designed and implemented based on qualitative ZMET findings. This survey helped verify the existing results in the mainland Chinese market and provided an opportunity to describe these travelers’ experiential luxury hotel experiences. Four cities (two tier-one and two tier-two cities each) were included: Beijing, Shanghai, Chengdu, and Hangzhou. Eight hundred participants (200 per city) were recruited. A 50/50 gender distribution was maintained for both survey rounds in an effort to balance the views of men and women. All participants were required to be at least 21 years old with a good age mix. They were also required to have stayed in a luxury hotel (5-star or higher) for at least one night in the past 12 months. Their monthly disposable income needed to be equal to or greater than their residential city’s average. In general, the survey data supported a three-dimensional structure of luxury hotel experiences among mainland Chinese consumers: supporting experiences, self/social experiences, and affective experiences. Supporting experiences encompassed hotel guests’ direct experiences (i.e., sensory interactions) via exclusive services, dining experiences, design, hotel images, and facilities. These experiences were derived from hotel offerings’ multisensory stimuli throughout consumption. Twenty-six luxury hotel attributes were included in the final measurement of supporting experiences. These attributes can provide luxury hotels guidance in terms of what should be prioritized for the mainland Chinese market to view these hotels as “luxury” options. Hotel offerings stimulated participants’ personal/social experiences, which then generated affective feelings toward luxury hotels. Three attributes were included in self-experiences; 10 attributes were included in the final measurement of social experiences at luxury hotels; and four attributes were retained for affective experiences. Customers’ affective feelings positively influenced their consumption intentions over the ensuing 12 months. Additional analyses indicated that self-experiences shaped affective feelings more strongly than social experiences in the luxury hotel setting. This pattern contradicts the usual understanding of motives behind luxury goods consumption, where social motives tend to play major roles. A further test of the relationship between luxury experiences and future consumption intention implied a positive relationship between the two. Qualitative and quantitative data jointly produced a sensory model of luxury hotel experiences for testing. The proposed model demonstrated an acceptable fit to the data.

15502019.label: Major findings and research outcome
15502019.value: Scholars have recently started exploring luxury service consumption in China. However, few studies have integrated verbal and nonverbal data when unraveling the customer experience, especially in hospitality contexts. This study is one of the first to enrich comprehension of luxury hospitality experiences among Chinese consumers with ZMET by combining verbal and nonverbal data. Customers’ experience formation appeared to come in response to sensory stimuli from products and services in luxury hotels corresponding to social and personal consumption needs. The structure and attributes of luxury hotel experiences were determined based on participants’ mental maps, summary images, imaginary stories, visual imagery, and verbal descriptions. Three dimensions emerged: supporting experiences, personal/social experiences, and affective experiences. The first dimension was rooted in sensory processing given customers’ initial encounters with hotel offerings. Self/social experiences were tied to supporting experiences depending on the multisensory incorporation of hotel stimuli into a specific consumption setting (e.g., social gatherings or personal enjoyment). Affective experiences reflected consumers’ emotions resulting from supporting or personal/social experiences. This study unveiled linkages between hotel offerings, sensory integration, experiences, and luxury hotel consumption intention. The proposed experience hierarchy demonstrates how luxury consumption experiences form in hospitality. The follow-up survey offered further evidence of the sensory model of luxury hotel experiences. Qualitative and quantitative data revealed Chinese individuals’ motivations for luxury consumption in hotel settings, the dimensionality of luxury hospitality experiences, and the attributes of experience measures. Findings also uncovered hierarchical relationships among experience categories. Both data sets vividly reflected experience construction. This study is the first of its kind to depict the mechanisms underlying consumption experience formation in luxury hotels on the bases of sensory processing and mental imagery. Sensory integration is fundamental in all service contexts but has been neglected in the luxury and experience literature. This study connected hotel offerings’ sensory stimuli with consumption experiences in luxury hotels. Its data-informed theoretical model explained how hotel input contributes to consumption experiences. This model also depicted how sensory stimuli in luxury hotels define Chinese consumers’ experiences, how customers respond to these hotels’ offerings, and how consumption experience dimensions emerge in these hotels. Hoteliers can refer to these conclusions to connect what hotels offer guests with customers’ actual experiences.

15502019.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15502019.value: Much work needs to be done to further develop research in this area. First, sensory processing can vary among people from different backgrounds. Participants in this study were not distinguished based on factors such as consumption history or cultural background when data were interpreted. Future studies can test whether consumers from diverse backgrounds view the same set of sensory stimuli differently in luxury hotels in light of their consumption experiences. Second, only Chinese consumers were included in the sample given this market segment’s prominence. Subsequent work can compare Chinese individuals’ consumption experiences with consumers from other countries to understand how guests’ consumption experiences vary in luxury hotels. Third, solely hotel-based luxury consumption was investigated. Follow-up research could include more experiential luxury consumption settings, such as high-end restaurants, luxury cruises, and private clubs, to verify the proposed model’s applicability. Fourth, the distinctions between luxury goods consumption and luxury services consumption need to be explored and compared in depth. Such studies are usually performed separately, making direct comparisons difficult. However, individuals’ consumption needs, consumption behavior, and perceived experiences could differ across tangible and intangible luxury consumption. Comparative studies will help to establish a complete picture of luxury consumption.

15502019.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15502019.value: Luxury consumption studies have focused on tangible products with less attention paid to experiential services. However, Chinese consumers are increasingly interested in luxury services. Yet little is known about what hotels can offer to inspire a sense of luxury among these guests. It is similarly unclear how hotel offerings may affect luxury consumption experiences and subsequent consumption intention. This study describes Chinese individuals’ experiential luxury consumption in hotel settings. Findings extend the understanding of luxury goods to luxury services. The results also clarify the connection between hotel offerings and Chinese consumers’ luxury experiences. Hoteliers can consider the identified experience-based stimuli to better understand how luxury consumption experiences can be built through hotel services, dining experiences, design, hotel images, and facilities. Practitioners will thus be prepared to meet customers’ personal and social needs. Overall, this study will help luxury hotels leverage their potential in the Chinese market.

15502419.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15502419.value: Although there are many attempts to identify determinants of destination competitiveness, the empirical research to estimate the relationship between productivity and competitiveness is limited. We plan to investigate labor productivity of various sectors that directly and/or indirectly affect destination performance (i.e., market share). More specifically, we will exploit a set of econometrics models considering variations of measuring destination competitiveness, in respect to different expenditure estimations (total expenditure, per arrival expenditure or per capita expenditure) and competitive sets (key competing destinations or an Asia Pacific region). The use of multiple competitiveness measures ensures of the robustness of the findings and a comprehensive understanding of competitiveness from various perspectives. The researchers will employ a series of advanced econometric techniques to accomplish rigorous analyses, such as the Bayesian time-varying parameter VAR model, to capture the possible time-varying nature at play in the context of destination competitiveness and productivity. This project focuses on Hong Kong as a case destination where tourism is one of key industries in the national economy. Since the global recession, in particular, it appears that the tourism contribution to Hong Kong’s GDP as well as the productivity growth of the economic sectors has been gradually decreased. Thus, this project is expected to provide important implications to not only policymakers in Hong Kong as an international tourism destination, but also tourism scholars. The findings are expected to suggest an appropriate method to evaluate destination competitiveness on the basis of the performance-based measures. This will assist policymakers in precisely assessing the success of the destination management. Recognizing that tourism is a broader system incorporating a set of stakeholders at diverse industries, this project will shed light on relative importance of productivity of the sectors associated with tourism on the destination competitiveness. This will facilitate for the policymakers effectively allocate resources to proper sectors, and identify certain industries to cooperate, in order to enhance tourism competitiveness. 雖然有許多嘗試來確定目的地競爭力的決定因素，但估計生產力與競爭力之間關係的實證研究是有限的。我們計劃調查直接和/或間接影響目的地業績（即市場份額）的各個部門的勞動生產率。 該項目利用一組計量經濟學模型，考慮到不同支出估算和競爭集合的測量目標競爭力的變化。多種競爭力措施的使用確保了調查結果的穩健性，並從各個角度全面了解競爭力。研究人員將採用一系列先進的計量經濟學技術來完成嚴格的分析，以便在目的地競爭力和生產力的背景下捕捉可能的時間變化性質。預計調查結果將提出一種基於績效衡量標準評估目的地競爭力的適當方法。這將有助於政策決策者準確評估目的地管理成功與否。 預計調查結果將提出一種基於績效衡量標準評估目的地競爭力的適當方法。這將有助於政策制定者準確評估目的地管理的成功與否。認識到旅遊業是一個更廣泛的系統，將不同行業的一系列利益相關者納入其中。該項目將闡明與旅遊相關的部門的生產力對目的地競爭力的相對重要性。這將有利於政策制定者有效地將資源分配到適當的部門，並確定某些行業進行合作，以提高旅遊競爭力。

15502419.label: Major findings and research outcome
15502419.value: To examine the effects of sectoral productivity on destination competitiveness, this study used the ADLM-ECM model to estimate the short- and long-term relationships between productivity in 10 sectors and destination competitiveness, with the latter measured in a performance-based framework as the total expenditure per resident in Hong Kong against the mean of the corresponding measures in competing destinations. Competitiveness was linked to productivity in 4 sectors. Only productivity in the retail sector had a positive complimentary effect on destination competitiveness. Productivities in the restaurant, finance and building and construction sectors had negative substitutive effects, which resulted from economy restructuring. Our results consistently show that demand-related factors are critical to influencing competitiveness. Competitive tourism products developed by the resources contributed from the other sectors in terms of human, capital, facilities and infrastructure capture expanding global wealth, though this process may feature a lag effect. Given product extension and efficiency improvements to optimize the complementary effect of sectoral productivity, sustained destination competitiveness should rely upon a road map of long-term strategic planning of sectoral economic development. As with other aggregate studies of destination competitiveness, this study has limitations. First, the use of labor productivity to represent tourism production efficiency may not have entirely reflected the effective utilization of all resources related to tourism, such as capital and technology, although these were embedded in labor productivity. Future studies should thus consider including both labor and capital productivities in the destination competitiveness function. In terms of the measure of destination competitiveness, the mean tourism performance of the competitors may vary, should different destinations be selected. To gain deeper knowledge of competitiveness and the corresponding relationship with sectoral productivity, competitors could be classified to define different benchmarks, such as direct and indirect competitors. Data availability also constrained this study. For example, the figures for total inbound tourism income (expenditure) obtained from BOP travel and transport accounts may have included expenditures unrelated to true tourism, such as those of gamblers, business travelers and overseas students, which could obscure the differences in actual tourism expenditure between destinations (IMF, 2010). Another data limitation is the small sample size. More data would have allowed more degrees of freedom and better understanding of the variables with longer lags. Furthermore, extrapolation methods were used to estimate missing data, but larger and more complete samples in the future could mitigate the potential biases in these methods. Finally, the use of a single equation approach to study destination competitiveness may be too restrictive, so future studies could explore the possibility of integrating both demand and supply perspectives using a system equations approach. The key contribution of this study is its use of a performance-based method to measure destination competitiveness, which is useful for policymakers because of its ability to examine the performance of a destination against that of its major competitors. By applying the ADLM-ECM technique, this is the first study to examine the short- and long-term relationships between the productivities of 10 sectors and destination competitiveness. The results are a valuable reference for future research on destination competitiveness and for the formulation of policies related to sectoral productivity and short- and long-term improvements in destination competitiveness.

15502419.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15502419.value: The study could be further expanded to study the destination competitiveness in other destinations than Hong Kong in order to generalize the research findings. The research team will continue the same line of research with a view to publishing more journal papers in this area.

15502419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15502419.value: To pursue a better quality of life in the context of an expanding global economy, destinations must sharpen their competitive advantages through increased productivity. This study investigates the effect of sectoral productivity on destination competitiveness, using Hong Kong as an example. The competitiveness of a destination is measured by the tourism-contributed quality of life relative to that of competing destinations. The autoregressive distributed lag model with error correction mechanism is used to model the relationship between destination competitiveness and various sectoral productivities. The productivity effects of several related sectors on the destination competitiveness are identified through empirical econometric analysis. This study makes three main contributions. First, it involves the development of a long-term measurement of destination competitiveness that accounts for rivalry dynamics, which provides a useful benchmark for policymakers and decision-makers to formulate appropriate policies and strategies to improve the competitiveness of their respective destinations. Second, this study is the first to examine the effect of sectoral productivity on destination competitiveness. The findings enrich our understanding of the short- and long-term relationships between destination competitiveness and sectoral productivity, which can help decision-makers effectively allocate resources to increase long-term competitiveness. Third, the case study of Hong Kong exemplifies the application of the method, and its implications can shed new light on tourism development aimed at long-term destination prosperity.

15503219.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15503219.value: In recent years, many countries have realized the increasing severity of global environmental issues and diligently contributed to the vision of sustainable development. For example, as pledged by President Xi, the Chinese government is gradually changing its policy focus from bottom-line economic growth to gearing more towards social and environmental sustainability to reflect the mission of building a “Beautiful China”. With the vision of sustainable development, many countries have invested extensively to advocate the research and development (R&D), production, and consumption of green products/technology, which require less energy and generate higher environmental benefits compared to their counterparts with traditional technology. When investing to advocate innovation and adoption of green products, policy makers usually have multiple interventions to utilize, out of which providing government subsidy has been widely adopted. When offering subsidy, the central challenge faced by governments is how to decide the appropriate subsidy timing, format, and amount to achieve the maximized benefit given limited investment budgets. In practice, there are three major subsidy schemes, with all finding their wide applications: (1) subsidy for product design and R&D innovation; (2) subsidy for mass production; and (3) subsidy for consumers’ consumption. Different subsidy schemes may offer distinct incentives that endogenously affect a firm’s product design and pricing decisions. The ultimate purpose for offering government subsidy is, through its impacts on product innovation and sale, to induce more consumers’ consumption and generate larger environmental benefits. However, as the key stakeholder, consumers usually exhibit inherent heterogeneity in their understanding and attitude towards green product. While a fraction can derive additional utility by generating environmental benefit through their consumption, the others may only focus on the base functionality and treat green product the same as its counterpart with traditional technology. Such consumer heterogeneity further complicates a firm's green product design and pricing decisions as it cannot price discriminate the two segments to fully explore its profit maximization opportunity. The central theme of this proposal is to provide systematic understanding on how the endogenous choices of government subsidy schemes affect a firm’s product design and pricing decisions in a segmented market with inherent consumer heterogeneity. Our proposal could provide not only clear guidance for governments to stimulate green product innovation and consumption by allocating its limited budget to different subsidy schemes, but also rich managerial insights on how the optimal subsidy policy is altered by the government’s resource, preference, and market conditions. 近年来，许多国家已经意识到日益严重的全球环境问题，并努力促进可持续发展的愿景。例如，正如习主席所承诺的那样，中国政府正在逐步将其政策重点从基本经济增长转向更加注重社会和环境可持续性发展，以反映建设“美丽中国”的使命。为推动可持续发展，许多国家已经投入了大量资金来倡导绿色产品/技术的研发，生产和消费。与传统技术相比，绿色产品/技术需要更少的能源并产生更高的环境效益。 在投资倡导创新和采用绿色产品时，政策制定者通常需要多种干预措施，其中提供政府补贴已被广泛采用。在提供补贴时，政府面临的主要挑战是如何在有限的投资预算下确定适当的补贴时间，形式和金额，以实现最大化的效用。在实践中，有三种主要的补贴计划，都有其广泛的实际应用：（1）产品设计和研发创新补贴; （2）批量生产补贴; （3）消费者消费补贴。不同的补贴计划可能会提供不同的激励措施，从而对公司的产品设计和定价决策产生内生影响。 提供政府补贴的最终目的是通过其对产品创新和销售的影响，促使更多的消费者消费并产生更大的环境效益。然而，作为关键利益相关者，消费者在对绿色产品的理解和态度上通常表现出内在的异质性。虽然一部分消费者可以通过消费产生环境效益来获得额外的效用，但其他消费者可能只关注基本功能并且将绿色产品与传统技术相等同。这种消费者的异质性进一步使公司的绿色产品设计和定价决策复杂化，因为它无法对两个细分市场进行价格区分，以充分发掘其利润最大化机会。 该提案的中心主题是系统地了解政府补贴计划的内生选择如何影响公司在具有固有消费者异质性的细分市场中的产品设计和定价决策。我们的建议不仅可以通过将有限的预算分配给不同的补贴计划来刺激绿色生产创新和消费， 从而为政府提供明确的指导，而且还可以为政府的资源，偏好和市场条件如何改变最优补贴政策提供丰富的管理见解。

15503219.label: Realisation of objectives
15503219.value: All the four research objectives have been fully investigated. The central theme of this research project is to provide a systematic understanding on how the a firm’s green product design and pricing decisions are affected by factors, such as government subsidy schemes and consumer heterogeneity in a segmented market. We aim to not only offer clear suggestions for government to stimulate green production innovation and consumption by allocating its limited budget to different subsidy schemes, but also provide rich managerial insights on how the design and sale of green product is affected by the government’s resource, preference, and the involving market conditions. To those ends, we develop a game theoretical model between a government and a firm. The government first devises a subsidy policy, including the recipient and the rate, to encourage green technology innovation, thereby maximizing social welfare. Three types of subsidy policies are considered: R&D, production, and consumer subsidies. Then, the firm designs the product by deciding whether to invest in green technology and subsequently sets the retail price of the product. To capture consumer heterogeneity, we consider two segments in the market. The first contains socially conscious consumers, who are willing to pay for the green product, while the other contains non-socially conscious consumers, who does not value green technology. We first solve the above model when the government offers a single subsidy scheme under limited budget to maximize social welfare. Then, we consider the case when the government offers a combination of subsidy schemes. With all these analyses conducted as building blocks, we make comparisons and derive insights to address our detailed research objectives, which are highlighted below. Objective 1: The first objective is to understand the distinct impacts of each individual subsidy scheme on the firm’s green product innovation. We understand this issue from two distinct perspectives: the condition for green innovation and the optimal green quality level. For the former one, we compare the condition needed for spurring green innovation in each scheme from both the perspectives of the government incentive, i.e., subsidy budget, and the market incentive, i.e., the fraction of socially conscious consumers. Specifically, the budget threshold needed is the lowest when subsidizing consumers, followed by the one when subsidizing production, and the highest when subsidizing R&D. By contrast, subsidizing R&D (resp. consumer) requires the greatest (resp. lowest) support from the market to stimulate innovation among all subsidy policies, i.e., the largest (resp. smallest) size of socially conscious consumers. On the other hand, when green innovation is successfully spurred, for the same budget, subsidizing R&D leads to the highest green technology level while subsidizing consumers leads to the lowest one. Those results could provide useful understanding on the strengths and limitations of each subsidy scheme. (Please see paper 1 in Part C). Objective 2: The second objective is to understand the government’s preference over different subsidy schemes. For individual subsidy case, the government prioritizes subsidizing consumers when placing more emphasis on economic performance and, conversely, subsidizing R&D. For portfolio subsidy case, we find that the optimal portfolio leads to greater social welfare, since the government can make better use of its limited subsidy budget and enjoy flexibility by rationally allocating the subsidies to different recipients. Such allocation usually leads to opposite impacts on the firm's profit and the environmental benefits. For instance, when the government places more emphasis on environmental protection, the optimal portfolio will generate a greater environmental benefit and a smaller firm's profit, compared to the case under single subsidy scheme. By contrast, when the government focuses on economic performance, the firm benefits from the subsidy portfolio, but the environmental benefit is lower. That is, although the portfolio cannot simultaneously increase the firm's profit and environmental benefit, its flexibility and superiority will certainly result in a better social welfare from government's perspective. (Please see paper 1 in Part C). Objective 3: The third objective is to conduct comparative statics analysis to understand how the subsidy policy and the associate social welfare are affected by some key model parameters. We have conducted comprehensive sensitivity analysis to derive a set of results. Among others, we highlight a few: When offering a single subsidy scheme, the government’s preference switches from consumer subsidy to production subsidy, and eventually to R&D subsidy when it becomes more concerned on environmental benefits. By contrast, the opposite trend in government’s preference usually occurs when the subsidy budget becomes larger. When offering a subsidy portfolio, we depict the trend of how the optimal portfolio is constructed as focal parameters change and demonstrate that a higher budget or a larger fraction of socially conscious consumers could lead to a higher green quality and social welfare. (Please see paper 1 in Part C). In addition, we build another general model to further capture two-dimensional consumer heterogeneity, i.e., heterogenous product valuation and heterogenous preference for certain product attributes. We study the pricing issue in a general product line setting, which can capture the situation when a green product competes with another product. Our results shows that consumer heterogeneity may lead to some adverse impacts, such as enhancing green quality or enlarging the fraction of consumers who values green product may not necessarily benefit the seller. (Please see paper 2 in Part C). Objective 4: The last objective is to provide some general insights regarding the design and sale of green products in a competitive environment with added complexities. The scope for this objective is broad but relatively qualitative in nature. Yet, we challenge ourselves by studying two detailed complexities in such a competitive environment, namely, network effect and learning-by-doing effect. For the former one, consumption of green product may induce social interactions. We categorize social interactions into market expansion effect and value enhancement effect, and study how each effect would affect competing firm’s green product quality and pricing (Please see paper 3 in Part C). For the latter one, firms may enjoy learning-by-doing benefit when launching new green products, as more consumption may better help firms improve their products. We study how such effect would affect competing firms’ pricing decisions when product qualities can be improved (Please see paper 4 in Part C). Both papers could help us better understand some intriguing challenges involved in the design and sale of green products in a competitive market. We have fully investigated the four research objectives and delivered four research papers. Specifically, paper 1 addresses objectives 1-3 to understand how the endogenous choices of government subsidy schemes affect a firm’s green product design and pricing decisions in a segmented market with inherent consumer heterogeneity. Paper 2 addresses objective 3 to provide a deep understanding on how consumer heterogeneity affects the design and sales of green products. Finally, paper 3 and paper 4 jointly fulfill objective 4 to provide understanding on how social interactions and learning-by-doing effect would affect the design and sale of green product in a competitive market. All the four papers are closely linked under the general theme of green product innovation and pricing. They all adopt the same methodology of building game theoretical models to analyze the focal research questions and provide managerial insights.
