16100219.label: Major findings and research outcome
16100219.value: All the data mentioned above are now summarized in a manuscript that is currently under the peer review assessment in a reputable journal. We believe that understanding the pivotal role of sex in health and disease is a cornerstone of personalized medicine. Sex differences have been well-documented in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the intrinsic cellular changes induced by the menopausal transition that underlie disease vulnerability remain unclear. Driven by an integrated analysis of single-nucleus transcriptomics, bulk transcriptomics, and metabolomics data available from the ROSMAP study, we identified female-biased metabolic network changes occurred to neurons. We then elaborated on and validated the relationships between these changes and estradiol signaling using mouse and cell models as mentioned above in Section 5.3, which led to the following major findings: 1. Sustained loss of estradiol from the peripheral is correlated with accelerated cognitive and memory decline, and this effect is independent of chronological aging (Objective 2) 2. Brain transcriptomic and metabolomic changes induced by the peripheral loss of estradiol production lead to similar changes observed in female AD brains, namely the impairment of the ERRα-regulated bioenergetic network in neurons (Objective 2 and 3) 3. Estradiol unexpectedly involved in supporting neuronal cholesterol homeostasis, which is crucial to sustaining the ERRα nuclear activity required to uphold the integrity of the TCA cycle (Objective 2) 4. TCA cycle 'truncation' induced by the loss of estradiol or ERRα leads to a net catabolic shift of N-acetyl-aspartyl-glutamate (NAAG), which is elicited by an adaptive aspartate-dependent response that attempts to reconstruct a 'mini-TCA cycle (Objective 1) 5. The net catabolism of NAAG unleashes the neuroexcitatory metabolites aspartate and glutamate. While the aspartate is consumed in the “mini-TCA cycle”, glutamate is stochastically released presynaptically and increases spontaneous neural activity (Objective 2) 6. Such alteration in electrophysiological properties, when combined with the bioenergetic deficiencies caused by estradiol loss, slowly depletes cellular ATP reserves and increases susceptibility to energy crises triggered by additional excitatory insults, ultimately contributing to the female-biased vulnerability to AD (Objectives 1 and 3). The public datasets requested (e.g., ROSMAP dataset) and analytical platforms associated with this proposal, including bioinformatics, metabolic isotopologue tracing, metabolomics profiling mass-spectrometry were also utilized by other publications form the lab and this grant is acknowledged.

16100219.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16100219.value: Based on the key findings from this project, we planned to extend our study in APOE-ε3 versus APOE-ε4 mouse model. APOE-ε4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. The protein encoded by the APOE-ε4 variant is poorly lipidated compared with that by APOE-ε3, and prevents efficient transport of lipids between glia and neurons. We are interested in investigating if the menopausal effect on neuronal cholesterol homeostasis would worsen in APOE-ε4 carriers. Furthermore, based on our current findings and the settings laid out in the proposed future work, we are also interested in investigating the timing effect of the hormonal replacement treatment with the VCD mouse mode (i.e., in mice carrying APOE-ε3/ε3, ε3/ε4 and ε4/ε4 variants), and to test when and if the transcriptomic, metabolomic and bioenergetic properties of the neurons could be better preserved. These future plans shall be able to better inform for whom, when and how long the menopausal hormone therapy shall be applied to maximize the benefits.

16100219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16100219.value: Sex differences have been demonstrated in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the intrinsic cellular changes underlying the enhanced disease vulnerability observed in postmenopausal women remain elusive. We demonstrate that sustained loss of peripheral estradiol is correlated with accelerated cognitive and memory decline. The resulting brain transcriptomic and metabolomic changes suggest the impairment of a transcription network mediated by estrogen-related receptor alpha (ERRα). Estradiol supports ERRα activity via its actions on neuronal cholesterol homeostasis. Consequently, this prevents truncation of the TCA cycle at the reaction catalysed by succinate dehydrogenase, which would otherwise cause a net catabolic shift of N-acetyl-aspartyl-glutamate (NAAG), driven by an adaptive aspartate-dependent response that attempts to reconstruct a “mini-TCA cycle”. The free glutamate released alongside the net catabolism of NAAG is stochastically released presynaptically and thereby increasing the spontaneous neuronal activities. Coupled with the bioenergetic incompetency that occurs during estradiol-loss, this slowly depletes cellular ATP and increases susceptibility to energy crises triggered by additional excitatory insults, which ultimately contributing to the female-biased vulnerability to AD.

16100719.label: Project Objectives
16100719.value: Conditional KO of TPC2 in SMCs during SP1: via the use of homologous recombination of Cre-LoxP. Our goals here are to generate lines of transgenic fish where tpcn2 is knocked out in a time-dependent or in a tissue-specific manner. Thus, the effect of tpcn2 knockout on Ca2+ signaling and myofibrilogenesis specifically during SP1, or specifically in the SMCs, can be investigated to a far higher level of temporal and spatial accuracy than has been achieved previously. Identify downstream targets of TPC2-mediated Ca2+ release during SP1: via mRNA-seq and lncRNA-seq, followed by validation by qPCR and high-resolution imaging. The aim here is to identify genes that are likely downstream-targets of TPC2/Ca2+ signaling in the SMCs during SP1. Thus, RNA-seq (both mRNA and lncRNA) will be conducted on wild-type (control) and tpcn2 mutant fish, as well as on transgenic fish lines where tpcn2 has specifically been knocked out in the SMCs during SP1. Extend our understanding of the precise location of TPC2 in the nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments of SMCs, and to determine if the nuclear Ca2+ transients are generated via TPC2. This will involve the use of STED-based super-resolution nanoscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and electron tomography, as well as the application of complementary luminescence and fluorescence-based Ca2+ imaging techniques.

16100719.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16100719.value: There is a growing interest in the developmental and physiological roles of a new family of cation channels, the two-pore channels (TPCs), which are found in the membranes of acidic-endo-lysosomal organelles. As TPC type 2 (TPC2) has been shown to act as a Ca2+ release channel, these organelles represent an alternative intracellular Ca2+ store to the endo-/sarcoplasmic reticulum. However, TPC-mediated Ca2+ signaling is now understood to be far more complex than originally envisaged. As a result, it has been proposed that TPCs might represent a signaling hub within a complex intracellular signaling interactome. This view is supported by the diverse number of human diseases that have been reported to result from dysfunctional TPC activity. Gaining a better understanding of the function of TPC-mediated signaling is therefore of immense importance to human health, as it might provide opportunities for new drug development; the novel application of existing drugs; and/or the introduction of innovative therapeutic practices. This, however, cannot take place until basic research provides clear and accurate information regarding the function of TPCs in situ. This is the goal of our application and one of the reasons why we selected zebrafish as a tractable model system. To simplify matters, we propose to focus solely on the role of TPC2-mediated Ca2+ release within the differentiating slow muscle cells (SMCs) of the zebrafish trunk, and to do so during a restricted developmental time-window (~17.5-20.0 hours post-fertilization), when a highly reproducible series of distinct Ca2+ signals are generated within the cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments. Our goal is to identify the specific contribution made to these signals by TPC2-mediated Ca2+ release, and to identify the down-stream targets of the nuclear and cytoplasmic Ca2+ transients. To achieve this, we propose to apply innovative conditional knockout of the tpcn2 gene specifically in SMCs, and RNA-seq, respectively. We also plan to utilize super-resolution nanoscopy and a number of electron microscopy techniques, to explore whether TPC2 acts on its own in generating the nuclear/cytoplasmic Ca2+ transients or whether it does so in combination with Ca2+ release channels in other organelles. We suggest that meeting the goals of our proposal will add a significant body of knowledge regarding TPC2 function in differentiating skeletal muscle cells, which we anticipate will have a future impact with regards to understanding the pathomechanisms underlying a number of muscle diseases that result from the dysregulation of Ca2+ signaling and homeostasis. 雙孔通道 (TPCs) - 陽離子通道的新家族，人們對於這種存在於酸性內溶酶體細胞器膜中的通道的發育和生理作用越來越感興趣。由於已顯示TPC 二型 (TPC2) 充當釋放鈣離子的通道，意味著這些細胞器是內/肌漿網以外的細胞內鈣儲存。然而，現在發現由TPC介導的鈣離子信號傳導比最初設想的複雜得多。所以， TPC可能是複雜的細胞內信號傳導相互作用中信號傳導的中樞。 而TPC活動功能失調導致的各種人類疾病支持了這種觀點。因此，深入了解TPC介導的信號傳導功能對人類健康非常重要，它可能提供了研發新藥的機會; 發掘現有藥物新的應用方式; 和/或引入創新的治療方法。然而，在未有基礎研究提供有關TPCs清晰準確的功能之前，這種情況不可能發生。 這正是我們這計劃的目標，也是我們選擇斑馬魚作為易處理模型系統的原因之一。為了簡化問題，我們建議僅關注TPC2在斑馬魚軀幹的分化慢肌細胞 (SMC) 中介導鈣離子釋放的作用，並限制於特定發育時間窗 (約受精後17.5-20.0小時)，此時間內細胞質和細胞核區室內產生一系列獨特且高度重複的鈣離子信號。我們的目標是要鑑定TPC2介導的鈣離子釋放對這些信號的特定貢獻，並鑑定細胞核和細胞質鈣離子瞬變的下游靶標。為此，我們建議分別在SMC和RNA-seq中應用條件性的tpcn2基因敲除。我們還計劃利用超分辨率納米顯微鏡和其他電子顯微鏡技術來探索TPC2在產生細胞核/細胞質鈣離子瞬變中是否起獨立作用，或是它與其他細胞器中的鈣離子釋放通道結合而起作用。實現此提案的目標將增加我們對TPC2在區分骨骼肌細胞方面的功能的知識，預計這將對由鈣離子信號傳導和體內平衡失調導致的許多肌肉疾病的病理機制帶來新的理解。

16100719.label: Realisation of objectives
16100719.value: Objective-1: We completed the first step of this objective by confirming, via Sanger Sequencing the sequence of our muscle specific TPC2 rescue construct. Next, we injected our tpcn2 homozygous embryos with this muscle-specific rescue construct and showed that due to the mosaic nature of the DNA injection, we were able to compare neighbouring slow muscle cells (SMCs), one expressing EGFP and the other not. In the SMC expressing the rescue construct (and EGFP), there was partial recovery of the sarcomeric banding pattern, whereas in the cell with no EGFP expression, no sarcomeric banding was observed. These experiments indicated that in SMCs, the tpcn2 knockout phenotype could be partially rescued by targeted intervention (Kelu et al., 2017). As similar effect was demonstrated for zebrafish caudal primary motoneuron growth cones following tpcn2-mediated knockdown (Guo et al., 2020). Generating a conditional tpcn2 knockout line of fish was a significant challenge even during an uninterrupted 3-year grant cycle. A key component of achieving this objective lay in our collaboration with our Consultant, Prof Grunwald (University of Utah). Due to travel restrictions and lockdowns, the timeline for generating a conditional tpcn2 knockout line was seriously compromised, and so we were not able to complete this objective. However, we did meet our mRNA rescue experiment objectives (see Objective 2) and this along with the TPC1 and TPC2 mutant lines we generated with previous RGC GRF funding, has brought the development of TPC conditional knockout lines closer to completion. Objective-2: To explore the genetic landscape of tpcn2 mutants and identify candidate genes implicated in zebrafish trunk development, whole-transcriptome RNA-seq analysis was performed on samples collected from the trunk of tpcn2 homozygous embryos or wild-type (WT) embryos at ~17 hpf, approximately when SP1 commences (Cheung et al., 2011), shown to involve TPC2-mediated Ca2+ release (Kelu et al., 2015; 2017). We conducted a principal components analysis and showed that the tpcn2 homozygotes formed a distinct cluster that was separate from the WT controls, indicating that most of the variation in the transcriptomes was caused by the different genetic backgrounds of the samples. Differential expression gene analysis was performed to better compare the transcriptomic landscape of the tpcn2 mutants with the WT controls. The efficacy of tpcn2 knockout in the tpcn2 mutant line was previously demonstrated by RT-PCR (Kelu et al., 2017) and RT-qPCR (Guo et al., 2020). These previous results were mirrored by our new RNA-seq data, where the tpcn2 transcripts were shown to be significantly downregulated in the tpcn2 homozygous embryos compared to the WT controls. Among the 14,005 genes identified by RNA-seq, 858 genes were shown to be down-regulated, whereas 785 genes were upregulated (with a cut-off of p < 0.05 and |fold-change|>1.5). The top 5 genes with the most significantly altered expression include: actin-depolymerizing factor/gelsolin, a key regulator of actin filament assembly/disassembly; annexin 1b, a Ca2+-dependent phospholipid binding protein; phosphatidylinositol glycan anchor biosynthesis class B, involved in glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchor biosynthesis; thymocyte nuclear protein, a poorly characterized nuclear protein believed to be involved in apoptosis, and methylthioribulous-1-phosphate dehydratase, an enzyme involved in the methionine salvage pathway. The full list of differentially expressed genes are in NCBI’s Gene Expression Omnibus, accessible through GEO Series accession number GSE229162. The top 50 differentially expressed genes that passed the statistical cut-off in the tpcn2-/- mutants compared to WT embryos were visualized in a heatmap. Notably, two members of the solute carrier protein encoding genes, slc7a2 and slc16a8, were among the top 50 most significantly downregulated genes. Other genes of interest include the β-tubulin gene, tubb5; a member of the biogenesis of lysosomal organelles complex 1 subunit 3, bloc1s3; and a member of the mitochondrial anion carrier protein, ucp2. The significant differentially expressed genes were matched to the D. rerio genome in the Gene Ontology (GO) Consortium database to identify biological processes that were affected in the tpcn2-/- mutants compared to WT. Upregulated processes in the tpcn2-/- mutants were mainly related to the response to extracellular signals and biochemical processes involved in metabolism. However, interestingly, the ‘negative regulation of secretion by cell’ was also upregulated, examples of which include anxa1a and asip2b. On the other hand, downregulated processes in the tpcn2-/- mutants included extracellular matrix binding, actin filament severing, cellular component morphogenesis, organelle assembly, Ca2+ binding, and structural constituent of cytoskeleton. Thus, our transcriptomic profiling data indicate that the tpcn2-/- mutants have significantly attenuated gene expression patterns and disparate biological processes compared to the WT controls. These data have recently been accepted for publication as follows: Rice, K.L., Chan, C.M., Miller, A.L., Webb, S.E. (2023). A role for two-pore channel type 2 (TPC2)-mediated regulation of membrane contact sites during zebrafish notochord biogenesis?” Contact (In Press). Objective-3: Location of TPCs in the nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments of SMCs: We confirmed the localization of TPC-EGFP labelled vesicles associated with the contiguous nuclear membrane, and the SR membrane, and at the myoseptal junction in the cytoplasmic domain (Figs 4, 5; Rice et al., 2022). TPC labelling was also visualized within the nucleus and in perinuclear domains associated with the nuclear membrane (Fig. 4Ba,4Cc; Rice et al., 2022). We also confirmed the presence of TPCs within the nuclear compartment of trunk notochord cells (Fig. 4; Rice et al., 2023). Identification of the endolysosomal vesicles expressing TPCs and their location within SMCs: Here, we injected embryos with TPC-EGFP and plasmids encoding mKate2-tagged Rab5c (early endosomes); Rab11ba (recycling endosomes); Rab32 (late endosomes and Golgi); or Lamp1 (late endosomes and lysosomes). See Fig. 4A, Rice et al., 2022 for the data. Investigating the possible role of microtubules in TPC-decorated endolysosomal dynamics: Here, we visualized TPC-decorated vesicles in cultured SMCs (Fig. 4B-D; Rice et al., 2022). The key involvement of microtubules was demonstrated via treatment with the microtubules inhibitor nocodazole, which resulted in a cessation of endolysosomal movement. Investigating the Ca2+ signaling events associated with TPC function in slow muscle cells. We tagged TPC1 with G-GECO and demonstrated that highly localized Ca2+ transients associated with Lamp1-labeled vesicles in cultured SMCs (Fig. 8; Rice et al., 2022). Our goals here are to generate lines of transgenic fish where tpcn2 is knocked out in a time-dependent or in a tissue-specific manner. Thus, the effect of tpcn2 knockout on Ca2+ signaling and myofibrilogenesis specifically during SP1, or specifically in the SMCs, can be investigated to a far higher level of temporal and spatial accuracy than has been achieved previously.

Identify downstream targets of TPC2-mediated Ca2+ release during SP1: via mRNA-seq and lncRNA-seq, followed by validation by qPCR and high-resolution imaging. The aim here is to identify genes that are likely downstream-targets of TPC2/Ca2+ signaling in the SMCs during SP1. Thus, RNA-seq (both mRNA and lncRNA) will be conducted on wild-type (control) and tpcn2 mutant fish, as well as on transgenic fish lines where tpcn2 has specifically been knocked out in the SMCs during SP1.

Extend our understanding of the precise location of TPC2 in the nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments of SMCs, and to determine if the nuclear Ca2+ transients are generated via TPC2. This will involve the use of STED-based super-resolution nanoscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and electron tomography, as well as the application of complementary luminescence and fluorescence-based Ca2+ imaging techniques.

16100719.label: Major findings and research outcome
16100719.value: Using zebrafish as the animal model, we demonstrated that TPC1 (encoded by tpcn1), generates highly localized non-propagating Ca2+ transients that play a distinct and required role in the capture and attachment of slow skeletal muscle cells (SMCs) at myoseptal junctions (MJs). Use of antisense morpholinos or CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to disrupt the expression of the tpcn1 gene in abnormal MJ phenotypes, including SMCs detaching from or crossing the myosepta. We also showed that TPC1-decorated endolysosomes are dynamically associated with MJs in a microtubule-dependent manner, and that attenuating tpcn1 expression or TPC1 function disrupts endolysosomal trafficking and results in an abnormal distribution of β-dystroglycan, which is a key component of the dystrophin-associated protein complex. This work is published in: Rice et al. (2022). Journal of Cell Science 135(9), jcs259564. We previously characterised the role of two-pore channel type 2 (TPC2, encoded by tcpn2)-mediated Ca2+ release in the establishment of the early spinal circuitry, a key event in the coordination of neuromuscular activity (Kelu et al., 2018; funded by GRF#16101714). Funding via GRF#16100719 allowed us to further investigate the in vivo role of TPC2 in the regulation of caudal primary motor neuron axon extension and subsequent innervation of developing SMCs. We used a combination of TPC2 knockdown (via a translation-blocking morpholino antisense oligonucleotide), TPC2 knockout (via the generation of a tpcn2dhkz1a mutant line of zebrafish using CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing), and pharmacological inhibition of TPC2 (via incubation with bafilomycin A1; an H+-ATPase inhibitor or trans-ned-19; an NAADP receptor antagonist) and showed that these treatments attenuate CaP Ca2+ signaling and inhibit axon extension. These findings are published in: Guo et al. (2020). Journal of Cell Science 133, jcs244780. Most recently, we showed that TPC2 plays a role in the development of the notochord of zebrafish embryos. For example, when tpcn2 was knocked down/out, increased numbers of small vacuoles were formed in the inner notochord cells, compared with that in control embryos. This abnormal vacuolation was associated with embryos displaying attenuated body axis straightening. RNAseq was used to identify differentially expressed genes in tpcn2 mutants compared to wild-type controls, and we found that those involved in actin filament severing, cellular component morphogenesis, Ca2+ binding, and structural constituent of cytoskeleton were downregulated in the mutants. Together, these data suggest that TPC2 activity plays a key role in notochord biogenesis in zebrafish embryos. This work is accepted for publication: Rice et al. (2023). Contact (accepted 16/10/23).

16100719.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16100719.value: As the PI retired at the end of June 2023, we will not be able to follow up with our research on two pore channels (TPCs) at the HKUST. However, our line of tpcn2 mutant fish was sent to the laboratory of Prof Jonathan S. Marchant (Department of Cell Biology, Neurobiology and Anatomy, Medical College of Wisconsin, USA) whose main research focus is on the role of Ca2+ channels and Ca2+ signaling in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Thus, following on from the basic research questions we were exploring regarding the role of TPC channels (especially TPC2), in developmental events, it is likely that the tpcn2 mutant line we generated via RGC GRF funding, will be used in the future for more applied research that will focus more on specific human diseases.

16100719.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16100719.value: Two pore channels (TPCs) are a novel class of non-selective Na+/Ca2+ channels located in cellular organelles called endolysosomes. Of the three types that have been described (TPC1-3), humans only have the first two. Using zebrafish as an animal model, we showed that when TPC1 or TPC2 is knocked-out, knocked-down or inhibited via drugs, then various distinct key developmental events are disrupted. For example, TPC1-mediated Ca2+ signaling plays an important role in the development of slow skeletal muscle cells as it is required for the capture and attachment of these cells at myoseptal junctions. Attenuating the expression of tpcn1 or disrupting normal TPC1 function results in an abnormal distribution of β-dystroglycan, a key component of the dystrophin-associated protein complex, which can result in muscular dystrophies when mutated. Moreover, TPC2-mediated Ca2+ signalling plays a distinct role in axonal extension in caudal primary motor neurons and thus is likely involved in neuromuscular junction formation. TPC2 also plays a role in the development of the notochord in zebrafish; this is a transient rod-like structure found in chordate embryos, replaced by the vertebral column in adults. Thus, the knowledge gained about TPCs in zebrafish has potential for furthering our understanding of human diseases.

16100819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16100819.value: 我們和其他科學家最近確定了AAA+ ATPase TRIP13透過重構MAD2於調節有絲分裂檢查點上有著關鍵作用。TRIP13的失調會導致染色體不穩定和增加癌症風險。TRIP13對其他細胞過程的調節會否也有助於腫瘤發生仍有待解讀。通過驗證文獻上蛋白質組學數據，我們發現TRIP13能夠與MDM4（也稱為MDMX）有交互作用，而MDM4是腫瘤抑制因子p53的調節因子。通過截短突變，我們觀察到MDM4的最後五個氨基酸的缺失能夠消除跟TRIP13交互作用，亦進一步證明MDM4和其結構同源蛋白MDM2的RING結構能夠與TRIP13結合。重要的是，MDM2和MDM4的C末端在MDM2和MDM4的寡聚化和p53泛素化中是必要的。基於這些初步發現，我們的目標是以降解决定子以條件滅活的方法去了解TRIP13在調節MDM2/MDM4-p53網絡中的潛在作用。我們計劃探討MDM2/MDM4的蛋白質表達是否受TRIP13影響，以及MDM2/MDM4的寡聚化是否跟TRIP13交互作用有關。此外，我們將研究TRIP13會否影響MDM2/MDM4的寡聚化、p53的交互作用以及其功能性失活。使用轉錄組分析和其他方法，我們亦會查考TRIP13對p53轉錄網絡的影響。鑑於TRIP13，MDM2和MDM4經常在腫瘤中過度表達，MDM2/MDM4在TRIP13的致癌功能中的作用會加以闡明。解決這些重要問題可以進一步擴展對癌症生物學的認知。從長遠來看，更好地理解TRIP13在MDM2/MDM4-p53的調節的關係可能有助於設計新的抗癌策略。

16100819.label: Realisation of objectives
16100819.value: To study the effects of TRIP13 on the protein expression of MDM2/MDM4 This aim has been achieved, while the TP53/AKT-dependent and independent mechanisms in MDM2/MDM4 stability are still in progress. Characterizing the functions of essential cell cycle control genes requires tight and rapid inducible gene inactivation. A conditional gene inactivation system avoiding the drawbacks of current conditional depletion approaches, which include slow responses and incomplete depletion, has been developed. A transposon-based method to implement the same conditional gene inactivation system can now be completed in a single step. A set of Sleeping Beauty transposon-based vectors for expressing auxin-inducible degron (AID)-tagged genes under the regulation of a tetracycline were generated. Moreover, multiple genes could be simultaneously or sequentially targeted, allowing inducible inactivation of multiple genes. The materials and methods in this part have been published in Molecular Biology of the Cell and the Journal of Cell Science. With these newly developed methods, we have generated the AIDTRIP13KO in multiple cell lines for later part of studies requiring rapid and tight suppression of gene expression. In HeLa and HCT116 cells with AIDTRIP13KO genetic background, we found that MDM4 was not stabilized upon AIDTRIP13 was targeted to degradation up to 72 h, but the stabilization of MDM4 can only be observed in HCT116, which highlighted the stabilization of MDM4 may have a p53-dependent and independent mechanism. This is consistent with the increase of MDM4/MDM2 mRNA expression in the HCT116 but not HeLa cells in RT-PCR and RNAseq experiments. Therefore, we separately investigated the transcriptional and post-translational control of MDM2 and MDM4 by using the HeLa and HCT116 cell line models. Interestingly, we observed the AKT activation (increased serine 473 phosphorylation) after AID-TRIP13 was targeted to degradation in HCT116 but not HeLa cell model, thus suggesting the TP53-dependent activation of AKT upon TRIP13 depletion. The treatment of the AKT inhibitor blocked the accumulation of MDM2 and MDM4 in HCT116, thus suggesting the involvement of the phosphorylation of MDM2 and its stability. Unfortunately, we have tested multiple commercially available phospho-specific antibodies for MDM2, but none of them provide satisfactory results in confirming the increase of phosphorylation when TRIP13 is depleted. They confirmed the induction of MDM2 phosphorylation upon depletion of TRIP13 in an AKT-dependent manner. On the other hand, we observed the change in the protein expression of multiple Ubiquitin-Specific Proteases (USPs) in HeLa cells upon depletion of TRIP13 using label-free quantitative proteomics, as the stability of MDM2 and MDM4 are tightly regulated by USP7; therefore, USP7 is up-regulated by TRIP13 and subsequently regulating the expression of MDM2 and MDM4 in the TP53-independent manner. We are now confirming the MDM2 and/or MDM4 phosphorylation using the mass spectrometry approach and will finalize the model on how TRIP13 regulates the MDM2 and MDM4 in a p53-dependent and independent manner. To investigate the binding mechanism between TRIP13 and MDM2/MDM4 These objectives have been completed. With the binding assays between TRIP13 and different MDM2/MDM4 mutants, we confirmed the RING domain is necessary for the binding. The point mutation C463A abolishes the dimerization of MDM2/MDM4, further stabilizing the interaction of MDM4/MDM2-TRIP13 binding. Using bacteria-purified proteins, we find that both the MDM4 and MDM2 RING domains can bind to TRIP13; the binding affinity of TRIP13 to MDM4 is significantly higher than MDM2. On the other hand, the binding of TRIP13 to MDM2/MDM4 is dependent on the ATP binding or hexamer formation (with Walker A mutant data) but not on the hydrolysis of ATP, as Walker B mutants don’t affect the binding of TRIP13 to MDM2/MDM4. Furthermore, the p31comet KO or additional of purified p31comet do not change the TRIP13-MDM2/MDM4 interaction, thus suggesting the dispensable role of p31comet between the interactions. To evaluate the effects of TRIP13 on MDM2/MDM4’s oligomerization, p53 binding and p53 ubiquitination activity This objective was completed. Since both the WT and WB mutants of TRIP13 bind to MDM2/MDM4, we directly compared the MDM2/MDM4’s oligomerization and p53 binding in the TRIP13 KO cells and the WT and WB mutant TRIP13 re-expressing cells. Notably, no change of p53 binding to MDM2/MDM4 was observed, while both homodimerization and heterodimerization of MDM2/MDM4 were reduced in the immunoprecipitation assay in WT and WB TRIP13-expressing cells than the TRIP13-KO-expressing cells. The WB mutant does not change the MDM2/MDM4’s oligomerization, which is contrary to the remodelling function to MAD2 and HOP1. The ATPase or protein remodelling activity is indispensable to its role in the MDM2/MDM4-TP53 axis. Together with our observation of MDM2/MDM4 RING-TRIP13 interaction data, we proposed the function of TRIP13 as a molecular chaperone that binds to MDM2/MDM4 via the stabilization of the RING domain and formation of functional E3 ligase, thus preventing/promoting its auto-ubiquitination. To assay the p53 ubiquitination, TRIP13 KO, WT, and WB-expressing cells co-expressing FLAG-p53 and HA-ubiquitin, followed by FLAG-immunoprecipitation, were analyzed; no significant changes of TP53 ubiquitin were observed. This is consistent with our initial observations of no changes of the TP53 level in KO or WT TRIP13-expressing cells. Taken together, the binding of TRIP13 to the RING domain of MDM2/MDM4 affects MDM2/MDM4 stability but not the binding to TP53 and the ubiquitination activity towards TP53. To characterize the effects of TRIP13 on the MDM2/MDM4-p53 transcriptional network These objectives have been completed. We have characterized the role of TRIP13 in transcriptional regulation by RNAseq. We have performed the RNAseq in both HeLa and HCT116 AID-TRIP13 cell lines in multiple timepoints. It’s important to note that little change in the transcriptome was observed up to 48 h depletion of TRIP13, but significant induction of typical p53 targets, including MDM2 and p21, was observed up to 1 week of depletion. Notable, HeLa cells, which do not have functional p53, did not show any change of p53 target in short or long depletion of TRIP13, thus highlighting the role of TRIP13 in the MDM2/MDM4-p53 transcriptional network. Notably, since we observed the p53 induction is accompanied with AKT phosphorylation and inhibition of AKT reduced the increase expression of MDM2/MDM4, and hence suggesting that the AKT-p53-MDM2/MDM4 transcriptional control, however, the mechanism of how depletion of TRIP13 in AKT activation is yet to be understood. Oncogenic TRIP13 function in MDM2/MDM4-p53 regulation This part of the objective is only partially completed. We have tested the overexpressing TRIP13 in the normal immortalized RPE-1 cells in WT and KO p53 genetic backgrounds. However, even with co-expression of the oncogenic RAS, we did not observe significant anchorage-independent growth in the soft-agar assay. Due to the change in the hosting dependent of the PI to the state-key lab of liver research, the PI has the new access to the hydrodynamic tail injection tumorigenesis model. Therefore, oncogenic TRIP13 function is then tested in the mouse via the HDTI model. The mouse liver cancer can be readily induced by the c-Myc/p53 KO; however, although overexpression of TRIP13 increases the tumor progression, including the onset time and size of the tumor, overexpression TRIP13 cannot replace the c-Myc or p53KO in mouse liver induction. Since the TRIP13 KO induction of MDM2/MDM4 cannot suppress the protein expression of TP53 and its transcriptional target, we did not test the effect of MDM2/MDM4 depletion in TRIP13 KO.

16100819.label: Major findings and research outcome
16100819.value: Tight and rapid inducible gene inactivation is necessary for the characterization of the functions of cell cycle control genes. We have created a system that addresses the limitations of existing conditional depletion methods, which encompass slow responses and insufficient depletion. We demonstrated that the combination of the tetracycline-controlled promoter system and the auxin-inducible degron (AID) system allows for more efficient reduction of AID-tagged proteins compared to the individual technology used separately. The technique enables the investigation of gene function through quick and precise conditional depletion when applied with CRISPR Cas9-mediated disruption of the endogenous locus. The materials and methods were initially published in Molecular Biology of the Cell, and the enhanced system facilitating dual protein degradation control was published in Journal of Cell Science. Utilizing these newly developed approaches, we have produced the AIDTRIP13KO in various cell lines for subsequent experiments necessitating quick and stringent suppression of gene expression. Importantly, the conditional TRIP13 inactivation cell lines generated were the useful reagents for later parts of studies requiring rapid and tight suppression of gene expression in mammalian cells. With the proposed conditional gene inactivation system, the role of TRIP13 in MDM2/MDM4 protein expression was characterised. With the binding assay, we found that TRIP13 did not change the activity of MDM2/MDM4 to the p53 but affecting the dimerization of MDM2/MDM4 via the RING domain. Unlike other functions of TRIP13, the ATPase activity is not required for the stabilization of MDM2/MDM4, which highlighted the potential of TRIP13 as the molecular chaperone of the MDM2/MDM4 RING domain. Strikingly, we found that loss of TRIP13 stabilizes MDM2/MDM4 in a transcription-independent manner in a p53-inactive cell line, but the AKT-mediated MDM2/MDM4 mRNA expression is in a p53-dependent manner. Notably, we do not observe the immediate effect on p53 downstream target expression even though MDM2/MDM4 has already stabilized; the effect on p53 upon prolonged loss of TRIP13 is likely due to the activation of AKT. Lastly, we did not find evidence for TRIP13 in tumor initiation, such as anchorage-independent growth or tumour initiation, but overexpression of TRIP13 resulted in faster cellular proliferation, resulting in a larger tumour. We are now collecting the important evidence of MDM2/MDM4 phosphorylation upon the loss of TRIP13 using the mass spectrometry approach, and the manuscript for this part of the work is being prepared.

16100819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16100819.value: The knowledge generated from this project extended our understanding of TRIP13 in controlling MDM2/MDM4 in a p53-dependent and in-dependent manner. Unlike the ATPase-dependent protein structure remodelling function of TRIP13, the molecular chaperone function in stabilization of the MDM2/MDM4 RING domain is novel. Interestingly, the molecular chaperone function of TRIP13 to RING domains is yet to be known. Therefore, we plan to further characterize the effect of TRIP13 on protein stability, especially the RING domain-containing proteins. To this end, with the reagents and the molecular chaperone hypothesis developed in this project, we will utilize the robust AID-TRIP13/KO system to set up the label-free proteomic study to generate further evidence on the non-ATPase function of TRIP13 in maintaining protein stability. Apart from the TRIP13-MDM2/MDM4-p53 axis, the project has also found the activation of AKT upon prolong loss of TRIP13 in the p53-dependent manner. We will further characterize this observation and plan to check factors such as SAC/DNA damage function result to the AKT activation.

16100819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16100819.value: We and others have recently established that the AAA+ ATPase TRIP13 plays a critical role in regulating the spindle-assembly checkpoint through remodelling of MAD2. Unlike the structural remodelling function of TRIP13 in MAD2, we found that TRIP13 can stabilize MDM4 and MDM2 via the RING domain in an ATPase-independent manner. The binding of TRIP13-MDM4/MDM2 does not change the ubiquitination activity towards p53 but negatively regulates the homo/hetero-dimerization of MDM2 and MDM4. With the degron-mediated TRIP13 conditional inactivation cell lines, we found that loss of TRIP13 can result in the increase of MDM2/MDM4 in protein and mRNA expression. Strikingly, change of MDM2/MDM4 mRNA expression is accompanied with AKT activation only in the p53 positive cell line, hence suggesting the two independent mechanisms in controlling MDM2/MDM4 by TRIP13. Using transcriptome analysis, the effects of TRIP13 on the p53 transcription network are only found upon prolonged loss of TRIP13. Furthermore, TRIP13 overexpression speeds up cancer cell proliferation but other transformation properties such as anchorage-independent growth and tumour initiation are not affected. Taken together, our work provides a comprehensive picture of how TRIP13 affects the MDM2/MDM4-p53 axis and opens up the ATPase-independent function of TRIP13 as molecular chaperone.

16101219.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16101219.value: Understanding how molecular mechanisms shape evolutionary novelties and new adaptations is one of the central goals in modern evolutionary biology. Mollusca has been identified as a phylum with substantial abilities in generating numerous evolutionary novelties to conquer a wide range of habitats and niches. For instance, the dermal scale-like structures can be found in both early Cambrian molluscs and the present-day aculiferans, even though they are structurally distinct. The discovery of scaly-foot gastropods from the hydrothermal vents in the Central Indian Ridge with numerous dermal scales has given us another opportunity to study the scale formation process in detail. In order to uncover the meticulous mechanism regulating scale formation and its evolutionary history, high-quality genome sequencing and tissue-specific gene expression is essential. Considering the genome is rather heterozygous, we propose to perform a complete genome sequencing with the newly available Oxford Nanopore Technology. Meanwhile, tissue-specific gene expression analysis in addition to evolutionary analysis will be implemented to shed light on the scale formation process. Furthermore, scaly-foot gastropod that resides in Kairei vent site has been uncovered to acquire mineralized scales and shells with iron sulphide, making it the only metazoan that adopts iron to build a part of its skeleton, where other individuals from Solitaire vent site have not been found to develop iron sulphide at all. Thus, comparisons between the morphotype with and without iron sulphide would help distinguish genes that are involved in iron sulphide mineralisation. Our study can not only unveil new evolutionary insights on how Mollusca develop diverse evolutionary novelties, but also elucidate the unique biomineralization process in this peculiar species. 在進化生物學中，一個比較核心的研究目標是揭示生物如何進化出形態或生理等方面的新特徵來適應周圍的環境。在眾多的物種中，軟體動物被公認為可以不斷的進化出新的特徵來“征服”各種各樣的棲息地。例如，在史前寒武紀軟體動物祖先的化石中發現了一種特殊的被覆鱗片的結構只能在當代的Aculiferans (例如石鱉等物種)中找到----雖然兩者的解構學結構不完全一致；而在另外的軟體動物類群，即Conchifera,卻鮮有發現。然而，2000年在中印度洋深海熱液區發現的一種屬於Conchifera的鱗足螺卻顛覆了這個認知：它們也被覆數以百計的鱗片。這個發現為我們重新審視鱗片的形成過程提供了新的機遇。為了闡釋相對應的分子生物學機理，我們計畫對該物種進行全基因組的測序，並結合器官特異性的基因表達結果和後續進化生物學分析的手段來解讀鱗足螺鱗片的形成過程。考慮到該基因組雜合度較高，基因組的組裝或許困難重重。為此，我們計畫採用最新的Oxford Nanopore Technology來克服這個困難。 此外，這個螺還有一個有趣的特徵：即在印度洋Kairei熱液區發現的鱗足螺的鱗片表面擁有硫化鐵的覆蓋，而在距離700公里以北的Solitaire熱液區發現的鱗足螺鱗片卻完全沒有這個特徵。為了解釋相應的硫化鐵生物成礦的機理，我們還會對採集自這兩個站位的多個鱗足螺進行鱗片組織的基因表達分析。我們認為該研究會對軟體動物如何進化出新的特徵這一科學問題提供嶄新的見解，同時也可以闡明一系列新的生物礦化的機理。

16101219.label: Realisation of objectives
16101219.value: 1. To assemble and annotate the scaly-foot snail genome The Scaly-foot Snail genome was assembled with a combination of Illumina and Oxford Nanopore Technology (ONT). The genome of the Scaly-foot Snail is relatively compact for Mollusca (444.4 Mb) and is highly heterozygous (1.38%), but with relatively low repeat content (25.2%). Genome was assembled by smartdenovo on the canu corrected ONT reads, which is a common strategy that has been successfully applied in many marine invertebrate genomes. Heterozygous contigs were removed by purge_dup pipeline from the assembled genome and further polished by the Illumina clean reads. A total of 1032 contigs were assembled with a N50 value of 1.88Mb, suggesting one of the most continuous genomes in Mollusca. With additional Hi-C data, 1032 contigs were anchored to 15 pseudo-chromosomal linkage groups. Genome were annotated with three different strategies (i.e. transcript evidence, homolog proteins, and ab initio evidence). RNA was extracted from different tissues of Scaly-foot Snail which was in situ fixed near the local colony to avoid the impact of hydrostatic pressure on the gene expression. The cDNA was Illumina sequenced, cleaned, de novo and genome-guided assembled into transcripts. Only the high quality transcripts were used to train Augustus, an ab initio gene predictor. Maker was used to collect all the three evidences to build 16,917 gene models. These gene models were functionally annotated by searching against various databases, including NCBI nr, SWISSprot, GO, and KEGG. The Scaly-foot Snail genome represents the most complete and continuous genome among the assembled mollusc an or lophotrochozoan genomes to date, with a metazoan BUSCO (Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs) score of 96.6% for the genome assembly and 87.5% for the predicted transcripts. Therefore, in this project, we have assembled and annotated a high-quality Scaly-foot Snail genome. 2. To identify genes that are highly expressed in the scale-secreting epidermis and compare with the mantle that secretes the shell Gene expression levels in five different tissue types (including the shell-secreting mantle, scale-secreting epithelium, oesophageal gland, the gill, and the foot musculature) of the Scaly-foot Snail were assessed by transcriptome sequencing. To assess tissue-specific functions, particularly in relation to biomineralisation, a paired test in DESeq2 was applied to distinguish tissue highly expressed genes (n = 5), further confirmed with real-time PCR (two replicates, five tissue types) and in situ hybridisation (ISH; for mantle and scale-secreting epithelium). Genes known to produce proteins involved in molluscan shell formation, such as pif, chitin-binding peritrophin-A domain gene, and chitin synthase, were also conserved and highly expressed in the shell-secreting mantle and scale-secreting epithelium of the Scaly-foot Snail. A GO enrichment analysis on highly expressed genes in the mantle and scale-secreting epithelium revealed that the categories integral component of membrane, scavenger receptor activity, and cell-matrix adhesion were enriched in both of these biomineralisation tissues, further indicating that they elements of a shared biomineralization toolkit. The gene exhibiting the highest expression level among the scale secreting epithelium highly expressed genes was chitin-binding peritrophin-A. This gene (CsqKR_Scaf21_18.25), together with its recent duplicated paralogue (CsqKR_Scaf21_18.24), were also highly expressed in the shell-secreting mantle but at lower levels than in the scale-secreting epithelium. They also show sequence similarity with the well-known shell matrix protein Pif, which by contrast was highly expressed in the mantle in the Scaly-foot Snail, similar to other Mollusca, but not in the scale-secreting epithelium. A similar pattern is seen in the chitin synthase gene family, as the Scaly-foot Snail genome possesses diverse subgroups of this family, and different paralogues were found to be highly expressed in the mantle or scale-secreting epithelium. We also identified 25 highly expressed transcription factors in the scale-secreting epithelium (12) and mantle (13), often confirmed by ISH; the two biomineralisation tissues did not share any highly expressed transcription factors. We propose that they control downstream novel and existing biomineralization genes in different ways to fabricate different kinds of armour or skeletal elements by upstream activation. 3. To determine the evolutionary process of the scale formation genes We discovered that the scale and shell formation in the Scaly-foot Snail employ independent subsets of 25 highly-expressed transcription factors. Several of these were only detected as highly expressed in the Scaly-foot Snail hard parts among the available lophotrochozoan tissue-specific data. However, all transcription factors reported to date from other lophotrochozoan skeletal elements (brachiopod mantle and chaetae, and annelid chaetae, n = 10 genes) were found to be also highly expressed in the Scaly-foot Snail, in either the mantle (n = 6 genes) or scale-secreting epithelium (n = 4). Some of these co-opted transcription factors, and others, have also been reported from other molluscs including aculiferan mantle and sclerite-secreting tissue, gastropod or bivalve mantle tissue, or tissues secreting the radula, beak, or operculum. The involvement of these transcription factors in the formation of various hard parts across different lophotrochozoan groups ranging widely from plesiomorphic (e.g. brachiopod shell) to more recently evolved armature (e.g. Scaly-foot Snail scales) signify that they together comprise the biomineralisation toolkit preserved from the ancestral lophotrochozoan genome. Collectively, comparisons with other lophotrochozoan genomes imply that this biomineralization toolkit is ancient, though expression patterns differ across major lineages. 4. To compare gene expression levels between scaly-foot snails with and without iron biomineralisation We compared gene expression levels in the scale-secreting epithelium and shell-secreting mantle of the Scaly-foot Snail from the iron-rich Kairei vent field with a second population from the iron-poor Solitaire vent field that naturally lack any iron sulfide mineral coating. In the Kairei population, with iron sulfide mineralisation, transmembrane transporter activity was comparatively enriched in highly expressed genes, supporting the hypothesis the iron sulfide precipitation is indeed mediated by the gastropod through transportation and precipitation of sulfur species. Another gene, metal tolerance protein (MTP) 9, exhibited over 27-fold increased expression level in the population with iron sulfide mineralisation compared with the one without. This gene is widely found in invertebrates, protists, and even plants34. Although poorly studied in invertebrates, functional assays of MTP in plants revealed potential pathways for enhanced tolerance of metal ions and maintaining intracellular homoeostasis. The Scaly-foot Snail biomineralises iron sulfide nanoparticles by allowing sulfur that it actively recruits or deposits in the scales to react with iron ions diffusing in from its highly iron-enriched environment, and the MTP9 gene likely helps the snail tolerate such high levels of iron in its surrounding environment. This would allow the Scaly-foot Snail to gain finer-scale control of nanomaterial-scale production, which is completed at much lower temperatures than can be currently controlled in laboratory settings. Many other species of molluscs incorporate iron into hard parts, particularly the radula. Molluscs have been highlighted as a model for generating biogenic nanomaterials at low temperatures, but the genomic tools to open this part of the biomineralisation toolkit for other applications were previously unavailable. In addition, we also discovered a new morphotype of scaly-foot snail from Tiancheng vent field on Southwest Indian Ocean Ridge. Unlike the previously examined populations, scales of the Tiancheng scaly-foot snails were coated in zinc sulfide, although this results only from precipitation. Population genetic analysis with partial COI sequence have revealed that the Tiancheng population was clustered with populations from the CIR, showing low connectivity with the Longqi field.

16101219.label: Major findings and research outcome
16101219.value: By comparing genomic elements and tissue-specific gene expression patterns in the scaly-foot snail scale- and shell secreting tissues, as well as other biomineralising tissues in lophotrochozoans, we revealed an ancient biomineralization toolkit comprising at least 25 transcription factors that contribute to biomineralisation across all lophotrochozoan hard parts investigated to date. Gene families in the Scaly-foot Snail genome have predominantly ancient origins, as seen in other lophotrochozoans, but their distribution and duplications across various lineages are nonsynchronous with phylogenetic positions, underlining rapid modifications. Although novel genes do appear to play important roles in downstream production of the hard parts, the hard parts themselves arise by deploying elements from the conserved biomineralisation toolkit. Comparison between sclerites from unrelated groups of molluscs —the Scaly-foot Snail, and aculiferan molluscs, or Cambrian fossils—may underline the longevity of these gene families. The true power of the biomineralisation toolkit lies in the capacity for dynamic combination of the components being switched on or off, expanded or reduced, and relocated within the genome, which creates compounding changes in phenome. The extreme morphological disparity of mollusc biomineralization underpins their successful diversification. Similarly, the re-use, rearrangement and re-deployment of conserved genomic elements over more than 540 million years explains both our challenges in obtaining genomic and phylogenetic resolution, and their evolutionary success.

16101219.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16101219.value: The discovery that the diversity of phenome is likely to be controlled by an ancient origin biomineralization toolkit is exciting. We suggest that the ability of lophotrochozoan lineages to generate a wide range of hard parts, exemplified by the remarkable morphological disparity in Mollusca, draws on a capacity for dynamic modification of the expression and positioning of toolkit elements across the genome. Further study shall investigate the potential role of gene regulatory net-work in shaping the diversity and speciation in major Lophotrochozoan lineages. Reverse genetic technique on several easy-to-be-cultured species on particular hard-part involving transcription factors would possibly reveal the gene regulatory network underlying the phenotypes.

16101219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16101219.value: Scaly-foot Ssnail, also known as “Sea Pangolin”, is a deep-sea hydrothermal vent endemic species. This species was listed as one of the “top-ten astonishing species” discovered in last century because it is not only the only extant gastropod alive that possesses armor-like scales but also the only organism in the world known to incorporate iron into its exoskeleton. Little is known, however, about its molecular mechanism and unusual morphology. By combining with genome sequencing and gene expression analysis, we discovered that most of the scaly-foot snail’s genes already existed in other mollusks. Particularly, the 25 transcription factors (a key protein that regulates many downstream gene expression levels) which contribute to the snail’s scale and shell formation, have also contributed to the formation of many other unique hard-parts in Mollusca and even Lophotrochozoa - such as operculum in gastropods, beak in squid, spicule in chiton, or chaetae in polychaetes. Uncovering scaly-foot snail’s genome advances our knowledge in the genetic mechanism of biomineralizations, laying the genetic groundwork which paves the way for application. Population genetics analysis of different populations indicated that gene flows between southwest and Mid Indian Ocean ridges were limited but were high between mid and northwest Indian Ocean Ridge populations.

16101419.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16101419.value: Both timing and kinetics of neurotransmitter release depend on positioning of clustered Ca2+ channels by a structure known as active zone, an electron-rich structure visible under electron microscopy, that is located right next to docked synaptic vesicles on presynaptic plasma membranes. However, how active zone protein complex assemblies might form is not known. Our preliminary data showed that two multi-domain scaffold proteins RIM and RIM-BP, via specific multivalent bindings, form dynamic and condensed assemblies through liquid-liquid phase separation. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCCs), via C-terminal tail-mediated direct bindings to both RIM and RIM-BP, can be enriched to the RIM/RIM-BP condensates. We further show that RIM and RIM-BP together with voltage-gated Ca2+ channels form dense clusters on the supported lipid membrane bilayers via phase separation, an observation suggesting that the condensed RIM and RIM-BP can cluster Ca2+ channels and thus regulate neurotransmitter release. In this proposal, we plan to test the hypothesis that RIMs and RIM-BPs, together with other active zone proteins such as Liprins, ELKS, and LAR may function as key organizers of active zone protein assemblies capable of clustering VGCCs into nano- or micro-domains and positioning the clustered Ca2+ channels with Ca2+ sensors on docked vesicles for efficient and precise synaptic transmissions. We will also investigate how the memberaneless active zone protein condensates may communicate with membrane-based SNARE vesicles to coordinate neurotransmitter releases in the nervous systems. 神經遞質釋放的時間特性以及動力學特徵都依賴於突觸前膜活性區對電壓門控型鈣離子通道的定位與聚集。突觸前膜活性區正好位於突觸小泡對接的突觸前膜，在電鏡下呈現出高電子密度特徵。然而，活性區的蛋白分子複合物是如何組裝的還不清楚。我們的初步結果顯示，兩種多結構域的支架蛋白，RIM和RIM-BP，通過特異性的多價相互作用發生液-液相分離，從而形成高度濃縮且動態的組裝體。同時，電壓門控型鈣離子通道（VGCC）也可以通過其與RIM和RIM-BP的直接相互作用而被富集進它們形成的濃縮相。進一步硏究表明，RIM，RIM-BP和VGCC可以通過液-液相分離在支撐性脂雙層膜上濃縮與組裝，提示RIM和RIM-BP形成的濃縮相可以富集VGCC並調節神經遞質的釋放。因此，我們計劃測試如下猜想：RIM和RIM-BP，與其他活性區的蛋白，比如Liprins，ELKS和LAR，也許會作為關鍵組織者去組裝活性區，並把VGCC富集為納米/微米級的結構域，且將其定位到突觸小泡上的鈣離子感應器附近，從而實現突觸小泡的高效和精準釋放。此外，我們還會探究這種無膜包被的活性區蛋白濃縮相與膜包被的突觸小泡可能的相互作用方式，以及它們如何協調神經遞質的釋放。

16101419.label: Realisation of objectives
16101419.value: Active zones are critical for docking readily releasable synaptic vesicles and coupling of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCCs) with membrane fusion machinery for precise control of neurotransmitter release. Active zones are believed to be formed by a family of proteins via extensively connected networks resulting in a highly dense “protein web”. Dense projections in active zones, electron-dense molecular assemblies viewable by electron microscopy on fixed synapses, are attached to the presynaptic plasma membrane on one side and open to axonal cytoplasm on the other side, form a grid-like structure to segregate docked vesicles and to position clustered VGCCs in close vicinity to Ca2+ sensors on the docked vesicles. However, it is not known how dense projection-like structures or the densely packed active zone “protein webs” might form, although RIMs and RIM-BPs are essential for the formation of dense projections as well as for essentially all known functions of active zones. We proposed that RIM and RIM-BP, via specific multivalent bindings, may form self-organized, dynamic and condensed assemblies through liquid-liquid phase separation. VGCCs, via C-terminal tail-mediated direct bindings to both RIM and RIM-BP, may be enriched to the RIM/RIM-BP condensates, thus mimicking VGCC clustering by RIM and RIM-BP in presynaptic active zones. Additionally, we proposed that VGCCs together with RIM and RIM-BP may form dense clusters on the supported lipid membrane bilayers via phase separation. Our key hypothesis was that RIMs and RIM-BPs are likely the key organizers of dense projections/active zone “protein webs” capable of clustering VGCCs into nano- or microdomains and coupling the clustered Ca2+ channels with Ca2+ sensors on docked vesicles for efficient and precise synaptic transmissions. In this project, we proposed to characterize the mechanisms of RIM and RIM-BP-mediated biological condensate formation via liquid-liquid phase separation. We aimed to investigate how other presynaptic active zone proteins such as Liprins and ELKS can modulate RIM and RIM-BP-mediated condensate formation and VGCC clustering. We also plan to investigate how the RIM and RIM-BP condensates may communicate with membrane-delimited SNARE vesicles. We had hope that successful execution of the current research proposal would make major conceptual advancement on how presynaptic neurotransmitter release machinery are formed and regulated. We are very pleased to report that we have made excellent progresses during the project period. We have fully achieved all of the objectives that we set out in the proposal. The following is a summary of the achievements made during the project. To investigate how active zones might form, we took an in vitro reconstitution approach using purified recombinant proteins. We showed that RIM and RIM-BP, via specific multivalent bindings, form dynamic and condensed assemblies through liquid-liquid phase separation. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCCs), via C-terminal tail-mediated direct bindings to both RIM and RIM-BP, can be enriched to the RIM/RIM-BP condensates. We further show that RIM and RIM-BP together with VGCCs form dense clusters on the supported lipid membrane bilayers via phase separation. Therefore, RIMs and RIM-BPs are plausible organizers of active zones, and formation of RIM/RIM-BP condensates may cluster VGCCs into nano- or micro-domains and position the clustered Ca2+ channels with Ca2+ sensors on docked vesicles for efficient and precise synaptic transmissions. This study was published as a research article entitled “RIM and RIM-BP form presynaptic active zone-like condensates via phase separation” in Mol Cell in 2019. Having established that active zones are formed by major scaffold proteins via phase separation, we next asked how synaptic vesicles (SVs) are tethered to the active zones. We made an exciting discovery that small unilamellar vesicles (SUVs) and SVs from rat brains coat on the surface of the condensed liquid droplets formed by active zone proteins RIM, RIM-BP and ELKS via phase separation. Remarkably, the SUV-coated RIM/RIM-BP condensates are encapsulated by the synapsin/SUV condensates, forming two distinct SUVs pools reminiscent of the reserve and tethered SV pools existing in presynaptic boutons. The SUV-coated RIM/RIM-BP condensates can further cluster Ca2+ channels anchored on membranes. Thus, we have reconstituted a presynaptic bouton-like structure mimicking SV-tethered active zone with its one side attached to the presynaptic membrane and the other side connected to the synapsin-clustered SV condensates. The distinct interaction modes between membraneless protein condensates and membrane-based organelles revealed in this study indicate that membraneless organelles formed via phase separation can interact with membrane-based organelles via distinct modes. Our study has general implications in cellular processes including vesicular trafficking, organelle biogenesis, and autophagy, as these cellular processes involve different kinds of interactions between membraneless organellesand membrane-based organelles. This study was published as a research article entitled “Vesicle Tethering on the Surface of Phase-Separated Active Zone Condensates” in Mol Cell in 2021. The finding described above, together with our studies funded by other UGC-funded research in my lab, has provided a convincing body of evidence showing that the highly dense signaling complexes on both the pre- and post-synaptic sides of neuronal synapses are likely formed via liquid-liquid phase separation. These findings establish a new conceptual framework for understanding synapse formation and function, as well as brain disorders caused by synaptic signaling complex malfunction. We are pleased to report that our research findings are appreciated by colleagues in the field. We have been invited to write reviews on synapse formation via liquid-liquid phase separation by various journals including Nat Neurosci, Dev Cell, Mol Cell, J Neurosci, J Biol Chem, J. Mol. Biol. and Biochemistry. The PI of this project has been invited to present our findings at numerous conferences and institutes/universities. Our systematic studies on phase separation have also sparked collaborations with many colleagues from different parts of the world.

16101419.label: Major findings and research outcome
16101419.value: We demonstrated that multivalent interactions between RIM and RIM-BP and their intrinsically disordered properties lead to formation of self-organized, highly condensed and dynamic assemblies through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro. VGCCs, via direct bindings of their cytoplasmic tails to RIM and RIM-BP, can not only be enriched to the condensed liquid phase, but also significantly promote LLPS of RIM and RIM-BP. Our biochemical reconstitution experiments indicate that RIMs and RIM-BPs are sufficient for forming the dense projection-like structure in presynaptic active zones. Our study also suggests that the RIM/RIM-BP condensates can effectively cluster VGCCs and position clustered VGCCs in close proximity with SNARE fusion machinery for fast and precise synaptic transmission. This work was published in Mol Cell in 2019. We then discovered that negatively charged liposomes as well as SVs purified from rat brains coat on the surface of the phase separated RIM/RIM-BP condensates. By tethering VGCC-CT to the giant unilamellar vesicle (GUV) membranes, we show that the RIM/RIM-BP condensates can bind to and cluster VGCC-CT on GUV membranes on one hand and link SUVs on the other hand, resembling active zone-mediated tethering of SVs to presynaptic membrane release sites. Remarkably, the synapsin-clustered SUV condensates and the SUV-coated RIM/RIM-BP condensates form phase-in-phase assemblies, which recapitulate coexistence of reserved and tethered pools of SVs in presynaptic boutons. The finding that the RIM/RIM-BP condensates can simultaneously link two totally different types of membrane-based cellular organelles suggests a wide range of unanticipated cellular roles of membraneless biological condensates formed by phase separation. This work was published in Mol Cell in 2021. We have made another major progress in the second half of the project period. In addition to long-distance molecular motor-mediated transport, cellular vesicles also need to be moved at short distances with defined directions to meet functional needs in subcellular compartments but with unknown mechanisms. Such short-distance vesicle transport does not involve molecular motors. We demonstrate, using synaptic vesicle (SV) transport as a paradigm, that phase separation of synaptic proteins with vesicles can facilitate regulated, directional vesicle transport between different presynaptic bouton sub-compartments. Specifically, a large coiled-coil scaffold protein Piccolo, in response to Ca2+ and via its C2A domain-mediated Ca2+ sensing, can extract SVs from the synapsin clustered reserve pool condensate and deposit the extracted SVs onto the surface of the active zone protein condensate. We further show that Trk-fused gene, TFG, also participates in COPII vesicle trafficking from ER to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment via phase separation. Thus, phase separation may play a general role in short-distance, directional vesicle transport in cells. This work has just been published in Cell (Qiu et al, (2024).

16101419.value: The original PI has left Hong Kong and thus does not plan to continue this line of work in Hong Kong any further. Nonetheless, the research completed in this GRF project has opened a new direction for understanding presynaptic vesicle organization and release. It is expected that many labs in the field will follow this line of research in the future. Indeed, there are several papers published describing involvement of phase separation of presynaptic vesicle release in the recent few years.

16101419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16101419.value: Rapid and precise controlled neurotransmitter releases from presynaptic termini is the foundation for animal brains including human’s to effortlessly perform complex tasks. This event is controlled by positioning right numbers of Ca2+ channels in a very small and defined area (known as Ca2+ channel nano-/micro-domains) and at precise distance to Ca2+ sensors on the SNARE fusion vesicles docked at active zones. A major challenge in synaptic transmission research in the past decades is what Ca2+ channel nano-/micro-domains are made of and how they are formed? In this project, we demonstrate that RIM and RIM-BP, two scaffold proteins essential for the active zone structures of presynaptic termini, can form self-assembled membraneless compartments via liquid-liquid phase separations. We further show that the RIM/RIM-BP condensates can cluster right numbers of Ca2+ channels on lipid membrane bilayers. Our study provides potential answers to several major questions in the field of neuroscience. Another general question in cellular organelle biogenesis, biomolecular trafficking and function is how membrane demarcated organelles interact and communicate with membraneless protein machineries, which are often formed via liquid-liquid phase separation. We demonstrated in the second half of the project that synaptic vesicles (SVs), which are densely protein decorated membrane-enclosed organelles, interact with different protein condensates formed via phase separation with totally different modes. SVs coat the surface of active zone condensates but coacervate with the synapsin condensates. This finding uncovers distinct and versatile modes of interactions between membrane organelles and membraneless condensates. Our results will likely prompt colleagues in the field of neuroscience and cell biology in general to re-evaluate numerous basic cellular processes by integrating membrane biology and membraneless organelles.

16101819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16101819.value: Ethylene regulates multiple aspects of growth and development in plants. However, the molecular mechanism underlying many later steps of ethylene signaling is largely unknown. Current data indicate that ethylene’s effect on root growth may be mediated via multiple signal transduction pathways, including novel post-translational modifications (PTM) and phosphor-relay cascades, ranging from ethylene receptor subfamily-1 and -2 to CTR1, to PDK1, and PIP2A water channels-mediated cell water transport and finally to the inhibition of root growth. The protein phosphorylation biomarker for such an EIN2-independent ethylene-induced phosphor-relay is the C-terminal S280/S283 phosphorylation of aquaporin. Given that a mathematical model has been formulated for the relationship between S280/S283 phosphorylation of PIP2A and water flux rate and that the PIP2 aquaporin family is an abundantly expressed water channel in root tissue, ethylene-regulated root growth will serve as a good biological model for Omics-based molecular systems biology research. To elucidate the molecular mechanism and novel signalling components underlying root ethylene response, we plan to first perform differential and quantitative phosphoproteomics on root tissues of two pairs of the loss-of-function ethylene receptor family mutants. Comparative analysis of these phosphoproteomes will allow us to identify receptor kinase subfamily-specific phosphoproteins regulating root growth. Secondly, we plan to perform in planta quantitative interactomics to identify the putative substrates or interacting proteins of either ethylene receptor subfamily proteins, CTR1 kinase and/or PDK1 kinase. Finally, we plan to perform molecular and cellular biology, reverse genetic analysis, and plant physiology experiments to analyze the molecular and cellular functions of these interactors as well as PDK1, and possibly other new putative ethylene signaling components in mediating root ethylene response. These studies might construct an previously undefined PTM network composed of an ethylene receptor family protein complexes, signaling components and ethylene-regulated PIP2A phosphorylation during water transport, delineating the molecular mechanism underlying the root cell proliferation, elongation, root growth and lateral root formation. The outcomes of the research project are expected to provide valuable information on the fundamentals and molecular mechanisms underlying multiple pathways of ethylene signaling in regulation of plant growth. This project will also allow us to disseminate the cutting-edge plant quantitative phosphoproteomics and interactomics technology into our bioscience community through collaboration. 16101819.value: 1. To perform isotopic labeling-based quantitative phosphoproteomics on ethylene response mutants 1.1 Stable isotope labelling of ethylene signalling mutant The seeds of the constitutive ethylene response mutant, etr1–6, were sown on both light nitrogen 14N- and heavy nitrogen 15N-coded agar media in glass jars. A total of four biological replicates were performed, each of which has 30, 36, 32 and 34 g of the mixed tissues mixed from both control and stimulated plants at a 1:1 ratio. 1.2 Quantitative PTM proteomic data The digested total cellular peptides from proteins went through a tandem affinity-based multi-step protocol for the phosphopeptide enrichment. A total of 51 phosphopeptide samples were finally produced from all four biological replicates and were analysed on a MS. All four biological replicates together generated a total of 67,822 PSMs. Consequently, we identified 5556 repeatable phosphopeptides (PSMs ≥2), which were derived from 2374 Arabidopsis protein groups. Our dataset contained 465 novel phosphopeptides and phosphosites. Since this PTM proteomic work is overlapping with the proposal writing, and the date of publication of the results is after the funding starting day, the work results have been included in this report. The pandemics affects the work process and interfered the plans on the initially intended spending. 2. To perform 4C quantitative interactomics to identify the putative interacting proteins of ethylene receptors and/or signaling component 2.1 Ethylene-treatment of plant tissues One batch of seeds geminated in containers filled with air as control tissues while the other were fumigated with 5 ppm ethylene. In total, 6 pairs of air-grown and hormone-treated etiolated seedlings were harvested. Control and Hormone seedlings were subjected to the nuclei isolation. The nuclei pellets were subsequently rinsed with 3 volumes (v/w) of Crosslinking Buffer containing an amine-reactive crosslinker cyanur biotin dipropionyl succinimide (CBDPS, in organello 2nd crosslinking). The nuclear protein pellet was subsequently extracted, air-dried and resuspended in Protein Resuspension Buffer. 2.2 Preparation of the stable isotope-labelled XL-peptides The crosslinked peptides (XL-peptides) were desalted using C18 Sep-Pak cartridges and concentrated. In the end, a total of 6 biological replicates were performed, consequently generating 12 experimental replicates of nuclear peptide mixtures. The 499 XL-peptide samples were finally desalted using the Ziptip. 2.3 Acquisition and confirmation of XL-peptide data These XL-peptides spectral data were acquired in a mass spectrometer. The XL-peptides searching from the spectrum data was performed by the mXlinkX. The formaldehyde and CBDPS crosslinkers coupled qXL-MS discovered 5,340 crosslinked peptides. 2.4 Conversion of XL-peptides into PPI The nuclear XL-peptides or crosslinks were converted into nuclear Protein-Protein Interactions (PPIs). The abundance of crosslinked nuclear proteins was measured using the nuclear proteome data by the Proteomic Ruler. These crosslinks were construed into 1,297 nuclear protein-protein interactions (PPIs), protein components of which contained 250 and 26 novel interactors of histone octamer and nucleolar box C/D snoRNP complex, respectively, in the intricately organized nucleome. Numerous interactors of both ERS1 ethylene receptor and AP2 transcription factor were found using the XL-interactomics. 2.5 Quantitation and bioinformatic analysis of PPI and MMI The NCBI blastp was firstly used to convert the soybean plant nuclear PPIs into Arabidopsis ortholog PPIs. The abundance of PPI was calculated using the following equation, which is the PSM count(s) of XL-peptide(s) (or called crosslink) that corresponded to a PPI as a single PPI could be described by multiple species of XL-peptides. Both the PPI and the abundance of PPI were incorporated by the M1 algorithm of the MONET toolbox to construct the Nuclear Protein-Protein Interaction Modules (NPIMs). Moreover, the entire constituent components of an NPIM can be converted to a single converging node, and the PPI and the abundance of PPI between the two interacting NPIMs can be converted to hybrid edge, respectively. Consequently, Module-Module Interaction (MMI, or called hybrid edge, defines a higher level of edge existing in between two interacting converging nodes (or two interacting modules). The abundance of MMI is the sum of the abundance of PPIs derived from all interacting components between these two modules. The module of modules (or NPIMs) was consequently defined as a Community. A higher level of organization of a Community is defined as a System. The bioinformatic workflow finally generated a nuclear protein System 1 of 4 communities including Genome and Nucleolus Community. The modulomic analysis of Control and Hormone datasets using the MONET toolbox constructed Control module variants (CV) and Hormone module variants (TV), respectively. The MONET-based modulomic analysis of these crosslinks captured 95 nuclear protein interaction modules (NPIMs), Some NPIMs captured 6 previously reported nuclear protein complexes . The comparison between module variant CV and TV was accessed by the Jaccard Coefficient (JC) calculated based on the modular components’ identification. A similar comparison method was performed at the Community level to determine the Control- or ethylene Hormone-specific Communities. CHAMPION (Capturing the Hierarchically Assorted Modules of Protein Interaction in the Organized Nucleome) approach has partitioned these NPIMs into ethylene-modified four hierarchically and topologically organized communities in nucleome ( or called 4-dimentional modulomes). 2.6 Confirmation of modules using known nuclear bodies in repository The third class of confirmation for the inter-crosslinks came from the comparison between the CBDPS-crosslinked proteins and the subunits of the gel filtration-determined protein complexes, such as RNA Polymerase II, 40S Ribosome, MOS4-associated, Proteosome, small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particle (SNRP) and 20S Proteosome . 3. To perform molecular and cellular biological, reverse genetic, and/or plant physiological studies on the cellular functions of the newly identified novel phosphoprotein in mediating root growth, root cell proliferation and/or root cell elongation. 3.1 Validation of PPI with imaging Rabbit polyclonal antibodies were raised against the synthetic peptide. Super-resolution imaging was performed using the Single Molecular Localization Microscopy mode of ZEISS Elyra 7 with Lattice SIM for each pair of proteins. Consequently, we generated four antibodies. The dSTROM microscope was used to validate the PPIs of these four interactors. 3.2 Validation of PPI and NPIM using molecular biology and immunoblot The plant proteins were extracted. The immunoblot assays were employed to validate the ethylene hormone up-regulation of the inter-crosslinks occurred in between hnRNPQ and histone H4 as well as in between RAE1 and NUP98. The protein amount changes of hnRNPQ, RAE1 and NUP98A were quantitated accordingly. As a result, the protein levels of hnRNPQ, RAE1 and NUP98A were increased under ethylene Hormone treatment, which was consistent with the qXL-MS results. 3.3 Physiological and biological studies of Arabidopsis genetic mutants, nup98a and rae1 Surface-sterilized etiolated Col-0, rae1 and nup98a seeds of Arabidopsis were geminated on half-strength MS-agar plates under the dark condition for 1 day, followed by 5 ppm hormone treatment for 4 days at room temperature under darkness condition. The comparison of the hypocotyl length between Col-0, and mutants (rae1or nup98a) was assessed using the two-tailed student’s t-test. Finally, the biological role of a Hormone-specific module variant, TV-1-77, containing RAE1 and NUP98A, was investigated by a seedling hormone triple response assay on the wild type Col-0 as well as rae1 and nup98a mutants of Arabidopsis. The results showed that there was no difference between these three lines of seedlings under untreated control condition. In contrast, there was a significant difference existing in between Col-0 and rae1 as well as in between Col-0 and nup98a under the hormone-treated conditions.
