16101819.label: Major findings and research outcome
16101819.value: All four biological replicates of phosphoproteomics performed on ethylene receptor mutant etr1-1 generated a total of 67,822 PSMs (FDR ≤ 0.01, Table 1). Consequently, we identified 5556 repeatable phosphopeptides (PSMs ≥2), which were derived from 2374 Arabidopsis protein groups. As compared to the phosphopeptides in the PhosPhAT 4.0 database, our dataset contained 465 novel phosphopeptides and phosphosites that have not been reported by PhosPhAT 4.0 . Our experiments detected much more acidophilic (41%) but less basophilic (14%) and proline-directed (28%) phosphor-S/T than those of known Arabidopsis phosphoproteome (23% acidophilic, 22% basophilic and 38% proline-directed phosphosites). To decipher the ethylene-regulated global connectivity of signaling nuclear proteins and the hierarchically organized modules of their interactions, we conducted two rounds of cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL- MS) analysis, one of which followed a quantitative double chemical cross-linking mass spectrometry (in vivo qXL-MS) workflow, and identified 24,140 unique crosslinks in total from the nuclei of plant seedlings. This in vivo quantitative interactomics enabled the identification of 5340 crosslinks that can be converted into 1297 nuclear protein–protein interactions (PPIs), 1220 (94%) of which were non-confirmative (or novel) nuclear PPIs compared with those in repositories. There were 250 and 26 novel interactors of his- tones and the nucleolar box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein complex, respectively. Modulomic analysis of orthologous Arabidopsis PPIs produced 27 and 24 master nuclear PPI modules (NPIMs) that contain the condensate-forming protein(s) and the intrinsically disordered region–containing proteins, respectively. These NPIMs successfully captured previously reported nuclear protein complexes and nuclear bodies in the nucleus. Surprisingly, these NPIMs were hierarchically assorted into four higher-order communities in a nucleomic graph, including genome and nucleolus communities. This combinatorial pipeline of 4C quantitative interactomics and PPI network modularization revealed 17 ethylene-specific module variants that participate in a broad range of nuclear events. The pipeline was able to capture both nuclear protein complexes and nuclear bodies, construct the topological architectures of PPI modules and module variants in the nucleome, and probably map the protein compositions of biomolecular condensates. 16101819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16101819.value: A modular cell biology theory predicts that the cellular proteins may interact with each other in a modular fashion to perform specific activities, several related questions are raised: (1) how can the physical organization and distribution of signaling proteins be systematically mapped? and (2) how can modules of protein interaction be associated with various signaling and nuclear events? Addressing these questions is certainly challenging. Application of hormone treatment to plant cells further complicated biomolecular modulome construction from a 3D issue to a 4D issue. To address these questions, the significantly regulated crosslinks (SRCs)and crosslinks (XL-peptides) identified by performing the qXL-MS pipeline on hormone-treated cells provided key information about the degree of signaling and nuclear protein components, the abundance of PPIs, and the ethylene hormone-specific PPIs necessary for building dynamic 4D biomolecular modulomes. Construing the SRCs into hormone-specific PPIs enabled MONET-based modulomics to capture novel module and community variants specific to the ethylene hormone treatment and was able to monitor the dynamically changing behaviors of modules and communities of signaling proteins. CHAMPION, a novel protein modulomics pipeline consisting of in vivo quantitative interactomics and protein interaction network modularization, might generate a much higher-resolution landscape of the hierarchically and spatiotemporally organized 4D biomolecular modulomes of kinase and protein substrate molecules in cells upon induction by various signals like ethylene and at different developmental stages.

16101819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16101819.value: Ethylene is an important plant hormone that controls the fruit ripening and leaf senescence as well as plant growth and development. Integration of multi-level Omics, quantitative PTM proteomics, quantitative interactomics and quantitative modulomics together (which is called CHAMPION) is able to construct ethylene-induced 4-dimensional biomolecular modulomics, revealing the organization and interaction of ethylene-regulated enzymes with their protein substrates, such as histone protein and transcription factors, in cell, and especially in nucleus. Application of bioinformatics, microscopic studies and molecular genetic analysis has provided both sound dry and wet laboratory evidences to the PTM proteomics and functional modulomics approach.

16102019.label: Realisation of objectives
16102019.value: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by memory loss. There is currently no effective cure for AD. Synapse loss and the weakening of synaptic connectivity in hippocampus, mediated by beta-amyloid (Aβ)-mediated neuronal degeneration, contribute to the cognitive decline in AD. Physiologically, astrocytes participate in the regulation of synapse formation, maturation, and elimination. In AD, the loss of synapses is primarily mediated by the engulfment of glial cells. However, our understanding of the molecular mechanisms that contribute to their malfunctioning in AD is limited. EphA4, a member of the Eph receptor family, is mainly expressed in the hippocampus and is involved in modulating synaptic plasticity (Fu et al., 2007, 2011). Our previous studies indicate that EphA4 is hyperactivated in response to Aβ (Fu et al., 2014). We previously showed that in the APP/PS1 transgenic mouse model of AD, blockade of EphA4 signaling using an inhibitor of EphA4, KYL peptide, restores impaired synaptic plasticity in the hippocampal CA1 region. Thus, the current research proposal aimed to investigate the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which EphA4 signaling mediates the hippocampal synaptic deficits in AD. We first conducted in situ hybridization to characterize the differential cellular expression of EphA4 in the hippocampus in APP/PS1 mice. Wild-type (WT) mice exhibited prominent expression of EphA4 in pyramidal neurons but minimal expression in astrocytes. At 12 months of age, the expression of EphA4 transcript was significantly higher in CA1 pyramidal neurons from APP/PS1 mice than those from WT mice. In addition, the proportion of EphA4+ astrocytes was significantly larger in the stratum radiatum and stratum lacunosum-moleculare layers of the CA1 region. We made similar observations in another AD transgenic mouse model: 5xFAD mice. These results suggest that dysregulated EphA4 expression is specific to the hippocampal CA1 region and EphA4 may play a role in both neurons and astrocytes in the synaptic dysfunction in AD. To investigate the roles of EphA4 in distinct cell types in synaptic deficits in AD, we selectively depleted neuronal and astrocytic EphA4 in the hippocampal CA1 region of APP/PS1 × EphA4lx/lx mice using a cell-type-specific, promoter-driven, Cre viral approach. Immunostaining analysis revealed that knockout of either neuronal or astrocytic EphA4 rescued the decrease of excitatory synapses, indicated by an increase of postsynaptic PSD-95 protein clusters in the stratum radiatum layer of the CA1 region in APP/PS1 mice. This indicates that both neuronal and astrocytic EphA4 signaling regulate excitatory synapses. Noteworthy, knockout of neuronal or astrocytic EphA4 produced different effects on the morphology of dendritic spines in CA1 neurons in APP/PS1 mice. While both conditions rescued the total number of dendritic spines, knockout of neuronal EphA4 increased mature spines (mushroom- and stubby-shaped spines) but decreased immature filopodia-shaped spines. Conversely, knockout of astrocytic EphA4 increased the number of mature spines but did not affect the number of immature spines. To examine the mechanisms by which dysregulated EphA4 expression in neurons and astrocytes impacts synaptic connectivity in AD pathogenesis, we administered an EphA4 inhibitor, KYL peptide, to APP/PS1 mice for 3–4 weeks. Blockade of EphA4 signaling resulted in increases in excitatory synapses and dendritic spine density in the CA1 region. Functionally, we showed that blockade of EphA4 signaling increased synaptic transmission in the hippocampal CA1 region in APP/PS1 mice. Moreover, in APP/PS1 mice, blockade of EphA4 signaling increased both presynaptic fiber valley amplitude and field excitatory postsynaptic potential slope, suggesting that blockade of EphA4 signaling improves synaptic strength in AD conditions. Together, our results suggest that suppression of dysregulated EphA4 activity strengthens synaptic connections between CA3 and CA1 neurons in AD transgenic mice. To examine the molecular and cellular effects of aberrant EphA4 signaling in the hippocampus in AD, we conducted single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) analysis of hippocampal samples in APP/PS1 mice with or without EphA4 blockade by KYL administration. Unbiased clustering of the nuclei categorized them into different brain cell types according to their top expressed genes and cell markers. Compared to WT mice, several differentially expressed genes were upregulated in CA3 and CA1 neurons in APP/PS1 mice. However, the upregulation of these genes was ameliorated in APP/PS1 mice upon EphA4 blockade. Pathway analysis of these genes showed that they shared biofunctions, including “response to oxidative stress” and “regulation of apoptosis process,” indicating that KYL exerts a neuroprotective effect on neurons in AD. Thus, these results provide insights into how the blockade of EphA4 signaling rescues synaptic transmission efficacy in AD. In CA1 neurons, KYL administration effectively restored the expression level of a cluster of genes associated with crucial functions, including “synapse organization,” “trans-synaptic signaling,” “synaptic membrane adhesion,” and “neurogenesis.” Although these genes were downregulated in APP/PS1 mice, after KYL treatment, their expression levels were comparable to those in WT mice. Protein–protein interaction analysis using synaptic genes from this module revealed that “synaptic cell adhesion molecules” (e.g., Ncam2, Cntnap2, Ntng1, and Pcdh9) centrally coordinate the processes of “synaptogenesis,” “synaptic transmission,” and “neurite outgrowth.” These results suggest that the synaptic functions in CA1 neurons were restored in KYL-treated neurons. These findings further support the involvement of neuronal EphA4 signaling in synaptic dysfunction in AD. In AD, besides neuronal-mediated synapse weakening, weakened synapses can be eliminated by glial cell engulfment. snRNA-seq analysis showed that compared to the controls, C4b gene expression increased significantly in the hippocampus in APP/PS1 mice upon KYL treatment. The C4b gene encodes complement C4b, a subunit of C3 convertase (i.e., C4b–C2a heterodimer), which is involved in the cleavage and activation of complement C3 in the complement pathway. The release of complement C3 from astrocytes is neurotoxic, inducing astrocytes to engulf synapses, which leads to synapse loss. This suggests that modulation of EphA4 signaling regulates the complement pathway in the hippocampus in APP/PS1 mice. Immunostaining analysis revealed that while there were more C3-expressing astrocytes in APP/PS1 mice than in WT mice, this was reduced upon blockade of EphA4 signaling. In particular, specific deletion of EphA4 in astrocytes but not in neurons abolished the increase of C3-expressing astrocytes in APP/PS1 mice, suggesting that EphA4 protein is critical for the activation of complement signaling in astrocytes. C3 in astrocytes is associated with the presence of complement C1q protein, which tags the weakened synapses for glial cell engulfment. We observed increased C1q staining at excitatory synapses (stained with PSD-95) in the hippocampus in APP/PS1 mice, which decreased upon KYL treatment. Notably, compared to APP/PS1 mice, APP/PS1 mice crossed with astrocytic EphA4-knockout mice exhibited significantly less C1q-tagged PSD-95 staining. These results support that astrocytic EphA4 activates the glial–synapse complement pathway. Given that astrocyte-mediated synapse elimination may be dependent on the interaction between C3 and C1q-tagged synapses, we examined the astrocytic engulfment of synapses by co-staining astrocytes and synapses with S100 and PSD-95, respectively. Astrocytic EphA4 knockout significantly decreased the number of PSD-95 clusters within astrocytes. Together, these results indicate that astrocytic EphA4 stimulates the engulfment of synapses through the activation of complement signaling at astrocytes in AD conditions.

16102019.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102019.value: Our study aimed to investigate the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying the increased EphA4 signaling in synaptic dysfunction in AD. The major research outcomes as are follows: EphA4 expression is increased in CA1 pyramidal neurons and astrocytes in the hippocampus in AD conditions. EphA4 is expressed in various brain cell types in AD transgenic mouse models (i.e., APP/PS1 and 5xFAD mice). In particular, we found that EphA4 expression is increased in neurons and astrocytes in the postsynaptic CA1 region but not the CA3 region in the hippocampus in the AD transgenic mouse models. These findings suggest that EphA4 signaling contributes to synaptic dysfunction within the CA3–CA1 circuit pathway in AD. Suppression of EphA4 activity by administration of KYL peptide (a specific EphA4 inhibitor) or conditional knockout of EphA4 rescues the loss of excitatory synapses in the hippocampal CA1 region in APP/PS1 mice. Similar to the effects of KYL administration, either neuronal or astrocytic EphA4 knockout is sufficient to rescue the loss of dendritic spines and excitatory synapses in APP/PS1 mice. This indicates that EphA4 is important for the loss of excitatory synapses in AD. Blockade of EphA4 signaling modulates synaptic connections within the hippocampal CA3–CA1 circuit. snRNA-seq analysis revealed that KYL administration increases the expression of genes that encode synaptic complex and synaptic adhesion molecules in in CA1 excitatory neurons in the hippocampus in APP/PS1 mice. These results suggest that in AD conditions, the activation of EphA4 signaling decreases synaptic connectivity within the hippocampal CA3–CA1 circuit, contributing to synapse loss and synaptic dysfunction in AD, whereas blockade of EphA4 signaling promotes excitatory synapse formation in CA3–CA1 neurons. EphA4 signaling modulates complement pathways in astrocytes. Complement C3 released from astrocytes mediates the loss of C1q-tagged excitatory synapses in AD conditions. Immunostaining revealed that knockout of astrocytic EphA4 but not neuronal EphA4 reduces astrocytic complement signaling (i.e., C3 and C1q expression). This demonstrates the specific role of EphA4 in the complement pathway in astrocytes. EphA4 signaling regulates engulfment of excitatory synapses by astrocytes. Specifically, EphA4 knockout in astrocytes significantly reduces the tagging of PSD-95 with C1q and the number of synaptic PSD-95 puncta engulfed by astrocytes. Thus, our results reveal a novel mechanistic role of astrocytic EphA4 signaling in synaptic failure in AD conditions. Most of the findings described herein are reported in the manuscript authored by Yang et al., which is under preparation (see attached).

16102019.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102019.value: Our current findings shed light on the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which dysregulated EphA4 signaling affects synaptic loss in AD. However, our understanding of the exact mechanisms remains limited. Further studies analyzing single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from different neural cells would clarify how neuronal and astrocytic EphA4 influences the reorganization of synaptic connections. Moreover, by investigating the bidirectional signaling of ephrin–EphA, we will gain a more comprehensive understanding of the cellular mechanisms involved. To further assess the potential of modulating EphA4 signaling to restore synaptic dysfunction in AD, we can further conduct functional studies to evaluate the impacts of modulating EphA4 expression in astrocytes or neurons on hippocampal synaptic transmission and synaptic plasticity in animal models of AD. Finally, our current study focuses on transgenic mouse models of AD, it is essential to extend our research to human subjects. To explore the therapeutic potential of targeting EphA4 for AD, we can investigate the expression and cellular localization of EphA4 in postmortem brain samples from individuals with AD. To validate the relevance of EphA4 in human AD cases, we can analyze AD-associated endophenotypes to determine how EphA4 levels are correlated with certain stages of disease progression and, cognitive decline.

16102019.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102019.value: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive brain disease that affects memory and cognitive abilities. As effective treatments are limited, it is crucial to search for therapeutic targets. In AD, the dysfunction and loss of synapses in the hippocampus may contribute to cognitive decline. Although the cell-surface protein EphA4 regulates the hippocampal synaptic dysfunction in AD, the mechanisms through which the dysregulation of EphA4 signaling results in the synaptic dysfunction in AD remain unclear. Here, we demonstrated that EphA4 level is higher in neurons and astrocytes in hippocampal regions in AD model mice. Improper activation of EphA4 signaling impairs communication among neurons and contributes to synapse loss in the hippocampus. We found that activation of EphA4 signaling in astrocytes stimulates the elimination of synapses via engulfment by glial cells; specifically, it stimulates the complement pathway (an innate immune response) to label weakened synapses to be engulfed by glial cells. Meanwhile, inhibiting EphA4 signaling modulates the complement pathway to block and reverse the synapse loss in AD conditions. In summary, EphA4 signaling is important for synaptic dysfunction in AD. Understanding the biology of EphA4 activation in the hippocampus in AD helps clarify the pathological mechanisms of the disease and develop new treatments.

16102319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102319.value: 骨骼肌幹細胞，又稱‘’衛星細胞‘’， 是一類緊貼於肌肉纖維的靜止幹細胞。在肌肉損傷後，衛星細胞脫離靜止狀態並且被激活，進而分裂分化，而後自我更新來進行肌肉修復。在成體組織中，幹細胞群體及其靜止狀態的保持對組織損傷後再生是至關重要的。很長一段時間以來，衛星細胞被認為處於一種休眠的靜止狀態。但是越來越多的數據表明衛星細胞的靜止狀態及其激活過程是受轉錄後調控機制活躍調節的。靜止衛星細胞表達大量的可編碼在激活過程起到關鍵作用的蛋白的信使RNA，但其翻譯過程被抑制。在收到肌肉再生的信號後， 衛星細胞會釋放被抑制的信使RNA，因此翻譯過程可以迅速激活從而引起衛星細胞的激活。一直以來，我們感興趣並致力於衛星細胞的靜止和激活的分子調控機理的研究。先前，我們證明了小分子RNA介導的翻譯抑制調節衛星細胞的靜止狀態。然而，目前衛星細胞靜止和激活過程的轉錄後調控機理的研究所用傳統的細胞分選辦法不是最優的。衛星細胞的正常生理狀態會被分選過程干擾，因此傳統分選辦法得到的衛星細胞不能表現完全的靜止和激活狀態的特徵。另外，細胞分選過程需要數個小時，這也導致了我們不能研究早期的衛星細胞激活過程。 為了解決技術上的限制，我們在細胞分選前先”固定”衛星細胞在肌肉纖維上。我們發現此辦法可以保留在肌肉纖維上的最原始的細胞狀態與特徵。這份項目書的第一個目標是應用高通量二代測序技術來獲取最真實的細胞靜止及其早期激活的轉錄組表達譜與特徵。我們將會鑑定在早期激活過程中開始起作用的基因和信號通路，並儘可能發現在細胞激活過程中最早發生的分子調控機制。下一個待研究的問題是：這些基因是怎麼被調控的？在這個項目裡，我們的目的是探索一個翻譯調節因子，細胞質多腺苷酸化原件結合蛋白1（CPEB1），是如何調節MyoD 翻譯和細胞激活的。我們首先檢測到在細胞早期激活過程中，CPEB1活性被激活。因此，我們認為CPEB1作為一個翻譯啟動的開關調節了細胞激活需要的蛋白的翻譯。為了證明這個假設，我們將會製造只在衛星細胞敲除CPEB1的轉基因老鼠品系。首先，我們會探索敲除CPEB1後引起的細胞早期激活和肌肉再生的缺陷表型。為了研究CPEB1如何調節翻譯，我們會探究CPEB1是如何處理其結合的RNA。此外，我們也將鑑定CPEB1 結合併調節的RNA和信號通路。這些實驗得到的數據將確立CPEB1是如何促進翻譯並調節細胞的快速激活的。 我們的研究不僅僅有助於理解目前仍缺乏足夠探索的細胞早期激活過程，並確立CPEB1調節細胞激活的主要作用機理。我們長期目標是提供更多更充分的關於幹細胞基礎研究的知識和觀點，並引導幹細胞基礎研究向再生醫學臨床治療的轉化。

16102319.label: Realisation of objectives
16102319.value: Aim 1: Molecular characterization of satellite cell (SC) early activation In the first part of this aim, we proposed to characterize the molecular regulation of early SC quiescence using our established in situ fixation technique that preserves the genuine quiescence signature. Initially, we isolated quiescent SCs (QSC, fixed), freshly isolated SCs (fiSCs, unfixed), and activated SCs (ASCs) to study their transcriptomic profiles. Gene ontology analysis was performed and we confirmed quiescence markers (Pax7, Calcr, Notch/Wnt associated genes) were present in QSCs and fiSCs, while activation markers (Mki67, Bub1, Plk1) were expressed in ASCs. In addition, fiSCs also showed signs of early activation, and so redefined these fiSCs as early ASCs. Previously, we discovered that MyoD1 transcripts localized to a cytoplasmic compartment containing CPEB1. As CPEB1 is known to promote mRNA translation, here we performed proteomic analysis of SCs during activation. We also compared whether the transcriptomes correlated with protein expression. Interestingly, we observed a significant number of proteins being translated, despite their transcripts being down-regulated. This suggested a translational control mechanism during SC activation. Another part of this aim to was to study 3’UTR processing during SC early activation. Here, we studied the profiles of 3’UTRs of transcripts in QSCs to identify what modifications this region of the transcripts undergoes during SC activation. We isolated poly(A)+ RNA from fiSCs and ASCs and found that the transcripts of the gene upregulated in ASCs were longer than that of transcripts from fiSCs. In addition, after determining the length of the 3’UTR transcripts, we found that the transcripts derived from fiSCs and ASCs were substantially shorter than that of the QSCs. We then used the MinION sequencer developed by Oxford Nanopore Technologies to investigate the length of the poly(A) tail. We encountered several difficulties during the library preparation. As the RNA content of QSCs is low and the number of QSCs isolated per mouse is also low, it was difficult to meet the RNA input requirement. Thus, we mixed the QSC RNA with C.elegans RNA to meet the required input. As Mus musculus and C. elegans are two distinguished species, the reads could be computationally separated. However, due to the relatively low RNA input and low sequencing depth of MinION (compared to Next Generation Sequencing), this limited our capacity to perform downstream bioinformatics analysis of the 3’UTRs. Aim 2: Elucidation of the functional role of CPEB1 during SC early activation Our findings from Aim 1 suggested SC activation is under post-transcriptional regulation. Here, we examined whether CPEB1 post-transcriptionally regulates the quiescence-to-activation transition. We hypothesized that CPEB1 regulates one of the activation associated proteins, MyoD. We found that the translation of MyoD transcripts is repressed in QSCs, where CPEB1 expression is low, but MyoD protein is evident in ASCs. We next pinpointed the cellular location of CPEB1 by Fluorescent In-situ Hybridization (smFISH). We observed that CPEB1 can binds to the cytoplasmic polyadenylation elements of MyoD transcripts to regulate its translation. Furthermore, inhibition of CPEB1 led to the reduction of MyoD-expressing SCs, as shown in immunofluorescence staining. We also investigated the functional impact of CPEB1 inhibition in SCs. CPEB1 expression was depleted in in vitro (freshly isolated SCs) and ex vivo (myofibers isolated from EDL muscle) by CPEB1-specific siRNA. MyoD expression levels and EdU incoporation on SCs were reduced post siRNA transfection. It was previously reported that CPEB1 phosphorylation is required to regulate translational control in various biological pathways and it is a target of Aurora Kinase A (Aurka). We treated SCs with either an Aurka-specific inhibitor, MK5108 or activator, insulin, to observe the impact on MyoD expression and EdU incorporation. We showed that CPEB1 phosphorylation is required for SC activation and proliferation. In addition, we modulated the CPEB1 phosphorylation levels in injured Tibialis Anterior (TA) muscle by MK5108 or insulin and found there was decline muscle repair. This shows the phosphorylation-dependent role of CPEB1 in SC activation and subsequent muscle regeneration. As CPEB1 is a RNA-binding protein, we used RNA Immunoprecipitation Sequencing (RIP-seq) to identify potential CPEB1 targets in SCs. Subsequent functional enrichment analyses identified transcripts encoding for mRNA transport regulators and mitochondrial ribosome components related to oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis. Taken together, our results suggest CPEB1 is a master post-transcriptional regulator for the reprogramming of the SC cellular environment during activation. In addition, we performed transcriptomic and proteomic analysis of SCs. We generated SC-specific CPEB1 conditional-knockout (KO) mice to confirm the role of CPEB1 in regulating MyoD and MyoG protein expression in freshly isolated SCs using immunofluorescence staining and western blotting, as well as its effects on SC activation and muscle regeneration. RNA-sequencing was carried out to compare the transcriptomes between wild-type (WT) and CPEB1 KO fiSCs. We investigated the post-transcriptional processing by CPEB1 using the MinION sequencer but the sample quality was limited by the cell number thus we did not reach the input threshold for direct RNA-seq. 16102319.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102319.value: In 2022, our work was published in Nature Communications titled “CPEB1 directs muscle stem cell activation by reprogramming the translational landscape”, reporting the proteomic changes during muscle stem cell activation. We first characterized SC early activation by studying the proteomes and transcriptomes of QSCs, fiSCs, and ASCs, observing that the gene expression levels did not correlate with their corresponding protein levels, showing discordance between translation and transcription during SC activation, indicative of a translational control mechanism during SC activation. This led us to discover SC activation is regulated by CPEB1, a RNA-binding protein. Comparison of the poly(A) tails length between fiSCs and ASCs showed a global trend of similar length. However, when studying genes that were differentially expressed between the two populations, we observed that upregulated genes in ASCs had longer poly(A) tails when compared to fiSCs. We also found that there was a global shortening of the 3’UTRs in fiSCs and ASCs, in comparison to QSCs. On average, we found the 3’UTRs were 40% shorter than in ASCs. SCs cultured on isolated muscle fibers showed increased CPEB1 expression co-localizing with MyoD, indicating CPEB1 expression was increased during activation. Furthermore, siRNA-mediated knockdown of CPEB1 decreased EdU incorporation, hence inhibiting SC activation, suggesting that CPEB1 is essential for SC activation. We observed that CPEB1 co-localized with MyoD transcripts, post-transcriptionally regulating MyoD by acting on the CPEs within its 3’UTRs to regulate its translation. This was further supported by our findings that CPEB1 influences MyoD protein levels in vivo. Furthermore, insulin (Aurka activator) injection into the muscle promoted SC activation and proliferation, demonstrating that phosphorylation of CPEB1 is important in SC functions. These results suggest CPEB1 could be a novel therapeutic target to improve muscle regeneration. The importance of CPEB1 in SC activation was studied using the CPEB1 conditional KO (cKO) mice. We observed that CPEB1 was highly expressed in differentiated primary myoblasts and regenerated fibers, whilst knocking out CPEB1 impaired muscle regeneration, evident 7 days and 14 days post-injury. Proteomic analysis between CPEB1 KO and WT mice fiSCs showed 3145 differentially expressed proteins. Gene ontology analysis showed that the spliceosome, ribosome, translation initiation ribosomal scanning and start codon recognition were downregulated. These data strengthen the important role of CPEB1 to maintain the proteomic landscape in SCs.

16102319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102319.value: In this study, we demonstrated that insulin promotes SC activation and proliferation partially via the CPEB1 pathway. Our in vivo data also indicated that insulin improves muscle regeneration. Our study suggests there may be a potential regulatory pathway which insulin regulates muscle hypertrophy by modulating SC proliferation via CPEB1. However, the insulin pathway is complex with many downstream targets so its effect on CPEB1 may not be direct. Hence, the mechanisms by which insulin acts on CPEB1 could be elucidated further. In addition, we could screen for positive regulators of CPEB1 using CPEB1-reporter mice (where CPEB1 protein levels correlated with changes in green fluorescent protein expression).

16102319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102319.value: Quiescent skeletal muscle stem cells (also known as satellite cells, SCs) can activate quickly in response to external stimuli. However, the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. In this study, we utilized our perfusion-based fixation protocol to isolate quiescent SCs and compared their protein expression profiles to freshly isolated and activated SCs. We reported massive protein expression level changes during the quiescence-to-activation transition, but it showed discordance with the gene expression levels, suggesting a post-transcriptional regulation upon SC activation. Here, we showed Cytoplasmic Polyadenylation Element Binding protein 1 (CPEB1) post-transcriptionally regulates the translational landscape of SCs during activation, identifying myogenic progression-associated protein MyoD as one of its targets. We showed that Aurora kinase 1 (Aurka)-mediated phosphorylation regulates SC functions in terms of activation. Furthermore, we found insulin, activator of Aurka promoted SC activation and proliferation. Moving forwards, we examined the role of CPEB1 in SC activation and proliferation by generating CPEB1 conditional-knockout (KO) mice. CPEB1 KO mice showed changes in protein expressions in pathways reflecting the phenotypes exhibited in our siRNA-mediated CPEB1 knockdown SCs. Furthermore, CPEB1 KO mice showed defects in muscle repair. In summary, our study lays the foundation for consolidating CPEB1 as a major post-transcriptional regulator of SCs during activation.

16102519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102519.value: Lipid metabolism is critical for maintaining neuronal integrity and activity. However, the role of lipid metabolism in axon regeneration of the central nervous system (CNS), and in particular its intrinsic molecular mechanism, remains elusive. We found that depleting neuronal Lipin1, a key enzyme controlling the balanced synthesis of glycerolipids, enhanced axon regeneration. Forced TAG storage blocked axon regeneration. Conversely, inhibiting neuronal diglyceride acyltransferases (DGATs), crucial enzymes catalyzing TAG synthesis, increased phospholipids and also promoted axon regeneration. In addition, Lipin1 depletion promoted corticospinal tract sprouting. Our proposal aims to elucidate the mechanisms underlying Lipin1-mediated growth inhibition. By using mutant mice, we will examine whether modulating the glycerolipid synthesis pathway by deleting neural Lipin1/DGATs in either retinal ganglion cells or corticospinal neurons can promote axon sprouting and regeneration after injury. Our study will reveal a critical role of Lipin1/DGATs as intrinsic regulators of glycerolipid metabolism in neurons, and indicate that tailoring neuronal lipid synthesis from TAG to phospholipids can be targeted for axon regeneration. 我們發現, 神經軸突損傷提高了視網膜神經節細胞lipin1。神經元 lipin1 是控制平衡合成甘油脂的關鍵酶, 降低 lipin1 可增強神經損傷後的軸突再生。增強的再生需要甘油三酯水解同磷脂合成。直接抑制甘油三酯合成也可以促進再生。我們提出作為儲存脂質的甘油三酯也許會為膜合成必須的磷脂質提供合成前體， 而且甘油脂代謝通路研究有轉化潛力。

16102519.label: Realisation of objectives
16102519.value: In the central nervous system (CNS) of adult mammals, severed axons cannot regenerate to recover lost functions. Failure of axonal regeneration is largely attributable to the low intrinsic growth potential of neurons and the presence of an extrinsic inhibitory environment. Axon elongation needs an increase in membrane expansion and, consequently, membrane lipid production. There are numerous classes of lipids with diverse functions in neurons, and not all lipids are necessarily essential for axon growth. Therefore, regeneration must necessitate coordinated alterations in the lipid homeostasis of damaged neurons. Glycerolipids are very prevalent cellular lipids. The physiological functions of lipids include energy storage (primarily triacylglycerol (TG)), membrane structure (phospholipids and other lipids), and cell signaling. The glycerol phosphate pathway is an essential mechanism for modulating the levels of various glycerolipids in cells through the regulation of a series of enzymatic reactions. Lipin1 protein, a phosphatidic acid phosphatase (PAP) enzyme, catalyzes the conversion of phosphatidic acid (PA) to diacylglycerol (DG) in the penultimate step of the glycerol phosphate pathway. DG is TG and phospholipids' precursor. The final and only irreversible phase of the glycerol phosphate pathway is the covalent bonding of a fatty acyl-CoA and DG molecule to form TG. This reaction is catalyzed by the DGAT1 and DGAT2 acyl-CoA:diacylglycerol acyltransferase (DGAT) enzymes. Both enzymes have been implicated in TG homeostasis regulation. Uncertain is the role of this metabolic pathway in neuronal response to injury and morphological change, particularly axon growth. We discovered that Lipin1 shRNA promoted axon extension. Then, we crushed the optic nerve and investigated axon regeneration two weeks later. Comparable RGC survival rates existed between two groups. Cholera toxin B (CTB) labeling of the optic nerves revealed significantly more regenerated axons in mice injected with AAV-shLipin1 compared to mice injected with scrambled shRNA (AAV-Scr), indicating that Lipin1 inhibits axon regeneration. Then, we utilized CRISPR to eliminate Lipin1 from RGCs and evaluated the results. After injection into Cas9 mice, we discovered that AAV-sgLipin1 stimulated axon regeneration. AAV-sgLipin1 eliminated Lipin1 in approximately 50% of RGCs. Consistent with the shRNA experiment, Lipin1 KO had no effect on RGC survival. In addition, the combination of AAV-shLipin1 and AAV-CNTF produced much more potent growth. Some axons even reached the chiasm in as little as two weeks, which was extremely uncommon with either treatment alone. Lipin1 KD may accelerate the rate of regeneration induced by CNTF. Thus, using two distinct methods, we demonstrated that neuronal Lipin1 functions as an intrinsic axon regeneration suppressor. Lipin1 possesses both PAP and transcription coactivator functions, and we examined whether or not both functions are implicated in lipin1-dependent growth. In RGCs with lipin1 depletion, we used AAVs to express human WT lipin1 (lipin1-WT), lipin1 with a PAP catalytic motif mutation (lipin1-PAPm), and lipin1 without a nuclear localization signal (lipin1-DNLS). Lipin1-WT and lipin1-DNLS suppressed axon regeneration to the level of the control, whereas lipin1-PAPm did not, indicating that PAP activity rather than transcription coactivator function was essential. The result also confirmed that the regeneration induced by lipin1 shRNA was not the result of potential off-target effects. Due to the fact that PAP activity was essential for Lipin1-dependent axon growth, we hypothesized that Lipin1 may control axon regrowth by regulating glycerolipid synthesis in neurons and tested this hypothesis in vitro. High suppression efficacy was achieved by adding AAV-shLipin1 or AAV-Scr to cultured cortical neurons. After eliminating glia, we directly measured glycerolipid levels using neuronal culture. The ultra-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS) system was utilized to analyze the lipid extraction of cortical neurons. We observed an increase in phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), as well as a decrease in triglyceride (TG). In addition, we measured TG and PC levels using an enzymatic hydrolysis assay and found similar outcomes. Injured neurons can regrow their axons by redirecting two limbs of the branch and shifting lipid storage to membrane lipid production by depleting Lipin1. Given that Lipin1 regulates the amount of TG in neurons, we sought to determine if neuronal TG metabolism is crucial for Lipin1-dependent axon growth. In the brain, two TG lipases, ATGL and DDHD2, are active and convert TG to DG and fatty acid. In cultured adult DRG neurons, inhibition of ATGL and DDHD2 with specific inhibitors significantly increased TG storage. In addition, 40% of axon elongation was inhibited in the primary culture. Two weeks after optic nerve crush, we injected AAVs containing ATGL shRNA and DDHD2 shRNA into the eyes of rodents deficient in Lipin1 and examined the effect. The suppression of both ATGL and DDHD2 inhibited axon regeneration. Consequently, our data suggest that TG hydrolysis was essential for Lipin1-dependent axon regeneration. Next, we determined if directly reducing the level of neuronal TG by inhibiting its biosynthesis could promote axon growth. In a model of optic nerve injury, we deleted DGATs in retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) using AAV-sgRNA against DGAT1 (AAVsgDGAT1) or DGAT2 (AAVsgDGAT2) in Cas9 mice and evaluated the effect on growth. Eliminating either DGAT significantly improved axon regeneration following injury. Consequently, neuronal DGATs inhibit axon regeneration and can be targeted to promote growth. We published the work above in Neuron in 2020. In addition to lipid metabolism, some glycerolipids, such as PA and lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), play an important role in cell signaling. Using a model of optic nerve injury, we discovered that mTOR and STAT3 activation induced axon regeneration that required Lipin1 downregulation. Additionally, Lipin1 knockdown-induced axon regeneration required mTOR and STAT3 signaling activation. We extracted lipids from cultured cortical neurons lacking Lipin1 and measured the lipid component using UPLC-MS. Lipin1 suppression was found to increase PA abundance. PA may serve as a crucial mediator between Lipin1 and cell signaling pathways. Then, we investigated whether Lipin1 inhibition affected the CST's regenerative capacity. We analyzed its effect on CST proliferation following unilateral pyramidotomy. The propagation of intact CST axons into the denervated side of the cervical spinal cord was investigated. AAV-shLipin1 injection induced extensive trans-midline sprouting of adult CST axons from the intact side of the spinal cord into the denervated side, in contrast to the limited sprouting of adult CST axons in the control group. Thus, Lipin1 inhibition may increase the proliferation potential of adult CSMNs. Next, we examined whether Lipin1 inhibition promotes CST axon regeneration after complete spinal cord injury in rats. In contrast to the inability of control animals to regenerate, animals with Lipin1 suppression induced robust axon regeneration across the lesion site for as much as 3 mm. These results demonstrated that Lipin1 inhibition increased the capacity for regeneration of CST axons. Our research reveals a novel mechanism that regulates CNS axon regeneration. We demonstrate that the glycerolipid metabolism mediated by Lipin1 and DGAT1 determines axon regeneration after optic nerve injury. Moreover, Lipin1 interacted with the mTOR and STAT3 signaling pathways to control axon regeneration. Lipin1 also determines the regenerative capacity of CST axons. These results are currently under review for publication. In addition, we also showed that boosting the neuronal innate immune responses can also promote axon regeneration. The initial paper was published in Neuron 2023 and we are currently investigating the cross-talk between lipid metabolism and immune responses. Due to the pandemic, we encountered higher consumable expense than what we proposed in the budget. Also, we did not go to any conferences and the conference expense was shifted to consumable.

16102519.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102519.value: To comprehend the role of lipid metabolism in axon regeneration, we manipulated the main factors that regulate lipid metabolism in RGCs. Lipin1, a crucial phosphatidic acid phosphatase (PAP) enzyme that regulates glycerolipids synthesis, controls axon regeneration capacity, we discovered. Lipin1 expression increased in RGCs following injury, which favors production of energy storage TGs over membrane component PLs. Lipin1 deletion redirected lipid metabolism to the synthesis of PLs, thereby facilitating axon regeneration. Moreover, reprogramming lipid metabolism by eliminating DGATs promoted axon regeneration. Moreover, this mechanism regulated the spontaneous axon regeneration of peripheral neurons. Consequently, our study demonstrated that rewiring lipid metabolism by manipulating Lipin1 and DGATs promotes axon regeneration in a model of the optic nerve. Lipids serve several functions within the cell, including energy storage, membrane component, and cell signaling. Whether glycerolipid metabolism orchestrates cell signaling pathways to promote CNS axon regeneration is not illustrated. Lipin1 overexpression suppressed mTOR and STAT3-induced axon regeneration, whereas Lipin1 knockdown facilitated axon regeneration required activation of both mTOR and STAT3 pathways, indicating a cross-talk between Lipin1 and classical signaling pathways in determining axon regeneration. In addition, we discovered that Lipin1 knockdown substantially increased corticospinal tract (CST) sprouting. Lipin1 knockdown also facilitates robust CST regeneration following complete spinal cord injury. Our research reveals a novel mechanism that regulates CNS axon regeneration. We demonstrate that the glycerolipid metabolism mediated by Lipin1 and DGAT1 determines axon regeneration after optic nerve injury. In addition, Lipin1 regulates axon regeneration by interacting with the mTOR and STAT3 signaling pathways. Lipin1 also determines the regenerative capacity of CST axons.

16102519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102519.value: Axon regeneration requires supply of fundamental materials. Our study demonstrates that increasing synthesis of membrane component PLs by targeting Lipin1 or DGATs promotes axon regeneration. Whether PLs could be directly delivered to the injured axons to facilitate axon regeneration requires further investigation. In addition, Lipin1 interplays with mTOR and STAT3 signalling. The underlying mechanism that mediates the crosstalk is unknown. Uncovering the underlying mechanism may provide novel target for rescuing axon regeneration failure. Moreover, Lipin1 knockdown dramatically increases CST axon regeneration capability. Whether the regenerated axons could be integrated into neural network to reconstitute motor function is of great interest.

16102519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102519.value: The ability of the central nervous system to restore itself is lacking. Therefore, persistent function loss results from traumatic brain damage or neuro degenerative illnesses. Our research offers an innovative method to restore the damaged neural network. Important genes that control lipid metabolism include Lipin1 and DGAT1. When Lipin1 or DGAT1 are removed, ocular neurons manufacture more building blocks, such as PLs. As a result, their nerve acquires the capacity for repair after damage. This could be applied to heal the nerve damage that resulted in blindness. Additionally, paralysis is a common consequence of spinal cord damage. We discover that Lipin1 inhibition encourages corticospinal tract regeneration, suggesting a potential treatment for patients with paralysis. Overall, our research identifies new targets to enhance neural healing following injury.

16102919.label: Realisation of objectives
16102919.value: Mitotic slippage involves cells exiting mitosis without proper chromosome segregation. In this project, we have Interrogated the fundamental mechanism of mitotic slippage. Although degradation of cyclin B during prolonged mitotic arrest is believed to trigger mitotic slippage, its upstream regulation has remained obscure. Whether mitotic slippage is caused by APC/C activity that is able to escape spindle-assembly checkpoint (SAC)-mediated inhibition, or is actively promoted by a change in SAC activity has been an outstanding issue. Our studies revealed that a major culprit for mitotic slippage is the reduction of MAD2 at the kinetochores, leading to a progressive weakening of SAC during mitotic arrest. A further level of control of the timing of mitotic slippage is through p31comet-mediated suppression of MAD2 activation. The loss of kinetochore MAD2 is dependent on APC/C, indicating a feedback control of APC/C to SAC during prolonged mitotic arrest. The gradual weakening of SAC during mitotic arrest enables APC/C to degrade cyclin B, cumulating in the cell exiting mitosis by mitotic slippage. Our findings were published in Oncogene (Lok et al., 2020). In a similar vein, we conducted studies to investigate the mechanism of chloroquine-induced mitotic slippage. By using an ATG5-knockout cell line, we demonstrated that chloroquine promotes mitotic slippage independent of the autophagy pathway. We found that chloroquine accelerates mitotic slippage by promoting cyclin B degradation. Inhibition of upstream mechanisms, including APC/C and SAC, effectively abolishes chloroquine-induced mitotic slippage. Prolonged mitotic arrest-induced mitotic catastrophe is a major anticancer strategy. We have also explored how p53 and members of the BCL2 family regulate cytotoxicity following mitotic slippage. Our studies revealed that, in addition to the dependency on p53, several BCL2 family members, including MCL1 and BCL-XL, plays crucial roles in controlling cell death both during mitotic arrest and after mitotic slippage. We observed compensatory changes in the expression of BCL2 and MCL1 when manipulating BCL-XL levels, highlighting the complexity of their regulatory network. To circumvent their reciprocal regulation, we utilized a degron-mediated system to acutely silence BCL-XL just before mitosis (Yeung et al., 2021; Yeung et al. 2023). Our results show that in epithelial cell lines including HeLa and REP1, BCL-XL and BCL2 act collaboratively to suppress apoptosis during both unperturbed cell cycle and mitotic arrest. By tagging BCL-XL and BCL2 with a common epitope, we estimated that BCL-XL is less abundant than BCL2 in the cell. Nonetheless, BCL-XL plays a more prominent antiapoptotic function than BCL2 during interphase and mitotic arrest. Loss of BCL-XL leads to mitotic cell death primarily through a BAX-dependent process. Furthermore, silencing of BCL-XL results in the stabilization of MCL1, thereby buffering apoptosis during mitotic arrest. Nevertheless, even in a MCL1-deficient background, depletion of BCL-XL accelerates mitotic apoptosis. These findings underscore the pivotal involvement of BCL-XL in controlling timely apoptosis during mitotic arrest, despite adaptive changes in the expression of other BCL2-like proteins (Yu et al., 2024). MCL1 an anti-apoptotic protein also plays a crucial role in delaying apoptosis during mitotic arrest. Progressive degradation of MCL1 occurs during mitotic arrest leading to the loss of its anti-apoptotic function. Surprisingly, the knockout of various components of ubiquitin ligases does not prevent mitotic degradation of MCL1, except for MARCH5 which determines the initial level of MCL1-NOXA network and the duration of MCL1 presence during mitotic arrest. Paradoxically, although knockout of MARCH5 elevates mitotic MCL1, mitotic apoptosis is in fact enhanced in a BAK-dependent manner. Mitotic apoptosis is accelerated after MARCH5 is ablated in both the presence and absence of MCL1. Cell death is not altered after disrupting other MARCH5-regulated BCL2 family members including NOXA, BIM, and BID. However, the disruption of the mitochondrial fission factor DRP1 reduces mitotic apoptosis in MARCH5-disrupted cells. These findings suggest that MARCH5 regulates mitotic apoptosis through MCL1-independent mechanisms, including mitochondrial maintenance, which can override MCL1 stabilization (Wang and Poon, 2023). In the context of mitosis following mitotic slippage, we have characterized several players that potentially regulate bipolar versus multipolar spindle formation. These include several components of the SAC, Aurora kinases, as well as members of the kinesin families. Knockout or pharmacological inhibition of several kinesins shifts the balance between bipolar and multipolar spindle formation after mitotic slippage. The length of mitosis, regulated by the SAC, may influence spindle polarity through kinesins following mitotic slippage. We also found that depletion of NDC80 complex (NDC80C), a kinetochore complex vital for kinetochore–microtubule (KT–MT) attachment, triggers a transient mitotic arrest followed by mitotic slippage. SPC24-deficient cells are unable to sustain SAC activation despite the loss of KT–MT interaction. Intriguingly, our results revealed that other subunits of the NDC80C are co-downregulated with SPC24 at a post-translational level. Silencing any individual subunit of NDC80C likewise reduces expression of the entire complex. Synergism of SPC24 downregulation with drugs that promote either mitotic arrest or mitotic slippage further underscores the dual roles of NDC80C in KT–MT interaction and SAC maintenance. The coordinated regulation of NDC80C subunits suggests that targeting individual subunits may disrupt mitotic progression and offer new therapeutic opportunities (Kim et al., 2024). In addition, we have published several invited review articles on SAC, Aurora kinases, and whole-genome duplication following mitotic slippage (Ma and Poon, 2020; Poon 2021; Poon 2023; Lau and Poon, 2023).

16102919.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102919.value: Mitotic slippage, the process by which cells exit mitosis without proper chromosome segregation, was investigated in this project to understand its mechanism and regulation. We addressed the question of whether mitotic slippage is caused by APC/C activity escaping SAC-mediated inhibition or by an active change in SAC activity. Our findings revealed that the reduction of MAD2 at kinetochores is a significant contributor to mitotic slippage, leading to a gradual weakening of the SAC during prolonged mitotic arrest. Additionally, p31comet-mediated suppression of MAD2 activation further controls the timing of mitotic slippage. The loss of kinetochore MAD2 depends on APC/C, indicating a feedback control mechanism between APC/C and SAC. The weakening of SAC allows APC/C to degrade cyclin B, ultimately leading to cell exit from mitosis through mitotic slippage (Lok et al., 2020). We also investigated the mechanism of chloroquine-induced mitotic slippage and found that it is independent of the autophagy pathway. Chloroquine accelerates mitotic slippage by promoting cyclin B degradation. Inhibition of upstream mechanisms, including APC/C and SAC, effectively abolished chloroquine-induced mitotic slippage. Furthermore, our studies revealed the crucial roles of BCL2 family members, MCL1 and BCL-XL, in regulating cell death during both mitotic arrest and after mitotic slippage (Yeung et al., 2021; Yeung et al. 2023; Yu et al., 2024). Silencing of BCL-XL resulted in the stabilization of MCL1, buffering apoptosis during mitotic arrest. However, even in a MCL1-deficient background, depletion of BCL-XL accelerated mitotic apoptosis, emphasizing the pivotal involvement of BCL-XL in timely apoptosis during mitotic arrest. In the context of mitosis following mitotic slippage, we investigated the regulation of spindle formation. Components of the SAC, Aurora kinases, and kinesin families were identified as potential regulators. Knockout or inhibition of specific kinesins shifted the balance between bipolar and multipolar spindle formation after mitotic slippage. Depletion of the NDC80 complex (NDC80C), a kinetochore complex essential for kinetochore-microtubule attachment, triggered a transient mitotic arrest followed by mitotic slippage. Silencing any individual subunit of NDC80C reduced the expression of the entire complex. The dual roles of NDC80C in kinetochore-microtubule interaction and SAC maintenance highlight its potential as a therapeutic target (Kim et al., 2024). In addition to our primary research, we have published several invited review articles on SAC, Aurora kinases, and whole-genome duplication following mitotic slippage (Ma and Poon, 2020; Poon 2021; Poon 2023; Lau and Poon, 2023).

16102919.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102919.value: • Our findings demonstrated that chloroquine induces mitotic slippage by promoting cyclin B degradation. However, the exact target(s) of chloroquine during this process, particularly at the kinetochores where enzymatic components of the SAC such as MPS1 are present, remain unknown. Further investigation is warranted to elucidate the precise mechanism of action for chloroquine-induced mitotic slippage. • This research underscores the potential of targeting mitotic slippage as a therapeutic strategy. Future studies can explore specific targets to further develop translational applications and therapeutic interventions related to this process.

16102919.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102919.value: Mitotic slippage, a phenomenon where cells exit mitosis without properly separating their chromosomes, was investigated to understand its mechanism. We found that a protein called MAD2, located at specific sites on our chromosomes called kinetochores, plays a crucial role in mitotic slippage. The levels of MAD2 decrease during prolonged mitotic arrest, resulting in mitotic slippage. Another protein called p31comet also regulates the timing of mitotic slippage by suppressing MAD2 activation. This weakening allows a protein complex called APC/C to degrade cyclin B, leading to cell exit from mitosis through mitotic slippage. Additionally, we investigated how the drug chloroquine induces mitotic slippage. They discovered that chloroquine accelerates mitotic slippage by promoting cyclin B degradation. Moreover, our studies identified the significance of two proteins, MCL1 and BCL-XL, in regulating cell death during mitotic arrest and after mitotic slippage. We also found that disrupting a protein complex called NDC80C caused a temporary cell division arrest followed by mitotic slippage. These findings suggest that targeting the NDC80C and other regulators of mitotic slippage could be a potential therapeutic approach. In summary, this study provides insights into the mechanisms and regulation of mitotic slippage and provide potential avenues for future therapeutic strategies.

16103319.label: Realisation of objectives
16103319.value: The trans-Golgi network (TGN) serves as a crucial transport hub in the secretory transport pathway. Arf family proteins and cargo adaptors are key players in the protein sorting process. Arf proteins function to mediate the membrane recruitment of cargo adaptors, enabling these adaptors to capture cargo proteins into vesicles. In this project, our aim is to perform spatial and functional analyses of the Arf protein and cargo adaptors that regulate TGN sorting. We developed an in vitro assay that reconstitutes the vesicular release of cargo proteins from the TGN to investigate their functional roles. Using this assay, we aim to reveal the spectrum of cargo proteins specifically recognized by the spatially segregated cargo adaptors, AP-1 and GGA2. Subsequently, we aim to explore and characterize the Arf proteins spatially associated with these two cargo adaptors. Additionally, we intend to analyze whether the spatially segregated cargo sorting machineries, which regulate the TGN sorting of PCP proteins in mammalian cells, are crutial for the propagation of PCP in vivo in the wings of Drosophila. In collaboration with Prof. Zhongping Yao’s lab at PolyU and Prof. Liwen Jiang’s lab at CUHK, we developed a large-scale vesicle formation assay in combination with label-free quantitative mass spectrometry analysis to examine the protein profiles of transport vesicles for proteomic analysis. This approach robustly reveals cargo proteins that depend on a specific cellular factor to be enriched in transport vesicles. The vesicle formation assay was performed using cytosol prepared from WT HeLa cells, AP1γ1 KO HeLa cells, and GGA2 knockdown cells. Label-free quantitative analysis of the vesicles produced from these experimental groups uncovered specific cargo proteins that depend on AP-1 or GGA2 for enrichment into transport vesicles. We then employed biochemical and cell biological approaches to verify the findings from the mass spectrometry analysis. We found that EGFR, one of the identified cargo clients of AP-1, relies on AP-1 to be exported out of the TGN. Further analysis revealed that AP-1 directly interacts with the tyrosine sorting motif on EGFR to enrich EGFR into TGN-derived vesicles. Knockdown of AP-1 causes defects in TGN export of EGFR and induces defects in EGFR signaling. Interestingly, the oncogenic mutant form of EGFR, EGFR(L858R), is independent of AP-1 for export out of TGN, suggesting EGFR(L858R) and the wild type EGFR utilize different cellular factors for export out of the TGN. We also verified that another identified cargo client of AP-1, CAB45, also depends on AP-1 to be exported out of the TGN. Through similar analyses, we found GGA2, but not AP-1, regulates TGN export of a planar cell polarity protein, Frizzled6. An Arf family protein, Arf1, mediates membrane recruitment of AP-1 and GGA2 in a GTP-dependent manner. The membrane recruitment of AP-1 can also be mediated by Arfrp1. Interestingly, we found that the amphipathic motifs of Arfrp1 are required and sufficient for determining its Golgi localizations. The spatial determination mediated by the Arfrp1 helix requires its binding partner Sys1. In addition, the acetylation modification on the Arfrp1 helix is important for spatial determination. Interestingly, Arfrp1 is recruited to their specific intracellular compartments independent of GTP binding, suggesting their GTP binding and membrane association are uncoupled. Based on these analyses, we propose a model to explain the process of membrane recruitment of Arfrp1. First, the amphipathic helices of Arfrp1 will be acetylated. Subsequently, the modified amphipathic helix motifs of Arfrp1 will interact with the membrane-localized phospholipids or transmembrane proteins to be recruited to specific membrane compartments. After being recruited to the membranes, the Arf proteins will meet with their corresponding GEF proteins to promote GTP binding and induce conformational changes of their switch domains. GTP-bound Arf proteins then recruit downstream effector proteins such as AP-1 to mediate vesicle formation and cargo packaging. Our analysis provides a novel mechanism for the membrane association of some Arf proteins. We utilized two-color STORM imaging to analyze the spatial distributions of cargo adaptors that participate in the TGN sorting process of PCP proteins, Vangl2 and Frizzled-6, at high resolution. We found that these cargo adaptors can be assembled into elongated punctate structures of over 250 nm in length at the juxta-nuclear Golgi area. We revealed that the cargo adaptors, AP-1 and GGA2, are spatially segregated and function in the sorting of Vangl2 and Frizzled-6, respectively. In contrast, another cargo adaptor, epsinR, showed a GGA2- and AP-1-associated pattern. Both GGA2 and epsinR regulate sorting of Frizzled-6. Using super-resolution imaging, we found that Vangl2 was spatially associated with AP-1, and Frizzled-6 was associated with GGA2 and epsinR upon exiting the TGN, providing a direct observation of the differential sorting of PCP proteins at the TGN. Using 2-color super-resolution imaging, we also found that Arfrp1 is located at the TGN distinct from Arf1 and colocalizes with its cargo client, Vangl2, but not Frizzled6 upon TGN export, suggesting Arfrp1 is located on a specific TGN microdomain to regulate TGN sorting of Vangl2. This work demonstrated with unprecedented clarity the spatial relationships among clathrin, cargo adaptors, and cargo molecules at the juxtanuclear area, suggesting Arf protein in association with cargo adaptors providesadditional specificity for recognizing cargo molecules. The Drosophila wing hairs, as a classical example of the PCP phenomenon, are oriented distally to the Drosophila body. Using the engrailed-Gal4 driver and UAS-RNAi to specifically induce gene knockdown in the posterior territory of the wing disc, it has been reported that AP-1 and Arf1 are important for wing hair orientation. Using the same genetic approach, we found that knockdown of Arfrp1 and epsinR, but not subunits from AP-3, causes defects in wing hair orientation and the localization of Frizzled on cell boundaries in Drosophila wing. These analyses provide novel insights into the functions of Arf proteins and cargo adaptors in the propagation of PCP in animals in vivo. In summary, we have addressed all of our objectives using the vesicle formation assay as well as other biochemical, cell biological, and genetic approaches, which revealed novel insights into protein sorting at the trans-Golgi network.

16103319.label: Major findings and research outcome
16103319.value: The trans-Golgi network (TGN) plays a crucial role as a cargo sorting station in the secretory pathway. Defects in the TGN sorting process can lead to protein mistargeting, causing disturbances in establishing cell polarity, immunity, and other physiological processes. Key players in the protein sorting process include Arf family proteins and cargo adaptors. Using the vesicle formation assay in conjunction with label-free quantitative mass spectrometry analysis, we identified novel cargo clients for two TGN-located cargo adaptors, AP-1 and GGA2. CAB45 and EGFR are two of the identified cargo clients of AP-1. Frizzled6 has been determined to depend on GGA2 but not AP-1 for export from the TGN. Further analysis revealed that AP-1 recognizes the tyrosine sorting motif in EGFR, enriching EGFR into TGN-derived vesicles. In contrast, the oncogenic mutant version of EGFR, EGFR(L858R), operates independently of AP-1, suggesting that the wild type EGFR and EGFR(L858R) rely on different cargo adaptors for delivery to the cell surface. An Arf family protein, Arfrp1, mediates the membrane recruitment of AP-1. We found that the amphipathic motifs of Arfrp1 are both necessary and sufficient to determine its Golgi localization. The spatial determination mediated by Arfrp1's helix requires its binding partner, Sys1. Further analysis indicates that Sys1 plays a significant role in the TGN export of AP-1 clients, Vangl2, and EGFR. Employing two-color super-resolution imaging, we discovered that the cargo adaptors, AP-1 and GGA2, are spatially segregated and function in the TGN sorting of Vangl2 and Frizzled-6, respectively. We also found that Arfrp1 is located at the TGN, distinct from Arf1, and colocalizes with its cargo client, Vangl2, but not with Frizzled6 upon TGN export. This suggests that Arfrp1 occupies a specific TGN microdomain to regulate the TGN sorting of Vangl2. Genetic studies in Drosophila suggest that Arfrp1 and epsinR, but not AP-3, are important for the propagation of planar cell polarity (PCP) in the Drosophila wing. These analyses provide novel insights into the functions and molecular mechanisms of the cargo sorting process at the TGN. Some of the work in this project is published in two PNAS papers in 2021 and 2022. Some of the work in this project is published in four JBC papers in 2020a, 2020b, 2022 and 2023. We also published other manuscripts and a protocol with support from this grant.

16103319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16103319.value: In this study, we employed a large-scale vesicle formation assay paired with quantitative mass spectrometry analysis to identify cargo clients of AP-1 and GGA2. We proceeded with a combination of biochemical, cell biological, and super-resolution imaging approaches to analyze the functional roles of the Arf protein and cargo adaptors in mediating protein sorting at the TGN. The physiological roles of these Arf family proteins and cargo adaptors in live animals were further analyzed through genetic studies conducted in Drosophila. This research establishes a platform using both biochemical and cell biological approaches to uncover molecular mechanisms, as well as a genetic approach to study physiological relevance in live animals. Our future plan is to expand this platform to conduct studies investigating vesicular trafficking, from molecular mechanisms to physiological relevance. Furthermore, an important future direction is to provide structural analysis to reveal how Sys1, Arfrp1, and AP-1 regulate the sorting of AP-1's cargo clients at the TGN. Another important future direction is to execute the vesicle formation assay in specialized cells, such as neuronal cells or pancreatic cells, to identify the cargo clients of specific cargo adaptors.

16103519.label: Project Objectives
16103519.value: Develop NIR light-responsive proteins through a combination of directed evolution and cofactor engineering: AdoB12 derivatives that are NIR-sensitive will be chemically synthesized. Structure-guided saturation mutagenesis of the CarHC protein will be performed to adjust the binding pocket to accommodate the altered cofactors. Synthesize and characterize NIR light-responsive protein hydrogels with tunable immunogenicity: The hydrogel synthesis will involve the combined use of genetically encoded click chemistry (SpyTag/SpyCatcher chemistry) and small-molecule induced protein oligomerization. Rheological tests will be performed to examine the viscoelastic properties of the materials. To modulate their immunogenicity, which is of great importance for in vivo applications, immunomodulators such as recombinant human clusterin proteins fused with SpyTag will be produced and used to decorate the protein networks. The interactions between the clusterin-containing materials and immune cells such as macrophages will be assessed in vitro. Micro-pattern the hydrogels mechanically and biochemically with light to guide 3D cell behavior and axon growth in vitro: Microchannels will be created within the hydrogel scaffold using a focused laser, and, as proof of concept, then decorated with biomolecules such as RGD cell-binding ligands for cell adhesion/migration and leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) for enhanced neurite elongation using orthogonal genetically encoded click chemistry (SnoopTag/SnoopCatcher chemistry). The resulting materials will be used to examine the combined influence of nerve guidance channels and biochemical signals on axon elongation of adult dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons in vitro.

Synthesize and characterize NIR light-responsive protein hydrogels with tunable immunogenicity: The hydrogel synthesis will involve the combined use of genetically encoded click chemistry (SpyTag/SpyCatcher chemistry) and small-molecule induced protein oligomerization. Rheological tests will be performed to examine the viscoelastic properties of the materials. To modulate their immunogenicity, which is of great importance for in vivo applications, immunomodulators such as recombinant human clusterin proteins fused with SpyTag will be produced and used to decorate the protein networks. The interactions between the clusterin-containing materials and immune cells such as macrophages will be assessed in vitro.

The resulting materials will be used to examine the combined influence of nerve guidance channels and biochemical signals on axon elongation of adult dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons in vitro.

16103519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16103519.value: Development of near-infrared light-responsive hydrogels that enable targeted delivery and in situ dynamic modulation of the microenvironment can provide solutions to a variety of problems facing regenerative biology and medicine. For instance, axon regeneration in the adult central nerve system (CNS) has been a long-standing challenge in the field of regenerative neurobiology, where the general consensus calls for an integrated approach that combines hydrogel scaffolds, nerve guidance channels, and spatiotemporally controlled delivery of cells and biomolecules to promote axon growth. Here we propose an approach that combines directed evolution, cofactor engineering and synthetic biology to create a near-infrared (NIR) light-responsive protein hydrogel. Such a gel might enable guided 3D axon elongation. We will leverage a previously reported photo-responsive protein hydrogel system that comprises polymerized photoreceptor CarHC proteins. These protein polymers undergo a liquid-to-solid phase transition upon addition of the photo-labile cofactor, adenosylcobalamin (AdoB12) and solid-to-liquid phase transition when exposed to green light. To shift the photo-responsiveness to the near-infrared, we will design and synthesize several NIR-sensitive AdoB12 derivatives. The photoreceptor protein CarHC will also be engineered through directed evolution to accommodate the altered cofactors and maintain its photo-responsiveness. The engineered proteins will be covalently stitched together to form linear (injectable liquid) polymers using genetically encoded click chemistry. The polymers will be further assembled into a hydrogel (an elastic solid) upon addition of a small-molecule cofactor. Through the combined use of genetic engineering, photo-micropatterning and orthogonal genetically encoded click chemistry, these hydrogels will be designed to contain micro-channels as well as biomolecules needed for guided cell behavior, axon growth or immunomodulation. Given the spatiotemporal control over their mechanical and biochemical properties, the proposed photo-responsive protein hydrogels will not only offer a versatile platform to study biological processes such as axon elongation in the CNS, but may also serve an injectable, optically controlled delivery/release system with minimal invasiveness for new therapies including the treatment of spinal cord injuries (SCI). This proposed research, if successful, will represent a paradigm shift in designing smart materials for CNS axon regeneration as well as regenerative medicine in general. 軸突再生一直是再生神經生物學領域的重大難題。本項目將結合小分子合成，蛋白質工程和合成生物學以構建近紅外光響應的蛋白質水凝膠並實現其對神經幹細胞的調節。水凝膠將由感光體CarHc蛋白質的分子網絡組成。CarHc的天然輔酶因子AdoB12對綠光敏感。在光照下,CarHc會由四聚體變為單聚體。為實現更好的生物兼容性，我們將設計並合成對近紅外光敏感的輔酶因子衍生物,然後通過定向進化來改造蛋白質以適應輔酶因子衍生物,進而通過諜化學聚合合成水凝膠。 這些水凝膠將含有軸突生長所需的促進因子等各種生物信號。我們會進一步利用原位近紅外光圖案化等手段在其內部創造機械性能和生化信號不同的微通道以誘導軸突生長。這些光響應水凝膠將提供一個多功能的平臺來研究幹細胞-基質相互作用和軸突再生。

16103519.label: Realisation of objectives
16103519.value: To achieve the objectives of this project, we used a combination of directed evolution, cofactor engineering, synthetic biology, and genetically encoded click chemistry. We started by developing NIR light-responsive proteins through protein engineering. We developed several variants of CarHC protein that can be modified through thiol-maleimide click chemistry with fluorescent groups. The modified proteins exhibited responsiveness towards red or NIR-light without the use of chemically modified AdoB12, reducing the phototoxicity of CarHc photodynamic activation. Once we had developed the NIR light-responsive proteins, we moved on to the second objective, which was to synthesize and characterize NIR light-responsive protein hydrogels. We used genetically encoded click chemistry and small-molecule induced protein oligomerization to synthesize the hydrogels. Rheological tests were performed to examine the viscoelastic properties of the materials. The third objective was to micro-pattern the hydrogels mechanically and biochemically with light to guide 3D cell behavior and axon growth in vitro. We used microfluidics to create microchannels within the hydrogel scaffold and decorated them with biomolecules such as RGD cell-binding ligands and leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF) using orthogonal genetically encoded click chemistry. The resulting materials were used to examine their influence on axon elongation of adult dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons in vitro.

16103519.label: Major findings and research outcome
16103519.value: We were able to develop several variants of CarHC protein that could be modified through thiol-maleimide click chemistry with fluorescent groups. The specific amino acid substitutions and reaction conditions were determined, and the resulting modified proteins were found to be responsive to long-wave-length (red or NIR) light (Journal Paper #3 Yang et al Science Advances 2022; Other impact: Fok et al. Chinese Patent, Filed, 2023). We were also able to synthesize and characterize NIR light-responsive protein hydrogels with tunable mechanical and biochemical properties. The hydrogel synthesis involved the combined use of genetically encoded click chemistry and small-molecule induced protein oligomerization (Journal Paper #1: Jiang et al Science Advances 2020). Rheological tests were performed to examine the viscoelastic properties of the materials, and bioactive proteins fused with SpyTag were produced and used to decorate the protein networks. Finally, we were able to micro-pattern the hydrogels mechanically and biochemically with light to guide 3D cell behavior and axon growth in vitro. The resulting materials were used to examine the combined influence of mechanical and biochemical signals on axon elongation of adult dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons in vitro.

16103519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16103519.value: The materials developed offer a versatile platform to study biological processes such as axon elongation in the CNS and may also serve as an injectable, optically controlled delivery/release system with minimal invasiveness for new therapies, including the treatment of spinal cord injuries (SCI). The proposed course of action could involve further studies to optimize the hydrogel synthesis and micro-patterning techniques, as well as in vivo studies to assess the efficacy of the hydrogels for targeted delivery and in situ dynamic modulation of the microenvironment. We will assess the injectability of protein hydrogels and their ability to deliver axon-growth promoting biomolecules and neural stem cells into spinal cord injury sites using mouse models. The mix of protein polymers and cells (liquid) will be injected toward SCI lesion sites, followed by injection of the cofactor, AdoB12 or its derivatives, to trigger the gelation in situ. Several criteria including viability of transplanted NSCs, regeneration of impaired host axons, and functional recovery will be used to gauge the efficacy of the materials.

16103519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16103519.value: The development of near-infrared light-responsive hydrogels that enable targeted delivery and in situ dynamic modulation of the microenvironment can provide solutions to a variety of problems facing regenerative biology/medicine. The combination of directed evolution, cofactor engineering, synthetic biology, and genetically encoded click chemistry used in this project has shown great promise in developing a near-infrared (NIR) light-responsive protein hydrogel that can be used for targeted delivery and in situ dynamic modulation of the microenvironment. The hydrogels developed in this project have tunable materials properties and can be micro-patterned mechanically and biochemically with light to guide 3D cell behavior and axon growth in vitro. These hydrogels offer a versatile platform to study biological processes such as axon elongation in the CNS and may also serve as an injectable, optically controlled delivery/release system with minimal invasiveness for new therapies, including the treatment of spinal cord injuries (SCI). This project represents a paradigm shift in designing smart materials for CNS axon regeneration as well as regenerative medicine in general.
