16203319.label: Major findings and research outcome
16203319.value: Integrating classification information as extra constraints within a weakly-supervised domain adaptation framework for MI segmentation poses a fundamental and challenging task. Our research addressed a range of perspectives, stemming from the practical challenges encountered in clinical settings. These include multi-source decentralized MI classification based on federated learning, development of an adaptive pruning Transformer for MI segmentation, enhancing representation learning for semi-supervised MI segmentation, and investigating uncertainty consistency and variational model ensembles for semi-supervised deep regression tasks. We successfully developed a series of innovative methods and achieved several state-of-the-art results with publications in top-tier journals and conferences. Firstly, we enhanced feature robustness learned from weak supervisions across different clients without sharing data. Observing that the federated model diverges at the classifier layer due to inter-client variations, we proposed a customized federated learning framework addressing this issue by regularizing the feature extractor learned at each client through feature alignment and recalibrating the classification layer at each client according to its characteristics. Secondly, we tackled the problems of daunting computational complexity, high computational costs, and redundant contextual dependency in Transformer-based MI segmentation, which have been largely overlooked in existing research. We proposed employing adaptive pruning to transformers for MI segmentation and introduced a lightweight network architecture called APFormer. Thirdly, we proposed an innovative two-stage learning framework for semi-supervised MI segmentation as an alternative to existing state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation methods that predominantly depend on pseudo supervision directly on predictions. Our approach emphasizes feature representation learning with both labeled and unlabeled images, allowing regularization of a more compact and better-separated feature space, facilitating low-density decision boundary learning, and ultimately enhancing segmentation performance. Lastly, we addressed the challenge of uncertainty estimation, which can be unreliable and unstable, especially in regression problems. We employed heteroskedastic regression loss for uncertainty estimation in regression tasks, involving joint estimation of the target label and the associated uncertainty value. Due to absence of ground-truth labels for uncertainty, these estimates can be unreliable and unstable. We observed that aleatoric uncertainty, which is solely associated with input data, should remain consistent for identical inputs, despite unknown true values. As a result, we enforced consistency between uncertainty estimates from co-trained models as an auxiliary training signal. More reliable uncertainty estimates enable better loss weighting, focusing model training on high-quality pseudo-labels. Our findings demonstrated that uncertainty consistency can efficiently enhance the quality of uncertainty estimates on pseudo-labels and improve training for other semi-supervised learning methods.

16203319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16203319.value: 1. Investigate the weakly-supervised domain adaptation federated learning framework in more complex clinical scenarios, such as those with noise or image occlusions, to enhance the model's adaptability in challenging real-world situations. 2. Develop efficient Transformer models for MI segmentation targeting edge computing devices, to alleviate the current requirement for expensive GPUs or cloud computing resources. By leveraging edge computing devices, we can significantly improve real-time image processing and patient privacy preservation in clinical research tasks. 3. Research more robust and generalizable semi-supervised MI segmentation models to further reduce the reliance of current MI processing machine learning models on labeled data, making the models more applicable in scenarios with limited annotations. 4. Develop methods for improving pseudo-label quality that are independent of specific learning models and datasets. These methods would not only benefit semi-supervised learning tasks but also extend their applicability to other weakly-supervised tasks, broadening their impact across various domains.

16203319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16203319.value: This research project presents a groundbreaking weakly-supervised domain adaptation framework for medical image (MI) segmentation, significantly improving the accuracy and efficiency of analyzing complex MIs. By incorporating classification information as extra constraints, the framework addresses real-world clinical challenges, such as data privacy and domain variations between clients, by implementing innovative techniques like federated learning and adaptive pruning Transformer models. The project's success in enhancing segmentation performance while maintaining data privacy and reducing computational complexity has far-reaching implications for the medical image analysis community. Improved MI analysis can lead to more accurate diagnoses, better treatment planning, and ultimately, improved patient outcomes. Besides, the framework's adaptability to various medical datasets and potential for extension to different types of medical data, such as X-ray images, fundus images, and surgical videos, showcases its versatility and broad applicability. In summary, the research project's innovative approach to MI segmentation not only contributes to the advancement of MI analysis techniques but also holds great promise for improving patient care by enabling more accurate and efficient diagnosis and treatment planning across various medical imaging modalities.

To design a parallel decoding scheme that can support more concurrent data streams than the number of antennas in backscatter networks. To design an affordable energy estimation scheme for the backscatter tags. It should not noticeably increase the energy consumption, cost, and complexity of the tags. 16203719.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16203719.value: With the latest advances in the Internet of Things (IoT), a new era has begun in the smart city domain, which opens up new opportunities for the development of applications that aim to improve the quality of life in cities. Although the total global worth of IoT technology is predicted to reach USD 6.2 trillion by 2025, energy consumption for wireless communication is a serious obstacle to this optimistic forecast. Backscatter communication is a promising solution to solve the energy burden, however, this technology is still limited in transmission range. Over the past couple of years, several efforts have been undertaken to design long-range backscatter communication, which could potentially open up new frontiers for IoT. However, backscatter tags do not have the capability to sense other tags’ on-going transmissions, which leaves multiple access control as an issue. In this project, we propose discussing multiple access control in long-range backscatter networks, which could consist of a vast number of tags dispersed over a large geographical area. We will explore the opportunity for multiple antennas at the receiver side and enabling parallel decoding for concurrent backscatter uplinks. Multiple antennas have been widely adopted in the IEEE 802.11ac/11ax and 4G/5G systems to increase the channel capacity. However, it is not easy to exploit multiple antennas in backscatter communication. The receiver in MU-MIMO requires the channel coefficient of each individual tag to decode the collided signals. This will increase the complexity of tags and incur coordination overheads. Moreover, in multiple-antenna systems, it is necessary for the number of concurrent links be no more than the number of receiving antennas. As the number of tags is usually large, it is not practical to have a large antenna array on the same scale as the number of tags. In this project, we will first consider the multiple access control for tags under one signal helper. We will explore the opportunity for multiple-antennas and the frequency agnostic property of backscatter tags to boost the throughput, combining both spatial and frequency domain diversity. Then we will discuss medium access control with multiple signal helpers in a large area. We will take advantage of the frequency-shifting capability on tags to decouple backscattered signals from different signal helpers and alleviate inter-cell interference. Our proposed research will enable IoT devices to be connected in an ultra-low power and long-distance manner, resulting in ubiquitous connectivity in smart cities, which has tremendous technological and social significance. 随着物联网（IoT）的最新进展，智能城市领域进入新的时代，为应用程序的开发开辟了新的机会。虽然预计到2025年物联网技术的全球总价值将达到6.2万亿美元，但无线通信的能源消耗是这一乐观预测的严重障碍。反向散射通信是解决能量负担的很有前景的解决方案，然而该技术在传输范围内仍然受到限制。在过去的几年中，学术界已经做出了一些努力来设计远程反向散射通信，这可能为物联网开辟新的发展。但是，反向散射标签无法感知其他正在进行的标签传输，这使得多标签访问控制成为一个问题。在这个项目中，我们提出了远程反向散射网络中的几种访问控制，讨论如何读取分散在较大地理区域上的大量标签。 我们将探索接收器侧多个天线的机会，并为并发反向散射上行链路启用并行解码。我们知道，今天在IEEE 802.11ac / 11ax和4G / 5G系统中广泛采用多个天线以增加信道容量。然而，在反向散射通信中利用多个天线并不容易。 MU-MIMO中的接收器需要每个单独标签的信道系数来解码冲突的信号。这将增加标签的复杂性并导致协调开销。而且，在多天线系统中，并发链路的数量是必要的。由于标签的数量通常很大，因此使用大型天线是不实际的。在这个项目中，我们将首先考虑一个信号助手。我们将探索多天线和频率复用的机会。然后我们将讨论在一个大的区域，如何利用频移功能来解耦来自不同信号助手的反向散射信号，并减轻小区间干扰。 我们提出的研究将实现超低功耗和长距离的方式，从而在智能城市中实现无处不在的连接，具有巨大的技术和社会意义。

16203719.label: Realisation of objectives
16203719.value: All the objectives proposed in this project had been achieved. 1) Explored how to enable concurrent backscatter communication using antenna arrays. The design paradigm for backscatter tags is to make tags as simple as possible. However, such a design principle leads to the prevalence of signal collision as tags cannot sense other tags' ongoing transmissions. Thus, medium access control for backscatter tags becomes a bottleneck. Although there are several existing approaches to enable a concurrent transmission in backscatter networks, they all suffered from the fact that channel capacity is limited in low SNR scenarios and is insufficient to support multiple concurrent data streams. In this project, we bring in antenna arrays to boost the channel capacity. We propose a system that can explore the opportunity of multiple antennas at the receiver side and enable scalable parallel decoding for concurrent backscatter uplinks. We leave tags as simple as possible and push the decoding complexity to the receiver side. Tags with data in the transmission buffer will start sending the uplink data freely and the receiving antenna array will perform parallel decoding. We implement the proposed system on USRP software-defined radios with a 4-antenna linear array. The experimental results show that we can enable up to 20 tags transmitting concurrently. 2) Explored how to leverage the reflected signals from the ambient smart environment to eliminate the requirement of bulky antenna arrays for accurate sensing (use localization as sensing example). Device-to-device (D2D) localization has achieved submeter localization accuracy, the basic idea of which is to leverage a large antenna array of the devices to extract the fine-grained physical-layer signatures. Nevertheless, the cost of such an infrastructure makes its realization expensive and unachievable. Fortunately, with the development of low-cost backscatter communications, new opportunities have emerged. In this project, we have our own observation. When a target is communicating with the receiver, the rich reflected signals from the ambient smart environment can be exploited to eliminate the need of bulky antenna arrays and sense the target. Specifically, the large number of backscatter tags in the smart environments can be used to form tag arrays. Then, the incident signal launched from a single-antenna device goes across the tags in an array will lead to the phase shift among the tags. Accordingly, the phase shift can be exploited to create the direction signatures, making the receiver enable to identify the direction from the transmitter to the tag array. As a result, our proposed scheme can localize the target by combining multiple arrays. We prototype our proposed scheme with two single-antenna Intel NUCs with off-the-shelf Intel 5300 WiFi cards and customized low-cost backscatter tags to evaluate our system in various environments. Our experimental results show that even when we construct the tag array by using only four tags, our proposed scheme can achieve a median localization error of 0.82m, which is acceptable for many applications in smart home and smart business. 3) Explored how to secure IoT devices by exploiting backscatter propagation signatures. The minimalist design of IoT devices is like the two sides of a coin: it enables IoT devices to communicate with low power while making IoT devices easily bear the risks of active attacks during devices pairing or data transmission. Many attempts to defend against attackers for wireless devices have been extensively studied during the past several years. Fine-grained physical-layer signatures, such as angle of arrival, channel state information and received signal strength have received much attention to mitigating these threats. However, these systems require at least two antennas or a large antenna array (e.g., an eight-antenna array) to construct sensitive signatures, and thus are not applicable for the systems where the APs and IoT devices are equipped with only a small number of antennas. This project presented ShieldScatter, a lightweight system to secure IoT device pairing and data transmission. Our key insight is that backscatter tags, communicating based on reflecting ambient signals, can be exploited to intentionally create fine-grained multipath signatures. We observe that, even though the IoT device is attacked by a powerful attacker who can create wireless channel signature to spoof the AP, the propagation signatures created by the backscatter tags can be used to construct a unique profile to identify the device. This unique profile then confirms whether these two signals are from the legitimate IoT device and help defend against active attacks. Moreover, when there are multiple APs, we combine all of them to construct a more stable profile to detect the attacker. We prototype ShieldScatter with USRPs and ambient backscatter tags to evaluate our system in various environments. The results show that even when the powerful attacker is close to the legitimate device, ShieldScatter can mitigate 95% of attack attempts while at the same time triggering false alarms on just 7% of legitimate traffic. 4) Explored how to improve the spectrum efficiency for Low-power Wide Area Networks (LPWAN) for IoT devices by exploring Partially Overlapping Channels. Recently, LPWAN becomes a promising networking paradigm for connecting billions of low-power IoT devices. Among which, Long-range WAN (LoRaWAN) is one of the most representative LPWAN technologies, which serves a large volume of coexisting IoT devices, and thus gained tremendous attention. However, the IoT devices can send data over one-hop uplink to an LoRaWAN gateway, resulting in more collisions in a larger coverage area within the same spectrum. Dynamic spectrum management (DSM) plays an important role to improve spectral efficiency. In this project, we propose a novel deep-learning-based spectrum sharing paradigm that explores partially overlapping channels (POC) for concurrent spectrum access in LoRaWAN. We proposed an Intelligent Overlapping paradigm to strategically leverage the extra coding redundancy in the existing error correcting codes (ECC) to enable low-power IoT device coexistence on POC. 5) Explored how to design the backscatter tag's signal and construct sensitive propagation profiles to secure industrial IoT robots. With the development of Industry 4.0 and Internet of Robotic Things concept, wireless devices have been widely deployed in the industrial robot area. However, industrial robots are reportedly suffering from serious active attacks due to cyber vulnerabilities. In this project, we present RobotScatter, a non-intrusive system that intentionally attaches several tiny and low-cost backscatter tags to the robot’s arm to defend again active attacks, such as man-in-the-middle attacks and replay attacks. The key insight of RobotScatter is that the propagation signatures of the tags significantly rely on the movement of the robot's arm, which are captured and fused by the nonlinear effect of RF circuits at the receiver, and thus can be extracted to detect the robot movement. The foundation of RobotScatter is to extract propagation features from the fused propagation caused by the nonlinear effect of the RF circuit. We extract unique amplitude and phase signatures from the second-order harmonic to construct robot movement profiles to defend against attacks. We implement RobotScatter on two common robotic platforms, Universal Robot and iRobot Create, using commercial LoRa chips SX1276, a diode nonlinear circuit, and several customized backscatter tags, and evaluate our system in a variety of environments. The experimental results show that RobotScatter achieves a high overall accuracy of 97.7%, and detects up to 94% of anomalies against small movement deviations of 10mm/s in velocity, and 2.6cm in distance.

16203719.label: Major findings and research outcome
16203719.value: IoT devices have been widely deployed as one important building block in smart homes, intelligent factories, and even smart cities. Backscatter communication is an ultralow-power paradigm, consuming several microwatts of power. With backscatter communication, millions of low power, or even battery-free IoT devices can be connected to the Internet. With this ubiquitous connectivity, a number of interesting applications are blooming. The design paradigm for backscatter tags is to make tags as simple as possible. However, such a design principle leads to the prevalence of signal collision as tags cannot sense other tags' ongoing transmissions. In this project, we explore the multiple antenna opportunity in backscatter networks. We bring in antenna arrays to boost the throughput in backscatter networks. We propose FreeScatter, which enables scalable parallel decoding by combining the spatial domain and frequency-domain diversity, overcoming the limitation of antenna numbers. Enabling Device-to-device (D2D) localization without the additional infrastructure to deploy would support a range of important applications. With the development of low-cost backscatter communications, new opportunities have emerged for the design of single-antenna D2D localization. In this project, we develop TagLoc, a lightweight system that enables D2D localization without relying on large antenna arrays. Our observation is that the reflected signals from the ambient environment can be exploited to eliminate the requirement of bulky antenna arrays that are unachievable for the simple-designed IoT devices. The minimalist design makes IoT devices vulnerable to many attacks. Recent advances use an antenna array to extract fine-grained physical-layer signatures to identify the attackers, which adds burdens in terms of energy and hardware cost to IoT devices. In this project, we present ShieldScatter, a lightweight system that attaches low-cost backscatter tags to single-antenna devices to shield the system from active attacks. The key insight of ShieldScatter is to intentionally create multi-path propagation signatures with the careful deployment of tags. These signatures can be used to construct a sensitive profile to identify the location of the signals’ arrival, and thus detect the threat. The openness of wireless medium exposes robots to the threats of Sybil attackers. In this project, we present ScatterID, a lightweight system that attaches backscatter tags to single-antenna robots to defend against Sybil attacks. ScatterID actively “manipulates” multipath propagation by using backscatter tags to intentionally create rich multipath features obtainable to a single-antenna robot. These features are used to construct a distinct profile to detect the real signal source.

16204019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16204019.value: In this project we will employ our recent achievements in topological photonics to realize topologically protected interlayer communications. Our approach could relax fabrication requirement for multilayer photonic circuits and ensure a low reflection for interlayer couplings, which is crucial for efficient signal processing. Its basic principle is summarized as follows: Photonic valley-Hall phases, which were recently discovered in topological photonics, could induce valley-projected back-scattering immune edge states whose propagations is robust against various impurities and defects. If a layer pseudospin is introduced, which mimics the spin of electrons in quantum mechanics, the topological edge states could become layer polarized and the layer polarization could be reversed if we introduce adequate interlayer couplings which mimic the famous Zeeman effect. Based on this effect, smooth and reflection-suppressed interlayer communication becomes possible. The proposed project aims to apply the most recent topological structures to photonic communications. It has at least the following two important features: 1) Topological structures can be easily integrated into photonic devices. We will adopt and adapt our previously researched designer surface plasmon (DSP) crystals . These DSP crystals are straightforward to fabricate and feature planar structures, which can ease the integration with existing photonic systems. DSPs, similar to the famous surface plasmons in optics but occur in much lower frequency regimes, have become one of the emerging platforms for future photonic communications owing to their unique advantages, such as tightly bound fields, structural flexibility, and low propagation losses. 2) The project will apply topological protection to interlayer communications for the first time. Previously, interlayer communications in multilayer photonic circuits are based on geometrically optimized three-dimensional structures , and their fabrications require complicated processes and has strict requirements. In contrast, our structure based on DSP crystals are planar in nature and the topological protection guarantees a robust transmission performance against possible fabrication defects. 我們將利用我們最近在拓撲光子學方面取得的成果實現拓撲保護的層間通信。我們的方法可以簡化多層光子電路的製造要求，並確保層間耦合的低反射，這對於信號處理至關重要。其基本原則概述如下： 最近在拓撲光子學中發現的光子谷 - 霍爾相可以誘導谷投射的反向散射免疫邊緣狀態，其傳播對各種雜質和缺陷是穩健的。如果引入層贗自旋，即模仿量子力學中的電子自旋，則拓撲邊緣態可以變為層極化，並且如果我們引入塞曼效應足夠的層間耦合，則層極化可以反轉。基於該效果，可以實現無衰減的信號層間連通。 我們將採用和設計我們之前的研究結果及（DSP）晶體。這些DSP晶體具有簡單的平面結構可以簡化與現有的光子系統的集成。 DSP類似於光學中著名的表面等離子體，可以在很低的頻率範圍內產生，由於其獨特的優勢，例如緊密束縛的場，結構靈活性和低傳播損耗，實現成為未來光子通信的新興平台之一。 以前，多層光子電路中的層間通信基於幾何優化的三維結構，並且它們的製造需要復雜的工藝並且具有嚴格的要求。相比之下，我們基於DSP晶體的結構本質上是平面的，並且拓撲保護保證了可靠的製造缺陷的穩健傳輸性能。

16204119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16204119.value: Lately, Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have received considerable attention due to the explosive growth of data generated by various sources, the increasing interest for novel processing tasks and their versatile abilities in problem solving. A recent innovative work proposed the concept of learned indexes for one-dimensional range query processing in databases. A learned index replaces the intermediate nodes of a conventional index with a hierarchy of models, where each model is an ANN, or some other machine learning technique. Experiments with various datasets suggest significant improvements with respect to efficiency and space consumption compared to B-trees, the de-facto index for one-dimensional ranges. In this proposal, we apply and extend this concept to learned spatial indexing. We believe that spatial indexes could benefit greatly from the application of machine learning for several reasons. (1) Spatial query processing is inherently more complex and expensive than one-dimensional ranges. Accordingly, ANNs could provide higher speed-ups. (2) Multidimensional structures are larger than conventional indexes, and therefore they present more opportunities for size minimization. (3) There are multiple spatial query types in different temporal contexts that could take advantage of alternative machine learning techniques. (4) Finally, ANNs are well suited for several spatial information processing tasks, such as handling uncertainty of location updates, and predicting future positions. We first propose a learned spatial index for query processing at the current time, and demonstrate how it can support most common spatial queries, including ranges and nearest neighbors. Then, we extend it to historical spatio-temporal processing, where queries also include a temporal aspect. Finally, we investigate location uncertainty and prediction of future positions based on past trajectory data. 近来，随着各种数据的爆炸性增长以及人们对新型处理任务兴趣的日益增加，人工神经网络（ANN）因其解决问题的多样性与通用性从而受到了人们极大的关注。 一项最近的创新工作中提出了学习索引的概念，其被提出用于数据库中一维范围的查询处理。学习索引利用具有层次的模型结构来替换常规索引的中间节点，其中每个模型为一个ANN网络或其他机器学习模型。与目前普遍采用的一维范围的索引算法B树相比，学习索引在多个数据集的实验中证明了其在效率和空间消耗方面有着显著的提升。在本项目中，我们将此概念应用并扩展到学习空间索引中。我们认为空间索引可以从机器学习的应用中获益很多，原因有以下几点。 (1)空间查询处理在本质上比一维范围的索引更复杂且高昂。因此，人工神经网络可以提供更高的加速。 (2)多维结构比传统索引更大，因此其为尺寸最小化提供了更多的机会。 (3)在不同的时间上下文中存在多种空间查询类型，这些时间上下文可以利用多种可替代的机器学习技术。 (4)最后，人工神经网络非常适用于几种空间信息处理任务，例如处理位置更新的不确定性问题以及预测未来的位置。 我们首先提出了当前时间查询处理的学习空间索引，并演示了其如何支持最常见的空间查询，如范围查询和最近邻居查询。然后，我们将其扩展到历史时空处理上，其中的查询还包括时间方面。最后，我们基于过去的轨迹数据来研究位置的不确定性以及对未来位置的预测。

16204119.label: Realisation of objectives
16204119.value: Our contributions regarding objective 1 include Waffle, a disk-based framework that auto-adapts to all spatial indexing purposes. Waffle includes (i) a novel bulk loading method that guarantees optimal disk page utilization and emphasizes square-like nodes; (ii) algorithms for dynamic updates that create non-overlapping nodes and (iii) a maintenance mechanism that monitors the query workload and distribution, continuously optimizing the index. Waffle combines concepts from space and data partition methods. Specifically, the bulk loading and dynamic update algorithms generate non-overlapping nodes, without causing top-down propagation of splits. As in the case of data partition indexes, the nodes do not have to cover empty space. The spatial extent of each directory node is a minimum bounding rectangle (MBR) that contains the combined extent of its child nodes. Waffle involves two parameters: data node capacity (C), and directory fanout (F). C is the maximum number of data points per data node. F is the maximum number of child pointers per directory node. Bulk Loading: Waffle bulk loads the data points using a two-step process. The first step creates the lowest level with the data nodes, assuming that initially there is a single data node N0 containing all data points, and a root R1 pointing to N0. To partition N0, we sort its points on the major dimension. After determining the split point S1, entries up to S1 in the sorted list are inserted to a new node N1, and the rest to N2. The MBRs of N1 and N2 are computed and inserted to R1, together with pointers to the new nodes and S1, while N0 is deleted. If either N1 or N2 contains more than C points, it is partitioned again. This recursive process continues until all data nodes hold at most C points and can fit on a disk page. The (possibly overflowing) root R1 stores (i) pointers to all data nodes, (ii) their MBRs, and (iii) a vector with the splits that generated these nodes in chronological order. The second step of bulk loading spans over multiple rounds. Starting bottom-up from level 1, each round splits an overflowing root, to create a new root at the next level. A round begins by checking if R1's fanout exceeds F, in which case R1 is split into two new directories D1 and D2 using the first split S1 stored in R1. The contents of R1 (i.e., pointers to child nodes and splits), except S1, are distributed to D1 and D2, depending on which side of S1 they lie. A new root R2 stores pointers to D1, D2 and their MBRs; S1 is inserted into the split vector of R2. If D1 and D2's fanout exceeds F, they are partitioned using their respective first splits. Split nodes are replaced in R2 with the new directories, and the splits that created them are kept in R2. The MBRs of the new directories are computed using the MBRs of their child nodes. Directory splitting and populating R2 continues until the fanout of all directories is at most F. If after the end of the round the fanout of R2 exceeds F, the process is repeated. Dynamic Updates: For disk-based indexes, the CPU-time of common queries is usually negligible compared to the disk I/O cost. Accordingly, they prioritize reducing the node accesses over optimizing directory traversal. For instance, during overflows, R*-Trees reinsert a subset of data points to improve the index structure and enhance the efficiency of future queries. However, frequent reinsertions may lead to slow updates on dynamic data sets. Also, a compact structure that maximizes dead space is counter effective to update-heavy workloads as nodes are expanded more often to fit the new data points. This leads to a vicious cycle of contractions (through reinsertions) and expansions especially when performing burst updates. In contrast, Waffle delays index optimizations until required by the query workload. Specifically, nodes that are often accessed by queries are re-organized more frequently than those that are prone to more updates. Consequently, different parts of the tree are maintained according to the workload in the corresponding part of the data space. Specifically, Waffle automatically adjusts the balance between node packing and update speed by locally bulk loading frequently queried nodes that deteriorate after updates. An extensive experimental evaluation in J1 verifies that Waffle outperforms all existing spatial indexes on common spatial queries, including ranges and nearest neighbours. Multi-version Waffle: Waffle is an ephemeral index because it manages spatial data at the current time. In the context of objective 2, we have developed MV-Waffle, a historical index based on the multi-version framework. MV-Waffle maintains a logical Waffle index per timestamp. Consecutive logical trees share common branches that are stored only once. We assume that physical deletions never occur. Instead, when a data point moves, a new version is created, and the old version is maintained, possibly indefinitely. Accordingly, past nodes remain a part of the index and pointers to their newer and older versions exist to facilitate query processing about any time in history. The temporal neighborhood captures the continuity between nodes in successive timestamps. Specifically, whenever a node N1 is version split to N2, N2 becomes the successor of N1. When the root of the last ephemeral Waffle splits, it corresponds to a new root at the current timestamp. We use a temporal estimator based on linear regression in order to find the Waffle roots responsible for processing historical spatio-temporal queries. Specifically, consider a point-timestamp query that retrieves the data point at location P at timestamp T. The temporal estimator outputs the last Waffle root created before T. Potential inaccuracies are handled by scanning the timestamps towards the direction of T. After the proper root has been found, P is fed to this root, and the point is retrieved using the corresponding ephemeral Waffle. Queries that involve intervals require duplicate elimination because the same node may be accessed multiple times (from different roots) and the same data point may be retrieved more than once. MV-Waffle eliminates this problem by visiting each node, only the first time it is encountered during query processing. In the context of objective 3, we use recent positions of data objects in order to predict their locations in the near future. We are exploring alternative approaches, such as exponential smoothing, applicable to different applications (e.g., ship movements versus network-constrained traffic). In addition, we are investigating the application of prediction models for handling inaccurate updates. For instance, if the last update received for a moving object differs substantially from the predicted position, this could signify an error and require special handling.

16204119.label: Major findings and research outcome
16204119.value: Spatial databases manage large data sets of objects with location information (e.g., GPS positions of smartphone users, vessel and aircraft coordinates). Due to the sheer volume of data, and since there is no natural ordering in multi-dimensional space, linear search for objects that satisfy some spatial predicate (e.g., airplanes in Hong Kong airspace, the nearest restaurant) is impractical. Thus, tree-based spatial indexes have been developed to efficiently filter and retrieve information. Although these indexes enable fast query processing, they are ineffective for highly dynamic data sets because updates may be very expensive due to extensive reorganization of the tree structure. Instead, simple grid-based solutions are often preferable to hierarchical indexes for update-intensive applications, despite their inferior query performance. Motivated by the query vs. update cost trade-off, we developed Waffle, a novel disk based spatial index, which delivers excellent performance and can accommodate both update- and query-intensive workloads. Waffle constitutes a complete indexing solution that includes efficient algorithms for bulk loading, dynamic updates and query processing. Our extensive experimental evaluation reveals that Waffle delivers excellent query and update performance for both static and dynamic data, whereas competitive spatial indexes, such as the KDB-Tree and the R*-Tree, fail in some settings. For static data, Waffle achieves the minimum number of data nodes through a fast bulk loading algorithm that avoids cascading splits. The output node extents have a desirable (i.e., square-like) shape that minimizes their average perimeter. For dynamic data sets, it automatically adjusts the balance between node packing and update speed. Depending on the setup, local bulk loading reorganizes subtrees of the index that deteriorate after updates. We have also developed a multi-version Waffle for maintaining the historical positions of moving objects. This structure consists of consecutive logical Waffle trees, covering disjoint time intervals. Given a spatio-temporal query, a temporal estimator returns the appropriate tree(s) covering the query's lifespan. Multi-version Waffle enables spatio-temporal queries in the past and the present (e.g., report all airplanes in Hong Kong airspace yesterday 1-2 pm). We are currently integrating prediction models in multi-version Waffle in order to enable queries in the future (e.g., based on their recent locations, which airplanes are expected to enter Hong Kong airspace within the next hour). We also investigate the utilization of the prediction models for handling update errors (i.e., when the last location update differs substantially from the prediction).

16204119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16204119.value: We are currently working on further optimizing Waffle. Specifically, all existing bulk loading methods, including that of Waffle, are based on repeated applications of external sorting, which is rather costly. Instead, we are experimenting with novel algorithms based on linear scan. Moreover, whereas Waffle, and the other methods, build the entire index at a single step, we investigate adaptive bulk loading, where the index is gradually built as a response to the query workload. The intuition is that only the parts of the data space that contain query results require a detailed structure. In this way, a query focused (as opposed to full) index can be created very fast. Regarding the multi-version framework, we are working on fine tuning its parameters in order to achieve a trade-off between data redundancy and query performance. Finally, we are exploring alternative spatial query processing tasks that are made possible by the maintenance of historical information in the index.

16204119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16204119.value: Spatial and in general multidimensional indexes are crucial for efficient query processing in several applications. Their importance can only increase due to the vast amounts of multidimensional data (e.g., coordinates, sensor readings) collected in an every day basis. Although there exists a plethora of spatial indexes in the literature, some of which are used in commercial products, they are focused on fast query processing, usually at the expense of update cost. Thus, they are ineffective for update-intensive workloads. In this project we developed Waffle, a complete indexing solution that integrates a novel bulk loading method, algorithms for dynamic updates, and a maintenance mechanism that automatically optimizes the index based on the query/update ratio, without any parameter tuning. A multi-version Waffle can be used to store the historical locations of moving objects and answer spatial queries in the past.

16204519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16204519.value: 丙型肝炎病毒（HCV）对大众的健康有着极大的危害。据统计，全球共有超过7000万人感染HCV，其中在中国有超过900万人感染HCV，并且HCV也是造成慢性肝病、肝硬化和肝癌的主要原因。在2017年，全球卫生组织（WHO）出台了第一项旨在2030年前根除HCV的计划。根除HCV的关键在于散发有效的抗病毒药物和研发有效的针对HCV的疫苗。 本项目旨在利用前沿的计算模型和机器学习算法，通过最近发布的多项生物数据库（例如基因序列数据，生物进化研究实验数据，病毒免疫实验数据等）来帮助实现疫苗研发的初级阶段，即旨在识别出能刺激肌体产生有效免疫反应的HCV表面抗原的位置。这项工作的难点在于HCV的表面蛋白的突变率很高，导致HCV能够逃脱机体免疫系统的攻击而不显著降低HCV在机体里的适应性。同时，HCV的上位效应也使得机体的免疫系统更难控制，即即使单个位点的突变会降低HCV在机体里的适应性，但HCV能通过其它位点的突变恢复其在机体里的适应性。 本项目将利用前沿的算法建立新的计算框架来模拟HCV膜蛋白（E2膜蛋白，免疫系统的主要目标）的适应性地形（即反应HCV在机体里的适应性）和HCV在机体里的进化过程。本项目最初由PI和合作研究员提出，利用信息论和统计物理学的理论成果建立模型模拟艾滋病病毒的适应性地形和对HCV一种亚型的初步研究，本项目将在之前的研究基础上进行。新的模型将使用2018年新发布的HCV E2膜蛋白数据训练，并使用公开的实验数据进行验证。 本项目计划提出的计算框架将能够识别HCV E2膜蛋白最易被免疫系统攻击的位点，并通过HCV的动态进化过程的研究预测免疫系统的有效性。由此，本项目计划提出的计算框架能给针对HCV的疫苗提供具体的能被疫苗成功攻击的HCV抗原位点。

16204519.label: Realisation of objectives
16204519.value: All key objectives have been successfully met. The project has produced numerous key contributions, leading to 8 journal publications, all in leading journals in computational biology, bioinformatics, and virus evolution. It has supported 2 Ph.D. students who have successfully defended their Ph.D. and found excellent jobs. Note that in the following, Objectives 1 and 2 and Objectives 3, 4, and 5 have been grouped together as they deal with construction and validation aspects of specific models. Objectives 1 and 2 aimed at developing and validating fitness landscape (FL) models for the E2 surface glycoprotein of HCV. Important contributions were made in this respect. A FL model was developed for HCV E2. This model was obtained by inferring a correlation-based probabilistic (maximum entropy) model using available patient-derived genetic sequence data. The general approach was described in [Journal Paper 1]. This paper was published in IEEE Potentials Magazine; a journal similar in scope to IEEE Spectrum, but with a focus on graduate engineering students. The approach described in [Journal Paper 1] was applied in [Journal Paper 2] (published in iScience) to infer an FL model for the E2 surface protein of HCV genotype 1b (one of the most prevalent genotypes of HCV globally). The accuracy of the FL model was established by checking its statistical properties (such as the low-order the moments) of the inferred model against those of the sequence data. Excellent model fit was established. In order to validate the FL model in terms of its ability to predict biological fitness, the model was assessed against independent fitness measurements reported in multiple in-vitro studies. Excellent prediction results were confirmed, returning Spearman correlations between fitness predictions and measurements of above 0.7. Further independent biological validation was also presented by assessing the correspondences between model coupling parameters and protein structural contacts, which again returned solid prediction results. These tests further confirmed the biological significance of parameters of the inferred model. Both of Objectives 3 and 4 were completely addressed. In [Journal Paper 2], evolutionary simulators were proposed for HCV E2. These incorporated the FL model described above into a Wright-Fisher-like evolutionary model from population genetics to describe the temporal evolution of viral quasi-species in a specific host. The model incorporated immune pressure imposed by antibody binding and neutralization. The parameters of the evolutionary model, such as effective population size and mutation rate, were selected in accordance with known values for HCV. A main purpose of the evolutionary model was to quantify and compare the expected time it takes for the virus to escape specific antibody responses. This is important since it can be used to determine which antibodies are the hardest to escape from, which can help to guide vaccine development. The model has been validated by comparing model-based predictions against independent clinical and experimental data. Specifically, data from known antibody escape mutations (observed in patients) was compiled, and the ability of the model to predict rapid escape relative to other mutations was confirmed. We also demonstrated that the predicted escape times for “buried” residues were considerably longer than for “exposed” residues, in line with biological expectations. Objective 5 was completely addressed. In [Journal Paper 2], evolutionary modelling was used to evaluate the expected escape times from a set of HCV “broadly neutralizing antibodies” (bnAbs) for which the binding footprint has been experimentally determined. Our results demonstrated that for a large majority of these antibodies, fast escape was possible. A selected subset of eight antibodies were identified as being particularly difficult to escape. Designing vaccines which seek to elicit these antibodies is therefore recommended, based on our analysis. In addition to the above objectives being addressed for HCV E2 protein, we also looked at two related problems within the umbrella of this project. We briefly describe them below: The first study focused on investigating the role of E1-E2 interactions in viral fitness and resistance to E2-specific antibodies. Using the same framework as Journal Papers 1 and 2, we developed a computational fitness landscape model called the joint model (JM) to capture the interactions between E1 and E2 proteins. The JM was compared to an independent model (IM) that considered E1 and E2 separately. In vitro infectivity data were used to assess the representativeness of JM and IM in capturing the intrinsic fitness landscape of E1E2. Incorporating the JM into an evolutionary model, we found that E1 plays a role in facilitating escape from E2-targeting antibodies. The study also identified potentially escape-resistant human monoclonal antibodies (HmAbs) against the E1E2 complex. These findings highlight the importance of understanding the interplay between E1 and E2 proteins in HCV infection, as E1 and E2 involve strong compensatory interactions. The study has been accepted for publication in Virus Evolution [Journal Paper 7]. In the second study, we examined the role of epistasis in conferring resistance to HCV drugs. Using globally prevalent HCV genotype 1a sequence data, we inferred a fitness landscape model for the NS3 protein, a target of HCV drugs, based on the framework used in Journal Papers 1 and 2. The model revealed that specific drug resistance mutations (DRMs), known as "SC-DRMs," were associated with strong compensatory epistatic interactions and enriched in NS3 drugs. Under selective pressure from drugs, HCV was more likely to acquire SC-DRMs compared to other DRMs. The number of SC-DRMs negatively correlated with the efficacy of each NS3-specific drug. Understanding epistatic interactions is crucial for studying resistance to current HCV NS3 drugs and developing new drugs targeting the NS3 protein. This study has been accepted for publication in Nature Communications [Journal Paper 8]. Furthermore, while T cells and T-cell based vaccines have not yet been considered for HCV in this project, closely related results have been achieved for other viruses such as COVID-19 . For COVID-19, bioinformatics methods were used, along with genetic data and immunological data for the related SARS virus, to quickly identify T-cell targets for COVID-19 vaccines. This work has had significant impact by guiding experimental studies to understand immune responses against COVID-19, and it has influenced the design of multiple commercial COVID-19 vaccines. This impact is described in more detail in Section 10 of this report. The initial publication in Viruses [Journal Paper 3] has been cited over 1300 times, while a web-platform for recommending vaccine targets was published in Nature Protocols [Journal Paper 4] and an updated webserver providing up-to-date information of COVID-19 T cells was published in Cell Reports Medicine [Journal Paper 6]. A subsequent review article was also provided in the medical journal Advanced Drug Delivery Reviews [Journal Paper 5], in a special issue focused on COVID-19 vaccines.

16204519.label: Major findings and research outcome
16204519.value: Below is a brief summary of the major contributions in this project: [Journal Paper 1]: This paper summarizes in detail how genetic sequence data can be used to guide vaccine design for highly mutable viruses like HCV and HIV. [Journal Paper 2]: This paper compared HCV subtypes 1a and 1b and found that the higher chronicity rate and disease severity associated with subtype 1b may be due to its ability to more easily escape antibody responses, suggesting differences in evolutionary constraints between subtypes as a factor in distinct disease outcomes. [Journal Paper 7]: This paper investigated the interplay between E1 and E2 proteins in HCV infection, revealing that E1 plays a role in facilitating escape from E2-specific antibodies and identifying potential escape-resistant antibodies against the E1E2 complex. [Journal Paper 8]: This paper focused on drug resistance in HCV and explored the role of genetic interactions in the NS3 protein. It discovered specific drug resistance mutations associated with strong compensatory interactions, highlighting the importance of understanding these interactions to develop effective treatments and combat drug resistance. [Journal Paper 3, 4, 5, and 6]: While this project did not specifically consider T cells and T-cell-based vaccines for hepatitis C virus (HCV), related studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of such approaches for other viruses, including COVID-19 [Journal Paper 3]. For COVID-19, bioinformatics methods were utilized, along with genetic and immunological data from the related SARS virus, to identify T-cell targets for COVID-19 vaccines, leading to significant impacts on experimental studies and the design of commercial COVID-19 vaccines [Journal Papers 3, 4, 6]. The initial publication in Viruses has been widely cited [Journal Paper 3], and subsequent articles were published in Nature Protocols and Cell Reports Medicine, providing recommendations and up-to-date information on COVID-19 T cells [Journal Papers 4, 6]. Journal Paper 3 was especially timely since we started this work on Jan. 15, 2020 when the first sequence of SARS-CoV-2 was publicly made available. By working day in and day out, we were able to perform research and submit this paper within 25 days. These works highlight the potential of bioinformatics and T-cell studies in vaccine development for various viral infections.

16204519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16204519.value: There are various avenues for further development. We briefly indicate a few such directions. Refinement of the proposed model can be achieved as more HCV genetic data becomes available. Computational methods can be developed to interpret the inferred landscape (which is extremely high dimensional) using approaches from statistical physics. These approaches, which seek to decompose the model landscape into its peaks and valleys and pathways between them, will help to provide further model validation, and may enhance our knowledge about the evolutionary dynamics of HCV E2. The work done in this project has so far demonstrated a model that is predictive of escape times for different antibodies. However, important work is still required for model validation, particularly in terms of its ability to predict the times required for virus to evade T cell responses. While the primary focus so far has been on antibodies, T cells are also important components of the adaptive immune system, and developing models that are predictive of T cell escape is important for rational vaccine design. In addition, the contributions made in this work to T-cell-based vaccine design, and associated bioinformatics platforms, provide a foundation for the T cell analysis and vaccine design for HCV.

16204519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16204519.value: In this project, the investigators focused on understanding various aspects of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, immune response, and drug resistance. They compared HCV subtypes 1a and 1b and found that the higher chronicity rate and disease severity associated with subtype 1b may be due to its ability to more easily escape antibody responses, suggesting differences in evolutionary constraints between subtypes as a factor in distinct disease outcomes. They investigated the interplay between E1 and E2 proteins in HCV infection, revealing that E1 plays a role in facilitating escape from E2-specific antibodies and identifying potential escape-resistant antibodies against the E1E2 complex. They then focused on drug resistance in HCV and explored the role of genetic interactions in the NS3 protein. They discovered specific drug resistance mutations associated with strong compensatory interactions, highlighting the importance of understanding these interactions to develop effective treatments and combat drug resistance. Overall, these findings contribute to the development of vaccines, therapies, and strategies for managing HCV infection and associated complications.

16204819.label: Project Objectives
16204819.value: To construct a framework that externalizes robot’s internal policy development states in LfD and creates an intuitive mapping to humans’ mental model of learning. To design motion-based transparency techniques that can communicate a robot’s mastery of policy in a reciprocal, user-friendly and unambiguous manner in three LfD scenarios: skill learning, task learning, and a hybrid of the two. To build simulation platforms for large-scale online experiments that allow researchers, industrial practitioners, and users to compare our motion-based transparency approach to state-of-the-art methods in various LfD scenarios, iteratively improving the proposed method. To develop tool suite and open-source software APIs such that the proposed approach can be tested by others and us in real-world LfD settings for iterative development.

16204819.label: Realisation of objectives
16204819.value: Upon the completion of this project, we realized the four key objectives. The research outcomes were demonstrated in four journal articles and four conference publications. In the progress report, we presented our approaches to meeting the first two objectives. In particular, regarding the first project objective, we employed the apprenticeship learning formalism to mathematically define and computationally model robot learning from demonstration (LfD). That is, a learner finds a policy Pi that performs better than or equal to an expert Pi_E (demonstrator/instructor) concerning an unknown reward function r(s, a) where s is the state and a is the action. Under this framework (RQ1.1 in the proposal), maintaining a transparent LfD process is translated into communicating the similarity between the learner’s current policy and that of the expert. The similarity can be measured by the distance between the state/action trajectory of the human demonstration and that reproduced by the robot student, which needs to be customized according to the actual skill/task to learn. With this mathematical model, we further got inspiration from human learning theory (RQ1.2) to explore how to determine the proper timing of transparency communication (RQ1.3 Configuration). More specifically, we learned from cognitive apprenticeship (CA), a situated learning theory that highlights collaborative social interaction and social construction of knowledge. Literature in this area suggested that virtual social signals (verbal or non-verbal) that follow social norms could achieve similar communication effectiveness as the real-world signals used in human-human teaching. In this project, our investigation revealed that gaze, gesture, and rhythm are viable signals to convey learning status and progress and providing such feedback during the demonstration is considered helpful for keeping the learning process transparent. To address the second project objective, we conducted a literature review and surveys with teachers and students to compile a comprehensive list of learning cues employed in teacher-student communication of the learning process (RQ2.2 the design space). In addition, we distilled the cues that are usually prioritized and how they could be sensed and expressed (RQ2.1 design requirements). We mapped these cues to a humanoid robot’s eye (head) and (upper) body motions. We then conducted a within-subjects user study in a simulation environment to investigate the possible influence of these different robot engagement cues on human users in comparison with a no-transparency cue condition. The results confirmed the effectiveness of our proposed design. As an extension to our original proposal which focuses on gesture-based communication of transparency in LfD, we also explore the use of text and casual visualization as means to infer and present the current learning status for robots/agents without a physical form. This is to verify the generality of our proposed concept of transparency in learning in a broader range of scenarios involving the collaboration between human users and artificial intelligence (AI) systems. To accomplish the third project objective, we developed an online human-robot teaching platform. It enables human instructors to perform a demonstration in front of a webcam, and the captured motions drive a skeleton-based human avatar to replicate the demonstration in front of a virtual robot student in a simulated environment (RQ3.1: LfD Simulator Development). Based on our designs and findings in Task 2, we further improved our approach to modeling adaptive expressions of robot engagement for transparent communication of robots’ learning status (RQ3.2: Iterative Improvement over Comparative Study). We revised and verified the design of two types of engagement expressions, namely gaze following and (behavioral) rhythm synchrony. We employed the normalized cumulative reward (NCR) as the LfD learning status indicator and computationally incorporated NCR into these engagement cues. It resulted in the Z2O-Mode (zero-to-one) and D2O-Mode (disorderly-to-orderly) of communicating dynamic learning progress. To address the last objective (Task 4: Public Release and Field Testing), we carried out an online user study using the simulation environment to investigate the effects of different engagement modes on users’ mental models of robots’ learning process and their perception of the overall teaching experiences. Our quantitative and qualitative results showed that the design of engagement expressions indeed affected human perceptions of robots’ learning status/progress, expected learning outcomes, intelligence, and acceptability, as well as human instructors’ self-assessment, self-reflection, teaching experience, and engagement. We also release the project page online for open access.

16204819.label: Major findings and research outcome
16204819.value: In the realization of Task 1, our journal article Journal Paper #2 presents our exploration of feedback timing and mechanism during situated, social learning. We compare how human users’ perception and behavior in the learning process could be affected by the three robot feedback conditions, i.e., immediate feedback, after-action feedback, and the combination of the two, conveyed through gesture, gaze, and speech. We developed a simulation platform and our user study results provide useful insights into the design of intelligent agents in apprenticeship learning. To accomplish Task 2, we constructed the design space and extracted the design requirements of verbal and non-verbal signals for maintaining transparency of the learning status and progress. We reported the findings in our conference paper Conference Paper #3. We learned that gaze behavior and upper body behavior are commonly used by instructors to infer students’ learning states such as engagement and confusion. Our second journal article titled Journal Paper #1 presented our proposed algorithms for transferring three types of engagement behavior (namely gaze following, gesture imitation, and both) to robots as a reciprocal cue of learning status to human instructors during LfD demonstrations. Experimental results suggested that all three cues impacted humans’ estimation of the robot’s learning progress and it is important to match the expression to the robot’s actual state. We also showcased that the proposed cues are applicable to other intelligent systems not in the form of humanoids. The related investigation led to one journal publication (Journal Paper #3) and three conference publications listed in Section C (text modality in Conference Paper #1 and Conference Paper #4 and visual modality in Conference Paper #2), as a supplement to enrich the application contexts of our approach. The research process and outcomes of Tasks 3 and 4 are documented in our Journal Paper #4. Our experimental result showed that it is feasible to convey a robot’s internal learning status through appropriate engagement cues in the process of robot learning from demonstration. In RLfD, robots’ instant reciprocal feedback can better motivate their instructors and reduce misunderstandings in the process. Our approach is expected to inspire novel designs of human-AI communication and transparency in broader contexts.

16204819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16204819.value: This research can be extended in several directions. 1) Exploring Alternative Learning Engagement Design. Besides eye gaze and rhythm, as suggested in our Task 2 findings, there are other engagement cues worth exploring, such as head nodding, head-scratching, hand raising, finger tapping, and body leaning, to name a few. We can further investigate the possible design alternatives to show the robot learning status by drawing insights from the common behaviors in human-human teaching and learning. 2) Extending our Approach to Other Forms of Robots and Types of LfD Tasks. The social cues exhibited by humans cannot be directly deployed on non-humanoid agents. We can extend the proposed designs to non-humanoid robots and goal-oriented tasks in which users focus more on the outcome than the process. 3) Extending to Other General Human-AI Interaction Scenarios. We can study how to transfer our proposed methodology to other modalities of human-AI interactions, such as via graphical interfaces and conversational interfaces.

16204819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16204819.value: For service robots to become an integral part of our lives, they need to have the ability to handle diverse, highly dynamic, and nondeterministic human environments. Robot learning from demonstration (LfD) is a paradigm that supports end-users with limited knowledge about robotics and/or programing to teach robots new skills or customize their functionalities to a new environment through demonstrations. Our project aimed to help human instructors form and dynamically maintain a good mental model of robot learners’ knowledge development in the LfD process through timely communication, allowing them to shape teaching accordingly. In other words, ensuring good transparency of robots’ state of learning is essential to reducing the workload of non-expert instructors and improving the flexibility and efficiency of LfD. We proposed to leverage social cues such as gaze, gesture, and rhythm for humanoid robots to reveal their learning status in LfD. We designed a novel approach to conveying a robot’s model training progress via common robot behavior (e.g., trajectory and pace of movements). We verified that our designs can help users master the robot’s learning progress more accurately, form a more positive perception of the robot, and have a better teaching experience.

16205619.label: Project Objectives
16205619.value: To develop a droplet microfluidic platform that generates and sorts droplets in high throughput, and gives precise control of the droplet composition, size and size uniformity. The microfluidic device will be coupled with a microscope and photomultiplier (PMT) detectors to allow in-line screening and measurement of the fluorescence signals from droplets. To identify and isolate exosomes with specific target proteins. Single-exosome enzyme-linked immunocomplexes will be randomly captured by magnetic beads and then encapsulated in droplets using droplet based compartmentalization technology. The droplets that encapsulate the target bead conjugates will be recognized and selected using reporter enzyme fluorescence and droplet sorting technology. Then, the isolated positive droplets will be pooled to retrieve the target exosome-bead complexes for further analysis of miRNAs within those individual exosomes. To detect and quantify specific target miRNAs in the isolated exosomes with identified proteins. Bead-exosome complexes and reagents for miRNA assays will similarly be encapsulated in droplets for single exosome analysis. The exosomes will be lysed in droplets and the target miRNAs will be amplified by real-time reverse transcription - polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), and quantified using imaging techniques. To evaluate the developed approach to analyze cancer-related biomarkers in individual exosomes using breast cancer serum samples. Exosome population distributions will be profiled according to the miRNA expression and protein signatures. The statistical information about single-exosome miRNA and protein signatures will be assessed in relation to the breast cancer subtypes and development stages.

16205619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16205619.value: 乳腺癌是女性中最常見的癌症，可以根據基因表達模式分為不同的亞型。早期監測和診斷癌症狀態對於正確治療和擊敗乳腺癌至關重要。最近，外泌體因其在癌症發病機制中的作用而備受關注。外泌體携带重要的生物標誌物并在血液和其他體液中循環。外泌體的功能由表面蛋白或由包裹的分子例如特定的小分子核糖核酸来反映。将外泌體携带的生物分子分類對於理解導致癌症侵襲和轉移是很有必要的。然而，在常規分析中常常只能得到样品的整体性息从而喪失了外泌體的个体和分子的差異性。於其外泌體低於100nm的尺寸，携带的信息複雜和群體異質性， 所以对單個外泌體逐一分析仍具有挑戰性。目前已有用於分析單個外泌體表面蛋白的新技術，但是还没有建立對單個外泌體水平的囊泡蛋白和核酸特徵的全面檢查。 我們在此提出一種基於液滴微流控平台用於開發單個外泌體分析的方法。該方法能夠探測由單個外泌體攜帶的生物分子的特徵。該系統將允許我們实现兩步過程分别对與膜蛋白和小分子核糖核酸的检测与分析。首先，基於泊松統計，外泌體將與磁珠綴合以形成用於特定膜蛋白靶向的單個外泌體酶聯免疫複合物，然後使用基於液滴微流控技術隨機打包封在液滴中。含有特定膜蛋白的外泌體-磁珠復合物的液滴將通過酶聯免疫測定識別並通過液滴分選技術選擇。合併分選出来的液滴以回收含有特定膜蛋白的外泌體，用於進一步分析其小分子核糖核酸。其次，將回收的外泌體-磁珠復合物用類似地包封在液滴中，用於在單個外泌體水平上進行小分子核糖核酸的測定。作為概念驗證研究，我們將將該方法應用於來自乳腺癌患者的外泌體样品进行外泌體亞型的分类。 我們期望所提出的單個外泌體分析方法可以建立更真實的多維視圖，以访问單個外泌體中的以前不可企及的信息。它將有助於闡明外泌體構建以及分析外泌體亞群在乳腺癌發展中的作用之間的功能關係，从而將極大地有益於乳腺癌的診斷，預後和治療。

16205619.label: Realisation of objectives
16205619.value: (1) Objective 1 was fully realized. A droplet sorting module has been integrated into the droplet generation and manipulation platform. The droplet sorting platform utilizes the fluorescent characteristics as feedback signal to sort droplet of interest, the mechanism adopted for the manipulation of droplets is dielectrophoresis which is fast in response and flexible in device design and fabrication. We have demonstrated fluorescent droplets containing targets can be separated from the waste droplets at a frequency of 50 Hz. This platform provides a very powerful tool for diagnosis and quantification of the following assays using extracellular vesicles (EVs). It is also applicable for a wide range of biological and chemical research. (2) Objective 2 was fully realized. We have developed droplet-based single-exosome-counting enzyme- linked immunoassay for identifying membrane protein biomarkers and digital quantification of the target exosomes. Using our droplet microfluidic platform, we were able to encapsulate single exosome complexes tagged with an enzymatic reporter that produces a fluorescence signal for detection. Using the droplet sorting system, we were able to select the positive droplets for further analysis of the sorted exosomes. (3) Objective 3 was fully realized. We developed a reverse transcription - polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) protocol on a droplet microfluidic platform for detection of microRNAs inside the exosomes. We captured exosomes on magnetic beads by ELISA and lyse exosomes by 0.2% Triton X-100 to for quantification of miR-21 in single EVs. (4) Objective 4 was fully realized. Collaborated with Nanfang Hospital, we performed clinical verification of the developed droplet digital PCR technology using breast cancer plasma samples. We applied a 4-plex detection assay to achieve more sensitive, accurate, and multiplex detection and quantification of mRNAs in exosomes. We applied a triplex droplet digital immuno-PCR (ddiPCR) assay for multi-subpopulation EVs counting through surface proteins profiling of individual EVs.

16205619.label: Major findings and research outcome
16205619.value: (1) We developed a 4-plex droplet digital PCR technology for simultaneous detection of four small extracellular vesicle (sEV)-derived mRNAs (PGR, ESR1, ERBB2 and GAPDH) for breast cancer diagnosis (J1, Biosensors and Bioelectronics, 2021), and a triplex droplet digital immuno-PCR (ddiPCR) assay for multi-subpopulation EVs counting through surface proteins profiling of CD9/CD63/CD81, HER2, EpCAM in a breast cancer cohort, and CD9/CD63/CD81, GPC-3, EpCAM in a hepatocellular carcinoma cohort (HCC) (J6, Chemical Engineering Journal, 2023). Droplet digital PCR achieved enough sensitivity, excellent stability, and applicability in clinic. (2) We applied Machine learning (ML) algorithms to improve breast cancer diagnosis. We evaluate the diagnsotic results with and without the assistance of the ML models. The results indicate that ML-assisted analysis exhibits higher diagnostic performance even using a single marker for breast cancer diagnosis, and demonstrate improved diagnostic performance under the best combination of biomarkers and suitable ML diagnostic model. (J1, Biosensors and Bioelectronics, 2021). (3) We designed a multiplexable injector which exploits a distinctive design comprising a circular electrode and a concentric fluidic channel to accommodate multiple injection ports for on-demand droplet injection and encoding. Droplet ingredients can be precisely injected via pressure pulse regulation. Through varying the fluorescence in droplets, binary coding and gradient coding are successfully demonstrated with droplet sequences. We also demonstrate that these color-coded droplets can be further collected and identified via an image analysis algorithm. This platform can potentially be used in applications such as multiplexed compound screening, combinatorial synthesis, or other multistep assays (J3, Sensors and Actuators B: Chemical 2022). (4) We developed a Picoinjection Aided Digital reaction unLOCKing (PADLOCK) approach utilizing droplet microfluidics to achieve droplet digital RPA (ddRPA) for absolute nucleic acid quantification. By coupling a microfluidic picoinjector with a droplet generator, the reaction initiator MgOAc is dosed into droplets containing MgOAc-deprived RPA master mix for controlled digital reaction unlocking, which completely circumvents premature amplification. The discretization of the targets to a single-molecule level in confined droplets endows absolute quantification of the copy number. Coupled with CRISPR/Cas13a sensing, the ddRPA demonstrates single molecule detection ability within 30 min with significantly enhanced signal-to-noise ratio (S/N ratio>6) and uniform fluorescence signal reporting, facilitating the precise quantification of nucleic acids (J2, Biosensors and Bioelectronics, 2022). This work is also included in our review paper (J4, Lab on a Chip, 2023).

16205619.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16205619.value: (1) The current droplet sorting system suffers from potential clogging problems that may lead to sorting errors. We will further improve the stability and accuracy of the droplet sorting platform. (2) The selected exosomes will be lysed to release the nucleic acids such as microRNA or mRNA for further analysis. The challenge is that the lysis buffer is not compatible with the reverse transcription or polymerase enzymes, we have employed a two-step process: complete lysis of exosomes in droplets in the first step, and injection of the amplification and detection reagents into droplets in the second step for final detection. This two-step process can be further optimized for a fully automated workflow.

16205619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16205619.value: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are phospholipid bilayer vesicles with a diameter of 30–2000 nm shed by almost all cells to the extracellular environment. Accumulating evidences indicate that EVs have enormous heterogeneity, not only in origin, size and morphology, but also in the various biomarkers secreted into EVs by parental cells. Many studies have shown that specific EV subpopulations based on the biomarkers (proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids) carried by EVs are more beneficial for cancer diagnosis. Moreover, the combined analysis of multiple subpopulations can greatly improve the diagnostic performance of cancer. Therefore, the development of new technologies for identifying these specific multi-subpopulation EVs from a group of heterogeneous mixed populations with the ability to analyze them quantitatively is highly desirable. We have developed droplet based microfluidic technologies to construct versatile assays for EVs profiling and quantification, and verified our method using breast cancer clinical samples. With the assistance of machine learning algorithm, our method exhibited great performance in differentiating breast cancer from healthy individuals. Therefore, this outcome of this project provides a promising strategy to count multi-subpopulation EVs at the single-vesicle level for cancer diagnosis.
