16301219.label: Major findings and research outcome
16301219.value: 1. We synthesize a single-layer 2D MOF and resolve the atomic structure of the Kagome Fe(II) lattice. The ground state comprises various degenerated spin configurations. Since realization of the Kagome antiferromagnetic (KAF) lattice is of high interest because the geometric frustration in the Kagome lattice is expected to give rise to highly degenerated ground states that may host exotic phases such as quantum spin liquid, this work points out a feasible route toward realizing spin 1/2 KAF, a candidate quantum spin liquid system. We also successfully synthesized 2D-piMOFs of Kagome Ni and Co lattices and investigate their spin properties. The first part of this work is published as J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 12, 3733 (2021). We are collaborating with the theory collaborators to complete the second part, which will be reported in a paper soon. 2. We grow single-layer two-dimensional (2D) cMOFs of M3(HAT)2, (M= Ni, Fe, Co). Using scanning tunneling microscopy and density-functional theory analysis, we resolve that the frameworks comprise a hexagonal lattice of HAT molecules and a Kagome lattice of metal atoms. The 2D frameworks are buckled to relieve the intermolecular steric hindrance. The DFT analyses show that Ni, Co and Fe carry a magnetic moment of 1.1, 2.5, and 3.7 mB, respectively. We anticipate that the small π-conjugated core of HAT and strong bidentate chelating coordination render appealing electronic and magnetic properties. We also successfully synthesized M3(HAT)2, (M= Ni, Cu, Co) on a graphite and a MoS2 surfaces and discovered that the inert substrate effectively decouple the 2D-piMOFs from the substrate. The first part of this work is reported in a publication Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. in press (2022). The rest part is reported in another paper under preparation. 3. We synthesize a two-dimensional Fe-coordinated bimolecular metal-organic framework which constitutes a honeycomb lattice and a Kagome lattice on a Au(111) substrate. Density-functional theory calculations show that the framework features multiple well-separated spin-polarized Kagome bands, namely Dirac cone bands and Chern flat bands, near the Fermi level. Using tight-binding modelling, we reveal that these bands are originated from two effects: the low-lying molecular orbitals that exhibit p-orbital characteristics and the honeycomb-Kagome lattice. This study demonstrates that p-orbital Kagome bands can be realized in metal-organic frameworks by using molecules with molecular orbitals of p-orbital like symmetry. This work is published as Communications Chemistry, 6, 73 (2023).

16301219.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16301219.value: Successful growth of 2D-piMOFs on inert substrates is of great significancy for future studies and applications because the intrinsic physical and chemical properties are largely preserved. In the next step, we plan to grow these structures on monolayer 2D materials to make composite heterostructures that may host exotic new properties.

16301219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16301219.value: Materials of single-atomic thick are of great potential to be used in future information and energy technology because of their unique physiochemical properties. We have demonstrated that a new type of single-atomic thick materials - 2D-piMOFs, is stable and can be synthesized and transferred to various platforms. This work has opened an avenue towards wide applications of this new type of materials.

16301319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16301319.value: 在流感病毒中，病毒RNA聚合酶（vPol）負責病毒基因組的轉錄和復制。該聚合酶與哺乳動物的聚合酶相比，由於其缺乏後者所具備的檢閱與校對機制，從而在病毒基因組的轉錄與復制過程中更容易產生錯誤，即擁有更高的基因突變率。然而，高突變率對病毒而言則意味著其在傳代過程中會增加其子代的遺傳多樣性，而遺傳多樣性的提升是病毒進化的主要驅動力。因此，了解vPol轉錄和復制的機制至關重要。 目前，尚缺乏關於病毒聚合酶轉錄方法學以及全基因組範圍內轉錄機制的研究。雖然先前研究者利用傳統的生物化學實驗方法揭示了個別轉錄現象的過程（如“帽狀結構捕獲”、多腺苷酸化和RNA編輯等），但是為了更加全面地揭示vPol如何讀取與翻譯基因組以及研究病毒調節及突變的分子起源，研究者仍需要開發壹種能夠精確映射vPol在全基因組範圍內分布的技術方法。 我們的目標是開發兩種全新的全基因組深度測序平臺（“病毒精準核內測序平臺”與“RNA聚合酶轉錄錯誤測序平臺”）來研究vPol的轉錄、突變和調控機制。目前研究病毒轉錄的技術僅僅可以捕獲病毒的成熟RNA，其中隱藏的轉錄機制的信息則無從得知。除此之外，判斷成熟RNA相對於基因組發生的變化是否由vPol導致則又是壹大難題。“病毒精準核內測序（ProV-seq）”技術可以將vPol在全基因組中的分布精確到單壹堿基對範圍（single base-pair）。而作為“ProV-seq”平臺的延續，我們隨後計劃開發“RNA聚合酶轉錄錯誤測序平臺”（rPOLE-seq）。其通過將ProV-seq與環狀測序（Cir-Seq）相結合，將RNA測序的準確度提高了1億倍，以完成對新生RNA中出現的轉錄錯誤的高精度偵測。我們使用酵母核醣體RNA作為樣本進行初步實驗，其結果證明了上述兩種測序平臺不僅可以在轉錄序列中以單壹堿基對為分辨率單位定位RNA聚合酶，而且能夠精準地計算出轉錄的錯誤頻率。與此同時，我們也發現了兩個特殊的現象：（1）聚合酶暫停位點附近屬於突變的高發區域；（2）新生RNA中的二級結構可以誘導轉錄活性位點的突變。 綜上所述，我們的工作為研究轉錄調節和vPol驅動的流感病毒突變機制提供了全新的觀點與方法。

16301319.label: Realisation of objectives
16301319.value: Aim 1: We developed a novel nascent RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) method, which is named EmPC-Seq using Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a model with preliminary results shown in the original grant proposal (Journal of Molecular Biology with PI as first author and grant collaborator John Lis as corresponding author). The underpinning experimental methodology was outlined in detail in our Bio-protocol paper (PI as corresponding author and John Lis as co-author). This protocol describes the steps to map RNA polymerases at base-pair resolution and identify TEELs. When applied to the yeast rRNA transcriptome, EmPC-Seq identified transcription error-enriched genomic loci (TEELs) within ribosomal DNA regions and discovered transcriptional errors are enriched at 3' ends of nascent rRNA transcripts. Building on this work, we adapted nascent RNA-Seq for a viral polymerase for the first time. Currently, nascent viral RNA-Seq remains unexplored due to great technical difficulties. After extensive testing with Biotin-NTPs on influenza A virus (IAV) RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP), we found much lower incorporation efficiency of Biotin-NTPs in RdRP than eukaryotic polymerases. Hence, we established a novel single-molecule viral nascent RNA-Seq with new bioinformatics pipeline for viral polymerases, named “STREP-Seq” (U.S. Provisional patent filed No. 63/606,365). STREP-Seq uses streptavidin affinity purification, whereby a Strep-tag viral RdRP is expressed in a live recombinant virus, allowing the enrichment of viral against host RNA and nascent against mature viral RNA by pull-down of transcribing RdRP complex. Also, we adapted a high-throughput Nanopore direct RNA sequencing platform to STREP-Seq which provides several advantages, particularly allowing direct sequencing of full-length single RNA molecules without reverse transcription and amplification. Therefore, the sense and position of the last nucleotide of RNA molecules can be easily pinpointed. Since nascent RNA lacks the poly(A) tail targeted by the Nanopore platform, we designed a custom DNA adaptor that allows direct ligation to 3’-end RNA nucleotides, thereby expanding its application to RNA-Seq of any RNA species. This work is published in BioRxiv and will be submitted to Nature for consideration. Aim 2: STREP-Seq provides valuable information that can only be captured by nascent RNA-Seq, such as revealing regulatory sequences for replication and transcription, elucidating mechanisms by which antiviral drugs act on viral replication in vivo, and unravelling viral adaptation via its replication machinery. We found that IAV polymerase pauses at regulatory sequences, thus pausing is not random. Highly reproducible pausing sites across three biological replicates were observed. By analysing the last nucleotide position, we identified transcriptional pausing sites in the 3' packaging signal region of all eight IAV segments in complementary and messenger RNA (c/mRNA). Surprisingly, we discovered that unlike yeast from our Journal of Molecular Biology paper, the most populated pausing sites in each segment were not mutational pausing. For all 8 segments, the percentage of correct vRNA sequence fell within the range of 96.82–100%. We speculated that one potential cause for transcriptional pausing is local RNA secondary structure barrier that RdRP encountered during transcription. We plotted the SHAPE-MaP reactivities for RNA secondary structures along the vRNA genome previously reported for influenza A/WSN/1933 (H1N1) (Nat Microbiol, 2019, 4(11), 1781) and compared with our c/mRNA pausing sites. We discovered that transcriptional pausing was driven by RNA structure but there could be exceptions. For PB2, PB1, HA, NA, M, and NS segments, the pausing positions were in the region with increasing RNA secondary structures. For the PA segment, the pausing position was located at sites immediately upstream and downstream of RNA secondary structures. Reassortment involves the exchange of gene segments between different IAV strains, leading to the evolutionary adaptation to jump species to humans and the emergence of new pandemic viruses such as that responsible for the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. We discovered that reassortant viruses exhibited different polymerase pausing spots along the viral genome compared to the control wild-type viruses. Aim 3: How IAV polymerase transcription affects genetic variation? Defective viral genomes (DVGs) are viral subgenomic materials with mutations, deletions, or gene rearrangements found in many viruses. DVGs have been found in many viruses and carry mutations, deletions, or gene rearrangements. DVGs with incomplete genetic information compete with full genomes as defective interfering particles. DIPs, viral particles with DVGs, replicate and package faster than “standard” particles with full-length genomes. Viral control of the DIPs subpopulation reduces virulence, promotes antiviral immunity, and increases host cell survival to improve transmission and virus persistence. With STREP-Seq, we observed lower internal gene coverages in PB2, PB1, and PA segments in viral RNA and similar defective segments in c/mRNA indicated DVGs in our system. IAV DVGs typically occurred in PB2, PB1, and PA genes and had a large internal deletion of gene segments while retaining packaging signals at 3'- and 5'-packing signals. Generated at a high MOI, they can hinder stranded virus replication. Though PB2 and PB1 DVGs had similar 3' and 5' regions, To elucidate the mechanisms of polymerase replication error, we treated IAV-infected cells with the nucleotide analogue antiviral drug Molnupiravir, which has been under great media and public health attention lately because it induces mutagenesis in the SARS-CoV-2 genome by converting one tautomer to another upon incorporation into the viral genome, leading to an overall error of G-to-A and C-to-U. The misincorporation of Molnupiravir in place of the correct NTP is known to be governed by the transcriptional fidelity of the polymerase. With STREP-Seq, we identified one dominant mutational site at each of the eight IAV c/mRNA segments (transcription/replication) and eight vRNA segments (replication). For c/mRNA, G-to-A mutation was observed in NP, NA, and M segments at three positions, and C-to-U mutation in PB2, PB1, PA, HA, and NS segments at five positions. For viral RNA (vRNA), G-to-A mutation was identified in HA, NP, and NA segments at three positions, and C-to-U mutation in PB2, PB1, PA, M, and NS segments at five positions. We did not observe the corresponding mutation at the template strand for all the mutation sites. One speculation is that during the 4-hour infection time, the majority of the IAV RdRP performs transcription using the original vRNA template to generate mRNA for protein synthesis instead of replication to generate cRNA, as such carry-on mutation in cRNA and vRNA generated by replication and the subsequent viral error catastrophe was not yet been reflected in the genetic pool. Strikingly, we discovered the existence of motifs that are more prone to error by analyzing template sequences upstream and downstream from the mutation position. For instance, all the G-to-A mutations in the three c/mRNA segments and three vRNA segments occur at the GGC (3’-5’) template motifs. While all C-to-U mutations in the five c/mRNA segments and three vRNA segments also occur at the correct AGA (3’-5’) template motifs, AGU and AGC motifs were also observed in two vRNA segments. It appeared that mutations are prone to occur after A or G in the template. Overall, we observed that IAV RdRP predominantly misincorporates Molnupiravir after a single A or G template sequence in transcription, and preferentially with GGC and AGA template motifs. The Nature Communications paper determined that IAV polymerase mutation dynamics can be useful to develop a predictive evolutionary model to forecast IAV strains and select vaccine strains for upcoming epidemic seasons.

16301319.label: Major findings and research outcome
16301319.value: Six publications resulting from this grant, including two related viral genomics papers in review in Cell (PartC8.no4) and Nature Communications (PartC8.no5). The Journal of Molecular Biology (PartC8.no1), Bio-Protocol (Part C 8.no2), and BioRXiv (PartC8.no6; to be submitted to Nature) papers demonstrated that all aims are completed. Journal of Molecular Biology and Bio-Protocol papers showcased a novel method EmPC-Seq that overcomes challenges in the transcription field and identified Transcription Error-enriched Genomic Loci (TEELs) from RNA sequencing data. EmPC-Seq integrates PRO-seq, Cir-seq, and a background error model to precisely map TEELs with unprecedented accuracy. Applying this to yeast rRNA transcripts revealed statistically significant TEELs and that errors are enriched at 3' transcript ends, suggesting polymerase pausing correlates to higher 3' error rates. Because PRO-Seq cannot be applied to viruses, as it relies on the viral polymerase to incorporate Biotin-NTP and then terminate RNA synthesis, we followed our alternative plan to successfully developed nascent RNA-Seq on influenza A virus (IAV) polymerase. This is an advancement in the virology and genomics field by reporting the first nascent RNA-Seq (not mature RNA-Seq) in a virus for the first time, opening up mechanistic studies for viral polymerases processing the viral genome in vivo, connecting protein to genomics levels (filed for U.S. provisional patent). Our method can enrich viral against host RNA and nascent over mature RNA, better than when we used traditional antibody-based protein capture methods. STREP-Seq provides valuable information about the viral replication process concealed in current sequencing methods. With nanopore direct RNA sequencing, the entire length of RNA molecules can be sequenced without the need for additional steps such as reverse transcription and PCR that remove sense and mutational information, respectively. Using this nascent RNA-Seq method, we discovered that pausing for viral polymerase is not random, with pausing mostly saturated at the 3’ packaging signal. We discovered that reassortment viruses like the pandemic H1N1 have different polymerase pausing sites compared to their wildtype counterparts. We identified dominant mutational sites within each IAV gene segment using Molnupiravir as a mutagen and correlated specific template motifs with polymerase misincorporation preferences. Our work has great implications for understanding the mechanisms of how Molnupiravir drives SARS-CoV-2 evolution, a major public health concern now. The success of this work puts us at the cutting edge of polymerase profiling. Our sequencing technique represents the first application of a virus and has the potential for high scientific and commercial impact.

16301319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16301319.value: Our first nascent RNA-Seq on a virus opened up many novel biological observations. We showed that polymerase pausing is not random and is tightly regulated in a virus genome, allowing us to identified novel regulatory sites within each gene segment. Further work will elucidate the mechanisms by which these novel regulatory sites regulate viral replication and transcription. We will explore how viral replication are affected by extrinsic factors such as reassortment and host cell adaptions. Reassortment is important evolutionary event wherein gene segments between IAVs adapted to distinct host species can give rise to chimeric viruses with enhanced potential for cross-species transmission (e.g. reassortant strains that gave rise to 1957, 1968, and 2009 influenza pandemics). We discovered that IAV polymerase exhibited different pausing landscapes in reassortant viruses compared to their respective wild-type viruses. Further work will reveal how these differences can be explained mechanistically, allowing reassortant viruses to replicate efficiently with the three polymerase genes from two different IAV strains. Our method will be applied to other viruses (e.g. SARS-CoV-2). This is one of our aims in our subsequent successful CRF grant. Investigating how viral or host factors impact polymerase pausing profiles mapped by STREP-seq may reveal novel intervention targets.

16301319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16301319.value: To elucidate the mechanisms by which influenza A virus (IAV) replicates its genome in vivo, and generates genetic variations, we developed novel STREP-Seq to sequence viral nascent RNAs and discovered that IAV polymerase pauses at specific sites along the viral genome. These pausing sites are not random and are likely influenced by RNA's secondary structures, such as those prominent at terminal packing signals. Reassortant strains of IAV exhibit different pausing patterns, which could contribute to the virus's ability to adapt and cause new pandemics. Furthermore, defective viral genomes (DVGs), which are subgenomic materials with mutations or deletions are commonly found in PB2, PB1, and PA genes and possess significant internal deletions but retain pausing patterns at packaging signals at their ends. Current public health concerns focus on how Molnupiravir causes SARS-CoV-2 mutation. Using STREP-Seq, we showed that it induces mutations in the viral genome, converting G-to-A and C-to-U. Surprisingly, we identified specific motifs in the viral genome that are more prone to these mutations. This research provides valuable insights into the replication process of IAV, its genetic variations, and the effects of antiviral drugs. Understanding these processes can help develop new strategies to combat viral infections and prevent future pandemics.

16301419.label: Realisation of objectives
16301419.value: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been instrumental in identifying numerous associations between single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and a wide range of complex traits and diseases. However, the majority of these risk variants are located in non-coding regions, presenting challenges in understanding their functional mechanisms. Emerging evidence suggests that many of these risk variants may impact traits and diseases through the modulation of gene expression levels. Therefore, there is a growing interest in precisely characterizing the role of genetically regulated gene expression (GREX) in human traits and diseases. 1. Develop statistical methods to quantify the impact of genetically regulated gene expression on complex traits. In this project, we have developed statistical methods to quantify the impact of GREX on complex traits. Leveraging existing GWAS and expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) resources, we have achieved success in identifying trait associations of GREX levels through transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). Our method called IGREX [1] precisely quantifies the proportion of phenotypic variation attributed to the GREX component. Additionally, we have developed Tis-CoMM [2], a tissue-specific approach to studying genetically regulated gene expression on complex traits. To improve the estimation accuracy of genetic and environmental covariances, we have introduced GECKO [3], which relies on composite likelihood and summary statistics for scalable computation across various scenarios. To explore regulated gene expression patterns at the single-cell level, we have developed FIRM [6], a re-scaling algorithm that accurately integrates single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets across multiple tissue types, platforms, and experimental batches. Furthermore, we have introduced Portal [4], a unified framework based on adversarial domain translation networks. Portal achieves the harmonization of large-scale atlas-level single-cell datasets while preserving biological variation and demonstrating high performance in integrating millions of cells in minutes with low memory consumption. Our method SpatialScope [8], leveraging deep generative models, integrates scRNA-seq reference data and spatial transcriptomics (ST) data, enabling the inference of transcriptome-wide expression levels for image-based ST data. Additionally, we have developed stVAE [7], a method for deconvolving cell-type composition in large-scale spatial transcriptomics. 2. implementation of the proposed algorithms. The implementation of the proposed algorithms has been done in either R or Python. The R software package IGREX is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/mxcai/iGREX. The Python code for the Portal software can be found at https://github.com/YangLabHKUST/Portal, and the R package for FIRM is available on GitHub at https://github.com/mingjingsi/FIRM. 3. Evaluate model performance using comprehensive simulation studies and compare analysis results with other related methods. To evaluate the performance of our methods, we have conducted comprehensive simulation studies and compared the results with other related methods. For example, we compared IGREX with RhoGE, a method developed by a research team from UCLA, and demonstrated that IGREX provides unbiased estimation while RhoGE substantially underestimates the variance of genetically regulated gene expression. In the context of cell type-specific gene expression patterns, we compared FIRM with various existing methods such as Seurat, BBKNN, BUSseq, LIGER, scVI, and ZINB-WaVE through simulation studies. 4. Apply the proposed methods to real data to examine scientific hypothesis. We have also applied our methods to real data to examine scientific hypotheses. For instance, using the IGREX method, we analyzed two individual-level GWAS datasets, the Northern Finland Birth Cohorts program 1966 (NFBC) and the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (WTCCC), with eQTL data from the GTEx project as a reference. Our analysis revealed significant heritability and genetic regulation of gene expression for various traits, such as Glucose, HDL, LDL, TG, TC, and SysBP. In liver, we observed substantial variance of gene expression explained by genetic regulation for LDL and TC, capturing a significant portion of their total heritability. These findings provide insights into the role of liver in gene regulation and the transport of cholesterol in the blood. 5. Investigate the theoretical properties of the proposed methods. The theoretical properties of our proposed methods have also been investigated. We developed BOLT-SSI [5], a method for ultra-high dimensional data analysis that guarantees the sure screening property for interaction identification. We established statistical theory for BOLT-SSI, demonstrating its computational efficiency and statistical accuracy through comprehensive simulations and real case studies. Our results indicate that BOLT-SSI outperforms competing methods in terms of computational efficiency and statistical accuracy, making it suitable for detecting interactions with a large number of predictors. 6. Set up a web portal to disseminate the results from this research. To disseminate the results of our research, we have set up a web portal on our lab website using GitHub (https://github.com/YangLabHKUST/SpatialScope). The portal contains all the codes, experimental settings, and datasets from this research project. Additionally, detailed documentation can be accessed at https://spatialscope-tutorial.readthedocs.io/en/latest/, providing guidance on how to use the methods developed in this research. Overall, our project aims to advance our understanding of genetically regulated gene expression and its impact on complex traits and diseases. Through the development of statistical methods, integration of single-cell data, exploration of tissue-specific gene expression patterns, and application to real data, we have made significant progress in this field. Our methods and findings contribute to the broader goal of unraveling the functional mechanisms underlying genetic associations with complex traits and diseases. Reference numbers are based on the submitted papers in Part C: Research Output. Regarding the budget and expenditure, a significant portion of the funds has been allocated to "Salaries." This decision was primarily influenced by the project's duration coinciding with the COVID pandemic, which rendered international conferences and visiting plans nearly infeasible. As a result, we had to reallocate some of the budget towards supporting research activities, particularly in recruiting additional PhD students and research assistants. The unforeseen circumstances brought about by the pandemic necessitated a shift in our priorities. With limited opportunities for travel and direct collaboration, it was crucial to invest in strengthening our research team. By recruiting more PhD students and research assistants, we aimed to enhance the productivity and depth of our research activities. While the expenses on salaries might appear relatively high, it reflects our commitment to maintaining the project's momentum and ensuring that valuable research continues to be conducted despite the challenges posed by the pandemic. Our focus on bolstering the research team demonstrates our adaptability and determination to make the most of the project's resources in the given circumstances.

16301419.label: Major findings and research outcome
16301419.value: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been highly successful in identifying tens of thousands of unique associations between single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and a wide range of complex traits and diseases (source: http://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/). However, a significant challenge arises from the fact that over 90% of the identified risk variants are located in non-coding regions, which makes it difficult to understand their functional mechanisms. Recent evidence suggests that many of these risk variants may influence traits and diseases by modulating gene expression levels in a cis-regulatory manner. Consequently, there is a growing interest in precisely characterizing the role of genetically regulated gene expression (GREX) in human traits and diseases. To address this, we have developed the IGREX method, which enables the quantification of the impact of genetic regulatory effects on phenotypes through gene expression levels. IGREX has been applied to two individual-level GWAS datasets: the Northern Finland Birth Cohorts program 1966 (NFBC) and the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (WTCCC). In these analyses, we utilized eQTL data from 48 human tissues obtained from the GTEx project as a reference. Our findings demonstrate that genetic regulation of gene expression patterns significantly contributes to tissue-level associations. Building upon this, we have developed Tis-CoMM, a method that allows the study of genetically regulated gene expression in a tissue-specific manner [2]. Additionally, we have created GECKO [3], a tool for estimating both genetic and environmental covariances. To further explore gene expression patterns in a cell-type specific manner, we have developed advanced methods for single-cell data analysis. For instance, FIRM [6] is an algorithm that accurately integrates single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets across multiple tissue types, platforms, and experimental batches, accounting for cell type compositions. To streamline the integration of single-cell data atlases, we have introduced Portal [4], a unified framework that utilizes adversarial domain translation to learn harmonized representations of datasets. Furthermore, we have aimed to enhance our understanding of gene regulation by incorporating spatial information. Our methodology includes SpatialScope [8], which integrates scRNA-seq reference data and spatial transcriptomics (ST) data using deep generative models. Additionally, we have developed stVAE [7], a method that deconvolves cell-type composition in large-scale spatial transcriptomics, providing valuable insights into gene regulation patterns within a spatial context. These innovative methods open up unprecedented opportunities for investigating gene regulation patterns using spatial transcriptomics technology, as well as for performing cell-type-specific analyses and integrating diverse single-cell datasets across different conditions and platforms.

16301419.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16301419.value: Genome-wide association studies have successfully identified numerous genetic loci associated with complex diseases. Interestingly, more than 90% of these loci are found in regions of our DNA that do not directly code for proteins. It is believed that these regions contribute to disease by affecting the regulation of our genome. In our research, we have developed statistical methods to investigate the patterns of gene regulation. We have discovered that the variation in gene expression can be divided into two components: steady-state variation and context-dependent variation. Our study has focused on comprehensively examining the genetically regulated gene expression in a steady-state. Additionally, we have begun exploring how gene expression patterns change depending on the specific context. Moving forward, we aim to develop new methods that integrate genetic data, single-cell data, and spatial transcriptomics data. This will enable us to further investigate genetic variations and their effects in specific cell types or in response to various physiological or environmental stimuli. By doing so, we can deepen our understanding of complex diseases and their underlying mechanisms.

16301419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16301419.value: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been successful in linking DNA variations (SNPs) to complex traits and diseases. However, most of these genetic differences are located in non-coding regions of our DNA, making it challenging to understand their impact on our health. Recent evidence suggests that these genetic differences may affect our traits by influencing gene expression in specific cells. This has led to the study of genetically regulated gene expression (GREX) in human traits and diseases. To address this challenge, statistical methods have been developed to quantify the impact of genetic effects on traits by examining gene expression levels. The results have shown that genetic regulation of gene expression patterns significantly influences the functioning of different tissues in our body. Advanced methods have also been developed to analyze single-cell data and spatial transcriptomics, providing insights into cell-type-specific gene regulation and context-dependent effects. These innovative approaches offer exciting opportunities to investigate gene regulation and the contribution of genetic variations to complex diseases. By integrating genetic data, single-cell data, and spatial transcriptomics, we can explore the effects of genetic differences in specific cell types and in response to different environmental factors, ultimately advancing our understanding of complex diseases.

16301519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16301519.value: In this proposed project, we will consider various deformed random matrix models including the deformations of the classical Hermitian and non-Hermitian random matrices, and also general additive and multiplicative models. We will consider both fixed- and large-rank deformations. We will study the distribution of the eigenvectors of these deformed models, in order to understand how the deformation affects the eigenvectors of the random matrix models on the fluctuation level. For Hermitian models, first, we will look to establish non-universality for the outlier eigenvectors for a large class of fixed-rank deformed random Hermitian matrices. Second, we will aim to derive the limiting distribution of the eigenvector corresponding to a deformation at the critical BBP transition point. Third, we will study the distribution of the eigenvectors of a general additive and multiplicative models, for which the eigenvalue distribution is known, with the aid of the free probability theory. We will also consider similar problems for the non-Hermitian random matrices. Finally, we will apply our results to some problems from the high-dimensional statistics. 在这个项目中，我们将考虑多种带扰动项的随机矩阵模型。这包括经典Hermite随机矩阵和非Hermite随机矩阵的扰动，以及更一般的加法和乘法模型的扰动。 我们既考虑有限秩扰动，也考虑扰动项的秩很大的情形。 对于这些模型，我们将主要研究特征向量的分布问题。特别的，我们将通过这些研究更好地理解扰动项是如何影响随机矩阵特征向量的分布的。对Hermite模型，我们首先研究有限秩扰动大于BBP相变点时时特征向量分布的非普适性问题。然后我们研究扰动在BBP相变点附近时特征向量的分布。 另外我们还将研究一般加法和乘法模型特征向量的分布。关于非Hermite矩阵的类似问题也会被研究。最后，我们会把得到的数学结果用到一些高维统计的问题当中。

16301519.label: Realisation of objectives
16301519.value: A random matrix with low-rank deformation is a model widely studied in random matrix theory. It plays a fundamental role in high-dimensional signal detection, factor models, PCA (Principal Component Analysis), and CCA (Canonical Correlation Analysis). An important task for this type of model is to study the limiting properties of its leading eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Regarding the leading eigenvalue, a famous result is the BBP transition discovered by Baik, Ben Arous, and Péché. This phase transition describes the changes in both the first-order limit and the second-order fluctuation of the leading eigenvalue when the intensity of the deformation exceeds a certain threshold. While many studies in the literature investigate such results for eigenvalues, corresponding results for eigenvectors largely remain at the first-order level. Studying second-order fluctuations is the main task of our proposal. We also apply the eigenvector fluctuation to various hypothesis testing problems. First, we studied eigenvector behavior in the most challenging regimes: the critical regime of the BBP transition and the supercritical regime, which is particularly important in applications. In one of our recent works, we established the eigenvector distribution for the deformed GUE in the critical regime. The distribution is given by an extended Airy process, a new distribution not previously seen in the literature. We further proved the non-degeneracy of this distribution, solving the critical regime part of Objective 1. In another work, we established the Gaussian fluctuation of the leading eigenvectors of the spiked sample covariance matrices in the supercritical regime, addressing the supercritical regime part of Objective 1. Second, we investigated the signal-plus-noise model, a non-Hermitian random matrix perturbed by low-rank non-Hermitian deterministic matrices. We established the limiting distribution of the leading left and right singular vectors of this model in the supercritical regime of the BBP transition. Notably, we discovered a non-universal phenomenon for this model: the limiting distribution may or may not be Gaussian, depending on the signal structure and the entry distribution of the noise matrix. This fulfills Objective 2. Third, in a recent work, we studied the sum of two random matrices, which can be regarded as a large-rank deformation of one of the two matrices. Beyond eigenvalue results, we also proved that the eigenvectors of this model are delocalized, providing evidence that the components of the eigenvectors are asymptotically Gaussian, of order 1/sqrt{N}. This addresses Objective 3. Finally, in a work concerning spiked covariance matrices, after determining the distribution of the leading eigenvectors, we applied it to various hypothesis testing problems. For results related to the signal-plus-noise model, we also used the findings in hypothesis testing concerning the singular subspace. This achieves Objective 4.

16301519.label: Major findings and research outcome
16301519.value: We first established the eigenvector distribution for three random matrices with low-rank deformation: the deformed GUE, the spiked sample covariance matrices, and the signal-plus-noise model. For the deformed GUE, we obtained the eigenvector distribution in the critical regime of the BBP transition. For the spiked sample covariance matrices and the signal-plus-noise model, we obtained the eigenvector distribution in the supercritical regime of the BBP transition and applied the results to several hypothesis testing problems, finding that our statistics outperform most of the other existing statistics in the literature. The first result was published in Probability Theory and Related Fields (2022); the second and third results were published in the Annals of Statistics in 2021 and 2022, respectively. Then we obtained an eigenvector estimate for the sum of two random matrices. This result was published in Forum of Mathematics, Sigma (2021).

16301519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16301519.value: In Objective 1, we consider the low-rank deformation of GUE. It is mainly because, for such deformed GUE, its eigenvalues and those of its minor have an explicit joint density function. Based on this explicit formula and the eigenvector-eigenvalue identity, we are able to perform explicit analysis and obtain the result for the eigenvector in the critical regime. However, if we turn to the real symmetric case, i.e., the deformed GOE, so far, there is no explicit formula for the joint density function of its eigenvalues and those of its minors. Hence, to extend this result to the real case, we must first derive this joint density function. Beyond the Gaussian ensembles, we also aim to develop a universality result for generally distributed deformed Wigner matrices. This will include the universality of both the eigenvalue and eigenvector in the critical regime of the BBP transition.

16301519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16301519.value: In this project, we work on the low-rank deformation of classical random matrices, such as Wigner matrices and sample covariance matrices. These low-rank deformations will not significantly change the global picture of the spectrum but may change a few leading eigenvalues and eigenvectors, depending on the strength of the deformations. We studied various such models and derived the limiting behavior of their leading eigenvectors in various regimes. We further applied our results to several hypothesis testing problems. The results of this project are important in the fields of Random Matrix Theory, Free Probability Theory, and High-Dimensional Statistics.

16301619.label: Project Objectives
16301619.value: To choose three-dimensional lattice models which can properly represent a Weyl semimetal (WSM) phase. The models should be easy to add disorders to (as with on-site random potential or random hopping coefficients in lattice models) without destroying the WSM phase within a certain range of the randomness. To properly define WSMs in disordered systems. This is important and non-trivial. Disorders exist inevitably in all materials and the physics of any genuine phase must deal with at least weak disorder. WSM was originally defined in terms of the linear crossing of conduction and valence bands, but that is valid only for crystals with translational symmetry so that the lattice momentum is a good quantum number. We shall examine whether the existence of surface states in a metallic bulk phase can be a good description of disordered WSMs. To use exact diagonalization to compute all the eigen-energies and eigen-functions of a finite disordered system that supports a WSM phase. We then plan to compute the distribution of the nearest-neighbour level spacings in various energy ranges, especially around the Weyl nodes (WNs). It is anticipated that the wave function at the WNs may be different from that of a normal, homogeneous extended state like a Bloch state of a pure crystal. We will use finite-size scaling to analyse the inverse participation ratio of the wave function around the WNs. In particular, we shall see whether the wavefunction at WNs is a fractal or not. If it is, one can ask many related questions: what is the fractal’s dimensionality? Is that dimension universal? How does the fractal wave function at a WN change to the usual homogeneous wave function away from the node? If the fractal nature of the wave function at WNs is the cause of non-Wigner-Dyson level statistics, the level spacing distribution in fractal spaces such as the electronic level in Sierpinski gaskets and Menger sponge with on-site disorders will be documented in both the localized state and extended state regions. The level statistics of random Hamiltonian matrices whose elements are octonion numbers will also be documented. 16301619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16301619.value: Weyl semimetals (WSMs) are a newly discovered quantum state of matter that is characterized by the linear crossing of conduction and valence bands at Weyl nodes (WNs). Topologically-protected surface states give rise to the formation of Fermi-arcs on sample surfaces. WSMs have attracted enormous attention in recent years because of their fundamental interest and because their exotic properties may be useful in possibly revolutionary applications. The WSM phase must survive with disorders in order to be a genuine physical state because disorders inevitably exist in all materials. Although almost all aspects of the new quantum materials have been under extensive and intensive investigations, the level statistics of disordered WSMs have seldom if ever been investigated so far. Level statistics are a fundamental property of disordered systems that can classify them into classes and phases according to their symmetries. For example, the level spacing of conventional metals follows the Wigner-Dyson distributions. Normal metals can be classified as either a Gaussian orthogonal ensemble in which the Hamiltonian matrix elements are real numbers, a Gaussian unitary ensemble in which the Hamiltonian matrix elements are complex numbers, or a Gaussian symplectic ensemble in which the Hamiltonian matrix elements are quaternion numbers. There is good evidences that the level statistics of disordered WSMs do not follow this classification, especially around WNs. Studying those level statistics is the focus of this proposed theoretical study. Specifically, we shall ask what are the level statistics of disordered WSMs near the WNs? Are they universally applicable? How does the level number variance, which relates to fluctuations in conductance, change with the average level? The conductance fluctuation of conventional metals is of order of the conductance quantum; it would be interesting to know whether WSMs also have a universal conductance fluctuation. If yes, what is its value? It would also be interesting to know whether the material’s level statistics have anything to do with the nature of the wave function near WNs, especially whether or not the wave function is fractal. So we shall also be interested in investigating the level statistics of electrons in fractal spaces. It is expected that the outcomes of this study will significantly impact condensed matter physics in general and the field of topological materials in particular. 外尔半金属是近年发现的一种新型量子态，其本征特性是价带和导带在外尔点处的线性交叉及由它引起的受拓扑保护的表面态和所伴随的表面费米弧。由于此态的奇异性质和其可能的应用前景，外尔半金属引起了广泛关注。人们对其的方方面面也进行了全面的研究。但外尔半金属要能成为自然界中这是的存在的状态，一定要能在无规系统中存活，这是因为绝对的晶体是不存在的，尽管对外尔半金属的研究很全面，但到目前为止，无规外尔半金属能级间隙统计分布还是一个没有研究过的问题。这是本项目计划研究的一个基础问题。能隙统计分布在通常的金属具有普适Wignor-Dyson分布，不同的Wignor-Dyson分布可以用来刻画不同对称性的金属。所以本项目希望回答无规外尔半金属的能隙统计分布是否有异于Wignor-Dyson分布。尤其是在外尔附近的能级。如果外尔半金属在外尔附近有不同于Wignor-Dyson的能隙，能否用于判定无规外尔半金属的准则。另外，在外尔点的态函数是否具有分形空间，如果是分形，它的分形维数是多少？是否能有普适性？对这个问题的深入研究也许能解决无规外尔半金属的描述这一基本问题。无论如何，此项目的实施必将加深我们对外尔半金属此一量子新状态的认识。

16301619.label: Realisation of objectives
16301619.value: The projective objectives 1-3 are well achieved with many interesting findings. We studied various topological phase of both Hermitian and non-Hermitian topological materials. Fundamental quantity of the nearest-neighbor level-spacing distributions are used to distinguish one quantum phase from the others and are classified into different universality classes. The Wigner-Dyson and the Poisson functions govern respectively extended and localized states in Hermitian systems. The Ginibre functions are for the non-Hermitian systems whose eigenvalues are complex and away from exceptional points (EPs). However, the level-spacing distributions of disordered non-Hermitian systems near EPs have not been adequately studied, and corresponding random matrix theory is absent. We studied the level-spacing distributions in the vicinity of EPs of a class of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. Two distribution functions for the symmetry-preserved phase and for the symmetry-broken phase, are needed. Surprisingly, both distributions show linear level repulsions, in contrast to cubic level repulsions of the Ginibre ensembles and follow universal distributions which depends on the localization nature of states at EPs rather than the dimensionality of non-Hermitian systems and the order of EPs. We have numerically studied the Anderson localization transitions in non-Hermitian two-dimensional (2D) systems with exceptional points by using the finite-size scaling analysis of the participation ratios. At the exceptional points of either second order or fourth order, two non-Hermitian systems with different symmetries have the same critical exponent of correlation lengths, which differs from all known 2D disordered Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems, a notion of superuniversality. In the symmetry-preserved and symmetry-broken phases, the non-Hermitian models with time-reversal symmetry and without spin-rotational symmetry, and without both time-reversal and spin-rotational symmetries, are in the same universality class of 2D Hermitian electron systems of Gaussian symplectic and unitary ensembles. The universality of the transition is further confirmed by showing that the critical exponent does not depend on the form of disorders and boundary conditions. For non-Hermitian topological insulators, we found that the chiral boundary states of higher-dimensional without parity-time symmetry can be Hermitian with real eigenenergies under certain conditions. Our approach allows one to construct Hermitian chiral edge and hinge states from non-Hermitian two-dimensional Chern insulators and three-dimensional second-order topological insulators, respectively. Such Hermitian chiral boundary channels have perfect transmission coefficients (quantized values) and are robust against disorders. Furthermore, a non-Hermitian topological insulator can undergo the topological Anderson insulator transition from a topologically trivial non-Hermitian metal or insulator to a topological Anderson insulator with quantized transmission coefficients at finite disorders. We found the absence of quasiparticle-level anticrossing in random non-Hermitian systems. The general Wigner-Dyson distributions of energy-level spacing of diffusive metals in the usual Hermitian systems is replaced by the Poisson distribution for quasiparticle-level (the real parts of complex eigenenergies) spacing of non-Hermitian disordered metals in the thermodynamic limit of infinite system size. This is a very surprising result because Poisson statistics is universally true for the Anderson insulators where energy eigenstates do not overlap with each other, so energy levels are independent from each other. For disordered metals where different eigenstates overlap with each other, one should expect different levels trying to stay away from each other, so the Poisson distribution should not apply there. Our results show that the larger non-Hermitian energy (dissipation) can invalidate the quasiparticle-level anticrossing that holds dearly in Hermitian metals. Thus, a unified picture for recently discovered “level attraction” in various systems is provided. This understanding provides a theoretical basis for manipulating quasiparticle energy levels.

16301619.value: The major findings are two distribution functions of the nearest-neighbor level-spacing for the symmetry-preserved phase and for the symmetry-broken phase are needed (Paper 23 in part C). The critical exponents of the Anderson localization transitions are the same for non-Hermitian two-dimensional (2D) systems with time-reversal symmetry and without spin-rotational symmetry, and without both time-reversal and spin-rotational symmetries, a notion of superuniversality (Paper 27 in part C). They are in the same universality class of 2D Hermitian electron systems of Gaussian symplectic and unitary ensembles. The universality of the transition is further confirmed by showing that the critical exponent does not depend on the form of disorders and boundary conditions. For non-Hermitian topological insulators, we found that the chiral boundary states of higher-dimensional without parity-time symmetry can be Hermitian with real eigenenergies under certain conditions (paper 1 in part C). We found the absence of quasiparticle-level anticrossing in random non-Hermitian systems when the damping is large enough (paper 1 in part C). Thus, a unified picture for recently discovered “level attraction” in various systems is provided. This understanding provides a theoretical basis for manipulating quasiparticle energy levels.

16301619.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16301619.value: It will be very interesting to see whether the findings in this project are also applicable to spaces and lattices with non-integer dimensions. Because of insufficient funds available in this project, we could not investigate the case when the Hamiltonian matrix elements are octonion numbers, instead of real, complex, or symplectic numbers. It is well known that random matrices with real, complex, and symplectic numbers belong to Gaussian orthogonal, unitary, and symplectic ensembles. Thus, it is fundamental interesting to see whether the random matrices with octonion numbers gives a new ensemble, and it is also highly interesting to find physical systems described by such an Hamiltonian.

16301619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16301619.value: Level statistics are fundamental property of disordered systems that can classify them into classes and phases according to their symmetries. This project investigated the level statistics of topological phases of both Hermitian and non-Hermitian disordered system. The important findings in this project is the absences of anti-crossing of the levels in non-Hermitian systems with strong dissipation. The consequence of this effect is the Poisson statistics of disordered non-Hermitian metals. Other important findings include the linear level repulsion near the exceptional points of non-Hermitian systems and superuniversality of non-Hermitian Anderson localization transition with exceptional points in which the critical exponents do not depend on the symmetry and many other details of a model.

16301719.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16301719.value: Massive eruption events and sudden changes in large-scale flow pattern are often observed in closed thermal convection systems of geophysical scale, such as in oceanic circulation, Earth's outer core convection, and dynamo generation of geomagnetic field, and in the convective zone of the sun and other stars and planets [1–6]. While the incidence of these events is rare, their impact on our living conditions is often dramatic. Examples include volcano eruptions, earthquakes and climate changes due to oceanic circulation reversals. Because these phenomena are complex owing to the extreme conditions and complex material parameters involved [7], our fundamental understanding of the geophysical-scale flow phenomena is often challenged by limited direct experimental observations and oversimplified computer simulations. In a recent experiment [8], we found that similar random reversals of large-scale circulation (LSC) may be realized and quantitatively studied in a specially designed thin-disk convection cell with its circular cross-section orientated vertically parallel to gravity. The experiment clearly showed that LSC reversals are caused by rare massive thermal plume eruptions that disrupt the existing LSC and reset its rotational direction. It remains unclear how these massive eruption events are triggered in the closed convection cell. In this research, we plan to conduct a systematic investigation aimed at understanding the physical mechanism of large-scale flow reversals and rare massive thermal plume eruptions in turbulent thermal convection. In the experiment, we will conduct systematic measurements in the thin-disk cell with different thicknesses and under variable asymmetric boundary conditions between the top and bottom conducting plates, and examine how the statistical properties of the plume eruption events are affected by the symmetry breaking in the boundary conditions of the convection cell. Particle image velocimetry, thermometry and shadowgraphic techniques will be used to study the interplay between the boundary layer dynamics, thermal plume instability and large-scale flow reversals with varying Rayleigh numbers, Prandtl numbers, cell aspect ratios, and bottom plate roughness. A parallel study using direct numerical simulation in the same convection systems will be conducted to complement the experimental investigation. The proposed research will fully characterize the LSC reversals and pinpoint their physical origin. This research will explore new physics in non-equilibrium flow systems and investigate rare extreme events of practical importance. New knowledge gained from this research will assist scientists in modeling the massive eruption events and large-scale flow reversals on a geophysical scale. 在具有地球物理尺度的封閉熱對流系統中，諸如海洋環流、地球外核對流、地磁場電機形成、太陽及其他恆星和行星的對流區，人們通常可以觀測到大規模噴發事件和大尺度流動模式的突然變化。雖然這些事件的發生率極低，但對我們的生活環境影響極大，例如火山爆發、地震和由於海洋環流反轉引起的氣候變化。由於這些複雜現象涉及到極端條件和複雜的物性參數，我們對地球物理尺度下的流動現象的基本理解常常受限於很少的直接實驗觀測和過度簡化的計算機模擬。 在最近的一項實驗中，我們發現類似的大尺度環流（LSC）隨機反轉可以在一個經過特別設計的薄圓盤對流槽（其圓形橫截面方向豎直並平行於重力方向）中實現並做定量研究。實驗清楚地表明，LSC的反轉是由於罕見的大規模熱羽流噴發所引起的，這種噴發破壞了現有的LSC並重置其旋轉方向。目前尚不清楚在封閉對流槽中大規模噴發事件是如何觸發的。我們計劃進行一項系統的研究，旨在理解湍流熱對流中的大規模流動反轉和罕見的大規模熱羽流噴發的物理機制。在實驗中，我們將在具有不同厚度、上下導熱板非對稱邊界條件可變的薄圓盤對流槽中進行系統的測量，並檢查羽流噴發事件的統計性質是如何被對流槽邊界條件的對稱性破缺所影響。我們將使用粒子影像測速、溫度測定和陰影技術，研究在不同瑞利數、普朗特數、對流槽寬高比和底板粗糙度下的邊界層動力學、熱羽流不穩定性和大尺度流動反轉之間的相互作用。我們將同時對相同的對流系統進行直接數值模擬，以補充實驗研究。 本擬議的研究將充分刻畫LSC的反轉規律並確定其物理本源。它包括了探索非平衡流動系統的新物理和研究罕見的極端事件，這些都具有重要的實際意義。從這項研究中獲得的新知識將有助於科學家對在地球物理尺度下的大規模噴發事件和大尺度流動反轉的建模工作。

16301719.label: Realisation of objectives
16301719.value: The original PI of this project was Prof. Penger Tong, whose contract as a Chair Professor at HKUST ended in June 2022. As a result, the PI of this project was changed to Prof. Qin Xu in July 2022, which is only three months away to the end date of this project. At that time, the major work of the project has been completed and the main purposes of the PI transfer were to get the results published and to produce a successful completion report. Prof. Tong retired at HKUST, partly because he planned to go back to the US to take care of his wife, who was diagnosed with the late-stage breast cancer. Unfortunately, his wife passed away in May 2022. Now Prof. Tong renewed his contract as a Chair Professor at HKUST for five more years, and he is fully responsible for the completion report of this project. To fulfill the three research objectives of this project, we carried out three subprojects to study of the dynamics of large-scale flow reversals in turbulent thermal convection. In a previous experiment, it was found that reversals of the large-scale circulation (LSC) in a closed convection cell are caused by rare massive eruption of thermal plumes, which disrupts the existing LSC and resets its rotational direction. It remains unclear how the massive eruption events are triggered in a closed convection cell. In one subproject, we conducted a combined experimental/theoretical study aimed at understanding the physical mechanism of the large-scale flow reversals and rare massive eruption of thermal plumes in turbulent Rayleigh-Benard convection (RBC). In particular, we investigated the dynamic instabilities of the two coupled nonlinear time-delay differential equations that was used to describe the coherent oscillations between the top and bottom boundary layers. By introducing two different sensitivity parameters to external perturbations for the instabilities of the two boundary layers, we studied how the broken symmetry of the boundary conditions near the conducting plates affects the dynamic instabilities of the system in a broad range of the parameter space. We found three different types of solutions, namely, in-phase single-period oscillations, multi-period oscillations and chaos. The chaos solution contains rare but large amplitude fluctuations. The statistical properties of these fluctuations are consistent with those observed in the experiment for the massive eruption of thermal plumes, which causes random reversals of the LSC in turbulent RBC. Our study thus provide new insights into the mechanism that triggers the massive eruption of thermal plumes in turbulent RBC. This work was published in Nonlinear Dynamics (2021). In the second subproject, we conducted a combined experimental/numerical study of the boundary conditions at a stable liquid–liquid interface. The hydrodynamic boundary condition, which complements the Navier-Stokes equation, serves as a pillar of continuum hydrodynamics. Unlike other partial differential equations in physics, such as Maxwell’s equations, for which the boundary conditions can be derived analytically from the equations themselves, the hydrodynamic boundary condition near a solid wall, which has been regarded as non-slip for more than a century, has never been derived from first principles. For this reason, the past decade has witnessed a surge of experimental and theoretical studies of the hydrodynamic boundary conditions at various liquid-solid interfaces. Compared with the large number of investigations of the boundary layer (BL) dynamics near solid surfaces, our understanding of the BL flow near stable liquid interfaces is rather limited. In this work, we showed that quasi-2D RBC in two stacking layers of immiscible fluids is a valuable experimental framework for the study of the boundary conditions at a stable liquid interface. With this experimental framework, We measured the mean temperature profile θ(δz) and temperature variance profile η(δz) across the stable and immiscible liquid interface. The measured θ(δz) and η(δz) as a function of distance δz away from the interface are found to have the scaling forms θ(δz/λ) and η(δz/λ), respectively, with varying thermal BL thickness λ. By a careful comparison with the simultaneously measured BL profiles near a solid conducting surface, we find that the measured θ(δz) and η(δz) near the liquid interface can be well described by the BL equations for a solid wall, so long as a thermal slip length L_T is introduced to account for the convective heat flux passing through the liquid interface. This work was published in J. Fluid Mechanics (2022). In the third subproject, we applied our knowledge on the LSC and boundary layer dynamics that we learned from the controlled convection experiments to the study of the vertical temperature profiles (thermocline) and LSC in oceans. A widespread permanent thermocline is observed beneath the relatively warm, well-mixed surface layer, from depths of about 200 m to about 1,000 m, in which temperature decreases rapidly from the mixed upper layer of the ocean to much colder deep water layer below with an approximately constant temperature. In the ocean, the thermocline is linked to the large-scale ocean circulation that is driven by global density gradients created by surface heating near the equator and cold water downward fluxes near the north and south poles. The stability of the thermocline structure plays an important role in maintaining the ocean circulation, which has a large impact on the climate of the Earth. In this study, we conducted field measurements of vertical profiles of the turbulent diffusivity and temperature at different stations in the South China Sea (SCS). Based on the data of turbulent diffusivity, we identified the vertical turbulence structure of the SCS and obtained the depth range of the three vertical layers: upper layer (UL), middle layer (M), and deep layer (DL). From the combined results of turbulent diffusivity and temperature fluctuations, we found that the vertical temperature profiles in the two regions have a self-similarity form. Our study of the multiple-layer structure of the CSC provides a better understanding of turbulent mixing in the SCS. This work was published in Acta Oceanologica Sinica (2022). With the above three sets of experimental and numerical investigations, the three objectives of the project were fully accomplished. Because of the COVID-19 pandemic in Hong Kong, HKUST took a series of special measures to reduce human contact and trafficking in the campus and banned all business travels for more than two years since 2020. As a result, the PI/Co-PI and their team members (research postgraduate students and postdocs) were unable to attend any international and regional conferences in person during this time. The research activities reported here were carried out mainly using the existing equipment and no major equipment was purchased during this time. The bulk of the funds obtained for this project was used mainly to support the research staff (research postgraduate students and postdocs).

16301719.label: Major findings and research outcome
16301719.value: 1. Symmetry-breaking-induced rare fluctuations in a time-delay dynamic system. Inspired by the experimental and numerical findings, we studied the dynamic instabilities of two coupled nonlinear delay differential equations that are used to describe the coherent oscillations between the top and bottom boundary layers in turbulent Rayleigh-Bénard convection. The chaos solution of the two coupled nonlinear delay differential equations contains rare but large amplitude fluctuations, which are consistent with those observed in the experiment for the massive eruption of thermal plumes. Our study provides new insights into the origin of rare massive eruptions and sudden changes of large-scale flow pattern that are often observed in convection systems of geophysical and astrophysical scales. 2. Fluctuation-induced slip of thermal boundary layers at a stable liquid–liquid interface. In this work, we demonstrate that turbulent Rayleigh-Bénard convection in two stacking layers of immiscible fluids is an ideal quasi-two-dimensional system for the study of the thermal boundary layer (BL) dynamics near the liquid–liquid interface. The convective flow in each fluid layer is turbulent and possesses the key features of turbulent convection. A well-developed thermal BL is formed on each side of the liquid interface, which is stable and remains at an (average) position with minimal movement. A central finding of this investigation is that the measured BL profiles near the liquid interface can be well described by the BL equations for a solid wall modified by a thermal slip length L_T, which is directly linked to the convective heat flux passing through the liquid interface. 3. Vertical multiple-layer structure of temperature and turbulent diffusivity in the South China Sea. Our study of the vertical profiles of the turbulent diffusivity and temperature at different stations in the South China Sea showed that the measured turbulent diffusivity follows a power-law distribution with a varying exponent in three different water layers. Similar multiple-layer scaling regimes were also observed from the temperature fluctuations. Combining the results of turbulent diffusivity and vertical temperature fluctuations, we identified the multiple-layer structure of temperature in the South China Sea. Furthermore, we found that the temperature profile in each water layer can be well described by a common scaling function under identical turbulence conditions. This study provided new clues for understanding the physical mechanism of maintaining a stable multi-layer temperature structure in the South China Sea.

16301719.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16301719.value: Our current study of the large-scale circulation and boundary layer dynamics near a liquid interface provides a useful theoretical framework that can be used to characterize the vertical temperature profile Theta(z) in oceans as a function of depth z away from the ocean-air interface. This research is, therefore, much relevant to the study of the ocean thermocline formation and large-scale circulation that is driven by global density gradients created by surface heating near the equator and cold water downward fluxes near the north and south poles. In particular, it would be very interesting to utilize the newly obtained analytical capabilities and conduct a systematic study of the functional form of the vertical temperature profiles Theta(z;phi,s) across the Atlantic Ocean at different latitudes phi and in different seasons s. The stability of the thermocline structure plays an important role in maintaining the ocean circulation, which has a large impact on the climate of the Earth. Given that the global climate is projected to continue to change over this century and beyond due to the global warming effects, it is high time to conduct research in this new direction. We plan to seek additional funding to support the research along this direction.

16301719.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16301719.value: Massive eruptions and sudden changes in large-scale flow pattern are often observed in closed thermal convection systems of geophysical scale, such as in oceanic circulation and Earth's outer core convection. The stability of the large-scale flow pattern in the closed convection system, such as in ocean circulation, plays an important role in stabilizing the global climate. Modelling of these phenomena require a better understanding of the dynamics of large-scale circulation and its response to intermittent eruption of thermal plumes, which can be realized in the well-controlled convection experiments. In this project, we conducted a combined experimental, numerical and theoretical study aimed at understanding the physical mechanism of the large-scale flow reversals and rare massive eruption of thermal plumes in turbulent Rayleigh-Benard convection. With a large volume of local temperature measurements near the liquid-liquid and solid-liquid interfaces, we are able to provide a quantitative description of the mean temperature and temperature variance profiles across a stable liquid interface in turbulent convection. This investigation laid a solid foundation for further study of the vertical temperature profile in oceans, which plays an important role in maintaining the ocean circulation and hence has a large impact on climate changes.

16301919.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16301919.value: When the thickness of polymer films is less than ~100 nm, the properties are often different from those of the bulk material. Most studies investigating the effects of confinement on the glass transition temperature (Tg) and related dynamics have found good consistency. For example, freely suspended (or free-standing) polymer films or films with weak polymer-substrate interactions have consistently displayed reduced Tg and enhanced overall dynamics. These findings have generally been attributed to the existence of a region near the free surface of the films where molecular motions are faster and freeze at a lower temperature than in the bulk material. However, studies of the effects of confinement on the elastic modulus of free-standing polymer films and films supported by a soft substrate have found variable results. In particular, enhanced, unaltered and depressed elastic modulus have all been reported. Here, we propose a program to develop a platform to mechanical test free-standing polymer films permitting a convenient check on the linearity and reproducibility of a measurement. The proposed platform will be versatile and allow various thermal and dynamic mechanical tests. Besides the room-temperature modulus confinement effect, we will also use the platform to study the short-time elastic modulus and relaxation modulus of free-standing polymer films over an unprecedented thickness range of ~10 nm to ~10 micron and temperatures varying from ambient to the Tg of the films. These measurements will enable us to clarify the mechanical properties of free-standing polymer films and address important fundamental questions concerning how the presence of a surface mobile region affects the elastic modulus and mechanical relaxation behaviors of a film at different temperatures below its Tg. As applications for flexible polymer films increase, as in flexible electronics and artificial skin, and given the well-known enhancement effects of free surfaces on the dynamics of polymers, it is imperative to have access to methods that allow comprehensive characterization of the time-dependent mechanical properties of flexible polymer films. The proposed method will allow us to determine the evolution of the stiffness of the film as it is stretched from the unstrained state until it breaks. It will also allow us to determine how the stiffness of a film relaxes with time at different elevated temperatures. All these are important engineering factors in the design of a product.

16301919.label: Realisation of objectives
16301919.value: Objective 1: We have successfully made freestanding single-layer and bilayer polymer films with various molecular weights between ~100k and ~1000kg/mol, and conducted stress-strain curve measurement on them at adjustable strain rates using our dynamic mechanical analyzer. For single-layer films, we determined the elastic modulus from the slope of the stress-strain curves in the linear regime. For bi-layer films, we determined the elastic modulus by using the rule of mixture. Measurements from the single-layer and bilayer films agree within experimental uncertainty. The elastic modulus values that do not change with further increase in the applied strain rate are identified as the short-time elastic modulus E. Objective 2: We have measured E as a function of temperature and found that it agrees with the published values of the bulk polymer and is independent of film thickness. Objective 3: We have successfully measured the relaxation modulus E(t) of freestanding polystyrene (PS) single-layer and PS-PDMS bilayer films with a wide range of PS thickness from 5 nm to ~200 microns. Objective 4: We found that all the E(t) measurements could be fit to the double or single Kohlrausch-Williams-Watts (KWW) function, where the latter is commonly used to describe glassy dynamics. Correspondingly, the films possess two and one relaxation mode, respectively. From the fits, we could determine the relaxation time(s), stretch exponent(s). If the data fits the double KWW function, the fit result also provides the relaxation strengths of the mode(s). As shown in the financial report, the project did not incur any general expense or conference expense. The reason for the absence of general expense is that our department had an expected surplus from running a new MSc program and dispersed it to the faculty in the form of general expense support. The reason for the lack of conference expense is that we had refrained from overseas travels due to the travel restrictions enforced during much of the grant period. With funds from these categories, we had supported a postdoc whom was not planned in the original budget.

16301919.label: Major findings and research outcome
16301919.value: One goal of this program is to clarify the origin of the inconsistent film thickness (h) dependences reported in the literature for the elastic modulus E of thin polymer films, where some researchers have reported a reduction in E with decreasing h while some reported an h-independent E. In this program, we developed a method to measure the time (t) dependence and strain rate dependence of E of polymer films at unprecedented ranges of h and temperature (T) of 5 nm–185 microns and 300–370 K, respectively. With this unique capability, we clarified that both decreases and constancy in E with decreasing h can occur. Specifically, longer t and higher T render E to decrease with decreasing h. Otherwise E is independent of h. We have also measured E(t) at different t and h and deduced the relaxation time(s) and strength(s) where appropriate. From the result, we discovered that the films with h < ~ 1 micron relaxed faster than the bulk. Moreover, tau decreased with decreasing h below ~100 nm, consistent with previous observations that enhanced molecular mobility existing within a nanoscale layer at the free surface. For thicknesses exceeding 1 micron, however, a bulklike relaxation mode emerged, and concomitantly, the fast mode changed to a long-range mode that extends over micrometers from the free surface. These findings evidence that the propagation distance of enhanced mobility at the surface is micrometers. Moreover, this surface region comprises not only a nanoscale mobile outermost layer, which is well-known, but also a hitherto unknown slower microscale sublayer that relaxes by a different mechanism. The existence of two different relaxation modes with nanometers and micrometers ranges from the free surface implies that studies probing the near-surface dynamics with different timescales may find different propagation distances of the enhanced mobility, providing an explanation for their vastly values found in the literature. This program has generated five refereed journal articles and eight conference presentations. Two of the presentations were invited talks while five were given at international conferences. It has provided training of one postdoctoral fellow, one Ph.D. student, and three undergraduates. Upon completion of the project, the postdoctoral fellow joined Zhejiang Sci-Tech University as an assistant professor. The Ph.D. student has joined ExxonMobile China as an engineer.

16301919.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16301919.value: The finding that the propagation distance of enhanced mobility at the surface is micrometers is surprising as both theoretical arguments and computer simulations indicate that it should be less than about 10 nm. A natural further development is to address the physical origin of the microscale of the propagation distance. We surmise that spontaneously excited shear modes on the surface could be the origin of the long-range mode we found as an estimate indicates that these modes can have relaxation times and propagation distances similar to those of the long-range mode. It would also be meaningful to examine if the long-range mode also exists in other polymer films. We have submitted a grant proposal to the RGC requesting support to pursue these ideas.

16301919.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16301919.value: For elastic solids, when a small force is applied to the solid for a duration and let go, the solid restores its original shape and dimension irrespective of the duration. For viscoelastic solids like polymers, however, the recovery is partial if the hold time of the force is longer than the relaxation time of the polymer. At room temperature, this relaxation time is very long, of the order of several months. Our result shows that if the polymer is made into thin films with thicknesses below ~50 microns, even a hold time of only several hours could cause permanent deformation to the film at room temperature. This finding suggests that devices like stretchable electronics, optoelectronics, and integrated systems made of thin polymer films that are subject to constant stress or strain during operation may change shape after each use. This would have significant impact on their reusability.
