16302319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16302319.value: The quantum anomalous hall Insulator (QAHI) has recently been engineered to show conductive quantum Hall edge states even in the absence of external magnetic fields. It is formed by introducing ferromagnetism into a topological insulator through doping it with magnetic materials. The availability of the topological quantum Hall state without the need for strong magnetic fields opens the possibility of creating a novel topological superconductor (SC) by introducing superconductivity into these chiral edge states. Two distinct topological superconducting phases with one and two chiral Majorana edge modes have been theoretically predicted, and are characterized by Chern numbers N of ±1 and ±2, respectively. Recent experiments on a QAHI/SC heterostructure have revealed the presence of integer and half-integer quantized conductance plateaus as a function of the magnetic field across a deposited superconductor strip and presented quantization evidence of these two distinct topological states. Most recently, we have provided spectroscopic evidence of a superconducting QAHI state using nano-point contacts at the edge of a QAHI/SC heterostructure and obtained unique signatures of these topological superconducting phases. The phase with N = ±1 with a conduction signature of 2e^2/h occurs in a narrow field regime during the reversal of the QAHI magnetization just before the QAHI enters a trivial insulating state without edge conduction. These results are consistent with the theoretical analysis and confirm the presence of chiral Majorana modes with quantized conduction. Unfortunately, these chiral Majorana modes in such a two-dimensional QAHI/SC heterostructure are delocalized and unsuitable for topological qubits. It has been predicted that when the heterostructure is reduced to a 100 nm wide strip, the Majorana modes on the opposite side of the heterostructure become coupled and form a single helical conductive channel with Majorana zero modes localized at the end of the one-dimensional strip. Such 1D QAHI/SC structures, when arranged to form cross-shaped structures, have been proposed as components of scalable qubit networks. We already have the capability to fabricate 1D QAHI and QAHI/SC nanoribbons, and in this proposed research, we want to probe the existence of quantized helical conduction in 1D QAHI and localized Majorana zero modes in QAHI/SC heterostructures by transport and spectroscopic experiments. If successful, our research could open an alternative path to future topological quantum computation with a scalable platform based on thin-film wafer technology, which is easier to develop than competing approaches. 近来，量子反常霍尔绝缘体（quantum anomalous hall Insulator, QAHI）已被用于显示即使在外磁场缺失条件下的导电量子霍尔边缘态。通过掺杂磁性材料将铁磁性引入拓扑绝缘体可以获得量子反常霍尔绝缘体。拓扑量子霍尔态无需强磁场，该特性开启了在手性边缘态中引入超导性从而创造出新奇拓扑超导体（superconductor, SC）的可能性。具有一个或两个手性马约拉纳边缘模的两种不同的拓扑超导相已经得到了理论预测，其特征在于陈数N分别为±1和±2。最近关于QAHI/SC异质结构的研究已经揭示了整数和半整数量子化电导平台作为穿过沉积超导体条带的磁场函数的存在，并且呈现了这两种不同拓扑态的量化证据。近来，我们通过在QAHI / SC异质结构的边缘使用纳米点接触提供了超导QAHI态的光谱证据，并且获得了这些拓扑超导相的独特特征。QAHI进入无边缘电导的平庸绝缘态之前，即QAHI磁化反转期间，N=±1且传导特征为2e^2/h的相位在窄场域内出现。这些结果与理论分析一致，证实了具有量子化传导的手性马约拉纳模的存在。不幸的是，这些二维QAHI/SC异质结构中的手性马约拉纳模是离域的，且不适用于拓扑量子位。经预测，当异质结构减小到100纳米宽的条带时，在异质结构对侧上的Majorana模会耦合并形成Majorana零模位于一维条带末端的单个螺旋形导电通道。当被构建成十字形结构时，该一维QAHI/SC结构可作为可扩展量子比特网络的组件。我们已经具备制造一维QAHI和QAHI / SC纳米带的能力，并且在该提议的研究中，我们想要通过输运和光谱实验探测一维QAHI中量子化螺旋传导的存在以及QAHI / SC异质结构中的局域化马约拉纳零模的存在。如果成功，我们的研究可以通过基于薄膜晶圆技术的可扩展平台来开辟未来拓扑量子计算的替代途径，开发新方法比在原有基础上竞争更加容易。

16302319.label: Realisation of objectives
16302319.value: Despite significant challenges posed by the pandemic and recent developments in the research field of Majorana zero modes, we have successfully met all objectives. We previously mentioned these difficulties in our midterm report, and we summarize them here for clarity. The pandemic severely slowed our progress during the first half of the project period. Our project heavily relied on the use of our nanofabrication facilities at HKUST, which were unavailable for extended periods during the pandemic. Additionally, our project depended on thin-film materials supplied by our collaborators at UCLA, who were even more severely affected by the pandemic. This situation forced us to work with a very limited number of samples and extend our work on similar heterostructures between superconductors and topological materials. Despite these challenges, we managed to successfully address all objectives, although we would have preferred better circumstances to achieve even more robust research results. Another difficulty, which did not affect our research pace but impacted our publication record, was a strong controversy that developed in the research community in the field of Majorana zero modes. Several leading publications in this field were retracted due to controversies over the reported data. This included a publication by our collaborators in the journal Science on the first report of chiral Majorana modes in a two-dimensional quantum anomalous Hall insulator/superconductor heterostructure. While we were not involved with this publication, it served as a basis for our research on quasi-one-dimensional quantum anomalous Hall insulator/superconductor heterostructures and its retraction caused a high level of controversy in the community. This forced us to proceed with caution when publishing our results. One experiment we aimed to achieve was the reproduction of the results in this Science article. Although we achieved this, the controversy surrounding the Science article made us feel that publishing these results could potentially harm our reputation. We thus decided to abandon this part and have only presented some results at a conference, as listed in this report. We therefore focused on the quasi-1D QAHI-superconductor devices, as stated in our objectives, and consolidated all our results into one comprehensive publication, which we successfully published in the journal Cell Reports Physical Sciences in 2024 (impact factor 8.9). Despite the need to formulate our findings very carefully, we successfully demonstrated that quasi-one-dimensional quantum anomalous Hall insulator/superconductor heterostructures are a promising platform for the realization of localized Majorana zero modes. We presented experimental results that perfectly aligned with theoretical simulations suggesting the existence of a localized Majorana zero mode formed at the interface where a bare QAHI nanoribbon meets a QAHI nanoribbon proximitized by a superconductor. These results were reproducibly demonstrated in at least three different devices. Furthermore, our research on a similar quasi-one-dimensional heterostructure, which is a combination of a superconductor and a topological material, yielded comparable experimental results. This topological material likely possesses characteristics of a quantum anomalous Hall insulator due to the presence of ferromagnetic impurities at the interface with a topological insulator. Notably, we observed a quantized zero bias anomaly in the tunneling spectrum at the end of a nanoribbon. This nanoribbon was fabricated identically to our quasi-one-dimensional quantum anomalous Hall insulator/superconductor heterostructures. This research was published in the journal Advanced Electronic Materials (Impact factor 6.64) in 2022, thereby contributing a second significant publication that promotes a novel experimental platform for realizing Majorana zero modes. In the following we explain how we achieved addressing the individual objectives. Objective 1 - 3 In our midterm report, we had already discussed these objectives. We developed a technique to fabricate narrow, quasi-one-dimensional QAHO nanoribbon structures. This process begins with two-dimensional QAHI films on a GaAs substrate and employs a focused ion beam milling technique. We successfully fabricated nanoribbon structures with widths as small as 70 nm and lengths up to the micrometer scale. We demonstrated that a conducting channel across the nanoribbon remains intact, allowing the transmission of the chiral edge mode from both sides. The narrow width of the nanoribbon ensures that the two opposing edge modes are closer than the predicted hybridization limit, facilitating the formation of a helical edge channel. This is a prerequisite for the predicted formation of a localized Majorana zero mode. Our subsequent experiments on quasi-one-dimensional QAHI/superconductor nanostructures further confirmed these results. These experiments provided evidence for a small hybridization gap within the topological band when the chemical potential was adjusted by applying a magnetic field perpendicular to the heterostructure. These experiments served as a test to determine whether we can successfully produce quasi-one-dimensional QAHI structures with the required narrow widths to meet the conditions necessary for the formation of a localized Majorana mode when proximitized by a superconductor. Objective 4 The first three objectives served as the preparatory stage for our main experiments, while the fourth objective pertained to the primary stage where we aimed to use our nanofabrication technique to prepare devices suitable for detecting localized Majorana zero modes. We successfully achieved this objective. In our publication in Cell Reports Physical Science, we presented experimental results from three different devices. Each device contained quasi-one-dimensional quantum anomalous Hall insulator/superconductor heterostructures and showed similar results. We fabricated narrow nanoribbons of approximately 100 nm width, extending from a region of a bare QAHI film to a region where the QAHI film was covered by a superconductor (niobium). We then conducted Andreev reflection spectroscopy at very low temperatures at the interface between the bare QAHI part of the nanoribbon and the part covered by the superconductor. Without applying a magnetic field, we observed a complex structure with several peaks and shoulders within the energy range of the superconducting gap of niobium, including a central zero-bias anomaly. Upon applying a magnetic field perpendicular to the QAHI/SC heterostructure, the shoulder structures were suppressed, leading to a single sharp zero bias anomaly. This occurred before the conductance disappeared in higher fields when the chemical potential was pushed into the small hybridization gap of the chiral edge mode. Our experiments conclusively demonstrated our success in inducing superconductivity in our quasi-1D QAHI nanoribbon structures. However, the experimental signature proved to be more complex than the theoretical predictions. In collaboration with Prof. K. T. Law, we utilized theoretical simulations for the same device geometry, which enabled us to interpret our results. The nanopatterning of our QAHI films led to a chemical potential that crossed not only the topological channel but also several bulk bands. Each of these contributed shoulder-like structures to the Andreev reflection spectra. We demonstrated that the application of a magnetic field perpendicular to the heterostructure relatively shifted the chemical potential down into the gap region. When we applied a field on the order of 3 T, only a single zero bias peak remained. According to the simulations, this suggested that the chemical potential only crosses the topological band, leading to a single zero bias peak, which theoretically originates from a localized Majorana zero mode. We were able to reproduce this in at least three different devices, thus successfully addressing objective 4. We also found similar results for another heterostructure, which we etched with the same technique into nanoribbons. This heterostructure was formed by FeTe and the topological insulator Bi2Te3, and it exhibited a very similar quantized zero bias conductance anomaly.

16302319.label: Major findings and research outcome
16302319.value: Localized Majorana modes hold significant potential for future fault-tolerant quantum computation strategies. These modes naturally form within topological superconductors under specific conditions. Quantum Anomalous Hall Insulators (QAHI), typically thin film samples derived from a topological insulator with magnetism induced by magnetic dopants, exhibit a chiral topological edge channel. This channel allows electrons to circulate without dissipation around the sample’s edge. It is proposed that when this edge channel comes into proximity contact with a superconductor, it transforms into chiral Majorana modes. Despite having provided previously evidence for these modes [PNAS 117, 238-242 (2019)], their dispersive nature makes them challenging to utilize for topological quantum computation. To localize these Majorana modes, we engineered quasi-one-dimensional narrow nanoribbons with widths around 100 nm in this project. Theoretical predictions suggest that in such geometries, the chiral Majorana modes should localize at the end of a QAHI nanoribbon proximitized by a superconductor [Phys. Rev. B. 97, 104504 (2018)]. We fabricated devices where a portion of a QAHI nanoribbon was covered by the superconductor niobium, forming a tunneling interface between a bare QAHI nanoribbon and a proximitized one. We conducted Andreev reflection spectroscopy experiments at this interface to search for localized Majorana zero modes. The experiments revealed multiple in-gap conductance peaks across different devices. As the magnetic field perpendicular to the film increased, the multiple-peak structure evolved into a single zero-bias conductance peak. Comparing our measurements with theoretical simulations for a similar device geometry, we found consistency with the scenario where the increasing field transitions the nanoribbons from a multi-channel occupied regime to a single-channel regime. This transition is a prerequisite for observing zero-energy Majorana modes. In this regime, we detected the characteristic single zero-bias-conductance peak indicative of localized Majorana modes. This demonstrates that quasi-1D QAHI/superconductor nanostructures offer a promising new platform for detecting Majorana zero modes [Cell Reports Physical Science 5, 101762 (2024)].

16302319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16302319.value: Our study illustrates that narrow quantum anomalous Hall insulator (QAHI)/superconductor heterostructures offer a promising platform for generating localized Majorana modes using a top-down approach from 2D films. However, more comprehensive experiments are required to confirm the Majorana origin of these experimental signatures. We consistently observed in our nanoribbons that the chemical potential shifts into the QAHI’s conduction band upon contact with the superconductor. Although the chemical potential can be adjusted back into the topological regime within the band gap using a magnetic field, it would be more efficient to use gate voltages to achieve this state without the need for a magnetic field. The use of sputtered niobium as the superconductor is suboptimal. A superior strategy would involve using 2D superconductors like NbSe2 to proximitize the QAHI via an atomically clean, epitaxially grown interface. Once this step is accomplished, the most compelling evidence for the presence of localized Majorana zero modes would be the fabrication of simple topological qubits. These could be constructed by intersecting two QAHI/superconductor nanoribbons with gate electrodes, allowing a pair of Majorana modes to be braided by moving them between the four ends of the cross-like structures.

16302319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16302319.value: This project is about the search for a special “elementary” particle called Majorana fermion, which can be found under certain conditions mimicked by the electrons in a material. These particles are interesting because they could make quantum computers more reliable. We searched for them using an innovative material - a “topological superconductor” - which can host these Majorana modes. We have made very narrow nanoribbons and found it to be a good place for Majorana fermions to exist. We used a technique called Andreev reflection spectroscopy to study the nanoribbons and found several peaks of conductance, which is a measure of how easily electricity can flow. When we applied a magnetic field to the ribbons, these multiple peaks turned into a single peak at zero bias, which is a good sign that Majorana particles are present. Our theoretical simulations support these experimental findings and suggest that the magnetic field changes the ribbon from a state where multiple channels of electricity can flow to a state where only one channel can flow. This single-channel state is necessary for Majorana particles to exist. Therefore, this research is a promising step towards using Majorana fermions in quantum computers.

16302419.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16302419.value: Techniques and concepts in statistical mechanics have increasing applications in devising and analyzing computational algorithms. In optimization and inference problems in which the unknown or probabilistic variables are related by a network structure, the belief propagation (BP) algorithm is a widely applicable method in which messages about the environment of a node are exchanged, and the solution is obtained after iterations. Since BP is a local approach, its computational complexity scales favorably with network size and is useful for decentralized control in large networks and evolving networks. For real-valued variables, BP yields the exact solution of the mean estimates when it converges. However, when the network structure contains loops, messages propagating along distinctive arms of a loop will be correlated. Since BP is derived by approximating the local network topology as a tree structure, variances and higher order statistics of the variables are greatly underestimated. To address loop effects, the generalized belief propagation (GBP) was developed from statistical mechanics. By including loop effects, GBP provides much more accurate marginal probabilities on the nodes than ordinary BP, but has not been applied to address real-valued variables and probabilistic inputs. In this project, we extend GBP to the problem of finding the real-valued optimal flow in transportation networks when the arrival and departure rates to the network at future instances can only be estimated from probability distributions. This is highly relevant to the dynamic control of network traffic. A typical example is the predictive control of power grids, especially when power generation relies increasingly on renewable sources. Although GBP equations are complicated, our insights on their parallelism with circuit theory greatly simplify their form and the computational steps, and our pilot study on small networks showed that they are much more accurate than BP. We will also apply GBP to Gaussian Markov random fields, in which real-valued field variables in spatial maps are estimated with uncertain and incomplete data. This is relevant to applications such as denoising spatial data (e.g., weather) and exploring resources. GBP enables us to estimate variances that are essential for tuning the model and active exploratory inquiries for optimization (technically known as hyperparameter estimation and Bayesian optimization, respectively). To accommodate a broader class of predicted distributions, we will further consider extensions to non-Gaussian distributions. 統計力學中的技術和概念在設計和分析計算算法方面具有越來越多的應用。在以網絡結構連繫未知或概率變量的優化和推理問題中，信念傳播（BP）算法是一種廣泛適用的方法，透過交換和迭代包含節點環境的信息之後，便可求解。由於BP是一種局域方法，其計算複雜度隨網絡規模擴展的程度非常有利，因而在大型和不斷演化的網絡中的分散控制非常有用。對於實值變量，BP在收斂時可以產生估計均值的精確解。 但是，當網絡結構包含迴路時，沿著迴路各臂傳播的消息將是相關的。因為在BP的推導中，是把局域網絡拓撲近似為樹結構而得到的，所以變量的方差和高階統計量被大大低估了。為了解決迴路效應，統計力學開發了廣義信念傳播（GBP）。通過包含迴路效應，GBP在節點上提供比普通BP更準確的邊際概率，但尚未應用於解決實值變量和概率輸入。 在這項目中，我們將GBP擴展到預測運輸網絡中的實值最優流量，其中這預測是基於在未來情況下網絡的到達率和離開率只能從概率分佈估計。這與網絡流量的動態控制關係非常密切。一個典型的例子是電網的預測控制，特別是當發電越來越依賴於可再生能源時。儘管GBP方程很複雜，但我們對它們與電路理論並行性的見解大大簡化了它們的形式和計算步驟，我們對小型網絡的試驗研究表明它們比BP更準確。 我們還將GBP應用於高斯馬爾可夫隨機場，其中必須在具有不確定和不完整數據的空間圖中估計實值場變量。這與需要去除噪聲的空間數據（例如天氣）和探索資源等應用，關係非常密切。GBP使我們能夠在調整模型和進行主動性探索（技術上分別稱為超參數估計和貝葉斯優化）時，能估計方差。為了適應更廣泛的預測分佈，我們將進一步考慮對非高斯分佈的擴展。

16302419.label: Realisation of objectives
16302419.value: The objectives of this project are realized in three areas: A. theoretical basis, B. neuroscience, C. applications. A1. Physical optimizers: Solving discrete optimization problems is useful in many modern applications, but they are well known for their hardness. With advances in technologies such as the Coherent Ising Machine and Simulated Bifurcation, there is an emerging interest in using physical dynamics of continuous variables to solve hard combinatorial optimizations. When the external drives of these machines are gradually tuned, non-trivial suboptimal solutions emerge at the so-called bifurcation point. Contrary to the conventional belief that these solutions are far from optimal, we found that they nevertheless contain rich information about the optimal solution [12]. Identifying the nodes near the bifurcation point as “trapped nodes” and “swing nodes”, we found that the values inferred by the trapped nodes can speed up the computation effectively. Using problem instances from the Biq-Mac library benchmark and random Ising models, we validated this approach’s superior convergence and accuracy. A2. Generalized associative memories: We proposed a generalized associative memory model of pattern sequences, in which pattern separations within an arbitrary distance along the sequences are learned [10]. The model can be analytically solved and predicts that a short-range correlation already significantly enhances the memory of the sequence, i.e., the stimulus-induced attractor can be highly correlated with a significant number of patterns in the stored sequence. We also derived the eigenvalue spectrum of the coupling matrix using the replica method, which is also shown to be consistent with the results obtained by applying the free probability method [11]. The maximum eigenvalue is then obtained by an iterative equation, related to the paramagnetic to spin glass transition in the model. The derivations of the eigenvalue spectrum provide useful methodologies in modeling other information processing problems with sequential correlations. A3. Importance of Prior Knowledge: Pattern inference with fluctuating data performs better if prior knowledge of the hidden information is available. This can be formulated as the prior distribution in Bayesian inference. In [2] we proposed a statistical physics model of unsupervised learning with prior knowledge. Compared with the prior-free scenario, we revealed that the prior knowledge strongly reduces the critical data size for symmetry breaking, and moreover, it causes the permutation symmetry-breaking phases to merge. We further verified that the prior can be estimated from data samples. A4. Gaussian Generalized Belief Propagation (GaGBP): Belief Propagation (BP) is a popular algorithm for performing approximate inference on general graphs. Generalized Belief Propagation (GBP), as an extension of BP, can be more accurate than BP but it is also perceived to be much more computationally expensive. We developed GaGBP which considerably improves accuracy while remaining reasonably efficient [7]. We further developed an algorithm based on GaGBP to demonstrate its feasibility for performing inference on dynamical graphical models, an example being the inference of current fluctuations in electrical network models where the statistics of injection currents are changing with time. Experiments show that the algorithm yields accurate results with quick response in settings of distributed processing for networks. B1. Rough-to-fine information retrieval: Categorical relationships between objects are encoded as overlapped neural representations in the brain. In [6], we proposed that neural feedback, which is widely observed in the brain, contributes to disentangle neural correlations to improve information retrieval. We studied a hierarchical neural network storing the hierarchical categorical information of objects, and information retrieval goes from rough-to-fine, aided by the push–pull neural feedback. Our model reproduces the push-pull phenomenon observed in neural data and sheds light on our understanding of the role of feedback in neural information processing. B2. Bimodular networks: We studied bimodular networks with excitatory and inhibitory inter-modular couplings in the presence of static and moving stimuli. We found non-trivial interactive behaviors depending on inter-modular couplings, inferred positions and magnitudes [5]. The dependence on disparity is consistent with the Bayesian framework. B3. Multisensory integration: To deal with probabilistic inputs from two modalities, we proposed a Bayesian approach to multisensory integration in the brain, based on a prior consisting of both a correlated and an independent component [9]. We found that the probabilistic model can be formulated in two steps, the first integrates the cues from the two modalities using the correlated prior component, and the second combines the correlated component with a further independent input. Thus, we proposed the corresponding network circuitry consisting of congruent and integrated neurons, providing important insights on well characterized brain functions. Next, to address the challenging problem of causal inference, we introduced the corresponding probabilistic model in the framework of probabilistic population coding and implemented the decision-making circuit with a gated neural network [13]. This work helps us to go deeper into the understanding of the nature of the causal inference, and how it can be linked to network dynamics with a well-designed architecture. C1. Robust transportation networks: We introduced the message-passing algorithm and discrete Green's function to elucidate how resource fluctuations determine flow fluctuations [1]. We developed the schemes of optimal bandwidth allocation in links and optimal resources adjustment in nodes. Compared with the conventional approach of proportionate bandwidth assignment or resources reduction, our optimization schemes greatly enhance the stability of the networks against fluctuations. We further verified the robustness of our scheme for long-tailed distributions recently found in power grids. Furthermore, we found that the two optimization schemes are correlated except in relay nodes. C2: Fluctuating data: To develop techniques for studying fluctuating data, we used real data from the Taiwan freeway system, and found that traffic congestion is characterized by a loopy trajectory in the fundamental diagram, and the area enclosed by the loop is a measure of the economic loss due to congestion [8]. In a study of the highway traffic through a tunnel, we found interesting switching behavior during congestion and the effects of control policy [4]. For fluctuating time series data, we studied the housing price data in Hong Kong from 1992 to 2010, and observed signs of quasi-periodicity in housing price and transaction volume [3]. We found that there is an overall periodicity of approximately 30 months in housing price changes and a strong lead-lag relationship between housing price and transaction volume. Our analysis reveals that this quasi-periodicity is potentially driven by prime lending rates. Incorporation of quasi-periodicity into the kernel of Gaussian processes further enables us to construct a predictive model of the Hong Kong housing price trends that outperforms other traditional kernel functions.

16302419.label: Major findings and research outcome
16302419.value: Three areas of major findings: A. theoretical basis, B. neuroscience, C. applications. A1. Physical optimizers: We discovered that when continuous physical dynamics (such as the coherent Ising machine) is used to solve discrete optimization problems, the bifurcation point in the energy landscape provides rich information of the final solution [12]. Freezing the bifurcated “trapped nodes” speeds up the computation effectively. A2. Generalized associative memories: We proposed generalized associative memories for pattern sequences with extended correlations, and found that a short correlation already strengthens the memory significantly [10]. The derivation of the eigenvalue spectrum of the coupling matrix provides a useful methodology in modeling other problems [11]. A3. Importance of prior knowledge: We proposed a statistical physics model of unsupervised learning with prior knowledge, revealing its advantages when compared with the prior-free scenario [2]. A4. Gaussian Generalized Belief Propagation (GaGBP): We developed GaGBP for inferring variances on dynamical graphical models [7], such as current fluctuations in electrical networks with fluctuating sources. The algorithm yields accurate results with quick response in settings of distributed processing. B1. Rough-to-fine information retrieval: We proposed that push-pull neural feedbacks, which are widely observed in the brain, contribute to disentangle correlations via a rough-to-fine mechanism [6]. B2. Bimodular networks: We found non-trivial interactive behaviors depending on inter-modular couplings, inferred positions and magnitudes [5]. B3. Multisensory integration: We proposed a Bayesian approach to multisensory integration in the brain, based on a prior consisting of both a correlated and an independent component [9]. We developed a neural circuitry consisting of congruent and integrated neurons that models optimal inference in the Bayesian framework. By introducing gated neurons, the system can perform causal inference [13]. C1. Robust transportation networks: We developed the schemes of optimal bandwidth allocation in links and optimal resource adjustment in nodes [1]. Compared with the conventional approach, our approach can highly enhance the stability of the networks against fluctuations. C2: Fluctuating data: Using real data from the Taiwan freeway system, we found that traffic congestion is characterized by a loopy trajectory in the fundamental diagram, and the loop area is a measure of the economic loss due to congestion [8]. In a study of the highway traffic through a tunnel, we found interesting switching behavior during congestion and the effects of control policy [4]. We also discovered quasi-periodicity in the Hong Kong housing price data [3]. Incorporating quasi-periodicity enables us to construct a performing predictive model.

16302419.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16302419.value: In the area of physical optimizers, we will benchmark their computational ability in solving hard discrete optimization problems by considering their behaviors in finding the ground state of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model, whose analytical solution is well known. We will calculate how the physical optimizers decode the ground state energy of the SK model and how it depends on the noise level and the external drive used to tune its energy landscape through the bifurcation point. Beyond the bifurcation point, we will consider other improved methods of selectively freezing a fraction of dynamical nodes of the physical optimizers. We will also consider whether decentralized optimization can speed up the convergence, using a message-passing approach. We will extend the analysis of highway traffic data to study other types of fluctuating data, such as air traffic data in the terminal maneuvering area of the Hong Kong International Airport (HKIA). An interesting and unique feature of HKIA is the extensive use of holding patterns to relieve air traffic congestions and the short duration of communications for flights arriving from the North and Northwest direction. These issues will be addressed by the techniques developed in the present project.

16302419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16302419.value: This project aims at developing algorithms for inferring variables in optimization problems in the presence of data fluctuations. With technological advances such as the Coherent Ising Machine, there is an emerging interest in using physical optimizers to solve hard combinatorial optimizations. By tuning the external drives of these optimizers, a nonzero-solution regime emerges at a point referred to as the bifurcation point. The solution near this point was not completely optimal, but we discovered that it still provides rich information of the final solution. Indeed, we identified some “trapped nodes” near this point whose inferred states facilitate speedy computation. In studying how the brain stores pattern sequences, we found that a short correlation among the patterns already strengthens the memory significantly. We also found that prior knowledge facilitates learning. For fluctuating network data, we developed accurate message-passing algorithms for inferring variances. Finally, we studied real fluctuating data in highway traffic and housing prices. In highway traffic we found that congestion is characterized by a loopy trajectory in the flux-density space. The loop area is a measure of the economic loss due to congestion. In housing price data, we discovered periodic fluctuations and constructed a predictive model accordingly.

16302519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16302519.value: A wide variety of natural phenomena, such as sound, heat and fluid dynamics, can be well described by partial differential equations (PDEs). They also interact decisively with other branches of mathematics such as geometry and probability, and other scientific fields such as engineering and economics. This proposed project will use analysis of PDEs to study best constants of fractional Sobolev inequalities and several related shape optimization problems. Sobolev inequalities are among the most famous and useful functional inequalities in analysis. They express a strong integrability and regularity property of a function in terms of the integrability property of its (fractional) derivatives. The significance of the best Sobolev constant is well known in widely diverse disciplines including PDEs, differential geometry and even quantum field theory. Shape optimization problems have strong relations to a number of applications in physics and engineering that require a focus on shapes instead of parameters or functions. The goal of these applications is to deform and modify the admissible shapes in order to comply with a given cost function that needs to be optimized. The isoperimetric problem, which is to determine a plane figure of the largest possible area whose boundary has a specified length, is among the most classical shape optimization problems. We know that this figure exists and it must be a disk. Many shape optimization problems can be seen in the larger framework of optimal control problems. Admissible shapes play the role of admissible control and the corresponding state variable is usually the solution of a PDE on the control domain. The intriguing feature is that the competing objects are shapes, i.e., domains in the Euclidean space, instead of functions as usually appearing in problems of calculus of variations. The object we study is a fractional Sobolev inequality in domains. Frank, Xiong and the PI discovered a new phenomenon that the best constants of these fractional Sobolev inequalities are sensitive to the shape of the domains and can be achieved for domains in a special class, which is in contrast to the classical Sobolev inequality. Here, the PI proposes to investigate whether the best constant is always achieved for all bounded smooth domains, and if so, the existence and the shape of the domain that has the least constant. The PI also proposes to study the Rayleigh-Faber-Krahn inequality for the first eigenvalues involving this fractional Sobolev norm, and related symmetry property of the solutions. 在这里我们主要研究有界区域上的分数阶Sobolev不等式。Sobolev不等式是一个用来表达函数的可积性和正则性之间的关系的不等式。 它是分析学中最有用的不等式之一。它在偏微分方程和微分几何中有着广泛的应用。我们主要的研究对象是有界区域上的分数阶Sobolev不等式的最优常数。我们同时也研究它的一个衍生问题。这个Sobolev不等式所对应的拟微分算子的第一特征值是可定义的。我们想要研究关于这个第一特征值所对应的Rayleigh-Faber-Krahn不等式。

16302519.label: Realisation of objectives
16302519.value: The classical Sobolev inequality expresses a function's strong integrability and regularity based on the integrability of its derivatives. The optimal constant in this inequality indicates its sharpness and has significant implications across diverse fields such as PDEs and differential geometry. Notably, while the optimal constant remains constant across different domains, optimality is only achieved in the entirety of Euclidean spaces. In previous research conducted jointly with R. L. Frank and J. Xiong, we explored a Sobolev inequality associated with the regional fractional Laplacian in domains. This study unveiled a novel phenomenon where the optimal constant varies depending on the domain's shape. Specifically, the optimal constant for the entire space is invariably greater than that for any other domain. Furthermore, in domains such as the half-space or those with a flat boundary, this optimal constant is attainable by certain functions, marking a clear divergence from the classical Sobolev inequality. The PI proposed here further investigation into whether the optimal constant is achievable for certain non-flat domains, and also to explore the Faber-Krahn inequality for the regional fractional Laplacian. In the research output 2, we investigated this regional fractional Sobolev inequality for non-flat domains. We obtained a fine expansion of the energy functional evaluated at a rescaled minimizer for the half space, which particularly shows that the optimal constant for other domains are always smaller than or qual to that of the half space. This fine expansion involves the mean curvature of the domain's boundary, as well as the first order variational of the energy functional evaluated at the half space with respective to a small standard parabola perturbation. During our analysis, the mean curvature naturally emerges after we demonstrating that the minimizer in the half-space is radially symmetric in the first n-1 variables following a possible translation. Determining the sign of the first variation presents challenges due to the strong nonlocality of the energy functional. Nonetheless, we demonstrated that if a part of the domain closely aligns with a Euclidean hyperplane, then the sharp Sobolev constant is strictly smaller than that for the half-space, and thus, its achievability is confirmed. In research output 1, we examined the Faber-Krahn inequality for the regional fractional Laplacian, focusing on identifying a normalized domain that minimizes the first eigenvalue of this operator. Specifically, within the category of convex domains with a fixed measure, we successfully established the existence of a convex minimizer. More broadly, we demonstrated the existence of a minimizer that is both bounded and represents a level set of a fractional Sobolev function. Additionally, we derived new a priori diameter estimates.

16302519.label: Major findings and research outcome
16302519.value: First, we investigated the regional fractional Sobolev inequality for non-flat domains. We proved that the minimizers in the half space case are radially symmetric in the first n-1 variable subject to a translation. We used these rescaled minimizers in the half space as test function to obtain a fine expansion of the fractional Sobolev ratio in any domain. A corollary is that optimal constant for other domains are always smaller than or qual to that of the half space. In this expansion, the first nontrivial leading error involves the mean curvature of the domain's boundary, as well as the first order variational of the energy functional evaluated at the half space with respective to a small standard parabola perturbation. We proved that if all the principal curvature of the boundary at one point are sufficiently small, then the sharp Sobolev constant is strictly smaller than that for the half-space and hence, is achieved. Second, we studied the Faber-Krahn inequality for the regional fractional Laplacian, which about finding a domain minimizing the first eigenvalue of the regional fractional Laplacian. We proved the existence of minimizers within the category of convex domain. Without the convexity assumption, we proved the existence of minimizers, which is bounded and represents a level set of a fractional Sobolev function. We also obtained new a priori diameter estimates.

16302519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16302519.value: One potential further development involves determining the signs of the first variation of the Sobolev ratio, evaluated at the minimizer in the half-space, subject to a standard parabolic perturbation. Direction calculation may be difficult. Perhaps it needs some new geometric ideas. The other potential further development is to show the global continuity of the Sobolev function whose level set is the minimizing shape for the Faber-Kahn inequality with respect to the regional fractional Sobolev Laplacian. Establishing this continuity requires a detailed understanding of the asymptotic behavior near the level set, aligning it with the behavior observed in its Green's function. These represent compelling open questions within the field. A notable challenge in these investigations is that the operator itself varies depending on the shape of the minimizer, adding complexity to the analysis.

16302519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16302519.value: This research project investigates advanced mathematical concepts known as Sobolev inequalities, which help us understand and predict the behavior of certain mathematical functions that are crucial in physics and engineering. Traditionally, these inequalities are known to behave consistently across different environments, but this project discovered that their effectiveness varies significantly depending on the shape and curvature of the space involved. Specifically, it was found that while these inequalities perform optimally in infinite flat spaces, their efficiency decreases in more complex, non-flat spaces. Additionally, the project explored another mathematical principle, the Faber-Krahn inequality, which deals with identifying the most efficient shapes for minimizing certain mathematical properties. This research not only challenges existing mathematical theories but also has practical implications in designing materials and structures in engineering, enhancing our ability to apply mathematics in real-world, complex environments.

To compare the quality of the analytical results of the voter model with zealots in objective (1) with numerical simulation for various concentrations of zealots. To perform the analytical calculation of the probability density function by solving the Fokker–Planck equation for the voter model with zealots in a co-evolving social network (Model 2 in the proposal). This study also aims to explore the nature of the solution as it depends on the concentration of zealots and the parameters describing the homophilic (heterophilic) nature of the susceptible voters. To compare the quality of the analytical results of the voter model with zealots in an adaptive network in objective (3) with numerical simulation for various concentrations of zealots and the homophilic (heterophilic) parameters. To collect and analyze numerical data from simulations in order to gain insights into the finite-size effects and the emergence of evolving community structure.

16302619.label: Realisation of objectives
16302619.value: This project studies the dynamics of adaptation in complex networks, which is applicable to social networks. Another example of adaptive networks is neuronal networks. Through the studies, the project also covers many fundamental aspects of network dynamics. The realization of the objectives of this project are described in the three sections below. A. Social Networks A1. Link cascades in complex networks Cascade models on networks have been used extensively to study cascade failures in complex systems. However, most current models consider failure caused by node damage and neglect the possibility of link damage, which is relevant to transportation, social dynamics, biology, and medicine. In an attempt to generalize conventional cascade models to link damage, we proposed a link cascade model based on the standard independent cascade model, which is then solved via both numerical simulation and analytic approximation [5]. We found that the probability that a node loses all its links due to link damage exhibits a minimum as a function of node degree, indicating that there exists an optimal degree for a node to be most resistant to link damage. We applied our model to investigate the sign distribution in a real-world signed social network and found that such an optimal degree does exist in a real-world dataset. A2. Effects of opinion leaders on the consensus of voters In [11], we applied techniques of statistical physics on the problem of consensus formation in politics. We studied the expected long-term consensus of a large society during a two-party election with the majority-rule voter model, which prescribes a voter to adopt the majority opinion of his neighbors drawn according to the principle of homogeneous mixing. We found that the initially more popular party always wins, but its popularity evolves in different manners depending on the number of a voter’s neighbors drawn. Once the parties are allowed to hire opinion leaders with fixed opinions (also referred to as zealots), the initially less popular party can turn the tables and win eventually by hiring many leaders. More details can be found in Chun Yin Yip’s PhD thesis. A3: Emergence and dissolution dynamics in traffic congestion The emerging and fading of traffic congestion is also a collective dynamical process of vehicles. Using real data from the Taiwan freeway system, we found that traffic congestion is characterized by a loopy trajectory in the fundamental diagram, and the area enclosed by the loop is a measure of the economic loss due to congestion [3]. B. Neuronal networks B1. Rough-to-fine information retrieval Categorical relationships between objects are encoded as overlapped neural representations in the brain. In [1], we proposed that neural feedback, which is widely observed in the brain, contributes to disentangle neural correlations to improve information retrieval. We studied a hierarchical neural network storing the hierarchical categorical information of objects, and information retrieval goes from rough-to-fine, aided by the push–pull neural feedback. Our model reproduces the push-pull phenomenon observed in neural data and sheds light on our understanding of the role of feedback in neural information processing. B2. Bimodular neuronal networks We studied bimodular neuronal networks with excitatory and inhibitory inter-modular couplings in the presence of static and moving stimuli. We found non-trivial interactive behaviors depending on inter-modular couplings, inferred positions and magnitudes [8]. The dependence on disparity is consistent with the Bayesian framework. B3. Multisensory integration Neuronal networks also exhibit adaptative behaviors when there are two modalities of inputs. We proposed a Bayesian approach to multisensory integration in the brain, based on a prior consisting of both a correlated and an independent component [4]. We found that the probabilistic model can be formulated in two steps, the first integrates the cues from the two modalities using the correlated prior component, and the second combines the correlated component with a further independent input. Thus, we proposed the corresponding network circuitry consisting of congruent and integrated neurons, providing important insights on well characterized brain functions. Next, to address the challenging problem of causal inference, we introduced the corresponding probabilistic model in the framework of probabilistic population coding and implemented the decision-making circuit with a gated neural network [10]. This work helps us to go deeper into the understanding of the nature of the causal inference, and how it can be linked to network dynamics with a well-designed architecture. C. Fundamental properties of network adaptation C1. Physical optimizers: Solving discrete optimization problems is useful in many modern applications, but they are well known for their hardness. With advances in technologies such as the Coherent Ising Machine and Simulated Bifurcation, there is an emerging interest in using physical dynamics of continuous variables to solve hard combinatorial optimizations. When the external drives of these machines are gradually tuned, non-trivial suboptimal solutions emerge at the so-called bifurcation point. Contrary to the conventional belief that these solutions are far from optimal, we found that they nevertheless contain rich information about the optimal solution [9]. Identifying the nodes near the bifurcation point as “trapped nodes” and “swing nodes”, we found that the values inferred by the trapped nodes can speed up the computation effectively. Using problem instances from the Biq-Mac library benchmark and random Ising models, we validated this approach’s superior convergence and accuracy. C2. Generalized associative memories We proposed a generalized associative memory model of pattern sequences, in which pattern separations within an arbitrary distance along the sequences are learned [6]. The model can be analytically solved and predicts that a short-range correlation already significantly enhances the memory of the sequence, i.e., the stimulus-induced attractor can be highly correlated with a significant number of patterns in the stored sequence. We also derived the eigenvalue spectrum of the coupling matrix using the replica method, which is also shown to be consistent with the results obtained by applying the free probability method [7]. The maximum eigenvalue is then obtained by an iterative equation, related to the paramagnetic to spin glass transition in the model. The derivations of the eigenvalue spectrum provide useful methodologies in modeling other information processing problems with sequential correlations. C3. Gaussian Generalized Belief Propagation (GaGBP) Belief Propagation (BP) is a popular algorithm for performing approximate inference on general graphs. Generalized Belief Propagation (GBP), as an extension of BP, can be more accurate than BP but it is also perceived to be much more computationally expensive. We developed GaGBP which considerably improves accuracy while remaining reasonably efficient [2]. We further developed an algorithm based on GaGBP to demonstrate its feasibility for performing inference on dynamical graphical models, an example being the inference of current fluctuations in electrical network models where the statistics of injection currents are changing with time. Experiments show that the algorithm yields accurate results with quick response in settings of distributed processing for networks. Expenditure Changes The project period coincided with that of the pandemic, resulting in modifications in the expenditure. In the “General Expenses” item, traveling costs supporting visits to collaborators, as well as international workshop attendance by students, were eliminated due to pandemic travel restrictions. Incidentally, the publication cost of [9] was paid by our industrial collaborator. These changes explained the reduction in general expenses.

16302619.label: Major findings and research outcome
16302619.value: Three areas of major findings: A. social networks, B. neuronal networks, C. fundamental properties of network adaptation. A1. Link cascades in complex networks: We proposed a link cascade model and found that the probability that a node loses all its links due to link damage exhibits a minimum as a function of node degree, indicating that there exists an optimal degree for a node to be most resistant to link damage [5]. A2. Effects of opinion leaders on the consensus of voters: We studied the problem of consensus formation in politics [11]. We found that by hiring enough opinion leaders with fixed opinions, the initially less popular party can turn the tables and win eventually. A3: Emergence and dissolution dynamics in traffic congestion: Using real data from the Taiwan freeway system, we found that traffic congestion is characterized by a loopy trajectory in the fundamental diagram, and the loop area is a measure of the economic loss due to congestion [3]. B1. Rough-to-fine information retrieval: We proposed that push-pull neural feedbacks, which are widely observed in the brain, contribute to disentangle correlations via a rough-to-fine mechanism [6]. B2. Bimodular networks: We found non-trivial interactive behaviors depending on inter-modular couplings, inferred positions and magnitudes [5]. B3. Multisensory integration: We proposed a Bayesian approach to multisensory integration in the brain, based on a prior consisting of both a correlated and an independent component [9]. We developed a neural circuitry consisting of congruent and integrated neurons that models optimal inference in the Bayesian framework. By introducing gated neurons, the system can perform causal inference [13]. C1. Physical optimizers: We discovered that when continuous physical dynamics (such as the Coherent Ising Machine) is used to solve discrete optimization problems, the bifurcation point in the energy landscape provides rich information of the final solution [12]. Freezing the bifurcated “trapped nodes” speeds up the computation effectively. C2. Generalized associative memories: We proposed generalized associative memories for pattern sequences with extended correlations, and found that a short correlation already strengthens the memory significantly [10]. The derivation of the eigenvalue spectrum of the coupling matrix provides a useful methodology in modeling other problems [11]. C3. Gaussian Generalized Belief Propagation (GaGBP): We developed GaGBP for inferring variances on dynamical graphical models [7], such as current fluctuations in electrical networks with fluctuating sources. The algorithm yields accurate results with quick response in settings of distributed processing.

16302619.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16302619.value: We anticipate our link cascade model to have applications in areas such as transportation, biology, and medicine. Our results regarding the dead probability suggest that when link damage is of concern to network design, node strengthening strategies through link addition should be performed in such a way that the degree of a node does not deviate too much from the optimal value. It will be fruitful to extend our current analysis to study the degree dependence of a link cascade in the non-equilibrium regime. The mean-field approximation in the present work would need to be modified to give a more accurate time-dependent description. Such an extension will shed light on the nature of link cascade processes and the distinction with its node-based counterpart. In the area of physical optimizers, we will benchmark their computational ability in solving hard discrete optimization problems by considering their behaviors in finding the ground state of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model, whose analytical solution is well known. We will calculate how the physical optimizers decode the ground state energy of the SK model and how it depends on the noise level and the external drive used to tune its energy landscape through the bifurcation point.

16302619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16302619.value: This project studies the dynamics of adaptation in complex networks. When a link in a complex network fails, the failure will spread to other links in cascades. We proposed a link cascade model and found that the probability that a node becomes isolated due to link damage is minimized at an optimal connectivity. When we studied the problem of consensus formation in politics, we found that opinion leaders with fixed opinions have strong influence on election results through their personal networks. In traffic networks, we found that congestion is characterized by a loopy trajectory in the flux-density space. The loop area is a measure of the economic loss due to congestion. In neuronal networks, we modeled how the brain retrieves information through a rough-to-fine dynamics, how bimodular networks perform multisensory integration, and how pattern sequences can be remembered even when the correlation among the patterns is short. We discovered that when continuous physical dynamics is used to solve discrete optimization problems, the dynamics already contains rich information about the final solution even when the dynamical state is near zero, and accelerated algorithms can be designed. For loopy networks, we developed accurate message-passing algorithms for inferring variances.

16302719.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16302719.value: Alkynes are basic readily available materials from nature. They are the starting material for many other useful materials in our daily life, from clothing, electronic devices to medicines. The transformations from simple alkynes to these highly useful materials require many important organic reactions. In many cases, the first step is to install functional groups to alkynes, which is called functionalization. After longstanding pursuit of organic chemists, there have been various approaches available for alkyne functionalization. However, selectivity problems still remain in certain cases and more solutions are in high demand. An important aspect for alkyne functionalization is that the majority of current methods are to add two functional groups to the two different carbons on the triple bond. There have been much less known reactivity modes and examples for the addition of two functional groups on the same side of the triple bond. The proposed study is focused on the latter case, which will provide not only fundamentally new knowledge to the currently known portfolio on alkyne chemistry, but also new practically useful approaches to the synthesis of valuable products from alkynes. The proposed study will have societal applications, spanning pharmaceutical industry and functional materials to other aspects of daily life. 炔烴是來自大自然的基本原料。它們也是我們日常生活中許多其他有用材料的起始原料，從服裝、電子設備到藥物。從簡單的炔烴到這些功能材料的轉化需要許多重要的有機反應。在許多情況下，第一步是將官能團安裝到炔烴上，這稱為官能化。经过有機化學家長期不懈的努力，目前已有多種方法可用於炔烴官能化。然而，在某些情況下仍然存在選擇性問題，並且需要更多解決方案。 目前炔烃官能化的最普遍的形式是在三鍵上的兩個不同的碳原子上加兩個官能團， 而在三鍵的同一側碳原子上添加兩個官能團的實例較少。本课题的研究将側重於後一種情況，該案例不僅為目前已知的炔烴化學提供了新的知识，而且還提供了從炔烴合成有價值產物的新方法。本研究將在製藥業、材料工业和日常生活等各个方面具有潜在應用。

16302719.label: Realisation of objectives
16302719.value: In this project, we have successfully developed a range of selective functionalization reactions of alkynes. Specifically, a range of geminal addition reactions, including hydrogenation, hydroboration and even diboration, have been developed. Some of these reactions represent unprecedented reaction modes. These processes provided access to important synthetic building blocks, such as stereodefined olefins, and biologically active molecules. The objectives of this proposal have been realized as expected. We have developed a new migratory geminal hydroboration of alkynes. With the proper choice of a [CpRu]-based catalyst, a range of silyl alkynes overcame the intrinsic 1,2-addition propensity observed for general internal alkynes and reacted in a 1,1-addition mode with concomitant silyl migration, providing efficient access to various vinyl boronates with excellent stereoselectivity. This study represents a new step forward not only for alkyne hydroboration, but also for more general geminal additions of alkynes. This work has been published in J. Am. Chem. Soc. While alkyne hydroboration and enyne cyclization are two types of well-established processes, their merger for direct hydroborative cyclization to construct boryl-incorporated cyclic structures from simple enynes have been less explored, despite of their bond-forming efficiency and atom-economy. Here we have developed the first geminal hydroborative cyclization of enynes. For the first time ruthenium was employed as catalyst for hydroborative enyne cyclization, leading to a new reaction mode. Further detailed DFT calculations indicated that the reaction mechanism is likely substrate-dependent. This work has been published in Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. We have discovered a new reaction mode for the hydroboration of ynones. Overcoming the strong propensity toward their typical reactivity (simple carbonyl reduction), ynones undergo an unprecedented formal inverse H-B addition to carbonyl with concomitant trans-hydrogenation of the triple bond with [Cp*Ru(MeCN)3]PF6 as catalyst, leading to structurally novel and previously inaccessible vinyl α-hydroxylboronate products. This work has been published in J. Am. Chem. Soc. We have developed a new approach for the mild synthesis of gem-diboryl compounds bearing an α-heterosubstituent, a family of less-explored, limitedly accessible, but versatile molecules. This process also represents the first dihydroboration of heteroalkynes leading to α-hetero gem-diboryl compounds. This work has been published in J. Am. Chem. Soc. Other studies, including stereoselective addition of electron-rich alkynes, such as siloxy alkynes, ynamides, thioalkynes, have also been performed, leading new methods for the synthesis of challenging molecules, including medium rings. Regarding the expenditure, due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the budget for conference was not used as expected. This part of budget was then used for general expenses.

The objectives of this proposal have been realized as expected. Details of the major finding and research outcomes are shown below. (1) We have developed the a new migratory geminal hydroboration of alkynes. With the proper choice of a [CpRu]-based catalyst, a range of silyl alkynes reacted in a 1,1-addition mode with concomitant silyl migration with excellent stereoselectivity. Chem. Soc. (5) We have developed a modular strategy for the rapid synthesis of the valuable β-functionalized electron-rich naphthalenes, specifically, β-naphthol, β-naphthylamine, and β-naphthyl thioether derivatives. This work has been published in Chem. Sci. (6) We have developed a new [3+2] annulation for the robust asymmetric synthesis of chiral pyrrolidinones. This work has been published in Chem. Commun. (7) We developed an efficient intermolecular process for the synthesis of medium-sized lactones. This work has been published in Tetrahedron. (8) We have developed a new approach for the synthesis of coumarins from siloxy alkynes and salicyladehydes. This work has been published in Synlett. (9) We have developed an efficient [3+2] cycloaddition of nitrile oxides with electron-rich alkynes, including thioalkynes, ynol ethers, and ynamides. This work has been published in Organic Letters. (10) We have discovered an unusual formal migrative cycloaddition of aurone-derived azadienes with siloxy alkynes. This work has been published in Chemical Science.

16302719.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16302719.value: As an extension of this project, the development of additional useful catalytic geminal addition to alkynes will continue to be our topic of pursuit in this area. In particular, we will continue to explore and push the boundary of geminal addition. For example, currently geminal addition is still limited to H,H- and H,B-addition by ruthenium system. We will spend more efforts to explore other metal catalytic systems and other addition reactions, including H,Si-, Si,Si-, B,B-addition to triple bond with concomitant formation of a carbene intermediate in the future.

In this project, we have developed a range of geminal addition reactions, including hydrogenation, hydroboration and even diboration. Some of these reactions represent unprecedented reaction modes. These processes provided access to important synthetic building blocks, such as stereodefined olefins and biologically active molecules. 16302819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16302819.value: The goal of this project is to develop efficient numerical methods to solve hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs) on hypersurfaces. These PDEs arise in various areas of the applied sciences and engineering. Examples include multiphase flow calculations, simulation of Hamiltonian dynamical systems, pattern formulation on surfaces, and understanding of dynamics of compressible fluids. In this project, we propose to extend and develop novel and flexible numerical methods to solve Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) equations and hyperbolic conservation laws on surfaces. In the first part of the project, we propose to extend the Modified Virtual Grid Difference (MVGD) scheme developed by the PI to solve some widely used HJ equations, motivated by the Level Set Method. The resulting algorithms can be applied to many areas of research, such as image processing of surfaces and dimension reduction for high dimensional data. In the second part of this proposal, we will develop numerical schemes that can be used to solve hyperbolic conservation laws on surfaces. We propose to first improve numerical approximations of differential operators on the tangent plane located at each sampling point on the surface. Then, based on these approximations, we will develop a finite-volume scheme of this tangent plane. The outcome of this proposal should lead to new numerical algorithms and will provide several alternatives to other numerical methods in a variety of applications. The project should also be important to many disciplines, including crystal growth modeling, surface regularization in image processing and computer graphics, high-frequency asymptotic solution to surface wave propagation in seismology and geophysics, multiphase flows with surfactants, and the simulation of gas dynamics. 項目的目標是開發有效的數值方法來解決超曲面上的雙曲型偏微分方程（PDE）。這些雙曲型偏微分方程出現在應用科學和工程的各個領域。例子包括多相流計算，哈密頓動力系統的模擬，表面上的圖案配方，以及對可壓縮流體動力學的理解。 在這個項目中，我們建議擴展和開發新穎而靈活的數值方法，以解決表面上的Hamilton-Jacobi（HJ）方程和雙曲守恆定律。在項目的第一部分，我們建議擴展由PI開發的改進的虛擬網格差異（Modified Virtual Grid Difference）方案，以解決一些由水平集方法而廣泛使用的HJ方程。得到的算法可以應用於許多研究領域，例如表面的圖像處理和高維數據的降維。在該提案的第二部分中，我們將開發可用於解決表面上的雙曲守恆定律的數值方案。我們建議首先改進位於表面上每個採樣點的切平面上的微分算子的數值近似。然後，基於這些近似，我們將開發該切平面的有限體積方案。 該提案的結果應該導致新的數值算法，並將在各種應用中提供其他數值方法的幾種替代方案。該項目對許多學科也很重要，包括晶體生長建模，圖像處理和計算機圖形中的表面正則化，地震學和地球物理學中表面波傳播的高頻漸近解，表面活性劑的多相流以及氣體動力學模擬。

16302819.label: Realisation of objectives
16302819.value: Fourteen relevant papers have been published in this reporting period. subsection*{5.3.1 Objective 1 (100% progress)} We have solved the surface eikonal equation $| abla_{Sigma} T | = n$, where $n$ is the slowness function defined on the surface. We propose to develop a fast-sweeping method based on the MVGD and the Lax-Friedrichs (LxF) Hamiltonian. The idea is to first approximate the Hamiltonian by the LxF Hamiltonian given by $$ | abla_{Sigma}^{mbox{ iny MVGD}} T_{i,j} | - sigma_{Sigma} epsilon_{Sigma} Delta_{Sigma}^{mbox{ iny MVGD}} T_{i,j} = n_{i,j} , . $$ where $sigma_{Sigma} ge frac{partial H}{partial p}$, $epsilon_{Sigma}=O(Delta x)$, and the differential operators $ abla_{Sigma}^{mbox{ iny MVGD}}$ and $Delta_{Sigma}^{mbox{ iny MVGD}}$ are computed using the MVGD method. Following the philosophy of the fast sweeping method, we can rearrange the express to obtain an update formulate for each $T_{i,j}$. In the proposal, we presented some preliminary solutions to the eikonal equation on the unit sphere represented by the GBPM. We have also tested the algorithm on some standard benchmarks, including the Stanford Bunny. The method is working reasonably well. We have also performed a convergence test. The method seems to be able to provide first-order accurate solutions. In [Chu-Leung 2021], we propose a simple level set method for the Dirichlet $k$-partition problem, which aims to partition an open domain into $K$ different subdomains to minimize the sum of the smallest eigenvalue of the Dirichlet Laplace operator in each subdomain. We first formulate the problem as a nested minimization problem of a functional of the level set function and the eigenfunction defined in each subdomain. As an approximation, we propose replacing the eigenfunction with the level set function so that the nested minimization can be converted to a single minimization problem. We apply the standard gradient descent method so that the problem leads to a Hamilton-Jacobi-type equation. We are extending the method to solve a related equation on surfaces. In this part of the project, we have also considered another nonlinear equation related to optimal transport. The solution to the transport problem satisfies the so-called Monge-Ampere (MA) equation. In [Liu-Leung-Qian 2022], we have developed a method for the numerical solution of the three-dimensional elliptic MA equation. Our methodology combines a time-discretization by operator-splitting with a mixed finite element-based space approximation where one employs the same finite-dimensional spaces to approximate the unknown function and its three second-order derivatives. A key ingredient of our approach is reformulating the MA equation as a nonlinear elliptic equation in divergence form involving the cofactor matrix of the Hessian of the unknown function. With the above elliptic equation, we associate an initial value problem with it, which we discretize by operator-splitting. To enforce the pointwise positivity of the approximate Hessian, we employ a hard thresholding-based projection method. In [Glowinski-Leung-Liu-Qian 2020], we construct an algorithm to determine the eigenfunction of the MA operator. subsection*{5.3.2 Objective 2 (100% progress)} The PI has developed a method for solving partial differential equations on evolving surfaces. Based on the grid-based particle method (GBPM), the method can naturally resample the surface even under large deformation from the motion law. We introduce a new component in the local reconstruction step of the algorithm and demonstrate numerically that the modification can improve the computational accuracy when a large curvature region is developed in the evolution. The method also incorporates a recently developed regularized least squares (RLS) formulation, which can lead to a better conditioned discretized matrix for computing some surface differential operators. The proposed framework can incorporate a large class of methods and link various approaches for the same problem. In particular, we will demonstrate that the so-called local tangential lifting (LTL) method can be naturally applied in our framework, while a recently developed regularized least squares method with RBF can also be used in our method. subsection*{5.3.3 Objective 3 (100% progress)} In [Fong-Leung 2023], we develop two new interpolation ideas on $mathbb{S}^2$. In this first part of the paper, we introduced a simple interpolation method named Spherical Interpolation of orDER $n$ (SIDER-$n$) that gives a $C^2$ interpolant given $nge 2$. The idea generalizes the construction of the Bezier curves developed for $mathbb{R}$. The second part incorporated the ENO philosophy and developed a new Spherical Essentially Non-Oscillatory (SENO) interpolation method. When the underlying curve on $mathbb{S}^2$ has kinks or sharp discontinuity in the higher derivatives, our proposed approach can reduce spurious oscillations in the high-order reconstruction. We will give multiple examples to demonstrate the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed approaches. subsection*{5.3.4 Objective 4 (100% progress)} We have successfully developed an efficient, accurate, robust hybrid approach for solving surface hyperbolic conservation laws in [Hung-Leung 2023]. The method is based on the embedding idea, where a level set function first implicitly represents the surface. Instead of explicitly solving the equation on the surface, we introduce a modified partial differential equation in a small interface neighborhood. This embedding equation is developed based on a push-forward operator that can extend tangential flux vectors from the surface to a neighboring level surface. This operator is easy to compute and involves only the level set function and the corresponding Hessian. The resulting solution is constant in the normal direction of the interface. In [You-Leung 2021a, You-Leung 2021b, Ng-You-Leung 2022, Chau-Leung 2023], we propose an Eulerian approach to compute the finite time Lyapunov exponent (FTLE). This work will be important in analyzing the dynamics governed by a hyperbolic conservation law.

16302819.label: Major findings and research outcome
16302819.value: Supported by this project, we have published 14 articles and trained one MPhil student and one PhD student. We have successfully developed an efficient, accurate, robust hybrid approach for solving surface hyperbolic conservation laws. Drawing inspiration from differential geometry, we introduce the push-forward operator to extend the surface flux function. The approach can provide a flux function in a small interface neighborhood that is still tangential to the interface. Therefore, this push-forward operator modifies the surface PDE and gives a PDE defined in a computational tube. Following the idea of other embedding methods, we can apply any well-developed numerical method to solve the modified PDE in the Cartesian mesh. More importantly, we can show analytically that the solution to the modified equation is constant along the normal directions of the interface. This property is essential for maintaining numerical accuracy in the finite difference scheme for the differential operator and the interpolation step when extracting the solution from the mesh to the surface. We have also developed a systematic approach to construct high-order interpolants from given data points on the unit sphere. The idea follows the construction of the Bezier curves based on the composition of multiple SLERPs. Therefore, the formulation is familiar with what has been widely used in the community. However, unlike the typical Bezier curves, our proposed approach determines the control points in Bezier curves to ensure that the reconstruction passes through all given data points. Once we have these high-order reconstructions on the sphere, we follow the ENO philosophy and propose a new Spherical Essentially Non-Oscillatory (SENO) interpolation method. This approach can provide a smooth, high-order interpolant even when the underlying curve has kinks. This property will be necessary to develop high-order numerical schemes for solving any quaternion-related differential equations.

16302819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16302819.value: Method for solving hyperbolic equations is still an extremely interesting and important field of research. There are plenty of problems we can continue to work on. For example, it is interesting to see how well these methods can be applied to nonlinear or nonlocal hyperbolic or higher-order nonlinear equations. Special attention might be needed to impose constraints due to the physical properties of the equation. For example, one might need the ENO/WENO philosophy in the local reconstruction when solving a hyperbolic equation on surfaces. Another possible future research direction is investigating methods for solving differential equations of $mathbb{S}^2$-valued functions.

The resulting algorithms can be applied to many research areas, such as image processing of surfaces and dimension reduction for high dimensional data.
