17100819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17100819.value: The tumor microenvironment is the immediate environment in which cancer cells reside. During tumor development and progression, cancer cells communicate with each other and with non-tumor cells (such as fibroblasts, endothelial cells and immune cells) by secreting signaling molecules that function as messengers to create a favorable microenvironment for tumor growth and metastasis. Recently, nanometer-sized vesicles called exosomes, which function as novel vehicles of intercellular communication, have become an exciting area in cancer research. However, very little is known about the significance and functions of tumor-secreted exosomes, and especially their protein cargo, in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Our preliminary data showed that normal esophageal epithelial cells exposed to exosomes purified from ESCC cells had increased migratory potential, which suggests that cancer exosomes can transfer aggressive phenotype to non-cancerous cells. We previously identified serglycin as the top upregulated gene in a highly invasive ESCC cell line, and our recent findings showed that serglycin secreted by ESCC cells could stimulate other cancer cells to be more invasive, and that this function may be mediated by a growth factor called midkine. Interestingly, our preliminary results showed that serglycin was also secreted in an exosome-associated form by highly invasive ESCC cells. Moreover, the exosomes secreted by serglycin-overexpressing cells were enriched in midkine, and had the ability to enhance the invasiveness of ESCC cells and the blood vessel-forming ability of endothelial cells in culture. We therefore hypothesize that both soluble and exosomal forms of serglycin exert autocrine and paracrine influences in the tumor microenvironment during cancer progression, and that these effects may be mediated by midkine. This regulatory mechanism has not been reported previously. We also speculate that the integrity of the glycoasminoglycan (GAG) attachment domain of serglycin is crucial in this regulatory mechanism because we found that the culture medium and exosomes of ESCC cells expressing serglycin without the (GAG) attachment region failed to induce autocrine secretion of midkine (including exosomal midkine). In the proposed study, we will investigate the autocrine effects of serglycin-induced midkine on malignant phenotypes of esophageal cancer cells, as well as the paracrine effects of serglycin and serglycin-induced midkine on non-tumor cells in the tumor microenvironment using in vitro and in vivo experiments. The contribution of cancer cell-secreted exosomes to these functions will be assessed. We will also determine whether serglycin interacts with midkine, and the significance of GAG side chains of serglycin in regulating midkine expression and secretion.

17100819.label: Realisation of objectives
17100819.value: OBJECTIVE 1: To study the autocrine effects of serglycin-induced midkine on malignant phenotypes of esophageal cancer cells. Previously, we found that highly invasive esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) cells overexpress serglycin (SRGN), and that SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells secrete midkine (MDK) into the tumor microenvironment. The concentrations of SRGN and MDK were positively correlated in serum samples of patients with ESCC. In this study, we used various in vitro approaches to prove that cancer cell-secreted MDK had autocrine stimulatory effects on proliferation, invasion, and activation of ERK signaling pathway in ESCC cells. Since autocrine communication between cancer cells may be mediated by exosomes (a class of nanosized extracellular vesicles), we hypothesized that cancer cell-secreted MDK might be carried in exosomes. Density gradient ultracentrifugation was used to obtain pure exosomes from SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells (abbreviated as SRGN Exo). Western blotting showed that MDK was found in the subcellular fraction which contained soluble proteins, but not in the fraction that contained exosomes. Nonetheless, we found that treatment with DMA (an exosome inhibitor) or knocking-down Rab27a (a gene involved in controlling the secretion of exosomes) negated the autocrine pro-invasive effect of SRGN-overexpressing ESCC. Furthermore, in vitro and in vivo experiments showed that recipient ESCC cells exposed to SRGN Exo had enhanced invasive and metastatic potential, which suggests that SRGN Exo could transfer malignant phenotype to ESCC cells. Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) was applied to identify differentially expressed proteins in SRGN Exo. Cation-dependent mannose-6-phosphate receptor (M6PR) and ephrin type-B receptor 4 (EphB4) were found to be consistently upregulated in multiple ESCC cell lines. We found that while exosomes isolated from M6PR-overexpressing ESCC cells did not facilitate invasion of ESCC cells, EphB4-knockdown attenuated the pro-invasive effect of SRGN Exo on ESCC cells. In summary, this objective was fully accomplished with novel data showing that soluble rather than exosomal MDK secreted by SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells could promote malignant phenotype in ESCC in an autocrine manner. Another significant finding was the identification of EphB4 as a novel SRGN-induced exosomal protein which can also mediate this autocrine function. OBJECTIVE 2: To study the paracrine effects of serglycin and serglycin-induced midkine in the tumor microenvironment. Fibroblasts constitute the main cellular component of tumor stroma. We treated human esophageal fibroblasts (HEFs) with conditioned medium (CM) of ESCC cells that overexpressed wild-type SRGN (SRGN CM) or truncated SRGN lacking the GAG attachment domain (ΔGAG CM). The results showed HEFs treated with SRGN CM, but not ΔGAG CM, had upregulated fibroblast activation markers, increased proliferation and migratory ability. Notably, SRGN CM-pretreated HEFs also facilitated tumor growth and tumor angiogenesis in vivo. Immunohistochemistry of tissue microarrays showed that SRGN expression in cancer cells was positively correlated with expression of fibroblast activated protein in stromal cells of ESCC. Because MDK-knockdown abolished these stimulatory effects of SRGN CM on these functions, our data suggest that SRGN-induced MDK was a trigger for HEF activation. Furthermore, the secretome of the HEFs were altered after treatment with SRGN CM, with significant increase of hepatocyte growth factor (HGF). Endothelial tube formation assay indicated that HEF-derived HGF had pro-angiogenic function in vitro. Since treatment with exogenous MDK elicited only a slight increase of HGF mRNA expression in HEFs, human cytokine arrays were used to identify the inducer of HGF. We found that SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells had increased secretion of interleukin 1β (IL-1β), which stimulated the transcription of HGF in HEFs by activating the PLCγ1/ERK/AP-1 signaling pathway in a paracrine manner. Co-immunoprecipitation assay showed that IL-1β directly interacted with glycosylated SRGN, which suggests that SRGN-induced IL-1β might be transported out of the cancer cells to the tumor microenvironment via interaction with the glycosaminoglycan (GAG) side chains of SRGN. Angiogenesis is required to support tumor growth. Our data showed that tumor xenografts of SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells had increased angiogenesis. In vitro angiogenesis assay showed that M6PR-rich exosomes promoted endothelial tube formation. Furthermore, knocking down M6PR in SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells abolished the pro-angiogenic effect of SRGN Exo in vitro and in vivo. These data suggest that cancer cell-secreted M6PR-rich exosomes are important angiogenic mediators in SRGN-overexpressing ESCC. This objective was well achieved by obtaining solid in vitro and in vivo data to support that SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells can exert paracrine influence on fibroblasts in the tumor microenvironment. SRGN-induced MDK activates fibroblasts, while SRGN-induced IL-1β stimulates the PLCγ1/ERK/AP-1 signaling pathway to upregulate HGF in fibroblasts. HGF secreted by activated fibroblasts in turn promotes angiogenesis to facilitate tumor growth. M6PR-rich exosomes secreted by SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells also play a role in tumor angiogenesis. OBJECTIVE 3: To determine the functional role of GAG attachment domain in serglycin on midkine expression and secretion. Cell lysates and CM of ESCC cells with ectopic expression of wild type SRGN, ∆GAG and mGAG (SRGN with mutated GAG attachment domain) were compared for MDK expression using western blots. The results showed that the expression of MDK in CM of ∆GAG- and mGAG-expressing ESCC cells was low compared with that of SRGN-expressing cells. Co-IP experiments were performed using the cell lysates and CM of ESCC cells overexpressing FLAG-fusion SRGN and FLAG-fusion ∆GAG, and we found that MDK was co-precipitated with SRGN in F-SRGN-overexpressing cells but not F-∆GAG-overexpressing cells. These co-IP results therefore showed that both intracellular and secreted forms of MDK bind to the GAG chains of SRGN. To identify the type(s) of GAG chains associated with SRGN secreted by ESCC cells, GAGs were isolated from the CM of SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells, and then digested with chondroitinases and heparinases. The results indicated that the secreted SRGN was mainly decorated with chondroitin sulfate (CS) GAG chains. Fluorophore-assisted carbohydrate electrophoresis (FACE) analysis showed that the GAG chains isolated from the CM of SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells were mainly decorated with ∆di-4S and ∆di-6S CS, which suggests that cancer cell-secreted SRGN may differ from that expressed in normal cells in terms of the composition of GAG chains in order to favor the recruitment of cancer-promoting binding partners. As in the case of MDK, IL-1 was identified as a novel binding partner of SRGN. Its interaction with SRGN also depends on the integrity of the GAG attachment domain. In summary, this objective was fully achieved. Our findings highlight the functional significance of SRGN’s GAG attachment domain in tumorigenic properties.

17100819.label: Major findings and research outcome
17100819.value: (i) SRGN overexpression in ESCC cells induces the secretion of MDK from cancer cells into the tumor microenvironment. Cancer cell-secreted MDK exerts autocrine stimulatory effects on proliferation and invasion of nearby ESCC cells by activating the ERK signaling pathway. Both intracellular and secreted forms of MDK bind to the GAG chains of SRGN which are mainly decorated with ∆di-4S and ∆di-6S chondroitin sulfates. Exosomal form of MDK has a negligible role in promoting malignant phenotype in ESCC cells. (ii) In addition to autocrine function, SRGN-induced MDK also has paracrine effects in the tumor microenvironment. It can activate esophageal fibroblasts, the major cellular component of tumor stroma, to increase their proliferation and migratory ability. These activated fibroblasts have the ability to facilitate tumor growth and tumor angiogenesis in vivo. (iii) In addition to MDK, SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells also secrete IL-1β which alters the secretome of fibroblasts in a paracrine manner. Activation of PLCγ1/ERK/AP-1 signaling pathway in the fibroblasts increases transcription and secretion of HGF. The fibroblast-derived HGF can in turn influence endothelial cells in the tumor microenvironment to promote angiogenesis. Like MDK, IL-1β also interacts with the GAG side chains of SRGN, and is therefore another novel binding partner of SRGN. Taken together, the integrity of the GAG attachment domain is critical in the pro-invasive function of SRGN. (iv) Exosomes secreted by SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells can promote invasion and metastasis of ESCC cells, as well as facilitate tumor angiogenesis. These exosomes are enriched in M6PR and EphB4 proteins. M6PR-rich exosomes mediate the pro-angiogenic function of exosomes secreted by SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells, while EphB4 contributes to the pro-invasive effect of these exosomes on ESCC cells. These findings were published in three peer-reviewed publications listed in Part C8. The Journal Citation CR 2021 Impact Factors are: 11.600 (Theranostics), 8.554 (Clinical and Translational Medicine) and 10.750 (International Journal of Biological Sciences). Some of the findings were presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Association for Cancer Research 2022 (see Part C9). This study was mostly the efforts of two PhD students, Yun ZHU and Dongdong YAN, whose training was made possible by this GRF grant. Their PhD theses are listed in (Part C10).

17100819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17100819.value: Our findings substantiate that SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells overexpress and secrete growth factors/cytokines, some of which are novel binding partners of SRGN. While our study focused on two signaling molecules (i.e. MDK and IL-1), it is perceivable that other overexpressed proteins may also have important functional roles. In our research output Zhu et al. 2021, we published a list of proteins that are differentially expressed in SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells, as determined using RPPA analysis. These proteins merit further investigation. Proteins are secreted from cells either as soluble molecules or as part of extracellular vesicles. The functions of cancer cell exosome-transmitted proteins are rarely studied. It is generally believed that exosomes are enriched with parent cell-derived molecules but our results showed that not SRGN-induced secreted proteins were enriched in the exosomes, and that exosomes may be responsible for transporting a distinct subset of functional proteins to target cells. In our research paper Yan et al. 2023, we profiled exosomal proteins purified from SRGN-overexpressing ESCC cells and corresponding control cells using Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. These data would be a valuable resource for researchers interested in further studying the significance of SRGN-induced exosomes in esophageal cancer.

17100819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17100819.value: During tumor development and progression, cancer cells communicate with each other and with non-tumor cells by secreting signaling molecules. We previously reported that highly invasive esophageal cancer cells secrete a proteoglycan named serglycin. In this study, we found that serglycin-overexpressing esophageal cancer cells release midkine and interleukin-1β, both of which bind with the glycosaminoglycan side chains of serglycin. Our data showed that cancer cell-derived midkine exerted autocrine stimulatory effects on proliferation and invasion of other cancer cells in the vicinity, whereas interleukin-1β could activate fibroblasts and stimulate them to secrete hepatocyte growth factor (HGF). Fibroblast-secreted HGF in turn influenced endothelial cells in the tumor microenvironment to promote tumor angiogenesis. In addition to this mechanism, we found that a non-classical secretion pathway involving exosomes (nanosized extracellular vesicles) also contributed to autocrine and paracrine tumor-promoting functions of serglycin. The exosomes secreted by serglycin-overexpressing esophageal cancer cells were enriched in M6PR and EphB4 proteins. Our data showed that M6PR- and EphB4-rich exosomes had the ability to promote angiogenesis and to transfer invasive phenotype to cancer cells, respectively. In conclusion, soluble proteins and exosomes secreted by serglycin-overexpressing cancer cells function as intercellular messengers to create a tumor microenvironment favorable for tumor growth and metastasis.

17101119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17101119.value: Hypoxia, low oxygen (O2) availability, is a key feature of all solid cancers due to the rapid expansion of tumorous regions lacking functional blood vessels. The key adaptive molecular cascades are mediated by hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) which coordinate the transcription of a wide repertoire of genes beneficial to survival under hypoxic condition. One important HIF-mediated adaptive response is the metabolic switch from oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) to glycolysis to prevent reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation at the electron transport chain (ETC). Compelling evidence amassed showing the clinical and functional importance of HIFs in cancer development. However, HIFs are difficult to target pharmacologically. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is considered to be one of the most hypoxic malignancies. HCC lacks promising curative treatment and continues to have dismal clinical outcome. To identify novel and reliable therapeutic targets responsible for hypoxic survival, high-throughput forward genetic screening approach involving CRISPR-Cas9 library was employed. We found that protein-tyrosine phosphatase mitochondrial 1 (PTPMT1), an important enzyme for cardiolipin (CL) synthesis, was the most significant gene, ranked just after HIF-1α and HIF-1β, crucial to hypoxic survival. CL makes up the mitochondrial membrane and ensures the correct assembly of stable ETC complexes for efficient electron transfer and respiration. Knockout (KO) of PTPMT1 significantly reduced mitochondrial CL content, destructed mitochondrial membrane, and impaired mitochondrial functions in HCC cells. KO of PTPMT1 drastically induced ROS accumulation in hypoxia. It is generally believed that hypoxic cells do not rely on mitochondria given that glycolysis could compensate for the energy output. Interestingly, our previous findings and current data suggested that mitochondria are not completely shut down but indeed are important for survival especially under hypoxic condition. We hypothesize that KO of PTPMT1 would affect the maturation of CL thereby impairing the assembly of ETC complexes leading to leakage of electrons and accumulation ROS at the ETC when the final electron recipient O2 is low. Excitingly, HCC cells especially under hypoxic condition showed great sensitivity towards PTPMT1 inhibitor, alexidine dihydrochloride (AD). In this study, we will thoroughly unravel the protective roles of PTPMT1 in hypoxic survival and HCC development. We will also study the therapeutic potential of PTPMT1 inhibitor using different HCC mouse models. Targeting hypoxic cells through PTPMT1 inhibition may represent a valid therapeutic opportunity in treating advanced HCC.

17101819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17101819.value: 寒冷或腎上腺素β3激動劑介導的白色脂肪棕色化，通過增加機體代謝率，是抵抗肥胖的有效手段之一。因此，尋找新型白色脂肪組織棕色化因子是熱門研究領域。 多種分子信號通路調控白色脂肪組織棕色化.β3腎上腺素/ cAMP / PKA及下游p38 MAPK信號激活通過增加非偶聯蛋白（UCP）1表達，促進脂肪細胞棕色化.ERK信號通路激活是前脂肪細胞增殖和分化的關鍵步驟。同時，盧-ROCK信號也是成纖維化祖細胞聚集並分化為脂肪細胞及棕色化的關鍵分子通路。 多配聚醣4（Sdc4），作為一種1型跨膜蛋白，調節細胞增殖，遷移和分化等一系列生物過程.Sdc4是多種生物配體的受體或輔助受體，通過多種結合方式調節細胞內信號通路.Sdc4的胞外域剪切後發揮自身或遠分泌功能。人類SDC4單核苷酸多態性與體重指數，糖代謝和心血管疾病緊密相關。脂肪SDC4缺失的線蟲出現寒冷抵抗性差，代謝率降低和體重增加的特徵。然而，SDC4在白色脂肪組織棕色化和適應性產熱的作用仍不清楚。 我們前期RNA測序結果顯示，高脂飲食誘導肥胖小鼠的腹股溝脂肪SDC4表達水平降低，但寒冷刺激促進SDC4表達。寒冷誘導的白色脂肪組織棕色化與SDC4表達升高和胞外域剪切呈正相關。棕色脂肪細胞分化過程中，SDC4水平先降低後升高，與PPARgamma表達趨勢一致。然而，SDC4缺失抑制脂肪細胞棕色化和UCP1等棕色化基因表達。這些前期數據暗示，SDC4在白色脂肪細胞棕色化和能量代謝中有重要作用。 SDC4能夠調節ERK和MAPK信號通路活性，並抑制RhoA的活性本項目假設：寒冷誘導的SDC4表達促進成纖維化祖細胞分化為脂肪細胞.Sdc4同時促進棕色化祖細胞增殖和分化為棕色化脂肪細胞。本假設將利用慢病毒介導的脂肪細胞SDC4缺失小鼠模型證明假設，並評價SDC4防治肥胖的效果。本項目的順利開展將創新性揭示SDC4在白色脂肪棕色化和能量代謝的作用，並提供針對脂肪組織的防治肥胖及其並發症的新方法。

17102119.label: Project Objectives
17102119.value: We will investigate the role of EDA FN in mediating tubulo-interstitial inflammation and fibrosis in two murine models of CKD using wild type, heterozygous and EDA FN knockout mice. We will isolate PTEC, interstitial fibroblasts and pericytes from wild type, heterozygous and EDA FN knockout mice to investigate the mechanism through which EDA FN regulates inflammatory and fibrotic processes, and also the pathogenic mechanisms that induce EDA FN expression. We will overexpress EDA FN in PTEC, pericytes and interstitial fibroblasts and determine its effect on cellular functions with particular focus on its role in cell proliferation, viability, inflammation and fibrogenesis. EDA FN expression will be assessed in renal biopsies obtained from CKD patients categorized according to severity of CKD and renal fibrosis. The relationship between tubulo-interstitial EDA FN expression and that of renal function and renal histological parameters will be assessed.

17102119.label: Realisation of objectives
17102119.value: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is an escalating global health problem associated with increased morbidity, mortality and treatment cost. CKD is characterized by progressive tubulo-interstitial fibrosis leading to end-stage kidney disease. There is no effective treatment for kidney fibrosis and current medication can at best reduce the rate of kidney function deterioration. Identifying mechanisms leading to CKD is therefore essential to develop novel therapeutic intervention. Fibronectin (FN) accumulation in the tubulo-interstitium is an early indicator of tubulo-interstitial fibrosis. Fibrotic lesions also contain FN isoforms such as extra domain A-spliced (EDA) FN variant, but its role in CKD remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the role of EDA FN in CKD. We have completed Objectives 1 and 4 and Objectives 2 and 3 are 90-95% completed, and will be completed in the coming 4-6 months. Two murine models of kidney injury, namely adenine-induced nephropathy and unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO), were used to investigate the role of EDA FN in inflammatory and fibrotic processes related to kidney injury in wild-type (WT) and EDA FN knockout (KO) mice. EDA FN deficiency in the KO mice was confirmed by qPCR. In the adenine-induced nephropathy model, excess adenine accumulates in the kidney and is converted to insoluble 8-dihydroxyadenine and 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which crystalizes in renal tubules causing injury. Adenine (0.2%) was incorporated into casein-based chow, and WT and EDA FN KO mice were randomized to receive casein-based chow (Control diet) or adenine-based chow for up to 12 weeks. Body weight of WT and EDA FN KO mice with CKD was comparable, and both were significantly lower than their counterparts fed with Control diet (P<0.05, for both). In WT CKD mice, proteinuria was observed after 4 - 8 weeks of adenine feeding and increased with CKD progression. Histopathological lesions in the kidney of WT mice included tubular dilation and atrophy, protein cast formation and infiltration of immune cells, in particular macrophages. Flow cytometric analysis showed increased CD45+ cells and F4/80+ / CD11b+ macrophages in the kidneys of WT CKD mice. This was accompanied by a marked increase in tubulo-interstitial expression of collagen, native FN and EDA FN, and alpha-smooth muscle actin especially in the proximity of dilated proximal tubules. RNA-Seq analysis demonstrated that pathways related to extracellular matrix organization, cellular senescence, inflammation and fatty acid metabolic processes were enriched in kidney specimens from WT CKD mice compared to WT control mice. Cellular senescence is a process whereby cells undergo cell cycle arrest and adopt a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) through the production and secretion of pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic mediators. Genes that induce cell cycle arrest, including cdkn1a, cdkn2a and cdkn2b, and genes encoding for pro-inflammatory and profibrotic mediators including il1a, il6, ccl2, tnfa, serpine1 and tgfb1 were increased in WT CKD mice. Cellular senescence has been shown to contribute to kidney fibrosis. Genes related to kidney fibrosis including tgfb1, fgf, fn and various isoforms of collagen and laminin were also enriched in the kidney of WT CKD mice. Proximal tubular epithelial cells (PTEC) are the predominant cell type in the tubulo-interstitium and undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) during injury. EMT precedes kidney fibrosis and endow PTEC with a migratory, invasive, and highly proliferative phenotype. Genes related to EMT including acta2, zeb1, zeb2, notch1, snail, mmp2, mmp9 and mmp13 were enriched in the kidney of WT CKD mice. We confirmed the expression of these inflammatory and fibrotic mediators in the kidney through Western blot analysis and cytochemical or immunohistochemical staining and demonstrated their localization in the tubulo-interstitium. Mediators of inflammation, cellular senescence, EMT and fibrosis were all significantly reduced in EDA FN KO mice, whereas proteinuria was comparable between WT and EDA FN KO CKD mice. In the UUO model, a murine model of tubulo-interstitial fibrosis, Sham and UUO mice were sacrificed 14 days post-surgery as this time-point showed a significant increase in FN expression in the kidney of WT UUO mice. In WT mice, tubulo-interstitial fibrosis was accompanied by tubular dilation and atrophy, infiltration of macrophages into the interstitium, increased expression of EDA FN, kidney injury markers (KIM-1 and NGAL), mediators of inflammation (CCL2, CCL5, IL-1beta, IL-6 and TNF-alpha), EMT (alpha-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, ZEB1, Notch1 and SNAIL) and fibrosis (FN, collagen I and III), and activation of p38 MAPK, ERK and PI3K signaling. These histopathologic abnormalities were significantly reduced in EDA FN KO mice with UUO suggesting that EDA FN contributes to tubulo-interstitial inflammation and fibrosis. In cultured HK-2 cells, an immortalized PTEC cell line, EDA FN expression was absent under basal condition. Exposure of HK-2 cells to TGF-beta1, IL-1beta and TNF-alpha, but not CTGF, induced EDA FN expression. Administration of both TGF-beta1 and CTGF to HK-2 cells further induced EDA FN expression in a synergistic manner, mediated in part through increased p38 MAPK, JNK and PI3K/Akt phosphorylation. To investigate the role of EDA FN in fibrotic processes, human recombinant EDA-lacking (EDA-) and EDA-containing (EDA+) peptides were generated. EDA+, but not EDA- peptide, increased SNAIL, ZEB1, native FN, collagen type I and laminin expression at the gene and/or protein level, and significantly reduced E-cadherin expression. EDA+ peptide, but not EDA- peptide, also increased IL-6, IL-8 and MCP-1 secretion (p<0.001, EDA- vs EDA+ for IL-6 and IL-8; p<0.05, EDA- vs EDA+ for MCP-1), mediated in part through PI3K, p38 MAPK and ERK phosphorylation. In human kidney specimens, native FN and EDA FN expression was determined in normal kidney specimens from patients undergoing nephrectomy (n = 6) and in renal biopsies from CKD patients comprising diabetic nephropathy, IgA nephropathy, hypertension-induced nephropathy and lupus nephritis (n = 70). Native FN was weakly expressed in normal human kidney specimens, whereas EDA FN was absent. Both native FN and EDA FN expression was increased in renal biopsies from CKD patients. Native FN was localized to the tubulo-interstitium and glomeruli, while EDA FN was predominantly localized to PTEC and interstitium. The intensity of staining was more prominent in renal biopsies from patients that showed a high chronicity index. Taken together, our findings demonstrated that EDA FN expression is increased in patients and mice with CKD and tubulo-interstitial fibrosis, irrespective of aetiologies, and suggests that EDA FN contributes to pathogenic mechanisms leading to tubulo-interstitial inflammation, cellular senescence and fibrosis, mediated through increased p38 MAPK, JNK and PI3K/Akt phosphorylation. Problems encountered At the end of January 2021, due to mouse hepatitis virus infection at HKU animal facilities, all our breeders were infected and the progress of our animal studies was severely delayed. It took almost 10 months to successfully rederive our EDA FN KO mice. Objectives 2 and 3 will be completed in the coming 4 -6 months. A postgraduate student wanted to take up the project as his PhD project but defaulted twice and subsequently took up a PhD placement overseas. The project was thus completed by research staff in Prof Chan’s team.

17102119.label: Major findings and research outcome
17102119.value: In this study, we demonstrated that WT mice with kidney injury, induced by adenine-feeding or UUO, was associated with increased EDA FN expression in PTEC and histopathologic abnormalities included tubular dilation and atrophy, macrophage infiltration and expression of mediators related to inflammation, cellular senescence, EMT and fibrosis, which included p38 MAPK, PI3K/AKT phosphorylation, cdkn1a, cdkn2a and cdkn2b, CCL2, CCL5, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, alpha-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, ZEB, Notch1, SNAIL, FN, laminin and collagen I expression. In EDA FN KO mice with CKD or tubulo-interstitial fibrosis, histopathological abnormalities were less severe, with a significant reduction in the expression of mediators related to kidney inflammation, cellular senescence, EMT and fibrosis. In human kidney specimens, EDA FN expression was absent from normal adult kidney tissue and induced in CKD patients, localized to tubular epithelial cells especially in tubules showing dilation or atrophy and in the interstitium. EDA FN expression was associated with chronicity index in CKD patients. EDA FN expression was induced in PTEC by inflammatory or fibrotic mediators such as TGF-beta1, IL-1beta and TNF-alpha, but not CTGF. Administration of TGF-beta1 together with CTGF to PTEC induced EDA FN expression in a synergistic manner, mediated in part through increased p38 MAPK, JNK and PI3K/Akt phosphorylation. To investigate the role of EDA FN in fibrotic processes, recombinant EDA-lacking (EDA-) and EDA-containing (EDA+) peptides were generated. EDA+, but not EDA- peptide, increased mediators of EMT and fibrosis including SNAIL, ZEB1, native FN, collagen type I and laminin expression at the gene and/or protein level, and significantly reduced E-cadherin expression. EDA+ peptide, but not EDA- peptide, also increased SASP and pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-6, IL-8 and MCP-1 secretion mediated in part through PI3K, p38 MAPK and ERK phosphorylation. Taken together, our data identified a novel role for EDA FN in tubulo-interstitial fibrosis through increased PI3K/Akt and p38 MAPK phosphorylation, macrophage recruitment, and induction of cellular senescence and EMT in PTEC, leading to kidney inflammation and fibrosis through secretion of SASP and matrix protein accumulation. Part of these findings were presented at The International Society of Nephrology, World Congress of Nephrology (ISN WCN) in 2021 (abstract published in Kidney Int Rep 2022; 7: S197) and American Society of Nephrology Kidney Week 2024 (abstract published in J Am Soc Nephrol 2024; 35:449-450). Both abstracts acknowledged RGC’s funding support.

17102119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17102119.value: In this research study, we made the novel discovery that EDA FN contributed to CKD through induction of EMT and cellular senescence in PTEC resulting in macrophage recruitment and an increase in mediators of inflammation and fibrosis. Potential for further development of this project will investigate how EDA FN induces EMT in PTEC with specific focus on how EDA FN regulates expression of Notch1, SNAIL and ZEB, transcription factors. Further studies will also investigate how EDA FN regulates cellular senescence and cell cycle arrest. Both EMT and cellular senescence have been reported to play key roles in kidney fibrosis but the mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated. Our findings may also be extrapolated to other organs that develop tissue fibrosis. Part of these findings will serve as preliminary data for a grant application to the RGC General Research Fund 2026/27 round for consideration of funding.

17102119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17102119.value: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is an escalating global health challenge with considerable morbidity, mortality, and treatment costs. There is currently no effective treatment for CKD. Irrespective of the primary aetiology, tubulo-interstitial fibrosis drives CKD progression to end-stage kidney disease and patients will require either kidney transplantation or life-long dialysis to sustain life. There is a huge knowledge gap in understanding the mechanisms that induce tubulo-interstitial fibrosis in CKD. In this study, we demonstrated that EDA FN, an isoform of native FN that is absent in healthy adults, was induced in the kidneys of patients and mice with CKD and contributed to kidney inflammation, cellular senescent in proximal tubular epithelial cells, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and fibrosis. Targeting EDA FN may alleviate or delay kidney fibrosis.

17102619.label: Realisation of objectives
17102619.value: 1. Utilizing the ChIP sequencing to identify the CTCF binding sites and transcriptional active and suppressive histone marks (H3K4me3, H3K27me3, and H3K27ac) in EBV+/- NPC We have utilized the assay for transposase accessible chromatin sequencing (ATAC-seq) to investigate the regions that are nucleosome free (open chromatin), which is found to positively correlate with active chromatin markers (H3K4me3) and can identify the distal regulatory regions that serve as enhancers (H3K27ac). The ATAC-seq data can also infer the close chromatin, indicating the suppressive marker (H3K27me3). The experiments have been completed for all three EBV-positive (+) and -negative (-) NPC cell lines, and two normal immortalized nasopharyngeal cell lines with biological duplicates. We also performed CUN&RUN sequencing for CTCF binding sites and histone marks including H3K4me3, H3K27me3 and H3K27ac proposed in this study. Deviations from the original plan and reasons: Instead of ChIP-seq for the selective histone marks, we utilized the cutting-edge ATAC-seq technology to investigate chromatin accessibility, which incorporates a genetically engineered hyperactive Tn5 transposase that simultaneously cuts open chromatin. This method does not involve size selection during library preparation, and thus, it is a fast and robust approach (Yan et al. Genome Bio, 2020). It provides a more comprehensive picture of the chromatin accessibility with gene regulation than the ChIP-seq data. Instead of conventional ChIP-seq for CTCF binding sites, we performed the CUT&RUN sequencing to identify the CTCF binding sites. This native endonuclease-based method relies on the binding of the antibody and the recruitment of a protein A-micrococcal nuclease fusion (pA-MN) to the antibody to efficiently cleave DNA surrounding binding sites (Skene PJ & Henikoff S, Elife, 2017). This method provides a high level of signal to noise ratio, so it is more cost-effective due to the reduced sequencing depth compared to the traditional ChIP-seq method. Therefore, we selected this new technology for evaluating the CTCF binding sites in this project. 2. Utilizing the RNA sequencing to examine miRNA profiles and transcriptome data in EBV+/- NPC The miRNA and total RNA were simultaneously extracted from the cell lines used for ATACseq with OD260/280 between 1.8 - 2.0. A total of 2μg RNA with a concentration greater than 50 ng/μL was used for miRNA sequencing and transcriptome analysis, respectively. The RNA sequencing with 10M raw reads per sample and miRNA with 15G raw reads per sample were obtained for EBV+/- NPC. The raw data were processed using bioinformatics tools STAR and HTSeq, and the quality of the data was evaluated by Picards. The differentially expressed genes/miRNAs between EBV+/- NPC cells were identified by DESeq2 R package. In addition, we have collected three sets of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNASeq) data for NPC and compared the gene expression between the NPC cancer cells with and without EBV infection to identify the EBV-associated genes. 3. Utilizing the ChIA-PET sequencing to investigate 3D genomics targeting CTCF binding sites in EBV+/- NPC We have utilized the Omni-C technology to investigate the compartments and topologically associating domains (TADs) in NPC. The boundaries of TADs are highly conservative and enriched with CTCF and cohesin binding sites. The robustness of the assay was evaluated with >90% reproducibility. The QC matrices including the mapping rate, duplication rates for the cis and trans read pairs and percentage of usable reads, were created to evaluate the quality of the sample and sequencing data. Two software of cooler and juicer were used to create the contact matrix for the downstream analysis. The 3D genome data have been generated for all EBV+/- NPC cell lines proposed in this study. 4. Integrating the ChIP-Seq, bisulfite sequencing, miRNA and RNA profiling data, and 3D genomics data to characterize cellular and EBV epigenetic landscape in NPC Integration of the ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN, miRNA and RNA profiling data, together with whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) and 3D genome data and comparison between EBV+/- NPC cell lines revealed that (1) two DNA methylation subtypes are present for EBV+ NPC with global hypermethylation and global hypomethylation, respectively; (2) EBV infection is highly associated with hypermethylation changes at the promoter CpG islands enriched for CTCF binding sites and has the role for chromatin accessibility remodelling in NPC; (3) EBV episomes could tether to host chromatin, and virus-host interacting regions (EBVIRs) on host and EBV genomes were non-random and associated with chromosome reorganization; (4) in addition to the EBV OriP region, which is known to tether to host centromere during mitosis, two additional regions covering oriLyt and BART regions on EBV episomes are important for virus-host chromatin interactions, and (5) virus-host interactions promote latent enhancer activation leading to the aberrant activation of the genes in NF-κB cascade and immune responses. In the original proposal, we did not include the paired EBV+/- NPC cell lines. To overcome this limitation, we further examined two paired EBV+/- cell lines derived from HK1 and NPC43 for genome organization, CTCF bindings and histone modifications. The results confirmed that EBV latent infection could modulate compartmentalization and promote inactive-active compartment transition, leading to latent enhancer activation and transcription activation of the nearby genes. We also compared the 3D genome data among the EBV+ NPC cell lines, EBV+ patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) and EBV+ clinical samples. A similar phenomon that EBV modulates compartmentalization for 3D genome reorganization was also observed in EBV+ PDXs and NPC clinical tissue.

17102619.label: Major findings and research outcome
17102619.value: (1) Epigenomic landscape study reveals molecular subtypes and EBV-associated regulatory epigenome reprogramming in NPC. In addition to the known global DNA hypermethylated subtype, we discovered a novel subtype with global hypomethylation in EBV + NPC. The consistent EBV-specific differentially methylated regions in the human genome were identified from both subtypes and associated with loss of CTCF binding. Importantly, CTCF is a master chromatin regulator and CTCF protein was reduced in 45% of NPC cases, especially in those with advanced NPC. This result links EBV with chromatin changes. The ATAC-Seq data suggest regulatory epigenome reprogramming through chromatin accessibility changes in EBV + NPC with altered CTCF binding and the switch of transcription factor binding from differentiation-associated KLF/SP family to the innate and adaptive immunity-related NF-ĸB and IRF families. Detailed chromatin accessibility analysis identified a potential EBV target gene CD74, which mediated EBV-specific cell-cell communications in the tumor microenvironment (TME) and was strongly correlated with T cell exhaustion. Our study reveals the unexpected epigenetic heterogeneity, providing insights into NPC pathogenesis and highlighting the involvement of host factors in virus-associated epigenetic changes. EBV infection is associated with epigenome reprogramming and may promote immune evasion. The results have been published on eBioMedicine in 2022 and presented in GRC conference in 2022. (2) Cross-species interactions modulate human 3D Genome reorganisation and promote NF-kB Activation and immunosuppression in NPC. We observed a much larger compartmentalization size in EBV+ NPC with a consistent increase of active to inactive (A to B) compartments, compared to NPE and EBV- NPC. Pathway enrichment analysis showed that these changes potentially influenced immune response, cell differentiation and development, metabolism, ERBB pathway, and calcium signaling transduction. In addition to the changes in compartmentalization, we observed a reduction of CTCF binding signals at the TADs boundaries and the loss of chromatin looping at the 10kb resolution. More importantly, we found EBV tethering to the host chromatins. In the EBV genome, the tethering sites were often located at the regions associated with OriP, oriLyt, and BARTs. In the human genome, the tethering sites were dramatically enriched in the inactive to active (B to A) compartments, which were highly associated with the enhancer regions with H3K27ac, leading to transcription rewiring at the NF-κB target genes, such as CD74. The results have been presented in GRC conference in 2022 and AACR annual meeting in 2023. The relevant manuscript is in preparation.

17102619.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17102619.value: 1. Investigate clinical impact of epigenomic molecular subtypes in nasopharyngeal carcinoma We have applied for the Health and Medical Research Fund (HMRF) to further investigate the clinical impact of two epigenomic molecular subtypes (HyperNPC vs. HypoNPC) after conventional treatment. 2. Investigate the role of molecular subtypes and EBV in immunosuppression in NPC Based on the findings from current study that EBV can modulate chromatin accessibility at the regulatory regions of genes relevant to immune response and cancer cell-immune cell communications in NPC tumor microenvironment (TME), we propose to systematically evaluate the genomic and epigenomic subtypes of EBV+ NPC and characterize their TME, assess the clinical impact of these molecular subtypes after immunotherapy, further elucidate the role of EBV on modulating epigenetic changes and understand how these changes contribute to the immunosuppressive TME in NPC. The proposal is included in the Theme-based Research Scheme (TBRS), which will start in January 2024. 3. Functional study of the genes regulated by EBV-host chromatin interactions We propose to utilize 4C-sequencing to capture the EBV-host chromatin interaction regions (EBVIRs) and study the functional impact of EBVIR-related genes in NPC pathogenesis. This GRF proposal has been submitted recently.

17102619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17102619.value: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is highly associated with Epstein-Barr virus. Our study focused on the role of EBV latent infection and the epigenomic changes, which regulates gene transcription activity. Two different subtypes of EBV-positive (EBV+) NPC based on their epigenomic landscape was discovered with excessive DNA methylation (global hypermethylation) and reduced methylation (global hypomethylation), respectively. EBV infection was found to be associated specific DNA hypermethylation enriched for CTCF binding sites, chromatin remodelling and genome reorganization. These changes were linked to immune responses, cell differentiation, metabolism and aberrant activation of NF-κB pathway. Importantly, the study revealed a new paradigm that EBV episomes could interact with the human genome, leading to altered gene transcription activity. This interaction was particularly prominent in regions associated with enhancers, which regulate gene expression. One of the affected genes was CD74, which plays a role to mediate communications between cancer and immune cells and contribute to T cell exhaustion in tumor microenvironment. Overall, these studies shed light on the complex molecular mechanisms underlying NPC, highlighting the impact of EBV infection on epigenome and genome organization. Understanding these processes could help to decipher EBV-associated NPC pathogenesis and develop epigenetic-based therapies for NPC patients.

17103819.label: Realisation of objectives
17103819.value: Objective #1 a. We improved echo planar imaging (EPI) image quality by devising new methods to correct EPI artifacts at 7 Tesla. Such EPI image quality improvement increases the BOLD detection sensitivity and specificity in all fMRI experiments. Specifically, we have developed a new method to remove EPI Nyquist ghosts by incorporating phase error correction with sensitivity encoding (PEC-SENSE) for robust EPI parallel imaging reconstruction. Further, we have extended PEC-SENSE to both in-plane and slice accelerated EPI parallel imaging. These two developments benefit not only our own rodent fMRI but also clinical EPI applications in general. These two works have led to several international conference abstracts in the International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine (ISMRM) and two full technical papers in Magnetic Resonance in Medicine (1, 2). Recently, we extended the aforementioned works above through the use of deep learning (i.e., convolutional neural networks) to further improve the temporal resolution of EPI images without compromising the sensitivity in detecting BOLD signals during fMRI experiments (i.e., signal-to-noise ratio) and spatial resolution of EPI images. The work was published in Magnetic Resonance in Medicine (3) and led to several abstracts at the ISMRM conference. Note that ISMRM and Magnetic Resonance in Medicine are the leading scientific research conference and journal, respectively, dedicated to MRI technology and brain imaging. b. We also Implemented the capability of stimulating the vestibular sub-nuclei with high precision (see Objective #2 below for the detailed summary of the fMRI experiments). We also successfully designed optogenetic pulse train stimulation paradigms (i.e., 1-5 optogenetic pulses) that enabled the presentation of periodic and/or aperiodic pulse trains. This is in contrast to conventional block-designed paradigms used in fMRI, which typically requires the presentation of ≥20s optogenetic stimulation (i.e., ≥20 optogenetic pulses). This work was published in Neuroimage (4), including abstracts in ISMRM. Note that Neuroimage is one of the leading general journals for reporting scientific and technical developments in preclinical/clinical neuroimaging. Further, a number of software tools have been developed to facilitate online optogenetic fMRI data analysis to improve the experiment efficiency. Objectives #2 & #3 a. We have performed the proposed experiments in two of the four vestibular sub-nuclei (i.e., medial vestibular nucleus, MVN; and superior vestibular nucleus, SVN), particularly related to the neural activity downstream propagation that is initiated by optogenetically exciting the pyramidal excitatory neurons in MVN and SVN respectively. Using optogenetic stimulation and brain-wide fMRI, we determined the large-scale effects of spatiotemporal-specific downstream propagation of vestibular nuclei activity. We demonstrated robust optogenetically evoked fMRI activations bilaterally at sensorimotor cortices and their associated thalamic nuclei (auditory, visual, somatosensory, and motor), high-order cortices (cingulate, retrosplenial, temporal association, and parietal), and hippocampal formations (dentate gyrus, entorhinal cortex, and subiculum). We then examined the modulatory effects of the vestibular system on sensory processing using auditory and visual stimulation in combination with optogenetic excitation of the MVN. We found enhanced responses to sound in the auditory cortex, thalamus, and inferior colliculus ipsilateral to the stimulated MVN. In the visual pathway, we observed enhanced responses to visual stimuli in the ipsilateral visual cortex, thalamus, and contralateral superior colliculus. Meanwhile, the stimulation of SVN resulted in activations that were distinct and not as widespread as those found with MVN stimulation. Optogenetically evoked fMRI activations were primarily observed in the cerebellar cortices and limbic regions (i.e., insula cortex and amygdala). Taken together, our imaging findings reveal multiple and distinct brain-wide central vestibular pathways. We demonstrate large-scale modulatory effects of the vestibular system on sensory processing. b. More detailed analysis and experiments are presently underway. The key experimental results remain to be summarized and published, they are presently being analyzed and prepared for publication in a leading brain imaging or neuroscience journal such as Neuroimage and/or PNAS, and in ISMRM conference proceedings. 17103819.label: Major findings and research outcome
17103819.value: Using fMRI, we examined brain-wide neural activity patterns elicited by optogenetically stimulating excitatory neurons of a major vestibular nucleus, the ipsilateral medial vestibular nucleus (MVN) and superior vestibular nucleus (SVN). We demonstrated robust optogenetically evoked fMRI activations bilaterally at sensorimotor cortices and their associated thalamic nuclei (auditory, visual, somatosensory, and motor), high-order cortices (cingulate, retrosplenial, temporal association, and parietal), and hippocampal formations (dentate gyrus, entorhinal cortex, and subiculum). We then examined the modulatory effects of the vestibular system on sensory processing using auditory and visual stimulation in combination with optogenetic excitation of the MVN. We found enhanced responses to sound in the auditory cortex, thalamus, and inferior colliculus ipsilateral to the stimulated MVN. In the visual pathway, we observed enhanced responses to visual stimuli in the ipsilateral visual cortex, thalamus, and contralateral superior colliculus. Meanwhile, the stimulation of SVN resulted in activations that were distinct and not as widespread as those found with MVN stimulation. Optogenetically evoked fMRI activations were primarily observed in the cerebellar cortices and limbic regions (i.e., insula cortex and amygdala). Taken together, our imaging findings reveal multiple brain-wide central vestibular pathways. We demonstrate large-scale modulatory effects of the vestibular system on sensory processing.

17103819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17103819.value: In the completed project, we only used CaMKIIα as our primary promoter to drive the expression of the optogenetic construct in only excitatory neurons in the vestibular sub-nuclei because the long-range projections in central vestibular pathways are predominantly glutamatergic (1-3). Nevertheless, we acknowledge that the stimulation of the inhibitory neuronal population in the VN, which is not included in the present project application, may also be important to fully examine the pathways and also functions of the central vestibular system. 17103819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17103819.value: Blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) fMRI has been a key neuroimaging tool utilized in our endeavor to map brain-wide functions in response to specific sensory tasks, and has been instrumental in the past decade in identifying certain regions important for vestibular processing. However, in these vestibular fMRI experiments, subjects positioned inside the scanner were not stimulated with vestibular tasks, such as head and body rotation and/or translational movements, due to the limitations of current scanner configurations that restrict the subject’s ability to move. Currently, vestibular fMRI by itself cannot clearly map important details of the large-scale spatiotemporal distributions in cortical and subcortical regions across both brain hemispheres. In this project, we interrogated brain-wide central vestibular pathways and their functions by combining the use of functional MRI (fMRI) and optogenetic neuromodulation. We showed that by using fMRI to monitor brain-wide responses to optogenetic stimulation of excitatory neurons in the vestibular nucleus (VN), we can (i) visualize the VN’s downstream activation targets; (ii) characterize the targets’ BOLD response properties; (iii) systematically categorize the central vestibular pathways involved in the response; and (iv) examine the vestibular system’s cross-modal functional effects on other sensory systems.

17104619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17104619.value: Protein engineering is impeded by the unpredictability of functional consequences of combining multiple mutations. Direct experimentation of sequence variants is important for identification of rare combinations that confer desired properties of proteins useful for biomedical and biotechnological applications. However, de novo synthesis is a prohibitively expensive way for generating libraries of protein mutants and site-directed mutagenesis alone is laborious and limited in throughput. Surpassing the limitations of pre-existing approaches, we aim to develop a new technology platform to enable simple one-pot, seamless and scalable assembly of variant combinations from a repertoire of fragments tagged with barcodes specifying predetermined mutations at defined positions, such that short-barcode sequencing can be used to track variants cost-effectively and allow the pursuit of large-scale systematic analyses of the functional impact brought by combinatorial mutations. We shall validate our approach by applying this new technology platform for high-throughput optimization of CRISPR enzymes to achieve their optimized performance for genome editing. This proposed work aims to tackle the unmet need for high-throughput building and testing of protein variants carrying combinatorial mutations. 科學家可借修改蛋白質的氨基酸序列，在多點位置換入其它氨基酸，以提高蛋白質的功能。然而多個氨基酸變化的組合效應難以預測，並且隨著每個額外氨基酸的修改，蛋白質變體組合數量亦大量增加。傳統定點誘變技術可逐一產生蛋白質變體，但不能建立具有多個變化的大型氨基酸變體文庫作大量的同時平行分析。我們的目標是開發一個新的技術平台，以序列條碼標籤蛋白基因的變體，以高通量測序方法，快速分析多點氨基酸的變化組合，以瞭解變體組合與蛋白酶活性的關係。這方法比傳統技術更為省時，成本較低，且可以廣泛應用於不同領域的實驗室，例如生物醫學、應用醫學，新藥及抗體開發和生物科技等，實現高通量表徵及篩選蛋白質變體。我們將應用這個新的技術平台於高通量優化CRISPR酶的基因編輯效率和準確性。

17104619.label: Realisation of objectives
17104619.value: This study aims to optimize CRISPR-based tools for efficient and accurate genomic perturbations via CombiSEAL technology that enables high-throughput profiling of combinatorial mutations. We have successfully achieved the objectives in this project. In Aim 1, we sought to identify the SpCas9 variants that show robust on-target activity and low off-target activity across multiple gRNAs. We have generated additional monoclonal reporter cell lines to stably express RFP and gRNA that targets another pair of matched and mismatched site of the RFP gene sequence (i.e., RFPsg5-ON and RFPsg5-OFF5-2). Cells were infected with the SpCas9 variant library, and sorted into bins based on the RFP fluorescence levels at 14 days post-infection. Illumina HiSeq was used to track the barcoded SpCas9 variants to isolate the subpopulation of variants that are enriched in the sorted bin that encompasses ~5% of the cell population with the lowest level of RFP when compared to the unsorted population. We successfully performed the large-scale profiling experiments in two biological replicates for both the RFPsg8 and RFPsg5 reporter systems. We defined high-fidelity variants as those with enrichment ratios that were at least >90% of WT for both RFPsg8-ON and RFPsg5-ON, and <50% of WT for both RFPsg8-OFF5 and RFPsg5-OFF5-2. Using the enrichment ratio as an index for editing activity of SpCas9, we constructed heatmaps presenting on- and off-target activities conferred by the combinations of mutations and the epistatic interactions involved. Our analysis provides insights into how the number and type of substitutions introduced at SpCas9’s amino acid residues that are predicted to interact with the target and non-target DNA strands (including R661, Q695, K848, Q926, K1003, and K1060) govern the optimal balance between maximizing the nuclease’s on-target editing efficiency and minimizing its off-target activity. In sum, we have successfully performed massively parallel analysis to optimize SpCas9’s genome editing specificity. We then followed up on characterizing the on- and off- target activities of Opti-SpCas9 and OptiHF-SpCas9 identified in Aim 1 to edit endogenous loci, which is Aim 2 of our proposed work. We performed T7 endonuclease assay to measure the on-target DNA cleavage activity of the high-fidelity variants when compared to WT. eSpCas9(1.1), SpCas9-HF1, HypaCas9, and evoCas9 was also included in the experiments to benchmark the on-target activity of Opti-SpCas9 and OptiHF-SpCas9. We also performed Western blot analysis to measure the expression of the different variants to confirm the difference of editing is not due to the decreased protein expression levels of the SpCas9 variants. To evaluate the editing specificity of the newly identified variants, we performed T7 endonuclease assay and GUIDE-Seq at off-target sites to detect the induced genomic indels. To compare the mismatch tolerance of different SpCas9 variants, we generated a panel of gRNAs containing one- to four- base mismatches against the reporter gene target (i.e., a genomically integrated green fluorescent protein (GFP) gene sequence). The panel include 20 individual gRNAs bearing single-base mismatch against the target GFP sequence, and gRNAs with two- to four- base mismatches that span across different positions of the gRNA’s spacer sequence against GFP. We measured the loss of GFP fluorescence to reflect DNA cleavage and indel-mediated disruption of the target site using flow cytometry. With the above experiments, we showed that Opti-SpCas9 and OptiHF-SpCas9 generated less off-target edits and displayed a higher on-to-off target ratio compared to WT. To facilitate genome editing in eukaryotic cells, a 5’-G is commonly included or added to the start of a gRNA sequence to promote its transcription under the U6 promoter. Unlike other high-fidelity SpCas9 variants including eSpCas9(1.1), SpCas9-HF1, HypaCas9, and evoCas9, we performed experiments to show that Opti-SpCas9 and OptiHF-SpCas9 are compatible with gRNAs having an additional 5’-G that is mismatched to the protospacer sequence. We further demonstrated that Opti-SpCas9 and OptiHF-SpCas9 showed better compatibility with the use of truncated gRNAs than other high-fidelity variants. In sum, we have completed the validation of our optimized SpCas9 variants using non-pooled assays. We moved on to Aim 3 of this study to try engineer off-target-minimized dSpCas9-VPR variants for programmable gene activation. Because of the large size of dSpCas9-VPR protein that could not fit in the viral vector for CombiSEAL, we explored the use of the non-viral, CRISPR-assisted recombinase-based integration system to deliver large constructs into human cells. Unfortunately, our attempts failed to obtain a high enough integration efficiency for large-scale protein engineering screen. Seeing the blooming of the use of artificial intelligence for protein engineering, we came up with an idea and shift our aim of Aim 3 of this study to try apply machine learning to assist the engineering of CRISPR proteins. The genome-editing Cas9 protein uses multiple amino-acid residues to bind the target DNA. Considering only the residues in proximity to the target DNA as potential sites to optimise Cas9’s activity, the number of combinatorial variants to screen through is too massive for a wet-lab experiment. Therefore we established the parameters for using machine learning models to cross-validate the in silico and experimental datasets of multi-domain combinatorial mutagenesis libraries for SpCas9 engineering, and we demonstrated for the first time that a machine learning-coupled engineering approach reduces the experimental screening burden by as high as 95% while enriching top-performing variants in comparison to the null model. We completed Aim 3 by validating a readily applicable workflow to enable resource-efficient high-throughput engineering of SpCas9’s activity.

17104619.label: Major findings and research outcome
17104619.value: Given the fast nature of the CRISPR field and fierce competitions, we tried to expedite and first focus on completing Aim 1 and 2, based on our prior and the promising preliminary data indicated in our original submitted proposal. This enabled us to maintain the significance and novelty of the study. The data described above are included in our paper published in Nature Methods. We also published a book chapter in Structural Genomics, Methods in Molecular Biology to describe the high-throughput protein engineering methods that was also applied in this work. For Aim 3, our work to establish the machine learning-coupled engineering approach for SpCas9 contributes to in part a paper published in Nature Communications and a review article published in Advanced Genetics. We also had several poster presentations at international conferences (Please refer to Part C for the details).

17104619.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17104619.value: Our established CombiSEAL strategy uses a pooled assembly approach to bypass the laborious steps for building individual combination mutants one-by-one, and exploits barcoding tactics to allow parallel experimentations on and identification of the top performers from a large number of protein variants to facilitate protein engineering. Using CombiSEAL, we successfully identified Opti-SpCas9 and OptiHF-SpCas9 – novel variants with superior genome editing efficiency and specificity across a broad range of endogenous targets in human cells. The CombiSEAL pipeline can be readily applied to build even more Cas9 variants to broaden the search for variants with multifaceted or other properties, such as those having broader protospacer adjacent motif flexibility. We envision that CombiSEAL will accelerate the engineering of various CRISPR nucleases and their derivatives (e.g., base editors) for precise editing of the genome. The generalizability of this approach will also expand our scope to systematically engineer diverse proteins that are relevant to many biomedical and biotechnology applications. In addition, our work also set up a useful workflow and establishes parameters that can maximize machine learning usefulness in succeeding screens and minimize wasted wet-lab resources for engineering the SpCas9 system and in future could be extended to other gene editing tools.

17104619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17104619.value: We have established new methods to address the unmet need for rapid and simultaneous profiling of high-order combinatorial mutations for engineering CRISPR genome editing proteins. Using our new methods, we successfully identified novel variants with superior efficiency and specificity for genome editing applications in human cells.

17104919.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17104919.value: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) is the causative agent of acquired immunodeficiency disease syndrome (AIDS). Despite increased coverage of combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) globally, HIV-1 continues to spread mainly via the route of unprotected sexual contacts in our country including Hong Kong. To win the battle against HIV/AIDS, it is necessary to discover novel immunotherapy and its related molecular mechanism to treat HIV-1 infection. The Nobel prize-wining discovery of programmed death-1 (PD-1 or CD279) not only has resulted in immune checkpoint inhibitors for cancer immunotherapy but also has allowed subsequent findings on PD-1 in regulating T cell exhaustion through interaction with its ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2 during HIV-1 infection. The biological function of PD-1 isoforms, however, remains incompletely investigated. In 2013, we first reported the discovery of a novel alternatively spliced isoform of human PD-1 (namely Δ42PD-1) with a 42-nucleotide in-frame deletion located at exon 2 near its IgV domain in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC)(Molecular Therapy, 2013). Δ42PD-1 functions distinctly from PD-1, as it engages neither PD-L1 nor PD-L2 but can induce pro-inflammatory cytokines in PBMC. We then reported two Δ42PD-1-specific monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) that do not cross-react with PD-1 by flow cytometry (mAbs, 2015). Using the Δ42PD-1-specific mAb namely CH101, we discovered that gut-homing Δ42PD1+γδ-T cells engage Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) to initiate innate inflammatory responses, leading to mucosal tissue damage in humanized mice during acute HIV-1 infection (Nature Microbiology, 2017). CH101 reduces these pathological effects in vivo. In a different disease model, our preliminary results indicated that TLR4 is one of the key factors underlying chronic inflammation in promoting human hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Importantly, we observed repeatedly that CH101 inhibits HCC progression significantly in humanized mice. Considering the importance of these findings to disease immunotherapy, we hypothesize that the humanized CH101 (huCH101) is a useful PD1-independent immunotherapeutic drug in treating HIV-1-induced immune activation and mucosal damage by blocking the Δ42PD-1/TLR4 pathway. To test this hypothesis, we plan to conduct a focused GRF study in humanized mice with two specific aims: 1) To determine the role of huCH101 and its variants in treating HIV-1-induced immune activation and mucosal damage (year 1-1.5), and 2) To determine the efficacy of huCH101 and immune checkpoint inhibitor in treating HIV-1 infection (year 1.5-3). By conducting the proposed studies, we will reveal the role of huCH101 not only in treating HIV-1 infection but also on engaging distinct immunotherapeutic interventions against HIV/AIDS.

17104919.label: Realisation of objectives
17104919.value: In this study, we hypothesize that the humanized CH101(huCH101) is a useful PD1-independent immunotherapeutic drug in treating HIV-1-induced immune activation and mucosal damage through blocking the Δ42PD-1/TLR4 pathway. The overall objective of the proposed study, therefore, is to investigate the role of a newly humanized Δ42PD1-specific mAb huCH101 and its variants primarily in treating HIV-1-induced immune activation and inflammatory mucosal damage during HIV-1 infection. During the study, we have successfully generated the huCH101 antibody drug and performed all necessary experiments. More importantly, based on our findings, the huCH101 antibody drug has been licenced by HKU TTO to ImmunoCure Hong Kong, Ltd for clinical development against HIV-1 infection and cancer immunotherapy. We conclude that the project objectives have been achieved. Objective 1: To determine the role of huCH101 and its variants in treating HIV-1-induced immune activation and mucosal damage. a)Engineering of huCH101-IgG1 and its variants. To engineer the huCH101-IgG1 and its variants, the variable heavy and light chains of murine CH101 were amplified from multiple clones of CH101 hybridoma using specific sets of primers. We made various modifications in the constant regions of the chimeric version or humanized version of CH101, resulting in CH101-huIgG1(N297A), CH101-huIgG1(L/S), CH101-huIgG4, hufrCH101-IgG1, hufrCH101-IgG4, CH101-huIgG1(chimeric CH101). The original murine CH101(parental) was included as a control. All humanized antibodies could recognize Δ42PD1 expressed on the cell surface but with different specificity (Figure 1). The detailed statistical analysis elucidated the activity of versions of humanized antibodies in interacting with Δ42PD1 at different specificity and sensitivity (Table 1). b)Half-life of humanized versions of CH101 in NSG-PBL mice. We tested three humanized CH101 antibodies, CH101-huIgG1, CH101-IgG4 and hufrCH101-IgG1 in NSG-PBL mice at the dose of 200 µg per mouse. The peripheral amounts of each antibody were measured subsequently by ELISA. The plasma levels of all three antibodies under investigation declined over time within 72 hours after the injection and subsequently plateaued at a low level after 5 days. The half-life of CH101-IgG4 was 45.35hr that was slightly longer than others as compared with CH101-huIgG1 (44.55hr) and hufrCH101-IgG1 (36.44hr). c)Chimeric huCH101 as a therapeutic intervention in HIV and HCC mouse models. We found that humanized NSG-huCD34 mice were not suitable for treating HIV-1 infection due to insufficient Δ42PD-expressing immune cells. To overcome the problem, we assessed the CH101-IgG1, for its potential as an immunotherapy in the well-established NSG-PBL/HCC model. Briefly, we found that CH101-huIgG1 group displayed an average of 3.83 mm3 smaller tumor than the hu-IgG1 control group on Day 14. At the same time, parental murine CH101 group had a comparable reduction of 4.12 mm3 as compared to the mouse IgG1 control group. At the endpoint, a significant reduction in tumor volume was consistently observed in the CH101-huIgG1 group at an average of 38.94 mm3 (data not shown). d)The hufrCH101-IgG1 as a therapeutic intervention in HIV and HCC mouse model. Importantly, we also evaluated the hufrCH101-IgG1, the 97.0% humanized version of CH101, for suppressing HCC in NSG-PBL mice. The animals received daily antibody treatment for 5 days one week after the tumor inoculation (Figure 4A). The tumor growth in mice was measured and the volume of tumor was recorded every week until the humane endpoint (Figure 4B-C). Encouragingly, the tumor size significantly reduced mainly in the hufrCH101-IgG1 group as compared with the control group (Figure 4C). The hufrCH101-IgG1 group presented an average of 7.82 mm3 in tumor size like 7.90 mm3 in the CH101-huIgG1 group as compared with 11.55 mm3 in the hu-IgG1 control group on day 14. The tumor size progressed slower in two humanized CH101 antibody groups, showing 13.33mm3 and 14.56 mm3 in hufrCH101-IgG1 and CH101-huIgG1 on day 21, respectively, which were contrasted with 23.96 mm3 in the control group. Subsequently, hufrCH101-IgG1 still showed a relatively better control of tumor size at the end point, with an average volume of 14.26mm3 as compared with 27.27 mm3 in the control group (Table 4.3). Significant decline was found neither with the tumor weight (Figure 4D) nor with the plasma inflammatory cytokines level (Figure 4E), which required further analysis. Objective 2. To determine the efficacy of huCH101 and immune checkpoint inhibitor in treating HIV-1 infection. Under this specific objective, we aimed to evaluate immune checkpoint inhibitors including anti-PD-1 (Pembrolizumab, IgG4, Merck), anti-PD-L1 (Atezolizumab, IgG1-NA, Genentech) or anti-CTLA4 (Ipilimumab, IgG1, BMS) mAbs for potential combination immunotherapy together with our huCH101-IgG1 or its variants. To promote the implications to patients’ clinical care, we sought to include cART for combination immunotherapy as originally planned. For this purpose, we conducted Pembrolizumab treatment experiments in NSG-PBL/HCC mice. To our surprise, Pembrolizumab showed no significant in vivo efficacy (Figure 3), affecting the further evaluation of combination therapy. To overcome the problems, we have continuously tried to establish HIV-1/NSG-huCD34 mouse model. a)NSG-huCD34 mouse model. To examine the efficacy of huCH101-IgG1 and hufrCH101-IgG4 with identical specifity, we sought to establish the NSG-huCD34 mouse model because they have diverse types of human immune cells as compared with NSG-huPBL mice. Our animal protocols will be approved by the Committee on the Use of Live Animals in Teaching and Research at the Laboratory Animal Unit of the University of Hong Kong. All physical procedures associated with this work were performed in animals under anesthesia to minimize the pain. Immunodeficient NOD.Cg-Prkdcscid Il2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ(NSG) mice were obtained from the Jackson Laboratory. Humanized NSG-huCD34 mice were generated. Briefly, human CD34 stem cells were inoculated intravenously into each of 20 NSG 3-4 weeks old mice 4 hours after the irradiation (Figure 5A). After four months of waiting, we were able to detect human immune cells in NSG mice, including CD4 and CD8 T cells with frequencies like humans (Figure 5B-F). We detected human NK, monocyte and dendritic cells but at low frequencies. b)HIV-1/NSG-huCD34 mice. To determine the mechanism of Δ42PD-1-specific humanized antibody huCH101 in treating HIV/AIDS, we sought to establish the HIV-1/NSG-huCD34 mouse model for combination immunotherapy. One day before the live viral challenge, blood samples from animals will be subjected to flow cytometry to determine the baseline CD4/CD8 ratios and immune activation state. Humanized animals were then challenged with 10 ng p24 of live HIV-1JR-FL. Blood were drawn weekly, and viral load and CD4+ T cell percentages were determined by Q-PCR and flow cytometry, respectively. Two weeks after the viral challenge, three animals were given cART (including 3TC, RAL and TDF) according to a schedule mimicking HIV-1-infected patients (Figure 6A). To maintain effective viral suppression, three anti-viral drugs were mixed food for intake (Figure 6B). This innovative approach was quite successful because viral loads were reduced to detection limits during the 40 day-treatment period (Figure 6C). In this pilot experiment. We did observe protected CD4 cells in all three animals (Figure 6D-F). These results have provided evidence to conduct proposed combination immunotherapy. However, we consistently found that humanized HIV/NSG-huCD34 mice were not suitable for huCH101 treatment of HIV-1 infection due to insufficient Δ42PD-expressing immune cells, preventing the further in vivo evaluation of combination therapy as originally proposed. To overcome the problem, we continue to optimize the model by inoculate HIV and HCC at the same time so that HCC will assist the induction of sufficient Δ42PD-expressing immune cells for evaluating huCH101 treatment against HIV-1 infection and HCC.

17104919.label: Major findings and research outcome
17104919.value: During this study, we have generated a panel of humanized CH101 (huCH101) antibody drugs as a useful PD1-independent immunotherapy in treating HIV-1- and HCC-induced immune activation and mucosal damage through blocking the Δ42PD-1/TLR4 pathway. For in vivo evaluation, we have successfully generated the time-consuming HIV-1/NSG-huCD34 mouse model after several times of trials. However, due to the insufficient number of Δ42PD1-expressing immune cells in these mice, it remains a technical challenge to use this model for in vivo evaluation of huCH101 antibody drugs. To overcome this technical challenge, we had to adopt the NSG-PBL/HCC model to evaluate the efficacy of several huCH101 antibody drugs. We showed similar half-lives of these huCH101 antibody drugs in NSG-PBL mice. We have generated promising and reproducible results on couple huCH101 antibody drugs in the NSG-PBL/HCC model for reducing HCC progression including the hufrCH101-IgG with over 97% humanization. We found that huCH101-IgG1 and hufrCH101-IgG4 displayed nearly 100% identical specificity to Δ42PD1 without evident cross reactivity to PD1. Critically, based on our findings, we have patented these nearly fully humanized hufrCH101-IgG antibody drugs, which have subsequently been licenced by HKU TTO to ImmunoCure Hong Kong, Ltd for clinical development against HIV-1 infection and cancer immunotherapy. We conclude that the GRF project objectives have been achieved and we look forward to using the optimized hufrCH101-IgG4 antibody drug to benefit patients in future clinical trials and application. Lastly, we have trained a faculty research award-winning PhD student Dr. Dongyan Zhou. The platform of antibody humanization will be useful for discovery of other antibody drugs for human use.

17104919.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17104919.value: After licencing out the humanized hufrCH101-IgG antibody drugs and securing industry matching fund, we have been shortlisted for RAISE+ application by HKU for clinical development of an optimized hufrCH101-IgG4 against HIV-1 infection and cancer immunotherapy.

17104919.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17104919.value: During this study, we have generated several humanized CH101 antibody drugs against a new target of host protein called Δ42PD-1. Since Δ42PD-1 is associated with HIV-1- and HCC-induced immune activation and disease progression, the humanized CH101 antibody drugs may have potential to be developed for future human treatment. Although we had difficulties in establishing the HIV-1/NSG-huCD34 mouse model, we were able to provide promising and reproducible results on huCH101 antibody drugs in the NSG-PBL/HCC model for reducing HCC progression including the hufrCH101-IgG with over 97% humanization. Critically, based on our exciting results, we were able not only to patent these nearly fully humanized hufrCH101-IgG antibody drugs but also to licence the patent by HKU TTO to ImmunoCure Hong Kong, Ltd for clinical development against HIV-1 infection and cancer immunotherapy. We also trained a PhD student Dr. Dongyan Zhou, who received the faculty research award. The platform of antibody humanization will be useful for discovery of other antibody drugs for human use. We, therefore, conclude that the GRF project objectives have been achieved.
