17114519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17114519.value: Our work explored the genetic basis and pathogenic mechanisms that lead to the development of idiopathic scoliosis in adolescents and implies a role of glycine synaptic transmission in the etiology of AIS. A moderate elevation of glycine may be a strong risk factor for AIS. In future, One of the efforts is to measure and compare EMG activities of the paraspinal muscles in patients and controls. Measuring EMG on the paraspinal muscle of asymptomatic or early-stage patients would be more informative. EMG screening in preadolescent children may help to identify potential AIS patients for preventive treatment. Glycine is found in many protein-based food sources and is used as a food additive or taken as supplements. However, the long-term safety of glycine supplements, such as their effects on plasma or CSF glycine levels, has not been fully tested. This is very important issue for those people carried mutations in GlyT1 gene. Further, large population study should be contacted. It would be highly valuable to investigate whether there are associations among plasma/CSF glycine level, EMG signals, and genetic variants with AIS, which could establish a new method to predict AIS in preadolescents as well as testing of sodium benzoate as a potential preventive therapy in AIS patients.

17114519.value: We have detected a mutation in a gene, which causes Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS) in a family. The gene involved in AIS is glycine transporter 1 (GlyT 1), of which transports glycine in glutamatergic synapse to keep glycine concentrations below saturation level. Furthermore, we also detected two new mutations in sporadic AIS. This implies a role of glycine synaptic transmission in the etiology of AIS. 17114619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17114619.value: 許多神經系統疾病是由中樞神經系統中神經元亞型的退化導致的，因此人們對鑑定控制神經元發育的調控因子產生了濃厚的興趣，以便於能夠從多能幹細胞定向分化為治療神經退行性疾病的特定神經元類型。脊髓運動神經元(MNs)是一種在中樞神經系統中發育途徑較為深入研究的神經元亞型。 Sonic hedgehog基因(SHH)決定了發育中的腹神經管中的部分細胞轉變為MN的祖細胞，並且觸發一系列轉錄因子從而開啟分化為不同的MN亞型的過程，這些MN亞型通過延伸到肌肉組織的軸突來控制肌肉的收縮。由於基因突變而死亡的MNs會導致MN退行性疾病。然而，目前對介導MN分化維持和存活的因子還不甚了解。此外，這些因子是如何被調控的以及它們的表達失調是否與MN疾病有關還不清楚。 我們發現DLC1亞型1 (DLC1-i1)僅在有絲分裂期後的MNs中表達。功能喪失研究表明，雞和人的MNs分化過程對DLC1-i1具有劑量依賴性。將DLC1-i1的表達量減半會破壞MN的分化，而進一步的表達量降低會導致MN的死亡。 SHH的下游轉錄因子可調控DLC1-i1的表達。重要的是，前人的RNA測序研究表明DLC1-i1是脊髓性肌萎縮症(SMA)患者MNs中下調最多的基因，並且我們發現DLC1-i1的下調導致人成熟的MNs的凋亡，這與SMA中MN的死亡相似。基於這些數據，我們假設不同水平DLC1-i1的表達調控正在分化的MNs的維持和生存，並且DLC1-i1是SHH下游MN轉錄級聯的一部分，DLC1-i1表達的缺失導致SMA患者MN死亡。在這個方案中,我們將通過操縱DLC1-i1在雞，小鼠胚胎以及人的MNs中的表達水平來驗證這些假設：1)確定DLC1-i1在MN分化中的能夠行使功能的保守劑量, 2 )研究DLC1-i1的表達時間、定位和表達水平在分裂後的MNs中是如何被調控的，及其在MN分化中的作用方式，3)闡明DLC1-i1 在SMA發病機理和治療中的作用。我們提出的研究將闡明DLC1-i1在MN分化和SMA發病機制中的作用，這將為目前尚不清楚的SMA基因治療提供明顯的導向作用。

17114619.label: Realisation of objectives
17114619.value: Objective 1: We have achieved most of the issues according to the plan: (i) Assessing the fate of DLC1-i1 knockdown (KD) cells in developing chick neural tube Our study revealed that DLC1-i1 is predominantly expressed in post-mitotic MNs found in the neural tubes of embryonic chicks and human-induced pluripotent stem cells. By using the knockdown approach in both chick embryos and human-induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), we observed that DLC1-i1 is required for the onset of MN differentiation that is consistent with its specific expression in MN lineage. We conducted lentiviral-mediated overexpression of DLC1-i1 (DLC1-i1 OE) in motor neuron progenitors to investigate whether DLC1-i1 alone can promote MN differentiation. Our results revealed a significant increase in the number of cells expressing the MN marker ISLET1/2 and in the axonal length marked by TUJ1, compared to the vehicle control. This suggests that DLC1-i1 overexpression can promote precocious MN differentiation. We observed no significant difference in the number of apoptotic cells between DLC1-i1 OE and vehicle control. However, the RhoGAP domain or the SAM domain of DLC1-i1 alone is not sufficient to induce MN differentiation. This suggests that the effect of DLC1-i1 OE is RhoGAP independent. Overall, our findings indicate that DLC1-i1 overexpression can promote MN differentiation. (ii) Evaluating the requirement of DLC1-i1 for MN maintenance and axon growth To address this issue, we attempted to electroporate DLC1-i1 siRNA or a scramble control into neural tubes of st 17-18 chick embryos. However, the transfection efficiency was extremely low when embryos were harvested at st 26-28, a stage at which distinct MN pools have already innervated different types of muscles. Despite multiple attempts, we were unable to achieve successful transfection. Instead, we adopted a different approach and performed knockdown in mature MNs at 21 days post-differentiation. By qPCR and immunofluorescence analysis, we observed a decrease in the expression of ISLET1/2, ChAT and TUJ1 in DLC1-i1 KD cells compared to the scramble control. In addition, more DLC1-i1 KD cells were positively stained for Caspase 3, indicating an elevated level of cell death in the absence of DLC1-i1. These findings strongly suggest that DLC1-i1 plays a crucial role in maintaining the maturation and survival of human MNs. Objective 2: (i) Investigating the potential molecules involved in regulating DLC1-i1 expression To further investigate whether SHH-induced NKX6.1 restricts DLC1-i1 expression in post-mitotic MNs, either dependent on or independent of OLIG2 activity, we electroporated the OLIG2-VP16, which acts as a dominant-negative form of OLIG2, to interfere with the endogenous OLIG2 function. Electroporation of OLIG2-VP16 resulted in the expansion of DLC1-i1 expression in post-mitotic MNs to the MN progenitor region. Based on these results, we conclude that OLIG2 is required for restricting DLC1-i1 expression in post-mitotic MNs. We prioritized objective 3 as the obtained results are highly significant for enhancing our comprehension of SMA pathogenesis and treatment. Objective 3: We showed a 60% knockdown of SMN in human MNs resulting in a significant decrease in the mRNA levels of DLC1-i1, ISLET1/2, TUJ1, and increased expression of cleaved Caspase 3 (cCaspase3). To further strengthen these findings, we generated MNs from urine-derived cells of SMA patients. These cells could be reprogrammed into iPSCs and differentiated into MN lineage. As a positive control, we used urine cells from healthy individuals (wild-type, WT), which can give rise to functional mature MNs with evident action potential activity. Urine cells were obtained from SMA patients type I, type II, and type III. Consistent with the disease severity, MNs derived from type I patient’s UiPSCs exhibited a significant reduction in the expression of DLC1-i1 compared to MNs from types II and III, as well as WT MNs. As anticipated, MNs from type I patients displayed a more pronounced decrease in the expression of post-mitotic MN marker ISLET1/2, mature MN markers, choline acetyltransferase ChAT and synaptophysin (SYN), and TUJ1+ axon length. Additionally, there was an increase in the expression of cCaspase 3, indicating higher levels of apoptosis. To further investigate the impact of reduced DLC1-i1 expression on MN differentiation and survival, we specifically targeted the N-terminal region of DLC1-i1 and DLC1-i3 (truncated and non-functional) mRNAs using two shRNA oligos in UiPSCs, while avoiding interference with other isoforms. Following 21 days of MN differentiation, we observed sustained high levels of OLIG2 expression in both knockdown samples. This resulted in a significant decrease in the expression of ISLET1/2, ChAT, and SYN, accompanied by a notable reduction in TUJ1+ axon length and an increase in cCaspase 3+ apoptotic cells. These findings provide evidence of the crucial role of DLC1-i1 in MN differentiation, axon outgrowth, and survival. The loss of DLC1-i1 expression is likely responsible for the observed MN defects in SMA. Furthermore, when DLC1-i1 was overexpressed in MN cultures from SMA patients, we observed a restoration of ISLET1/2 and ChAT expression, an increase in TUJ1+ axon length, and a reduction in apoptosis. These results collectively indicate that the reduced expression of DLC1-i1 contributes to the impaired MN differentiation, maturation, and survival observed in SMA patients. In addition to the reduced expression of DLC1-i1 in MNs of SMA patients, we found a significant decrease in Dlc1-i1 expression in the lumbar spinal cord of moderate type II SMA mice that coincided with pronounced MN loss. In contrast, the expression of DLC1-i1 remained unaltered in the thoracic spinal cord of both SMA mice and WT mice. These findings indicate that the dysregulation of Dlc1-i1 expression exhibits similar changes in MNs of both SMA mice and SMA patients. Since DLC1-i1 OE can rescue differentiation of SMA patients’-derived MNs, we aimed to investigate whether the delivery of DLC1-i1 to SMA-mice could improve the lifespan, increase weight, and enhance locomotor behavior compared to the FDA-approved AAV9-SMN1 which is controlled by the ubiquitous hybrid CMV enhancer/chicken -actin promoter (CAG) which drives high levels of transgene expression in both CNS and non-CNS tissues. However, the size of DLC1-i1 cDNA (~4.7 kbp) exceeds the AAV9 packaging capacity, which could result in low titer or truncated protein production when driven by CAG. To achieve efficient expression of DLC1-i1 in CNS tissues, we utilized an enhanced AAV variant, AAV-PHP.eB vector which has been shown to facilitate a 40-fold increase in transduction efficiency in most CNS neurons compared to the parental AAV9 vector. We, therefore, generated AAV-PHP.eB-DLC1-i1 under the control of the human synapsin (SYN) promoter which is smaller in size than CAG to enable high viral titer preparation and restrict DLC1-i1 expression in a neuron-specific manner. In addition, we observed that the administration of AAV-PHP.eB-SYN-SMN1 (SYN-SMN1) was as effective as CAG-SMN1 in improving the lifespan and locomotor behavior of SMA mice. This indicates that using SYN-SMN1 to compare the therapeutic effects with SYN-DLC1-i1 in SMA mice is a valid approach. Intracerebroventricular injection of SYN-DLC1-i1 in SMA mice at P0 extended the median lifespan to 46 days (although there was no significant difference in weight between treatment groups). Moreover, mice treated with SYN-DLC1-i1 showed a significant improvement in motor function compared to those injected with SYN-SMN1 (median survival: 30 days) or vector control (median survival: 14 days). These results demonstrate that administering SYN-DLC1-i1 yields better therapeutic effects than SYN-SMN1 treatment in terms of lifespan extension, improvement of locomotor activity, and muscle strength in SMA mice.

17114619.label: Major findings and research outcome
17114619.value: Major findings: DLC1 isoform 1 (DLC1-i1) is expressed in postmitotic motor neurons in chick embryonic neural tubes and is regulated by the SHH-NKX6.1-OLIG2 axis. Similarly, DLC1-i1 is also expressed in motor neurons derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). The level of DLC1-i1 expression is reduced in motor neurons differentiated from spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) patients’ urine-derived iPSCs (UiPSCs), and this reduction is correlated with disease severity. When DLC1-i1 was knockdown in motor neurons derived from wild-type UiPSCs, motor neuron differentiation, axon growth, and survival were impaired, resembling SMA. However, overexpression of DLC1-i1 restored these defects. These results suggest that the decreased expression of DLC1-i1 contributes to the impaired differentiation, maturation, and survival of motor neurons in SMA patients. Additionally, Dlc1-i1 expression is significantly reduced in the lumbar spinal cord of SMA mice which is accompanied by a loss of motor neurons. Notably, gene therapy with DLC1-i1 in the neuronal population is more effective than SMN1 in improving the lifespan and locomotor activity of SMA mice. Altogether, our findings indicate that the deficiency of motor neuron-specific DLC1-i1 expression can lead to motor neuron degeneration in SMA patients, explaining why the loss of ubiquitously expressed survival motor neuron 1 predominantly affects motor neuron integrity. Restoring DLC1-i1 expression represents a more effective gene therapy approach for SMA. Research Outcome: The research findings have been presented at several local and international conferences. Dr. Tianyuan Shi, a PhD student who was trained in my lab, conducted most of the studies. She successfully graduated in Dec 2022 with her dissertation receiving an “excellent” grade from the three examiners. Additionally, we have filed a patent for AAV-SYN-DLC1-i1 as a novel gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy. Furthermore, we published a review article titled “Urine-derived induced pluripotent stem cells for modeling neurological diseases” in the journal “Cell & Bioscience”. The manuscript, titled “Restoring DLC1 isoform 1 expression is a more effective gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy” is currently being prepared for submission to Science Translational Medicine”.

17114619.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17114619.value: We have successfully utilized patients’ UiPSCs to generate neuromuscular organoids, which provide a more physiologically relevant model for recapitulating different stages of neuromuscular development in an SMA patient-specific manner. This approach allows us to identify new pathogenic factors and treatment targets through single-cell transcriptomics. Using alpha-bungarotoxin as a neuromuscular junction marker, we observed a decreased number of neuromuscular junction (NMJ) formations in SMA NMOs compared to healthy ones, indicating a deficiency in NMJ formation. Similar NMJ defects were also observed in DLC1-i1 KD NMOs. These findings highlight the role of DLC1-i1 in contributing to NMJ formation and SMA pathogenesis. Based on these findings, I applied for the Research Impact Fund 2023/2024 as a Project Coordinator and was recently awarded HK$5.7M for a project titled “Application of Neuromuscular Organoids for the Development of personalized therapy in spinal muscular atrophy”. This fund involves collaboration between Principal Investigators from HKU, City University of Hong Kong, and Families of SMA.

17114619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17114619.value: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a rare, genetic neuromuscular condition and the leading genetic cause of infant death. SMA is caused by the loss of the widely expressed survival motor neuron (SMN), which leads to selective degeneration of spinal motor neurons (MNs). Although current SMN-enhancing therapies can reduce disease severity, they do not effectively reverse motor axon degeneration. Additionally, the reason why global SMN deficiency causes MN loss remains unclear. Here, we show that DLC1-i1 is predominantly expressed in human embryonic MNs, and reduced expression was detected in MNs differentiated from SMA patients’ urine-derived iPSCs that contributed to the impaired MN axon growth, and survival. However, overexpression of DLC1-i1 restored these defects. Additionally, Dlc1-i1 expression is significantly reduced in the lumbar spinal cord of SMA mice. Notably, gene therapy with DLC1-i1 in the neuronal population is more effective than SMN1 in improving the lifespan and locomotor activity of SMA mice. Altogether, our findings indicate that the deficiency of motor neuron-specific DLC1-i1 expression can lead to motor neuron degeneration in SMA patients, explaining why the loss of ubiquitously expressed survival motor neuron 1 predominantly affects motor neuron integrity. Restoring DLC1-i1 expression represents a more effective gene therapy approach for SMA.

17115119.label: Project Objectives
17115119.value: Objective 1. Compare different facets of diversity in urban, agricultural and natural habitats With increasing conversions of natural habitats into agricultural and urban habitats, we will compare how taxonomic and functional diversity within (alpha) and between communities (beta) vary between three habitat types (natural/agricultural/urban). This will establish general patterns of diversity loss due to land-use intensification. Objective 2. Investigate how increasing land use intensity affects taxonomic and functional alpha diversity of bees We will determine the role of different land-use characteristics in driving diversity at local scales. This will illuminate how local diversity varies between agricultural and urban habitats with different environmental conditions or management. Insights into habitat management can be drawn such that conservation values of agriculture and urban habitats can be enhanced. Objective 3. Examine the importance of land-use characteristics in driving bee taxonomic and functional beta diversity within urban and agricultural habitats We will assess the influence of different land-use variables in determining bee beta diversity between sites. Additionally, we will disentangle taxonomic beta diversity into species loss and replacement components such that we can draw insights into how specific land-use drivers generate beta diversity. This will reveal the environmental variables driving spatial patterns of beta diversity (and its components) in agricultural and urban habitats, which can have direct applications for management in maintaining diversity at large spatial scales. Objective 4. Determine if regional climate or other factors modulate the impacts of land use intensification While land-use intensification is known to reduce diversity, the extent of diversity decline remains variable between studies. Our study will explore whether regional climate or other large scale regional factors can influence the ecological impacts of land-use intensification on bee diversity. This will highlight regions that are likely to be most vulnerable to land-use intensification based on regional factors and climate. Objective 5. Identify traits associated with land-use and climatic variables Using a species-level analysis, we will examine species-trait-environment associations. The framework directly links interactions between traits and environmental conditions in determining species abundance within communities, which would highlight the environmental variables driving community assembly. This would mechanistically show why some species are vulnerable to land use intensification.

17115119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17115119.value: With rapid human population growth, the planet is undergoing widespread intensifying land-use pressures to accommodate living (urban) and food (agricultural) demands. Examining the impact of land use intensification on multiple facets of diversity, especially for ecologically important taxa such as bees, is essential for the maintenance of future biodiversity, ecosystem functioning and services. While species richness declines are widely recognized with intensifying land-use, it is unclear if other facets of diversity exhibit similar trends. By collecting species traits (e.g. body size, nesting location) and examining the role of land-use characteristics in altering different dimensions of bee diversity (taxonomic, functional, alpha and beta), we will mechanistically examine the ecological impact of land-use intensification across large spatial scales. We will collect existing data on bee communities in natural, agricultural and urban habitats globally, as well as different land-use characteristics of sites to examine how these drivers affect bee diversity. Additionally, the results have strong conservation implications, as conservation actions can prioritize regions that are shown to have higher ecological impacts, and better design or management can be applied to urban and agricultural habitats to maximize their conservation values. Moreover, we will analyze how different traits are associated with environmental variables. This offers a mechanistic understanding for why some species decline under land-use intensification and improve projections of species vulnerability towards on-going land use intensification. Altogether, this study will reveal important patterns and ecological processes in determining global biodiversity. For bees specifically, this research will serve as a foundation for bee conservation and ultimately aim for maintaining ecosystem function and services. 基於全球人口急速上升，人類把不同生境改作城市或農業用途。研究土地利用如何影響對生境運作非常重要的生物(如蜂類)有助保護全球生物多樣性、生態系統功能和服務。已知土地利用一般會令物種數目下降，但現今仍缺乏研究指出這些活動如何影響其他生物多樣性的指標。透過收集不同蜂類物種的特徵(例如身體大小、築巢位置)和研究土地利用如何影響不同指標(物種多樣性、功能多樣性、α多樣性、β多樣性)，我們希望得知全球生物多樣性如何受土地利用影響。我們會搜集蜂類群落於農地、城市和自然生境的資料，亦會理解當地環境狀況，再去分析土地利用如何影響蜂類多樣性。此研究的結果有助理解什麼地區的蜂類特別容易受土地利用影響，亦可指出如何改善農地和城市的生態價值，從而保育蜂類物種。另外，我們亦會分析不同的環境狀況如何影響擁有不同特徵的蜂類。分析結果將顯示那些蜂類物種對土地利用特別敏感，有助預測不同物種的數目會否因此而大幅下降，甚至絕種。綜合所有資料，此研究將揭示全球生物多樣性受什麼因素影響。此研究亦將為日後保育蜂類物種的工作提供重要依據，亦有助保護由牠們提供的生態系統功能和服務。

17115119.label: Realisation of objectives
17115119.value: Data collection To achieve the objectives, we developed a dataset containing bee compositional data of 3,783 taxonomic units from 3,077 sites globally through reviewing the literature, searching for open-access databases and contacting bee researchers for primary data. We also developed a database of six traits for bees, including 1) whether they are free living or parasitic; 2) below ground-nesters or above-ground nesters; 3) build their own nests or rely on pre-existing cavities; 4) pollen generalists or specialists; 5) eusocial or non-eusocial species and 6) intertegular distance. Trait data were primarily provided by other collaborators; however we also conducted a literature review to fill data gaps within our dataset. Objective 1. Compare different facets of diversity in urban, agricultural and natural habitats Using the compositional, trait and phylogenetic data, we assessed taxonomic, functional and phylogenetic alpha and beta diversity for different sites. We asked data contributors to classify whether their sites are primarily natural, agricultural or urban habitats, as well as the sampling strategies and efforts in each site. We used Google Earth Pro to minimize mistakes in land-use classification, and removed sites when a category could not be confidently assigned. We additionally obtained the sampling effort and strategies in each site from the data contributor to control for differences in sampling efforts affecting diversity estimates. For alpha diversity, rarefaction analyses were further used to provide standardized diversity estimates for each site, while for beta diversity analyses, we included sampling completeness (estimated from rarefaction analyses) as a covariate and obtained mean pairwise beta diversity for habitats of each study. We additionally partitioned beta diversity into abundance difference and replacement components. For all analyses, we also included regional climatic variables to control for its effects of bee diversity at site-levels. To analyze diversity changes across land-uses, we built mixed models to control for methodological differences across datasets and spatial autocorrelation. The results established a general pattern for how land-use change could drive bee diversity decline globally (Tsang et al., in prep for PNAS). Diversity changes can reduce temporal stability of species populations and their communities, and we evaluated this using a global dataset of multiple taxa (BioTIME). We originally intended this analysis to be an examination of land-use affects on community stability as a means of trailing our statistical approaches for the bee data – however, over time the study instead focused more specifically on the relationship between community stability and diversity. We used structural equation models and revealed mechanistic pathways on how diversity changes can destabilize the stability of ecosystem at different levels, and identified consistencies and inconsistencies among taxa (Tsang et al. Minor revision, Diversity & Distributions). Thus, this research provides key insights into how bee diversity loss can destabilize their communities, and eventually the ecosystem functions contributed by them. Objective 2. Investigate how increasing land use intensity affects taxonomic and functional alpha diversity of bees For land-use intensity, we collected grassland, shrubland and forest within 1 km of each site in the sampled year using the ESA-CCI land cover time series. We then summed the area of the three land-cover to obtain natural habitat within 1 km. Sites with lower natural habitat within 1 km are considered to have lower land-use intensity. Additionally, we collected fertilizer application rate for 17 crops within 5 arcminute grid cell globally for each site during 1999-2000. Fertilizers considered include potassium, nitrogen and phosphorus, and they were summed to obtain total fertilizer application rate. Sites with higher total fertilizer application rate were considered as having higher land-use intensity. We then analyzed how these two land-use intensity variables affected bee taxonomic, functional and phylogenetic alpha diversity using mixed models. The results help explain the strong variations of land-use effects across studies, and provide mechanistic insights on how individual drivers affect bee diversity. Objective 3. Examine the importance of land-use characteristics in driving bee taxonomic and functional beta diversity within urban and agricultural habitats We used the two land-use intensity variables (see Objective 2) to analyze effects of land-use intensity on bee taxonomic, functional and phylogenetic beta diversity. For each beta diversity metric, we calculated mean pairwise beta diversity for urban and agricultural sites in each study. We also obtained mean land-use intensity across sites for each study, and built mixed model separately to assess their effects on different beta diversity metrics. However, we suspected our approach could be biased by uneven environmental conditions in each study, indicating some environments may be more common than others, which can in turn affect beta diversity conclusion. We therefore have developed a statistical method that addresses this artifact. Using simulation and empirical datasets we found our approach is more unbiased compared with conventional approaches. We have submitted a manuscript documenting this novel method (Tsang et al. submitted to Methods in Ecology & Evolution). Objective 4. Determine if regional climate or other factors modulate the impacts of land use intensification We obtained regional climatic conditions of each site using the CHELSA database. Specifically, mean annual temperature and precipitation, as well as their seasonality were obtained. We also included fertilizer usage and proportion of natural habitat within 1km for this analysis. We again used a mixed model to analyze whether alpha and beta diversity changes by land-uses are higher under certain climatic and land-use conditions. The results here highlight regional effects that are more sensitive to land-use change, complementing results from objective 1. Objective 5. Identify traits associated with land-use and climatic variables. To explain declines in different dimensions of diversity, we used the trait database to quantify community-weighted mean of each trait in each site, and analyzed how they were affected by different land-use and climatic variables. Furthermore, we also analyzed whether specific genus are more susceptible to land-use change to complement results of the trait analyses, and if evolutionary history constrained responses of bee. The latter part has been included in a manuscript documenting taxonomic and phylogenetic bee diversity change across land-uses globally (Tsang et al. in prep, PNAS). Overall, both results provide indications on what species are more sensitive to land-use changes, which can be useful for conservation management. Ecosystem function such as pollination are highly linked with floral visitation behaviours of pollinators, while other behaviours such as resting and reproducing are key to persistence of pollinators. However, we noted that diversity declines rarely focused on behavioural aspects of species in the literature. We thus developed a set of behavioral metrics at community-levels, such as number of species exhibiting certain behaviours and the average number of behaviours exhibited by different species within a particular environment, to indicate site importance to behaviours of species. We put these metrics into practice through an empirical study led by HKU MSc student Fiona Lo, who collected butterfly behavourial data in protected areas and urban parks of Hong Kong. Results from this study showed that how specific environmental variables can have differential effects on the behavioral of different species, and thus may explain their sensitivity to land-use change (Lo et al. 2022, Ecological Applications). Conclusions Overall, our results showed that land-use change have negative impacts on different facets of bee diversity. Furthermore, while the relationships between diversity and environmental change at the global scale can be complex and difficult to disentangle, we’ve developed tools through the development of this research for scientists to examine these key processes.

17115119.label: Major findings and research outcome
17115119.value: Using our global bee dataset, we established general patterns on how multiple dimensions of bee diversity are affected by land-use changes (Objective 1). We found that all dimensions of alpha diversity, namely taxonomic, functional and phylogenetic, were lower in agricultural habitats compared with native habitats. For beta diversity, we also found that their replacement components were lower in agricultural habitats, but abundance differences components were larger, leading to no net change in beta diversity. For urban habitats, taxonomic and phylogenetic alpha diversity were reduced, but not functional diversity. No beta diversity metrics nor their components exhibited significant differences between urban and natural habitats. We additionally analyzed whether land-use intensification, represented by the amount of fertilizer added and proportion of natural habitats within 1km of sites, affected different alpha and beta diversity measures in urban and agricultural habitats. We found that the two land-use drivers did not affect any dimensions of alpha diversity in both urban and agricultural habitats (Objective 2). Yet, amount of fertilizer reduced taxonomic and phylogenetic total beta diversity in agricultural habitats, as well as the phylogenetic replacement component (Objective 3). No beta diversity metrics, including their components, were affected by fertilizer usage and proportion of natural habitats within 1 km. We further examined the effects of land-use change under different climatic conditions (Objective 4), and revealed that effects of agricultural sites were more negative in areas with lower mean temperature and higher temperature seasonality (i.e., more temperate environments). None of the climatic and land-use drivers were significant in determining any beta-diversity metrics and their components in urban habitats. However, increasing fertilizer usage exacerbated the impacts of agricultural sites through reducing total beta diversity and the replacement component based on taxonomic and phylogenetic identities. Finally, we analyzed how environmental conditions can drive trait composition of bee communities (Objective 5). We found that agricultural sites were more characterized with non-parasitic and social species. Areas with lower mean precipitation and higher precipitation seasonality were more characterized with smaller species that does not rely on pre-existing cavities for nesting. Overall, our results show that land-use change can affect different dimensions of alpha and beta diversity, as well as the components of the latter, although the exact effects can vary across different land-uses. This indicates the need for conservation management to consider different dimensions of alpha and beta diversity to mitigate the effects of land-use change completely. Effects of land-use change on bee diversity can also be modulated by climatic conditions of the regions and land management, explaining the high spatial variations in different diversity metrics within the dataset. This also helps in identifying and predicting areas that are most severely impacted by land-use change, and thus have higher urgency for protection or restoration projects. Effects of land-use and climatic drivers can strongly vary across diversity dimensions, and considering their exact effects can help conservation management to target specific drivers and develop strategies accordingly to maximize different diversity dimensions.

17115119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17115119.value: Our research gathered community data from 3,077 sites, however the dataset is more represented by agricultural (N = 1,779) and natural (N = 967) habitats, while urban habitats were underrepresented (N = 331). More research is therefore needed in urban environments to better assess their effects on bee diversity. Additionally, although we used multiple strategies to minimize spatial bias in our dataset, regions such as Central Asia and India remain underrepresented, highlighting the need for future studies to assess effects of land-use change on bee diversity in these regions. We also experienced difficulties in conducting the functional diversity and trait analyses, due to a lack of trait data and poorly resolved taxonomy for many bee species, particularly those from the tropics. Functional diversity analyses, however, require all species to have complete trait data, and only ~30% of 3,783 taxonomic units met this requirement. As a result, we only included sites that are dominated by this species subset in trait analyses, which only include 1,796 sites. More studies are needed to understand the taxonomy and natural history of bees to fill these data gaps, and therefore increase spatial coverage of trait analyses. Although missing data in trait studies have frequently been addressed using imputation, the performance of these statistical means can be questionable, especially when trait data are biased towards certain regions or taxonomic groups. This is particularly true for our study, since trait data from Europe and North America are more complete compared with others. Thus, a potential development is to improve imputation methods under strongly biased data.

17115119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17115119.value: Land-use change is known to be a primary threat to global biodiversity, and understanding their impacts of ecologically important taxa are crucial for provisions of ecosystem services. Here we analyzed how bees, an important taxon driving pollination, are affected by land-use change globally, focusing on different components of diversity. We found that, compared with natural habitats, diversity of bees based on taxonomy, evolutionary histories, and ecological strategies were reduced in agricultural habitats, but in urban habitats only the former two were reduced. We also analyzed between-site diversity, and recorded reduction in all dimensions in agricultural habitats, yet in urban habitats we found no reduction. Further analyses revealed fertilizer usage and climatic conditions can exacerbate impacts of land-use changes. We also found that agricultural sites are more associated with non-parasitic and social species. Overall, our results uncovered impacts of land-use changes across different dimensions of bee diversity, highlighting their threats to bees and their associated pollination services. This also provides support for the supposition that conservation measures can be more effective in mitigating impacts of land-use change if all dimensions of biodiversity are considered.

17115619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17115619.value: The vascular remodeling of maternal spiral artery is crucial to placentation and successful pregnancy. Dysregulation of this process is associated with various pregnancy complications leading to significant maternal and fetal death. Preeclampsia is one of these complications characterized by insufficient invasion of the trophoblast and maternal spiral artery remodeling. It affects 2-5% of all pregnancies, and is the leading cause of prenatal mortality and morbidity. The causes of vascular remodeling dysregulation in preeclampsia are unclear, but it is suggested that hormone imbalance would be one of the causes. Currently, there is no reliable diagnostic test for prediction of preeclampsia. Successful vascular remodeling requires both trophoblasts and decidual natural killer (dNK) cells. Trophoblasts invade the decidua and spiral arteries during early pregnancy. Besides invading, trophoblasts undergo endovascular differentiation to assume an endothelial phenotype and replace the endothelial lining of the spiral arteries, leading to the vascular remodeling. The primary role of dNK cells is to promote placental vascular remodeling via both direct interaction with the spiral arteries and indirect interaction with trophoblasts. This primarily occurs via the secretion of various vascular and trophoblast regulatory factors. Glycodelin-A (GdA) is an abundant glycoprotein in the human decidua during early pregnancy. It interacts by its unique carbohydrate side-chains with the cell surface of various cell types in the feto-maternal interface, particularly the trophoblasts and the immune cells, and modulates their functions to permit successful pregnancy. Our unpublished data show that sex hormones treatment alters the glycosylation pattern of endometrial GdA. We hypothesize that hormonal regulation of GdA glycosylation during the menstrual cycle and early placentation is crucial to control the vascular remodeling activity of GdA. Aberrant hormonal status in preeclampsia is associated with alteration in glycosylation and defective vascular remodeling activity of GdA, which contributes to the pathophysiology of preeclampsia. The hypothesis will be tested by (1) studying the glycosylation heterogeneity of GdA derived from endometrium of different menstrual phases/early gestation; (2) studying the role and mechanism of glycosylation in regulating the vascular remodeling activities of GdA; (3) to determine the expression/glycosylation of GdA in pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia. The outcome of this project will give a better understanding on the regulation of early placentation in human. It will provide the evidence that changes in the glycosylation of decidual glycoprotein is associated with the defective vascular remodeling process. Clinically, the results will indicate the possible use of GdA glycosylation for early prediction of preeclampsia. 母体螺旋动脉的血管重塑对胎盘形成和成功妊娠至关重要。该过程的失调与各种妊娠并发症相关，导致母体和胎儿的死亡。先兆子痫是这些并发症之一，其特征在于滋养层细胞的侵袭不充分和母体螺旋动脉重塑。先兆子痫在妊娠中的发生率为2-5％，并且是导致产前死亡和发病的主要原因。 先兆子痫中血管重塑失调的原因尚不清楚，但有人认为激素失衡是其中的一个原因。目前，没有用于预测先兆子痫的可靠诊断性测试。 成功的血管重塑需要滋养层细胞和蜕膜自然杀伤（dNK）细胞。 滋养层细胞在妊娠初期侵袭蜕膜和螺旋动脉。除侵袭外，滋养层细胞经历血管内分化呈现内皮表型，并代替螺旋动脉的内皮内衬，从而导致血管重塑。dNK细胞的主要作用是通过与螺旋动脉的直接相互作用和与滋养层细胞的间接相互作用来促进胎盘血管重塑。这个过程主要通过各种血管和滋养层细胞分泌的调节因子实现。 Glycodelin-A（GdA）是妊娠早期人类蜕膜中的一种丰富的糖蛋白。它通过其独特的碳水化合物侧链与胎儿-母体界面中的各种类型细胞的细胞表面相互作用，特别是滋养层细胞和免疫细胞，并且调节它们的功能以保证妊娠成功。我们未发表的数据表明，性激素治疗改变了子宫内膜GdA的糖基化模式。 我们假设在月经周期和胎盘形成早期，GdA糖基化的激素调节对于控制GdA的血管重塑活性至关重要。先兆子痫中异常的激素状态与GdA的糖基化改变和血管重塑活性缺陷有关，这有助于先兆子痫的病理生理学研究。该假设将通过以下方法进行检验：（1）研究不同月经时期/早孕期子宫内膜GdA的糖基化异质性;（2）研究糖基化在调节GdA血管重塑活性中的作用和机制;（3）确定妊娠并发先兆子痫中GdA的表达/糖基化。 该项目的成果将有助于更好地理解人类早期胎盘形成的调节。它将为蜕膜糖蛋白糖基化的改变与缺陷性血管重塑过程有关提供证据。 在临床上，该结果显示了使用GdA糖基化来进行早期先兆子痫预测的可能性。

17115619.label: Realisation of objectives
17115619.value: Early human placentation involves the intricate coordination of maternal decidua and fetal trophoblasts. The trophectoderm of human blastocysts differentiates into cytotrophoblasts and then to syncytiotrophoblasts or extravillous trophoblasts (EVT) after implantation. Poor remodeling is associated with placental insufficiency and obstetrical syndromes like preeclampsia, fetal growth restriction, and preterm birth. From 11 days into gestation until late first trimester, the embryo and trophoblasts rely on histotrophic nutrition from endometrial glandular secretions, which promote placental development and modulate maternal-fetal interactions. Endometrial gland activity peaks during the early secretory phase and is enhanced in early pregnancy. Studying endometrial gland functions was previously challenging, but advancements in organoid technology enable long-term 3D endometrial organoid (EO) culture. EOs replicate uterine gland characteristics and respond to hormonal stimuli. Glycodelin-A (GdA), a glycoprotein found in the secretory endometrium, decidua, and amniotic fluid, interacts with various cell types at the human feto-maternal interface, such as trophoblasts and immune cells, modulating their functions for a successful pregnancy. GdA glycosylation regulation is poorly understood, and this project hypothesizes that hormonal regulation of GdA glycosylation during the menstrual cycle and early placentation is crucial for controlling its vascular remodeling activity. Aberrant hormonal status in preeclampsia (PE) may lead to altered glycosylation and defective vascular remodeling activity of GdA, contributing to PE pathophysiology. Objective 1: To confirm the glycosylation heterogeneity of GdA derived from endometrium of different menstrual phases and early gestation Endometrial tissue samples from women in the mid-luteal phase were obtained with written consent for hysterectomy. Endometrial organoids (EOs) were formed by digesting tissues with collagenase and DNase, isolating gland fragments, and culturing them in a specific medium with Matrigel support. Hormonal treatments (E2, 10 nM; P4, 1 µM; hCG, 1 µg/mL) were applied to simulate the proliferative phase (E2), secretory phase (E2+P4), and early pregnancy (E2+P4+hCG) for seven days. EO secretomes (EOS) were collected following a modified protocol. Hormone-treated EOs were washed and cultured in blank medium for 24 hours before collecting the EOS. GdA was purified from the conditioned medium, endometrial homogenates, and first trimester amniotic fluid using immunoaffinity chromatography. No significant differences in EO morphology, quantity, or EOS protein levels were observed across hormone treatments. Lectin-Antibody Sandwich ELISA and tandem mass spectrometry revealed changes in GdA glycosylation during different menstrual phases and early gestation, with a notable decrease in sialylation levels in EOS during early pregnancy conditions. The expression and activity of sialyltransferases and neuraminidases (sialidases), enzymes responsible for sialylation changes, were studied in hormone-treated EOs. ST6GalNAc1 mRNA and protein expression significantly decreased in EOs mimicking early pregnancy compared to the proliferative phase. However, neuraminidase activity remained unchanged across hormone treatments. To investigate the sialylated glycoprotein profile in hormone-treated EOS, we used SNA lectin-based lectin weak affinity chromatography to purify α-2,6 sialic acid-bearing glycoproteins and conducted sialo-proteomics analysis. Differentially expressed proteins were identified across hormone-treated EOS groups. From 1,036,939 spectra, 16,142 peptides and 2,690 proteins were identified with 1% FDR. Five candidate proteins with the largest fold change were selected for further study. An enzyme-linked antibody/lectin-binding assay was conducted to verify sialylation of these proteins across hormone-treated EOS. Sialylated S100A9 was upregulated in EOS mimicking the proliferative phase compared to the secretory phase, while sialylated AHSG and MIF increased in EOS mimicking the proliferative phase compared to early pregnancy. These expressions were confirmed in human full-thickness endometrium, primarily located in endometrial glandular areas. OBJECTIVE 2: To study the role of glycosylation in regulating the vascular remodeling activities of GdA Human first-trimester placentas were obtained with written consent from women undergoing surgical abortion and hysterectomy during the mid-luteal phase, respectively. EVTs and decidual natural killer (dNK) were isolated through immunomagnetic separation using HLAG and CD56 antibodies, respectively. The vascular remodeling activity of trophoblasts was determined by their ability to migrate, invade, and subsequently integrate into the endothelial cell network. EO secretion and GdA in the early gestation phase induced invasion and migration of primary EVT in transwell assays, without affecting EVT proliferation. This induction of invasion was also supported by the upregulation of matrix metalloproteinase activities in the treated EVT. However, the medium did not affect the integration of trophoblasts into endothelial cell networks during EVT-endothelial cell co-culture. None of the hormone treatments of eosinophils (EOS) affected endovascular differentiation of trophoblasts. dNK cells contribute directly to spiral artery remodeling by expressing various vascular regulatory factors. The spent media of GdA-treated NK cells promoted tube formation of human umbilical vein endothelial cells. GdA also had an ERK-activation dependent stimulatory effect on the production of VEGF and IGFBP-1 by the NK cells. This GdA-NK cell interaction was reduced by de-sialylation. GdA interacted with L-selectin, expressed only in the CD16-CD56bright dNK cells, but not in the CD16+CD56dim peripheral blood NK cells. Anti-L-selectin functional blocking antibody suppressed the binding and biological activities of GdA on the NK cells. OBJECTIVE 3: To determine the expression and glycosylation of GdA in pregnancy complicated by PE Endometrial tissues were obtained with written consent from biopsies of preeclampsia (PE) and normotensive (NT) patients who had cesarean sections. The criteria for defining PE during pregnancy include: (1) blood pressure (BP) of 140/90 mm Hg or greater after 20 weeks of gestation, (2) proteinuria of 300 mg/L or greater, and (3) no previous history of hypertensive or renal disease. Human endometrial organoid cultures were established. In general, PE pregnancies have reduced total glycodelin-A (GdA) expression and increased sialylation compared to controls, while GdA in the PE organoid secretome has increased sialylation and impedes angiogenesis and primary extravillous trophoblast (EVT) invasion compared to controls. PE is a gestational disease that affects maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide. Endometrial gland secretions, such as GdA, are detectable in maternal serum. To determine if sialylated GdA would be suitable as a serum biomarker for early detection of PE, maternal serum samples were obtained from pregnant women in their first trimester who were later diagnosed with PE or not at term pregnancy. The total and sialylated forms of GdA were detected by ELISA and ELALBA, respectively. The total protein expression of GdA was significantly decreased in first-trimester PE serum compared to control serum. In terms of sialylated forms, sialylated GdA was significantly upregulated in first-trimester PE serum compared to NT serum. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve indicated the diagnostic ability of sialylated GdA. The area under the curve (AUC) value for sialylated GdA was 0.70, with a sensitivity and specificity of 71.43 and 49.34, respectively. In summary, the results of this study suggest that hormonal regulation of GdA sialylation during the menstrual cycle and early placentation regulates the vascular remodeling activity of GdA. Aberrant hormonal status in PE is associated with alterations in sialylation and defective vascular remodeling activity of GdA, which contributes to the pathophysiology of PE.

17115619.label: Major findings and research outcome
17115619.value: - In early pregnancy, after the embryo implants the uterus, intensive communication begins between the developing placenta and the uterus. Human endometrial epithelium, endometrial gland secretions, decidual immune cells and trophoblasts are highly enriched with glycoconjugates and glycan-binding molecules important for healthy pregnancy. The secretion of endometrial glands plays a crucial role in the communication between the human fetus and mother. In this study, 3D organoid models from normal and preeclampsia patients were established to investigate the biological functions of endometrial gland secretion. (Li J et al., 2022; Li X et al, 2022; Zhong et al, under preparation; Dong et al, 2023). - Hormonal treatments were applied to EO to simulate different menstrual phases. There are no significant differences in EO morphology, quantity, or protein levels, but observed changes in glycosylation, especially sialylation level, of glycodelin-A. Sialyltransferase ST6GalNAc1 expression decreased in early pregnancy EOs, while neuraminidase activity remained unchanged. Sialo-proteomics analysis revealed differentially expressed proteins across hormone-treated groups. Sialylated S100A9, AHSG, and MIF expressions varied across phases, with these proteins primarily located in endometrial glandular areas (Zhong et al, under preparation). - EVT and dNK cells were isolated from first trimester termination of pregnancy tissues. EO secretion and GdA in early gestation induced EVT invasion and migration without affecting proliferation, but didn't affect endovascular differentiation. GdA-treated dNK cells promoted tube formation in endothelial cells and had an ERK-activation dependent stimulatory effect on VEGF and IGFBP-1 production. This interaction was reduced by de-sialylation. GdA interacted with L-selectin in dNK cells, and anti-L-selectin functional blocking antibody suppressed GdA's binding and biological activities on NK cells. Additionally, GdA and placenta-derived exosome also plays a role in mediating the differentiation and functions of decidual macrophages. (Zhong et al, under preparation; Dong et al, 2023; Vijayan et al, 2020; Bai et al, 2021; Bai et al., 2022). - Endometrial tissues from preeclampsia (PE) and normotensive (NT) patients were studied. PE pregnancies have reduced GdA expression, increased GdA and EOS sialylation, and impaired angiogenesis and EVT invasion. First-trimester PE serum showed decreased total GdA and increased sialylated GdA compared to controls. Sialylated GdA had a diagnostic ability with an AUC value of 0.70, sensitivity of 71.43, and specificity of 49.34. Hormonal regulation of GdA sialylation affects vascular remodeling, and alterations in sialylation due to aberrant hormonal status in PE contribute to its pathophysiology. (Zhong et al, under preparation; Dong et al, 2023)

17115619.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17115619.value: This study offers valuable insights into the role of the endometrial gland secretory product, glycodelin-A, in the development of preeclampsia and the regulation of spiral artery remodeling. Following this study, there are several areas that warrant further exploration to deepen our understanding and translate the findings into practical applications. Firstly, additional research could examine the specific mechanisms by which changes in glycosylation lead to trophoblast malfunctions. Delving deeper into the molecular signaling mechanisms contributing to these effects could enhance our understanding by identifying key therapeutic targets for interventions. Secondly, given the crucial role of sialylation of glycodelin-A in regulating placental development, it is reasonable to hypothesize that deficiencies in normal glandular functions may contribute to the pathophysiology of various pregnancy-associated diseases. We have submitted clinical trial applications aimed at determining the expression of total sialylation in endometrial secretions and sialic acid receptor in early maternal serum from women who experience preeclampsia during term pregnancy. Our objective is to measure the serum levels of these identified proteins in pregnant women at different gestational ages and to determine the sialylation levels and characteristics of these proteins in early maternal blood samples from women who develop preeclampsia during term pregnancy.

17115619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17115619.value: Preeclampsia is a pregnancy-related condition that can cause significant health problems for both the mother and baby. It is believed to be caused by issues with blood vessel development in the placenta. A protein called glycodelin-A (GdA) plays a critical role in this process, and its activity depends on a specific chemical modification called glycosylation. This study hypothesized that hormonal regulation of GdA glycosylation during the menstrual cycle and early placentation is crucial for controlling its vascular remodeling activity. Our data provided evidence supporting the idea that the sialylation of endometrial gland secretions plays a role in regulating spiral artery remodeling functions of trophoblast and decidual natural killer cells. This impaired sialylation of the endometrial secretome is associated with inadequate invasion of the spiral arteries and contributes to the development of preeclampsia. The findings of this study offer direct evidence of how glycosylation of endometrial secretions mediates maternal blood vessel remodeling in the uterus. Moreover, this research could lead to the development of tests that enable early detection of preeclampsia by identifying the sialylation of glycodelin-A, which can help healthcare professionals provide better advice and monitoring for high-risk pregnant women, ultimately reducing the risk of complications.

17116819.label: Realisation of objectives
17116819.value: Eight-week-old C57BL/6J male mice followed the consumption of a high-fat diet (HFD, 45% kcal% fat) or low-fat diet (LFD, 10% kcal% fat) ad libitum for 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 weeks. Then, other eight-week-old mice were assigned 4-week (5 days/week) exercise training and different diets (HFD/LFD): sedentary with HFD/LFD (HS/LS); moderate-intensity exercise with HFD (HM) or high-intensity exercise with HFD/LFD (HH/LH). Serum and multiple tissues were harvested and tested at study endpoints. One-way analysis of variance followed by Bonferroni post hoc tests was carried out. The mice assigned to different groups (diet/exercise) consumed similar quantities of food. Body weight and body fat increased over time under HFD, and the HH group significantly attenuated weight gain and fat accumulation. Glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity were impaired after HFD, while HH mice showed significantly better glycemic control. HS mice showed multiple organ changes, i.e. liver fat infiltration and hypertrophied adipocytes, with reduced changes in the HH group. HS mice showed an increased apical coronal distance from the alveolar crest to cementoenamel junction (dAcCej) between the mandibular first (M1) and second (M2) molars, as well as a reduction in bone mineral density (BMD) at M1 and M2 furcation area (realization of Objective 1). HH mice suffered from less dAcCej and appeared with better BMD at M1/M2 furcations and tibia metaphysis (realization of Objective 2). Bone resorption and osteoclastic activity were detectable in the HS jaw and tibia. Mice serum fatty acids and selected obesity-related cytokines/factors were characterized: three saturated fatty acids (palmitic acid, stearic acid, and hexanoic acid), one monounsaturated fatty acid (transgondoic acid), two poly-unsaturated fatty acids (arachidonic acid and DGLA), two adipose endocrines (leptin and FGF21), and two adipose factors (MMP-9 and Dkk-1) were significantly associated with dAcCej or BMD (M1 furcation or tibia). The effects of typical fatty acids on human periodontal ligament stem cells (hPDLSCs) were studied. 0.025 mM palmitic acid appeared to inhibit osteogenic differentiation of PDLSCs, while 0.1 mM oleic acid positively affected osteogenesis (realization of Objective 3).

17116819.label: Major findings and research outcome
17116819.value: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacteria. Increasing studies revealed obesity might be a risk indicator of periodontitis as overactivated adipose tissue may negatively influence bone remodeling and systemic health. The underlying mechanism, however, remains unclear. Exercise training exerts protective effects on obesity-related chronic diseases. Therefore, this study investigates the role of obesity in periodontal health and the impact of exercise on the obesity-associated adverse effects in alveolar bone remodeling and its possible mechanism in an animal model. In summary, disruptive bone homeostasis was observed in an obese mouse model. High-intensity exercise alone attenuated in part the negative systemic impacts of obesity on bone metabolism, including periodontal supporting bones. Major adipose endocrines in serum, like leptin, FGF21, and a few fatty acids, were associated with reduced tibia and dental BMD. Weight control, proper nutrition, and regular exercise may be needed to prevent disruptive bone homeostasis, especially for those who are obese or at risk for periodontitis.

17116819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17116819.value: The study enabled further understanding of the impacts of poor nutrition and improper lifestyle in general on periodontal health in an animal model. The study indeed showed exercise, or an active lifestyle, did significantly nullify the problem of overnutrition, notably the involvement of adipose endocrines (leptin and FGF21) and adipose factors (MMP-9 and Dkk-1). A research report is being drafted for submission at this juncture, as well as the formulation of a follow-up project and grant application focusing on investigating the mechanisms of the positive impacts of exercise on adipose endocrines and bone metabolism/turn over and, hence, better resistance against host-mediated alveolar bone resorption due to periodontal inflammation or the improved osteoimmunology.

17116819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17116819.value: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacteria. Increasing studies revealed obesity might be a risk indicator of periodontitis as overactivated fat tissue may negatively influence bone remodeling and systemic health. Disruptive bone turnover was observed in an obese mouse model. High-intensity exercise alone attenuated in part the negative impacts of obesity on bones, limbs, and jaw. Some adipose endocrines or factors appeared to play critical roles in the process. Further studies are underway to pursue and clarify the related mechanism(s).

17117019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17117019.value: Hepatocellular carcinoma is the major form of liver malignancy worldwide. Recent advances in next generation sequencing has provided us a revolutionary way to understand the mutational landscape of human HCC. HCC is mainly affected by loss-of-function mutations in tumor suppressor genes which includes TP53, AXIN, ARID1A and TSC1/2. Unlike other cancers, HCC lacks representative activating mutations in oncogenes. So far, β-catenin and TERT promoter mutations have been identified as oncogenic mutational events in HCC patients but they are regarded as non-druggable targets. Due to the highly heterogeneous nature of HCC plus the different etiological background of the patient samples being recruited among different studies, the identification of novel recurrent mutant genes in HCC is much more challenging than expected. RPS6KA3 encodes for p90 ribosomal S6 kinase 2 (p90RSK2 or RSK2), which functions as a direct downstream protein kinase of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK). RSK2 has dominantly been proposed to play oncogenic role in a number of human cancers in relation to the MAPK signaling pathway. However, the role of RSK2 in liver cancer is likely to be unique when compared to the other cancers. Among the four RSK and two RSK-like (MSK) isoforms, RSK2 is the dominantly expressed isoform in the non-tumorous human liver. Of note, RSK2 mutation was observed in a subset of liver cancers and liver cancer is among the top-ranking cancer being affected by RSK2 mutation. Multiple sequencing cohorts have identified recurrent RSK2 mutations in HCC clinical samples, irrespective of the etiological background. However, there is no hotspot mutation identified in RSK2. More interesting, the RSK2 mutations identified are likely to be inactivating mutations instead of activating mutations. This observation actually challenges our current view of RSK2 functioning as an oncogene in various human cancers. However, the functional role, the underlying biological processes and the significance of RSK2 mutations in HCC has never been followed up. Based on our preliminary observations, we hypothesize that loss-of-function mutation of RSK2 may support HCC development through the upregulation of MAPK signaling, and activate the downstream biological processes contributing to the increased aggressiveness of HCC. In this proposal, we aim to uncover the novel functional roles of RSK2 mutation in HCC including (1)the mechanism on how RSK2 mutation regulates MAPK signaling in liver cancer; (2)the significance of RSK2 mutation in modulating the cholesterol biosynthesis in HCC and (3)the potential role of RSK2 mutation in supporting cancer stemness in HCC.

17117019.label: Realisation of objectives
17117019.value: Objective 1. By whole-exome and targeted DNA sequencing analyses, RSK2 mutations were identified in 6.3% (7/111) of the HBV-associated HCC patients. RSK2 mutations are likely to be loss-of-function in nature as more than half of them are nonsense and INDEL mutations. To identify relevant models for characterizing the role of RSK2 mutation in HCC, its mutational status was first examined in a panel of four HCC cell lines by RNA-sequencing. Specifically, Hep3B, an HBV-associated HCC cell line was found to carry the intrinsic RSK2 mutation, with a specific truncation happening at the Exon10 in the RSK2 gene as indicated by the absence of the RNA read beyond the Exon10. The result was confirmed by complementary PCR analysis and Western blotting. We engineered a bicistronic lentiviral-based RSK2 overexpressing system which allows us to rescue the RSK2 expression in Hep3B cells. As RSK2 is reported to be a downstream kinase of MAPK, we examined how the restoration of RSK2 in Hep3B cells could affect the activity of MAPK signaling. For instance, RSK2-rescued Hep3B cells showed a reduction in the phospho-c-Raf, phospho-MEK, and phospho-ERK1/2 levels but not their total protein levels, suggesting the potential role of RSK2 played in exerting negative feedback on MAPK signaling. In contrast, expression of the RSK2 mutants in Hep3B cells are failed or significantly less efficient in suppressing MAPK signaling. The loss-of-function RSK2 mutations in HCC thus serve as a means to relieve this inhibition and ensure the MAPK signaling is always on in supporting the pro-oncogenic functions in HCC cells. Importantly, we delineated the underlying molecular mechanism behind RSK2-driven negative feedback on MAPK signaling. By subjecting the control (RSK2 mutant) and RSK2-rescued Hep3B cells to different dosages of sorafenib treatment in vitro, we found that RSK2 mutant cells, with higher MAPK activity, are more sensitive to sorafenib treatment and more cells were killed at a lower concentration of Sorafenib as compared to the RSK2 mutant cells. Similarly, the tumor xenografts derived from an RSK2-low HCC cell line (with high MAPK activity) were also found significantly suppressed by Sorafenib but the RSK2-overexpressed control (with significantly lower MAPK activity) was comparatively less sensitive to Sorafenib. Taken together, our results support and lead us to propose a model of RSK2-mediated SOS1/2-Ras-dependent negative feedback loop on MAPK signaling. A molecular subset of HCC tumors could bypass the negative feedback loop by gaining RSK2 loss-of-function mutations in exchange for sustained MAPK activity. Furthermore, RSK2 mutations may function as a potential genetic marker to reflect the high MAPK activity in HCC tumors, which are more prone to Sorafenib treatment. Objective 2. To understand the underlying biological processes associated with RSK2-mutation, global differentially expressed genes between the control (RSK2 mutant) and RSK2-rescued Hep3B cells were identified by RNA-seq analysis and were then subjected to pathway enrichment analysis. Employment of two different software packages consistently suggested the significant downregulation of the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway-related genes in the RSK2-rescued Hep3B cells, which indicate the potential functional association of RSK2 mutation in supporting the cholesterol metabolism in HCC cells. By qPCR, we verified the downregulation of a panel of signature cholesterol pathway genes in RSK2-rescued Hep3B cells as compared to the control. Conversely, the upregulation of these genes could be detected in CRISPR/Cas9-mediated RSK2 knockout Huh7 cells, an HCC cell line with wildtype RSK2, and with increased MAPK signaling activation upon RSK2 being knocked out. Upregulation of several committed step enzymes in the cholesterol biosynthesis could also be detected in an immortalized normal liver cell line with RSK2 being knocked out. We then further questioned whether the downregulation of the enzymes responsible for the cholesterol biosynthesis would eventually lead to changes in the intracellular cholesterol metabolism. Consistently, results from both Filipin staining and mass spectrometry analysis have shown the significant downregulation of the intracellular cholesterol in the RSK2-rescued Hep3B cells as compared to the control cells. To further establish the linkage between MAPK signaling and cholesterol biosynthesis, parental Hep3B cells were challenged with U0126, a MEK-specific inhibitor followed by the examination of the signature cholesterol pathway gene expression by qPCR. Interestingly, U0126 treatment could induce a significant upregulation of SOS1, suggesting that Hep3B cells exhibit a strong compensatory mechanism upon MAPK blockade. Also, SOS1 upregulation was coupled with the upregulation of the cholesterol pathway genes. On the other hand, cholesterol biosynthesis gene expression was found to be significantly suppressed by rapamycin, an mTOR-specific inhibitor which recapitulates the effects caused by RSK2-rescue. These experiments further provide us molecular insight into the modulation of cholesterol biosynthesis by MAPK signaling in an mTOR-dependent manner in HCC. By comparing the RNA-seq data of the RSK2 WT- or DA-expressing Hep3B cells with the control cells, global differentially expressed genes with ± 1.5-fold changes were identified and subjected to pathway enrichment analyses. Interestingly, RSK2 WT- and DA-expressing cells consistently showed a global downregulation of genes encoding key metabolic enzymes in cholesterol biosynthesis. Then we confirmed the downregulation of the expression of HMG-CoA synthase (HMGCS1), the rate-limiting enzyme HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR), and the genes in the mevalonate pathway of cholesterol biosynthesis. The downregulation of cholesterol biosynthesis in RSK2 WT and DA cells was further supported by reduced intensity of intracellular cholesterol staining by Filipin complex, as well as the lower intracellular cholesterol levels detected by mass spectrometry. In contrast, RSK2 knockout in MIHA and Huh7 cells led to upregulated expression of a number of cholesterol biosynthesis genes. Objective 3. To examine whether RSK2 mutations might serve as a marker to stratify HCCs and define a molecular subgroup of patients, the co-occurrence of RSK2 mutations and mutations of HCC driver genes was examined in our exome-seq and targeted DNA-seq data. Interestingly, RSK2 and TSC2 mutations were almost mutually exclusive, while RSK2 mutations showed very limited co-occurrence with TSC1, CTNNB1, ARID1A and AXIN1 mutations. Even for the high mutation rate of TP53 in HCC, only less than half of the RSK2 mutant cases concurrently carried TP53 mutations. RSK2 mutations may characterize a new molecular subgroup of HCC. To explore the clinical significance of this subgroup, RSK2 mutations were subjected to clinicopathological correlation. By stratifying the HCC tumors into 4 distinct molecular subgroups: 1) RSK2 mutations; 2) TSC1/2 mutations; 3) known HCC driver mutations and 4) others, we found that the presence of either RSK2 or TSC1/2 mutations was significantly associated with the presence of venous invasion (p=0.036; ANOVA). Also, RSK2 or TSC1/2 mutations tended to be associated with larger tumor size (p=0.055; ANOVA) and more advanced tumor stage (p=0.072; ANOVA). Since both RSK2 and TSC1/2 are Ras/mTOR signaling pathway-related genes, the collection of these 2 groups of patients, namely the subgroup with novel Ras/mTOR mutations, was found to be significantly associated with more aggressive tumor behavior, including larger tumor size (p=0.027; ANOVA), presence of venous invasion (p=0.017; ANOVA) and more advanced tumor stage (p=0.049; ANOVA). Functionally, RSK2-rescued Hep3B cells showed significantly reduced proliferative and migratory abilities, as well as a lower tumor incidence rate in a subcutaneous xenograft model in nude mice, whereas the somatic RSK2 mutants exhibited a reduced suppressive effect on Hep3B cell migration. Interestingly, upon stable expression of RSK2 WT, the RSK2-low expressing 97L cells formed significantly smaller tumors in a subcutaneous xenograft model.

17117019.label: Major findings and research outcome
17117019.value: Mutational profiling of patient tumors has suggested that hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) development is mainly driven by loss-of-function mutations in tumor suppressor genes. p90 ribosomal S6 kinase 2 (RSK2) functions as a direct downstream kinase of ERK1/2 and elevated RSK2 expression has been reported to support oncogenic functions in some cancers. We investigated if RSK2 was also dysregulated by inactivating mutations in cancers including HCC. To this end, we performed exome sequencing and targeted DNA sequencing on HBV-associated HCCs to examine recurrent RSK2 mutations. The functional significance and mechanistic consequences of RSK2 mutations were examined in natural RSK2-null HCC cells, and RSK2-knockout HCC cells. The potential downstream pathways underlying RSK2 mutations were investigated by RNA sequencing, qRT-PCR and mass spectrometry. We detected recurrent somatic RSK2 mutations at a rate of 6.3% in our HCC cohorts and revealed that, among many cancer types, HCC was the cancer most commonly harboring RSK2 mutations. The RSK2 mutations were inactivating and associated with a more aggressive tumor phenotype. We found that, functionally, restoring RSK2 expression in natural RSK2-null HBV-positive Hep3B cells suppressed proliferation and migration in vitro and tumorigenicity in vivo. Mechanistically, RSK2-inactivating mutations attenuated a SOS1/2-dependent negative feedback loop, leading to the activation of MAPK signaling. Of note, this RSK2 mutation-mediated MAPK upregulation rendered HCC cells more sensitive to sorafenib, a first-line multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced HCC. Furthermore, such activation of MAPK signaling enhanced cholesterol biosynthesis-related gene expression in HCC cells. Taken, together, our findings reveal the mechanistic and functional significance of RSK2-inactivating mutations in HCC. These inactivating mutations may serve as an alternative route to activate MAPK signaling and cholesterol metabolism in HCC.

17117019.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17117019.value: Our RNA-seq analysis identified significant downregulation of the expression of enzymes involved in cholesterol biosynthesis in RSK2-rescued Hep3B cells. Cholesterol biosynthesis is positively controlled by SREBP2, a transcription factor that drives the expression of cholesterol biosynthesis genes. SREBP2 activity has been reported to be potentially regulated by Akt/mTOR and Ras/MAPK signaling, and the specific SREBP regulator SCAP. In liver cancer, p53 loss-induced HCC tumorigenesis has recently been shown to be dependent on the activation of the mevalonate pathway through the maturation of SREBP2. Given that p53 and RSK2 mutations are recurrently mutated in patients with HCC, they may potentially serve as genetic markers in reflecting the activation status of the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway. Notably, emerging evidence has suggested that serum cholesterol could also function as a tumor-suppressive mediator in HCC. Similarly, cholesterol supplementation to HCC cells could suppress HCC-associated phenotypes by inhibiting SCAP-mediated de novo synthesis of fatty acid or by disrupting the assembly of a protein complex involved in promoting HCC cell invasion and metastasis. However, whether the biological consequence of increased cholesterol biosynthesis inside the HCC cells is directly equivalent to the context of increased systemic cholesterol levels would be an interesting area for future research.

17117019.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17117019.value: In this study, we identified and functionally characterized RSK2-inactivating mutations in human hepatocellular carcinoma and demonstrated their association with aggressive tumor behavior. Mutations in RSK2 drive signaling pathways with known oncogenic potential, leading to enhanced cholesterol biosynthesis and potentially sensitizing tumors to sorafenib treatment.

17117519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17117519.value: 肝細胞癌（HCC）是一種侵襲性腫瘤，出現轉移是其發展到後期的一個標誌。在約一半有肝外轉移的病人中，肺是最常見的轉移灶。在腫瘤轉移的過程中，為傳播的肝癌細胞在遠端器官建立一個支持的微環境是其遷移，存活和生長所必不可缺的。癌細胞和微環境之間的相互交流在肝癌發展和轉移中起重要作用。近來，外泌體是細胞之間交流的重要渠道逐漸為大眾所關注。 為了研究外泌體在肝癌中的作用，我們從侵襲性肝癌細胞中分離外泌體來研究其功能性。侵襲性外泌體可以增強細胞的遷移和侵襲性。通過動物實驗發現侵襲性外泌體促進了肝癌的形成，增加了肺轉移的機率，協助肝癌細胞在肺的存活以及增強了肺血管的通透性。外泌體蛋白質譜分析確認了nidogen1（NID1）在侵襲性外泌體的功能裡起關鍵作用。雖然NID1被報導在多種癌症出現，其在外泌體中的功能從未被研究。我們的研究顯示抑制外泌體NID1（exo-NID1）顯著減低了侵襲性外泌體的生物活性。侵襲性外泌體促進肺成纖維細胞的生長提示侵襲性外泌體誘導的成纖維細胞的激活參與了轉移前微環境的建立。外泌體處理後的肺成纖維細胞分泌腫瘤壞死因子受體1（TNFR1）顯著加強了癌細胞的活動性。並且exo-NID1的含量和肝癌細胞株的侵襲性顯著相關。更令人鼓舞的是，在肝癌晚期病人循環外泌體的NID1含量要高於早期病人。 綜上所述，根據前期研究結果我們假設外泌體NID1通過誘導肺成纖維細胞分泌TNFR1增強HCC細胞的侵襲性及幫助建立幫助轉移的微環境來促進腫瘤肝外轉移。本課題的主旨是1）闡明外泌體NID1在HCC發展和轉移中的作用；2）剖析外泌體NID1在肺調節轉移前微環境建立中的功能；3）評價外泌體NID1和血清TNFR1作為臨床診斷HCC的生物標記及通過阻斷外泌體信號通路作為HCC的治療手段。我們的研究將釐清外泌體分泌的NID1如何誘導HCC的轉移。本研究的順利完成還將揭示外泌體蛋白的表達譜和外泌體介導信號通路的臨床意義。

17117519.label: Realisation of objectives
17117519.value: We have used the term “extracellular vesicles” in place of “exosomes” in this report and related publication. 1. To characterize the effect of exo-NID1 in HCC tumorigenesis and metastasis To determine the role of NID1 in HCC, NID1 expression was knocked down in MHCC97L cells and engineered to be expressed in extracellular vesicles (EVs) from Hep3B and HLE cells using an expression vector with an EV targeting signal (XP-NID1). Knockdown of NID1 resulted in diminished ability of the tumor cells to grow, migrate and invade. Conversely, overexpression of EV-NID1 showed opposing effects. Treatment with EVs from nontarget control cells (CTL-KD-EVs) enhanced the migration and invasiveness of naïve cells. However, this enhancement was abolished in cells treated with NID1-KD-EV. XP-NID1-EVs displayed a more potent effect on promoting cell motility and invasion than did EVs derived from vector control cells (XPack-EVs). Consistent with the effect of parental MHCC97L-EVs, CTL-KD-EVs demonstrated the positive effect on liver tumor formation and distant metastasis in the EV treatment model. The augmented metastasis to the lungs was not observed in mice injected with NID1-KD-EVs. These functional characterizations provide evidence about the imperative activity of EV-NID1 in tumor growth and metastasis. 2. To characterize the role of exo-NID1 in the modulation of tumor microenvironment in lung tissues The role of EV-NID1 in modulating the microenvironment in lungs was examined. MHCC97L CTL-KD-EVs enhanced vascular permeability when compared to untreated mice. However, the enhancing effect was not observed in mice injected with NID1-KD-EVs. In addition, NID1 knockdown cells resulted in the release of EVs that abolished the promotion of tube-like structure formation of HUVECs and microvessel formation in the Matrigel plug angiogenesis assay, while XP-NID1-EVs promoted the formation of tube-like structures in endothelial cells. Compared to cells injected with PBS, mice injected with p53-/-; Myc hepatoblasts and CTL-KD-EVs showed a profound increase in the colonization of hepatoblasts to the lungs, whereas the colonization of hepatoblasts in the lungs was largely diminished in mice injected with NID1-KD-EVs. Conversely, in mice injected with XP-NID1-EVs, augmented colonization of hepatoblasts in the lungs was observed. Taken together, these findings suggest the role of EV-NID1 in destabilizing the vascular architecture and promoting angiogenesis in the lung, thereby facilitating tumor cell colonization. In addition, EV-NID1 also activated fibroblasts, which secreted tumor necrosis factor receptor 1 (TNFR1), facilitated lung colonization of tumor cells and augmented HCC cell growth and motility. 3. To evaluate the clinical applications of exo-NID1 and serum TNFR1 as biomarker of HCC and the blockage of exosomal signaling as a therapeutic strategy The circulating EVs obtained from non-HCC control subjects and HCC patients with early and late stage disease were collected for the analysis of NID1 level. Compared to control subjects, early stage patients showed a significantly higher overall level of EV-NID1. Late stage patients displayed an even higher EV-NID1 level than early stage patients. Serum TNFR1 showed concomitant upregulation with the HCC stages, and TNFR1 level increased progressively from the control group to the early stage group and late stage group. The level of EV-NID1 was well correlated with serum TNFR1 level. Our findings showed that sTNFR1 was crucial to HCC metastasis; therefore, neutralization of serum TNFR1 could potentially block the communication between cancer cells and the target tissue microenvironment, leading to the suppression of metastasis. The therapeutic effect of the anti-TNFR1 antibody was tested in mice implanted with metastatic MHCC97L cells in the liver. Our findings provide preclinical evidence supporting the efficient blockage of oncogenic signaling mediated by HCC EVs using an anti-TNRF1 antibody.
