17504319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17504319.value: A growing body of research analyzes the role of network structures in transmitting and amplifying idiosyncratic shocks to individual nodes in the network; examples include trade networks (Du et al. 2018), sectoral networks (Acemoglu et al., 2010), production networks (Gabaix, 2011), interbank networks (Denbee et al.,2018), and margin-holdings networks (Bian et al.2018). While this line of research generally finds that networks play a vital role in the propagation of idiosyncratic shocks, it remains silent on an arguably more fundamental issue: the formation and evolution of the network. What are the determinants of connections among firms/individuals? Why are some nodes in the network more central than others? What are the economic consequences if the network is formed under a different mechanism? This project addresses these issues by exploiting a unique market in China – guaranteed bank loans. In contrast to conventional bank loans (e.g., secured loans), in a guaranteed loan agreement, a third party promises to repay the loan if the borrower defaults. Each firm can act both as a guarantor for others and a guarantee backed by others. Consequently, firms are linked to each other through guaranteed loans. Using proprietary data of all guaranteed bank loans from 2007 to 2013 compiled by the People’s Bank of China, we are able to map out this entire network of guaranteed loans. Moreover, since our data contain granular information about each loan contract (e.g., loan performance, geographic and business of all guarantees and guarantors), we can study the causes and consequences of the guaranteed-loan network. The development of the guaranteed-loan market in China are likely the results of information asymmetry. While banks, particularly state-owned banks, may not have the expertise to analyze private firms, the guarantor (who is likely to have business links with the guarantee) can provide useful screening services. Moreover, since the guarantor is liable for the loan in case the borrower defaults, the guarantor bears the entire credit risk, and hence has all the incentives to screen the borrower. Guided by theory (e.g., Acemoglu et al., 2012), we plan to exploit cross-region, as well as time-series, variation in the data to analyze how idiosyncratic shocks are transmitted and amplified in the network. Moreover, we use the 2008 Sichuan Earthquake (the most devastating natural disaster in China in the past 20 years) to better identify the causal channel through which idiosyncratic shocks are transmitted to other firms in the guaranteed-loan network. 目前有关网络的研究在学术界越来越得到关注。目前的研究主要关注网络结构如何把个体风险扩大以及传到整个网络。相关研究包括但不限于：贸易网络（Du et al.，2018），经济部门网络（Acemoglu et al.，2010），产品市场网络（Gabaix，2011），银行间网络（Denbee et al.，2018），以及股票杠杆网络（Bian et al.，2018）。尽管已有文献发现网络对于风险的传导起到了重要的作用，但是尚无文献研究一个更为深层次的问题：网络是如何形成以及演化。具体而言，文献还不是很清楚什么决定了公司或个体之间的关联？为什么一些网络节点比其他节点更中心化？不同的网络形成机制是否会带来不同的经济后果？ 本研究项目以中国担保贷款市场这一独特的实证研究情景来回答上述问题。担保贷款相对于传统银行贷款的一个重要特征是，担保贷款违约时将由第三方（担保方）代为偿还。在担保贷款市场上，一家公司既可以作为一个担保贷款的担保方也可以同时作为另一个担保贷款的被担保方（借款方）。因此，不同的公司就可以通过相关的担保贷款形成网络上的关联。通过来自中国人民银行的2007-2013年间所有担保贷款的独特数据，我们可以构建出完整的担保贷款网络。此外，我们的数据包含了每一笔担保贷款各方面的具体信息（例如，贷款后续清偿状况，担保方和被担保方的地理位置、财务状况等），我们可以用这些信息来研究担保贷款网络的形成原因和经济后果。 信息不对称可能是中国担保贷款市场的发展的重要原因。作为传统贷款审核机构的银行（尤其是国有银行），不一定拥有足够的“软信息”去分析申请贷款的民营企业。而担保贷款中的担保方，由于通常与借款方企业有业务往来，则能够起到有效的贷款审核作用。更重要的是，由于担保方在贷款发生违约时有义务代为偿还，他们承担了担保贷款全部的信用风险，因此更有动力去审核借款方。 在相关理论研究（例如，Acemoglu et al.，2012）的指导下，我们计划利用担保贷款数据中截面上与时间上的变化，来分析企业特质风险如何在担保网络中传导并加剧。此外，我们将采用2008年汶川地震（中国近20年来最为严重的自然灾害）作为外生冲击，在因果关系层面去识别特质风险是否真正地通过担保网络进行传导。

17504319.label: Realisation of objectives
17504319.value: In this report, I summarize the outcome of the project and how I achieved the outcome of this project. Overall, this project aims to study the network in the guaranteed loan market in China and its implications. I also extend the study to the US financial market and study how information transmits in the economic networks of firms. In the proposal, I have four objectives (see Part. 5.2). Based on Objectives (1), (2), and (3), I have finished one research paper titled “Endogenous Formation of Guaranteed Loan Networks”. Based on Objective (4), I have finished one research paper titled “A frog in every pan: Information discreteness and the lead-lag returns puzzle.” The first paper is coauthored with Jian Feng (PhD. student from the University of Hong Kong), Xinhai Liu (from Beijing Credit Society), and Prof. Dong Lou (from London School of Economics), and Prof. Kathy Yuan (from London School of Economics). The second paper is coauthored with from Prof. Charles M.C. Lee (from the University of Washington), Prof. Yang Song (from the University of Washington), and Hong Xiang (who is a previous PhD. student from the University of Hong Kong, and now is an Assistant Professor of the Hong Kong Polytechnic University). Meanwhile, the second paper is published in the Journal of Financial Economics 2022. I provide details of how I achieved the proposal's objectives in these two papers. In the paper titled “Endogenous Formation of Guaranteed Loan Networks”, I exactly followed the stated Objectives (1)-(3) and study the guaranteed loan networks in China. Specifically, I and my coauthors mainly use the China guaranteed loan data which covers 902.8 thousand guarantee loans and involves 164.6 unique firm entities as borrowers or guarantors. The sample period is from October 2006 to April 2012. For each guaranteed loan, we track its performance and the characteristics of the borrower and its guarantors. We also use two supplementary data: (1) RESSET Industrial Enterprise Database; (2) the China Business Registration Information Database. These two data can provide information on industry characteristics at the city level and provide information about more than 20 million business entities. Based on these data, we first describe the distribution of guaranteed loans across provinces and industries (see Figures 1- 2). We find that three provinces, Zhejiang (14%), Guangdong (12%) and Jiangsu (12%) take the largest share of firms. We also find that 10 major industries from our sample (manufacturing, accommodation & catering, construction, wholesale, energy, real estate, business service, utility, agriculture-forestry-husbandry-fishery, and mining) account for 97% of firms in the guaranteed network. Nearly half of the firms (49%) belong to the manufacturing industry. We further follow the network literature and detect network structures from the guaranteed relationships among firms. We focus on two common network structures-core-peripherals and circle-and we characterize the geographic distribution of these structures (se Figure 3). We find that Zhejiang has the largest number of loans and circle member members and core peripherals are more popular in inland provinces. These descriptions are novel to literature and achieve Objective (1). After we characterize the guaranteed loan network, we move to study what determines the network formation (objective (2)). Inspired by the successful example of the Grameen Bank, we argue that information advantage and local industry characteristics are the key determinants to the network formation. Specifically, we conjecture and empirically find that firms in the same city/industry are more likely to form connections and build core-peripherals or circles (see Table 2 and Online Appendix Table A.2). We further examine what drives firms to form circle and core-peripherals and find that local industry concentration is the key determinant. That is, local industry with large leader(s) are more likely to have core-peripherals and have less likely to have guarantee circles (see Table 3 and Online Appendix Table A.3). We also acknowledge the endogenous issues and use the historical local industry structure as the key independent variable to show that the industry structure indeed determines the guaranteed loan networks. This work achieves Objective (2). We further take advantage of our granular data and study the implications of network for the loan default risk. We are particularly interested in comparing the implications of circle and core-peripherals networks on loan defaults. We find that loans in both circle and core-peripherals networks have better performance (see Tables 4-6 and Online Appendix Tables A.4-A.6), which is consistent with monitoring and selection in endogenous network formation. What is perhaps surprising is that the larger the core-peripheral structure (i.e., more peripherals attached to the same core), the better the loan performance of the peripheral firms. These results are consistent with information advantage in the core-peripherals as the central guarantors have better information advantage when they have contacts with other firms. But the results on the circle network suggest that a long circle lengthen can harm monitoring effects in guaranteed loans. We also find that circle members are similar in terms of firm size and creditworthiness (Tables 7-9). This is consistent with the framework of positive assortative mating (Becker, 1991; Ghatak, 1999); that is, the more credit-worthy firms form a group to guarantee each others’ loans and so do the less credit-worthy firms. Moreover, members of shorter circles have better loan performance than members of longer circles. Finally, circle members in local areas with a core-peripheral structure have worse loan performance, consistent with the view that the core attracts better firms in the city-industry (so leave worse firms to form circles). Overall, the work in Tables 4-9 and Online Appendix A.4-A.6 achieves Objective (3). The results in the paper titled “Endogenous Formation of Guaranteed Loan Networks” uncovers that economic links among firms have important information in forecasting firm fundamentals. We extend the study and study whether and how information in various economic networks helps forecast stock returns in the US market. The economic network can include customer-supplier network, industry network, geographic network, and so on (Objective (4)). I have finished one research paper titled “A frog in every pan: Information discreteness and the lead-lag returns puzzle.” In this paper, we first show that stock returns from lead firms (in the economic network of customer-supplier, industry network, geographic network, and shared-analyst-coverage network) indeed can help forecast follower firms’ stock returns, which suggests that there exists slow information transmission along the economic networks. We push further and attempt to understand what drives such a slow information transmission. Consistent with the “frog in the pan” (FIP) momentum eﬀect (i.e., a cognitive bias), we find that investors consistently underreact to information from lead ﬁrms that arrives continuously, while information with the same cumulative returns arriving in discrete amounts is quickly absorbed into price. Overall, these results suggest that the “frog in the pan” (FIP) momentum eﬀect is pervasive in co-momentum settings, suggesting that information discreteness (ID) serves as a cognitive trigger that reduces investor inattention and improves inter-ﬁrm news transmission. The work from this paper achieves Objective (4). In summary, in this project, I study the network in the guaranteed loan market in China and its implications. I also extend the study to the US financial market and study how information transmits in the economic networks of firms. The works from the two papers mentioned above have achieved Objectives (1)-(4).

17504319.label: Major findings and research outcome
17504319.value: Based on Objectives (1), (2), and (3), I have finished one research paper titled “Endogenous Formation of Guaranteed Loan Networks” (see attached file in Part C). This paper is coauthored with Jian Feng (PhD. student from the University of Hong Kong), Xinhai Liu (from Beijing Credit Society), and Prof. Dong Lou (from London School of Economics), and Prof. Kathy Yuan (from London School of Economics). We presented this paper at London School of Economics, Renmin University, the University of Hong Kong, Macquarie University. In this paper, we study the endogenous formation of the guaranteed-loan network and its impact on firm outcomes. First, there have emerged two types of network structures: core-peripherals and circles, and the local industry concentration determine which network structure occurs. The core and its peripherals are vastly different from each other; moreover, the larger the core-peripheral structure, the better the loan performance of the peripheral firms. In contrast, circle members are similar to each other, consistent with a framework of positive assortative mating; furthermore, the shorter the circle, the better the loan performance of circle members. Finally, circle members in local areas with an existing core-peripheral structure have worse loan performance. Based on Objective (4), I have finished one research paper titled “A frog in every pan: Information discreteness and the lead-lag returns puzzle” (see the attached file about the working paper version in Part C). This paper is coauthored with Prof. Charles M.C. Lee (from the University of Washington), Prof. Yang Song (from the University of Washington), and Hong Xiang (from the Hong Kong Polytechnic University). We presented this paper at Baruch College, Tsinghua SEM, Morgan Stanley Quantitative Research Colloquium, 2020 Chinese Finance Annual Meeting, and the Wolfe Research Global Quantitative and Macro Investment Conference for helpful comments.. Meanwhile, the second paper is published in the Journal of Financial Economics 2022 (see Part C for details). In this paper, we study information transmission among economically-linked firms, and we find that investors consistently underreact to information from lead frms that arrives continuously, while information with the same cumulative returns arriving in discrete amounts is quickly absorbed into price. Our results suggest that the "frog in the pan" effect is pervasive in network settings, suggesting that information discreteness (ID) serves as a cognitive trigger that reduces investor inattention and improves inter-firm news transmission.

17504319.value: As I have published the paper titled “A frog in every pan: Information discreteness and the lead-lag returns puzzle” at the Journal of Financial Economics, I will focus on the first paper (titled “Endogenous Formation of Guaranteed Loan Networks”). The further development of this research has two steps. First, while we have collected some comments/suggestions from various seminars, we plan to present this paper at academic conferences, which can help increase the visibility and impact of this paper. We also can have more suggestions from the conferences to improve this paper. After that, we aim to submit our paper to top economics/finance journals. So far, we submit this paper to many conferences, including CUHK-RAPS Conference on Asset Pricing and Investment, UT Dallas 2023 Fall Finance Conference, 36th Australasian Finance and Banking Conference. In the second step, we aim to develop this project further and can potentially write another research paper. Specifically, we plan to understand what determines the circle length and its implications for bank loan default contagions. We have some preliminary results.For example, we find that banks will take aggressive actions to prevent bank defaults by reducing credit lines to banks on the circle network.

17504319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17504319.value: The works from this project are important for both academics and practice. In fact, enabling credit access by small and medium enterprises (SMEs), especially in developing countries, has been for decades at the forefront of intense regulatory and political debates. In absence of a sound and comprehensive credit rating system for SMEs, banks in developing countries have limited ability and resources to screen credit-worthy SMEs from unworthy ones and to monitor the ones that actually receive credit. Banks’ general lack of information on SMEs have significantly curtailed credit access by SMEs, and consequently their development. To tackle these challenges, Chinese banks followed the successful example of the group-lending program pioneered by the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh in the 1980s and implemented guaranteed loans. My first paper can help characterize the economic links among guaranteed loans network and shed light on the formation determinants and the economic implications of different guaranteed loan networks. The information content inspires the second paper in economic links and studies whether and how information in various economic networks helps forecast stock returns in the US market. The work in this paper can help us understand what drives information transmission along various economic networks.

17504619.label: Project Objectives
17504619.value: We first solve the competitive bidding equilibrium in the refinancing stage with asymmetrically informed creditor and noisy public signals, following a standard first-price common-value auction with asymmetric information among bidders. Next, we solve the borrower's optimal technology choice, conditional on the expected future debt repayment, which depends on the bidding outcome conditional on the state and realized signals. We then plan to analyze how the change of accounting information precision affects the borrower's risk shifting incentive. We expect to find that accounting information precision might have a nontrivial effect on the risk-shifting incentive. We also plan to provide additional analysis about how the change of (public) information precision affects the firm's expected payoff, expected debt repayment, and the borrower's creditor switching decision. We may also show some empirical supports to our model.

17504619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17504619.value: We examine the role of public information quality on the borrower's risk-shifting incentive in the presence of asymmetrically informed creditors. In the model, a firm seeks financing the initial stage of a project with uncertain states through the credit market. The initial creditor gains private information about the firm's realized state, and competes with the outside creditor for refinancing the second stage of the project, the return of which depends on the technology chosen by the firm to implement the project. In the bad state, multiple technologies are available, but the choice is not verifiable or contractible. The borrower has incentive to choose a more risky technology to implement the project when the realized state is bad, particularly when the informed creditor observes the true state and requests a high debt repayment. Competition from the outside creditor may lower the expected debt repayment, thus alleviating the risk-shifting incentive of the borrower. We examine how public accounting information can play a role in the competitive bidding game, and affect the risk-shifting incentive of the borrower. We also investigate the impacts of accounting information quality on the borrower's expected payoff, the cost of debt, and the creditor switching decision, accounting for the endogenous risk-shifting incentive of the borrower. 我们研究当企业债权人之间存在信息不对称时，公开信息质量对借款人风险转移的影响。在模型中，公司需要通过借款为有风险的项目进行初始阶段融资。初始债权人在项目开始后，能观察到关于项目状态的信息，之后与外部债权人竞争项目第二阶段的再融资，其回报取决于公司为实施项目所选择的技术。在项目预期不好的情况下，公司可以选择不同技术来执行该项目，但是技术选择是不可验证的。借款人有动机选择一种风险更大的技术来实施项目实现时状态较差，特别是当债权人观察真实状态，并要求高负债偿还时。来自外部债权人的竞争可以降低预期的债务偿还，从而减轻风险转移的动机。我们将考察公共会计信息在竞价博弈中发挥的作用，并如何影响风险转移的动机。考虑到借款人相应的风险选择，会计信息质量会影响借款人的预期收益、债务成本和债权人转换决定。

17504619.label: Major findings and research outcome
17504619.value: Excessive risk-taking is a first-order consideration in the context of debt contracting. Debt financing induces borrowers to take on risky projects, especially if the firm’s current economic condition is weak. This is known as the risk shifting (or asset substitution) problem. If the only source of borrower-specific information accessible to the competing lenders is public accounting data, our paper shows that the risk-shifting incentive for weak borrowers will always be exacerbated if accounting information becomes more precise. In practice, banks often lend repeatedly to the same borrower. As a result of past loan monitoring, these banks gain privileged information, which they can use in the pricing of follow-on loans. To avoid lock-in and limit the rent extracted by relationship lenders, borrowers often invite competition among multiple lenders for new loans. Anticipating their information disadvantage, outside lenders will price-protect by bidding more cautiously for the loan terms. As a result, the expected face value of debt goes up, as compared with a setting where all potential lenders have access only to public information. Hence, the borrower again takes on excessive risks. Publicly available accounting information levels the playing field between “inside” (relationship) lenders and outside lenders. We show that if the main concern is risk-shifting on the part of the borrower, then regulations that increase the precision of accounting reports can improve or harm investment efficiency, depending on the beliefs held by the market participants about the borrower’s condition at the outset. In times where these beliefs lean towards pessimism, increasing the precision of accounting information tends to mitigate the risk-shifting problem for weak borrowers, at the margin; optimistic beliefs tend to have the opposite effect. Our study also sheds new light on the stability of lending relationships over time. We show that more precise accounting information often decreases the incidence of creditor turnover. We relate this finding to recent empirical studies that have found evidence consistent with our predictions using data on platforms where lenders share information about borrowers. In summary, our paper contributes to the understanding of lending in the presence of information frictions. We identify a novel cost of relationship lending – exacerbated risk shifting by weak borrowers – and show that leveling the playing field among differentially informed creditors may have unexpected consequences for the stability of lending relationships.

Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17504619.value: Should financial reporting regulations be procyclical or countercyclical, with greater scrutiny applied during economic downturns or boom periods? While this question has received much attention in the aftermath of the recent financial crises, often directed at the issue of how particular accounting choices (e.g., fair value accounting) affect equity markets, it remains largely unexplored in debt markets. We study the consequences of accounting quality for debt contracting when banks compete to extend loans. Specifically, we ask how the availability of information, public or private, about the economic condition of a potential borrower affects the cost of debt, the borrowers’ incentive to take on risky projects, and the stability of lending relationships over time. We show that regulations that increase the precision of accounting reports can improve or harm investment efficiency, depending on the beliefs held by the market participants about the borrower’s condition at the outset. In times where these beliefs lean towards pessimism, increasing the precision of accounting information tends to mitigate the risk-shifting problem for weak borrowers, at the margin; optimistic beliefs tend to have the opposite effect. Therefore, standard setters should consider loosening financial reporting standards in boom times and tightening them during economic downturns when the sentiment about individual firms’ outlook darkens.

17504819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17504819.value: Implementation of optimal mechanisms is typically difficult as it is informationally demanding for the auctioneer. We propose to tackle this issue by identifying a format that taps into market feedback for information. This design has the virtue that it is less sensitive to the assumed structure of the environment. We focus on equity auctions. Prelimiary results reveal that our proposed format is not only simple to implement, it also generates close-to-optimal revenues. 实施最优拍卖机制在实际中通常是非常困难的，因为需要拍卖者掌握大量相关信息。本文提出可以通过市场反馈来获取信息以解决该问题。本文设计的拍卖机制对特定假设的拍卖环境的依赖程度低。本文以股权拍卖为研究对象，初步结果显示我们设计的拍卖机制不仅易于施行，且可提供接近最优的拍卖收益。

17504819.label: Realisation of objectives
17504819.value: We have been working hard on the project which has been progressing steadily. The draft version of the paper has been presented by my coauthor at several universities and international conference. Our paper has received positive and constructive comments from seminar audiences. Based on the feedbacks, we have slightly adjusted the title to "Simplifying Auction Designs via Market Feedback." The working paper version is complete, we plan to submit it to a good outlet soon. I am confident that the paper will be published at an elite journal. Our working paper (attached to this report in part C concerning the Lancaster University Conference where this paper was presented) has addressed all the objectives listed in the proposal. Specifically, our Proposition 1 (page 12 in the paper) derives the bidding strategies in our dollar-denominated security-bid auction (we sometimes also term our design as “floating-parameter auctions”); Proposition2 (page 12) shows that when bidders are ex-ante identical and they bid with the same type of securities, then an revenue equivalence obtains between our dollar-denominated auction and the “fixed-parameter auctions” that are used in existing studies. The above two results set the stage for our more interesting results concerning heterogeneous bidders, which I describe below. Proposition 3 (page 17) shows that once bidders are heterogeneous, problems arise with the standard fixed-parameter auctions security-bid auctions: with sufficient heterogeneity in bidders, nondiscriminatory fixed-parameter auctions security-bid auctions generate lower revenues than cash auctions, and that steeper securities generate even lower revenues. Then theorem 1 on page 18 presents our main result: unlike fixed-parameter auctions, our dollar-denominated auctions are robust to bidder heterogeneity or any differences in the type of securities that bidders use. Specifically, Theorem 1 establishes that regardless of how bidders differ in their characteristics or the types of securities used, (1) expecteds revenue in our dollar-denominated security-bid auction are always higher than cash auctions, and (2) if any subset of bidders switch to using steeper securities than what they were using previously, then expected revenue always goes up. Theorem 1 (and the preceding results that led to the theorem) addresses the first two objectives in section 5.2 of this report. First of all, theorem 1 shows that if bidders use the same set of securities, but bidders have heterogeneous characteristics, then steeper securities always lead to higher revenues in our design. Second, theorem 1 shows that in even more general settings where bidders not only have different characteristics (for example they can differ in their standalone values) but also they use different types of securities (for example, some bidders pay with equities and others pay with call options), again our dollar-denominated auctions deliver superior seller revenues. We view our theorem 1 as a significant advance to the theory on security-bid auctions, because existing theories cannot accommodate such settings where bidders pay with different securities. In Section 3.1 (starting page 26), we compare revenues from optimal and dollar-denominated equity auctions when bidders share the same distribution of synergies with uniform distribution but differ in standalone values. Proposition 8 shows that seller profits with dollar-denominated security offers are identical to those in the optimal equity mechanism when the standalone values of bidders and the seller are far larger than the extent of synergies. And that section provides intuition on this result from several different angles. This addresses the third objective in section 5.2 of this report in terms of examining the revenue properties of our proposed format in equity auctions in comparison with the corresponding optimal equity auction, and here we have identify conditions in which our proposed mechanism generates the same, or nearly the same revenues as the optimal mechanism. In addition to addressing all the objectives listed in the proposal, our paper has gone beyond. Proposition 7 (p24) extends beyond equities to prove that if bidder standalone values are negligible relative to the sum of the seller's standalone value and expected synergies---e.g., bidders could be private equity firms that are far smaller than a target and pay the cash price by issuing debt---then dollar-denominated security auctions yield the same revenues as the optimal auction, even if (1) the rates at which standalone values go to zero vary across bidders, (2) the common distribution for expected synergies is arbitrary (not just uniform), (3) bidders offer general securities (not just equity), or (4) different bidders use different types of securities. In addition, in section 3.2, which is the end of the analysis, we provide conjectures about how our findings extend to even more general settings where both standalone values and the extent of synergies are finite, and bidders pay with general securities. We make two observations. First, when bidders use the same type of security (e,g., they all use debt), smaller bidders in dollar-denominated security auctions are more likely to win (Proposition 5). This reflects that smaller bidders in dollar-denominated security auctions have greater incentives to signal because they would pay a larger fraction of cash flows upon winning, and thus are more concerned with the market's beliefs. As a result, smaller bidders bid more aggressively and hence are more likely to win. Second, if bidders use different types of securities, bidders who use steeper securities in dollar-denominated security auctions are more likely to win, reflecting that steeper securities induce more aggressive bidding (Proposition 4; a point not previously highlighted). Both features raise seller profits in dollar-denominated security mechanisms. Intuitively, reductions in standalone values or the use of steeper securities reduce bidders' informational advantages by increasing the tying of security payments to the winner's type. Thus, it enhances seller revenues to have bidders with smaller standalone values or steeper securities win more often, as the seller can extract a larger fraction of their rents. We conjecture the optimal mechanism for general securities shares these features (i.e., the allocation should favor smaller bidders and bidders who use steeper securities). That is, our dollar-denominated security mechanism (with its simplicity and anonymity facilitated by use of market feedback) provides guidence for future efforts to identify optimal designs of fixed-parameter auctions that do not use market feedback in settings with general securities and heterogeneous bidders.

17504819.label: Major findings and research outcome
17504819.value: Our paper tackles a serious drawback of optimal mechanisms for securities auctions with heterogeneous bidders, where the mechanisms invariably require complex discriminatory winner selection and payment rules, and they impose implausible information demands on the auctioneer, as the optimal design is sensitive to the features of each bidder. We identify a simple mechanism that imposes minimal information burdens on the auctioneer and is invariant to the environment, yet generates high revenues regardless of how bidders differ in their ex-ante attributes or the securities they use. In our second-price dollar-denominated security auction, bidders submit cash bids, the high bid wins and pays with securities priced in a competitive capital market that sees the winning price. That is, bidders offer securities with guaranteed cash equivalent values, and the market determines the security parameter paid so that the security's expected value equals the winning cash price. Our mechanis has many virtues. It is detail-free and nondiscriminatory, removing legal and moral hazard concerns about discriminatory auctions. In takeovers, our mechanism lets a seller satisfy fiduciary duties requiring it to accept the "highest" bid, even if bidders use different securities or differ in other ways. The seller uses the same mechanism no matter how bidders differ ex ante, or how their securities differ; .It alleviates information demands. A seller can be uninformed (but need not be). Collectively, the market only needs to learn about the winner, and it can acquire the information post-auction, after a winner's selection. By contrast, in a fixed-parameter auction, a seller must know all information about all bidders pre-auction to design its evaluation rule properly. Our mechanism is practically relevant. It applies to both collars and cash bids that are financed after the auction with securities, as occurs for a large share of takeovers. It always generates higher revenues than cash, and is robust to bidder heterogeneity, exhibiting the properties that revenues rise when any single bidder uses a steeper security, or has a lower standalone value. By contrast, for a fixed-parameter auction to have these properties, it must incorporate complex and discriminatory rules, else it could generate lower revenues than cash when bidders differ sufficiently ex ante.

17504819.value: As discussed earlier, our findings have implications about general settings where both standalone values and the extent of synergies are finite, and bidders pay with general securities. In future studies, we plan to look into the optimal mechanisms for general securities, making use of the following two observations. First, when bidders use the same type of security (e,g., they all use debt), smaller bidders in dollar-denominated security auctions are more likely to win. This reflects that smaller bidders in dollar-denominated security auctions have greater incentives to signal because they would pay a larger fraction of cash flows upon winning, and thus are more concerned with the market's beliefs. As a result, smaller bidders bid more aggressively and hence are more likely to win. Second, if bidders use different types of securities, bidders who use steeper securities in dollar-denominated security auctions are more likely to win, reflecting that steeper securities induce more aggressive bidding.

17504819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17504819.value: Implementation of optimal or near-optimal mechanisms with heterogeneous bidders is informationally demanding for auctioneers, and such mechanisms invariably employ discriminatory winning and payment rules---creating legal and moral hazard concerns. We show how an auctioneer can alleviate informational burdens and avoid discrimination by exploiting information aggregation by capital markets, linking auction outcomes to post-auction market prices to obtain high revenues even when arbitrarily heterogeneous bidders pay with different securities. Our insight is that the market will collect information and respond to details ex post when pricing the winner, so the selling mechanism can be detail-free ex ante and informationally un-demanding for the auctioneer. We show that steeper securities always generate greater revenues than flatter securities and cash, and identify conditions where near-optimal revenues can be obtained.

17505219.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17505219.value: In Economics, power is everywhere. Sellers with market power can set prices above marginal cost. Powerful executives can use their bargaining power to extract better compensation terms. Employers have the power to reward and discipline employees through bonuses, promotions and the threat of termination. Countries use their power to influence international trade agreements. But what is power? Despite its widespread use in the social sciences, there is no universally agreed definition of power. In an influential paper, Dahl (1957) proposes that “A has power over B to the extent that he can get B to do something that B would not otherwise do.” One way to get B to do something is by rewarding or punishing B. Thus, according to this definition, power is intimately linked to the ability to punish or reward someone. Thinking of power as the ability to punish or reward is a useful way of understanding the different uses of power in Economics. Based on this idea, in this paper, we develop an economic theory of power relations. We propose a simple and flexible framework for modeling power relations. This framework helps us make sense of the various economic applications of the concept of power. We apply this framework to the design of optimal power structures. 这项研究探索经济学（和相关社会科学）的一个核心概念——权力。我们提出一个简单而灵活的建模框架。这个框架有助于我们理解权力概念的各种经济学应用。我们将此框架应用于最优权力结构的设计。该应用有助于阐明各种类型组织的低效率--搭便车和滥用权力。

17505219.label: Major findings and research outcome
17505219.value: We present a model of an autonomous organization that produces a common good with individual inputs (i.e., effort) from its members. Members can write contracts specifying effort provisions. However, crucially, the enforcement of such contracts must be carried out by organization members. Specifically, some members have the power to punish members who do not fulfill their contractual obligations. This power is, however, limited by members' right to exit the organization. The model is as follows. Two ex-ante identical agents contribute individual inputs to the production of a non-excludable good. Because inputs are costly, agents have incentives to underprovide such inputs. External enforcement is not feasible, implying that contracts in autonomous organizations must be relational. Because the game is infinitely repeated, the efficient outcome can be sustained by the threat of exit only if agents are sufficiently patient. If, instead, the discount factor is low, agents play the inefficient static Nash equilibrium. Our main result is what we call the Organizational Trilemma: the goals of autonomy, decentralization, and efficiency typically conflict with one another. In an optimally designed autonomous organization, there is a trade-off between efficiency and decentralization. If decentralization is a goal in itself, efficiency needs to be compromised. Similarly, our model makes it clear that organizational autonomy comes with benefits and costs. The cost of autonomy is that the organization cannot resort to third parties for contract enforcement. The benefit of autonomy is the avoidance of dishonest, incompetent or expensive enforcers. The Organizational Trilemma implies that, in autonomous organizations, the optimal (i.e., surplus-maximizing) governance structure is centralized. That is, in an optimal structure, the power to punish others should reside with a few selected members. This power asymmetry leads to asymmetric payoffs across members. In equilibrium, powerful members (i.e., managers) abuse their power to extract higher ex-post payoffs than those without power (i.e., subordinates). This abuse of power takes the form of asking subordinates to ``overwork,'' under the threat of punishment. Because managers benefit from the extra effort that subordinates exert, managers benefit significantly from an ongoing organization and are thus also incentivized to exert effort, in order to keep the organization intact. This is The Paradox of Power: by letting the strong party abuse his/her power, the weak party gains power over the strong party via exiting.

17505219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17505219.value: We study the governance design in autonomous organizations, which are organizations that can design and enforce their own rules. Our main result is what we call the Organizational Trilemma: the goals of autonomy, decentralization, and efficiency typically conflict with one another. In an optimally designed autonomous organization, there is a trade-off between efficiency and decentralization. If decentralization is a goal in itself, efficiency needs to be compromised. Our model helps understand the strengths and limitations of the Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs), which serve as our main motivation and application. The typical DAO is a blockchain-based entity that raises funds from its members and allocates such funds towards a common goal. Members decide on the allocation of funds collectively, typically through voting. DAOs resemble the canonical notion of an autonomous organization because all rules and contracts must be designed and enforced by the organization members themselves. Our results suggest that DAOs face the Organizational Trilemma: A truly decentralized autonomous organization will be inefficient. Our model thus helps us understand many of the practical difficulties encountered by DAOs. In fact, real-world DAOs have been plagued by issues such as centralization (and often abuse) of power, lack of contractual enforcement, and poor performance.

17505319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17505319.value: Does access to finance affect the healthcare quality hospitals provide to patients? Hospitals need credit for daily operation, capital expenditures on major surgical and diagnostic equipment, buildings, and other expenditures on salaries and travel expenses. This study employs three novel identification strategies to evaluate how credit supply affects the quality of hospital services in the United States. We examine various measures of hospital service quality (e.g. mortality rate, unnecessary treatment), as well as patient-level outcomes. To establish the casual link between credit supply and hospital performance, we exploit (a) hospital debt maturity structure right before the 2008 financial crisis, (b) local credit shortage due to bank branch closings, and (c) liquidity windfalls triggered by technological breakthroughs that facilitate shale development. 17505319.label: Realisation of objectives
17505319.value: Objective 1: We approach to address this objective by conducting two related projects. The first project, Barbarian or Vanguard? Private Equity Buyout and Physician Opioid Prescription, focuses on the impact of credit improvement via private equity (PE) buyouts of physician groups on the quality of healthcare provision, particularly in terms of opioid prescription. It utilizes the plausibly exogenous shock from PE buyouts to identify credit shocks to healthcare providers, which not only addresses the research questions as originally proposed to be examined with a set of credit events associated with the structure of immediately maturing debt before the 2008 financial crisis, bank branch closures, and liquidity windfalls triggered by deposit flow arising from significant discoveries of natural resources, but provides four more distinct advantages compared to them. (1) PE buyouts offer a novel angle with rising interests to study the impact of credit condition on healthcare provision and can help generate important policy implications. Over the past decade, the U.S. healthcare sector has witnessed a remarkable surge in PE investment, marking an astounding almost threefold increase from $41.5 billion in 2010 to a staggering $119.9 billion in 2019, as noted by Scheffler, Alexander, and Godwin (2021). This substantial growth trajectory shows no signs of abating and is poised to persist in the foreseeable future. A notable shift has been observed in the focus of PE firms, which have exhibited a vigorous appetite for acquiring an array of healthcare providers, encompassing hospitals, nursing homes, and emergency centers. Intriguingly, this trend has expanded to encompass physician-owned group practices, a segment which constituted a significant 54% of U.S. patient care physicians in 2018, according to the American Medical Association (2021). Demonstrating an unmistakable pivot, PE buyout transactions involving physician groups have remarkably surged by over six times between 2012 and 2021, underscoring a transformative wave in the sector (Scheffler et al., 2021). By analyzing the impact of PE buyouts of physician groups, this project helps us understand whether and how this form of credit shock affects healthcare provision and provides important policy implications given the concerns raised by policymakers regarding the implications of PE ownership in the healthcare domain – whether the role of PE ownership is benevolent or merely profit driven. (2) This novel setting is less contaminated by the confounding effects associated with the traditional ways of identifying credit shocks. Existing studies have shown that the credit events associated with (a) hospital debt maturity structure right before the 2008 financial crisis, (b) local credit shortage due to bank branch closings, and (c) liquidity windfalls triggered by technological breakthroughs that facilitate shale development, have potential impact on a variety of different corporate outcomes (e.g., Almeida et al., 2011; Nguyen, 2018; Gilje et al., 2016). In this regard, the PE buyouts can be of greater potentials to pin down the channel of the impact from relaxing financial constraints. (3) By focusing on the PE buyouts, the study extends the domain of credit shock beyond that of the banking sector, this can be more relevant to the financing of healthcare groups, which may not be typically financed by bank credit. (4) By focusing on the physician groups, the study can use a more homogeneous measure of healthcare quality, i.e., opioid prescription, which reduces the noises of hospital financial information, morality rates and other service delivery metrics. This also addresses the limitations on the acquisition of hospital related metrics in the U.S. that requires a U.S. residing coauthor in the team. Moreover, the opioid prescription also reflects the ESG/CSR preference of the physician groups, which provides implications on the ESG/CSR provision of healthcare sector. In validating the buyouts of PE as a plausibly exogenous shock to the healthcare outcomes of the physician groups, we conduct probit test on PE selection and find no evidence for it. Our placebo tests also show that the findings are not driven by unobservable confounding factors that may affect both PE acquisitions and healthcare outcome. In implementing the research, the project employs a Difference-in-differences (DiD) method with rigorous fixed effects at the physician-by-group level, state-level, specialty level, and year level. We also conduct a series of channel test and find evidence in support of the role of PE in reliving financial concerns of acquired physician groups. Taken together, this study has successfully addressed the research question in the spirits of the research design in the original proposal. In addition, we approach to address the question from an indirect manner. In the second project, Credit Market Conditions and Mental Health, we examine how bank regulatory reforms that improved credit conditions, e.g., by enhancing the efficiency of credit allocation and lowering lending rates, impacted mental health. While the study does not examine healthcare quality directly, it identifies an indirect channel, i.e., mental health, through which credit condition could potentially influence the healthcare sector. The paper is now under R&R at Management Science. Objective 2: The first project examines whether and how influence of PE buyouts can spillover to non-acquired physician group via the network of physicians working in multiple sites. While this is not transmitting through the internal network of the hospital system per se, it adds to our understanding on the positive impact of PE financing and related credit advantages.

17505319.label: Major findings and research outcome
17505319.value: The first project delivers the following findings: PE investors, by acquiring physician groups and improving their credit conditions, contributes to a notable decline in the rates of opioid prescriptions among physicians. The impact of this reduction is particularly pronounced when considering PE firms that exhibit fewer financial constraints, and it is further amplified when these firms target physician groups facing significant pre-acquisition financial limitations. Moreover, an intriguing finding is that PE firms displaying a heightened commitment to CSR exhibit a more substantial influence on reducing physician opioid prescription rates. Notably, the observed reduction in opioid prescriptions can extend beyond the acquired physician groups to encompass non-acquired groups, notably through physicians engaged in multisite practices. Furthermore, the project highlights that the regulatory environment plays a pivotal role. Regulatory risks serve as an incentivizing factor for PE firms to actively encourage acquired physician groups to curtail their opioid prescription practices. This influence is notably more potent when physicians' state-level policies adopt robust opioid monitoring initiatives. Moreover, the effect is significantly intensified following the initial legal repercussions faced by PE firms in relation to allegations under the False Claims Act. This underscores the evolving dynamics between PE firms, physician practices, and regulatory frameworks, shedding light on the multifaceted factors influencing opioid prescription behaviors within the healthcare landscape. The findings are summarized in the working paper, entitled “Barbarian or Vanguard? Private Equity Buyout and Physician Opioid Prescription”. The second project explores the impact of credit conditions on mental health. This is accomplished through an evaluation of regulatory reforms aimed at enhancing credit allocation efficiency and reducing interest rates. Additionally, the project scrutinizes the consequences of mergers involving large regional banks, which often result in branch closures and the subsequent imposition of more stringent credit constraints within the affected counties. Through these multifaceted investigations, the project endeavors to uncover the intricate interplay between credit conditions and mental health outcomes, providing implications for the service provision quality of the healthcare sector. The findings are summarized in the paper, entitled “Credit Market Conditions and Mental Health”, which is under revise and resubmit at Management Science.

17505319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17505319.value: Moving forward, this research presents compelling avenues for further exploration and action. Building on its insights, a comprehensive investigation could delve deeper into the mechanisms through which private equity (PE) takeovers influence healthcare provision and mental well-being. This could involve conducting interviews or surveys with doctors, patients, and administrators to gain qualitative insights into the decision-making processes behind opioid prescriptions and the broader impact of PE acquisitions on healthcare practices.

17505319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17505319.value: This research underscores how changes in credit conditions, whether through private equity buyouts or banking reforms, can impact both healthcare provision and mental well-being, with potential positive and negative consequences for different groups of people. The first part examined how private equity (PE) takeovers of physician groups influence doctors' prescription of opioid medications. The research showed that after a PE takeover, physicians in the acquired groups reduced their opioid prescription rates. This reduction was more pronounced when PE firms had fewer financial constraints and when the physician groups being acquired were financially constrained. Moreover, PE firms with a strong commitment to Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) had a greater impact on lowering opioid prescriptions. Interestingly, this reduction spilled over to other non-acquired physician groups through doctors who practice in multiple locations. The study also found that regulatory risks motivated PE firms to encourage acquired physician groups to prescribe fewer opioids. The second part investigated how changes in banking rules that improved access to credit affected mental health, providing indirect reference on the effect of condition on healthcare quality.

17505519.label: Project Objectives
17505519.value: To perform a quantitative analysis of the relative importance of various theories (“modernization”, class conflict, peasant grievances, media and propaganda, peasant nationalism, etc.) put forth to account for the rise of communism in China using a unique data set newly digitized from a wide variety of historical sources. To undertake a causal analysis of those theories showing significant correlations with the rise of the Chinese Communist Party especially during the Sino-Japanese War period of 1937-1945 measured in terms of both the enrollment of mid-rank Party officials (colonel and above) and the size of guerilla bases across the Chinese counties. To examine if nationalistic sentiment aroused during the Sino-Japanese War has a persistent effect measured in terms of political trust in, and attitudes toward, the Chinese government and the Party in the present day by analyzing data digitized from local gazetteers, China’s General Social Survey (CGSS), other survey data on political attitudes, and also online data available from the Baidu search engine.

17505519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17505519.value: With the collapse of the Soviet Union and the former Eastern Bloc, China is easily one of the most successfully reformed economies in the world that continues to be ruled by a single-party communist regime. While many have attributed the Chinese Communist Party (CCP)’s success in reforming the formerly centrally planned economic system to the deliberate combination of political centralization and a decentralized economy, there remains little consensus as to how the CCP overcame a myriad of adversities and rose to power some 80 years ago. For instance, they were nearly wiped out when were forced to embark upon the deadly Long March in 1934 by their political adversary—the Nationalist Party (Kuomingtang); the Japanese army which invaded in 1937 posed another severe threat. In terms of economic institutions, the CCP also needed to convince the people of the virtues and appeal of communism when private ownership had long been the norm, and industrial progress that would nurture a class consciousness required for spawning a revolution was woefully lacking. Nonetheless, endeavors have been made to account for the phenomenal rise of communism in the Chinese context. The “modernization” theory, for instance, emphasizes the role of rising education of the masses in general and among the revolutionist elites in particular. In contrast, those of a Marxist orientation ascribe the Chinese revolutionary success to the role of class struggle which points to the grievances of the peasants exploited by either the landlords or the state, if not both. There is also the claim that the CCP succeeded in staging a revolution despite its initially small power base thanks to its clever use of the media and propaganda. Last, but not least, the “peasant nationalism” hypothesis attributes the mass support of the Party to a new “national salvation” sentiment unwittingly aroused among the peasantry when the Japanese invaded and inflicted massive casualties. None of these hypotheses, however, have been substantiated with data or analyzed within a unified framework encompassing all of the contesting claims. We thus propose to subject the foregoing hypotheses to empirical testing by first digitizing various hitherto unavailable data sources from the archives of the Republican government, Japanese wartime intelligence documents, and various historical accounts and gazetteers compiled by the CCP.

17505519.label: Realisation of objectives
17505519.value: A primary goal of this project is to conduct a quantitative analysis of the various theories that have been put forth by scholars in accounting for the rise of communism in China – one of the most momentous events of the twentieth century. These theories include “modernization” (Lipset, 1959; Wickham-Crowley, 1992), “class consciousness” – based on incidents of workers’ protests in factories located in treaty ports and industrialized towns before the Sino-Japanese War (Perry, 1993), peasant grievances resulting from “exploitation” by landlords (Hofheinz Jr., 1969; Moore, 1966; Selden, 1971; Skocpol, 1979) or exorbitant taxes and unregulated levies imposed by local warlords (Bianco, 1971; Chen, 1992; Duara, 1991; Gillin, 1964; Goodman, 2000; Keating, 1997; Selden, 1971, 1995), respectively, rural social organization such as lineages and secret societies – examples of the latter include the “Red Gun Society” and the salt smugglers (Feng and Goodman, 2000; Kataoka, 1972; Li, 2009; Perry, 1980; Thaxton, 1997), “violent culture” that might have feed the communist movements (Rowe, 2007), and the influence of the Nationalist Party or Guomingdang on the rise of communism, etc. While these theories help elucidate the diffusion of communism in China, they have not been systematically verified due to the lack of data. What we have done is that we constructed a unique dataset by digitizing a large number of variables from various historical data sources as proxies for these theories and tested their empirical relevance. For example, using the density of middle-to-upper ranking cadres and martyr soldiers for the 1921-45 period as dependent variables, we find that proxies for modernization (treaty ports, number of respectively modern firms and primary and secondary schools) do not significantly explain the rise of communism even in the early period (viz. 1921-36) of communist expansion. While the proxy for “class consciousness” is significantly correlated with the two dependent variables in question, it cannot explain the growth of the communist party in wartime China (viz. 1937-45). We find the same for “exploitation”, using the share of tenancy and per capita land tax, respectively, as proxies. In the case of social networks and organization, lineages can account for the partial significance of the rise of communism in the pre-war period (as measured by cadre density), those of secret societies, conflicts, and early influence of the Nationalist government (specifically the Tongmenhui) have no significant effects whatsoever insofar as CCP growth is concerned. During the Sino-Japanese War, none of these variables are significantly correlated with the growing influence of the CCP; by contrast, an indicator variable that demarcates a county by whether or not it was occupied by the Japanese Army significantly correlates with markers of communist growth (refer to Figure 1 for details). Our second goal is to conduct an empirical (causal) analysis of the above theories especially during the Sino-Japanese War of 1937-45 to ascertain whether any of these theories can be shown to have caused the rise of the Chinese Communist Party, where the latter is measured at the county level by the enrolment of middle-to-upper-ranking Party officials (colonel and above), whether a Party Committee had been established in a county (as a proxy for the Party in building its organizational capacity), and the size of guerrilla bases across the Chinese counties. The causal analysis is conducted by means of a spatial regression discontinuity analysis (SRDD), whereby the pertinent proxies are employed as control variables, while the geographic variable of whether a county was occupied by the Japanese (Japanese Occupied Area) is considered the key independent variable (as an alternative explanation to the existing theories). The underlying assumption of this competing hypothesis is two-fold. First is “power vacuum”. The underlying idea is that, although it was easy for the Japanese Army to conquer China, the Chinese territory proved to be too vast for them to adequately garrison and govern. To prevent the communists from taking over the deserted villages, the Japanese relied on the militarily weaker “puppet troops” to garrison and govern. But the communists took advantage of their weaker military capacity and built up both their guerrilla bases and Party apparatus there. The second channel through which the communists developed in wartime China is that they exploited the sufferings and humiliation in counties occupied by the Japanese in fostering a nationalist sentiment because sufferings and humiliation – as proxied by civilian deaths and rape victims, respectively – were distinctly higher in these counties. Indeed, we find that communist growth as measured by all the markers of communist growth (mid-to-high-ranking cadre officials, Party Committee, and size of guerrilla base) was strongest in the occupied counties. As with the first goal, this goal is also well realized. Premised on the finding that nationalism was what spurred the rise of the Chinese Communist Party in the context of the Sino-Japanese War, our third and final goal is to examine whether the allegedly stronger nationalistic sentiment aroused during wartime has had a persistent effect in both the short-to-medium and longer terms. To estimate the former, we construct a new dependent variable that measures the growth in the density of CCP membership over time, defined simply as the number of party members in a county divided by its population. To ensure consistency, we measure this value in five separate years: 1950 (the year after the founding of the People’s Republic), 1960 (a decade into its rule), 1966 (the year the Cultural Revolution began), 1976 (the year the Cultural Revolution ended), and 1985 (several years into the economic reforms), and find that the communist influence in the Japanese Occupied Area in wartime China exerted a significantly persistent effect even long after the war ended. To estimate the long-term effect of war-induced nationalism, we measure political trust in, and attitudes toward, the Chinese Communist Party and government in the present day. For example, we find that nationalism was significantly stronger (as measured by an individual nationalism scores obtained from the China Political Compass survey – an online attitudinal survey conducted in 2014) in counties formerly occupied by the Japanese; that the perception of residents living in the same counties towards Japan was significantly more negative (based on a question taken from the Asian Barometer Survey of 2014); that these counties imported merchandise of distinctly lesser value from Japan, that residents of these counties were more likely to search on Baidu for the term “China Dream” (an aspiration revered by the Chinese national leader), and that these residents exhibited significantly greater trust in the Chinese government (based on analyzing a question in China’s General Social Survey), etc. On the question of long-term persistence, we have collected further data of a much more fine-grained nature and begun writing computer programs to explore the persistence of nationalist sentiments. This third and final objective is more than fully realized.

17505519.label: Major findings and research outcome
17505519.value: The rise of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is one of the most momentous events of the twentieth century, yet its rise to power has received surprisingly little scholarly attention. Our primary goal is to examine the causal rise of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) in wartime China using a spatial regression discontinuity design and several measures to proxy for the Party’s rise during the Sino–Japanese War. Designed to encompass both military and organizational dimensions, these novel measures include: middle-to-upper-level cadre officials (military), grassroots party organizations (political-cum-organizational), and size of the guerrilla bases (military). As we are able to identify the counties occupied by the Japanese, we are thus able to test the hypothesis that the more intense war suffering (using civilians killed as a proxy) and humiliation (using reported rape victims as a proxy) experienced by residents of the Japanese Occupied Area (JOA) were what was driving the rise of the Chinese Communist Party in wartime China. The research yields three key findings. First, we confirm that the three markers of communist growth were significantly higher in counties occupied by the Japanese Army, and that, its pre-war popularity notwithstanding, the same markers are not statistically significant before the war. Second, we identify two primary channels behind the CCP’s political ascendancy. The first is what we call “power vacuum”, meaning that the communists took advantage of the militarily weaker “puppet troops” in charge of administering the loosely held occupied areas. Our second channel is more general, implying that support for the CCP was powered by a strong anti-Japanese sentiment spurred by war suffering and humiliation. Our third and final finding is that the CCP’s wartime influence persisted after the war: former Japanese-occupied areas exhibited a significantly higher party membership density from 1950 to 1985.

17505519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17505519.value: There are two additional projects developed in the course of this study. The first pertains to the possible impact of cultural propaganda on war mobilization. After focusing on war suffering and humiliation as primary causes of rising nationalism among the Chinese people, an important question arising from this inquiry concerns the potential effectiveness of cultural propaganda. Specifically, how did the Red Army make use of a repertoire of (local) folk songs with newly written anti-war lyrics in fanning the nationalist sentiment of the Chinese people? How can we account for the varying success of this cultural mobilization across regions? We will explore these questions in our project extension. Currently a PhD student that I co-supervise at the Australian National University is investigating the differences in primary school curricula during the Sino-Japanese War between regions governed by three different political parties – the Nationalists, the Japanese, and the Red Army. The project is motivated by the premise that, by shaping political preferences, school curriculum can importantly affect nation building, and the first step is to compare and contrast the textbooks adopted in the three broad regions governed by the different political regimes with respect to the importance they paid to nationalism.

17505519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17505519.value: The rise of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is one of the most momentous events of the twentieth century, yet its rise to power has received scant scholarly attention. For example, what enabled the Party to emerge victoriously from the Sino–Japanese War, when it was militarily the weakest of the three powers? And why did it gain popular support only after the Japanese invasion of 1937 but not beforehand? By assembling a unique dataset based on a wide variety of historical sources, we show that the Japanese invasion had inadvertently facilitated the Red Army’s development via the expansion of many counter-Japanese guerrilla bases and state building (specifically the building of party committees at the county level) – the latter laying the foundation of party organization building in the years to come. We also provide systematic evidence showing that war sufferings and humiliation provide the basis for a growing nationalist sentiment that continues to deeply affect the Chinese people to this day, and a vantage point from which to understand the “deep roots” of nationalism as repeatedly stressed by various national leaders in a context where China’s influence in the current global economic and geopolitical order has been growing.

17600419.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17600419.value: What are the consequences of older adults being incapable of walking with appropriate focus of attention in an urban environment? Can we design a targeted intervention to augment the possibility that older adults at risk of falling could walk safely even in a complicated environment requiring capability of optimizing focus of attention? Walking is one of the commonest fall-related activities of older adults. Regrettably, older adult falls were well-proved to affect walking ability and lead to high fear of falling. To deal with movement difficulties and/or fear of falling during walking, older adults allocate their attention internally to the mechanisms of their movements through conscious motor processing, in an attempt to ensure the effectiveness of their movements when encountering movement difficulties or under stress. Ironically, previous research showed that conscious motor processing requires the processing of movement-related rules using working memory and it could cause movement disruption by constraining or interfering with automatic motor control mechanisms. Focusing internally by conscious motor processing was discovered to interfere with allocation of attention for navigation of the environment and/or multitasking in older adults during walking that overloads resources of working memory. It could consequently cause movement failure and increase risk of falling of the older adults, especially in a complicated environment requiring capability of optimizing focus of attention. Although conscious motor processing in older adults during walking was suggested to be influential, no completed research has investigated a potential intervention to ameliorate the propensity for conscious motor processing in older adults during walking. It is therefore clinically important to develop the targeted and effective intervention during gait rehabilitation by physiotherapists. The aim of this randomized controlled trial is to examine the effect of external, internal and no attention focus walking training during gait rehabilitation on real-time conscious motor processing, balance, walking ability and fear of falling by older adults at risk of falling in Hong Kong. Our pilot studies successfully established the rehabilitation training protocol and the training feasibility, safety and preliminary effectiveness have been assured. The proposed study can contribute significantly in the application of a novel, simple and effective evidence-based rehabilitation training method to ameliorate propensity for conscious motor processing by older adults. It could subsequently help improve older adults’ capability of optimizing focus of attention during walking and decrease their risk of falling when walking in the complicated urban environment.

17600419.label: Realisation of objectives
17600419.value: Objective: Examine the effect of external, internal and no attention focus walking training during gait rehabilitation on real-time conscious motor processing (reinvestment), balance, walking ability and fear of falling by older adults at risk of falling in Hong Kong. Hypothesis: Older adults who completed the external attention focus walking training during gait re-education will have lower real-time conscious motor processing propensity and better rehabilitation outcome than older adults who completed the internal or no attention focus walking training. The main objective has been fully achieved and the hypothesis has been evaluated comprehensively. Utilizing a well-designed and approved research methodology in our funded project, we had successfully investigated the main objective and its corresponding hypothesis of our project comprehensively. We recruited a total of 108 community-dwelling older adults in Hong Kong according to our plan of the funded proposal (6 participants have been excluded and therefore have not completed the assessment). We followed the inclusion criteria, according to the funded proposal, during recruitment: (1) Age 65 or above; (2) No history of cerebral vascular disease, Parkinson's disease, or any other neurological deficit; (3) Chinese version of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE-C) total score of equal or more than 24; (4) Able to walk independently indoor for at least 40 meters continuously with comfortable pace; (5) Older adults with moderate to high risk of falling, as indicated by the score of less than 24 out of 28 in the Tinetti Balance Assessment Tool (POMA). All the experimental procedures followed our funded and approved proposal, including all the measurements of different outcome measures. We assessed real-time conscious motor processing by the electroencephalogram (EEG) T3-Fz coherence, functional balance and gait by the Tinetti Balance Assessment Tool (POMA), balance ability by the Berg Balance Scale (BBS), functional mobility by the Time "Up and Go" test (TUG), walking ability by 10-meter comfortable and fast walking speed, trait conscious motor processing propensity by the Chinese version of the Movement Specific Reinvestment Scale (MSRS-C), fear of falling by the Chinese version of the Falls Efficacy Scale International (FES-I (Ch)), and number of falls by self-report diary, according to our funded proposal. Twelve training sessions were provided to each of the three randomly assigned groups: no attention focus walking group (NAFWG), external attention focus walking group (EAFWG), and internal attention focus walking group (IAFWG). Each participant completed assessment sessions (total 3 assessment sessions) before training at baseline (T0), just after completion of all training sessions (T1) and 6 months after completion of all training sessions (T2). To achieve the project objective, we extracted data and compared the real-time conscious motor processing, functional balance and gait, balance ability, functional mobility, walking ability, trait conscious motor processing propensity, fear of falling, and number of falls among the three groups of older adults at risk of falling. As a result, the objective of this funded project was achieved comprehensively. Additionally, the corresponding hypothesis was thoroughly evaluated and supported by substantial evidence. The primary outcome, which focused on real-time conscious motor processing (EEG T3-Fz coherence), demonstrated a significant result as anticipated in our hypothesis. Specifically, the EAFWG exhibited significantly lower levels of real-time conscious motor processing compared to the other groups immediately after training. Regarding the secondary outcomes, all groups demonstrated a significant immediate post-intervention enhancement in functional balance and gait as well as balance ability. However, no significant improvements were observed in any of the psychological fall-related outcomes, such as FES-I (Ch) and MSRS-C scores across all groups. The observed significant effects in EEG T3-Fz coherence, functional balance and gait as well as balance ability were mostly immediate. Benefits from functional balance and gait were sustained in the long-term over 6 months after completion of all training sessions in EAFWG compared to the other two groups. The findings of this research illustrated a clear immediate positive effect in our primary outcome as suggested in our hypothesis and objective of this study. Further research could be investigated to specifically evaluate the possible long-term effect of external focus gait training. The major findings of this research have been disseminated by different journal publications and conference presentations.
