17614519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17614519.value: Decoding Chinese orthography is complex because Chinese characters’ constituents shared very similar stroke patterns and morphemes which can correspond to the same character. Given the complexity, learners of Chinese as a second language(CSL) often encounter great challenges in word reading. A recent study suggests a series of top-down mental processes, also known as executive function(EF), has a significant association with Chinese word reading in Chinese students (Chung, Lam, & Cheung, 2018), to see patterns and figure out the abstract relations underlying analogies. Yet, the extent to which EF affects CSL learners’ word reading, and the underlying mechanism itself in Chinese word reading remain underexamined. This study aims to fill three important research gaps which are fundamental to understanding word reading difficulties of CSL learners. First, there is no research on the association between EF and word reading in CSL learners. Second, and relatedly, there is no research compares such relation between CSL learners and Chinese students. Word reading process for first- and second-language readers is different in the way that second-language readers are interfered by the dominant language simultaneously. As such, word reading in L2 potentially needs the inhibitory system in EF to suppress the interferences. Whether difficulties in interference control predicts the greater challenges to recognize Chinese written words for CSL learners than the Chinese students is not known. Third, previous studies on the link between EF and Chinese word reading focused on early childhood. The potential differences of the underlying cognitive processes at different stages of reading development has not been considered. This study is designed to address the above issues in order to enrich literature on the decoding of L2 learners. We will recruit two groups of 300students(CSL and Chinese-speaking students) in grade 3,5& 7. Their EF, orthographic knowledge, morphological knowledge, and word reading will be measured; while the effects of age, vocabulary and non-verbal IQ will be controlled. The effects of EF on word reading will be compared between two groups of students across different reading stages, and in relation to those linguistic knowledge. The study will identify the cognitive underpinnings of word reading difficulties among CSL learners at different stages of reading development, and enhance our understanding of the decoding process as a second language. The findings will suggest teachers may develop learning strategies and teaching activities that evoke the awareness of the orthographic structures to facilitate interferences control process and memorize the Chinese characters. 中文字詞的學習並不容易，其中一個原因是漢字由部件構成，許多漢字因而都含有字形相似的部件，而且漢字作為詞素，在不同的語境中往往會對應不同的意思。這讓以中文為第二語言(CSL)的學生在學習中文詞語時頗感困難。當前的研究顯示，學生如需掌握中文字詞潛在的特徵和法則，需進行一系列自上而下的認知過程，這些過程被稱作執行功能。近來的研究表明，在以中文為一語的學生中，他們認讀詞語的能力與執行功能有緊密關聯(Chung, Lam, & Cheung, 2018)，但在二語領域，二者的關係如何，尚未得到專門探討，一系列問題亦有待解答。例如執行功能在多大程度上影響學生的詞語認讀、哪些執行功能會影響以及如何影響認讀詞語的表現等。回答這些問題，有助於進一步認識造成二語學生中文閱讀困難的原因。 本研究可彌補當前研究中的三項空白。首先，二語領域中未見探討執行功能與詞語認讀關係的研究；其次，較少研究探討一語和二語學習中，執行功能和認讀詞語的關係會否不同。理論上，二語學生受到其一語的影響，其認讀詞語的過程可能與一語有所不同。特別是二語者可能更多運用執行功能中的抑制功能去排除一語的幹擾，因而抑制功能可能對二語學生認讀表現有更大的預測作用。最後，現有執行功能的相關研究多數以幼兒為對象，尚未探討學生在不同的學習階段執行功能和認讀詞語的關係是否有變。 針對以上研究空白，本研究探討一語和二語學生在認讀詞語時的認知因素。在以中文為一語和二語的三年級、五年級學生中，分別抽選出200名進行研究，總共400名學生。這些學生將接受多項評估，包括執行功能、字形意識、構詞意識、詞語認讀能力等。作為控制變量，學生的年齡、詞匯量和非言語智能的信息亦會被採集。研究小組將分析執行功能對詞語認讀的作用及其與中文語言知識的關係，並比較這些效應在不同年級、不同類型學生中會否不同。 本研究將從認知角度揭示不同階段二語學生詞語認讀困難的影響因素，有助學界更好地認識二語學習字詞時解碼過程。本研究結果亦有助於教師明確非華語學生中文學習困難中的一些成因，從而引導教師制定適切的教學方法和活動，提升學生閱讀相關的執行功能，最終提升學生的中文學習表現。

17614519.label: Realisation of objectives
17614519.value: Overall progress In alignment with the recent trend in understanding the role of executive function in literacy learning, this study aims to examine the respective effect of executive function on word reading among Chinese native and Chinese as a second language (CSL) students in Hong Kong. As a set of cognitive skills encapsulating the ability to update information, suppress interferences and shift attention that is necessary to control behavior, executive functions have been believed to place an important effect on Chinese word reading partially due to the complexity of the Chinese written system. In this study, we hypothesized that the pathways of its effect include both direct and indirect ways, with orthographic and morphological awareness as mediators. As approved by UGC, this research planned to recruit a total of 400 primary students in grades 3 and 5 (including 200 CSL students and 200 Chinese-speaking students). Due to the Covid-19 pandemic in the past two years, the project has encountered huge difficulty in collecting research data because the primary schools in Hong Kong were not able to conduct face-to-face teaching. Under such circumstances, the research team has made substantial efforts in completing various aspects of research, such as: (1) Kept close communication with the participating schools. (2) We have completed two meta-analysis studies during the period of face to face teaching suspension. It was found that the two key variables of this project, orthographic knowledge, and working memory, could correlate significantly with word reading/Chinese proficiency among CSL students at r=0.429 and r=0.286, respectively. These two studies lay a solid foundation in literature preparation; (3) Based on our previous studies and existing literature, the research team has developed or adapted a series of research instruments as stated in the approved proposal, including a Chinese word reading task, four meta-linguistic tasks (i.e., lexical decision, orthographic choice in context, morpheme recognition, and morpheme discrimination), three computerized executive function tasks (i.e., color-word interference test, sorting test, and digit span task measuring inhibitory, shifting and working memory respectively), and three instruments for measuring control variables (i.e., nonverbal intelligence, vocabulary, and background questionnaire). As these instruments have been widely used in previous research, they all have good validity and reliability. In the end, we have successfully completed the data collection among 204 CSL students and 419 Chinese native students although the schedule was a little delayed. Such data volume has exceeded the expected size. For the whole project, we have three research papers (two journal papers and one book chapter) published and four papers under review. We also have one research student graduated by exploring effect of inhibition skill in Chinese reading comprehension under supervision of team member (principal supervisor: Dr. Loh Elizabeth Ka Yee). Based on the tentative results, we believe that the research objectives have all been achieved. Realisation of three objectives 1. To examine the predicting effect of executive function on Chinese word reading for CSL learners and Chinese speaking students at different reading stages The objective has been fully achieved. Using the data collected, we performed regression analysis and found that for the whole sampled students, the overall prediction of executive functions on word reading was statistically significant, R square = .259, F (4, 618) = 53.962, p < .000. Among the four executive function skills, inhibition, verbal working memory and visual working memory are unique predictors. Furthermore, the significant prediction was found among Grade 3 students, R square =.335, F (4,234) = 29.404, p<.000. Verbal and visual working memory are significant predictors. The contribution of inhibition was marginally significant. Regarding the result of Grade 5 students, executive functions explained 15.9% of the variance in word reading, F (4,379) = 17.960, p<.000. It was found that verbal and visual working memory significantly predicted word reading. Based on the above results, the executive functions appear to be more important in Grade 3 than in Grade 5. 2. To compare the effect of executive function on Chinese word reading between CSL learners and Chinese-speaking students The objective has been fully achieved. To compare the effect of executive functions on Chinese word reading between CSL learners and Chinese-speaking students, linear regression analysis was conducted. The results indicated that executive function explained 14.8% of the variation in word reading, among Chinese-speaking students, F (4,414) = 18.018, p<.000. All subskills significantly contribute to word reading. Executive functions also significantly predicted CSL students’ word reading, R square = .236, F (4, 199) = 15.358, p < .000. Among executive function skills, inhibition, verbal working memory, and visual working memory were statistically significant to the prediction. The above results indicate that executive functions shed a greater predictive effect on the CSL student’s word reading, which might partially due to the complex linguistic properties of Chinese. The CSL students may not have sufficient practice and exposure to Chinese. Therefore, they may need to be more skillful in deploying their EF resources to memorize and recognize the Chinese words. 3. To identify any difference on the effects of executive function on Chinese word reading at different reading stages The objective has been fully achieved. The moderating analysis was performed to investigate the potential differences in the effects of executive function on word reading at different reading stages. Interaction items, namely inhibition×grade, attention shifting×grade, visual working memory×grade, and verbal working memory×grade, were added together in the regression model with word reading as the dependent variable and executive functions as independent variables. The interactions were also significant, ΔR square =.020, F (4,374) = 7.462, p<.000. Further focus was given to the moderation effect of grade on the contribution of each sub-skill using structural equation modelling (SEM). It was found that both the effect of inhibition and working memory on word reading could be negatively moderated by grade. That suggested, inhibition and working memory could play a less important role when students advance to higher grades.

17614519.label: Major findings and research outcome
17614519.value: There are several key findings emerged based on the tentative analysis. First, we confirmed the importance of executive function to students’ Chinese word reading. Our correlation and regression results indicated that 25.9% of the variance of students’ performance in Chinese word reading can be explained by the executive functions among Grade 3 and 5 students. Inhibition, verbal working memory, and visual working memory remain significant in terms of their predictive effects. Second, we gained evidence about the developmental impact of executive functions on wording reading. Although our data is cross sectional, it is shown that executive functions contributes 33.5% of variances in the Grade 3 students’ group whereas the value reduces to only 15.9% in the Grade 5 students’ group. The moderation found that both the effect of inhibition and verbal working memory on word reading decrease with grade. This reveals that the relationship between executive function and wording reading weaken along with students’ progressing to higher grade level. Third, the executive functions could be more important among CSL students than among Chinese native students, explaining word reading’s 23.6% and 14.8% variance respectively. Furthermore, we also found that executive function can significantly predict the performance in morphological awareness and orthographic knowledge tests, which in turn could significantly predicate the word reading performance. The indirect effects of executive function on word reading via the mediating of orthographic knowledge in CSL students was found higher than in Chinese native students (Please see our paper entitled “The effect of executive function on word reading: a comparison between CSL and Chinese native students” for more details in Part C) All the above findings indicate that executive function is a set of domain-general cognitive skills that bear significance in word reading across different ages and linguistics backgrounds in the present study. These findings have not been reported in previous studies and could further widen our understanding of executive function’s role in learning of logographic languages such as Chinese.

17614519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17614519.value: Based on the results obtained, there are two lines of future research directions. The first one is to initiate more longitudinal studies. During elementary education, students simultaneously develop their different aspects of reading skills and capacity of deploying executive function, for which researchers have suggested their relationship could be reciprocal. Therefore, it is necessary to provide a longitudinal perspective to deepen our understanding of the relationship between executive function and Chinese learning. Meanwhile, along with researchers’ ever-deepen understanding of executive function, it is recognized that investigation of executive function does not only involve the “cool executive function” (e.g., inhibition, shifting, and working memory) but also the “hot executive function” (e.g., delayed satisfaction) (Kerr & Zelazo, 2004; Zelazo, & Carlson, 2012). To provide a more comprehensive understanding of the role played by the executive function in language learning, it is rather necessary to include more identified of executive function in future research.

17614519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17614519.value: As a foundational skill of reading comprehension, Chinese word reading is rather challenging for learners with Chinese as second language (CSL) or even Chinese native students due to Chinese language’s logographical properties. Recent research has shown that executive function (EF) could be an important factor in explaining students’ differences in academic performance. However, its role in Chinese learning among different groups of students at different stages has not been addressed. In light of the crucial role of EF, the present study examined the effect of executive function on word reading among two groups of Chinese native (N=419) and CSL students (N=204) in Hong Kong. The study shows that EF significantly predicts students’ word reading performance across the two groups of students while such predictive effects are greater in the CSL group than in native Chinese group, and EF provides greater predictive effects in the lower grade level (i.e., Grade 3) than in higher level counterpart (i.e., Grade 5). The results of this project could provide theoretical insights into the important role of EF in Chinese language learning, which are also rather valuable in terms of the implication on curriculum design as well as teaching practice.

17615019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17615019.value: BACKGROUND: The latest advances in treatments, along with recent developments in recovery approaches, are enabling persons with bipolar disorder (BD) to live with purpose and to value their life roles, which often include the pursuit of creative occupations. Individuals with milder forms of the illness, those at risk of BD, and those who have a family history of the condition all tend to do well in creative tasks and in achieving creative accomplishments. What are the mechanism behind creativity in people with BD? OBJECTIVES: This study is informed by the two psychological concepts of novelty and reward sensitivity. Its specific objectives are to: 1) Quantitatively examine how the severity of BD symptoms, ambition, and decision-making indices of willingness to explore novel options, relate to real-world creative accomplishments and behaviors; and 2) Qualitatively explore the processes of creative activity over a three/four-month period among people living with BD, particularly in relation to tackling difficult goals and reaching important milestones in producing creative outputs. METHOD: We will conduct mixed-method research involving the collection, analysis, and integration of quantitative (Part 1) and qualitative (Part 2) research data. Part 1: Through advertisements in outpatient clinics, social media, and local newspapers, we will recruit 96 people living with BD (clinical group) and 96 individuals without a diagnosis of mental illness (control group). People in both groups will self-identify as being involved in creative arts, focusing on writing and/or painting (for which we anticipate strong recruitment). All participants will take three clusters of tests: real-world creativity; cognitive and decision-making variables; relevant clinical variables. Part 2: We will gather qualitative data from 14-16 BD participants (focusing on two subgroups, writing and painting) over a three/four-month period, using Photovoice projects and three focus group meetings for each subgroup. Photovoice is a methodology whereby research participants take photos of moments in which they have overcome major hurdles toward creative goals or have produced a creative output. At project completion, we will organize a half-day public art event to present the participants’ creative work and the photos they have taken. IMPACTS: This will be the first study to draw data from both quantitative and qualitative methods to better understand creativity in the arts among Chinese people with BD. Clinically, the findings will hold the potential to reduce the stigma associated with BD, and inform health workers how to support clients to pursue creative goals without compromising their health.

17615019.label: Realisation of objectives
17615019.value: 1) EXECUTION OF THE PROJECT TO ACHIEVE THE RESEARCH OBJECTIVES The study had two key objectives: 1) Assess how the severity of bipolar disorders (BD) symptoms, ambition, and decision-making relate to real-world creative accomplishments and behaviours. It was hypothesized that those with BD would exhibit greater reward-seeking and exploratory decision-making, accounting for higher creativity. 2) Explore the creative processes of individuals with BD, particularly in tackling goals and reaching milestones in producing creative outputs. 1.1 First objective: Outcome evaluation. This study consisted of two groups: a BD group and a control group (no current or history of mood/psychotic disorders), as assessed by the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5. All participants were currently engaged in creative activities related to writing and/or painting. Initially, 222 interested individuals (71 BD, 151 control) filled out an online form. A clinical psychologist and trained research assistant screened and recruited 151 eligible participants aged 18-65 (53 BD, 98 control) from March 2021 to May 2023. The remaining 71 were excluded because they did not meet the selection criteria, had relapsed, became sick (unrelated to bipolar), were admitted to the hospital, were worried about the COVID-19 outbreak, were not vaccinated, staying in quarantine, and already left Hong Kong. An in-person session was conducted at the university to collect additional data using a handgrip device connected to a laptop. Adults aged 18 to 70 with primary BD-I and BD-II and age-matched adults with no current or history of mood or psychotic disorder, as assessed by the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 (SCID-5) were recruited for the present study. Additional inclusion criteria for both groups included being of ethnic Chinese, currently participating in at least two hours per week or eight hours per month in creative activities related to writing and/or painting. Exclusion criteria included inability to provide written informed consent, to concentrate for more than 15 minutes during the study tasks or measures, use of medications or medical illnesses that could impair cognitive functioning or interfere with task completion, or other indications of impaired mental status; history of brain injury or neurological illness; substance use disorder within the past year; electroconvulsive therapy within the past year; or being a danger to self or others. The study chose to focus on writing and painting for several reasons: 1) They are widely considered prototypical domains of creativity; and 2) They are among the more common creative occupations, which enhanced the feasibility of recruiting participants. Participants were recruited through a variety of channels, including: • Notice boards on university campuses • Community healthcare agencies • Art supply stores and galleries • Advertisements to writers' support groups • A press release about the project • Social media, e.g., Facebook, Instagram, etc. Measures included the following: Carson Creative Achievement Questionnaire (CAQ): This is the primary dependent variable, a self-report measure designed to assess lifetime creative accomplishments across 10 domains - visual arts, music, creative writing, dance, drama, architecture, humor, science, invention, and culinary skills. Participants rate their level of accomplishment in each domain on a scale from 0 (none) to 7 (exceptional, e.g., national recognition). Unusual Uses Task (UUT): A widely used measure of divergent thinking, which has been associated with elevated subsyndromal manic symptoms. Participants are given 3 prompts (screwdriver, toothpicks, sheet of paper) and asked to generate as many different uses for each item as possible within 2 minutes. Effort Discounting Task: This task presents choices between an easy-to-obtain small reward and a larger reward requiring physical effort (measured via handgrip strength). It assesses how much the subjective value of the larger reward is "discounted" by the effort required. Participants made choices between a "no grip" option and a larger monetary reward requiring a given grip strength. Grip strength and reward size varied across 128 trials. Observe or Bet Task: Measures the tendency to make exploratory versus exploitative choices. In each block, participants experienced a sequence of blue or orange lights, with one color being more frequent (75%). They could either simply observe the light (explore) or guess the color (exploit). Guessing could win or lose points, so it was a riskier, exploitative choice. The color bias switched at an unknown point in each block. WASSUP Popular Fame and Financial Success Subscales: Assesses high life ambitions, which have been found to be elevated in bipolar disorder. Participants rated the likelihood of achieving 10 goals related to fame and financial success. PANAS: Self-report measure of positive and negative affect over the past week. YMRS: Interview-based assessment of current manic symptom severity. Brief QoL.BD: Self-report measure of quality of life across 14 domains in bipolar disorder. 1.2 Second objective: A process evaluation. The qualitative study addressing the second research objective did not wait for completion of the quantitative study. Invitations for focus groups were sent to the 13 interested participants in the BD group. A briefing session was held on campus, where 10 participants learned about the photovoice methodology and procedures. Over the 9-month study period, participants engaged in three focus groups, photo logging for 180 days (6-month), and a concluding public art exhibition and human library. During the study, researchers logged participants’ photos and work, tracking how mood state affected creative output. In the focus groups, researchers facilitated discussions on participants' creativity experiences and journeys. The focus groups lasted approximately 75 minutes. Each session began and ended with participants providing updates on significant events since the last meeting, and planning for the next session. The discussions were conducted in Cantonese, and full transcripts were prepared after each meeting. Two individual interviews were also conducted to gather personal insights not suitable for group settings. All discussions were transcribed in Chinese, with relevant portions translated to English for analysis. 2) CHALLENGES The research team faced significant difficulties recruiting participants with BD for the study, which involved screening, questionnaires, and lab tasks. Barriers included: 1. COVID-19 outbreaks in Hong Kong, including the 4th and 5th waves starting in 2022. 2. Campus access restrictions, requiring negative tests and vaccination proof. 3. Prospective participants' lack of interest due to pandemic-related concerns (e.g., staying vigilant against the pandemic, household’s finance) and their mental health challenges. The "BIOPAC" dynamometer for the "Effort Discounting Task" was faulty in November 2021. Participant recruitment was suspended for two months due to hardware issues and resumed in January 2022, but stopped again in February 2022 due to the COVID-19 outbreak. A part-time student was hired to promote the project and recruit participants, using posters and social media outreach. A promotional plan was developed, including posting flyers on the university campus and reaching out to community centres and leisure groups. The project was also introduced on social media pages for people and artists with BD, inviting them to participate. 3) BEYOND ACHIEVING THE OBJECTIVES To disseminate the research findings to the public, a 6-day art exhibition was held from 24 June 2022 to 29 June 2022 on the university campus. Ten participants with BD joined the exhibition to showcase their creative works and share their recovery stories through the exhibited artwork and accompanying narratives. Other activities (e.g., human library, presenting conference, items published in local Chinese newspaper) were completed to create a greater impact on different sectors of the community.

17615019.label: Major findings and research outcome
17615019.value: Regarding the first objective, the quantitative study produced two sets of findings. The first set of findings examined the relationship among bipolar disorders (BD), creativity, ambition, and socioeconomic factors. The full sample consisted of 151 participants. The BD group had lower education and employment levels, and higher manic symptoms, but no significant differences in creativity compared to the non-BD group. However, decision-tree analysis revealed that for highly ambitious individuals, creativity was high regardless of BD status. However, for those with low ambition, higher education was associated with greater creativity in the non-BD group compared to the BD group. Further analysis showed the links among creativity, ambition, and education were stronger for the non-BD group. The second set of findings focused on the relationship among BD, creativity, ambition, effort-based decision-making, and exploration in a sample of 113 participants (44 BD, 69 non-BD). 38 individuals were excluded because the grip trial did not meet the required threshold and did not show enough variation. There were no significant differences in creativity, ambition, or decision-making measures between BD and non-BD participants. A decision-tree algorithm found that ambition was the strongest predictor of creativity - those with higher ambition showed greater creative accomplishment, regardless of BD status. Among low-ambition participants, the non-BD group was more creative. For highly ambitious individuals, higher effort was linked to lower creativity, but maintaining a balance between exploration and exploitation allowed for strong creativity outcomes. Regarding the second objective, the qualitative study revealed four main themes related to ambition, bipolarity, and creativity. 1) Participants viewed creativity as a safe outlet to express their emotions, with creativity fluctuating alongside mood episodes. 2) They pursued ambitious creative goals during mood episodes, driven by meaningfulness and determination, though these tasks were often challenging. 3) Creativity was seen as healing and facilitating self-understanding. 4) Sharing creative work online fostered connection, confidence, and the ability to impact others. This project made unique contributions, including a focus on drawing and writing, an innovative decision-tree algorithm approach, and a participatory photovoice methodology. Initiatives to reduce stigma, such as an art exhibition and human library, provided a platform for participants to share their experiences and challenge societal misconceptions about BD. Overall, the findings reveal the complex interplay among ambition, bipolar status, socioeconomic factors, social connection, and creative potential. To our knowledge, this represented the first study to investigate these issues among Chinese participants with and without BD.

17615019.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17615019.value: The findings highlight the complex, multifaceted relationship among mood changes, ambition, decision-making, and creativity in individuals with bipolar disorders (BD). Ambition, characterized by a strong desire for success and determination, appears to be a driving force that can transcend the challenges of the illness while also leveraging the potential benefits of mood variability to further support their creative accomplishments. We make four recommendations: 1) Deepen the understanding of these dynamics, cross-cultural studies involving diverse individuals could provide insights into the connections among ambition, creative expression, mood episodes, and the recovery process. 2) Investigate the long-term effects of sustained creative engagement may determine if it contributes to greater stability, resilience, and improved functioning over time. 3) Explore the integration of technology, such as mobile apps or virtual platforms, into creative interventions for individuals with BD could enhance accessibility, engagement, and self-expression. 4) Finally, public education efforts highlighting the unique creative journey of individuals with BD, including their creativity, ambition, and self-management, can challenge prevailing stereotypes and foster greater public understanding. Collectively, these suggestions can advance the understanding of BD and lay the groundwork for developing innovative, multimodal methods to assist the well-being and creative potential of individuals living with this condition.

17615019.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17615019.value: This mixed-method study explored the connections among bipolar disorders (BD), creativity, ambition, and other factors. The quantitative results showed that while people with BD had lower education and employment levels, their creativity levels were similar to those without BD. High ambition was linked to strong creativity regardless of diagnosis status. But for people with lower ambition, higher education was associated with greater creativity in the non-BD group. Additionally, highly ambitious people tended to have lower creativity when they put in too much effort, though finding the right balance between exploration and taking risks allowed for high creativity. The qualitative findings revealed that participants viewed creativity as a safe way to express their emotions, with their creative output fluctuating alongside their mood changes. They pursued ambitious creative goals, driven by a sense of purpose and determination. Participants saw creativity as healing and helping them better understand themselves. Sharing their creative work online also fostered connection, confidence, and impact on others. Overall, this study highlights the complex interplay between BD and creative potential. The findings challenge negative stereotypes about people with mental illness and provide novel insights, likely representing the first investigation of these issues among Chinese participants with and without BD.

17615419.label: Project Objectives
17615419.value: Re-examine intellectual leadership in the post-Soviet context of higher education and explore challenges experienced by young scholars in joining the global networks of science and innovation. 17615419.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17615419.value: This study will explore how young scholars of post-Soviet universities conceptualize and build capacities for intellectual leadership in the age of globalization. The research on de-Sovietization of higher education shows a big gap between generations of academics driven by different expectations, experiences and accomplishments. Many seasoned scholars are still disconnected from the global discourse in their disciplines and shape environments that preclude trans-boundary exploration and collaboration. In the absence of globally-minded mentorship, young scholars are vulnerable in their efforts to enable innovative ideas, as well as lead interdisciplinary explorations in global networks of science. Transgressing boundaries often implies for young scholars to break the norms controlled by the local hierarchies. According to the Soviet standards, leadership still denotes bureaucratic control and compliance rather than experimentation with curricula, research agendas, academic service and community outreach. To advance new benchmarks of academic practice, the post-Soviet institutions require a new framework for evaluation and empowerment of transformative leadership. This study will shed light on competing expectations and emerging strategies in resolving the problems of leadership in the post-Soviet space of higher education. The analysis will be guided by data from semi-structured interviews with young scholars in China, Georgia, Russia and Ukraine. By engaging representatives from the faculties of social sciences, humanities and arts, health sciences, science and engineering, this project will illuminate epistemological and cultural variations in leadership conceptualization and capacity building for more openness and global engagement. Moreover, the cross-country empirical data will provide an opportunity for comparison of intellectual leadership perspectives across higher education systems that differ politically, economically, and culturally. The focus on intellectual leadership provides an exceptional opportunity to understand inter-generational tensions in creating opportunities for globally-linked research in post-Soviet universities. By delving into young scholars’ experiences and expectations, this study will elucidate best practices and challenges in creating transformative intellectual space and guidance in post-Soviet academic communities. Insights from the post-Soviet scholars will also allow to re-examine the premises of intellectual leadership that are discussed in the literature on global higher education. This study will show how and why local and international perspectives on knowledge production, academic service, and public contribution come into conflict at times, and where they converge for productive and sustainable impact. In the long run, this project will galvanize a discourse on freedoms and duties of young academics in reintegrating local institutions and epistemic communities with global networks of science and innovation. 本研究将阐明后苏联时代高等教育应对领导力问题的矛盾期待和新兴策略。本文的分析基于有中国、格鲁吉亚、俄罗斯和乌克兰的年轻学者参与的半结构访谈数据。通过分析社会科学、人文艺术、健康科学、科学与工程等学院的代表学者的观点，本文将说明认识论和文化的因素如何影响学者对领导力的构想，以及如何促进包括开放性和全球参与方面在内的能力发展。另外，作者将利用跨国实证数据，对比在政治、经济和文化各异的高等教育系统中，学者对智力型领导力的看法。

17615419.label: Realisation of objectives
17615419.value: This project commenced shortly before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, which had a profound impact on the post-Soviet region, where public healthcare infrastructure and internet connectivity were already strained. The PI's planned travels were severely disrupted for two years, necessitating the engagement of local researchers who were able to maintain connections with their colleagues. Despite these efforts, the local outreach was often hindered by the fluidity of schedules and the fear of virus transmission, leading to disruptions in normal work and the closure of public spaces and facilities that could be used for interviews. The interviewees were often reported to get sick or had to take care of their families and thus were unable to contribute to the interview process fully or timely. In February 2022, the war in Ukraine further worsened research conditions within the region while creating major disturbances for the interview processes in Ukraine and Russia. The pandemic and war urged for investigation of new conceptual and practical dilemmas that related to organizational legacies and challenges and thus stimulated to go deeper into the new topics. Despite the tremendous challenges related to this conflict, the research objectives remained steadfast, and the PI is grateful to the EdUHK and RGC for providing additional time to collect and analyze data. All three objectives of the research project were successfully accomplished, as outlined below: 1/ The project re-examined the concept of intellectual leadership in the post-Soviet context of higher education, drawing on case studies from Georgia, Lithuania, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, Ukraine, and Uzbekistan. This analysis explored the challenges faced by senior and junior faculty members as they strive to join global networks of science and innovation. 2/ Building on the collected data, the PI was able to re-conceptualize the relationship between intellectual leadership and institutional leadership and administration. Specific concerns around academic freedom and institutional rigidity were addressed in detail through several research papers. The study also explored the role of epistemological communities and their path dependencies in shaping academic leadership through knowledge production, boundary transgression, academic citizenship, and public intellectualism. 3/ The published papers have contributed to a cross-cultural discourse on the challenges of capacity-building for intellectual leadership in post-Soviet systems of higher education where institutional transformations are weak and inconsistent and are affected by multiple economic and political disruptions. This discourse allows for enhancing the comprehension of the complex dynamics managed by leading scholars and their students and provides valuable insights for policymakers and educators seeking to develop effective strategies for promoting intellectual leadership.

17615419.label: Major findings and research outcome
17615419.value: The research project has had a profound and far-reaching impact on our understanding of intellectual leadership in the post-Soviet context of higher education. The project's findings have shed new light on the complex challenges faced by senior and junior faculty members as they strive to join global networks of science and innovation. By examining case studies from Georgia, Lithuania, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, Ukraine, and Uzbekistan, the project has provided valuable insights into the intricate issues surrounding institutional transformations where prominent scholars pursue opportunities for academic freedom and global engagement. One of the key findings of the project is that intellectual leadership is not solely the domain of senior faculty members, but is also a crucial aspect of academic citizenship and public intellectualism displayed by younger colleagues who engage in institutional transformations. This cumulative approach to intellectual leadership highlights the importance of seeing the processes of capacity-building for intellectual leadership as collective, cross-generational, and multi-layered. Furthermore, this perspective challenges traditional notions of intellectual leadership as a singular, individualistic endeavor, instead emphasizing the importance of transnational knowledge production and collaboration. The project also showed that boundary transgression, as observed in interdisciplinary and international initiatives, is an important factor in intellectual leadership. However, rigid institutions cherishing the Soviet legacy often deny opportunities for policymakers and educators who pursue global science and networking. This highlights the need for post-Soviet reformers to develop mindful strategies for fostering a culture of innovation and experimentation in the entire academic ecosystem rather than exceptional centres of excellence. The project's findings have emphasized the importance of capacity-building for research education and internationalization in social sciences and humanities as a key factor in enhancing the global engagement of post-Soviet researchers. The project's findings have also underscored the importance of addressing the historical legacies of institutional rigidity and limited academic freedom in post-Soviet systems of higher education. By recognizing the complex interplay between institutional structures, cultural norms, and historical contexts, policymakers and educators can develop more effective strategies for promoting institutional transformation and intellectual leadership.

17615419.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17615419.value: This research project has opened up new avenues for further inquiry into the complex dynamics of intellectual leadership in the post-Soviet context of higher education. Future research could explore the specific ways in which institutional leaders and policymakers can foster a culture of globally-oriented innovation and experimentation, promoting intellectual leadership and academic citizenship by global standards rather than by the old templates of institutional relations. Additionally, studies could investigate the role of international collaborations and global engagement in enabling modern standards of organizational work in academic institutions and redefining epistemological communities. Furthermore, studies could investigate the experiences of junior faculty members and their role in promoting intellectual leadership, as well as the impact of capacity-building initiatives on their professional development and academic productivity. Moreover, future research could explore the intersection between intellectual leadership and other factors, such as student engagement, community outreach, and interdisciplinary research, to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics at play in post-Soviet systems of higher education. By exploring these areas, researchers can continue to shed light on the challenges and opportunities facing post-Soviet systems of higher education, ultimately informing policy and practice aimed at promoting intellectual leadership and academic excellence.

17615419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17615419.value: This research project has explored how intellectual leadership emerges and works at universities in post-Soviet countries. The study has exemplified various contextual conditions shaping professorial abilities and responsibilities to drive innovation and knowledge creation at institutions which are often regarded as affected by the administrative legacy of closed-mindedness and rigidity. The significance of this study is that it highlights the importance of academic freedom in developing globally-minded collaborations in post-soviet academic institutions. It shows that intellectual leadership is not just the domain of senior professors, but also involves younger colleagues who are working together to transform their institutions for greater public and international engagement. The cross-generational dynamics often create unexpected developments, which can have either positive or negative effects. Rather than being enforced or regulated, intellectual leaders achieve success when idea-generations are driven by freedom of expression, creativity, and collegial support. The significance of the project lies in its exploration of how different academic stakeholders and their leaders work together and create a collective agency to drive innovation and knowledge creation at their institutions.

17616419.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17616419.value: 在虚拟实境环境中的交互常常会导致晕动症，有时被称为虚拟实境晕动症。一个主要的原因被认为是冲突的感知反馈，这是由不匹配的模拟的和物理的自我运动引起的。在一个环境中模拟运动是虚拟实境应用的一个优势，但这种情况不可避免地会造成感知线索之间的非自然冲突。 当感知冲突无法避免时，感知冲突的理解和体验仍有可能被影响。本研究借鉴了可能与晕动症相关的知觉特性研究的思路，如临场感、视觉引起的移动、以及视觉诱发的姿势反应 。观察到的这些特性的自顶向下的影响可能同样调节感知冲突对虚拟实境晕动症的影响。 虚拟实境的应用需要临场感与沉浸感，但可能会增加对冲突感知线索的敏感度。临场感被证明会被一些自顶向下的因素例如逼真性影响，逼真性几乎和自我运动的低层线索无关。本研究将会操纵影响临场感的因素，并测试是否临场感更好会导致更多的虚拟实境晕动症。 在虚拟实境中模拟的自运动通常被看作为观察者在固定环境中的移动，但也可以被理解为周围环境的移动，后者应该较不易引起晕动症。以往的研究显示环境和预期可以调节感知到的移动以及姿势反应。本研究将测试在虚拟实境中对一个任务的高层理解是否可以调节模拟自我运动时的晕动症。 在虚拟实境显示器里绘制虚拟的鼻子曾经被发现会减少晕动症，但是关于这个效应的可靠性和普遍性所知甚少。本研究将研究这个效应以及它如何普遍化。 个体表现出对虚拟实境晕动症的很大的敏感性差异。可靠地预测晕动症可以有助于鉴别有风险的个体，以及有助于理解潜在起因。各研究间控制条件的聚合数据会被分析用于测试基于姿势不稳定性、视觉诱发的姿势反应、和临场感的潜在预测因子。

17616419.label: Realisation of objectives
17616419.value: Objective 1: Presence and cybersickness We completed two experiments that tested whether visual realism affects cybersickness. Visual realism has been found to increase presence, so varying visual realism provides a way to manipulate presence in a controlled way. Neither experiment found evidence that visual realism affects cybersickness. The first experiment tested a modest difference in realism and found a null effect. This was reported in the mid-term report. We then performed a second preregistered experiment with a more extreme difference between realistic and unrealistic conditions and still found no effect. We will present these results at the Annual Meeting of the Vision Sciences Society (VSS) in May 2024 and are currently preparing a manuscript for submission. Based on our results and other recent findings, we suspect that sense of presence does not directly affect cybersickness. The reported correlations in previous studies may reflect dependence on similar factors rather than a causal relationship. Objective 2: Imagined self vs world motion We did not pursue this planned line of research. Instead, we conducted other research on the role of attention in cybersickness: the experiments reported in Yip & Saunders (2023), and an ongoing study on the effect of multi-modal cue congruence. At the start of the grant period, we discovered a recent study that suggested that attention to the visual periphery during simulated motion could reduce cybersickness. The previous study was only correlational and did not test this directly. We attempted to manipulate attention to central or peripheral vision experimentally. This was not part of the original grant proposal. Our first experiment, reported in the mid-term report, found no effect on cybersickness, but may not have manipulated attention. Our second experiment used a stronger manipulation of attention and observed a clear effect: focused attention to the central visual field reduced cybersickness. This is a novel finding and contrary to hypothesis of the previous study that inspired our study. We also failed to replicated the correlational results from the previous study. The results from these experiments have been published in Cognitive Research: Principles & Implications (Yip & Saunders, 2023) and were presented at VSS in 2023. Objective 3: effect of virtual nose on cybersickness We used the registered report format to investigate the question of whether a virtual nose reduces cybersickness. Registered reports go through the peer-review process before data collection. This is helpful to avoid a bias against reporting null results. Another group recently reported a benefit from a virtual nose (Weinrich et al, 2022). However, their study was very underpowered, and our pilot testing suggested that the effect may not reliable. We submitted a registered report to Cognitive Research: Principles & Implications and received in-principle-acceptance in Oct 2023. In-principle-acceptance means that the journal has committed to publishing our results provided that we adhere to our research and analysis plan and draw appropriate conclusions from the results. We completed data collection in Jan 2024 and are near completion of the final report. The results will be reported at VSS in May 2024, and the final report will be published by CRPI in 2024. We did not find any evidence that a virtual nose reduces cybersickness, despite having good power to detect an effect. We suspect that the previous reports of a benefit from a virtual nose were false positives. The lack of effect of a virtual nose is a further reason to doubt that there is a direct relationship between presence and cybersickness. Objective 4: individual differences in cybersickness We plan to complete this objective after finishing some additional data collection. The proposed study uses pooled data across multiple studies to test possible predictors of cybersickness. Data collection for the virtual nose study was only recently completed, and two other cybersickness studies are ongoing. We will complete the analyses for Study 4 after completing this data collection. Other published research The grant funded a graduate student research project on navigation in virtual reality that was not related to the specific aims of the project. The navigation study was published in the Journal of Environmental Psychology (Chan, Ding & Saunders, 2023). The funding also supported an unrelated student-led project on the attentional blink that was published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception & Performance (Chan & Saunders, 2023).

17616419.label: Major findings and research outcome
17616419.value: Some of the major findings were null results. We failed to replicate a previously reported finding that a virtual nose can reduce cybersickness (Objective 3). We also found no effect of visual realism on cybersickness (Objective 1), which was contrary to expectations based on some previous findings. In both cases, the previous evidence came from underpowered studies. The null results from our studies shows that there is a need for preregistered studies with good statistical power in this area of research. Publication of our virtual nose study will be a valuable contribution even though the results cast doubt on a potentially promising intervention. The initial reports of a virtual nose effect received coverage in the popular press, and were even the basis for a patent application, despite the fact the effect was not well established. Our results show that this enthusiasm was premature. Using a peer-reviewed protocol, we found no evidence of a benefit from a virtual nose. Similar null findings may have gone unreported due to publication bias. By conducting a registered report, we ensured that results would be published even though no benefit from virtual nose was observed. In our study of the effect of attentional distribution on cybersickness (Yip & Saunders, 2023), we discovered that cybersickness was reduced when participants performed a task that required a narrow focus of attention. This is a novel finding with potential for further investigation, as discussed in the next section. Our study is one of the few published studies to investigate the effect of attention on cybersickness. The multiple experiments performed for this project have generated a data set to be used for analysis of individual differences (Objective 4). Although the grant period has ended, we are still collecting data for some related studies. We plan to do the analysis of individual differences when we have a larger data set.

17616419.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17616419.value: In a new GRF grant application, I have proposed studies to follow-up on the findings reported in Yip & Saunders (2023). Our published study compared attentional tasks that encouraged either a narrow or wide distribution of attention, and found that cybersickness was reduced with a narrow focus of attention. One possible explanation is that a narrow focus of attention acts like a restricted field of view, attenuating motion signals from the periphery. Alternatively, the effect could be due to a difference between the cognitive load imposed by the two tasks. Few studies have investigated the effect of cognitive load on cybersickness, and previous findings have been mixed. The follow-up experiments proposed in my new grant application will manipulate cognitive load and compare conditions that would direct attention toward or away from the virtual scene. Although the time period for this project has ended, we will still perform the planned analysis of postural control data across experiments. The results will likely provide some insight to whether postural instability measures can predict individual differences in tendency toward cybersickness.

17616419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17616419.value: We conducted experiments to investigate possible factors that could affect motion sickness in virtual reality (cybersickness). The factors included: visual realism of the virtual displays, the presence of a rendered nose (virtual nose), and the spatial distribution of attention (narrow vs wide). We found that cybersickness was not affected by visual realism or the presence of a virtual nose. Taken together, these results suggest that sense of presence is not directly related to cybersickness. The lack of benefit from a virtual nose is contrary to some previously reports. We suspect that the previously reported results were false positives. Our study was preregistered and had better statistical power than the one other published study. Our study of the effect of attention found that cybersickness was reduced with a narrow focus of attention. This is a novel finding that suggests some directions for further research. We collected data that can be used for an analysis of how individual differences in posture control are related to differences in motion sickness susceptibility. This analysis will be performed used pooled data from multiple experiments after some ongoing experiments are completed.

17616519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17616519.value: 自2015年來，世界頂尖的媒體公司推出了數款高質素的虛擬實境（VR）裝置。Facebook（Oculus Rift and Go），谷歌（Daydream），三星（Gear VR），HTC（Vive和Vive Pro）和索尼（PlayStation VR）的產品令虛擬實境（VR）能被普及於大眾使用。這引發了VR製作的內容的爆炸性增長，並創造了一種新形式的紀錄和敘事方法：電影虛擬實境（CVR）。 如之前出現的新主流媒體（印刷，廣播，電影，電視，互聯網）一樣，VR和CVR電影將改變我們如何展現現實，回憶過去，和想像虛擬世界。CVR電影與之前的深入式敘事方法一樣，甚至更大程度地顛覆我們批判的距離和批判性思維。我們迫切需要對CVR電影片提出一些批判分析的方法。這項目提倡定義CVR電影的術語，從而提供更好地辨識和提出批判CVR電影的證據。 沒有人能比Facebook更廣泛地於財務和戰略方面投放資源於VR。作為未來主義者，首席執行官馬克·扎克伯格將虛擬實境視為他的平台和人機界面的未來。社交媒體已經對我們的文化，社會和政治產生了巨大的影響。現實與故事，事實與假新聞之間的界限日益消失。在這情況下，人文學科必須跟上文化生產的技術發展步伐。我們必須提供工具和培訓，以便對目前以電影虛擬實境形式發展的新媒介進行批判性分析。

17616519.label: Realisation of objectives
17616519.value: 1. Cinematic Virtual Reality (CVR) encompasses linear narrative in virtual reality that use and extend form and style developed in the medium of feature film to create immersive and embodied storytelling. These cinematic elements include narrative form, mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing, and sound. Based on this definition of CVR, the PI will start a new research center at the University of Hong Kong to support and disseminate future research on the new medium. 2.We have created a comprehensive CVR database, which includes currently more than 1100 CVR films and experiences. The database includes key filmographic data and, if available, the link to the online stream. The database continues to be regularly updated as new CVR works are released. To our knowledge, this is the largest database on CVR in existence. Upon publication of the main research output of the GRF project (see #7), the database will be made available to the public through the website of the new research center. The database will be an essential online resource for film and media scholars, practitioners engaged in the production and distribution of CVR content, as well as the public interested in learning about and experiencing CVR. 3. We have systematically evaluated CVR films and experiences regarding their contribution to the development of CVR film form, collecting paradigmatic examples of the use of mise-en-scène, cinematography, editing, and sound in CVR. CVR film form includes the adaptation of conventional film form and the development of formal style unique to the new medium of CVR. The research on CVR film form focuses on documenting and analyzing the specificity of the new medium, namely the immersive and embodied experience of narrative. The research on CVR film form will be published in a monograph (see #7). Preliminary findings on CVR film form and style have been presented at one international conference and two invited lectures: Gruenewald, Tim and Cecilia Chen. "Virtual Reality as a Memory Machine." Seventh Annual Meeting of the Memory Studies Association, Newcastle, UK, June 2023. Gruenewald, Tim. “Narrative Virtual Reality” School of Journalism and Communication, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, 3 November 2021. “Cinematic Virtual Reality: Emergence of a New Narrative Medium.” Academy for Creative Media, University of Hawaii, 4 May 2021. 4. We have identified, defined, and described the genres prevalent among CVR films to date. So far, we have identified the following genres in CVR: Action, Animation, Anime, Comedy, Crime and Mystery, CVR of Attraction, Detective, Documentary, Drama, Educational, Experimental, Fantasy, Historical, Horror, Humanitarian, Memoir, Nature, Romance, Music Promotion, Science Fiction, Theatre, Thriller. The films and experiences in our CVR database are all assigned to one or more genres, which is a key feature to make the database more valuable for researchers and the public. The topic of CVR genres will also be introduced in the monograph (see#7). 5. We define CVR style as the systematic use of CVR film form to achieve aesthetic goals. While CVR is still a young medium, we have identified emerging styles in the works of a small group of CVR filmmakers and production studios. Second, we have analyzed styles of CVR filmmaking in the context of two genres: First, in the humanitarian CVR film in the published journal article "Feeling good: Humanitarian virtual reality film, emotional style and global citizenship" (co-authored with Saskia Witteborn, Cultural Studies, 36.1 2022, 141-161) Abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) film has been described as an empathy machine. Filmmakers and producers have claimed that VR film’s immersive qualities can amplify empathy for victims of humanitarian crises and move the viewer to support humanitarian aid organizations. This paper questions these transformative assumptions about VR film. We call attention to how humanitarian VR films are techniques that promote emotional styles like empathy through the script of suffering and hope. Through analysis of humanitarian VR films, the use of character, narrative, and formal VR film devices, we show how empathy is created. Thereby, we focus specifically on the simulation of particular locales, intimate encounters with the suffering Other, and gratification of viewer needs. Second, in an article on the traumatic memory in CVR film in the article "The VR Memory Machine: Traumatic Memory and Narrative Virtual Reality" (co-authored with Cecilia Chen, currently under review). Abstract: In recent years, a new narrative medium has been developing in the form of cinematic virtual reality film (CVR film). Early VR filmmakers have shown much interest in memory. We argue that CVR is a memory machine, meaning that it affords authors certain narrative opportunities of sharing real or imagined memories unlike any other narrative medium. The primary and unique characteristic of narrative VR is that it enables an embodied experience of narrative, which has privileged memory as a significant theme. We will show how traumatic memory functions in two innovative CVR films. First, The Book of Distance (2020, 25 minutes) recreates in VR the family history of writer and creator Randall Okita, centering on his grandfather, who emigrated from Hiroshima to Canada during the 1930s. Second, Is Anna Ok? (2018, 21 minutes), visualizes the memories of twin sisters Anna and Lauren Khan, who experienced a traumatic accident that left Anna with brain injury. 6. We have collected existing technical terms and defined new terms to describe film form specific to CVR. Such terminology is required for the analysis of CVR to name and discuss elements such as immersive 360° diegetic space, the cinematic construction of the spectator in narrative VR, forms of interactivity and viewer agency, to name just a few examples. Those terms will be introduced in the monograph on CVR film form (see #7). Upon publication of the monograph, the terminology database will be published online through the new CVR research center at HKU. 7. The main outcome of this GRF project is a comprehensive introduction into cinematic virtual reality from a film studies perspective. The monograph contains six chapters: 1. Introduction to CVR: Basic Concepts and Brief History, 2. Mise-en-Scène, 3. Cinematography, 4. Editing, 5. Sound, 6. Conclusion: CVR Film Form, Style, and Genre The monograph publishes the key research findings of the GRF project. It contributes to defining and theorizing CVR as a new narrative medium and provides the theoretical and methodological instruments required for further research on CVR. The manuscript is 80% complete and is expected to be ready for submission to an academic press during Q1 of 2024. The completion of the monograph manuscript has been delayed for two reasons. First, the rapid expansion of CVR film production has been unexpected and overwhelming (as documented in the extensive CVR film database.) The text corpus to be considered and analyzed for the monograph has significantly increased accordingly and is demanding more time than originally scheduled. Second, the PI has prioritized the publication of two journal articles for strategic reasons. VR technology and CVR production and distribution is progressing and changing so rapidly that it is advantageous to first complete shorter research outputs that can be published faster and generate greater impact in a quickly emerging field of research by exploiting the first-mover advantage (see #5 for titles and abstracts.)

17616519.label: Major findings and research outcome
17616519.value: This GRF project has compiled a comprehensive database of Cinematic Virtual Reality (CVR) films, and it has theorized CVR film form, style, and narrative. The database contains 1130 entries, including key filmographic data and file location for films with online access. The database begins with the VR experience Hunger in Los Angeles (dir. Nonny de la Peña) from 2012, includes VR films released in recent months, and continues to be updated. The VR database documents the dynamic growth during the past eight years with only nine films completed from 2012 to 2014. 2015 marks a tipping point with 43 films added and more than 100 films per year since 2016. The CVR database also documents the breath of film production spanning the entire globe and most established genres from conventional film. The database is the foundation on which the project's research on CVR film form and style was built and it will become a foundational resource for the emerging field of CVR film studies upon its online publication. More than 100 films were selected from the CVR film database for their historical significance or contribution to the development of CVR film form. They have been analyzed in order to define the formal language of CVR film according to the four categories mise-en-scène, cinematography, editing, and sound. The research shows how CVR filmmakers have developed techniques for each category to take advantage of the unique immersive and embodied experiences that CVR makes possible. For example, we show how aspects of mise-en-scène, such as lighting or staging, are used to direct the attention of the viewer within the 360° virtual space. An important example of cinematography is camera movement and position in relation to other characters, which filmmakers employ to shape the subject position of the immersant. Editing is used radically differently in CVR film compared to conventional film due to the embodied nature of the new medium. We show how conventions emerge that either attempt to mask or take advantage of the immersant's impression of being literally teleported to a different place. Sound is used in many innovative ways, for example, to orient the immersant in the diegetic world, to create continuity, or to design interactivity. Finally, the research outputs demonstrate how CVR filmmakers combine CVR film techniques strategically to create a distinct style that supports immersive and embodied experience of narrative.

17616519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17616519.value: The research outcomes of this GRF project pave the way for the emerging field of CVR film studies. First, CVR film studies applies existing film and media studies methodologies to the new medium of narrative CVR. Second, CVR film studies develops new theories and terminologies specific to the new medium that help understand its unique immersive, embodied, and interactive experiences of narrative. The GRF project has provided the PI and his team with a substantial head start in CVR film studies research. To further capitalize on this unique advantage, the PI is setting up a Center for Narrative Virtual Reality Research at The University of Hong Kong. This will allow the PI and HKU to leverage the project outcomes in several ways: 1. Attract outstanding postgraduate students and postdoctoral researchers 2.Network with and invite world-leading researchers and practitioners in CVR 3.Attract external funding to support the Center's research and other activities 4. Provide resources for the use of CVR in teaching and learning (for example, workshops) to universities in Hong Kong Finally, the PI is planning on submitting a follow up GRF application in October 2024 to further research important emerging genres in CVR.

17616519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17616519.value: Overall, this GRF project has documented, described, analyzed, and theorized the emergence of a new narrative medium: Cinematic Virtual Reality (CVR). It has compiled a database of currently more than 1100 CVR films, including key filmographic data. The prevalent genres in CVR have been identified and all database entries have been assigned to one or more genres. Drawing selected films from the CVR database, the formal language of CVR has been identified, described, and analyzed according to the four categories mise-en-scène, cinematography, editing, and sound. The research has shown how CVR filmmakers have developed techniques for each category to take advantage of the unique immersive and embodied experiences that CVR makes possible. In a second step, we have analyzed key examples to show how CVR techniques are coordinated to create distinct styles in support of CVR narratives. The research outputs include two journal articles and one monograph, which focus on the specificity of the new medium and explain how filmmakers create immersive and embodied virtual experiences. The research theorizes the viewer as an immersant who becomes part of a narrative's virtual world and always has at least some degree of agency over the experience through interaction.

17616619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17616619.value: While low level of concerns about the potential threat of cancer recurrence is a normal, realistic response, high fear of cancer recurrence can be detrimental, affecting individuals’ quality of life and functional capacity. Locally, one in four cancer survivors reported high fear of cancer recurrence. Patients with high fear of cancer recurrence report excessive intrusive thoughts which often lack identifiable triggers, making them difficult to dismiss. The manifestations of fear of cancer recurrences share similar characteristics of other emotional disorders such as anxiety and depression. Therefore, it may be useful to apply a theoretical model which explains the development and maintenance of emotional disorders. The Self-Regulatory Executive Function (S-REF) model adopted a transdiagnostic approach attempting to identify features that cut across different emotional disorders. S-REF suggests that metacognitive beliefs about negative thinking play an essential role to the development and maintenance of emotional disorders as these metacognitive beliefs promote intrusive thinking. A S-REF model based, manualized intervention, namely ConquerFear, was recently developed to reduce fear of cancer recurrence. So far, the effectiveness of the intervention had only been tested on longer-term cancer survivors. Fear of cancer recurrence is often chronic leading to disabling, suggesting early intervention targeting to promote strategies for controlling worry and managing unhelpful beliefs about worry may be beneficial to prevent persistent fear of cancer recurrence. The present study, using randomized controlled trial approach, aims to assess the effect of ConquerFear intervention on fear of cancer recurrence among Chinese patients newly diagnosed with curable cancer. We aims to (1) test the direct effect of ConquerFear intervention on fear of cancer recurrence and on maladaptive metacognition, and (2) to test the indirect effect of Conquerfear intervention on fear of cancer recurrence through its effect on maladaptive metacognition. Eligible participants are Chinese patients newly diagnosed with curative breast or colorectal cancer, completed the primary surgery within 6 months, and with the cut-off scored ≥ 13 on the Fear of Cancer Recurrence Inventory-Short Form. 174 eligible participants will be randomly allocated into either the ConquerFear intervention or the active control relaxation intervention. Both interventions consist of 5 individual face-to-face sessions over 10 weeks. Participants agreeing to participate will complete the Fear of Cancer Recurrence Inventory (primary outcome measure) and Metacognition Questionnaire (process outcome measure) at baseline, immediate post-intervention, 3rd months and 6th months post intervention. 對於癌症復發的潛在威脅有輕微擔心是正常及合理的反應，但對癌症復發有高度的恐懼就可能危害健康，影響個人的生活素質及能力。本港每四位癌症倖存者當中就有一位對癌症復發有高度的恐懼。這些患者指出他們有過多侵入性想法，而這些想法通常沒有明確的觸發原因，從而難以消除。癌症復發的恐懼所呈現的方式跟焦慮症及抑鬱症等其他情緒相關的疾病有類似的特徵。因此，使用解釋情緒病發展和持續的理論模型有助於理解癌症復發的恐懼。 自我控制執行功能(S-REF)的模式採用了一種跨診斷的方法去識別不同情緒病中共同的特徵。在S-REF的模式裏，有關消極想法的後設認知信念會助長侵入性思想，從而影響到情緒病的發展及持續 。「克服恐懼」是一套基於S-REF模式建立的指引性介入，旨在減少患者對癌症復發的恐懼。目前為止，「克服恐懼」這套介入已知有效的對象只有癌症長期倖存者。癌症復發的恐懼對生活造成的影響大多是慢性的，所以在早期進行一些控制憂慮及管理無益想法的介入可以更有效預防對癌症復發的持續恐懼。 本研究利用隨機對照試驗方式去評估「克服恐懼」介入對新診斷為可治癒癌症的中國患者的癌症復發恐懼的影響。本研究旨在 (1) 測試「克服恐懼」介入對癌症復發恐懼及不當後設認知的直接效果；以及(2) 測試「克服恐懼」介入透過對不當的後設認知的效果，從而影響癌症復發恐懼的間接效果。患者需是新診斷患上可治癒性乳癌或結腸癌的中國患者，在過去六個月內已完成手術，及在癌症復發恐懼量表（簡短版）中取得多於十三分，才符合條件參加這個研究。174名符合條件的參加者將被隨機分配到「克服恐懼」介入組或慣常護理組。兩個組別都需要在十星期裏出席5個面對面的會談。同意參與的參加者將會在基線，完成介入當天及在介入完成後的三個月及六個月後填寫癌症復發恐懼量表 （主要評估指標）及後設認知問卷（次要評估指標）。
