17617819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17617819.value: International flows of capital, migration and other social and political forces have resulted in deep social and economic inequalities in Hong Kong society. These inequalities are reflected in Hong Kong’s schools as high numbers of children from poor families study in low-ranking schools. Academic achievement and proficiency in English language as a core subject and global lingua franca remains elusive for many in high-poverty schools, hindering students’ socioeconomic advancement in adulthood. Teaching and learning English is deeply implicated in this social stratification and educational inequality: Hong Kong therefore needs English teachers committed to social justice and inclusion to serve high-poverty schools, and teacher preparation programmes and professional development must equip English teachers with the understandings, dispositions and sustainable practices to teach for justice and inclusion. Amongst the challenges to this aim are tenuous partnerships between teacher education programmes and local schools, one-way research and development, and an English curriculum disconnected from the lives and identities of poor children and their communities. This study aims to work at the nexus of teacher education, schools and communities to develop culturally responsive, socially just and sustainable pedagogies for teaching and learning English in high-poverty primary and secondary schools in Hong Kong. One of the key principles of this study is that of participation in the research process. In this study, teams of English teachers, student-teachers and their primary and secondary school students will collaborate with teacher educators to research, interrogate and design a responsive and academically rigorous English language curriculum for children in high-poverty schools. These collaborative participatory research teams will first conduct an in-depth examination of the English language classroom and school-based English learning context, and investigate the lives of students in their classes to identify and understand students’ individual and community competencies, knowledge and other cultural, creative and intellectual resources which can enhance the learning of English. Based on the findings, each team will then engage in cycles of classroom-based action research involving planning, teaching, data collection and reflection to develop pedagogies which are context and relationship driven and which potentially transform the teaching-learning culture and pedagogic relationships therein. The study aims to develop theories of social justice teaching in English language education and impact positively upon English teaching and learning in high-poverty Hong Kong schools. Finally, the study will develop sustainable approaches for preparing teachers for high-poverty schools with diverse student populations within initial English language teacher education programmes. 國際資本的流動、移民問題以及其他社會和政治力量的參與導致了香港社會中深層次的社會和經濟不平等問題。由於大批來自貧困家庭的學童就讀於低排名學校，香港的學校亦成了這些社會經濟不平等情況的寫照。英語是一門核心學科和世界通用語，然而對於來自高度貧困學校的學童來說英語學習和能力仍然是一大困難，這阻礙了他們日後取得更高的社會經濟地位。因此，英語教學和社會分層以及教育不平等息息相關；在高度貧困學校中，對致力於實現社會公平和包容的英語老師有著強烈的需求。教師培訓和發展項目必須培養英語教師對於平等和包容的認識、信念、和可持續的教學實踐能力。達成這個目標所面臨的挑戰主要有教師教育項目和本地學校的不緊密合作，研究發展與教學實踐的脫離，以及英語課程與貧困學童的生活和身份認同及社區文化的脫節。 本研究聯結教師教育、學校和社區，意在為香港高度貧困中小學的英語教學建立符合當地文化、促進社會公平、可持續的教學法。本研究着重研究過程的參與性；研究過程中，多組英語教師、實習教師、和中小學學童與教師教育者將一起研究、探尋、設計一個互動性強並且理論嚴謹的英語語言課程。這些協同合作的研究團隊將首先深入調查英語課堂和學校的英語學習環境，了解學生的課堂生活，從而理解學生個人能力、社區生活能力、知識、以及其他文創智力資源，用以幫助英語學習。基於此研究成果，團隊將進行多輪課堂行動研究，包括設計、教學、數據收集和反思，從而建立符合情境、改變教學文化和師生關系的教學法和教學實踐。本研究意在發展出關於英語教學中社會公平的理論，並對香港高度貧困學校的英語教學產生實際影響。最後，本研究將為初期英語教師培訓項目提出可持續的教師培訓方法，以適應高度貧困學校中不同背景學生的英語學習需求。

17617819.label: Realisation of objectives
17617819.value: The Covid-19 pandemic and suspension of in-school learning from February to May 2020, school restrictions in Sept 2020 and suspensions in December 2020, posed a great challenge to the project. In Phase 1 (secondary schools), the teaching practicum was suspended. Online teaching and learning posed logistical and pedagogical challenges to the school, and to the project. Some schools needed weeks to develop ways of teaching remotely, many students could not be contacted and struggled to participate in online lessons. Gaining access to online lessons was not possible in three schools. The project’s access to students to carry out ‘funds of knowledge’ inquiry was restricted. In Phase 2 (primary schools), the teaching practicum was hampered by curriculum pressures due to the shortened school day and class suspensions. Prior to the pandemic, the social unrest in 2019 made the term ‘social justice’ contentious for some of the participating schools. To overcome these challenges, the project team made every effort to achieve the core activities of the project and develop inclusive pedagogies. A two-week (online) practicum was arranged for each school in May 2020. We adjusted the original project activities when they proved to be unfeasible, such as student participation in the research process. We sought opportunities for further engagement with students when restrictions were eased in the summer of 2021. Objective 1 Through lesson observations, teacher and student interviews and study group meetings, it was found that students’ English language learning needs were unique to the sociocultural context of the school and classroom. In most lessons observed, students were engaged and motivated to participate. Many students had limited English proficiency and low confidence in learning English, which were magnified by the fixed DSE English and textbook learning targets, and when English was the language of instruction. Thus, a significant number of students could not participate in English lessons in a meaningful way. However in School D, which served South Asian heritage students, and in School E which had a strong oral English classroom culture built over two years with their teacher, students’ higher English proficiency and fluency in spoken English allowed for engagement in richer lesson content around social issues and students’ lifeworlds. We interviewed students in (only) two secondary classes and one primary class, and four students from the other primary class. We also used online diaries for secondary students, and “instagram” profiles in a primary class to explore their funds of knowledge. Students expressed love for their English teachers and many commented on the caring and supportive school culture. For secondary students, English was the most challenging subject at school, and they often felt daunted by the demands of the DSE English exam and the high stakes on their academic careers. We found that students’ funds of knowledge were rich, challenging deficit discourses of ‘Band 3’ students: they shared their aspirations and interests, views on local and global issues, and their multilingual and multicultural identities and resources. Some shared their critiques of economic, social, gender and racial and educational inequality. Objective 2 Across the 7 schools and 8 classrooms, project teams explored different facets of enacting social justice and inclusive pedagogy. Several teams used an issue of social justice as the lesson content. They also centred students’ identities and experiences in classroom activities and developed close and trusting relationships as core principles of a social justice pedagogy. Teachers and student-teachers designed workshops and teaching strategies to widen students’ access to English as cultural and institutional capital. Student-teacher Miss J discussed with their F4 class English language stratification in Hong Kong and the impact on students’ learning trajectories; Miss Y used a Langston Hughes poem to discuss and share experiences of racism with her F2 class; and Miss R examined gender stereotyping with her P4 class through the topic of toys. Miss K, through online one-to-one interaction, became close to a few of the most disengaged students in her F2 class, which she described as a “humanising” experience. Miss C ran an after school English club for four marginalised students in her P4 class, fostering mutual affection and developing strategies for increasing participation in English classes. Teams challenged existing classroom ‘practice architectures’, for example, Miss E, a “native” English speaker, used students’ L1 (Chinese) in her lessons and engaged with her F4 students’ use of banter as a classroom participation structure. In follow up interviews with five student-teachers, meanings of social justice education developed during the project, how they are engaging with them in their current teaching posts, and how consciousness of their own identities are salient in their practice were shared. Two teachers sought teaching positions in schools serving low-income families and “Band 3” schools. They reported being more aware of issues of inclusion and justice in the teaching profession and in their school and had more confidence in raising issues with school management. Objective 3 The findings suggest that theorising English language teaching for social justice and inclusion requires challenging dominant notions of “English language” as structural and fixed, and “teaching and learning” as methods-driven, skill-based and decontextualised, and taking up more rigorously theories of language and language learning as socially, culturally and historically situated and constructed. English language teaching for social justice and inclusion to traditionally marginalised groups is founded on humanising pedagogic relations between students and teachers. Through such humanising relations, students and teachers build their practice from the funds of knowledge in their classrooms and communities, and develop responsive, local and situated pedagogies which explore and interrogate both micro-classroom practice architectures and the wider social structures that influence language learning. This includes interrogating what it means to participate in class, what ‘good behavior’ is, what one’s identity in relation to English is, how mainstream ELT pedagogies serve or not serve students, how institutional structures such as textbooks and high-stakes examinations position and serve different students, and how English manifests as both a colonial and globalised language in Hong Kong society and in teachers’ and students’ lives. Objective 4 A collaborative community of practice amongst educators and students committed to teaching for social justice and inclusion provided an educational, social and cultural context for praxis around inclusive education, strengthening school-university partnerships in the process. However, the project also highlighted the challenges of building and sustaining such a community within a university culture of competitive individualism emphasising metrics and performance, transactional approaches to school partnership, a performance-based teaching practicum, and an entrenched institutional dichotomy between research and teaching. An approach to social justice ITE should involve 1) staffing ITE programmes with social justice scholar-teachers, 2) recruiting teacher candidates from diverse cultural, linguistic and socioeconomic backgrounds, 3) forming professional partnerships with teachers and schools serving socioeconomically marginalised families and low-English proficient students 4) curriculum content which develops critical consciousness of competing epistemologies in English language education, 5) a teaching practicum which prioritises understanding students’ funds of knowledge, mentoring relationships and collaborative classroom inquiry, and; 6) extending student-teachers’ practice via service-learning (for example, the PI’s work on youth mentoring in teacher education). We acknowledge the challenge of this comprehensive approach, therefore an embedded ‘stream’ of study within initial teacher education programmes for teacher candidates who wish to develop social justice and inclusive pedagogies is recommended (Lampert & Burnett, 2016).

17617819.label: Major findings and research outcome
17617819.value: This study found that English language learners and teachers in schools serving socioeconomically marginalised face many challenges and their ‘low attainment’ was socially constructed within DSE English exam driven curriculum, global capitalism and the demand for English as an international language. Many students did not have ready access to English language environments, had very low English proficiency which often precluded their meaningful participation in English language learning. The findings challenge the stigma surrounding low-English proficient students and their disengagement in English learning. In addition students’ have multilingual resources, academic and career ambitions, a wide range of interests and hobbies, opinions and concerns about global and local issues, and reflections and views about their education and English language teaching and learning. These ‘funds of knowledge’ challenge the stereotypes and deficit discourses of children from low-SES backgrounds and ‘low-banding’ schools, and offer rich content on which to develop a more responsive English language curriculum. Student-teachers, mentor-teachers and teacher educators collaborated to develop ways of challenging English language lessons in each participating school, to develop social justice and inclusive pedagogies. These pedagogies were foremost centred on humanising relationships between teachers and students. They also prioritised students’ identities and lived experiences, engaged in issues of social justice as content for English lessons, and challenged dominant participation structures and practices of English language teaching including English-only teaching and communicative, task-based language teaching. It was found that ‘social justice’ emerged differently in each classroom context and school-based team, highlighting the sociocultural situatedness of social justice pedagogy. Two conference papers were presented reporting the findings from the project’s school-based inquiries (see Part C). Another conference paper has been proposed, reporting on how student-teachers developed humanising pedagogies and challenged aspects of mainstream English language methodology (“Language teacher education for social justice and inclusion: Humanizing English language teaching pedagogy and practice”, paper proposal submitted to Second Language Teacher Education: Challenges and New Horizons, 15-17 September 2022, University of Vienna). A book chapter is being written about how the project members grappled with shifting meanings of ‘social justice’ education and how these mapped onto the terrain of desire (“Psychoanalytic interrogations of ‘social justice’ and desire in teaching English for social justice and inclusion in Hong Kong schools.” In F. Sanjakdar, editor. Using Critical Pedagogy in Education: Global phenomenon, Local praxis. Routledge). The PI and Co-I’s will be preparing other manuscripts in the coming year.

17617819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17617819.value: Given the major disruptions to this project due to the Covid-19 pandemic and school closures, further research is needed into the experiences, needs and lifeworlds of students from grassroots families, with a specific focus on how access to English language is socioculturally and socio-politically structured in Hong Kong society and the consequences of a stratified education system. In addition, longitudinal and in-depth case studies of the development of asset-based, inclusive English language teaching in high-poverty schools are needed to further conceptualise social justice and inclusive pedagogy in English language education, and to engage with international scholarship in this area. Collaborative, participatory and community-based research is strongly recommended to address the ethical issues of traditional, one-way research. As the PI’s contract was not renewed at the university in which this project was hosted, the PI is currently engaging in collaborative research into inclusive pedagogy as an independent scholar.

17617819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17617819.value: Hong Kong needs English language teachers who are committed to equity and justice in education. This study aimed to understand the needs of English language learners and their teachers in schools serving grassroots families and other socioeconomically marginalised groups, and to develop approaches to English language teaching which values and includes all students. Teams of student-teachers, mentor teachers, teacher educators collaborated to develop ways of teaching English that respected and built upon the individual strengths of students and which challenged negative stereotypes of poor families and ‘low-band’ schools in Hong Kong society. In the classroom, student-teachers and their students discussed social issues relevant to students’ lives in the classroom and built strong and caring relationships with each other. Student-teachers learned within a community of teachers and teacher educators who embraced inclusion in their practice. The study helps to enhance English language teaching at a time when educational social advancement is elusive for many Hong Kong youth. It also suggests that university programmes which prepare English language teachers would benefit greatly from a collaborative, community-based approach, and that they must critically engage with the social inequalities created by the global market for English.

17619219.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17619219.value: 青少年期至成年早期出現的精神病，對病者的社交及情緒可以有非常深遠的影響。因此，在早年生活中，尋找出影響精神病病發率的決定性因素至為重要，讓我們可以作出篩查並及早提供治療方案。此研究計劃目的在於檢示1) 家長對子女的精神健康評估的差異；及 2) 研究此異差能否預測子女日後在成年早期出現常見精神病的機率。 一直以來，當醫護界需要評估小童的精神健康時，一般會收集小童的自我評估以及家長對小童的評估。過往研究顯示這兩份對同一位小童的精神健康評估往往出現落差。由於收取家長及小童評估的做法於國際間非常普及，弄清兩個評估中的差異與日後精神病發病率的相關性，對精神病學在理論及臨床上皆有重要性。過去的研究亦有初步證據顯示，家長與子女對子女的精神健康評估的落差與當事人的操行問題、自殺傾向、及抑鬱症有所關聯。 不過，過往對此落差的研究方法亦有一個通病。 落差通常被定義為小童及家長評估之 「得分差異 亅(a difference score approach) ；但是統計學學者指出此定義會導致不準確的研究結果。此研究計劃將會克服過往研究的通病，並成為首項在此領域中採用 「response surface analysis」 的研究方法。Response surface analysis其中一項突破就是能夠將落差分別分析為落差的「大小」及「方向」。例如，一位是明白子女的家長( 以落差「大小」為基礎) ；而另一位卻是漠視子女情緒問題的家長 (以落差「方向」為基礎) ；response surface analysis能夠分析出那類型的差異與精神健康有關聯。 要達成上述目標，我們將會用到兩個為期約十年的大型隊列研究，分別為香港的「愛┼人」隊列研究及英國的Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children。此項研究比過去研究具以下優勢：1) 約十年長遠的追蹤數據 、2) 運用response surface analysis 去全面研究家長與子女的評估差異與精神病發病的關聯、3) 於東方及西方人口中分別去求證此研究的假設。此研究項目將為青年精神病學帶來理論及統計上的突破，亦有助篩查有精神病風險的青年人。

17619319.label: Project Objectives

To determine whether and how classroom quality interacts with the home learning environment in influencing children’s English language and literacy skills and growth.

17619319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17619319.value: English is one of the official languages in Hong Kong. Proficiency in English is highly prized because the language is used not only in Government but also in the legal, professional, business and tertiary sectors. The teaching of English is prioritized and well supported in schools starting from the kindergarten years. However, there has been ongoing debate over the city's English proficiency levels among academic, business and professional communities. Early childhood is known to be a critical period for language and literacy development and can have a lasting impact. Given the potential importance of this period in the promotion of English proficiency, there is an urgent need to examine factors that contribute to the attainment and progress of English among young learners. Emerging evidence suggests that the home and school contexts are powerful influences in shaping children’s early experiences and in contributing to disparities in language and literacy development. Against this background, this study aims to examine the role of the home and school in children’s English language and literacy development and growth in Hong Kong. Specifically, it investigates the separate and combined effects of the home learning environment (e.g., parent-child activities) and classroom quality (e.g., instructional practices, materials and resources, teacher-child interactions) on children’s English language and literacy skills and growth. This three-year longitudinal study, which follows children from the time they enter kindergarten until their final year of kindergarten (i.e., K1 to K3) will adopt qualitative and quantitative methods in the analyses of data collected from: (i) parent questionnaires and interviews that tap information on family demographics and practices in the home learning environment; (ii) classroom observations; and (iii) direct assessments of children’s English language and literacy skills, namely vocabulary, phonological awareness, letter knowledge and word reading. The findings will advance the field by providing culture-specific information on the home and school setting and enabling a more nuanced understanding of children’s development of English, particularly in a context where English is used as a second or foreign language. This study will provide much needed empirical evidence for program development and policy decisions and will inform teacher practices and parental engagement in supporting early English learning. 英國語文(英語)是香港的官方語言之一。這語言不僅被政府採用，還被用於法律，專業，商業和第三産業，因此精通英語被高度重視。從幼稚園時期開始，學校已提供優先及良好的英語教學支援。然而，關於香港的英語水平在學術，商業和專業社區一直存在爭議。幼兒時期是語言和讀寫能力發展的關鍵期，並可產生長遠的影響。鑑於這可提升英語水平的關鍵期至為重要，因此有迫切需要研究有助於幼兒習得英語和學習進展的因素。越來越多的證據顯示, 家庭和學校環境對幼兒早期學習有重大的影響，因而塑造幼兒英語發展的差距。家庭和學校因素對塑造幼兒早期學習經驗及促成語言和讀寫能力發展方面的差異具有重要影響。在此背景下，本研究旨在觀察及檢視香港家庭和學校在幼兒英語發展及成長中的角色。具體而言，本研究調查家庭學習環境（例如：親子活動）和課堂的教學質量（例如：教學實踐，教材和資源，師生互動）對幼兒英語技能及發展的的獨立和綜合影響。這項為期三年的縱向研究開始於幼兒進入幼稚園初班直至最後一年的高班, 期間會採用定性和定量研究方法分析從以下方向收集的數據：（一）家長問卷調查和訪問從而深入了解有關家庭背景及在家學習環境 （二）課堂觀察 （三）評估幼兒的英語技能，即詞彙，語音意識，字母知識和文字閲讀。研究結果將透過提供有關家庭和學校環境的文化特性資料，尤其是使用英語為第二語或外語的情況下，對幼兒英語發展作更深入的了解以及推動該領域的發展。本研究將為課程發展和政策的決策提供重要實質的證據，並將奉告教師實踐及家長參與支持早期英語學習。

17619319.label: Realisation of objectives
17619319.value: The project’s objectives have been extensively addressed by considering a broad range of factors within the home and preschool learning environments and through data collected via parent questionnaire, parent and teacher interviews, classroom observations and direct child assessments. Specifically, this research examined family socioeconomic status (SES), marital satisfaction, parental beliefs and self-efficacy and home literacy practices within the home learning environment, and teacher characteristics and classroom quality within the preschool learning environment. New measurement tools have been developed to assess parental beliefs on and attitudes towards children’s English as a second language (ESL) development and to evaluate the quality of teaching practices and environments in supporting early English language and literacy development in classrooms. Data collected in this study adequately address the project objectives. As this research taps into an understudied area in Hong Kong, , analyses are under way to examine the separate and combined effects of the home and preschool learning environments on children’s ESL development. A comprehensive set of factors associated with the home learning environment and children’s English language and literacy outcomes has insofar been identified. This study was conducted during the peak periods of COVID-19 in Hong Kong. The commencement of the project was severely delayed and data was collected at a time when schools re-opened after months of closure and social distancing measures were strictly implemented. As such, strategies for recruitment and retention of participants over three years of the study were limited and visibility of the project to the general public and schools through promotion and dissemination activities were compromised. Nonetheless, the recruitment of 28 kindergartens in this study provided an adequate sample size to address the project objectives.

17619319.label: Major findings and research outcome
17619319.value: Considering data collected through questionnaires, interviews, classroom observations and assessment of children’s English language and literacy outcomes with a sample of children aged 3 to 6 and their parents, the results of this study have provided important insights into contextual influences on children’s English language and literacy development in Hong Kong. Findings generated thus far have considered the influences of family characteristics, parental beliefs and home literacy practices on children’s English as a second language development. First, SES disparities in the home learning environment and children’s English language and literacy outcomes were found between children from higher-SES families as compared to their lower-SES counterparts. Aspects of the HLE mediated the relations between SES and children’s English language and literacy skills (Jiang et al., 2023). Second, this research developed and validated a questionnaire to assess parents’ beliefs about and attitudes towards supporting children’s ESL development (Zhang & Lau, 2022). This study found that Hong Kong parents generally valued their role in children’s English language development. Parents who valued their role in their children’s English language learning tended to provide more resources and activities at home and engage in more recommended practices for supporting English language development. Third, parents’ beliefs about their children’s English ability and their self-efficacy were related to children’s interest in learning English. Children’s interest uniquely contributed to their English language and literacy skills (Zhang & Lau, 2024). This research further explored (1) the cross-lagged relations between the home literacy environment and children’s ESL development; (2) parental self-efficacy, marital satisfaction and home literacy environment in supporting children’s second language development; and (3) parental involvement at home, in school and outside school and its influences on children’s ESL learning, all of which are currently under review. Additional findings on (1) the development and validation of a classroom observational tool; (2) classroom quality, teacher characteristics and children’s ESL outcomes; and (3) interactional effect of the home and preschool learning environment on children’s English as a second language development are under preparation. Findings from this research have been presented in the Biennial Meeting of the Society for Research in Child Development in Salt Lake City, United States and the Annual Meeting of the American Educational Research Association in Philadelphia, United States.

17619319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17619319.value: The newly developed and validated measures from this research – (i) questionnaire to assess parental beliefs and attitudes on children’s ESL development; and (ii) classroom observational tool to measure the quality of teaching and the environment in supporting English language learning – lead to further validation work with larger sample sizes, broader range of participants and different types of kindergartens across Hong Kong to enhance the cultural appropriateness and sensitivity of the tools. In view of the limited existing work on classroom quality and children’s ESL development in Hong Kong, the classroom observational tool can be used to evaluate teaching practices and the classroom environment across kindergarten settings to enhance professional development of teachers and improve children’s English language and literacy outcomes. The findings on the role of family characteristics, parental beliefs and home literacy practices on children’s English as a second language development and their interest in learning English prompt the need for intervention research to empower and support parents’ involvement in providing an enriched home learning environment and to promote the understanding of the importance of parental beliefs and attitudes towards children’s early English language learning.

17619319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17619319.value: This research aims to identify and examine home and school influences on children’s English as a second language development in Hong Kong. Specifically, it investigates the separate and combined effects of the home and preschool learning environments on children’s English language and literacy skills and growth. Through data collected from questionnaires, interviews, classroom observations and direct assessments of children’s English language and literacy skills, this study enables a nuanced understanding of children’s second language development and provides culture-specific information on family characteristics, parental beliefs and home literacy practices within the home learning environment and on teacher characteristics and classroom quality within the preschool learning environment. This research contributes to the measurement of the home and preschool learning environments by developing and validating a parent questionnaire and a classroom observational tool. Findings from this study provides insights into the processes and practices that support early English as a second language development in Hong Kong. This research has the potential to contribute to program improvement, parent education and policy investments and decision making in supporting children’s English language and literacy development.

17620219.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17620219.value: Ageism, meaning age-related stereotyping, can be experienced by both elderly and young people. The perception of being unfairly stereotyped can have negative effects, including poorer mental health and lower self-esteem. Although ageism has been discussed in the social psychology literature, its relationship with spatial segregation has been relatively under-explored. Spatial segregation by age is often viewed as natural, compared to racial segregation, which has been problematized more extensively. Spatial age segregation can be found in housing developments targeted at specific age groups, such as elderly housing and youth housing. There are some pragmatic reasons for living in age-segregated housing, such as opportunities to socialize with peers of similar age and convenient access to purpose-design facilities. Nevertheless, intergroup contact theories suggest that lack of interaction across social groups may exacerbate negative stereotypes. It is possible that living in age-segregated housing might influence levels of ageism, since age-segregated housing may reduce opportunities for face-to-face interaction across age groups. The aim of this research is to empirically investigate the relationship between spatial age segregation and ageism in Hong Kong. The first phase of the study involves establishing the nature of spatial age segregation in Hong Kong, and how this relates to cross-age interaction at the neighbourhood level. The second phase of the study involves quantitative survey research, to investigate ageist perceptions amongst residents of elderly-specific and youth-specific housing, compared to people living in conventional housing. The final phase of the study involves qualitative, in-depth interviews with residents of elderly-specific and youth-specific housing, to understand the factors which shape cross-age interactions, and how the quantity and quality of these cross-age interactions shape their ageist perceptions. The study bridges the gap between micro-level research on ageism in social psychology and macro-level research on spatial segregation in urban studies. Given the high-rise, high density urban environment in Hong Kong, segregation by vertical space may be more intensive than horizontal space, meaning that research on age segregation, cross-age interaction and ageism in this city might reveal relationships and explanations that are different from elsewhere. Through its dual focus on ageism toward the elderly as well as young people, the study supports development of methodologies for measuring ageism towards young people, which are less well-established. The study also has practical policy implications, by offering insights into the spatial and institutional interventions that may be relevant to counteracting ageism and improving intergenerational relations. 不論任何年齡，是長者或是青年，都有可能遭受年齡歧視。文獻顯示年齡歧視可能對精神健康造成各種負面影響。然而，較少學者研究空間隔離與年齡歧視的關係。空間隔離意指年齡相近的人聚集一處，與其他年齡的人隔開。例如長者屋的住戶只有長者；青年宿舍的住戶只有青年。長者屋或青年宿舍固然有其好處，例如提供長者專用設施，或提供機會給年齡相近的人士互相認識。然而，社會學家指出，空間隔離可能減少不同年齡人士之間的互動，有機會加深年齡歧視。本研究旨在比較不同住房模式的青年，對長者的印象及想法；透過大型問卷調查及深度訪談，分析空間隔離及其他因素與年齡歧視的關係。研究有助未來空間規劃，推動跨年齡共融。

17620219.label: Realisation of objectives
17620219.value: The primary aim of this research was to investigate the nature of age segregation and ageism in Hong Kong, and to understand how ageism is related to cross-age interactions in residential neighbourhoods in Hong Kong, This addresses a gap in the urban studies literature, which tends to focus on socio-economic and racial segregation, with fewer studies being conducted on age segregation and cross-age interactions, especially in high-density Asian cities. The first objective of the research was to establish the extent of spatial age segregation in Hong Kong. This objective was successfully achieved through analysis of secondary census data over a period of ten years, from 2006 to 2016, as well as qualitative in-depth interviews. Two key measures of age segregation were investigated, including dissimilarity index and p-measures of social isolation. The original plan was to include the latest census data collected in 2021. However, this was not possible, since the age distribution data were not available from the Census and Statistics Department at the time of data analysis. Nevertheless, the PI focused on analysing age distribution across a 10-year period, hence the analysis was able to achieve the first research objective, by illustrating how age segregation has changed over a longer period of time. The second objective was to investigate young people's ageist perceptions towards older people, including those living in age-specific housing and conventional housing. This objective was successfully achieved, although it was necessary to modify the sampling strategy due to practical constraints. As mentioned in the previous progress report, the sampling frame was slightly modified, since the progress of constructing youth-specific housing (youth hostels) was slower than expected. A more inclusive definition of age-specific housing was adopted – instead of focusing on age mix at the building level, the survey focused on the household level. Respondents were asked whether only young adults aged 18-34 lived in their housing unit. Respondents were also asked whether they lived with retired older people aged 65 and above. In other words, instead of comparing the attitudes of young people living in youth-specific housing and conventional housing, the PI modified the sampling frame by comparing young people who were co-living (or not co-living) with older people. Subsequently, the PI collected both quantitative (448 surveys) and qualitative data (23 in-depth interviews) to address the second research objective. The quantitative survey asked young adults aged 18-34 to indicate their level of agreement with ageist statements, while the qualitative in-depth interviews asked young adults to elaborate their positive and negative stereotypes of retired older people, and to offer possible explanations of their attitudes. In terms of the sampling approach, since the study period (2020-2022) coincided with successive waves of covid outbreak, it was not feasible to recruit interviewees through street interception, due to social distancing regulations and the need to safeguard the health of project research assistants. The face-to-face survey was converted to online survey – interviewees were initially recruited from students in the department, and were subsequently recruited via snowball sampling through referrals by the students. The referrals were screened to ensure ensure that the sample characteristics (gender, housing type, employment status) were as diverse as possible. The third objective of the study was to investigate the quantity and quality of cross-age interactions in residential neighbourhoods in Hong Kong. This objective was also successfully achieved through the 448 surveys and 23 in-depth interviews with young adults, as well as 26 in-depth interviews with retired older people. Respondents were asked to quantify their frequency and depth of interactions with both kin and non-kin retirees. In-depth interviews were subsequently conducted to better understand the reasons for varying frequency and depth of interactions between younger and older neighbours. Due to the ongoing pandemic, the face-to-face interviews were converted to telephone interviews, in order to safeguard the health of older interviewees. The fourth objective was to analyse the inter-relationship between ageist perceptions and cross-age interactions. This objective was also successfully achieved through the qualitative interviews with both older and younger people. As elaborated in one of the journal publications, previous literature on Western contexts have highlighted the strong influence of media representations on ageism, such as negative representations in television programmes. The new evidence from this study indicates that everyday cross-age interactions in high-density Hong Kong neighbourhoods can help counter negative stereotypes, since it is easier for young people to observe the diverse and positive activities of retired older people in public open spaces. Overall, all of the study objectives have been achieved. Apart from slight modifications to the sampling strategy due to the pandemic, other elements of the research plan have been successfully implemented, including collection of a mix of census, survey and in-depth interview data. The data were thoroughly analysed by applying concepts and theories from the literature review, and new explanations have been generated through qualitative data analysis.

17620219.label: Major findings and research outcome
17620219.value: The major findings from this research have been disseminated through four papers published in international peer-reviewed journals. The first set of important findings were published in the paper entitled “"Residential age segregation: Evidence from a rapidly ageing Asian city ", published in the Journal of Population Ageing. This paper addresses the first project objective by providing evidence of the extent of residential age segregation in Hong Kong. The findings reveal that the extent of age segregation between older people and young adults has remained consistently low from 2006 to 2016, although age segregation appears to be more pronounced between young adults in their early 20s and older adults above 65. The second set of important findings were published in two papers, the first one entitled “Beyond ageism: A qualitative study of intersecting forms of prejudice towards retired older people”, published in Societies, and the other one entitled “Intergenerational interactions, ageism and ableism in community settings”, published in the Journal of Intergenerational Relationships. These two papers address the second and fourth project objectives, by providing empirical evidence of young adults’ ageist perceptions. The survey findings reveal that young adults are not motivated to interact with retired older people beyond their family, which is partly explained by their busy schedules, and partly explained by ageism. The findings also counter the misconception that ageism is less prevalent in Asian societies, while highlighting more complex intersections between ageism, classism, and ableism. The third set of important findings were published in the paper entitled “Fostering intergenerational interactions in high-rise residential neighbourhoods: Towards culturally-informed interventions?”. This paper addresses the third project objective, by providing evidence on the quality of cross-age interactions between older and younger neighbours living in high-rise residential buildings. The findings reveal that the two generations rarely interact, partly due to generational differences in the use of neighbourhood public spaces, and partly due to socio-cultural factors, especially the pervasive culture of digital communication and aversion to small talk in public spaces. Apart from the above research publications, the major findings from the research were presented in two international conferences, including the 2021 Virtual Annual Meeting of the American Sociological Association (ASA), and the 2022 Asia-Pacific Network for Housing Research (APNHR) Virtual Conference. Due to covid-related travel constraints throughout the project period, both conference papers were presented via online mode.

17620219.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17620219.value: The qualitative research findings highlight an interesting issue which has potential for further investigation. In the conclusions section of the paper published in Housing Studies journal, it was noted that younger people may be more prepared to interact with and support older neighbours via digital platforms. Further research can be conducted to achieve better understanding of the influence of local cultural beliefs on younger and older people’s perceptions of digital intergenerational interventions in high-rise residential neighbourhoods. For example, how do younger and older people in different cultural contexts perceive the exchange of intergenerational support through digital platforms? How do older people perceive informal care from younger neighbours compared to formal caregivers? Further exploration of these questions could help reveal the most effective ways to foster meaningful intergenerational interactions in residential neighbourhoods, especially in high-rise, high-density Asian cities. The Principal Investigator plans to develop a new research project to explore these research questions.

17620219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17620219.value: This research investigates age segregation (spatial separation between older and younger people), ageism (prejudice towards older people) and cross-age interactions in Hong Kong. While there are plenty of studies on socio-economic and racial segregation in various cities across the world, there are very few studies on age segregation, especially in Asian cities. Through a mix of quantitative and qualitative methods, this study generates new knowledge on changing patterns of age segregation in Hong Kong, which highlights the importance of ageing-in-place policies, which may contribute to lower levels of age segregation. In addition, the study identifies young adults’ positive and negative stereotypes of retired older people, and the underlying reasons, which indicates the types of interventions that may be more effective in combating ageism. Furthermore, the study examines the quantity and quality of cross-age interactions in high-rise neighbourhoods in Hong Kong, which illustrates the types of socio-cultural factors that may affect the willingness of younger and older neighbours to interact with each other. This new knowledge helps inform future neighbourhood interventions, by drawing attention to new initiatives that may be more effective in fostering meaningful cross-age interactions in Hong Kong and other high-density Asian cities.

17620919.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17620919.value: Background Child maltreatment, including physical, sexual, or psychological abuse and neglect, is a prevalent problem worldwide. Among all types of child maltreatment, physical abuse is particular prevalent in Chinese communities because corporeal punishment is a well-accepted child rearing method in Chinese parenting culture. Various biopsychosocial conditions have been linked to child maltreatment, including mental disorders, academic underachievement, physical health, and elevated stress markers, but causality has not been confirmed due to cross-sectional or self-report retrospective design. A well-planned prospective cohort study is much needed to elucidate the role of child maltreatment in health and development. Objectives This study aims to investigate the longitudinal association between child maltreatment and mental disorders (depression, anxiety, substance abuse, and self-harm/suicidal attempts), educational/social outcomes (academic achievement and employment), physical health (injury and obesity), and biological markers of stress exposure (interleukin 6 and telomere length). In addition, the study will also examine the various potential effect modifiers for the relationships, such as gender, socioeconomic status, social support, and resilience. Study design This is a prospective cohort study. The cohort was formed from the Hong Kong Hospital Authority database of 7,473 child maltreatment cases and 26,957 control cases. The control cases were minor cases (e.g. non-recurrent flu, minor injury) with matched gender, age in years, socioeconomic background, and month of index hospital visit. This study will be conducted in two stages. The first stage is a database follow-up to compare the morbidity outcomes as captured in the Hospital Authority system of the whole cohort. The second stage is a detailed assessment, including a questionnaire survey and physical and biomedical measurement of a random 3% subset of the cohort. Study contribution The proposed study will provide reliable estimates of the burden of child maltreatment in Hong Kong and will be the first in Chinese society to investigate the long-term impact of child maltreatment. This study will also provide first-hand evidence of the value of individual, family, and extra-familial resources in promoting positive well-being among maltreated children. 研究背景 兒童虐待（包括身體虐待，性虐待或心理虐待）在全球均普遍存在。在中國傳統文化中，體罰是廣為接受的教養方式，因此在華人社區中，身體虐待尤其普遍。兒童虐待與各種生理心理社交狀況均有相關性，包括精神問題，學業成績不佳，身體健康和壓力生物標記升高。但大部分證據均來自橫斷面或自我報告的回顧性設計，因果關係尚未得到證實。精心策劃的前瞻性追蹤研究能夠闡明兒童虐待在健康和發展中的影響。 研究目標 本研究旨在調查兒童虐待與精神障礙（抑鬱，焦慮，藥物濫用和自我傷害/自殺未遂），教育/社會成果（學業成就和就業），身體健康（傷害和肥胖）之間的縱向關聯，和反映壓力感受的生物標誌物（白細胞介素6和端粒長度）。此外，該研究還將研究各種關係的潛在影響調節劑，如性別，社會經濟狀況，社會支持和適應力。 研究規劃 本研究採用前瞻性追蹤設計。研究群組從香港醫院管理局數據庫組成，共有7,473名兒童虐待個案及26,957名對照個案。對照個案為輕微求診個案（例如非複發性流感，輕微損傷）。他們與虐兒受害者的性別、年齡、社會經濟背景和就診月份匹配。本研究分兩個階段進行。第一階段是數據庫跟進，利用醫院管理局系統以檢視整個群組的各項發病率。第二階段是詳細評估，覆蓋隨機3%群組，內容包括問卷調查和各項生物醫學測量。 學習貢獻 本研究將對香港兒童虐待負擔提供可靠估算，並將是中國社會裡首次調查虐待兒童的長期影響。這項研究還能檢視為受虐兒童提供正向健康發展的用處。

17620919.label: Realisation of objectives
17620919.value: This was a 2-phase cohort study which comprise two groups: the maltreatment group (those with confirmed/diagnosed child maltreatment from the database of Hong Kong Hospital Authority (HA)) and the comparison group (those without any records of maltreatment experience). A cohort of 7,473 cases with prior maltreatment experience was established in a previous study using the HA databases, namely the Clinical Data Analysis and Reporting System (CDARS). In this study, the International Classification of Diseases, 9th revision (ICD-9) system for diagnosis to reflect the disease outcomes. All cases in this study were defined as those who were aged 0 to 19 years and had been admitted to public hospital with a first-listed record of maltreatment episode (ICD-9 codes 995.5, 955.8, and E967.0–E967.9) from January 1, 2000 to December 31, 2010 in the CDARS database. For each exposed cases, patients of the same gender and age that were admitted into the same hospital in the same calendar year and month without any records of maltreatment, congenital anomalies, severe chronic illnesses, or an index hospital stay >14 days at any point in the CDARS database were randomly selected as the comparison group. After the matching, the matched comparison group consisted of 26,834 patients who fulfilled the criteria. In Phase I, relevant medical records during the follow-up period such as the diagnosis of mental disorders, total number of hospitalisations, and number of prescriptions were retrieved from CDARS database. All retrieved data were then uploaded to an encrypted server for data matching, cleaning, and analysis. In Phase II, a subset was randomly selected from the cohort for detailed assessment. Upon obtaining the informed consent from the adult participants or the parents of adolescent participants, a series of physical assessments were conducted. In addition, 4mL of peripheral blood samples were collected from the participants and sent to out laboratory for further testing. Although we failed to recruit the proposed number of participants for Phase II of the study, the data collected sufficiently and satisfactorily achieved all the four proposed objectives. 1. To study the longitudinal association between child maltreatment and mental disorders, including depression, anxiety, substance abuse, and self-harm/suicide attempts After the matching, data on the psychiatric diagnoses records of all cohort participants from the date of admission to 31st January, 2019 were extracted. Cox proportional hazard regression model was then employed to estimate the associations between childhood maltreatment exposure and diagnosis of mental disorders, in hazard ratio (HR, with 95% confidence intervals). After adjusting for age at index visit, sex, and government welfare recipient status, our study found that childhood maltreatment exposure was significantly associated with an increased risk for both overall (HR, 4.12, 95% CI [3.75, 4.53]) and specific mental disorders (conduct disorder/oppositional defiant disorder: HR, 11.37, 95% CI [7.43, 17.38]; ADHD: HR, 10.62, 95% CI [8.35, 13.50]; personality disorders: HR, 6.03, 95% CI [4.38, 8.30]; anxiety disorder: HR, 3.88, 95% CI [3.23, 4.66]; psychosis: HR, 3.60, 95% CI [2.69, 4.84]; depressive disorder: HR, 3.48, 95% CI [2.65, 4.58]; bipolar disorder: HR, 2.08, 95% CI [1.16, 3.71]). To test whether there is any potential reverse causation (e.g. undiagnosed mental health problems that may cause first-time child maltreatment), a one-year landmark analysis was conducted by excluding patients diagnosed with the mental disorder of interest within the first follow-up year. Our one-year landmark analysis showed that all HRs were attenuated but remained significant after excluding events in the first follow-up year (p < 0.05). 2. To study the longitudinal association between child maltreatment and educational/social outcomes, including academic achievement and employment In Phase II, a total of 126 individuals (63 from maltreatment group and 63 matched comparison group) attended our detailed assessment. Upon informed consent, participants were asked to complete a set of questionnaires to assess their educational and social outcomes. For those who attended detailed assessment, 50 (39.7%) were male and 76 (60.3%) were female. The mean age at follow-up was 23.1 and 23.3 years in the maltreatment group and comparison group, respectively. The average follow-up duration was 14.8 years among all who attend detailed assessment. Although it was found that percentage of individuals who completed Bachelor’s degree or above was higher in the comparison group (41.3%) than maltreatment group (27.0%), our comparative analysis found no significance in the association between maltreatment history and academic achievement (p = 0.17). Similarly, no significant difference was observed in the employment status between maltreatment and comparison groups (p = 0.69). On the other hand, it was observed that the average monthly household income was significantly higher in the comparison group (HKD$39,810) than the maltreatment group (HKD$27,542) (p = 0.006). 3. To study the longitudinal association between child maltreatment and indicators of physical health, including injury, obesity, as well as biological markers that reflect the stress exposure, including interleukin 6 level and telomere length To examine the association between child maltreatment history and incidence of injury, the ICD codes 950 – 959 was used to identify the incidence of suicide and self-inflicted injury. Using the Cox proportional hazard model, it was found that child maltreatment history was significantly associated with an increased risk for suicide and self-inflicted injury (HR, 4.33, 95% CI [3.57, 5.25]). A total of 4ml peripheral blood samples were collected from the participants during the detailed assessment for the level of various biological markers including interleukin (IL) 6 and 10 levels and telomere length. All these biological markers have been suggested as a stress-related biomarker. Our adjusted regression models suggest that individuals from the maltreatment group had significantly higher level of IL-6 (β = 0.15, p = 0.001) and IL-10 (β = 0.11, p = 0.011). Although individuals from maltreatment group (Mean = 22.84) also had higher telomere length than those from comparison group (Mean = 21.78), the association between maltreatment history and telomere length was not significant (p = 0.47). No significant difference was observed in the body mass index, a well-adopted index for obesity status, between the maltreatment and comparison groups (p = 0.36). 4. To examine the roles of demographics (gender and socioeconomic status), abuse characteristics (type and age of maltreatment), and psychological assets (resilience and social support) on the association between child maltreatment and outcomes To examine whether there are any differences between subgroups defined by history of childhood sexual abuse (yes/no), age of onset (older/ young age), and gender (male/female), ratio of HR was computed as HRsubgroup/HRcomparison subgroup, with a ratio greater than 1 indicating that the association between childhood maltreatment and later psychiatric disorders for the numerator subgroup was stronger than that for the denominator subgroup. In our study, the risk of psychiatric disorders following childhood maltreatment did not vary by history of childhood sexual abuse, age at maltreatment exposure, and gender. Subgroup analyses by age of onset and follow-up duration were also conducted on the association between child maltreatment and biological outcomes. It was observed that there were significant between-group differences in log10-transformed IL-6 and log10-transformed IL-10 values only when the analyses were restricted to those with follow up duration less than 14 years and age of onset above or equal to 8 years (log10-transformed IL-6: β=0.19, p=0.029; log10-transformed IL-10: β=0.21, p=0.013). These differences were found to remain statistically significant in the adjusted model (Adjusted for monthly household income at follow-up).

17620919.label: Major findings and research outcome
17620919.value: This project is one of the first studies in Chinese community to investigate the long-term effects of child maltreatment on mental disorders (depression, anxiety, substance abuse, and self-harm/suicidal attempts), educational/social outcomes (academic achievement and employment), physical health (injury and obesity), and biological markers of stress exposure (IL-6, IL-10 and telomere length). In Phase I of this study, we identified a significant impact of child maltreatment on the mental disorder risk of the exposed individuals. Specifically, after adjusting for age at index visit, sex, and government welfare recipient status, our study found that childhood maltreatment exposure was significantly associated with an increased risk for both overall and specific psychiatric disorders (conduct disorder/oppositional defiant disorder, ADHD, personality disorders, anxiety disorder, psychosis, depressive disorder, bipolar disorder. In Phase II of this study, we found that there was no significant effect of child maltreatment on the academic achievement and employment status of the individuals with exposure to childhood maltreatment. However, the average monthly household income was significantly higher in the comparison group than the maltreatment group. Regarding the biological outcomes, our study found that individuals from the maltreatment group had significantly higher levels of IL-6 and IL-10. But no significant difference was observed in the body mass index and telomere length between the exposed and unexposed groups. Subgroup analyses were also conducted to examine whether the association between child maltreatment and biological outcomes vary by the age of onset and follow-up duration. Our adjusted regression model displayed that both age of onset and follow-up duration could significantly influence the impact of childhood maltreatment on the biological outcomes of the individuals with exposure to childhood maltreatment.

17620919.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17620919.value: The findings of this study lay an important foundation for future epidemiological research on child maltreatment by providing a reliable estimate on the burden of child maltreatment. Since existing evidence on child maltreatment heavily relies on self-report questionnaires, our study results provide substantiated and reliable evidence on the child maltreatment burden and demonstrate the value of linking databases from multiple sectors. Even more importantly, this study made use of a 2-phases design to prospectively examine the long-term effect of childhood maltreatment history to the psychiatric, social and biological outcomes. Since psychiatric disorders are very likely to worsen into adulthood without proper treatment, future longitudinal studies can be designed to study whether the psychiatric disorders would continue into adulthood. Additionally, this study was the first to investigate the long-term impact of child maltreatment in the Chinese community, in which corporal punishment is still a widely acceptable means of parenting. The findings could contribute to the international discourse and cross-cultural comparison on the link between child maltreatment and adverse health conditions, particularly in the biopsychosocial outcome aspects. Guidelines and recommendations based on the findings can be issued to schools, parents and professionals, alerting them the adverse consequences of child maltreatment and the potential benefits of early detection of child maltreatment.

17620919.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17620919.value: This research study examined the long-term impacts of childhood maltreatment. Results indicated that individuals with history of maltreatment in childhood are more likely to have psychiatric disorders in their adolescence and early adulthood. These findings add to the limited current evidence over the long-term impact of exposure to childhood maltreatment. Also, this study made use of data from various local databases to provide reliable evidence on the child maltreatment burden. This suggests the importance of prompt action by the government and healthcare providers to illustrate a cross-sector platform to establish a timely monitoring on the trend and burden of childhood maltreatment in Hong Kong. More resource should be allocated to promoting the knowledge of proper detection and management of childhood maltreatment.

17621119.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17621119.value: 講述自己的故事：移動的研究方法和移民知識

17621119.label: Project Objectives
17621119.value: To decolonize knowledge production on migrant labour issues; To examine the impact of migrants’ stories and narratives on labour migration trajectories within their families, communities and networks; To develop innovative modalities for constructing, analysing and disseminating migrant domestic workers’ stories, narratives and perspectives;
rows: To decolonize knowledge production on migrant labour issues;
To examine the impact of migrants’ stories and narratives on labour migration trajectories within their families, communities and networks;
To develop innovative modalities for constructing, analysing and disseminating migrant domestic workers’ stories, narratives and perspectives;

17621119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17621119.value: This project examines (1) the construction of migrant domestic workers’ stories and narratives about labour migration, (2) the impact these stories and narratives have in sustaining or shaping labour migration flows, and (3) the process by which these narratives become forms of transnational knowledge that can sustain, shape or transform labour migration trajectories. Domestic workers comprise one of the single largest migrant worker populations around the world. Currently, an estimated 11.5 million migrants are in domestic work or 7.7 per cent of the estimated number of all international migrants (ILO, 2015). Approximately 71.1 per cent of migrant workers are employed in the service sector which includes migrant domestic workers. Seventy-three per cent of migrant domestic workers are women. The existence of labour export policies in sending countries such as the Philippines (Battistella, 1995; Lindio-McGovern, 2003) has by now produced successive generations of migrant domestic workers. In the context of these global flows of migrant labour, the narratives or stories that migrant domestic workers share – with their families, communities and networks – constitute one important source of experiential knowledge. This project explores the transformation of migrant domestic workers’ experiences into stories, and their stories into knowledge. This involves investigating the transnational work that migrant workers’ stories do in shaping global migrant labour flows and in shaping potential migrants’ decisions about where to work, how to work and how to share their experiences. This project aims to expand ways for migrant domestic workers to create, share and reflect on their narratives. Therefore, a decolonizing approach to knowledge production provides the theoretical foundation for this work. This involves centering migrant domestic workers as knowledge producers and using innovative, visual and participatory methodologies, such as participatory video, photovoice and walking methodologies. These methods permit participants to exercise greater authorial agency, offer utility beyond the research project, and produce outputs that may be more readily channeled into activities for knowledge exchange and social impact. By exploring how labour migration experiences are understood or re-thought through stories and narratives that are then shared, this project considers whether migrant domestic workers’ stories and narratives can transform or change the role of migrant knowledges in labour migration flows. 該項目審查了（1）以外籍家庭傭工的故事為載體,進行共同敘述的構建，（2）這些故事和敘述對維持或塑造勞務移民流動產生的影響，以及（3）這些敘述成為各種形式的跨國知識的過程，這些知識維持、塑造或改變勞務移民的軌蹟。家政工人是世界上最大的移民工人之一。目前，估計有1,150萬移民從事家政工作，佔所有國際移民人數的7.7％（勞工組織，2015年）。大約71.1％的外籍工人受僱於服務部門，其中包括外籍家庭傭工。 73％外籍家庭傭工是女性。菲律賓等派遣國的勞務輸出政策的存在迄今已產生了連續幾代的外籍家庭工人（Battistella，1995; Lindio-McGovern，2003）。在這些全球移民勞工流動的背景下，外籍​家庭傭工與家人、社區和網絡共享的敘述或故事構成了體驗知識的重要來源。該項目探討了將外籍家庭傭工的經歷轉化為故事，將他們的故事轉化為知識。這涉及調查外籍家庭傭工的故事在塑造全球移民勞工流動方面所做的跨國工作，以及影響潛在移民決定在哪里工作，如何工作以及如何分享經驗。該項目旨在擴大外籍家庭傭工創造、分享和反思其敘述的方式。因此，知識生產的非殖民化方法為這項工作提供了理論基礎。這涉及將外籍家庭傭工作為知識生產者的中心，並使用創新的、視覺的和參與性的方法，如參與式錄影、影像發聲和行走的研究方法。這些方法允許參與者行使更大的作者能動性，提供研究項目以外的效用，並產生可能更容易引入知識交流和社會影響活動的產出。通過探索如何通過隨後分享的故事和敘述來理解或重新思考勞務移民經歷，該項目考慮外籍家庭傭工的故事和敘述是否可以重塑或改變移民知識在勞務移民流動中的作用。

17621119.label: Realisation of objectives
17621119.value: The first objective was achieved in three academic publications and extensive collaboration with Migrant Writers of Hong Kong. The first publication is a co-authored book chapter with two project collaborators, Christine Vicera and Jemima Joy Gbadago, titled ‘Knowledge production and cultural production in labour migration’ for The Handbook of Global Social Theory (SAGE), which provides a theoretical and methodological resource on how researchers and stakeholders can use a decolonial approach when working with migrant worker-led creative initiatives. This chapter is currently in revision. The second publication is a co-authored journal article with Vivian Wenli Lin and Merina Sunuwar, titled ‘Migrating methods in a pandemic: Virtual participatory video with migrants in Hong Kong’ for the International Journal of Qualitative Methods. This article explores how research methodologies can be informed by migrant realities by examining the methodological adaptations that were necessitated during the pandemic. This article is currently in press. The third publication is a forthcoming sole-authored book chapter, titled ‘Anti-pandemic measures, labour rights and the legibility of harm in domestic work’ for A Criminology of the Domestic (Routledge). This chapter centres the work of domestic worker-led activist organizations during the pandemic in Hong Kong in order to analyse the legibility of harm in domestic work, within institutions (e.g. the criminal justice system) and domestic worker communities. The first project objective was also achieved through extensive collaboration with the Migrant Writers of Hong Kong (MWHK), a creative writing network founded by migrant domestic workers in March 2021. I and project collaborators, Christine Vicera (founder of be/longing), Jemima Joy Gbadago and Yvonne Yu, have worked with MWHK since their inception. This has involved, among other activities, providing two series of creative writing workshops for MWHK members, titled The Writer’s Toolbox I and II. This comprised four workshops from May to August 2021 and nine workshops from January to July 2022. These workshops have centred migrant workers’ writing as a site for knowledge production about migrant labour and created a space where domestic workers can centre their creative roles, interests and aspirations. The second objective has been achieved, primarily through the project’s collaboration with MWHK in two workshop series, titled The Writer’s Toolbox I (Summer 2021) and The Writer’s Toolbox II (January-July 2022). The workshops introduced participants to creative writing methods and instruction, and involved peer reviewing one to three pieces by participants per workshop. Participants were asked about the development of their writing, authorial intentions and choices. The short stories submitted by participants reflected a wide range of interests and genres, including fantasy, historical fiction, mysteries and thrillers, memoir, drama, and social realism. Major themes that emerged across participants’ work and in workshop discussions included sacrifice, grief and the costs of labour migration. One notable finding was the impact of labour migration on workers’ intimate relationships and the silence and stigma experienced by workers within their communities. The third objective has been achieved, primarily in collaboration with the Migrant Writers of Hong Kong network. The project’s involvement with the Migrant Writers of Hong Kong network and writing submitted for peer review in The Writer’s Toolbox I and II workshop series have led to plans for an anthology titled Ingat (a term in Tagalog and Bahasa with multiple meanings, including to take care, to remember, to protect, to say goodbye). The creation of this anthology is led by leaders of Migrant Writers of Hong Kong, Lensational (an organization that provides photography training for domestic workers) and Guhit Kulay (a migrant worker-led arts collective) and will feature poetry, photography and creative works by domestic workers in Hong Kong. The third objective was also achieved in a small online exhibition of writing, video and photography by members of migrant communities in Hong Kong created in three pilot online participatory arts workshops held in November and December 2020, and in a website, previously hosted at mmmk.hku.hk (this website is in the process of being transferred to a new domain at Brock University).

17621119.label: Major findings and research outcome
17621119.value: The major findings that will be disseminated in academic publications (see Part C.8) speak to the interaction between migrant narratives and diverse audiences, and between migrant realities and research methodologies. An important project aim was to centre creative work by migrant communities as a significant site of knowledge production. In collaborative efforts with organizations such as the Migrant Writers of Hong Kong, major themes were the risks and challenges that domestic workers face if they explore other roles, interests and aspirations outside of domestic work (Ham, Vicera & Gbadago, under revision). In Hong Kong, this results in a criminalization of creativity or penalties that domestic workers risk if they are compensated for creative labour that they produce. Therefore, collaboration with migrant-led initiatives involves an astute awareness of the structural conditions in which creative work is produced. In addition, the reception of migrant narratives speaks to public expectations for migrant domestic workers. In Ham, Vicera & Gbadago (under revision), we explore how this emerges in respectability politics in creative initiatives with migrant communities, and the role of migrant narratives that challenge dominant narratives about domestic workers. Collaboration with MWHK and engaging with domestic workers’ stories revealed other lives, realities and narratives that contest Hong Kong’s insistence on the dehumanization of domestic workers. This also relates to the selective legibility of harm in domestic work analysed in a forthcoming book chapter (Ham, under review), in which some harms are recognized in institutional mechanisms and systemic remedies (e.g. physical assault, sexual violence) whereas other harms are routinized into the day to day household (e.g. overwork, unsuitable accommodation, food insecurity). The pervasive expectation that domestic workers should orient their lives around their employers’ priorities has obscured awareness of the costs of labour migration. This includes the toll of family separation and consequences for domestic workers’ intimate relationships. Another important finding or outcome was the adaptation of participatory arts methods necessitated by the pandemic. This project originally included plans for extensive in-person community engagement through creative arts workshops. In November and December 2020, I and project collaborators, such as Voices of Women Media, piloted a series of online participatory video-making workshops for members of migrant and ethnic minority communities. We found that recalibrating participatory video methods in an online environment mirrored long-term, ongoing migrant realities, such as physical separation, restriction of physical mobility, and connections mediated through technology.

17621119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17621119.value: I plan to continue my collaboration with MWHK and was asked to sit on their advisory panel when they registered as a new organization. Immediate plans include collaborating on their anthology, Ingat. Longer-term plans involve the potential development of a global platform for migrant workers? creative initiatives, or a platform that permits migrant workers? creative trajectories to continue developing alongside their labour migration trajectories. I also plan to continue developing my website, Mobile Methodologies and Migrant Knowledges, which was hosted at mmmk.hku.hk but will be moved to a new domain linked with Brock University (where I will be working from August 2022 onwards).

17621119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17621119.value: This project contributed to the decolonization of knowledge production on migrant labour issues through collaboration with migrant-led creative initiatives, most notably with the Migrant Writers of Hong Kong (MWHK), a creative writing network founded by migrant domestic workers in March 2021. Project activities included two workshop series, The Writer?s Toolbox I and II, in collaboration with MWHK and be/longing (a participatory arts initiative for ethnic minority communities). Workshops involved participants peer reviewing each other?s work, which spanned a diverse range of genres including memoir, fantasy, drama, thrillers, and historical fiction. Workshop discussions with authors raised issues concerning the toll of labour migration on intimate relationships, family separation, grief and sacrifice. Collaboration with migrant worker-led creative initiatives can challenge societal expectations that workers should not explore roles, identities or aspirations outside of domestic work, and legal parameters that restrict migrant workers? participation in creative endeavours. If collaborative efforts with migrant-led creative initiatives are to contribute fruitfully to social change efforts, partnerships should be grounded in an astute awareness of the structural conditions in which creative labour is produced.

17621819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17621819.value: The proposed project will be the first research study to investigate the use of intersex/DSD (and related) terminology in an Asian context or a multilingual context through a focus on Hong Kong. In alignment with international trends, in 2016 the UN Committee against Torture released a report on Hong Kong in which they unequivocally identified intersex children as a group being “subject to unnecessary and irreversible surgery” and expressing concern about the “long term physical and psychological suffering caused by such practices” (UN Committee against Torture (CAT), 2016, sec. 28). The committee made the strong recommendation that the HKSAR should guarantee respect for the bodily autonomy and psychological wellbeing of intersex people via sound communication. The proposed project builds on insights from published research by the Principal Investigator. Participants (in the USA) identified medicalized language as a key barrier to their efforts to convey intersex lived experience as part of the logic of understanding intersex bodies. The nature and scope of such communication across stakeholders in Hong Kong has not been studied empirically. In light of the existing plethora of competing/flexible language in English, the proposed research is interested in how communication in Hong Kong might further be affected by the combined use of English and Cantonese across language domains (e.g. home, hospital, or clinic). Intersex traits are statistically uncommon body traits that do not meet medical and social norms for genital and/or chromosomal arrangements. Such traits are also sometimes described, mainly in medical contexts, as “Disorders of Sex Development” or “DSDs” whereas large numbers of those born with intersex traits reject this terminology as unnecessarily pathologizing (because it conflates benign bodily variations with malignant medical threats) and prefer “Differences of Sex Development” (InterAct & Lambda Legal, 2018). This varied terminology and its deployment has serious material consequences for intersex-bodied people worldwide. To investigate communication of these bodily variations, the project proposes an innovative research design that: (a) integrates the insights from a range of disciplines; (b) draws on a large corpus of recorded interview and focus group data; (c) uses a metapragmatic discourse analytic framework; and (d) examines the sociocultural dimensions of the local perception of intersex traits. Perspectives on localized structures around intersex embodiment will be sought through up to 50 recorded interviews with Hong Kong stakeholders. The proposed research has great potential to manifest itself in policy changes surrounding health care practice and public understanding of intersex traits. 提議的項目將是首項以香港為重點，在亞洲或多語言環境下研究如何使用雙性人/性發育障礙（及相關）術語的研究工作。為了配合國際趨勢，2016年聯合國禁止酷刑委員會發布了一份關於香港的報告，其中明確指出雙性兒童是一個「需要接受不必要的、不可逆轉的手術的群體」，並對「此類行為造成的長期身心痛苦」表示關注（聯合國禁止酷刑委員會（CAT），2016，第28節）。委員會強烈建議香港特別行政區應通過良好的溝通去尊重雙性人的身體自主權和心理健康。 提議的項目是基於首席研究員出版的研究成果。（美國的）參加者認為醫學化的語言是他們傳達雙性人生活體驗的主要障礙，而這些語言也是理解雙性人體的邏輯的一部分。在香港的權益關係者之中，此類溝通的性質和範圍尚未得到實證研究。鑑於英語中存在過多的競爭/靈活語言，本研究旨在探討英語和廣東話的綜合使用如何在不同的語言領域中（例如家庭、醫院或診所）影響本地的交流。雙性特徵是統計學上不常見的身體特徵，亦不符合醫學和社會上的生殖和/或染色體慣例。有時候，這種特質在醫療背景中也被描述成“性發育障礙”（DSDs）。然而，大多數先天雙性人並不認同這個術語，認為這是不必要的病理化（因它將良性的身體變異與惡性的醫療威脅混為一談），並更傾向於稱其為“性發育差異” (InterAct & Lambda Legal, 2018)。這種有差異的術語及應用會在國際範圍內對雙性人產生嚴重的物質性後果。為了研究如何溝通這些身體上的差異，本項目提出了一個有如下特徵的創新性研究設計：（a）結合不同學科的研究發現；（b）使用包含大量訪談和焦點小組紀錄數據的大型語料庫；（c）使用元語用分析框架；（d）剖析本地對雙性特徵的社會文化認知。此項目將透過多達五十份在港權益關係者的訪談紀錄，去探討雙性人特徵在本地化結構的觀點。 提議的研究在圍繞醫療實踐的政策改變以及公眾對於雙性人特徵的理解方面具有很大的潛力。

17621819.label: Realisation of objectives
17621819.value: Obective 1 - Fully achieved because a database of perspectives on intersex/DSD terminology in both English and Cantonese has begun to be built in relation to diverse populations. It is being built from the interview recordings and is being published in research articles. Objective 2 - The innovative and respectful research design was developed and used with productive success. Metapragmatic discourse analysis of interviews with doctors and intersex people has proved to be a more respectful approach in which the language theorizations of stakeholders themselves are examined for the insights they can provide. Objective 3 - This objective was achieved, as the researcher secured access to intersex perspectives, with frank reflections from them about their lived experiences on Hong Kong. This is no mean feat given that sensitive-topic research often founders when potential informants are unwilling to participate. Achieving this objective has brought intersex embodied experience into this Hong Kong oriented research conversation for the first time. Objective 4 - Fully achieved via the analyses that have been published already (one chapter and nine conference presentations), as well as the analyses in preparation for publication (Cambridge Element and numerous articles being adapted from the previously mentioned conference talks). All of these contributions to international research bring with them the innovation of Hong Kong accounts in Hong Kong's plurilingual context, showing clearly the importance of considering the global circulation and local translation of medical and activist terminologies and how intersex experience in hospitals and the rest of society are directly affected by this linguistic reality. Objectives 5-6: Achieved via emailing recommendations and findings to doctors who participated in the study as well as by posting information resources on the HKU website.
