18607519.label: Major findings and research outcome
18607519.value: In this project, we have proposed a new VS approach, which is an integrated structural equation modeling (SEM) approach for conditional path analysis to address the limitations of the traditional methods for assessing mediated moderation (meMO). To evaluate the adequacy and the application of the new VS approach for assessing meMO, two simulation studies were conducted and the following outlined the major findings of these studies. In Simulation Study 1, we focused on evaluating the VS approach and compared it with the traditional regression-based method for assessing meMO. The results of the simulation study revealed that: (i) the VS model specification of meMO showed a good performance in terms of the accuracy of parameter and standard error estimates, statistical power, and coverage probability of 95% confidence interval of the meMO effect, supporting the adequacy of the VS approach for assessing meMO (Kwan et al., 2023); (ii) among all the methods, only the new VS approach had the ability to recover the total moderation effect in the effect decomposition process, supporting the distinctiveness of the VS approach in studying the meMO effects (Kwan et al., 2023). In Simulation Study 2, we focused on applying the VS approach for doing cross-group comparisons of the meMO effects. Specifically, we have looked at two different methods, namely, the likelihood ratio test and the difference in coefficients test for making statistical inference about the differences in the meMO effects between the groups using multi-sample SEM. The results of the simulation study suggested that: (i) both methods showed satisfactory performance in the two-group condition with good control in Type I error rate in the null condition and sufficient statistical power to detect the group differences when sample size was large as 200 in most conditions except when the difference was trivial; (ii) the likelihood ratio test is more flexible as it can handle the comparison of two or more groups. Although the Type I error rate in the null condition increased as the number of groups increased, the statistical power for detecting the differences among the groups also increased when there were more groups. In summary, the findings of this research project supported the adequacy and practical significance of the VS approach for assessing meMO. As an outcome of this project, we have also developed a statistical R package “VS” to assist researchers conduct the conditional path analysis using the VS approach. For details, see the VS website at https://vsquanpsy.wixsite.com/home.

18607519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18607519.value: There are two potential areas for further development of the research. The first area is about the practical issues related to the implementation of the VS approach for conditional path analysis. These practical issues include missing data analysis, sample size determination, power analysis, and handling multicategorical variables in conditional path models. To extend the project outcome and increase the sustainability of the project, the project team has already successfully secured a knowledge transfer grant (see Part C) to support future upgrade of the VS package and some of these practical issues will be addressed in future version of the VS package. The second potential area of development is about the methodology for testing multilevel conditional path models with clustered data. Theoretically, the moderator and mediator in the conditional path models may be measured at different levels, and therefore multilevel modeling technique has to be applied in order to study the conditional direct and indirect effects appropriately. The testing of multilevel conditional path models allows researchers to study both the group dynamics and individual psychological process simultaneously. In the future, the team will explore how to extend the VS approach for assessing conditional indirect effects in the multilevel context.

18607519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18607519.value: Mediated moderation (meMO) is one type of integrated models that combine mediation and moderation for explaining human processes and helps researchers explore the mechanism of how the relation between two variables changes in different conditions. Although meMO is conceptually useful, there has been much debate about its statistical representations and practical meaning. This project aimed to study the analytical framework of meMO and address the long existing myths and confusions about meMO. Specifically, we have refined the variable system (VS) approach that we previously proposed to address the limitations of the existing methods for assessing meMO. Through the simulation studies, we have provided empirical evidences to illustrate the distinctiveness and practical significance of the VS approach for assessing meMO. In addition, based on the research findings, we have also developed a new statistical R package “VS” to support researchers conducting the analysis of meMO using the VS approach. The significance of this project lies in its capacity to provide a guiding framework and statistical tool to more effectively capture the complex relations among variables in human processes, and hence contributes to the improvement of theory development by facilitating researchers in achieving more accurate and insightful results in theory testing.

18608319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18608319.value: In the years surrounding the second World War from the 1930s-50s, numerous new theatres opened in different districts across Hong Kong including Majestic Theatre (1928 in Jordan), Cathay Theatre (1939 in Wanchai), Capitol Theatre (1952 in Causeway Bay), etc. These buildings indicated a flourishing of entertainment businesses in Hong Kong and the high demand of this form of leisure from the local society. Interestingly, most of these theatre buildings were built in the Art Deco architectural style. Most of these theatres are now demolished or abandoned, but a socio-history of entertainment and theatre buildings in Hong Kong are missing in academia and there is a need of repositioning in the field. This research argues that Art Deco, a modern architectural style, can be understood as a form of entertainment and demonstration of resistance of the colonized in early twentieth century Hong Kong. The study also aims at demonstrating that these theatre buildings are not passive objects, but rather subjects that are able to consume the dominating culture to ‘self-fashion’ and ‘self-represent’, in using postcolonial theoretical terms. Previous research has been done on Chinese cinema operators and cinema business in Hong Kong in the early twentieth century, but little research has been conducted to link the architecture or socio-cultural landscape of Hong Kong cinema to postcolonial theories. This project will envision a three-tiered impact. First, the research will reveal the ways in which the patron, architect and the audience of the theatre buildings interacted with each other in laying the foundation of modern cinema and public entertainment history in Hong Kong. Second, based on archival research and visual ethnography, the research will adopt postcolonial theory to analyse and problematize the architectures, and investigate the ways that they ‘self-fashion’ and ‘self-represent’ different identities. Third, on top of formulating a database on Art Deco theatres, the research will propose ways of strengthening the conservation policy for the remaining few surviving Art Deco theatres in Hong Kong. The project will ultimately examine the reach of Art Deco into everyday life of Hong Kong in the form of architecture and cinema, critique the dynamics between the dominated-subjugated in colonial Hong Kong, and offer a new way to conserve architectural heritage through emphasizing its aesthetic and socio-cultural implications. 約在30至50年代第二次世界大戰之時，大量新型戲院於香港各處開業，包括佐敦的京華戲院(1928)、灣仔的國泰戲院(1939)和銅鑼灣的京華戲院(1952)。這些戲院建築均代表了香港當年娛樂事業的蓬勃發展，以及本地社會對戲院的需求。值得一提的是，這些戲院建築大多以裝飾藝術風格建成。這些建築大多現時已消失於歷史洪流，但在學術研究界中關於香港娛樂事業的社會歷史和戲院建築的一頁仍有待填補。本研究議論裝飾藝術作為一種新的建築形式，可以詮釋為一種對娛樂的視覺表達；也是二十世紀中葉香港扺抗殖民化的表現。本研究亦希望以後殖民理論，解構這些戲院建築如何把建築硬件，轉化為主流文化下的自我形像塑造。在此之前，只有零星的學者曾對二十世紀初中資院線和香港戲院產業作出研究，但把這類戲院建築或整個產業的文化景觀以後殖民理論串連起來的研究則寥寥可數。 是次研究盼望帶來三方面影響。首先會研究事業者、建築師及用家如何影響及推動香港戲院業以及娛樂事業的發展歷史。其二，本研究會以後殖民理論加上資料搜集，導出戲院如何以不同的自我形像塑造建構不同的身份認同。再者，本研究會建立一個以裝飾藝術風格的戲院建築作為重點的資料庫並作為引子，為香港碩果僅存的戲院建築保育作建議。本研究最後將會以建築和戲院為基本，以評估裝飾藝術風格在香港的深入程度，評述在殖民地時代香港的權力和自由，並提出著重於建築特色和期社會文化價值的全新保育方針。

18608319.label: Realisation of objectives
18608319.value: Objective 1: Understand the importance and implications of an architectural style upon the socio-cultural and political dynamics in the local community Realisation: The project demonstrated how Hong Kong’s theatres have transformed during the turn of the twentieth century in response to government ordinances, public health and safety concerns, as well as socio-cultural development and international exchange. By adopting a postcolonial theoretical framework, the theatres can be better understood under a clearer light by ‘decolonising’ and unravelling the narratives that the architectures presented. Objective 2: Identify the players and stakeholders (architect, patron, etc.) behind the construction and design of theatre buildings: why was Art Deco chosen as an architectural style and what message(s) of modernity it brought to the society Realisation: The data obtained from the interviews correlate with narratives about the role of Chinese theatres in the local community in the late 19th and early 20th century, as well as confirming global influences at the time where design trends were being brought in, evident in both Chinese and European individuals in the city. Some of the interviewee’s statements as well as historic personal writings were quoted directly as they play a crucial role in re-painting a picture of the local microcosm a century ago, ranging from the theatre operator’s point of view, the late architect of the theatre, the clientele and the community at large. Objective 3: Reconstruct and map Hong Kong’s early modern cinema and entertainment history by documenting the theatre buildings, architects and cinema operators and via using visual ethnography Realisation: By adopting a postcolonial analytical framework as well as interpretive-historical and archival research methods to examine primary resources including government documents, historical photos and drawings, interviewing descendants of cinema operators and architects, as well as film archivists and architectural historians, the project details how socio-cultural factors, evolving building regulations and the local industry had impacted upon the transition of theatre architecture over half a century, witnessing indigenous efforts that resisted certain colonial narratives in the design process. The project also scrutinises what potentials the architectures, demolished or still existing, can serve in the context of theatre heritage in postcolonial Hong Kong. Objective 4: Formulate and expand on a database of Art Deco theatres and entertainment buildings in Hong Kong Realisation: Through unveiling a large number of previously unexamined materials, including government documents and personal archives, as well as engaging in interviews, the project listed out the theatres that transformed from ‘Chinese theatres’ to 'Western cinemas' in Hong Kong, and are also presented in the journal papers. The history of the plague and the enaction of the Entertainment Ordinance also reflect in colonial policies directly influencing the earlier architectural designs of the theatres, followed by a ‘resistance’ of Western culture and empowerment of indigenous efforts resulting in localised movies as well as architectural styles beginning in the 1910s. Through the efforts of the descendants of historic but under-researched architects and theatre operators, the Hong Kong Film Archives, and various local researchers, the stories behind these theatres are able to be re-represented. Objective 5: Re-examine and enhance the policy for conserving heritage buildings in Hong Kong, paving the way for a special focus on theatre buildings and cinema heritage Realisation: From resisting colonial narratives of ‘imported’ theatre culture and architecture to resisting bureaucratic heritage conservation processes and policy, of which is regarded as a ‘product of colonial governance’ that reflects ‘Eurocentric biases’, the theatres investigated in this paper can be interpreted as a ‘cultural process’, understood together with the body of social interactions and movements. Afterall, heritage movements come from many directions, and it shows the various ways and depths in which collective identities are made and contested for the theatre buildings.

18608319.label: Major findings and research outcome
18608319.value: The PI has one paper accepted and one other paper resubmitted, respectively to Surveying & Built Environment journal and the International Journal of Heritage Studies. Both papers are direct outcomes of the project. The major findings from the project are that certain theatres in interwar Hong Kong were characterized by a decorative architectural style that shifted away from revival or neoclassical forms to signify a modern era in theatre design. The project also traced intercultural exchange among architectural practices of the time, contributing to the history of modern Hong Kong theatre by delineating the socio-historical context of Art Deco, the development of local cinema industry in the early 20th century, and analysed the reasons behind the transformation of theatre design in the interwar years.

18608319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18608319.value: As discovered in the project and also mentioned in the journal papers, some interesting new leads are found, particularly the architect of an Art Deco theatre in Hong Kong (Alhambra Theatre) Wong T.C. was also the architect of a still existing Art Deco theatre in Macau (Apollo Theatre). In fact, this architect is related to Lai Man-wai, regarded the father of modern cinema in Hong Kong (Wong's wife was the sister of Lai). This is a greatly interesting lead and indicates that perhaps there was a close network of relations in the cinema industry during 1930s Hong Kong, and the PI anticipates to continue to uncover more hidden links and narratives behind these architectures.

18608319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18608319.value: Based on interviews, old newspapers, photographs, as well as personal writings and tracing family lineage of interwar architects, this project revealed that certain architects produced unique regional responses to an adaptive modern architecture in Chinese cities including Hong Kong and Macau. Modern architecture in this region, particularly theatres, may therefore be understood in the context of the dynamics of these architects in reflection of their country’s architectural milieu and adapting to local conditions. It also shows the autonomy of the architect to be able to implement their own preferences and being able to convey unique adaptations of decorative (at times Chinese) elements with modern Western expressions. This project and research will act as a bridge to understand the framework of architectural practices in early twentieth century Hong Kong and China, placed within an international context, and their contribution towards modernist architecture in their urban manifestations in the Chinese cities.

18608619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18608619.value: This project responds to the need for research into how to address the educational challenges confronting ethnic minority students (EMS) in Hong Kong, defined as “people from non-Chinese ethnicities” (Census and Statistics Department, 2017). It has been argued that developing the cultural intelligence of Hong Kong teachers should be a priority of teacher education and that teachers must learn to recognize diversity across multiple sites, including classrooms, homes and the community. To address this need, there have been calls for initiatives that build connections between EMS, their families and Hong Kong schools. This project responds to that need. The project investigates the expectations and experiences of home-school relations amongst different groups of EMS in Hong Kong schools. Using in-depth interviews, the project comprises three case study schools that have been identified as enrolling significant numbers of EMS. It aims to explore the needs and wants of different stakeholders - EMS, their parents/ guardians and their teachers – about home-school relations. Using in-depth interviews, data gathered from stakeholders will be used to design tailor-made home-school partnerships that responds to the needs of wants of stakeholders within each of the case study schools. The findings of the study are expected to have implications for educational policy makers and school authorities who wish to establish partnerships between schools and the families of EMS in Hong Kong and other analogous settings worldwide. These results will also be of interest to educationalists involved in the design and delivery of in-service teacher professional development programmes that foster the cultural intelligence of school-based teachers. Finally, the findings will provide insights for teacher educators tasked with designing preservice teacher education programs that reduce prejudice and support anti-racist education. 此項目回應了研究如何應對香港少數族裔學生所面臨的教育挑戰的需要，少數族裔被定義為“非華裔人士”（政府統計處，2017）。有人認為，發展香港教師的文化智慧應該是教師教育的重點，教師必須學會識別地點的多樣性，包括教室，家庭和社區。為了滿足這一需求，有人呼籲在少數族裔學生，其家庭和香港學校之間建立聯繫。該項目滿足了這一需求。 此項目調查了香港學校不同少數族裔學生組別之間家庭與學校關係的期望和經驗。項目採用深入訪談三所有大量的少數族裔學生註冊的學校案例以探索不同持份者(學生，他們的父母/監護人和他們的老師)對家校關係的需求和願望。通過深入訪談所收集的數據將用於設計特制的家校合作夥伴關係，以滿足每宗研究學校案例的持份者之需求。 預計研究結果將對教育政策制定者和學校當局產生影響，他們希望在香港和全球其他類似環境中建立學校與少數族裔家庭之間的合作關係。這些結果也將引起參與設計和提供在職教師專業發展計劃的教育工作者的興趣，這個計劃旨在培養校本教師的文化智慧。最後，調查結果將為教師教育工作者提供見解，他們的任務是設計減少偏見和支援反種族歧視教育的職前教師教育計劃

18608619.label: Realisation of objectives
18608619.value: To identify the situated needs and wants of EMS, their parents/guardians and their teachers for home school-school relations in three case study schools in Hong Kong The project has explored the needs and wants of a group of participants in an HSP scheme. The project gave voice to one group of schoolteachers in Hong Kong. Employing a framework of teacher identity construction, the project explored the needs and wants of stakeholders in an HSP setting and how teachers, parents, and students experienced setting up and running a home-school partnership that responds to their needs. The results suggest that the participants faced challenges in setting up and developing partnerships but found solutions to address challenges. The project outcomes have implications for both schools and individual teachers who want to establish home-school partnerships, as well as for school leaders and policymakers wanting to support the HSP development in their own districts and schools. To design and implement HSPs that responds to these situated needs and wants. The HSP took place in a secondary school located in an urban area of Hong Kong. The school offers classes in grades eight to thirteen and contains a large number of ethnic minority students, primarily of Pakistani and Indian ethnicity but also including some students from the Philippines. The school is, in Hong Kong terms, a band 2 school, with some content subjects taught to more able students using English as the medium of instruction. Less academically able students are assigned to classes that use Chinese as the medium of instruction. The principal participant in the study is a family of Indian ethnicity, termed here the Kohli family (a pseudonym as anonymity was promised to all participants and institutions taking part in the study). Although several EM families were invited to participate in the study, this paper reports on the experiences of a single family in order to examine meaning-making processes for individuals and group members in depth. To identify best practices in the design and implementation of HSPs for EMS in Hong Kong. A key finding of the study that should impact best practices for the design and implementation of HSP was that the participants must became collaborators as they work together to address the challenges and issues that arose. In addition, they should be promoters and builders. For instance, they should promote and built linguistic, academic, cultural knowledge amongst each other in a two-way process of collaboration. They should also be influences and informers, as they share experiences and views that impacted what and how learning and teaching occurred within the school. There was also some degree of role reversal. Parents, for example, should become educators of teachers as they share cultural and religious knowledge and practices. Teachers, in turn, should take on the role of learners of this knowledge. The HSP design must also assist in valuing and validating the history and experiences of the EM participants. The results of the study are also suggestive the ways in which context can impact the form and outcomes of HSPs. In particular, there must exist in the HSP implementation a strong feeling of community at the school participating in the study. Teachers, parents, and students should feel a strong commitment to the school and hence willingness to engage in the HSP and were therefore invested in doing their best to ensure its success. Indeed, the parents must communicate on a regular basis with other parents, thus making it easier to establish and nurture relationships that could draw other parents into the HSP. This has implications for schools wishing to set up HSPs. For instance, it might be that schools do not need to be as proactive as might otherwise be the case in recruiting parents and families to participate in the HSPs. If this is not the case, then intermediate outreach teachers might need to make these links between the school and parents in the establishment of HSPs. To draw out implications for in-service teacher professional development and preservice teacher education programs for supporting EMS and their families in Hong Kong and settings worldwide. To be successful, the results of the study suggest that HSPs require teachers to commit to a long-term vision of the HSP. This requires that teacher professional development programs as well as preservice teacher education programs prepare teachers for these challenges. These programs should require teachers to experience a mini version of an HSP through, for example, role-playing the different stakeholders in an HSP meeting. These experiences can be recorded and then participants critically reflect on the needs and wants and roles of different stakeholders. This would allow teachers to better understand the perspectives of different stakeholders, in particular parents and students. If ethnic minority students and their parents could be included in these role plays and also provide lectures to teachers on their needs and wants within the education system then the value of such teacher development initiatives could be further enhanced.

18608619.label: Major findings and research outcome
18608619.value: The findings suggest that goals and objectives of HSPs should be shared ones amongst the stakeholders. Teachers can invest time and effort in finding out, for example, what the aspirations for their children are. Teachers can then work in a HSP setting with parents towards achieving these aspirations. In this way all participants in the HSP are seen to take on the role of problem solvers and moreover that this is a team investment. If problems can be dealt with openly and in a respectful two-way communication process parents can come to feel that the HSP is open and respectful of their wishes and concerns, and they are more likely to feel comfortable expressing their ideas and suggestions within the HSP. Homework is another possible area in which such two-way communication can be encouraged. Homework could be designed in ways that actively involve parents by, for example, allowing them to contribute unique cultural, social and religious knowledge to homework activities which the EM students can then share with classmates and other members of the wider school community. Results indicate that teachers can take certain actions to support the development of HSPs. First, teachers should reflect on their own practices and processes. IS a HSP part of these practices and beliefs? If so, teachers are inclined to make contact with families of EM students. Such an approach can be part of the teacher recruitment processes followed by schools. These supportive beliefs can in turn be a significant inducement to parents become more willing to take part in a HSP. The findings also suggest that teachers can position parents as a very valuable resource. This can help in developing trust between all the different stakeholders and this can be essential to the success of an HSP. Indeed, teachers are an crucial input to encouraging EM parents to believe that they are welcome participants in the life of a school and this can be achieved by teacher displays of interest and care in students, issues which include but also go beyond the mere achievement of high grades. Teachers, and schools in general, should also be ready to take advantage of any opportunity for communication with parents, be that formal or indeed informal. Such communication, moreover, should be from teacher to parent but equally important is that communication is valued from parent to teacher.

18608619.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18608619.value: The HSP initiatives can be extended to other schools and focus on specific ethnic minority groups to give a more tailored approach to the development of HSPs. This is not to suggest that all issues facing EM students can be addressed successfully by simply setting up and running a HSP. In this respect the results reported above suggest opportunities for future research. A larger scale study, for example, could be undertaken that involves multiple schools to determine if the results reported here can be reproduced over multiple settings. In addition, quantitative investigations can be undertaken to determine if HSPs do have a significant and long-term impact on students’ academic performance. This research can also be a means of exploring different ways for teachers and families to exchange knowledge and experiences, for teachers to explore new ways of constructing meaningful learning opportunities for their students based on their HSP experiences, to determine what types of learning resources different

18608619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18608619.value: The results show that HSPs are a valuable contribution to the school life of ethnic minority students. There are barriers to their success, however. These include relations of power. teachers are often seen as being in a more powerful position than students or parents. Cultural barriers also exist. Some parents are reluctant to share critical comments with teachers for fear of negative implications. Therefore, HSPs need to establish clear guidelines for their conduct. These include valuing all contributions equally, treating the participants with respect and sharing topics that might be uncomfortable in a atmosphere of trust. it is also essential that a long term view be taken for all HSPs as benefits will be unlikely if a short term approach is taken. This means policy makers and school officials must be willing to make a long-term commitment in terms of time and other resources if HSPs are to achieve their true potential.

18609719.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18609719.value: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) demonstrate limitations in social communication and social interaction across home, school and community contexts. Restrictions on participation in activities impinges further on the social development of individuals with ASD. Teaching and intervention programs using humanoid robots for children with ASD has rapidly been developed with an aim to improve their social functioning. Increasing resources have been invested in the development of artificial intelligence engineering to aid in the programming and design of humanoid robots to enhance the learning of children with ASD, and local special schools have been subsidized to enable the purchase of humanoid robots for use with students with ASD. However, there is no standardized policy, guidelines or protocols to guide practice. The evidence-base of robotic intervention programs for children with ASD is limited. There is, as yet, no evidence to inform therapists, teachers and service providers on a best practice program design to ensure program effectiveness. This study will develop and test a Robotic Intervention Framework for Children with ASD in the real context. It will be built from a synthesis of literature review, verification with the evidence collected in the real context; and testing of effectiveness using scientific methods. The first part of this study will focus on the identification and initial testing of core elements of effective robotic intervention programs to form a practice framework. Part II will use a randomized control trial to test the efficacy of the robotic intervention programs that incorporates all elements of the framework. Part III will use a qualitative approach to examine the outcomes of the program with reference to the elements of the practice framework. With a framework that is built upon evidence and tested sufficiently, practice guidelines and an intervention protocol will be delineated to ensure the success of robotic intervention programs. 自閉症孩童常會在不同生活處境中表現出溝通和人際闗係方面的問題，社交障礙窒礙了孩子在社交發展方面的身心健康。近年，應用機械人科技於自閉症孩童的教育和訓練越趨普及，工程師致力研發相關的人工智能，特殊學校亦投放資源購置了機械人，惟這方面的科研實證仍未充足，最徍執行的成功的訓練方案仍未見有所準則。有見及此，此研究計劃會建構一個成功的機械人訓練方案執行框架，此框架會應用在自閉症孩童訓練中，並且會在真實的訓練環境中被驗證其成效。整個框架的建立是建基於科研實證，在第一個研究階段中，團隊會初步測試並找出機械人訓練方案的成功執行因素；在第二部份的研究中，我們會採用隨機對照試驗以測試這個方案的成效；於第三部份，團隊會採用質性的研究方法以深入查證這個方案對自閉症孩子在社交參與和生活上的影響。這個成功的機械人訓練方案執行框架在經過多重驗證和確立後，就可以編制成實務的訓練指引和執行手冊，以促進機械人能成功地應用於自閉症孩童的社交訓練中。

18609719.label: Realisation of objectives
18609719.value: Objective 1 is fully achieved. Methods. In Phase I of this study, an initial framework was built based on a scoping review. This review aimed to identify the core elements conducive to effective robotic intervention programmes for children with ASD. In Phase II, the content of the initial framework was validated using a case study approach in a real-life setting. Results. The robotic intervention framework, which comprised three domains, was built and tested. The three domains were robot-, child-, and programme-related factors. Elements within each domain were identified and verified in real-life contexts. Phase I: Formulation of an initial framework based on the scoping review Twenty-seven papers were included. The results of the analysis show that three categories of core elements related to effective robotic intervention were collated: (1) robot selection; (2) participant characteristics and (3) activities and instructions. Descriptions of the elements in the respective domains are identified in Table 2. Phase II. Testing the initial framework using a case study approach Review of the framework, placement of new elements into the framework and review of the robotic intervention programmes were required. The two new elements were placed under the domain of child-related factors. The final framework is formed. Objective 2 is fully achieved. Part II used a randomised control trial to test the efficacy of robotic intervention programmes incorporating all elements of the framework. The study developed and tested a Robotic Intervention Framework for Children with ASD to ensure the best use of robots in such programmes. Results Performance-based behavioural change in social communication The overall ADOS score was used as an outcome measure to assess the performance-based change in social behaviours. A one-way ANCOVA was performed to compare the effectiveness of the three interventions while controlling for the pretest score. Levene’s test and normality checks were performed, and the assumptions were met. There was a significant difference in the posttest overall ADOS scores between the groups (F(2,56) = 44.07, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.612). Post hoc tests showed significant differences between the experimental and comparison groups (p = 0.002) and between the experimental and control groups (p = 0.002). Moreover, there was a significant difference between the comparison and control groups (p < 0.001). A low overall ADOS score (O) indicates high performance in social communication and behaviour. When the estimated marginal means were compared, the lowest ADOS score was found in the experimental group (O = 12.69), followed by the comparison group (O = 19.21) and the control group (O = 23.353). The three subscales, namely communication (C), reciprocal social interaction (RSI), and restrictive repetitive behaviours (RRB), reflected the essential aspects of social communication and behaviours. A one-way MANOVA was used to determine whether there were any differences between the three groups in their pretest and posttest scores across the three subscales. The MANOVA indicated no significant differences between the groups for the C, RSI, and RRB scores (F(2,57) = 1.187, p = 0.318) in the pretest. In the MANOVA for the posttest scores, there were statistically significant differences in the subscale scores between the three groups (F(2,57) = 4.16, p < 0.001; Wilk’s Λ = 0.253; partial η2 = 0.497). Significant differences were found in the three subscale scores: communication (F(2,57) = 56.02, p < 0.001, effect size partial η2 = 0.663), reciprocal social interaction (F(2,57) = 33.06, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.537), and restrictive repetitive behaviour (F(2,57) = 5.73, p = 0.005, partial η2 = 0.167). Post hoc univariate tests revealed the source of the significant main effects. Significant differences were found in the communication and reciprocal social interactions scores between the experimental group and the control and comparison groups (p < 0.01). However, no significant differences were found in restrictive repetitive behaviour between the experimental group and the other two groups (p > 0.05). Parent-perceived change in social responsiveness The SRS was used to measure changes in the participants’ social responsiveness as reported by their parents. A one-way ANCOVA was conducted to evaluate the changes and compare the effectiveness of the three interventions while controlling for the pretest score. Levene’s test and normality checks were performed, and the assumptions were met. There were significant differences in the posttest SRS total scores between the groups (F(2,56) = 5.56, p = 0.006, partial η2 = 0.166). Post hoc tests showed significant differences between the experimental group and the comparison group (p = 0.041) and between the experimental group and the control group (p = 0.041). Moreover, there were significant differences between the comparison group and the control group (p < 0.001) and between the comparison group and the control group (p = 0.008). A low SRS-T score indicates high performance in social communication and behaviour. When the estimated marginal means were compared, the lowest SRS-T was found in the experimental group (73.49), followed by the comparison group (74.72) and the control group (79.94). Hence, the experimental group performed best under all three conditions. Objective 3 is fully achieved. This part aimed to (1) identify the qualitative outcomes of a robot-mediated social skills training programme for children with ASD, (2) examine the impact of such programmes on children’s social participation and (3) identify the essential elements of robotic interventions that are conducive to children’s social development. Results The COPM results identified the successful outcomes related to social participation. The unit of analysis in this part of the study is the outcome of robotic intervention program. A total of 48 items, which measured social development outcomes, were collected from the 16 participants. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed that the robotic intervention programme brought statistically significant changes to the scores for both performance (Z = -5.755, p < 0.001) and satisfaction (Z = -5.811, p < 0.001). The median scores for performance were 3.5 in the pretest and 7 in the posttest. The median scores for satisfaction were 3 in the pretest and 6 in the posttest. Content analysis was performed on the transcripts of the COPM interviews. Forty-eight successful outcomes relating to the social development of children with ASD were extracted and collated into themes and subthemes. The 12 collated themes were matched against the three essential diagnostic criteria of ASD, namely communicative behaviour, socio-emotional reciprocity and social relationship (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). The most commonly reported changes as revealed in the matching of codes against the themes, were verbal expression, social awareness and emotional reciprocity, in order of priority. Semi-structured interviews. Semi-structured interviews with the parents and instructors were conducted before, during and after the training programme. Content analysis of the interviews with the parents and instructors revealed the key themes regarding (1) the impact of the robotic intervention programme on the personal growth and social development of the children with ASD and (2) the elements of the programme perceived to be conducive to the growth and development of children with ASD. Impact on personal growth and social development. 18609719.label: Major findings and research outcome
18609719.value: Part I – building of a robotic intervention framework The robotic intervention framework, which comprised three domains, was built and tested. The three domains were robot-, child-, and programme-related factors. Elements within each domain were identified and verified in real-life contexts. Part II – Testing the effectiveness of robotic intervention program using a randomized controlled trial A robotic intervention program was designed based on the Robotic Intervention Framework as built in Part I. The program was successfully tested using a RCT and the participants in the robotic intervention groups demonstrated a statistically significant change in communication, social behaviours and social responsiveness. Part III – Examining the qualitative outcomes of the designed program The results from the COPM analysis showed a statistically significant change in both the levels of performance and satisfaction regarding the children’s social participation. The parents satisfaction with the performance of their children was enhanced. These results showed that the improvement in the children’s social participation was substantial, impressive and observable to their parents. The results of this study confirmed the impact of robotic intervention programmes on the daily living and social participation of children with ASD. It demonstrated that the improvement of children with ASD resulting from robotic intervention programmes had moved beyond improvement in component skills (such as eye contact and joint attention) to that in social participation in daily living. Impressive qualitative and behavioural changes were observed and reported throughout the training. The most commonly reported changes, in order of priority, were improved verbal expression, social awareness and emotional reciprocity. The personal growth and social development of the children with ASD were enhanced. Three important impacts of the programme on the children with ASD were enhanced self-esteem, self-confidence and presence. This finding is interesting. The programme was not meant to build self-esteem or self-confidence. Its primary objectives were to teach social skills. This result implies that robotic intervention programmes are not limited to enhancing social skills. It sheds lights on the implications of enhancing social development for children with ASD through their interaction and relation with a social robot. The programme elements that were perceived as important in contributing to the positive changes in the children’s social development were (1) robot friendship; (2) the robot acting as a facilitator and model; and (3) the presence of a human instructor capable of leading the programme. Robot friendship was the most commonly reported element.

18609719.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18609719.value: Reconciling evidence across the three parts of this project, the research team used a mixed source of data for testing and triangulation to enhance the empirical validity of the framework in this study. It proved robotic intervention programmes impact the social development of children with ASD. Robotic intervention programmes are complex in nature, and they involve multi-dimensional skillsets to design, plan, implement and evaluate. This study attempted to integrate these multi-faceted dimensions to build a framework. The robotic intervention framework is in fact a generic model. It integrated evidence into practice. We used mostly the NAO robot in our study. There are also other humanoid and animated robots. Thus, future studies may test this framework using other robots to further enhance its validity. In part III, it highlights the importance of robot friendship for children with ASD. Robot friendship is an area that is worth studying.

18609719.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18609719.value: This study has developed and tested a Robotic Intervention Framework for Children with ASD in the real context. It was built from a synthesis of literature review and testing of effectiveness using scientific methods. The literature review of this study is focused on the identification and initial testing of core elements of effective robotic intervention programs to form a practice framework. Part II used a randomized control trial to test the efficacy of the robotic intervention programs that incorporated all elements of the framework. Part III identified the qualitative outcomes of a robot-mediated social skills training programme for children with ASD, and examined the impact of such programmes on children’s social participation. This is significant as there is no evidenced-based framework or protocol to guide the design and implementation of robotic intervention programs for children with ASD. A good program design incorporating all essential elements for effective interventions ensures the success of the training program.

18610719.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18610719.value: Teacher innovation, which is collective introduction and application of novel and useful ideas initiated by teachers, is crucial for inherently rewarding teachers, cultivating creativity in students, sustaining professional learning communities, and differentiating “stuck schools” from “moving schools”. However, despite the well documented merits, open exchange and exploration of creative ideas in schools could entail a risk because other school members, especially school leaders, may interpret and react to the creative ideas and practices differently. Moreover, engagement in deep, integrative dialogue among teachers, which is essential for transforming creative resource inputs into teacher innovation, has been a constant challenge for schools. In contrast to the vast literature on top-down introduction and implementation of innovative projects in schools, little is known about the types of teacher innovation, and even less on how voluntary, bottom-up innovative practices emerge among teachers. Using a two-phase research design, the project team attempts to address three questions: (1) what are the prevalent types of teacher innovation in Hong Kong? (2) how does teacher innovation emerge in schools, and (3) under which conditions are schools more conductive to teacher innovation? Based on extant literature on innovation, a provisional four-type taxonomy of teacher innovation is proposed. The study also draws on the componential theory, the interactional perspective, and school improvement literature, and proposes hypotheses regarding the factors and processes that enable teacher innovation. In the first phase, we will approach innovative primary and secondary schools in Hong Kong, and adopt document studies, individual interviews, and focus group interviews to seek a qualitative taxonomy of teacher innovation and an exploratory understanding of factors enabling teacher innovation. The former part of the results will be used to formulate a more sensitive instrument of teacher innovation, and the latter part will be used to refine the hypotheses to be tested in the next phase. In the second phase, the research team will approach approximately 600 teachers from 30 primary schools and 30 secondary schools, and focus on testing a general theoretical model of teacher innovation. This project is expected to generate at least two contributions. First, this project will enable a timely documentation of teacher innovative practices in Hong Kong, which facilitates a more nuanced understanding of the educational achievements as well as challenges in the society. Second, establishing a theoretical model that predicts teacher innovation will lay a useful foundation for future studies on teacher innovation in Hong Kong and elsewhere. 教師創新，意指教師在群體層面引進和應用新穎及有用的想法。它對於內在激勵教師、培育學生創新、維系專業學習群體，以及區分‘陷入困境的學校’和‘持續前進的學校’，都有關鍵的意義。 儘管創新有許多的優點，在學校裡公開討論和探索創新仍然可能帶來風險，因為學校其他成員， 特別是學校領導，可能對新穎的想法和實踐有不同的闡釋和反應。此外，將創意思維轉化成創新實踐，教師們需要參與深度的、結合式的對話，而這素來是學校工作中的一大難題。 相較于大量探討學校至上而下引進和推行創新專案的文獻，專門研究教師當中湧現的、自發的、自下而上的創新實踐的文獻少之又少。 本項目團隊計畫採用兩階段的研究設計，致力於回應三個問題：1）香港的學校裡有哪些盛行的教師創新實踐？ 2）教師創新在學校中是如何產生的？ 3）怎樣的學校條件最有利於教師創新？ 基於已有的創新研究文獻，我們提出了一個暫行的四類別教師創新，再基於創新成分理論、互動的視角，以及學校改進領域的文獻， 本研究就教師創新生成的前因和過程提出了具體的研究假設。 在第一階段，我們會聯繫香港社會公認有創意的小學和中學，採用文檔研究、個體訪談、和焦點訪談的方法，以辨識教師創新的類別和進一步探索教師創新的過程及情境因素。 前一部分研究的結果將會用於開發更具敏感度的教師創新測量工具，而後一部分的結果將被 于完善我們提出的研究假設。 在第二階段，研究團隊會聯繫大約30所小學和30所中學的600名教師，著重于檢驗教師創新的理論模型。 這個研究在兩個範疇可能作出貢獻。 首先，本項目及時記錄香港學校的教師創新實踐，這有助於我們這個社會中的教育成就和挑戰形成更豐富的認知。 第二，本專案建立起能夠預測教師創新的理論模型，這會對香港和其他地區的教師創新研究奠定有利的知識基礎。

18610719.label: Realisation of objectives
18610719.value: As stated in the proposal, the project team attempted to address three research questions: (1) what are the prevalent types of teacher innovation in Hong Kong? (2) how does teacher innovation emerge in schools, and (3) under which conditions are schools more conducive to teacher innovation? In the following section, the research team report the research activities carried out and explain how the research activities help to achieve each of the research objectives. The first research objective deals with the development of a parsimonious taxonomy of teacher innovation at primary and secondary schools. The research team had planned to individual interviews school principals and ask them about the type and nature of all important innovations initiated by teachers at their schools in the last five years. However, from the beginning of the project (January 2020) to the extended end date of project (June 2022), schools were either suspended or operated on a very tight half-day schedule with stringent health measures. The research team was not able to interview individual teachers or focused groups at multiple schools. More importantly, although the research team managed to collect semi-open online survey data from 156 teacher leaders during the COVID in Hong Kong, almost all the innovative practices reported during the pandemic period dealt with the adoption of online learning, which greatly constrained the conceptual breath of teacher innovation. Therefore, the project team sought to engage in alternative research activity to achieve the designated research objectives. Specifically, the research team analyzed a secondary dataset, the online discussion forum of three classes of one part-time master’s degree course taught by the PI. In the three classes, participants were in-service school leaders, and leading school innovation was one of the intended learning and teaching topics. Course participants shared more than 85 concrete, valid, and detailed examples of teacher innovation on the discussion forum. These cases confirmed that teacher innovation can occur in the areas of school life, including teaching and learning, supporting students, structuring professional learning and collaboration, designing management infrastructure and procedures, and developing school-family community partnerships. These cases also enabled verification of the proposed taxonomy of teacher innovation along two dimensions: the extent of novelty (exploitative innovation or exploratory innovation) and orientation type (prevention orientation or promotion orientation). Along these two dimensions, teacher innovation can be divided into four types: entrepreneurial, proactive, contributory, and responsive (Lu & Chen, under preparation). The second project objective aims to examine the individual and group-level determinants and process of teacher innovation. Three lines of research activities were carried out in this regard. Firstly, the PI delved into an underutilized existing Experience Sampling Method (ESM) dataset and examined individual level determinants and process of teacher innovation. The result revealed an immediate, same-day effect of work enjoyment on creativity of teacher leaders, as opposed to a one or two-day incubation process documented in the literature. Furthermore, the results also indicated that quality of recovery reported by teacher leaders in the morning precedes their work enjoyment reported by the teachers at the end of work in a day (Lu, 2021). Secondly, we found teacher entrepreneurial behavior enables teachers to seize innovation opportunities and scale-up innovation in schools. Through four-interconnected studies with four different groups of teacher informants, we aimed to develop and validate a multi-factor scale of teacher entrepreneurial behavior and tested its association with several key teacher outcomes including school innovation. As a result, we identified four stable and distinct factors of teacher entrepreneurial behavior, i.e., four typical sets of behavioral items commonly engaged by entrepreneurial teachers to advance innovations at schools. These behaviors include advocating innovative ideas and initiatives in schools, taking active measures to mitigating potential risks, mobilizing peer teachers through demonstrating humility, and securing professional and financial resources. The initial findings were presented at an international conference (Ho & Lu, 2022) and the full manuscript was submitted to journal in 2022 (Ho & Lu, under review). Thirdly, based on the proposal, the PI published a conceptual paper which posited a reciprocal relationship between professional learning and teacher innovation and suggested that teacher professional learning could enable teacher innovation and teacher innovation reversely sustains teacher professional learning (Lu & Campbell, 2020). The PI also collaborated with two external researchers and further tested an enriched theoretical model about teachers’ engagement in professional learning communities and teacher innovation. The research collaborator based in the East China Normal University collected a sample of 3419 senior high school teachers. We investigated how professional learning communities as the environmental structure influence teachers' efforts towards innovation. We also explored mechanisms through which professional learning communities promote teacher innovation in schools with different levels of innovation climate (Liu, Lu, & Yin, 2022; full reference is provided under section 11. Other impact > collaboration with other research institutions). The third research objective sought to investigate under which conditions schools are most conducive to teacher innovation. The research team conducted in-depth case studies of four innovative schools which demonstrated radical innovations over the past five years. The case schools were composed of three primary schools and one secondary school. For each school, at least two rounds of interview data were conducted with school principals, with at least one year interval in between. Additionally, individual interviews were also conducted with key staffs and teachers from each school. Different formats of supplementary data were also collected at each school, such as meeting with parents or students, ethnographic attendance at school information day or other relevant events. Initial findings of the case study have been presented at an international conference (Lu, 2022) and the full manuscript based on the case study of four schools is under preparation (Lu & Walker, under preparation). The analysis of case studies also revealed that school innovation is not only a school-based professional pursuit of educational ideals in vacuum, but also an institutional response in addressing the burgeoning school competition in Hong Kong. We extended this line of research by delving into secondary data, including school student intake data from Secondary School Profiles 2021/22 published by the government advisory committee on Home-School Co-operation, and school development plan, annual schools’ reports retrieved from the websites of 327 secondary schools. Using hierarchical regression analysis, we found that a dual emphasis of both academic achievement and whole-person development orientation can enhance a school’s competitiveness in terms of student enrolment (Ho & Lu, under review). The results of secondary data analysis affirm a quasi-market condition of schooling in Hong Kong and implies parents are increasingly concerned about both their children's academic achievement and whole-person development in schools.

18610719.label: Major findings and research outcome
18610719.value: Teacher innovation in Hong Kong and nearby regions can largely be classified into four distinct types: entrepreneurial, proactive, contributory, and responsive. The entrepreneurial type of teacher innovation represents a high degree of novelty and is driven by a promotion orientation. Proactive innovation, on the other hand, exhibits a low degree of novelty and is also driven by a promotion orientation. Contributory innovation is characterized by a high degree of novelty and a prevention orientation. Responsive innovation, on the other hand, involves a low degree of novelty and a prevention orientation. The innovation cases vividly illustrated teacher innovation as a responsive, responsible, and resilient process undertaken by teaching professionals to enhance student learning and gain greater control over professional lives (Lu & Chan, under preparation). This project identified three individual and group level determinants of teacher innovation. At individual level, this project identified an emotional path for understanding the creativity of teacher leaders in schools. It is found that immediate, same-day effect of work enjoyment has significant positive effect on the creativity level of teacher leaders (Lu, 2021). This project also found that teacher entrepreneurial behavior (including advocating innovative ideas and initiatives in schools, taking active measures to mitigating potential risks, mobilizing peer teachers through demonstrating humility, and securing professional and financial resources) has significant positive effect on school innovation (Ho & Lu, 2022; under review). Thirdly, we found that teacher creative self-efficacy mediated the positive relationship between professional learning communities and teacher innovation, and innovative climate moderated the effects of professional learning communities on both teacher creative self-efficacy and teacher innovation (Liu, Lu, & Yin, 2022). This project found two layers of conditions which are most conducive to school innovation in Hong Kong. At school level, the analysis of the case studies revealed that school principals’ combined use of conventional leadership practices (operational and enabling leadership) and innovative-specific leadership practices (reorientation, integrating innovative initiatives into school strategic planning, shouldering ethical risks, and leveraging external stakeholders) are common and crucial for facilitating psychological safe, learning-oriented environment (Lu, 2022; Lu & Walker, under preparation). At system level, the results of secondary data analysis corroborated a quasi-market condition of schooling in Hong Kong. Together the findings indicate that schools need to constantly seek continuous improvement, handling the challenges of uncertain conditions, developing innovative pedagogy, and implementing new school-based curricula in order to present a balanced orientation of promoting both student academic performance and cultivating student whole-person development.

18610719.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18610719.value: The execution of this project facilitated a necessary documentation of teacher innovative practices in Hong Kong and nearby regions, which enables a more nuanced understanding of the educational achievements as well as challenges in the high-performing education system. The findings accumulated from this project, regarding the individual and group-level determinants and process of teacher innovation, as well as the conditions under which schools are most conducive to teacher innovation, provide some useful basis for future research on teacher innovation. The research findings also generated relevant, up-to-date leadership training materials for more than 2000 school leaders in Hong Kong during 2020 and 2023. The research findings flagged the importance of open, cooperative interactions with external stakeholders, including cross-school professional learning communities, parents and other schools. Following the project, the PI will investigate whether schools’ engagement in networked school improvement communities can contribute to and sustain continuous school innovation. The PI has participated in an application for the Research Impact Fund for 2023/24 on forming reciprocal improvement communities and developing collective school leader capacity across the GBA (pending).

18610719.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18610719.value: This research sheds light on teacher innovation in Hong Kong and nearby regions, identifying four main types: entrepreneurial, proactive, contributory, and responsive. These innovations differ in their degree of novelty and orientation but ultimately serve to enhance student learning and empower teachers in their professional lives. The study found three factors that influence teacher innovation. First, work enjoyment positively impacts teacher leaders' creativity. Second, entrepreneurial behavior of teachers significantly boosts overall school innovation. Lastly, a strong connection was found between teachers’ engagement in professional learning communities and teacher innovation, with the innovative climate playing a moderating role. The research also pinpointed two key conditions for fostering school innovation in Hong Kong. At the school level, effective leadership that combines conventional practices with innovation-specific approaches including reorientation, shouldering ethical risks and leveraging external stakeholders is essential for creating a psychologically safe and learning-oriented environment. At the system level, a quasi-market schooling landscape compels schools to strike a balance between academic achievement and whole-person development orientations.

18611019.label: Realisation of objectives
18611019.value: This study adopted design-based research in three stages with different focuses to address the three objectives from 2019 to 2022. How the objectives have been achieved is presented below: Initiation: Design and development of by the mobile-user-generated-content (m-UGC) tool (12 Aug. 2019 - 04 Oct. 2019) This stage included four main activities: (a) preparing the initiation plan, and contacting and discussing the details with school teachers for implementation; (b) constructing instruments to be used in the implementation stage of the study; (c) preparing and conducting a pilot study; and (d) preparing and organising a 3-hour teacher professional development. Cycle 1 – Implementation of the self-regulated learning model with the m-UGC tool (16 Oct. 2019- 31 Aug. 2020) To help achieve the project objectives in Cycle 1, six teachers with their students were expected to participate in the project. In the end, four school teachers with their students were involved (School A, B, C & D) due to the school suspension in mid Nov 2019 resulted from the social event in Hong Kong, as well as the outbreak of COVID-19. Two schools participated in the project at the end of 2019/2020 Semester I and the other two schools joined the project in 2019/2020 Semester II. Six main research activities (a, b, c, d, e and f) involved in Cycle 1-Implementation of the self-regulated learning model with the m-UGC tool. (a). Vocabulary tests: pre-, post- and delayed-post vocabulary tests; (b). Self-regulated learning survey: pre- and post-self-regulated learning questionnaire; (c). Student self-reported plan of their self-regulated learning; (d). Student self-regulated learning reflection form; (e). Student focus group interviews: the interview questions would be follow-up questions on the survey, using the five dimensions of the questionnaire as a framework; (f). Student created vocabulary learning logs recorded on the m-UGC tool in the experimental group beyond the classroom. Cycle 2 Implementation of the self-regulated learning model with the m-UGC tool (Sep. 2020 - Sep. 2021 ) Due to a revision of the tool used in this project, the end date for Cycle 2 has been extended to Sept. 2021 (the original plan was Feb. 2021). This stage included four main activities: (a) revising the tool; (b) preparing and organising a 2-hour teacher professional development; (c) collecting data: vocabulary tests, self-regulated learning survey, student created vocabulary learning logs recorded on the m-UGC tool (also the Vocab+ app), student focus group interviews: the interview questions would be follow-up questions on the survey, using the five dimensions of the questionnaire as a framework; and (d) refinement of the m-UGC tool (also Vocab+). (a) Adoption of a new m-UGC tool (Sep. 2020 – Mar. 2021) Because technical issues and drawbacks of the original web-based m-UGC tool provided by the Co-PI from Kyoto University could not be solved without installing the virtual machine by the Co-PI during the COVID-19 period, the newly developed m-UGC tool named Vocab+ was adopted in Cycle 2 and Cycle 3’s implementation. The newly developed app - Vocab+ can work both on Android and IOS mobile devices and can be freely downloaded. The application interface and interactive function development of Vocab+ was supported by the Unity platform, which enabled the application to be installed and run on the two mainstream mobile operating systems of iOS and Android. Its network services and data interaction services were provided by the Laravel PHP Web Framework. With the support of AJAX and related Unity packages, this mobile app can keep all contents updated in real time automatically. The learning content and operation records of the database were stored in the MySQL database. For IOS users: https://apps.apple.com/hk/app/vocab/id1529237367 For Android users: https://vocabgo.eduhk.hk/unity/vocabgo.apk (b) Preparing and organising a 2-hour teacher professional development (Mar. 2021) The researchers conducted a 2-hour online meeting with six teachers (School A, B, C, D, E, F) via Zoom to (a) introduce the updated version of m-UGC tool (also Vocab+); (b) do hands-on practices in using Vocab+; and (c) discuss about how to implement self-regulated vocabulary learning with the Vocab+ during the COVID-19. (c) Collecting data (Mar. 2021- Sept. 2021) Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the initial plans for the implementation of the self-regulated learning model with the m-UGC tool (also the Vocab+ app) in six school teachers with their students (School A, B, C, D, E & F) had to be postponed. Six experimental groups and six control groups were involved in Cycle 2 in April 2021. Students in the experimental groups did their vocabulary learning using the self-regulated learning approach with the Vocab+ app; and the control group did their vocabulary learning using the self-regulated learning approach without the Vocab+ app. Vocabulary tests, self-regulated learning surveys, and student created vocabulary learning logs recorded on the m-UGC tool (also Vocab+) were collected and six student focus group interviews (10 students in each group) were conducted. (d) Refinement of the m-UGC tool (also Vocab+) (Sept. 2021) Based on the findings of the interviews, technical bugs were identified and refined. The self-regulation scheme was developed and embedded on the Vocab+ app to support students’ self-regulated learning more effectively. The self-regulation scheme includes: (1) Goal-setting; (2) My progress; and (3) My reflection. To be specific, the general features are presented below: (1) Goal-setting: Students are able to set vocabulary learning goals in terms of words in the current learning units and words beyond the learning units. In addition, they are able to generate their own learning strategies to achieve the goals they set. (2) My progress: Students are able to observe and monitor learning status via dashboards and a leaderboard. (3) My reflection: Students are able to reﬂect and evaluate their achievements according to their performance on the Vocab+ app and adjust goals in the next round. Adjustments and adaptations to vocabulary learning occur when students evaluate their progress and determine what areas are needed to improve. Cycle 3 Implementation of the self-regulated learning model with the m-UGC tool (Sept. 2021 – Mar. 2022) This stage includes four main activities: (a) preparing and organising a 2-hour teacher professional development; (b) collecting data: vocabulary tests, self-regulated learning survey, student created vocabulary learning logs recorded on the Vocab+ app, student focus group interviews; and (c) making the final version the Vocab+ app with a self-regulation scheme. Six experimental groups and six control groups were involved in Cycle 3. Students in the experimental groups used the Vocab+ app with a self-regulation scheme to conduct vocabulary learning; and the control group used the Vocab+ app without a self-regulation scheme to conduct vocabulary learning. We felt thankful to collaborate with six teachers from six schools to conduct the research to support primary students’ self-regulated vocabulary learning studies.

18611019.label: Major findings and research outcome
18611019.value: In the design-based research, both qualitative and quantitative methods were adopted to analyse data. The research results in relation to the three research questions are presented below: Regarding RQ1 – Do learners’ vocabulary learning outcomes differ across the control and experimental groups? Students’ prior English vocabulary learning outcomes of the experimental group and control group were checked by the non-parametric test, Mann–Whitney U test, indicating no significant difference. An independent samples t-test was used to analyse any signiﬁcant diﬀerences between the experimental and control groups students in terms of their post- English vocabulary tests. The results show that the students in the experimental group showed better English vocabulary learning performance than that of the students in the control groups. Regarding RQ2 – Does the perceived self-regulated learning of learners differ across the control and experimental groups? The results show that student in the experimental group showed better perceived self-regulated learning skills than that of the students in the control group. Regarding RQ3.1 – What are the relationships between learners’ vocabulary learning outcomes and their perceived self-regulated learning? The latent growth modelling was used to explore the change of vocabulary learning outcomes in the consecutive three cycles of intervention. The results show that the initial level of students’ perceived self-regulated learning and the initial level of vocabulary learning outcomes were positively correlated but not statistically significant. However, the change of students’ perceived self-regulated learning had a significantly positive effect on the change of vocabulary learning outcomes. Regarding RQ3.2 – How do the relationships between learners’ vocabulary learning outcomes and their perceived self-regulated learning differ across the control and experimental groups? Using the multivariate growth modelling, the results show there was a significant correlation between the change of students’ perceived self-regulated learning and the change of vocabulary learning outcome for the experimental groups. But the relationship of the two in the control groups was not significant. Regarding RQ 4.1 – What are the technology use patterns (e.g. technology use regarding time, place, picture-taking, audio-recording, and vocabulary input) of learners in the experimental and control groups? By using Gephi – an open graph visualisation tool, two technology use patterns were identified: active learners and passive learners. Compared to control groups, students in the experimental groups (1) created more learning logs and multiple logs for the same word; (2) used pictures taken in real life settings, wrote descriptions of the logs and (3) made more comments on peers’ logs. Regarding RQ 4.2 – How do these technology use patterns affect learners’ vocabulary learning outcomes and their perceived self-regulated learning? The research found that students had higher perceived self-regulated learning were more engaged in the technology use, but the positive relationship was not observed for the vocabulary learning outcomes. To sum up, there were difficulties encountered during the project due to the social event and the COVID-19 pandemic, but by working together with the researchers and using the newly developed m-UGC tool - the Vocab app, the students overcame the obstacles and developed self-regulated vocabulary learning skills and enhanced vocabulary learning outcomes. This study would not have been successful without their sustained efforts. This project also had the support and contribution of a research assistant and a PhD student who made a substantial contribution.

18611019.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18611019.value: After the three cycles of iterative implementation of the mobile-generated tool, the researchers identified further potentials in upgrading the tool and made a plan of promoting the project in wider learning contexts. The following presents the details. • Further development of the app (1) To add gamification elements: gamification elements (e.g., badges, completion, points) can be used to create joyful and interactive learning environments for students to be engaged in vocabulary learning and develop self-regulated skills.. (2) To focus on adaptive learning design: The app can be further developed to adapt to individual needs, providing customised self-regulated vocabulary learning experiences. AI technology can be used to identify students' learning behaviours. By using AI, the app can help students become more self-directed, autonomous, and motivated learners, and better equipped to succeed in a rapidly changing world. • Promoting the project in wider learning contexts: Researchers will keep promoting the Vocab+ app and inviting K-12 students or students in higher education to participate in research. Thus, more students will benefit from the innovative design of the app to develop self-regulated learning .

18611019.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18611019.value: The research findings show the positive effects of the mobile-user-generated-content (m-UGC) tool (also Vocab+) on primary students’ vocabulary learning outcomes and perceived self-regulated learning. The significance of this study lies mainly in four aspects: 1. It is the first empirical study that addresses the use of a self-regulated vocabulary learning approach mediated by the m-UGC tool (also the Vocab+ app) to enhance primary learners’ learning performance in Hong Kong. 2. It is a novel study to examine primary learners’ perceived self-regulated learning with a technology-assisted learning model in vocabulary learning. 3. The development and evaluation of the m-UGC tool (also the Vocab+ app) lay a valuable foundation for future extended research, such as exploring primary students’ self-regulated vocabulary learning progress and identifying their learning patterns to inform instructional practices. 4. Finally, the findings provide a comprehensive knowledge base for scaling up the self-regulated vocabulary learning practices mediated by a mobile app in Hong Kong primary schools and across a broader Hong Kong learning community and beyond.
