24604819.label: Major findings and research outcome
24604819.value: The major findings of the project are tripartite. Firstly, in terms of primary sources and textual analysis, the PI has identified a collection of literary works from late Qing period to contemporary period written in Wu dialect. This collection includes the most famous works such as The Sing-song Girls of Shanghai written by Han Bangqing, Blossoms by Jin Yucheng, some recently republished fiction about prostitutes by Zhou Tianlai, and most importantly the scripts for local opera and other oral performances collected in the local gazetteers. It paves the way for the rewriting of Chinese literature from a dialect tradition. Secondly, the project also contributes to the rewriting of modern Chinese literary history. Existing literary history approaches mainstream writing written in Mandarin. Discussion about dialect writing also features Cantonese and Hokkien literary works with an established writing system. This project thus offers an overview of the historical development of a prominent literary and oral tradition that has attracted many readers’ and scholars’ attention, but not yet discussed systematically. Thirdly, through textual analysis, the PI has also made contributions to the existing research about modern Chinese literature and enriched the studies of Sinophone studies. Sinophone studies has most significantly contributed to the studies of Hong Kong, Taiwan, Southeast Asian, overseas Chinese communities, and ethnic minority literature and culture in the past. This research project has bridged the gap between modern Chinese literary studies and Sinophone studies.

24604819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24604819.value: The PI has prepared a revised manuscript based on the research findings. Due to the delay of archival works caused by COVID-19, the writing has been delayed. In the next few months, the PI will send the revised manuscript to potential publishers and develop the project into a scholarly book. Furthermore, contemporary Wu dialect literature has given rise to a series of media adaptations in China and abroad. Wong Kar-wai’s ongoing adaptation of Blossoms is a great example. Inspired by Jin Yucheng, a younger generation of writers have started literary experiments in the same vein, leading to a booming publishing industry in dialect writing. The PI will devote time and energy to studying these new works and adaptations in the next project.

24604819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24604819.value: This research traces the history of Wu dialect literature in the twentieth and twenty-first century Chinese history. By looking at a variety of literary genres, including serialized novel, short story, folk song, and poetry in Shanghai, the research connects written and oral traditions that had previously been largely neglected by modern Chinese literary history. The importance of the project first lies in the excavation of primary sources in Wu dialect. It also expands the discussion of Sinophone studies by engaging literary works produced in Han Chinese in mainland China who are equally marginalized in many ways. Moreover, this research contributes to the expansion and rearticulation of Chinese literary history by unraveling the cultural and linguistic plurality of Chinese literature from the perspective of the local.

24608019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24608019.value: Introduction Stroke in adults aged between 18–64 years old is increasing significantly worldwide. Studies have reported that this group of young stroke survivors encounters enormous difficulties reintegrating into their social roles. Individualised discussions with healthcare professionals and learning from other survivors are imperative for them to reconstruct their identities after stroke. There is also great demand for community support during their chronic stage of recovery to help them rebuild life skills to promote reintegration. Aim This project will investigate the effects of a 24-week Narrative and Skills-building Intervention (NSI) on young stroke survivors’ community reintegration and psychosocial outcomes. Methods A randomised controlled trial (RCT) will be conducted. Adults aged 18–64 years old with a first-ever or recurrent ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke and have been discharged home will be recruited from three acute hospitals, a community-based service unit and a support group in Hong Kong (HK). An estimated sample of 208 participants (104 per group) will be required. Eligible participants will be randomly assigned to receive usual care or usual care with NSI. The NSI is grounded in Narrative Theory and Bandura’s principles of Self-efficacy and Outcome Expectation. It will consist of eight individual sessions over six months delivered by a facilitator with a workbook and 15 videos about other survivors’ recovery experience. Participants will be facilitated to narrate their survival experiences and rebuild core life skills. Outcomes including community reintegration, depressive symptoms, health-related quality of life, self-efficacy, outcome expectation and satisfaction with performance of self-management behaviours will be measured before (T0) and immediately after NSI (T1), then six (T2) and 12 months after NSI (T3). Analysis will be performed using the intention-to-treat principle. A mixed-effects model will be used to compare the differential changes in outcomes across time between the two groups. Focus group interviews will be conducted with the facilitator at T1 and with the participants in the intervention group at T1 and T3. Discussion and significance This is a novel RCT to test the short and long-term effects of a theory-based NSI on young stroke survivors’ community reintegration. It will establish a new model of community reintegration after stroke to inform future research. The results will provide valuable evidence to develop clinical guidelines for survivors’ community reintegration, which are not currently available in HK. The NSI is expected to be integrated into existing stroke care services to benefit young stroke survivors in the long run. 年齡在18-64歲之間的中風人士在全球顯著增加。研究顯示這組年輕中風康復者在重新投入社會角色方面遇上重大困難。為了在中風後重建身份，康復者有必要與醫療人員進行個別討論及向其他康復者學習。在慢長的恢復階段，幫助他們重建生活技能及促進他們重返社會的社區支援尤其重要。 目的 計劃將研究一項為期24週的敍事與生活技巧培訓措施對年輕中風康復者重新融入社區和對他們的心理社會後果的影響。 方法 研究採用隨機對照試驗方式。計劃將從香港的三間急症醫院，社區服務單位及支援小組招募年齡在18-64歲患有首次／複發性中風（包括缺血性或出血性）並已出院的康復者。估計需要招募208名參與者（每組104人）。符合條件的參與者將被隨機分配接受敍事與生活技巧培訓及常規護理或只接受常規護理。 敍事與生活技巧培訓措施以敘事理論和班杜拉的自我效能和結果期望原則為基礎。內容包括由協調員帶領橫跨六個月的八次單獨會談，亦會為參與者提供一本工作簿和15位中風康復者復康經歷的影片。措施將引導參與者敘述他們的復康經歷並協助他們重建核心生活技能。研究指標包括社會融合狀況，抑鬱症狀，健康生活質量，自我效能，結果期望以及對自我管理表現的滿意度，計劃將在措施介入之前（T0）和之後（T1），介入六個月後（T2）及12個月後（T3）收集數據。意向治療原則將用於進行分析。混合效應模型將用於比較兩組之間於不同時間點的差異。協調員將在T1和T3與實驗組參與者進行焦點小組訪談。 討論及含義 此研究為一項創新的隨機對照試驗，用於測試基於理論的敍事與生活技巧培訓措施對年輕中風康復者重新融入社區的短期和長期影響。它將為未來中風後重新融入社區的研究建立新的模式。研究結果將為製定年輕中風康復者重新融入社區的臨床指引提供寶貴的證據，而目前香港尚未有這類型的指引。這項計劃預計會與現有的中風護理服務結合，將有益於往後的年輕中風康復者。

24610519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24610519.value: China is a diverse country home to many ethnic peoples, but it is at the same time often considered to be the centre of a homogenous culture and writing system. Chinese minorities, after decades of cultural integration, now write the majority of their literature in Chinese, despite having their own language and often scripts. For their voices to be heard, they write in the language of the cultural colonizer (the language of the Han, Hanyu 漢語), hence they can be classified as “Sinophone” writers. Sinophone studies leads us to the study of Sinitic language as it is used by ethnic minorities within China. Tibeto-Burman minorities have their own native languages that share very little in common with the other half of the Sino-Tibetan language family, Sinitic. Tibeto-Burman peoples living in the PRC are caught between two linguistic and cultural worlds: somewhere between the “Sino” and the “Tibetan”, a situation that is reflected in their writing. As they write in Chinese, some choose to translate their own traditional language and culture, inserting non-Chinese words and cultural context into the Chinese text. While plenty has been written on Sinophone writers in Hong Kong, the United States and across the global Chinese diaspora, comparatively little has been done on such writing by minority groups within China proper. This research addresses the question of what roles language and translation play in Tibeto-Burman Sinophone writing. If it is true that “[Tibetan Sinophone author] Alai’s literary construction gives voice, perhaps for the first time, to a people whose identity and history have never emerged in the world’s vision” (Wang 2013, 124), then we must ask what kind of voice this is. How does he construct identity through language and translation, and, crucially, what other unheard minority voices are there in China? It is the aim of this research to see how Sinophone minority authors from Tibeto-Burman speaking minorities employ translational strategies to negotiate their own cultural identities in their writing, further challenging homogenized notions of both “Chineseness” and “ethnic-ness”. A wide array of distinct and original voices will be revealed, voices that work to champion cultural identities, leading to hybridized understandings and, hopefully, a remapping of modern Chinese minority literature through the lens of cultural translation. 漢藏之間：藏緬語少數民族的翻譯式華語文學 中國是一個多民族國家，卻同時也被視為一個單一文化和書寫體系的中心。中國境內許多少數民族雖然擁有自己的語言和文字，但在經歷了數十年的文化融合之後，現在主要以中文進行文學創作。為了讓本民族的聲音更廣泛地傳播，少數民族作家使用“文化主導者”的語言（即漢民族的語言——漢語）進行寫作，故此他們也可以被納入“華語”作家群。華語文學研究自然需要研究漢語族的語言，因為中國境內的少數民族亦使用漢語。但藏緬語少數民族擁有本民族的語言，且與漢藏語系的另一分支——漢語族的語言鮮有交集。因此，生活在中國境內的藏緬語使用者似乎身陷在兩種不同語言和文化的世界中：即在“漢”、“藏”的中間地帶，這種境況也反映在他們的寫作之中。當他們以中文寫作時，有些作家選擇翻譯本民族的傳統語言和文化，在中文文本中嵌入非中文詞彙和少數民族特有的文化語境。儘管已有大量關於香港、美國和全球華人聚居地的華語文學研究，但相對而言，較少有人涉及中國境內少數民族作家的華語文學。 本研究旨在探討語言與翻譯在藏緬語作家的華語文學創作中所扮演的角色。如果我們認可“（藏族華語作家）阿來的文學構建，很可能是首次，為一個從未在世界視野中展現其身份和歷史的民族發聲”（Wang Yiyan 2013, 124）這一論斷，那麼必須去探究這是一種怎樣的聲音。他如何通過語言和翻譯構建身份認同？更重要的是，中國還有哪些少數民族的聲音仍未得聞？本研究的目的即是探究使用藏緬語族語言的少數民族華語作家，如何運用翻譯策略在寫作中爭取文化認同，進而挑戰“中國性”與“民族性”這兩個同質化概念。藉此，各種各樣獨特的、原生態的聲音將會被發掘，這些聲音將努力捍衛其文化認同，以文化翻譯的視角實現對現代中國少數民族文學的多元理解、甚至重新定位。

24610519.label: Realisation of objectives
24610519.value: A total of 18 ethnic groups within China were included in the project: Achang, Bai, Derung, Hani, Jingpo, Jinuo, Lahu, Lisu, Menba, Lluoba, Naxi, Mosuo, Nu, Pumi, Qiang, Tibetan, Baima and Yi. As Mosuo and Baima are not official ethnicities recognised by the PRC, their lists, while separate, have been included alongside the ethnicities to which they ostensibly belong (the Naxi and Tibetan, respectively). The project has resulted in the creation of a bilingual website “Tibeto-Burman Sinophone Writing” (https://www.minzuwriting.com/) that now houses the two databases created during the course of this project: these are the minority author lists and lists of native language words used in minority literature in Chinese, both organised by ethnicity. The website is navigable in both English and Chinese and represents the completion of the first two project objectives (objectives one and two). In total the word lists contain over 2,500 comprehensive entries, enough to fill a small-scale, specialist dictionary. The research was particularly fruitful in the realm of Tibetan literature in Chinese, with over 700 entries of Tibetan words written in Chinese discovered across the literature. The author lists contain over 300 Sino-Tibetan authors and their works. They have been organized by minority group and form a relatively complete list (or, as complete as possible based upon the repositories of texts used during the data collection) of those writers who use Sinoxenic Chinese in their minority writings. The project has focused on how Chinese minorities (specifically those who speak Tibeto-Burman heritage languages) use these minority languages even when ostensibly writing Chinese, so authors who do not use their heritage language (i.e., they only write in standard Chinese) have not in this case been considered for the purposes of the project. In the analysis of minority literature, this project focuses on language and not thematic issues. In this way the author list is complementary to the glossaries, which represent I believe the major research achievement of the project. The glossaries are exhaustive lists of minority language words used by minority authors. They include English translations, example usages and back translations into minority script. Back translation proved to be the most difficult part of this project: as the project team did not have expertise in many of the languages involved, it was on occasion necessary to find consultants who were. The services of language consultants were used for the Bai, Hani and Tibetan lists in particular, with consultants identifying native script renderings of Sinoxenic words from minority literature. In many cases, however, it was simply not possible to identify the word in the original language and script, especially considering the issues of dialect diversity and transcriptions into Chinese. Some of the languages had no official romanisation system in which to back-translate, such as Achang. A research assistant was hired using project fund to assist primarily with data collection and database creation. The major sources for data collection were two printed collections of minority literature in multiple volumes (particularly the Xinshiqi Zhongguo shaoshuminzu wenxuezuopin xuanji新时期中国少数民族文学作品选集 and Xinshiqi Yunnan shaoshu minzu wenxue zuopin xuan 新时期云南少数民族文学作品选, alongside back issues of Border Literature, a Chinese journal focusing on minority authors. Individual works outside of such collections were also included. While two research trips were originally planned (to Yunnan and Sichuan) to collect examples of more hard-to-find literature not available in online bookshops or libraries in Hong Kong, these had to be cancelled due to the pandemic and the PI’s inability to travel to mainland China during the course of the project. It was hoped that the border would re-open in early 2022 and the project was extended for six months to accommodate this possibility, but the border remained closed until early 2023. This meant that the general expenses for the project went unspent. I do not however believe that the failure to collect materials “on the ground” in mainland China has impacted the attainment of the project objectives. It may be assumed that the majority of the words collected in this manner will be culturally specific – names of deities, local delicacies etc., but while culturally-specific words are a prominent category in the glossaries, we can see plenty of simple phrases, as well as verbs and adjectives, or non-culturally-specific nouns also appearing in the glossaries, suggesting that there is indeed linguistic choice at play in this this writing. For example, the Tibetan phrase ཐུགས་རྗེ་ཆེ།, “thank you”, has two Sinoxenic equivalents in the glossary: tujiqi “土吉其” and tujiqie “图吉切” (see https://www.minzuwriting.com/tibetanwordlist). Even for culturally-specific terms such as duoma 朵玛 (Tib. gtor-ma), a Tibetan religious offering made from roasted barley flour and ghee, the use of this transcribed Tibetan word in Chinese is still a linguistic choice made by the author even if there is no direct Chinese equivalent, because the author could simply have chosen to use the domesticating translation mian’ou 面偶 [flour-puppet] common in the literature. No matter what the authors, choose, these are all valid translational strategies, however Sinoxenic equivalents (essentially phonetic translations) reveal the negotiation of a distinct cultural identity in the way that a domesticating, Sinicizing translation does not (objective 3). Two conference papers at international conferences were presented during the course of the project, both in March 2021: “Minority literature as a translational ecosystem”, presentation at IATIS 2021, Barcelona (via Zoom), and “Literary Heteroglossia and Language Preservation”, presentation at the 18th International Conference on Minority Languages in Bilbao (via Zoom), the published research and the conference presentations, together with the creation of the projection website, can be seen as embodying the goals of objective four, i.e. essentially promoting the existence of this particular kind of writing (objective 4). The Chinese government has placed emphasis on minority literature without defining what exactly counts as minority literature explicitly: the end result is generally the promotion of minority authors who write in Chinese. The danger is in assuming such writing is only Chinese: this leads to a homogenization of both literature and language, homogenization that this project challenges. While we cannot expect many of the words featuring in the glossaries to enter the broader Chinese lexicon or indeed be inserted into the major Chinese dictionaries, it is nevertheless important to highlight their existence in Chinese, in printed material widely available to the Chinese-speaking public, and I believe the project has reached this goal.

24610519.label: Major findings and research outcome
24610519.value: The glossaries prove that minority authors from all ethnic groups included in the study (and by extension, we can surmise all ethnic groups in China) engage in this mode of Sinoxenic writing - to varying degrees of both extensiveness and efficacy. I have published three peer-reviewed articles (two in open access journals to enable maximum reach) based upon this research, and a book chapter is currently under preparation. As stated in my study drawing on Achang, Bai, Hani and Naxi examples, “Sinoxenic Writing and Chinese Minority Literature” (Journal of Chinese Writing Systems 6:2, 2022), the contemporary Sinoxenic writing as described in this project depicts what can be generally described as vernacular non-Chinese language within fiction or non-fiction texts that belong to the genre of minority literature; it is not indicative of a standardized script used for bureaucratic or other official purposes. While Sinoxenic writing as it can be seen within Chinese minority literature does not directly indicate the perseverance of systematic Sinoxenic writing in the same way that David Holm has, for example, documented for Zhuang, these Sinoxenic readings are more appropriate in their context than Chinese language readings, and they point to the still wider possibilities of this mode of writing, perhaps even toward avenues of development for minority writing as a genre in China. As I conclude in the article “Ethnic minority language and Sinophone minority literature in China” (Writing Chinese: A Journal of Contemporary Sinophone Literature 1:1, 2022), it is in Sinophone literature such as has been described in the project that there is reconceptualization of the literary territory itself, evidence that the minor can be more major than the major, that minority practices do not have to always be situated by and explained only in terms of the hegemony. While many of the minority authors whose works appear in the databases cannot be labelled as “major” authors, even so, the deterritorialization of Chinese embodied by Sinoxenic writing suggests a refusal to recognize the necessity of a binary of major/minor, pointing the way to new possibilities for Sinophone authors who would go beyond reproducing majoritarian narratives in their writing. For scholars and writers alike, the borders of “Sinography” have room to be widened further still.

24610519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24610519.value: The word lists produced for this project have the potential to be compied into a dictionary of Sinoxenic Tibeto-Burman language; such a tool would be a useful resource for minority authors and researchers alike. The PI will propose such a publication to Yunnan Nationalities Press, a publisher which specialises in the ethnology of minority groups of Yunnan and other related topics. This project has focused on traditional printed texts for its data. I believe that non-traditional texts, such as social media postings, are also a major dataset for minority language. The published texts that formed the focus of this project have to be carefully curated through to publication, and are subject to constraints from a number of different parties and factors (censorship, editing, sales concerns etc.). Widening the parameters of the “literature” being studied could become the focus of a future article based upon the foundations provided by this research. There is also room for a monograph on the minority Sinoxenic writing/Sinophone literature in China that draws more comprehensively on the data found in the glossaries than a research article can achieve.

24610519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24610519.value: China’s minority authors may compose poems and stories in Chinese, but it doesn’t mean that they have forsaken their heritage languages. It is possible for them to record, preserve and perhaps even revitalize their own languages using Chinese characters. In this sense, their Chinese writing does not always reflect Chinese language, for it is possible to write Tibetan in Chinese, for example. All minority authors become translators, working between cultures and languages. Minority writing that moves between languages like this can help us to change how we think about the literary landscape: the “minor” can be “major” just as the “major” can be “minor” (or that perhaps these terms are less meaningful than we might think, or only useful up to a point). We do not have to always understand “minority literature” in terms of the powerful centre, and there are ways for lesser-known authors to write back to the centre, even while using the writing of the centre. To really “read” minority literature, we need to be reading the text in terms of both languages and cultures.

24612619.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24612619.value: It is common in both public and academic discourse today to trace the origins of human trafficking and “modern slavery” to the Transatlantic Slave Trade in enslaved Africans, to which our modern scourge represents a departure in its global impact, multiethnic character and the preponderance not of manual labor (e.g. plantation agriculture), but of domestic, military and sexual exploitation. In contrast, this project argues that this Atlantic-centric view is historically myopic, and thereby less appropriate for framing our current problems. Indeed, if we look beyond the Atlantic, we see that slavery and human trafficking in the early modern world (c. 1500-1800) mirrored our current situation closely. In particular, the global slave system created by Iberian (i.e. Spanish and Portuguese) expansion produced an interrelated series of slave-trading networks that reached across the globe, from Macau to Mexico and from India to Peru, and entrapped people enslaved in different places for different purposes. This included South and Southeast Asians forced to work in Iberian homes, Africans bought and sold as plantation laborers and Korean women trafficked as sex slaves. In order to inform discourse on the origins of “modern slavery” and human trafficking, this project will study the interconnected history of the Iberian slave trade from a global, rather than a regional or proto-national perspective. Using Iberian history as a point of departure for studying early modern global history, the project will focus on Iberia’s global slave regimes and their interactions with contemporary slave systems in Asia, Africa and the Americas. In particular, it will address the ways Iberians and those with whom they interacted conceived of slavery and freedom, both in their own and other societies, using thematic case studies, rather than a geographically-defined structure. In this way, this project will contribute both to globalizing the field of Iberian history, and make an important contribution to global intellectual and legal history, especially debates surrounding the origins and uniqueness of western concepts of freedom and slavery. It will do so not by studying western and non-western concepts separately and then comparing them, but by studying their connections and interactions, especially in the field of slave law (both secular and religious), where such issues were discussed explicitly in this period. The ultimate outcome of this research will be two peer-review articles and a book proposal to be submitted to a major North American university press.

24612619.label: Realisation of objectives
24612619.value: The project has resulted in 7 conference presentations, the two peer-reviewed articles that I had proposed (including one in the prestigious Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies) and a book proposal that has been accepted by Harvard University Press. Both the intellectual and publication objectives of the proposal were therefore successfully achieved. While I was not able to travel to Spain due to COVID, I used the funds to hire an RA to undertake the archival research for me and order reproductions of documents that I could then read in Hong Kong. The secondary reading was done at Oxford, which complemented the primary sources and allowed me to formulate and situate the eventual arguments. East Asian language sources were also integrated into the project with the help of my Research Assistant. In the end, I decided to formulate the project as a global microhistory focused on the first slave voyage to British North America in 1619. These slaves were originally captured by English privateers from an Iberian vessel (San Juan Bautista) and so connected to the larger Iberian world. Through a series of connected microhistories arranged in concentric circles around the voyage of the San Juan Bautista, the project as it has emerged can show for the first time that the Africans transported to Virginia in 1619 were part of a global trade in slaves of various origins that took place at the edge of legality in multiple jurisdictions. This would not have been possible without the widespread pre-modern custom of commodifying human beings. At the same time, the desire for profit constantly pushed the boundaries of what was acceptable, as both European buyers and non-European sellers fudged (and sometimes even forged) documents to make the trade seem legitimate. As a result of this troublingly vast commerce, parallel and connected ideas about race developed from the Caribbean to Canton, setting in motion many of the prejudices we see today. As such, the line of research that has emerged from this project has succeeded in archieving the original objectives of the application.

24612619.label: Major findings and research outcome
24612619.value: Overall, the project made substantial contributions to the historigraphy on the global history of slavery. This includes the role of Iberian imperial expansion in the globalization of the slave trade, as well as the particular role of gender in shaping the lives of slaves in Asia. As regards the widely-accepted dichotomy between western and non-western concepts of “slavery” and “freedom” it appears that these were much more compatible than previously thought, especially within the context of commercial interactions. 24612619.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24612619.value: It is common today to trace the origins of human trafficking and “modern slavery” to the Transatlantic Slave Trade, to which our modern scourge represents a departure in its global impact, multiethnic character and the preponderance not of plantation agriculture, but of domestic, military and sexual exploitation. In contrast, this project has shown that if we look beyond the Atlantic, we see that slavery and human trafficking in the early modern world (c. 1500-1800) mirrored our current situation closely. The global slave system created by Iberian (i.e. Spanish and Portuguese) expansion produced an interrelated series of slave-trading networks that reached across the globe, from Macau to Mexico and from India to Peru, and entrapped people enslaved in different places for different purposes. This Iberian slave system in turn fed off of other human trafficking networks throughout the world, which provided the merchandize for the trade. This was undergirded by shared legal ideas about the alienability of human beings (the “commensurability of commerce”), although there were frequently also misunderstandings and conflicts. The ultimate outcome of this research has been two peer-review articles and a book proposal that has been accepted by Harvard University Press.

24613019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24613019.value: Why are the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, the two largest Christian denominations in the world, separated from one another? It was not always so. In the early Middle Ages (c.400-1000), most Christians in Western and Eastern Europe viewed themselves as part of the same religious community. However, European Christianity divided into two distinct churches by the end of the medieval period: the Latin-speaking Church of Rome and the Greek-speaking Church of Constantinople (known today as the Catholic and Orthodox Churches). The crucial period for this development was the eleventh to thirteenth centuries, when relations between Latin and Greek Christians degenerated to the extent that the Church of Rome sanctioned a holy war, the Fourth Crusade, against the Greeks in 1204. Previous studies of the subject have focused on theological and political explanations for this East-West schism, highlighting moments of conflict that can be identified as decisive ‘rupture points’. However, the eleventh to thirteenth centuries were also a time of evolution and revolution in the legal structures of the Churches of Rome and Constantinople. Both developed sophisticated, independent systems of codified law, institutional courts, and professional legal scholarship in this period. Drawing on recent insights from legal anthropology, I wish to pursue my hypothesis that the emergence of these distinct systems of religious law in the Greek East and Latin West was critical in shaping their identities as separate Christian denominations. This interdisciplinary research project aims to investigate how and why the Byzantine Church of Constantinople created a sophisticated religious legal system in the period in question, how this shaped Greek Christians’ sense of identity, and how the Greek church’s legal institutions survived the Latin conquest of Constantinople in 1204. The primary sources for this project are a body of eleventh- to thirteenth-century Byzantine religious law texts, most of which are known but largely untranslated and unstudied. These consist of legal codifications, scholarly commentaries, court proceedings, professional correspondence, and lists of ‘frequently asked questions’. In terms of practical outcomes, I aim to produce a monograph that will provide the first historical study of the development of Byzantine church law in this period and at least two peer-reviewed articles on specific aspects of the project. The resulting publications will be useful to those in neighbouring fields and sub-fields of history, religious and cultural studies, and others. 世界上最大的兩個基督教教派: 羅馬天主教和東正教教會，為何彼此分離？這種情況並非一直如此。在中世紀早期（c.400-1000），西歐和東歐的大多數基督徒將自己視為同一宗教社區的一部分。但是，到了中世紀末期，歐洲基督教逐漸分為兩個不同的教會：拉丁語的羅馬教會和希臘語的君士坦丁堡教會（也就是今天的天主教和東正教）。這一發展的關鍵時期是十一世紀到十三世紀，當時拉丁和希臘基督徒之間的關係逐漸惡化，直到羅馬拉丁教會最終在1204年發動了一場聖戰，即第四次十字軍東征，對抗希臘教會。 過往關於這個主題的研究集中在對東-西分裂的神學和政治解釋，重點在被認為是決定性“破裂點”的衝突時刻。然而，在羅馬教會和君士坦丁堡教會的法律結構中，第十一至第十三世紀也是一個重要的演變時期（在某些情況下，也是革命）。在此期間，兩者都建立了成熟獨立的法律系統，法院機構和專業的法律學術研究。借鑒法律人類學新近的見解，我的中心假設是：希臘東部和拉丁西部這些獨特的宗教法體系的出現對於將其身份塑造為不同的基督教教派至關重要。 我的主要研究重點是君士坦丁堡拜占庭教會在十一世紀到十三世紀如何以及為何創造了一個成熟的宗教法律體系，這個體系又怎樣影響了希臘基督徒對自己的看法，以及希臘教會的法律制度如何在1204年的拉丁第四次十字軍東征後存活下來。此項目的主要資料來源是十一至十三世紀拜占庭宗教法律的文本，其中大部分是已知的，但大部分未翻譯和未經研究，包括法律編纂，學術評論，法庭訴訟，專業信函以及希臘語稱為erotapokriseis的“常見問題”。除了該項目的直接研究成果外，我還希望它可以為一些重要資料來源的英語翻譯提供基礎。

24613019.label: Realisation of objectives
24613019.value: I originally developed this ECS project as stage of intitial research and publication in preparation for the production of a sole-authored book. The six objectives outlined above express the spirit and aims of both the research and the book. Unfortunately, the COVID-19 pandemic emerged at the beginning of the project period and severely disrupted my original plans, which I had first drawn up in 2018. In order to prepare for the book, my original plan was to conduct an initial study of published primary source texts, manuscript microfilms, and secondary literature at the Dumbarton Oaks Collection in Washington D.C. in 2020; then I would move on to study the manuscripts themselves in more depth in their various European collections (e.g. Vatican Library, Biblioteca Marciana, etc.) in 2021; then I would complete a synthesis of the research in 2022. The vast majority of the project budget was dedicated to international travel for research and conferences. I must address at the outset the fact that I was unable to carry out my original research plans, which is why I was only able to spend a small portion of my project budget. The beginning of the project coincided almost exactly with the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, which lasted throughout most of the project period. From March 2020, the HKSARG implemented quarantine policies that made travel difficult and costly, while the CUHK administration forbade all but absolutely essential international travel. Moreover, all of the major research institutes and collections that I planned to visit were closed in the summers of 2020–2021, with some beginning to re-open in autumn 2021 (others, such as Dumbarton Oaks, did not reopen to researchers until 2022). My inability to carry out my original plans due to the COVID-19 pandemic is the reason for the large unspent portion of the project budget. I was unable to leave Hong Kong in 2020 for either research or conferences (one major conference that had accepted a paper proposal from me, the International Medieval Conference in the U.K., was cancelled). The situation remained similar in 2021, although I was able to obtain permission from the university to travel to the United States to make use of the Library of Congress’ Law Library, which re-opened to visitors in that year had some useful secondary literature that I could not easily access in Hong Kong. I was also able to make a virtual presentation to the 2021 Byzantine Studies Association of North America conference over Zoom. Without the ability to travel to most research institutes and collections, I relied mostly on digital scanned document delivery and on digital reproductions of some manuscript sources. Although this is obviously not a substitute for studying the manuscripts in person, I was able to gain some useful research data this way. The pandemic situation gradually began to improve in 2022, with the HKSARG reducing compulsory quarantine for international arrivals to three days in August. I was able to make a trip to Europe in August 2022, visiting the British Library (London), the Bodleian Library (Oxford), Trinity College (Dublin), and eventually the Biblioteca Marciana in Venice, where I also presented a paper at the 24th International Congress of Byzantine Studies. This was a very useful trip, but, again, it was not on the scale that I had originally planned when I first proposed the project. Due to the setbacks arising from COVID-19, I was only able to complete around 50% of the research that I had originally planned and was not in a position to begin writing the book that would have embodied the six research objectives outlined above. Nonetheless, I have been able to fulfil all these objectives to some extent through the outputs that have resulted from this project: two peer-reviewed journal articles (in Dumbarton Oaks Papers and the Revue des études byzantines) and two papers at international conferences (the aforementioned BSANA and ICBS conferences). I completed the first journal article, on the ‘Appendix’ to Alexios Aristenos’ canonical commentary (see Part C for further details) in mid-2021 and it appeared in issue 76 of DOP in 2022. Through the study of a so-called ‘appendix’ of legal texts transmitted in manuscripts of Aristenos’ influential commentary, I was able to show how legal debates in the late eleventh century shaped attitudes to Greek Christian identity in the twelfth. This contributed to all six of my objectives. The same was true of my second journal article, on erotapokriseis (‘question-and-answer’ texts) on Byzantine religious law. These texts acted as a form of medieval legal ‘FAQs’, in which a legal practitioner (usually a bishop or an abbot) asked questions on points of law to expert jurists in the Byzantine church, receiving lists of answers in return. There are several large bodies of these texts that can be found in varying combinations throughout manuscripts of the twelfth century and later and they offer a fascinating insight into the kinds of legal questions that were being asked at the time, as well as the answers of ecclesiastical jurists. However, many of the texts remain unpublished and there have been no dedicated studies of the material. As such, my article provided the first historical study of these sources, but it also showed how they embody the development of jurisprudence in the Byzantine church at the time and emerging legal definitions of Orthodox Christianity. To return to my original objectives, I was able to completely fulfil objectives 2-6 through the publications that emerged from the project. However, the restrictions of working during the COVID-19 pandemic delayed my longer-term progress towards writing a monograph; as a result, objective one (providing the first dedicated historical study of the major primary sources of Byzantine religious law in the period c. 1000-1260) is only partially fulfilled. Nonetheless, I have demonstrated the basic soundness of my approach in using legal anthropology to better understand religious and cultural history in medieval Byzantium. In that sense, it has laid the foundations for future work on this topic specifically, and for future comparative research on the medieval Latin and Greek systems of Christian religious law more broadly.

24613019.label: Major findings and research outcome
24613019.value: This project’s key outputs (see Part C) were two peer-reviewed journal articles: (1) ‘Law and Orthodoxy under the Komnenoi: The Appendix to Alexios Aristenos’ Synopsis of Canons’; (2) ‘Frequently Asked Questions: Erotapocritic Canon Law Texts in the Komnenian Church (ca. 1080–1170)’. Although they covered different materials, both articles shared common goals: to provide the first historical study of key source texts and manuscripts of Byzantine religious law; to make these studies more accessible and easier to understand; to connect these texts/manuscripts to their historical context; and to demonstrate how a legal anthropological approach can improve our understanding of religious culture and identity. The first article focused on a collection of legal texts that are frequently transmitted in Byzantine manuscripts as a so-called ‘appendix’ to an influential twelfth-century legal commentary, Alexios Aristenos’ Synopsis of Canons. I showed in the article that these texts were not meant to be an appendix at all, but were unfinished notes from a period of legal debate and scholarship in the late-eleventh-century Byzantine church. Most notably, many of them concerned heretics, Latins, and other non-Orthodox groups. The article demonstrated that these unfinished legal texts were important evidence for the formation of Byzantine Christians views of themselves and others. The second article introduced the reader to Byzantine erotapokriseis (‘question-and-answer texts’) that were produced on the topic of religious law in the late-eleventh and twelfth centuries. Besides giving key historical information on the texts and details of their content and manuscript sources (which are not otherwise available), it analyzed how they reveal the development of legal science in the Byzantine church for the first time. It showed that this was an under-appreciated period of intellectual change in Byzantine religious law and that the texts reflect the development of a judicialized identity of Orthodox Christianity. In short, both articles showed that these poorly known legal sources are important for the understanding of the historical emergence of Orthodoxy as a distinct branch of the Christian church. Besides these articles, which were a proof-of-concept for my historical approach, the research project also provided me with a valuable body of data on several key source manuscripts. Unfortunately, the COVID-19 pandemic meant that I was not able to conduct the full research programme that I had originally planned.

24613019.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24613019.value: This project was conceived as a key step towards the preparation of an academic monograph, which is still my plan. Although it did not achieve all of the goals that I originally set due to the difficulties of researching during the COVID-19 pandemic, it did validate my basic concept and establish some extremely useful foundations for the book. In 2022, I applied for an RGC-funded GRF grant to write the book and a further peer-reviewed journal article; this application was successful and I have already begun work on it. At present, I have finished that journal article, which is due to be published in July this year, and have completed two of the book’s appendices: a forty-four-page overview of the book’s 150 main manuscript sources; and an overview of key statistical and historical information about the manuscripts and the texts that they contain. Over the next year and a half, I aim to complete writing the book and submit it to Oxford University Press for consideration in their Oxford Studies in Byzantium Series, with which I have previously published in 2021 (N.B. OUP does not offer a contract for book until the manuscript has been completed).

24613019.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24613019.value: The project aimed to conduct preparatory research that would form the basis of a single-authored book. This book would use explore how the development of legal systems and scholarship in the Byzantine church (11th–12th centuries) contributed to the development of a distinctly Orthodox Christian religious identity and the medieval schism with the Catholic Church. The research would consist of in-person study of manuscripts and analysis of texts, focusing on how the texts shaped (and were shaped by) the information environment. Unfortunately, the COVID-19 pandemic was a major setback: not only did international travel become significantly harder in 2020–2022, but key research collections such as the Vatican Library in Rome and Dumbarton Oaks in Washington D.C. were completely closed to visitors for much of the period. Nonetheless, I was able to conduct some research remotely and make an in-person visit to some key collections in summer 2022. I was therefore able to produce two peer-reviewed articles in top journals on some sets of the manuscripts and primary sources. Although I was not able to complete all the preparatory research for the book, I have demonstrated the merit of using legal sources and concepts to understand religious history.

24613819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
24613819.value: This proposed project aims to study the use of “soft regulation” employed by regulators and stock exchanges in China to curb wrongdoings by corporations. Soft regulatory measures are not legally binding and not compulsory. They rely on persuasion rather than legal sanctions as enforcement strategies. An important soft regulatory measure used in corporate governance in China is the letter of enquiry (LoE). In 2014, the two stock exchanges in China started to employ LoEs to address many decisions made by listed corporations, including distribution of dividends, issuance of new shares, executive compensation, related-party transactions and adoption of takeover defenses. These LoEs merely pose questions to listed corporations on whether their decisions promote shareholder welfare. Apart from the LoEs, regulators often use “interviews” or “informal conversations” to regulate the conduct of listed corporations. Current studies have neither provided an adequate explanation for the development of LoEs nor a sufficient evaluation of the strengths and weaknesses of this regulatory approach in developing countries such as China. The objective of the first part of this project is to present the basic facts of the use of soft regulation in corporate governance and the responses by corporations in order to provide an overview of the practice of this regulatory method in China and to evaluate whether this regulatory technique is effective overall. The major question in the second part is why soft regulation is effective or ineffective and how it affects the decisions made by corporations. The LoEs may be effective because they impose pressure on corporations by affecting the prices of their stocks. Corporations may also comply with the soft regulation because they believe it is the right thing to do. This part will collect evidence to examine different mechanisms through which these measures affects corporate decisions. The third part aims to evaluate the importance of soft regulation in the context of China’s special institutional and market environment. A comparative study will be conducted to examine the differences in the scopes and effects of soft regulation between China and certain developed countries and to identify the major factors that may explain these differences, including legal origin, the capacity of court and legislature, and the ownership structure of corporations in these different countries. Based on the above empirical and theoretical analysis, the final part will provide normative implications on how China may better improve the current regime and promote corporate governance in China. 本項目旨在研究中國監管機構和證券交易所採用的“軟規制”措施。軟規制措施不具有法律約束力與強制力。監管機構依靠說服而不是法律制裁作為執法手段。在中國公司治理中使用的壹項重要的軟監管措施是證券交易所的問詢函或關註函。從2014年起，中國的兩家證券交易所開始采用問詢函來監管上市公司的許多決策，包括分配股息，發行新股，高管薪酬，關聯交易和採用收購抵禦措施。這些問詢函只是向上市公司提出有關其決策是否促進股東福利的問題，而非對上市公司的懲罰。除了問詢函以外，監管機構經常使用“訪談”或“非正式對話”來規範上市公司的行為。目前的研究既沒有為問詢函的發展提供充分的解釋，也沒有充分評估這種監管方法在中國等發展中國家的優勢和劣勢。

24613819.label: Realisation of objectives
24613819.value: Realisation of objectives (1) Examine the use of soft regulation in corporate governance in China. I have examined the use of soft regulation in the form of letters of concern (LoCs) in China. From 2015, the stock exchanges gradually developed other important regulatory measures, such as the issuance of letters of concern (“LoCs”) against a variety of corporate governance issues; including the takeover defenses, related-party transactions (RPTs), and information disclosure in the financial reports. When an RPT is suspected to be unfair, the stock exchanges will request the listed corporation who enter into such a transaction to demonstrate its fairness. To analyze the regulatory effect of LoCs, I conducted an empirical analysis of all LoCs issued by the Shanghai Stock Exchange from 1 January 2021 to 31 December 2021. Among them, 133 LoCs were issued against RPTs. The Stock Exchange inquired about the fairness of transactions in 61 of these LoCs. However, after receiving the LoCs, most listed companies continued their transactions according to their original plans, with only eight RPTs being modified or withdrawn due to LoCs. LoCs likely have some regulatory impacts over RPTs. However, considering the considerable number of RPTs in listed companies, LoCs failed to affect the arrangement of RPTs in a vast majority of cases. I explored the reasons behind in the article “The effectiveness of judicial and public enforcement of regulation on related-party transaction in China.” (2) Identify the strengths and weaknesses of soft regulation in China compared with formal corporate governance mechanisms. I have found several reasons to believe that the LoCs mechanism can encourage listed corporations to self-regulate to some extent. The stock exchange possesses a certain degree of expertise in dealing with RPTs and identifying tunneling transactions. Soft regulatory measures such as LoCs may attract the attention of public investors and allow shareholders to “vote with their feet.” Meanwhile, the LoCs do not incur significant regulatory costs. Compared with the prior approval and regulatory sanctions imposed by the CSRC, the LoCs are “soft” regulatory measures. LoCs from the stock exchange are not subject to as many procedural requirements, which significantly reduces regulatory costs. Moreover, compared to the court, the stock exchange can rapidly respond to RPTs without going through lengthy litigation. However, LoCs are not without their shortcomings. One of the major disadvantages of the LoCs is that the stock exchanges are not authorized by the law to impose any coercive sanctions on the listed corporations if they simply ignore the LoCs and proceed with the proposed tunneling transaction. Other regulatory approaches may have different impacts. I conducted an empirical study on Chinese courts’ regulation of defensive tactics with mandatory rules in corporate law. Evidence suggests that the court’s approach had a negative impact on corporations with dispersed ownership structures and small market capitalization. These results suggest that employing mandatory rules to regulate the holding-period requirements in China is likely to harm shareholders’ interests. A soft regulation approach may be more appropriate given the empirical evidence presented. (3) Explain whether and why soft regulation plays a larger role in in corporate governance in China compared with other developed countries. Compared with other developed countries, Chinese law has certain characteristics that render it more appropriate to use soft regulation. First, Chinese legislature makes and amends laws slowly, rendering it more difficult to regulate wrongdoings. By contrast, soft regulation employed by stock exchanges can react to new circumstances quickly. Second, courts in China usually lack the ability to regulate corporate wrongdoings because of the lack of entrepreneurial litigation. Third, most corporations have concentrated ownership structures, with the controlling shareholder frequently engaging in activities harming the minority shareholders’ interests. These characteristics render soft regulation important in China’s context. (4) Identify the factors that made soft regulation successful or unsuccessful in China. Whether soft regulation is successful and effective depends on whether regulatory authorities can employ them in a responsive regulation approach. if they hold a “benign big gun” and can escalate the intensity of regulation when the regulated parties fail to comply with the soft regulation, the soft regulation would be more effective itself, as I illustrated in my article “Responsive Regulation of Related-Party Transactions of Listed Corporations” (上市公司关联交易的回应型规制). (5) Examine how the reliance on soft regulation affects the ownership structure and corporate finance in China. The literature on law and finance posits that as corporate governance improves, the ownership structure of listed corporations would become more dispersed, and more corporations would seek equity finance from dispersed investors. The average proportion of shares held by the largest shareholders of China’s listed corporations has dropped from 35.3% at the end of 2014 to 31.6% at the end of 2020. The ownership structure of most listed corporations remains concentrated during the period of examination. However, there is a sign that the ownership structure has become more dispersed and the corporate governance has been improving. To be sure, during this period, some other reform measures have also been adopted. However, some empirical evidence suggests that the increase in the use of soft regulation has improved the corporate governance while the courts continue to play a relatively trivial role in regulating wrongdoings of listed corporations. (6) Provide policy suggestions on how China may further improve corporate governance with soft regulation. First, regulators can employ both hard regulatory measures, such as prior approval, regulatory sanctions; as well as soft regulatory measures, such as LoCs. Regulators should prioritize soft regulatory measures and impose hard regulatory measures when listed corporations intend to engage in tunneling transactions. Apart from the stock exchange, the CSISC can also express concerns about listed corporations’ conduct in the form of shareholders’ letters. Regulators can consider combining soft and hard regulatory measures and adopting a responsive regulation approach, as proposed by Ian Ayers and John Braithwaite.94 The intensity of responsive regulation can be adjusted according to the company’s behaviour. Second, another way to enhance the regulation of RPTs is to adopt rules that promote the development and activities of institutional investors who have incentives to participate in the corporate decisions or initiate lawsuits, and thus curb wrongdoings of the controlling shareholder. Finally, the types of legal sanctions offered by current regulatory measures remain limited and there is a lack of punitive sanctions. China should consider adopting various forms of civil, administrative, and criminal sanctions. The CSRC can sanction directors and ban them from the securities market.

24613819.label: Major findings and research outcome
24613819.value: Soft regulatory measures such as letter of credit (LoCs) likely have some regulatory impacts over RPTs. However, considering the considerable number of wrongdoings in listed companies, LoCs failed to affect the arrangement of RPTs in a vast majority of cases. Soft regulatory measures have certain advantages over alternative regulatory measures. They take effects by attracting the attention of public investors and allow shareholders to “vote with their feet.” Meanwhile, they do not incur significant regulatory costs. Compared to the court, the stock exchange can rapidly respond to RPTs without going through lengthy litigation, which protects the investors’ interests promptly. Instead of waiting for post-transaction remedies through litigation, the LoCs can prevent an RPT that harms the corporation at the early stage. However, LoCs are not without their shortcomings. The stock exchanges are not authorized by the law to impose any coercive sanctions on the listed corporations if they simply ignore the LoCs and proceed with the proposed tunneling transaction. Compared with other developed countries, Chinese law has certain characteristics that render it more appropriate to use soft regulation. First, Chinese legislature makes and amends laws slowly, rendering it more difficult to regulate wrongdoings. By contrast, soft regulation employed by stock exchanges can react to new circumstances quickly. Second, courts in China usually lack the ability to regulate corporate wrongdoings because of the lack of entrepreneurial litigation. Third, most corporations have concentrated ownership structures, with the controlling shareholder frequently engaging in activities harming the minority shareholders’ These findings offer several policy implications. Regulators can employ both hard regulatory measures, such as prior approval, regulatory sanctions; as well as soft regulatory measures, such as LoCs, to regulate wrongdoings. Regulators should prioritize soft regulatory measures and impose hard regulatory measures when listed corporations intend to engage in tunneling transactions. In future law enforcement, the CSISC can cooperate with stock exchanges to strengthen the regulatory effect of shareholder letters. Additionally, soft regulatory measures alone may not sufficiently curb tunneling activities. The CSISC should also more actively bring lawsuits against a corporation if it insists on carrying out transactions that harm the corporation. China should consider adopting various forms of civil, administrative, and criminal sanctions. The CSRC can sanction directors and ban them from the securities market. Regulators can consider combining soft and hard regulatory measures and adopting a responsive regulation approach.

24613819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24613819.value: The soft regulatory measures taken by the stock exchanges play a significant role in China’s securities regulation. This study is more broadly connected to the question of how China protects shareholders against wrongdoings of listed corporations. After examining how stock exchanges regulate corporate wrongdoings, this project shows that there is still insufficient understanding of how courts enforce corporate wrongdoings and what are the reasons behind. In the future, the PI is to further explore alternative means of regulatory measures and how they affect the ownership structure of listed corporations in China. China’s economic rise has drawn increasing attention to how it organizes its financial market and economic activities. The various concerns that shape Chinese law and the forces that evolve with the law and the financial market provide valuable references for not only China’s policymakers, but also other developing countries seeking to achieve similar success.

24613819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24613819.value: This study examines to what extent soft regulatory measures without strong coercive forces exerted by the stock exchanges on listed corporations can protect shareholders and improve corporate governance in China. It conducts empirical analysis on how effective this regulatory measure is in curbing wrongdoings of listed corporations. This study identifies some strengths and weaknesses of this type of regulatory measures. Compared with more formal regulatory measures, these measures are more flexible and can respond to new circumstances quickly. They are thus important in China where lawmaking generally takes a long time and where the market is changing drastically. However, soft regulatory measures may not be effective if the regulatory authorities lack the means of escalating the regulatory intensity since listed corporations may simply ignore them. China should develop a range of administrative, civil, and administrative regulatory measures and combine hard and soft regulatory measures with different regulatory intensity in protecting shareholders and promoting corporate governance, which facilitates a strong capital market that is essential for economic development.

24615319.label: Realisation of objectives
24615319.value: Objectives of this study This is the final report I prepared for this ECS project titled Investigating kindergarten teachers’ content knowledge and pedagogical content knowledge of visual arts education in Hong Kong. The study aims to investigate the content knowledge and pedagogical content knowledge possessed by local kindergarten teachers of visual arts and to identify areas where they could be further developed. The specific objectives of this study are to (1) investigate in-service kindergarten teachers’ views on and their competence in visual arts education in Hong Kong; (2) examine how in-service kindergarten teachers deliver their visual arts knowledge (content knowledge) and pedagogies (pedagogical content knowledge); and (3) explore which kinds of visual arts knowledge and pedagogies in-service kindergarten teachers need in order to teach visual arts more effectively to young children. I report that I achieved 100% of three objectives designed in this project. Problems encountered This project started to be implemented on 1 January 2020. Since its outbreak in December 2019, the coronavirus disease has affected the health of people worldwide. Due to the COVID-19 outbreak, kindergartens in Hong Kong have been closed for face-to-face instruction since early February 2020. Face-to-face lessons were being resumed and suspended repeatedly. The kindergartens only had 31 to 54 days of class, varying by grade, in 2020. All government-subsidized kindergartens must follow the regulations to stay closed until the Education Bureau allows up to a third of a school’s student capacity to return for in-person classes after the lunar New Year holiday after February 2021. The project timeline has been dramatically affected, especially the data collection work, which covers class K1, K2, and K3 class observations and post-observation interviews. This phase of research work had to be postponed until the school year of 2021-2022 since kindergarten principals claimed that they were uncertain about the school operation in the coming months (i.e., from March to August 2021). The scope of investigation undertaken and the result achieved Nevertheless, I managed to complete the first two stages of my research project. Two research assistants were recruited for this project. Specifically, our research team has achieved the following tasks: (1) Obtaining the approval of the relevant institutional ethics committee; (2) reviewing literature of content knowledge and pedagogical content knowledge of visual arts education; (3) designing an e-survey for peer review; and (4) conducting a series of focus group interviews for developing the survey. In general, 30% of research has been achieved for each of the objectives at the mid-term progress in March 2021. In April 2021, my collaborators and I kicked off a sequential mixed-method study for my ECS project. A focus-group interview study was conducted in Phase 1 to explore Hong Kong kindergarten teachers’ beliefs regarding early visual arts education and establish a conceptual structure based on the TPB model. The interview data were the basis for developing the questionnaire used in Phase 2, a large-scale survey to examine how far teachers' practices aligned with the TPB model suggested in Phase 1. The qualitative part (Phase 1) was an interview study of 19 kindergarten teachers in two focus groups, aiming to develop a conceptual structure of the teachers’ behavioural, normative and control beliefs. The quantitative part (Phase 2) was a survey of 243 teachers from 21 randomly sampled kindergartens regarding their EVAE beliefs and practices. Most teachers believed in child-centred teaching while practising teacher-directed instruction and supported creativity while delivering closed-ended instruction. Four influential factors were identified to account for this gap: (1) practising child-centred pedagogies due to behavioural beliefs, (2) undervaluing visual arts due to normative beliefs, (3) instructing children directly due to normative beliefs and (4) delivering subject knowledge in studio teaching due to control beliefs. In the study, the TPB model could explain the teachers' beliefs and practices well, especially regarding how their behavioural, normative, and control beliefs affected their behavioural intentions in early visual arts teaching. In January 2022, my collaborators and I conducted another explanatory study for my ECS project. The study highlighted kindergarten teachers' teaching behaviours in their kindergarten classrooms. The study used a mixture of direct observations and post-observation interviews to investigate kindergarten teachers' knowledge of and pedagogical approaches to visual arts. In an observation study, 18 classrooms with 76 children in two local kindergartens in Hong Kong were observed during a 30-minute visual arts activity. Altogether, 540 minutes of video data were recorded and analysed using field notes and a time sampling strategy. In addition, 18 class teachers from the observed classrooms were invited to give post-observation interviews, and 810 minutes of data were recorded. The interview participants supported the importance of non-directive early childhood arts. However, the observation findings revealed that they still relied heavily on directive teaching in implementing early visual arts teaching. The study uncovered a discrepancy between integrating pedagogies and the subject knowledge of kindergarten teachers’ visual arts education. In September 2022, my collaborators and I conducted another mixed-methods study investigate kindergarten teachers’ content knowledge and pedagogical content knowledge in early visual arts education (EVAE) and to identify the challenges they face in teaching visual arts to children. The study surveyed 342 in-service kindergarten teachers in Hong Kong and conducted individual interviews with 12 participants, collecting a total of 480 minutes of data. The findings revealed that: (1) kindergarten teachers in Hong Kong generally performed well in terms of their pedagogical content knowledge; (2) they lacked content knowledge in various forms of early visual arts (EVA); (3) they faced challenges in teaching visual arts effectively. This study can potentially change how early childhood visual arts teaching is conceptualized and taught in Hong Kong and other Asian regions. Finally, 100% of the research has been achieved for each objective at the final stage. The first study used the theory of planned behaviour further to explain the gap between teachers' beliefs and practices. The study's preliminary findings have been translated into Chinese to disseminate to all local kindergartens in Hong Kong through emails in April 2022 during the pandemic. The second study, a continuation of the ECS project, observed kindergarten teachers' teaching and behaviours in their visual arts classrooms through observations and post-observation interviews. The adapted observation framework in this paper was shared in a professional development workshop for HKEC Elite Kindergarten in July 2022, and the school adopted the framework for peer observation of teaching early visual arts. The third study is currently under review (Title of the manuscript: Early Childhood Visual Arts Education: Teachers’ Content Knowledge, Pedagogical Content Knowledge, and Challenges), by a top-tier journal in the field of teacher education.

24615319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
24615319.value: The first output applied the TPB model to identify a significant belief–practice gap in implementing early visual arts activities based on various factors and constraints. The findings could be used to design and implement a responsive teacher education programme in visual arts, in partnership with existing teacher education institutes and kindergartens in Hong Kong. Given Hong Kong's location in Asia, the insights gained from examining early visual arts in this study may be relevant to other parts of the Asia-Pacific region, and they may even hold lessons for worldwide educators, policymakers and researchers. The second output used a mixture of direct observations and post-observation interviews to investigate kindergarten teachers' knowledge of and pedagogical approaches to visual arts. This study uncovered a discrepancy between integrating pedagogies and the subject knowledge of kindergarten teachers’ visual arts education. This study adapted the Early Childhood Teacher Behaviour Observation (ECTBO) instrument as a visual arts–specific rather than a general tool. The newly adapted ECTBO version will be helpful for worldwide researchers and educators seeking to investigate kindergarten teachers’ pedagogical knowledge of and approaches to visual arts education in the future.

24615319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
24615319.value: This study aimed to examine the level of content knowledge and pedagogical content knowledge that local kindergarten teachers possess in the field of visual arts and to identify areas where further development is needed. In the past, visual arts teaching was not considered a central aspect of early childhood education, but this study aimed to fill in the gaps in research in this area. The proposed study took a teacher education and development perspective to investigate the kindergarten teachers' views and competence in visual arts education in Hong Kong, how they deliver their knowledge and teaching techniques, and the areas where they need improvement to teach visual arts more effectively. The study utilized a mixed-method approach. The findings of this research had the potential to impact the way early childhood visual arts teaching is perceived and conducted in Hong Kong. On a practical level, the results could be used to design and implement a teacher training program in visual arts in collaboration with existing teacher education institutes and kindergartens in Hong Kong. Ultimately, the findings may improve the quality of visual arts teaching by local kindergarten teachers and contribute to future educational policymaking in Hong Kong.
