27608219.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27608219.value: The theoretical discussion of institutions and organizational behaviors accentuates the importance of legitimacy or social endorsement for organizations to survive and grow. Organizations are nonetheless exposed to pressures from multiple demands and expectations from key constituents in the organizational field. This state of affairs is known as institutional complexity, a situation where organizations confront a plurality of institutional logics that can be inherently incompatible. Past studies offer important insights into the interplay between field-level characteristics and organizational attributes in shaping organizational strategies for handling pressures across institutional logics. The accounts advanced in the literature, however, usually focus on the organizational responses at a single point in time and thus give insufficient attention to how organizations change their strategies over longer time spans. Also, most studies suggest that institutional complexity is transitional, as organizational fields will eventually move from one dominant logic to another. This assumption is oblivious to a theoretical issue that remains understudied: how do organizations respond to the incessant pressures precipitated by the coexistence of multiple logics? To fill this lacuna, this study will examine how the film production companies from Hong Kong coped with the institutional pressures in China after the People’s Republic of China (PRC) government implemented the Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement in 2003 – a policy that encouraged Hong Kong’s film companies to develop co-production projects with Mainland companies. The Chinese film market offers a rich context to pursue this theoretical inquiry because it is an organizational field characterized by enduring institutional complexity encompassing a multiplicity of political and market logics. The Hong Kong film companies’ experience also presents an intriguing case: they were once prominent players in the field, best known for their market orientation that sometimes entailed their challenging the officially permissible line in China’s censorship regulations. During the early 2010s, however, many of them shifted their focus to producing propaganda-like movies. Against the backdrop of this development, this project will conduct a longitudinal study of the dynamic responses of Hong Kong’s film companies to the institutional pressures operating in China. It develops a theoretical framework based on insights from institutional theory about organizational decoupling. It will compile a movie dataset and an event-history database on Mainland-Hong Kong film co-productions between 2003 and 2017, and conduct about 70 in-depth interviews with industry practitioners in Hong Kong and mainland China in order to explicate how organizations recalibrate their strategies in response to institutional complexity. 組織如何在矛盾的制度中生存？本研究分析自2003年中國內地與香港簽訂《內地與香港關於建立更緊密經貿關係的安排》香港電影製作公司如何面對中國電影制度的挑戰。本研究引用組織研究的制度理論，分析2003年至2017年出產的中港合拍片，並訪問約70位電影從業員探討以上問題。

27608219.label: Realisation of objectives
27608219.value: All objectives of this research are accomplished. First, this study elucidates the process of how organizations respond to the incessant and conflicting pressures precipitated by the coexistence of multiple institutional logics (the first objective). As committed in the proposal, I interviewed 38 CEOs, film producers, and film directors in Hong Kong, 25 CEOs and film producers in mainland China, and 8 government officials in the Chinese Film Bureau. I elucidate the censorship system for movie production and screening in mainland China and examine how Hong Kong’s film producers and directors recalibrated their strategies to handle the institutional complexity in the Chinese film market. My study suggests that the Chinese film censorship and screening system is capricious and contingent on four key factors: (i) The geo-political environment that affects the diplomatic relations between China and other countries. For example, the diplomatic tensions between China and South Korea since 2020 led to the suspension of Korean movies and TV programs from the media in China. (ii) The dynamic of domestic politics – in particular when the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is about to hold the national congress, where the Party’s leadership changes are conferred – the government would tighten the movie censorship. During this period (typically from September to October), the state would urge, if not command, the cinemas to show movies that promote patriotism and nationalism. Some recent examples of the quasi-propaganda movies include My People, My Country (2019), The Captain (2019), The Moment of The Sunrise (2019), The Battle at Lake Changjin (2021), and many others that were shown in cinema around the time of the national congress. Other movies, especially foreign movies imported from abroad, ought to give way to the quasi-propaganda movies during that period. (iii) Movies could hardly overcome censorship if they touch on any incidents of dissent in the society, which would potentially arouse the people’s grievances against the government and lead to dissension. For example, when the government sought to decrease the workload of primary and middle school students and to promote more equal access to education by barring for-profit after-school tutoring in 2021, movies that allude to the issue of education equality had to undergo a strict process of vetting from the state censors before they could gain approval for production and screening. (iv) Ad hoc measures from the National Radio and Television Administration would ban the movie and media contents that it considered detrimental to the society. These measures are, however, erratic as the government rarely gives the industry any advisory or cautionary notice before launching the policies – for example, banning “sissy” or “effeminate” male celebrities and public figures with tattoos on their body from the media in 2021 and 2022. Actors and actresses who infringed these measures have to be trimmed from the movie they performed. Second, my data show that film practitioners in Hong Kong and mainland China have adopted two strategies to handle the institutional complexity. In my analysis of these strategic responses, I draw insights from institutional theory and build a theoretical account of how Hong Kong’s film producers and directors coped with the institutional pressures and capricious censorship in China. As such, I attained the second and third objectives of this project. I argue that the film practitioners interpreted and addressed the institutional complexity in two ways. (i) Some film directors from Hong Kong are well-connected with the Chinese film censors. They would consult the government officials about the plot at both the pre- and post-production stage. They also bargained with the state censors for a higher degree of autonomy and freedom of expression in film production. Some of them could convince the government officials that their movies conformed to the censorship regulations. This strategy, however, is applicable to very few film directors who have a “clean” and “strong” track record – namely, those who never transgress the film censorship and collaborated with the state-supported film companies in producing quasi-propaganda movies. Their “clean” and “strong” track record, therefore, provides them with the “political capital” that allowed them to bargain with the state censors for more freedom in the course of film production. Some prominent examples of these film directors whom I interviewed are Derek Yee [爾冬陞], Dante Lam [林超賢], Herman Yau [邱禮濤], Tsui Hark [徐克], Andrew Lau [劉偉強], Wilson Yip [葉偉信], and others. (ii) Besides the forenamed strategies of the renowned film directors, some film producers from Hong Kong have assumed an important role in the top management of the major film companies in China. These film producers may not possess much “political capital” as the renowned film directors do. However, they acquired strong “social capital” through gaining trust from and building acquaintances with the film investors and CEOs of the major film companies in China. Some of these film investors and CEOs are closely-connected with the officials of the National Radio and Television Administration and the politburo of CCP, known also as the Political Bureau of the CCP’s Central Committee. These film investors and CEOs thus resemble the brokers who connected the film producers with the state censors, through which the film producers could have access to first-hand information about the requirements and expectations of the Film Bureau. Lest the government implements or amends the censorship policies abruptly due to the four factors discussed earlier, these film producers are better able to respond swiftly so that they could alleviate the loss incurred. Some prominent examples of these film producers and CEOs whom I interviewed include Yu Dong [于冬], Song Dai [宋岱], Nansun Shi [施南生], Jeffrey Chan [陳永雄], Chu Yam-chi [朱任之], Tang Wai But [鄧維弼], and others. Third, in theorizing the filmmakers’ responses to the institutional complexity in the Chinese film market, I developed a theoretical account that contributes to cultural sociology with particular reference to the power struggles between the cultural producers. In this respect, I achieved the fourth and fifth objectives of this project. I attribute the success of the renowned Hong Kong film directors and producers in mainland China to the director-centric culture of film production in Hong Kong and the Mainland. This market convention made some Hong Kong film directors highly-appraised and espoused by their Mainland counterparts. As a result, the Chinese film investors and CEOs are eager to collaborate with the renowned Hong Kong film directors and the film producers who worked closely with the renowned Hong Kong film directors. Moreover, my sociological account highlights the threat and shortcomings of the director-centric culture amidst the rise of multiplex cinemas in China. I argue that under the director-centric culture, film directors enjoyed the autonomy in film production but they have to bear great responsibility for the performance of their movies in the box office. If the movies did not achieve a certain level of success at the box office in their opening week, the multiplex cinemas would reduce their screening after a short period of time or pull the movie from the screen. As a result, many Hong Kong’s film directors are mired in difficulties in surviving in the Chinese film market and regaining their recognitions among their Mainland counterparts. My analysis sheds light on the relations between market change and the strategic interactions among the market players who possessed different types of political and social capital in the Chinese film market. I elaborate on this in my manuscripts.

27608219.value: As noted in 5.3, I elucidate the censorship system for movie production and screening in China and examine how Hong Kong’s film producers and directors recalibrated their strategies to handle the institutional complexity in China’s film market. I show that the Chinese film censorship and screening system is capricious and contingent on four factors – (i) the geo-political environment, (ii) the dynamic of domestic politics, (iii) the occurrence of incidents of dissent in the society, and (iv) ad hoc government measures that banned the movies it deemed detrimental to the society. I argue that some film directors acquired “political capital” from their “clean” and “strong” track record which allowed them to bargain with the state censors for more freedom in film production. Some film producers possessed strong “social capital” through building acquaintances with the film investors and CEOs of the major film companies in China, who connected the film producers with the state censors. I elaborate on this in a paper manuscript but I am seeking my interviewees’ consent for publishing their interview quotes in my manuscript. Although I have preserved their anonymity by concealing their name and identity, they would like to review my manuscript before revealing the interview data to the public. I will submit the manuscript to journal for review once acquiring their consent. Besides, my analysis attributes the success of the renowned Hong Kong film directors and producers in China to the director-centric culture of film production – I developed two journal articles on this (see Research Outputs No.1&2 in Part C) that are now under review. My sociological account also highlights the threat and shortcomings of the director-centric culture amidst the rising popularity of multiplex cinemas in China – I discussed this in my research output no.3 (in Part C) that is currently under review. Moreover, I shared my research findings in academic conferences and several public events, including two seminars organized by The Hong Kong Film Directors’ Guild and the Hong Kong Film Critics Society in 2021, and a talk show [五夜講場—學人串社科2021：從港產片到香港電影] at Radio Television Hong Kong (RTHK) on June 30, 2021, available at . The show was widely discussed in the media as one of the most popular episodes in its series with over 40,380 views on YouTube before it was pulled. As such, I reached out to the public and promoted a sociological perspective on studying media and culture as a public intellectual.

27608219.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27608219.value: This project sheds light on the study of Hong Kong’s film industry by illuminating the strategies film producers and directors adopted to secure their foothold in the Chinese film market. It also contributes to the theoretical advancement in sociology and organization studies by theorizing the process of which industry players attain recognitions amidst institutional complexity. This draws three important implications for further development of the research. First, sociological and organizational studies have to generalize the process of how competing institutional logics and the struggles among players shape economic development. Second, to do so, I propose to delve into the conditions of the forenamed process with reference to (i) the macro societal changes that shaped the opportunity space for players to acquire legitimacy, (ii) the institutional condition at the meso level that affects the possibilities of resource mobilization, and (iii) the strategies and frames that players adopted to construct their identity and mobilize support from the stakeholders that allowed them to attain legitimacy. Third, future studies should compare the conditions discussed above across social contexts in order to generalize the pattern of interplay between field-level characteristics (structure) and organizational attributes (agency) in shaping organizational strategies for handling pressures across institutional logics.

27608219.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27608219.value: This research examines how Hong Kong’s film producers and directors developed and adjusted their strategies for handling the institutional pressures in China’s film market since 2003. These pressures are derived mainly from the Chinese film censorship and screening system that is contingent on (i) the geo-political environment, (ii) the dynamic of domestic politics, (iii) the occurrence of incidents of dissent in the society, and (iv) ad hoc government measures that would ban the movies it deemed detrimental to the society. To cope with these pressures, some film directors bargained with the state censors for more freedom in film production. Some film producers developed acquaintances with the film investors and CEOs of the major film companies in China, who connected the producers with the film censors. Lest the Chinese government implements or amends the censorship policies abruptly, these film producers are better able to respond swiftly. The success of the renowned Hong Kong film directors and producers in mainland China can be attributed to the director-centric culture of film production in Hong Kong and the Mainland. Although this market convention made some Hong Kong film directors highly-appraised and espoused by their Mainland counterparts, it mired many film directors in difficulties in surviving in the Chinese film market and regaining their recognitions in China.

27611719.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27611719.value: Why do great powers intervene in foreign elections? What are the effects of such interventions on the targeted elections results? The 2016 U.S. election exhibited such an intervention by Russia in favor of Donald Trump, and my data show that the U.S. and the USSR/Russia have intervened in one out of every nine elections around the world using various covert and overt methods for this purpose. Nevertheless, electoral interventions remain understudied. As for the causes, I argue that partisan electoral interventions occur when two concurrent conditions exist. The first is that the great power perceives its interests as being highly endangered by another significant candidate/party within the target. This candidate/party has different and inflexible preferences on important issues and is either ideologically committed to them and/or is severely constrained by its political base. The second is that a significant domestic actor within a democratic target wants or is willing to be aided by the great power in this risky manner. When one or both of these conditions are missing, partisan electoral interventions will rarely, if ever, occur. As for effects of electoral interventions on the election results, I have three main hypotheses. First, I argue that such interventions usually increase the electoral chances of the aided candidate. Second, I claim that overt electoral interventions are more effective than covert interventions. Third, I argue that electoral interventions are less likely to effectively help an aided party/candidate competing in a founding election than in a non-founding/later election and will frequently harm it. I propose to complete the writing of a single-authored book for publication with a university press on these two questions tentatively entitled Meddling in the Ballot Box. This project uses a multi-method framework in order to answer these questions, including in-depth archival research into six cases in which the U.S. seriously considered intervening in this manner, the statistical analysis of my original dataset of electoral interventions by the U.S. and the USSR/Russia, and a micro-level analysis of election surveys from specific intervention cases. Most of the research for this book has been completed. I am requesting funding for the following remaining key components: archival research for two yet-to-be written case studies, and for the extension of this electoral intervention dataset to 2010.When finished, this book will provide the first empirically supported answers to these questions, increasing scholarly and public understanding and providing the tools for further study of this important phenomenon. 為什麼大國干預外國選舉？這些干預對目標選舉的結果有何影響？2016年俄羅斯對美國大選進行有利於唐納德特朗普的干預，而我的數據顯示，美國和蘇聯/俄羅斯在全球每九次選舉中就有一次採用各種隱蔽或公開的方式進行干預。儘管如此，干預選舉這個課題至今未得到充分研究。 關於干預選舉的原因，我認為當兩個條件同時存在時，干預就會發生。首先，大國認為其利益受到目標國內另一個重要候選人/政黨的高度威脅。這個候選人/政黨在重要問題上與干預國有不同的偏好而且不易改變其偏好：這要麽是出於對意識形態的忠誠，要麽是受到其政治基礎的嚴重限制。第二，在實行民主制的目標國中一個重要的國內行動者希望或願意以這種危險的方式得到大國的幫助。當缺少這些條件中的一個或全部時，干預黨派選舉的情況很少會發生。 關於干預選舉對選舉結果的影響，我有三個主要的假設。首先，我認為這種干預通常會增加受助候選人的獲選機會。其次，我聲稱公開的干預方式比隱蔽的更有效。第三，我認為干預選舉的措施在奠基性的選舉中較在非奠基性的/後期的選舉中有更少機會能有效地幫助受助的一方/候選人競爭，並且經常會傷害它。 通過此項目，我會撰寫一本獨作的書來系統研究這兩個問題。該書將在大學出版社出版，暫名為 “干涉選舉”。是項研究使用多方法框架來回答這些問題，包括對美國認真考慮以這種方式干預選舉的六個案例進行深入的檔案研究，對我原有的美國和蘇聯/俄羅斯干預選舉的數據集進行統計分析，以及對個別干預選舉案例中的選舉調查進行微觀分析。本書的大部分研究工作已經完成。我希望大學的研究基金能為以下的剩餘關鍵組成部分提供資金：兩個尚待撰寫的案例分析的檔案研究和將此干預選舉數據集擴展到2010年所需的研究 。 本書完成後將對這些問題提供第一批有實證支持的答案，提高學術界和公眾對此問題的理解，並為進一步研究這一重要現象提供理論及證據支持。

27611719.label: Major findings and research outcome
27611719.value: As for objective 5.1 (causes) I find in my analysis that partisan electoral interventions are usually an “inside job,” occurring only if a significant domestic actor within the target wants it. Likewise electoral interventions won’t happen unless the great power fears its interests are endangered by another significant party or candidate with very different and inflexible preferences. As for objective 5.2. (effects), I find through a statistical analysis of my new electoral intervention dataset (PEIG), as well as post-election surveys from particular cases of such interventions, that electoral interventions increase the vote share of the side aided by the foreign power by 3% on average. That is a significant effect on the election results, sufficient in many situations to determine the identity of its winner-and in some known cases clearly did. I also find that such interference also tends to be more effective when it is conducted overtly increasing the vote share of the preferred side by 3% more than when it is done covertly. However such meddling is usually ineffective, if not counterproductive, when done in a founding election reducing the vote share of the preferred side by 6.7% on average. As noted most partisan electoral interventions involve close coordination and cooperation between the intervening state and the assisted side. Such interventions, therefore, tend to usually occur in marginal elections, i.e. those in which the result is highly uncertain or one side lags but remains electorally viable. In such situations, election interference is most likely to have a significant effect on the results of the election. Likewise, because of these dynamics, the intervening State will usually not intervene overtly unless informed by the aided side that a domestic backlash will not occur prior to the elections. When backlash is unlikely, overt interventions are expected to be more effective because the intervening State can outbid the local politicians for the target State public’s support. It can also usually provide more resources to the preferred side in an overt intervention than in a covert one. As for the effect in founding elections, the contrary effect in these situations is due to the inexperience of the assisted side with elections and with how to campaign effectively for office, leading it to frequently request from the intervening State methods of interventions that are ineffective or counterproductive in that electoral context, thus leading to unintentional harm to itself.

27611719.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27611719.value: There are two potential directions for further development of research on this topic (partisan electoral interventions). One potential direction for further research examines other longer-term effects of partisan electoral interventions aside of on election results- e.g. the results of successes by foreign powers in getting their preferred candidate/party elected or, more generally of the public in question becoming aware of such significant meddling in their domestic affairs. This is planned to be further done in the near future using the expanded dataset of such interventions (PEIG) to analyze other such effects statistically- an expanded dataset made possible thanks to this grant. The second direction focuses on public opinion, examining the situations in which publics in countries whose governments frequently meddle in this manner (such as the American, Russian, and British publics) would support, if ever, such interference by their governments. I have applied in the recent GRF application cycle for a GRF grant for the funds needed in order to investigate this question in an empirical manner (via survey experiments in multiple countries etc.) and thankfully I was just informed that I have received it.

27611719.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27611719.value: Great powers have tried for centuries to intervene in elections occurring in other states through various methods with the Russian interventions in the 2016 and 2020 U.S. elections being recent examples. Indeed there has been such an American or Soviet/Russian intervention in one of every nine national-level elections. There is however scant scholarly research on this topic. This book, the first academic monograph to focus exclusively on this type of foreign meddling, begins to remedy this situation through an investigation that combines the historical analysis of six actual and potential interventions with a statistical study of a new dataset of partisan electoral interventions (PEIG) and of election surveys. It also analyzes the 2016 Russian intervention. It finds that electoral interventions happen when two concurrent conditions occur: a local actor agrees to collude with the intervener in such an activity and the great power feels deeply threatened by a different actor with divergent preferences. It also finds that electoral interventions frequently affect election results, enough in many situations to determine their winner. The effects are stronger when the intervention is done in public and it is more likely to work when that isn’t the first national election held in that country.

27612019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27612019.value: 该项目旨在了解自治和问责制的运作方式 在大中华区的两个高绩效地区 - 香港的教育系统中表现良好 和上海许多高度独特的国家和国家正在应对严峻的压力 通过学校自治与责任制（SAWA）政策进行教育改革， 其中包括高风险测试，绩效评估和支付费用等政策 性能。受新公共管理（NPM）私营部门原则的支持， 这些政策是由有影响力的中介组织传播的，例如 经济合作与发展组织。倡导者建议NPM和 SAWA改革将导致学校改善。但是，没有经验共识 自治和问责制政策可以改善教育机会 公立学校的成果。现有的研究显示出消极的，有时甚至是矛盾的 这些政策的效果，特别是对弱势学生。香港和上海 已经取得了令人满意的教育成果的全球声誉，但几乎没有 这些地区的NPM和SAWA政策结果的经验知识。鉴于 SAWA在全球教育改革中的突出地位，这个项目要求，是什么性格和 SAWA政策在香港和上海（SAWAhks）的后果？的问题 性格侧重于政策采用和多层次的制定，而问题 后果集中在围绕SAWA政策效果的情况。以人为本 在关键政策制定的角度来看，该项目首次展示了如何，为什么， 通过多种政策采纳和重新制定SAWA的行动理论 香港和上海的多个演员。发展关于这些现象的理论 SAWAhks采用混合方法生成方法学上严谨的结果 研究设计借鉴定性案例研究，调查和多元数据分析 方法。 SAWAhks以强大的项目为基础，在全球范围内改革学校：多元化 教育部门自治和问责政策的标量分析 （重整）。 REFORMED研究小组正在西班牙审查这些相同的问题， 挪威，荷兰和智利。就其本身而言，SAWAhks本身提供了第一次看 这个全球性的政策解决方案展现了两个表现最好但未充分考虑的问题 世界教育系统。与REFORMED项目集成时，这些 研究结果可以帮助世界各地的教育政策行动者和研究人员了解 自治和问责制可以改善学习的效力和条件 和教学。当教育不公平现象和政策上升时，这种影响至关重要 解决方案正在缩小。

27612119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27612119.value: Our every-day interactions with the environment rely on our brain’s ability to retrieve 3D structures from the barrage of information in a visual scene. To resolve 3D structure, the visual system must compute depth by reconciling the slightly different images projected to each eye (binocular disparity). Our current understanding of how the brain achieves depth from disparity is based primarily on studies employing rather simplistic stimuli, such as basic geometric forms. While this approach has advanced our understanding the neural architecture that serves 3D vision, it important to ask whether current knowledge has been hindered by using stimuli that are simplified (e.g., geometric planes), and that are hence far removed from the complex forms that are typically encountered day-to-day. The proposed project will approach the problem of 3D vision from a novel perspective – testing the role of object context on depth sensitivity, in order to better understand the utility of 3D information. Motivated by a growing body of work in other visual domains that have indicated surprising modulation of both behavioural and neural responses to basic visual properties (e.g., lightness, colour) as a function of object context, we ask here whether our ability to extract and encode depth is affected by the context of the object that the visual system is trying to decipher. Indeed, recent data acquired within the PI’s laboratory suggest that contextual modulations in vision extend to disparity processing. Here, the neural mechanisms underlying depth perception will be explored in contexts with varying degrees of natural relevance (faces versus non-faces); contexts with varying degrees of physical-plausibility (plausible versus implausible structures); and in terms of the plasticity of the underlying networks (depth representations before and after extensive training). The project’s experiments will integrate state-of-the-art fMRI and brain stimulation (TMS) methods, with concurrent behavioural (psychophysical) measures, allowing neural activity to be linked to perceptual states. Findings from this project will provide a better understanding of the neural substrates that underlie the perception of (disparity-defined) 3D structures in the human brain, and potentially inform the development of artificial and entertainment technologies. 人類的大腦可以將視覺場景裡的大量信息整合加工成立體圖像結構，這一能力在我們的生活中扮演着重要的角色。視覺系統必須通過協調投射在兩眼視網膜上圖像的細微差異來計算深度（雙眼視差）。我們目前對大腦如何通過視差來取得深度的理解主要是基於採用相當簡單刺激（例如：基本幾何形狀）的研究。雖然這種方法增加了我們對立體視覺的神經結構的理解，但因為使用簡化（例如：幾何平面）的刺激，與日常生活中所遇到的複雜形狀有所不同，所以可能會對了解這個課題造成阻礙。有見及此，本項目將會從一個全新的角度來處理立體視覺的課題 —— 測試物件環境在深度敏感度中的角色，以便更好地理解立體圖像信息的效用。近年多項研究指出，無論行為反應或神經反應，皆對作為物件環境的基本視覺特性（例如：光、顏色等）呈現超出預期的調控。此類研究近年越發增加，然而由於它們均是圍繞其他視覺領域為考證重點，故啟發了我們進行本次研究。而最近，本項目的研究團隊所獲得的研究數據表明，視覺的環境調控的確能夠擴展到視差的處理。在本研究中，深度感知背後的神經機制將在具有不同程度的自然相關性（面孔與非面孔）和具有不同程度的物理合理性（合理與不合理的結構）的環境下進行探索，也會研究背後的神經網絡的可塑性（在大量訓練之前和之後的深度表示）。本項目的實驗將會結合最先進的功能性磁振造影技術和神經刺激（顱磁刺激）方法，同時也會有行為學（心理物理）的測量，使神經活動與感知狀態能夠聯繫起來。本項目的結果將使我們能夠更好地了解人類大腦對（視差定義的）立體結構感知背後的神經基礎，並可能有助人工和娛樂技術的發展。

27612119.label: Major findings and research outcome
27612119.value: The perception of depth (from disparity) has long been shown to be governed by a network of regions extending from retinotopic visual cortex to both dorsal (parietal) and ventral (temporal) cortex. We now know that the particular sites engaged depends largely on task demands. Using a combination of behaviour and neuroscience (fMRI, TMS) paradigms, we highlight in this project a second important factor that modulates stereoscopic responses in the human brain: object context. Notably, we show that object plausibility, however task-irrelevant, exerts considerable influences on depth-position judgments, and depth-relevant responses in the human brain (Wong, Ban, & Chang, 2020 J Cog Neuro). We also show that behavioural and neural sensitivity to depth-position changes strikingly in biological (face) vs non-biological (random surface) contexts, and that these changes are task-dependent (Chou, Ban, & Chang, 2021 eNeuro). Depth responses in cortex are influenced by object (biological) relevance, particularly along the depth-related intermediate region V3, and fusiform cortex. Temporary disruption of such regions abolishes these contextual influences (Wong & Chang, 2022, eNeuro). This suggests a higher-order processing architecture that leads to an active reweighing of disparity computations against object familiarity. Such a mechanism would be consistent with models of vision that suggest inferences made in higher-order areas project back to lower regions to affect sensory encoding. Importantly, context-stereo interactions are largely expertise-dependent (i.e., can be changed through re-attaching meaning to objects!) (Li & Chang, 2023 Cerebral Cortex). This suggests that the underlying mechanisms, while potentially serving to enhance the efficacy of the visual system, are also not innately featured.

27612119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27612119.value: This work challenges our current understanding of the disparity processing network in the primate brain, signalling a need to recognize the potential for dynamically changing mechanisms that closely interact within the larger, object recognition problem. This work should provoke a re-think in the way in which the community views (and teaches!) visual processing.

27612119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27612119.value: We show that an observers' sensitivity to- and neural responses to stereoscopic depth are dependent on object-level context. For example, while entirely task-irrelevant, an observers’ ability to judge the position of an object in (depth) space is surprisingly influenced by whether the object is geometrically plausible, or implausible; or a face vs non-face. The work challenges conventional understanding of the hierarcharchical manner in which visual stimulus-solving occurs in the human brain, particularly as it pertains to its independence from higher-order object perception. We suggest that such object-to-feature modulations in the brain serve an ecological importance towards filtering irrelevant from relevant sensory data.

27614319.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27614319.value: 研究背景：中國目前有13%兒童（3,581萬）為城鄉流動兒童。這些兒童面臨著家庭低收入、歧視、適應困難、有限的父母支持、以及缺乏社會資源等多方面的挑戰，其情緒與行為問題因而往往顯著高於城市本地兒童，如抑鬱、自殺意念、自我傷害行為、社交焦慮、多動、行為問題、適應不良行為等。儘管大量流動兒童亟需情緒行為相關服務，目前的服務缺少實證干預。西方文獻正愈發關注建立兒童抗逆力的干預研究，而針對中國流動兒童抗逆力的研究仍然有限。西方國家近年來基於學校的一些正念干預表現出對學生情緒與行為的積極作用，初步證據亦表明正念所包涵的概念與抗逆力密切相關，但現有研究缺少以嚴謹的方法對其原理的探討。現有研究也缺少檢視在非西方文化環境中正念干預的效果，除了我們之前的探索性研究，目前並沒有關於中國流動兒童的正念干預研究。 研究方法：本研究將採用兩組隨機對照試驗，檢驗針對中國流動兒童的16節學校正念干預效果，以及探索抗逆力在這一過程中的作用。我們將邀請深圳民辦學校的300個四至五年級學生參與研究，參加者將被隨機分為16星期正念干預組以及16星期心理社會教育對照組，主要測量結果為情緒與行為健康。在17個月裡，參加者將參加4次測量：隨機分組前基準測量（T0）、干預中期測量（T1）、干預完成即時測量（T2）、和一年後追踪測量（T3）。我們的研究假設為：1）和對照組相比，正念干預將更顯著、持續地提高兒童抗逆力；2）抗逆力的提高將提升兒童的情緒與行為健康；3）抗逆力作為中介變量，調節正念與兒童情緒行為的關係。 理論意義：本研究將在一個缺乏相關研究的文化環境中探索抗逆力對童年中期發展的作用，並為在這一人群中的正念干預效果及抗逆力在干預中的機制提供實證基礎。 服務意義：這些實證基礎將為社區服務機構及學校提供服務建議，以幫助流動兒童應對情緒與行為方面的困難。本研究的結果也將為如何提高中國和其它地區的弱勢青少年群體的抗逆力提供啟示。

27614319.label: Realisation of objectives
27614319.value: For Objective #1, we used a 2-arm randomized experiment to test the effects of mindfulness intervention on child resilience. The treatment group joined 16 weeks mindfulness sessions in one semester, while the control group joined 16 weeks of psychosocial education sessions. The intervention manual and format were used in our pilot study and showed good acceptability and feasibility. Both intervention and control groups completed four assessments at baseline before intervention (T1, March 2021), mid-point during intervention (T2, May 2021), immediately after intervention (T3, June 2021), and one year after intervention (T4, June 2022). Our power analysis suggested 216 participants were required. We screened 2,361 students across five schools, and 278 students met our inclusion criteria. Excluding 12 participants who did not provide consent, we randomly assigned 266 students into a treatment group and a control group. 5.6% of participants were lost before posttest due to no show, schedule conflict, or withdrawal; 16.2% of participants were lost before follow-up due to reasons such as transferred to other schools. All withdrawn participants were invited to complete an exit assessment. An additional 1.5% of participants who showed invalid response patterns were excluded. In total, our attrition rate was 23.3%. Our intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis included 247 participants. We used regression analyses to examine the intervention effect on participants’ resilience over time, controlling for assessment timepoint (given that all the assessment timepoints were nested within individuals) and school (given that participants were nested within schools). Considering our literature review suggested that mindfulness interventions’ effects on children may vary by age (Dai et al., 2022) and gender (Xie et al., 2021), we also tested the intervention effect by gender (girls vs. boys) and grade (4th vs. 5th grade). In summary, compared with the psychoeducation group, the intervention showed no significant effect on the overall sample, but showed significant effect on boys, especially immediately after the intervention (B=2.88, p=0.046). It also showed long-term effect on resilience at 1-year follow-up for participants who had a low level of mindfulness at baseline. For Objective #2, we used regression analyses to examine whether the change in resilience from baseline predicts changes in mental health outcomes over time, controlling for child age, gender, family income, and parental educational level—background attributes that may affect child mental health. The mental health outcomes were measured by positive and negative affect, anxiety and depressive symptoms, behavioral difficulties and strengths, and sociocultural adjustment. Our analyses showed that improvements in resilience predicted reduced total depression and anxiety scores immediately after the intervention (B=-0.42, p=0.025 at T3) and one year later (B=-0.37, p=0.047 at T4). Improvements in resilience also predicted marginally reduced total behavioral difficulties one year after intervention (B=-0.13, p=0.058 at T4). Resilience improvements showed some effect on reducing negative affect shortly after the intervention (B=-0.11, p=0.015 at T2), but this effect diminished over time. Interestingly, resilience improvements significantly predicted increasing positive affect, and this effect grew larger across timepoints (B=0.12, 0.13, and 0.15 at T2, T3, and T4, respectively). The same growing effect also showed for child adjustment improvements (B=0.75, 1.05, and 1.41 at T2, T3, and T4, respectively). In summary, improvements in resilience predicted improvements in child emotional and behavioral outcomes in multiple domains. In particular, the effects on positive indicators (i.e., positive affect and adaptation) grew larger over time. For Objective #3, we conducted two sets of analyses to test the mediating role of resilience between mindfulness and child emotion and behavior. First, we conducted a path analysis using the cross-sectional pilot study baseline data to test the association among the constructs of mindfulness, resilience, and child emotion/behavior. The results showed that mindfulness was directly associated with child well-being, including sociocultural adaptation (β=0.13, p<0.01), anxiety (β= -0.37, p<0.01), depression (β= -0.43, p<0.01), positive affect (β=0.18, p<0.01), and negative affect (β= -0.29, p<0.01). However, resilience only mediated the relationship between mindfulness and sociocultural adaptation (p< 0.01) and positive affect (p< 0.01) but had no impact on anxiety, depression, or negative effect. Second, we used structural equation modeling to test whether changes in resilience mediated the relationship between receiving the mindfulness intervention and changes in emotion/behavior outcomes at T2, T3, and T4. Overall we identified no mediation relationship, except for a marginal indirect effect for boys’ adaptation at T3 (p=0.052) and T4 (p=0.086). In summary, our findings suggest that among our nonclinical Chinese school sample, resilience appears to exert promotive effect by further enhancing positive well-being indicators, whereas it did not exert protective effect to buffer negative indicators. However, although we were able to establish the mediation relationship in the cross-sectional data, we did not find resilience to mediate the relationship between mindfulness and child outcomes over time, except for a marginally significant effect for boys’ adaptation. As suggested by Gerber & Green (2012), mediation tests in experiments may be subject to estimation bias, especially when the mediator was not directly manipulated in the experiment. Our findings warrant further research to explore why the mediating effect of resilience is not maintained over time. Future experimental studies could also directly target resilience as a treatment component, such as comparing a mindfulness and resilience intervention with a mindfulness-only intervention. For Objective #4, based on our findings, we have provided a series of service recommendations that improve the emotional and behavioral well-being of migrant children in China and beyond. First, given that the mindfulness intervention showed significant effects for boys and children who reported lower levels of mindfulness at baseline, future interventions should be more targeted toward these student populations. Second, given that resilience showed more sustainable effects on positive mental health indicators (e.g., positive affect, adaptation), future interventions should adopt a more strength-based practice as mindfulness may promote children’s positive development rather than only reducing children’s emotional symptoms or behavioral problems. Third, given our overall promising findings on the intervention’s feasibility and effectiveness among migrant children, particularly with promising effects on their sociocultural adaptation, mindfulness training could be applied with more migrant youths in China and other countries. To disseminate our service recommendations, we held debriefing sessions with local school teachers and nonprofit organizational staff. Although COVID-19 caused significant delays in our project, we were able to provide timely services for the participants through mindfulness practices and psychological development knowledge, which likely helped the migrant students cope with the mental health challenges due to COVID-19, school closure, and neighborhood lockdowns. Last, to encourage mindfulness practice among younger children beyond China, we also developed short mindfulness cartoon videos for children, which are publicly available and have received over 1,800 total visits for the English videos (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=InnyfAE9fos&list=PLqkm8auOdUDEO1Mu7qAI_TXf6R8EpDkFf) and 1,871 total visits for the Chinese videos (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EkOiTtH1OkU&list=PLqkm8auOdUDEhQvETeWpgTfFItPd579U_). 27614319.label: Major findings and research outcome
27614319.value: First, the mindfulness and psychoeducation groups both showed mental health improvements over time, while mindfulness showed additional benefits on social adjustment and on boys. In addition, the literature suggested mindfulness may yield additional social benefits in peer relationships, which is particularly important for migrant youths’ social adjustment. Related research output: Presentation: - Lu, S., & Ng, S-M. (Jan 2021). Building resilience through school-based mindfulness intervention with Chinese migrant children: Feasibility and acceptability. Society for Social Work and Research annual conference. Invited talks: - Lu, S. (Jan 2022). School-based socio-emotional intervention with migrant children using a mindfulness approach. (under review). Effects of school-based mindfulness intervention on migrant adolescents’ mental health and adjustment: a randomized controlled trial. Second, among our nonclinical Chinese school sample, resilience appears to affect positive well-being indicators (e.g., positive affect, social adjustment) more so than negative indicators (e.g., depression, negative affect). Resilience is positively linked with the mindfulness intervention and positively with child emotion/behavior, but we did not find mediation relationships over time except for boys’ adjustment. Related research output: Presentation: Hu, H., Wang, Y., & Lu, S. (Jan 2022). Mindfulness, emotional well-being and sociocultural adaptation among Chinese migrant children: The mediating role of resilience. Society for Social Work and Research annual conference. Washington, DC. Journal manuscript in progress: Hu, H., & Lu, S. (under preparation). Mindfulness and adaptation among migrant children: The mediating role of resilience. Third, we found preliminary evidence of the reliability and validity of measuring Chinese migrant youths’ mindfulness with a brief version of the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire, including Observe, Attention, Nonreact, and Body–Mind Awareness subdomains. But the Nonjudgment subdomain in the original scale did not seem to apply to our sample. Related research output: Journal manuscript: Hu, H., Lyu, R., Dai, X., & Lu, S. (under review). Validating a Short-Form Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire Among Chinese Early Adolescents.

27614319.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27614319.value: Our findings suggest three future research directions. First, the gender effect—why and how do male participants benefit more from mindfulness than females, warrants further exploration. Second, given that resilience is a sociocultural context-specific process, and that resilience may exert both promotive (i.e., enhancing positive outcomes) and protective (i.e., reducing negative outcomes) effects, our findings should be replicated in diverse populations, such as youths in clinical settings or students from other cultures. Third, our findings warrant further research to explore why the mediating effect of resilience is not maintained over time. Future experimental studies could also directly target resilience as a treatment component, such as comparing a mindfulness and resilience intervention with a mindfulness-only intervention. As multiple mediators may link cause and effect in experimental studies (Gerber & Green, 2012), it would also be interesting to explore other potential mediators. Moving forward, we expect to applying for further funding in order to: 1) conduct qualitative research with male and female participants to understand the gender difference; 2) conduct cross-cultural research in school as well as clinical settings to explore the role of resilience in different populations; 3) develop an experiment study that examines alternative mediators, such as self-compassion.

27614319.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27614319.value: Thirteen percent (35.81 million) of children in China are rural migrant children living in cities, many of whom face challenges such as emotional, behavioral, and adjustment difficulties. This project examines the effectiveness of a school-based mindfulness intervention on the mental health and social adjustment of Chinese migrant youth compared with an active control condition (psychoeducation). In a randomized controlled trial, Chinese migrant students (mean age=11 years, 75% from low-income families) with relatively high depression and anxiety were randomly assigned to a 16-session mindfulness program or a psychoeducation program. The mindfulness and psychoeducation groups both showed some level of resilience and mental health improvements over time, while the mindfulness intervention showed additional benefits, including social adjustment and particularly for boys. This study identifies the role of mindfulness and resilience in middle-childhood development of a group of Chinese migrant children in a previously unexamined cultural context. The project provides service recommendations for community agencies and schools to help migrant children cope with adversities. The findings also inform resilience building in other vulnerable youth populations in China and beyond.

27614819.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27614819.value: Adaptive instruction is where teachers intentionally adjust curriculum design and classroom instruction based on student needs. As a key indicator of effective teaching, it is positively related to student outcomes (Brühwiler & Blatchford, 2011). Most current studies on enhancing teachers’ professional skills in adaptive teaching rely on formal programmes, with limited success in continuously improving daily instructional practices (Kennedy, 2016). In contrast, there is substantial evidence that spontaneous learning experiences in teachers’ daily lives; that is, informal teacher learning, is crucial to enhancing professional capability and, in turn, the success of adaptive instruction. However, few studies have directly examined the association between informal teacher learning and adaptive instruction. The proposed study thus aims to uncover the impact of different types of informal teacher learning activities on adaptive instruction, thereby enriching knowledge on the types of teacher learning that feed into improved adaptive instruction capability. The proposed study will first identify key categories of informal teacher learning experience, and then develop and test a model of their potential association with and influences on adaptive instruction. A mixed-method approach consisting of two phases will be adopted to achieve the project goals. In Phase 1, a case study of four Hong Kong primary schools involving 24 participants will be undertaken to identify informal teacher learning activities. This data will be used to refine the categories of informal teacher learning experience and the conceptualization the relationship between informal teacher learning and adaptive instruction. The data will also be used to develop an instrument for use in Phase 2. In this phase, a questionnaire related to informal teacher learning and adaptive instruction will be validated and delivered to 500 primary teachers in Hong Kong. Structural equation modelling and bootstrap analysis will then be used to examine the complicated nexus among various informal teacher learning activities and adaptive instruction. Informal teacher learning permeates teachers’ everyday lives and plays a pivotal role in their continual professional development. By identifying key categories of informal teacher learning experience and investigating their relationships with adaptive instruction, this proposed study can provide a theoretical framework to gauge the contributions of different informal teacher learning activities and generate practical guidelines supporting educational programmes and policy-making aimed at effectively facilitating teacher learning and improving the professional performance of teachers. 適應性教學是指教師根據學生需要對課程設計以及課堂教學進行調整。作為有效教學的一個關鍵性指標，適應性教學與學生的學習成果緊密相連。目前研究多利用正式培訓來提升教師開展適應性教學的能力，但收效不盡如人意。相比之下大量數據指出教師日常的學習經驗能夠提升教師專業能力以開展適應性教學，然而目前少有研究探討教師非正式學習和適應性教學之間的關係。因此本項研究致力於揭示不同類型的教師非正式學習行為如何影響教師的適應性教學。本研究將首先對教師非正式學習行為進行分類，進而嘗試建立非正式學習和適應性教學的關係模型。 本研究採用混合研究法來收集數據。在第一階段，本研究將邀請24名來自四所香港以及深圳小學的教師參加訪談，了解他們非正式學習以及適應性教學的情況。這些數據將會被用來分析非正式學習的類型以及初步建立非正式學習和適應性教學的關係。在第二階段，本研究將會根據第一階段的數據形成問卷并邀請700位香港以及深圳教師填寫問卷。本研究將會使用structural equation modelling和 bootstrap analysis來分析教師非正式學習行為和適應性教學之間的關係。 非正式學習充斥在教師日常的教學與生活中，它在教師專業發展過程中扮演重要角色。通過明確教師非正式學習的類型以及探討非正式學習和適應性教學的關係，本研究能夠為討論多元的非正式學習行為提供一個理論框架。與此同時本研究也能夠為教師培訓以及教育政策提供有效建議以更好的提升教師學習的質素以及教師的專業表現。

27614819.label: Realisation of objectives
27614819.value: Objective 1: To identify key categories of informal teacher learning (ITL) activity and the relationships between them We conducted two pilot studies (i.e. one qualitative and one quantitative) to develop, revise and validate the questionnaire on informal teacher learning (ITL). For the qualitative pilot study, we interviewed around 17 teachers to understand their informal learning activities (Huang & Lai, 2020). Thereafter, we used social cognitive theory and learning theories as guides to categorise various activities based on recurrent themes. Accordingly, ITL activities were divided into five categories. Thereafter, we invited two experts in the teacher education field and three frontline teachers to comment on the questionnaire items. The revised questionnaire assessing the five types of ITL was validated through a quantitative pilot study. The developed questionnaire was published by Huang et al. (2020). We collected qualitative data to understand the relationships amongst the different types of ITL. The qualitative data were used as bases to understand the close associations between the different ITL types with teachers’ personal meaningful experiences. The findings were published by Huang and Lai (2020). Objective 2: To develop and test a theoretical model of the effects of different categories of ITL activity on adaptive instruction For the second objective, we developed a model to investigate the effect of each ITL type on adaptive instruction. We invited around 2000 teachers to participate in the survey. We utilised structural equation modelling to examine how various ITL activities are related to adaptive instruction in varying degrees. Moreover, we tested the model across different teacher groups in terms of teaching experience. Differences in the model amongst novice, mid-career and late-career teachers were identified. The findings were published in the highly prestigious journal Metacognition and Learning (Five-year Impact Factor = 4.170) (Huang et al., 2022). We further focused on one type of adaptive instruction, which is teaching for creativity (TfC), and explored its association with ITL. On the basis of structural equation modelling, we found that five types of ITL have differentiated relationships with TfC behaviour. The findings were published in the journal Thinking Skills and Creativity (Impact Factor: 3.652) (Huang, 2021). We focused on another type of adaptive instruction, which is the integration of technology in adaptive instruction, and investigated its relationship with ITL. The findings confirmed the critical role of ITL, particularly teacher reflection, in teachers’ decision-making on technology adoption during adaptive instruction during COVID-19. The findings were published in the leading journal Computers & Education (Impact Factor: 11.182) (Huang et al., 2022). The qualitative data collected in this study enabled us to determine how teachers’ daily learning activities drive their adaptation in classroom teaching. We found that ITL can promote teachers’ can to, reason to and energised to motivations of adaptive instruction. Additionally, ITL can provide teachers with relevant sources for conducting adaptive instruction. The findings were published by Huang and Lai (2020). In summary, aligning with our research proposal, we collected quantitative and qualitative data to address two proposed objectives. Both objectives were answered using substantial data and by conducting solid analysis. The ITL questionnaire was developed, published and cited by other scholars, thereby showing this study’s impact on the teacher learning field. The developed model of ITL and adaptive instruction were presented at AERA conferences and published in prestigious international journals, significantly contributing to the teacher learning field. 1. 27614819.label: Major findings and research outcome
27614819.value: The project has generated substantiated findings in the field of teacher learning, as discussed below. 1. The project grouped various informal teacher learning into five main categories which are learning through media, learning through colleague interaction, learning through stakeholder interaction, learning through student interaction and individual reflection. Among the five types of ITL activities, individual reflection served as a mediator during the relationship between the other four ITL activities and adaptive instruction. Among different teacher groups, we found that senior teachers access more professional literature than novice teachers do. Senior teachers engaged in more student interaction, colleague interaction, and reflection than novice teachers (for detailed results, see Huang et al., 2020). 2. The project confirmed that ITL and adaptive instruction are generally positively related. We also identified different relational patterns between the five types of ITL and adaptive instruction across different career stages. At all three career stages, learning through colleague interaction was significantly and positively associated with teachers’ adaptive teaching. Regarding the other four ITL activities, only learning through student interaction was a strong impetus for novice teachers’ adaptive instruction. This study also found that late-career teachers’ adaptive instruction is more influenced by learning through reflection than novice and mid-career teachers (for detailed results, see Huang, Lin et al., 2022). 3. The project confirmed that ITL is critical to teachers’ adaptive instruction in terms of creative teaching. Four of the five types of ITL activities (not stakeholder interactions) were positively related to process-oriented TfC, and the strongest association was with reflection. Next, four of the five types of IWL (not colleague interactions) were significantly related to product-oriented TfC, and the strongest association was with student interactions (for detailed results, see Huang, 2021). 4. The project confirmed that ITL is vital to teachers’ adaptive instruction in terms of innovative technology adoption intention. Among the five types of ITL activities, learning through reflection and learning through media showed the strongest direct associations with teacher technology integration. No effect of learning through stakeholder interaction was found in this study (for detailed results, see Huang, Lai et al., 2022).

27614819.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27614819.value: The PI is developing a comprehensive ITL model that considers outcomes and antecedents. In this ECS project, the PI examines the critical role of ITL in teachers’ perceptions and behaviour. In the future, the PI will conduct a longitudinal study to examine the impact of ITL on student learning motivation and performance. The questionnaire has been developed, and the first wave of data will be collected in December 2022. The PI will also explore how ITL evolves from the dynamic interaction between teachers and the school context. The PI explored the impact of school climate and psychological capital on ITL. The findings were published in the top-tier journal Teaching and Teacher Education (Huang & Wang, 2021). In the future, the PI will develop a comprehensive ITL model by examining other antecedents of ITL, such as leadership, basic need satisfaction and calling. For the relationship between leadership and ITL, the PI has collected quantitative data and is currently conducting an analysis. Huang, X., & Wang, C. (2021). Factors affecting teachers’ informal workplace learning: The effects of school climate and psychological capital. Teaching and Teacher Education, 103, 363–369. (IF: 3.782) The PI strongly believes that these pioneering studies will lay a solid foundation for future investigation of teachers’ informal learning across various educational contexts.

27614819.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27614819.value: This project is amongst the first to systematically examine informal teacher learning (ITL) activities and their impact on adapting teaching. Different from the qualitative approach adopted by prior research, this study uses a mixed-method design to advance the ITL research beyond the initial stage of documenting various ITL activities towards a markedly critical understanding of the learning potential of these activities. Accordingly, a theoretical model is provided to gauge these activities’ contributions to teachers’ adaptive instruction performance. This study also uncovers the distinct relationship between each ITL activity with adaptive instruction across different career stages. This study develops and validates an ITL questionnaire, thereby enabling researchers, school leaders and policymakers to understand how teachers implement ITL and likewise enabling comparisons across districts or nations. The findings of this study yield valuable implications on how to enhance teacher awareness of ITL and improve teacher capability in managing specific ITL activities. Furthermore, the findings offer practical implications on how to build ITL-friendly schools or community environments that can help teachers transform ITL experiences into effective teaching performance.

27616019.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27616019.value: From the Bauhaus to Black Mountain College, collaboration between dancers and architects was part of an ethos of experimentation that marked some of the 20th century’s most influential cultural moments. In recent decades, research into intersections between dance and architecture has expanded: performance studies, digital media and neurology are fields that have put forward questions. Within architecture, scholars have examined specific collaborative relationships: for example, between the dancers Anna Halprin and Lucinda Childs and the architects Lawrence Halprin and Bernard Tschumi, respectively. While such research documents the mutual influence that dancers and architects have on each other, the practice of collaboration has been little studied. The proposed research investigates the impact that collaboration with dance has on architectural practice. When architects work with dancers, how does this creative exchange take place? How does collaboration between dancers and architects influence the making of architecture? The continued enthusiasm for partnerships between the disciplines would suggest that these questions have established answers, when in fact, they do not. This project tests a method for addressing those questions in order to achieve a qualitatively richer understanding of collaboration’s functioning and impact. Through this understanding, it could also be possible to characterize those collaborative practices that lead to innovations. The research is based on case studies comprising contemporary instances of collaboration between dancers and architects. These case studies will be subject to interviews and the documentation of materials (drawings, texts, videos, etc.) generated during the collaboration. Interviews and documentation will be analysed to identify knowledge, processes and mediating instruments: knowledge through a lexicon of terms debated and defined by participants; working processes through the abstraction and graphic representation of temporal, spatial and personal relations that form a network of dynamics; and mediating instruments through a catalogue that classifies and describes materials generated during the collaboration. Architectural production that post-dates the partnership will be documented and analysed to identify those instances where knowledge, processes and mediating instruments endure to influence the making of architecture. Project findings will be disseminated in conference talks, journal articles and a book-length publication. These outputs will contribute to the diverse critical discourse on architecture and dance, but also to questions of how interdisciplinary exchange generates knowledge, learning and creative production. The research methods and findings ultimately have the potential to impact the way architecture is investigated and taught as a collaborative process. 從包豪斯學院到黑山學院，舞者和建築師之間的合作是20世紀最具影響力的文化實驗精神的一部分。 近幾十年來，對於舞蹈與建築之間的研究越來越多，伸延至表演研究、數據媒體和神經病學等都被列入討論的範圍。 在建築學中，學者們曾經研究舞者與建築師的具體合作關係，如舞者安娜·哈爾普林與露辛達·奇爾茲；以及勞倫斯·哈爾普林和建築師伯納德 ·特斯庫米等。 這些研究雖然記錄了舞者和建築師之間互相影響，但卻對具體合作的實踐方式鮮有研究。 是次研究建議探討與舞者的合作對建築實踐的影響。 當建築師和舞者一起工作時，創作是如何發生的？ 舞者和建築師之間的合作是如何影響建築的設計及製造的？ 兩學科之間緊密的合作關係似乎表明了這些問題已經有確定的答案，但事實上卻並非如此。 該項目嘗試用新的方法去探討這些問題，讓協作的過程和影響能更豐富及全面地被理解；亦希望透過更深入的理解，能歸納創新的協作模式及特性。 這項研究以當代舞者和建築師之間的合作實例為基礎，透過訪談和分析檔案紀錄（如圖紙、文本、視頻等）歸納出協作「知識」、「過程」和「媒介」三方面。 通過與參與者辯論、界定詞彙歸納出「知識」；通過研究表達時間、空間及互動關係的抽像圖譜歸納出「過程」；通過將協作過程中產生的材料分類以描述出「媒介」—— 研究將記錄和分析合作關係的成果，總結出「知識」、「過程」和「媒介」對實踐建築的影響。 項目成果預計將於研討會、學術期刊和書籍中發佈。 它將有助於豐富建築和舞蹈之間的批判性討論，亦有助於理解跨學科交流產生知識、學習和創作的過程。 研究的方法和結果最終有可能影響建築作為一門協作學科的研究和教學方式。

27616019.label: Realisation of objectives
27616019.value: 1. To test a methodology for tracking, describing and categorizing the interactions that comprise collaborations between architecture and dance. The research achieved this objective through the implementation of a multistep method for studying identified collaborations between architects and choreographers. Semi-structured interviews with participants in the collaboration were followed by the transcription and light editing of the interviews. The transcripts were then analyzed using the parameters of language, place, people and time. We looked at language through a process of coding that led to the creation of concordance lists that made it possible to identify how key terms were understood. Information about sites of collaboration described in the interview were represented as a multi-scalar map that charted movements. A constellation chart described people mentioned in their interview and their relation to the trajectory of the collaboration. A graphic timeline made it possible to visualize the temporal cadences of the work. Finally, each interview also resulted in an archive of material related to the collaboration. This archive includes material provided by the collaborating project team, references mentioned during the interviews, and, in some case, external reviews or mentions of the work. For architects, we also collected documentation of work that came after the targeted collaboration. 2. To assess how these collaborations generate new forms of knowledge that contribute to existing discourses. The chosen case-studies fell outside of what we called instrumental modes of working together in which architects are called up to fulfil a largely pre-given task, or choreographers are asked to perform a traditional role within an already given architectural context. Instead, the case-studies were open-ended about the exact nature of the outcome, and instead motivated by a general desire to work together. The case studies ranged from architects and dancers who are highly regarded in their field, to others who are just beginning to establish an identity. Nevertheless, in nearly every case, the “open-endedness” of the collaboration allowed for a play of ideas and processes that contributed an expanded set of issues within architectural discourse. Taking place over the period between 2010 and 2019, the chosen case studies address issues that are increasingly important for architecture discourse including: the non-human, aging and care (Anchises), participation (Punt Point), embodiment (Sea Sea), queering and decolonizing space (Brasilia), gender and public space (Corpo Estraneo) and the material agency of objects (Vague Intérieur Vague). The research suggests that in each instance, the collaboration made possible ways of addressing these issues that would not have been possible through architecture alone. 3. To analyse ways in which architects and dancers structure the work of collaboration in terms of patterns of communication, distribution of time and tasks and spaces of work. This work took place through the method described in “Objective 1”. While no “patterns” appeared as such, what became legible through the analysis were the affective bonds that were necessary to ensure that exchanges could function in a productive way. I theorize these bonds as an infrastructure that underlies collaboration. It comprises: a capacity to trust that makes disagreement and frank exchange possible; a mutual respect that allows for the carving out of zones of expertise and competence; and an ethic of care that puts a concern for the quality and health of the relationship alongside a concern for the work. 4. To assess how architects and dancers use and generate instruments -- drawings, diagrams, models, writing, video-recording -- to develop ideas and communicate during a collaborative process. The interviews and the archive mentioned in Objective 1 made it possible to assess the role of these various instruments. While each collaborative pair worked in different ways, mediating instruments served three important roles. First, they were critical as part of a process of play in which media were used irrespective of which partner may have more disciplinary ease with that material’s manipulation. Second, was a dialogical role, in which instruments became shared supports for the exchange and development of ideas. Third, was a technical phase in which the partners worked within their disciplinary competences to create instruments necessary for the fabrication and finalization of a collaborative work. For example, architectural plans or a movement score. In these technical documents, partners trusted in the other’s competence to complete and verify such instruments. 5. To bring into focus how architects adopt the knowledge, processes or instruments generated through collaborations with dance into their own architectural practice and whether these appropriations go on to have a lasting impact on their architecture. The project was able to identify the integration of knowledge, processes and instruments into architectural work that followed the targeted collaboration. There were at least three levels in which this integration took place. First, particularly in situations where one partner had more experience that the other, the collaboration offered an important model for working quasi-independently that helped practitioners to develop their own practice afterwards. Second, working processes introduced within the collaboration, were carried forward by architects into their own practice. For example, play, improvisation, and the temporal scripting of a work, were identified as “lessons” that architects took from dance and tested out later in their work. More generally, the “open-ended” nature of the collaborations was translated into an attitude toward making and fabrication, so that and ad-hoc, experimental tectonics would come to characterize architectural production. Third, as mentioned in the section on “Objective 2”, the collaborations opened architects to issues that were otherwise not a part of their disciplinary understanding. These issues -- for example aging and the non-human for one collaboration -- would go one to be central to themes for the architects concerned and would influence the direction of their careers. 6.To develop a process-oriented interdisciplinary methodology that brings together the conceptual knowledge of architecture, the technical skills of the design studio, and the experimental practices of the rehearsal room. This objective was achieved despite the constraints created by the pandemic and limitations on in person teaching. Over the course of three years, we developed a collaboration with teachers and students in the contemporary dance department at the Hong Kong Academy of Performing Arts. In the first year, this comprised presentations about distinctions between ways of creative making in architecture and dance. Architecture students were introduced to choreographic exercises in an afternoon long workshop that they introduced into a participatory design process. In year two, the collaboration involved students from both institutions. Teams of architects and dancers worked with film to create works of movement for given sites throughout the city. The experience helped to inform design processes, site briefs, and the spatial articulation of the final architectural project. In year three, the collaboration was further expanded with a month-long working together. Student teams comprising one architect and one or two dancers worked together to “read” a common site through movement that was documented through film. Choreographic practices including improvisation and scoring, along with choreographic devices such as accumulation, embellishment, and force became tools for architectural design that informed a final project.

27616019.label: Major findings and research outcome
27616019.value: The findings of the research coalesce around an expanded field of issues that characterize collaboration. This field reflects and comprises changes taking place in the two disciplines and in their expectations for working together. Where earlier forms of collaboration privileged autonomy, disciplinary knowledge, and an instrumental relationship aimed toward an objective goal (a physical intervention for the stage), architects and dancers today also work together in ways that privilege process-oriented explorations that begin with open-ended expectations and a willingness to devote time to indeterminate contingent forms of knowledge. I argue that this expanding understanding of working together can change how we think about architecture’s potential impact on human environments and describe it as a collaborative infrastructure. Infrastructure describes both the logistical and affective underpinnings of relations that sustain a prolonged engagement with a collaborative partner, site, community or object of study. As a structuring of movement, infrastructure replaces fixed conceptions of roles, expertise, or objectives, by foregrounding exchange, mediation and support. These ideas developed through published and in process articles and chapter contributions. In “When Zoom Roomed the World” (Global Performance Studies) a study of the impact of tele-conferencing technologies on collaboration, I was able to develop an understanding of the affective bonds that underly collaborative engagements. In “Notes on Architecture and Collaboration” (chapter contribution to Embodied Practice in Art Making, Intellect Press), I articulate a way of thinking about collaboration that foregrounds the relations of empathy and trust that make the infrastructural movement of thought between partners possible. I developed ideas about infrastructure, drawing from the work of critical geographer Doreen Massey, in relation to movement and architecture in an accepted article for Manifest Journal and in an under peer-review article for Future Anterior. Conference interventions that contributed to the articulation of the research include: “Architectural de-placing (Transgression—A new paradigm, European Architectural History Network Thematic Conference, ENSA Bretagne, Zoom); “Collaborative Workings” (Artistic Research Working Group, Performance Studies International Annual Conference, Zoom); and “Walking as infrastructural practice / or a practice of infrastructure” (Dancing Resilience, Dance Studies Association, In-person). A synthesis of the research, Collaborative Infrastructures: Movements through architecture and dance, is currently in draft form, with a proposal ready to send to publishers. The book situates the case studies that comprise the research within the theoretical framework of “collaborative infrastructures”. Drawing from writings across dance, architecture, the humanities and social sciences, the book offers a new way of thinking both about architecture’s relation to dance and about how collaboration can expand architecture’s agency. Material for the book can be found at the following link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/12nykjC0AZLB57MJZaHKaKLN40WGM-iXf/view?usp=drive_link

27616019.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27616019.value: The project established important links between the Department of Architecture at the University of Hong Kong and the dance department at the Hong Kong Academy of Performing Arts. These institutional links involved multiple people from each institution and have been set up to continue despite the PI’s departure from Hong Kong. Future collaborations between students from the two institutions, already planned for the fall of 2023, will continue to test methods that bring dance and architecture together as a design tool. Over the course of the project, and in his collaborations with HKAPA, the PI also began a dance practice that shaped observations within the research. He will continue to develop this practice as an interdisciplinary method for spatial perception and the making of creative form that can be implemented in the analysis and design of the public realm, building on historical precedents. More broadly, the PI will continue to pursue the notion of “collaborative infrastructures” outside of the context of architecture’s relation to dance, to identify and propose ways of working together with different types of clients – individuals, institutions, and communities – that foreground longer-term relationships and open-ended processes that address ill-defined problems.

27616019.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27616019.value: Architecture and dance have sometimes been described as two opposite creative forms: the former dealing with the putting together of an enduring, stable realm and the second existing in the instant as a fleeting experience. Nevertheless collaborations between architects and dancers have been a rich source of inquiry since at least the modern movement, the two disciplines coming together to consider time, space and the body – issues where overlaps would seem to enliven our understanding of both creative practices. The project looks at contemporary collaborations between dancers and architects to move beyond traditional understandings of the productivity of these partnerships. Through interviews with six collaborations from practitioners at various points in their career, the project looked at architects and dancers who work together in open-ended processes with sometimes ill-defined objectives. The contingent nature of these partnerships is sustained by affective bonds that allow for doubt, while trust and mutual respect sustain a work together as a collaborative infrastructure that makes innovative insights in creative form possible. The project proposes that through the development of “collaborative infrastructures” architecture can engage with communities and clients to address the complex, ill-defined issues that pose challenges to the built environment in an age of uncertainty.
