28604519.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28604519.value: Twenty years after its 1997 handover back to China Hong Kong remains a unique place on the world’s stage. British colonialism has left many enduring marks on Hong Kong identity as well as on its physical landscape. One of the most peculiar, and controversial, is the legacy of the Small House Policy of the New Territories; an agreement reached between the British and the village leaders after it leased the New Territories in 1898. In a city of severe land scarcity, this unusual law grants decedents of ‘original villager’s’ families (mainly Hakka people), upon their 18 birthday, rights to build a maximum three story house of no more than 2100 sqft. With skyrocketing housing prices downtown this has created a boom of these ‘village houses’ being build and sold, mainly to ‘new villagers’ migrating from the city, on lands that once were Hong Kong’s farms and rice paddies. This has led to rapid changes in the visuality of these once traditional villages. The most notable visual change among these communities is the disappearance of traditional Hakka ancestral family homes, which are now scattered throughout a maze of stylistically unrelated modern village houses. The vanishing of these unique homes continues at rapid pace and since commencement of a pilot study in the spring of 2018 at least half a dozen additional ancestral homes, some dating back over a century, have been demolished during the summer. This makes the study of these traditional homes, their visual culture, and how they once formed the backbones of these villages all the more urgent. In order to do so this visually driven study employs both audio and visual methods to seek a more in-depth picture of current village life in North Eastern New Territories, Hong Kong by observing, documenting, collaboratively creating, and jointly analysing the multimedia data captured. This study documents the derelict, intact, restored, in ruin ancestral structures, attempting to trace revitalized elements of traditional Hakka villages via their design, layouts, and relationship with the natural environment. The study looks at how the making and sharing of imagery can foster dialogue and analyse the current state of flux of these villages and their lands to reconsider the ‘place’ they occupy how these changes may affect visual cultural identity and connections with the past. 在香港的“香港”被殖民之前，這些土地由客家人定居，他們在珠江三角洲盡頭不確定地逃脫並開始了新的生活。他們主要在現在被稱為“新界”的地區定居。隨著殖民地隨著移民潮的不斷增長，香港的房屋在壓力下緊張，導致騷亂和騷亂。政府期待新界提供發展和建設新城鎮的空間。一百二十年後，英國殖民主義在香港的身份及其自然景觀上留下了許多持久的印記。其中一個最奇特且最有爭議的是“小房子政策”的遺產。與香港和九龍不同，新界是租賃而非割讓，由於直接管理土地使用的雙重政策，香港的發展情況大為不同。小房子政策被視為對村民放棄發展的祖傳土地的補償。這項政策授予“原始村民”家庭的死者，建造一棟不超過2100平方英尺的三層樓房的權利。隨著市中心房價暴漲，這些“村屋”的建設和銷售蓬勃發展，許多人成為家園“新村民”從這座城市遷徙到幾個世紀以來一直是農業和漁村的土地，曾經一度為香港提供食物。這為村民擺脫貧困提供了新的機會，但也導致了這些曾經傳統的村莊的視覺形象的迅速變化。最值得注意的是傳統客家祖屋的消失。祖先的土地和傳統的祖先住宅已經商品化，以換取經濟優勢和社會收益。通過這些簡陋住宅的外牆和入口，我們目睹了過去兩個世紀的緊張局勢，政治，文化，商業和追踪。

28604519.label: Realisation of objectives
28604519.value: 1. Comprehensive Audio-Visual Documentation and Archival Materials The study employed image-based methods to capture a detailed and high-quality documentation of the current state of villages and village life in North Eastern New Territories, Hong Kong. This included photographing and filming the derelict, intact, restored, and ruined structures of traditional Hakka villages, their design layouts, and their relationships with the natural environment. The research documented the visual cultural elements still present, such as architectural styles, and used these visual representations to foster dialogue and analysis about the villages' current states. This comprehensive documentation served as a vital archival material, preserving the visual and cultural heritage of these villages. 2. Identifying Significant Issues and Changes in Visuality and Local Culture The research identified significant issues facing the communities by engaging directly with the villagers through interviews and image elicitation methods. Villagers were asked about the most pressing challenges they faced, particularly regarding the preservation of ancestral homes and other forms of Hakka visual culture. The study found that many traditional homes were being demolished to make way for modern constructions, leading to the disappearance of unique architectural and cultural motifs. The feedback from villagers highlighted concerns about the loss of cultural heritage and the impact of new developments on their sense of community and identity. 3. Exploring Visual and Sensory Methodologies The study contributed to the burgeoning field of visual and sensory methodologies by employing innovative methods like image elicitation and collaborative visual documentation. Participants were involved in the production and analysis of visual data, making them active contributors to the research. This approach allowed for a deeper exploration of how visual culture influences identity and community issues. The use of high-resolution images and drone footage provided new ways of understanding and documenting the changing landscape and cultural heritage of the villages. 4. Educational Framework for Community and Formal Education The comprehensive documentation and the findings from the study provided valuable data that could be used for educational purposes. The research highlighted the importance of preserving traditional and changing ways of life through alternative forms of knowing, such as sensory (audio-visual) methods. The visual materials and the insights gained from the study can be used to develop educational programs and materials for both the community and formal education systems, helping to raise awareness about the cultural heritage and the challenges facing these villages. 5. Providing a Platform for Villagers to Share Their Stories The study provided opportunities for villagers to share their stories and voice their opinions on the challenges and issues facing their communities. By involving villagers in the documentation process and using image elicitation techniques, the research gave them a platform to express their perspectives and concerns. The visual exhibition created as part of the study allowed villagers to engage with the visual materials, share their reactions, and contribute their own stories and memories. This collaborative approach helped to amplify the voices of the villagers and fostered a sense of ownership and participation in the research. 6. Informing Educational and Governmental Policies The detailed analyses from the study provided insights that could inform educational and governmental policies on historical and small community ways of life. The research highlighted the impact of development in the green belt and country park village areas, emphasizing the need for policies that balance development with the preservation of cultural heritage. The findings suggested the importance of involving local communities in decision-making processes and recognizing the value of traditional cultural practices and architectural styles. The study's recommendations aimed to address the issues of development while preserving the unique cultural identity of the Hakka villages. Summary "No Heritage Found on Map: The Vanishing Villages of Hong Kong" successfully achieved its objectives by employing a comprehensive and innovative approach to documenting and analyzing the visual cultural heritage of the Hakka villages in the NE New Territories. Through detailed visual documentation, engagement with villagers, and the use of sensory methodologies, the study provided valuable insights into the challenges facing these communities and highlighted the importance of preserving their cultural heritage. The findings and materials generated from this research offer a rich resource for educational purposes and policy development, aiming to support the preservation and revitalization of these unique cultural landscapes.

28604519.label: Major findings and research outcome
28604519.value: "No Heritage Found on Map: The Vanishing Villages of Hong Kong" highlights the urgent need to document and preserve the traditional Hakka villages in Hong Kong. The study's comprehensive visual methodology and direct engagement with villagers provide a rich archive of cultural heritage and offer valuable insights for educational and policy-making efforts aimed at preserving these unique cultural landscapes amidst rapid urbanization. The major findings were: 1. Disappearance and Transformation of Traditional Villages: The research reveals that traditional Hakka villages are either disappearing or undergoing significant transformations. Many ancestral homes and village structures, characterized by unique architectural styles and cultural motifs, are being demolished to make way for modern developments. This transformation is leading to the erosion of the physical and cultural landscape that has historically defined these communities. 2. Cultural and Visual Heritage: The study emphasizes the importance of traditional Hakka architectural elements, such as specific design layouts, decorations, and construction materials, which are integral to the villagers' identity and heritage. The comprehensive visual documentation, including photographs and videos, captures these elements, providing a valuable archive for future generations and emphasizing the need for their preservation. 3. Community Concerns and Identity: Interviews and image elicitation with villagers highlight their concerns about losing their cultural heritage and sense of community. Many villagers express a sense of displacement and a loss of identity as their ancestral homes are replaced by modern structures. The visual documentation serves as a platform for villagers to voice their concerns and share their stories, thus preserving their cultural narratives. 4. Impact of Urban Development: The construction of the Plover Cove Reservoir, the building of Ting Kok Road, and the land reclamation in Taipo, along with the establishment of the industrial estate, brought about profound changes and challenges to these communities. These developments led to the loss of farmland, traditional homes, and communal spaces, disrupting the cultural and social fabric of the villages.. 5. Educational and Policy Implications: The findings underscore the need for educational programs and policies that recognize and preserve the cultural heritage of these villages. The study provides a framework for using the visual and sensory data collected to develop educational materials that can raise awareness about traditional Hakka culture and the challenges it faces. Moreover, the research suggests that government policies should involve local communities in decision-making processes to ensure that development is balanced with the preservation of cultural heritage.

28604519.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28604519.value: The study on the vanishing Hakka villages of Hong Kong sets a foundational basis for further development in several key areas. Future research can delve deeper into comparative studies between the preservation efforts of Hakka villages in Hong Kong and those in other regions, such as Mainland China or Taiwan, to identify best practices and innovative preservation strategies. Expanding the scope to include digital heritage initiatives, like virtual reality (VR) reconstructions of the villages, could offer immersive educational tools and promote global awareness. To effectively implement the proposed course of action, a multi-faceted approach is recommended: Policy Advocacy: Engage with policymakers to advocate for stronger heritage conservation laws that integrate local community input and prioritize cultural preservation alongside development. Community Engagement: Foster active participation from villagers in preservation projects, ensuring their voices and needs are central to conservation efforts. Educational Programs: Develop comprehensive educational materials and curricula based on the documented visual and sensory data, aimed at both local schools and international platforms to raise awareness and appreciation of Hakka heritage. Collaborative Projects: Partner with universities, NGOs, and cultural organizations to fund and support ongoing research and preservation initiatives.

28604519.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28604519.value: This research project looks at the Hakka villages in Hong Kong, which are quickly disappearing. I recorded these villages with photos and audio to capture their unique culture, traditional buildings, and community life. The research is important because it helps preserve the history and traditions of the Hakka people, which are a key part of Hong Kong's cultural diversity. By creating these recordings, I ensure that future generations can learn about and appreciate their heritage. The project is valuable for several reasons. It provides visual and interview data that could be used to create educational materials for schools and the community, helps villagers share their stories and concerns, and offers information that can guide policies to protect these historical areas while allowing for modern development. In short, this project helps keep the culture and traditions of Hong Kong’s Hakka villages alive, making sure their stories are not forgotten.

28606419.label: Realisation of objectives
28606419.value: We not only reached but also went above and beyond all three objectives we set out to achieve, showing great progress and success in our endeavors. Our first objective was to examine the neural mechanisms associated with how Chinese children learn the intricate patterns present in Chinese characters. To accomplish this, we have the participation of 164 primary school children in study. These young participants engaged in a series of behavioral assessments and event-related potential (ERP) experiments to elucidate the neural signatures underlying their statistical learning processes. The ERP analysis unveiled a complex, multi-component system that underpins children's acquisition of orthographic regularities. Specifically, our findings highlighted three distinct ERP components - the P1, N170, and P300 components - which, in conjunction with reaction times, provided valuable insights into the cognitive processes involved in the statistical learning of orthographic regularities among Chinese children. The N170 component, for instance, appeared to signify the extraction and encoding of orthographic patterns within the occipitotemporal brain region, accompanied by neural adaptation. On the other hand, the P1 and P300 components were associated with various cognitive mechanisms that play a role in the statistical learning process. Furthermore, an additional ERP experiment focusing on orthographic-semantic connections shed light on a distinctive P1-N1-P300-N400 pattern characterizing the statistical learning of orthographic-semantic associations. Here, the P1 and N170 components in the occipitotemporal region seemed to represent initial attentional modulation and orthographic identification during the early stages of learning, while the P300 and N400 components were indicative of attentional allocation and semantic activation in the later stages of online statistical learning. Our second objective was to investigate how the ability of Chinese children to learn patterns in Chinese characters changes as they grow older, both in terms of behavior and brain activity, over a three-year period spanning from first grade to third grade. To broaden our scope, we extended this objective by including data from kindergarten to primary five students and tracking one grade for two years. In total, 119 children from a kindergarten and 164 children from a primary school were recruited in this study. We analyzed the developmental changes by fitting three different models to the accuracy rates of each age group across various consistency levels using a power function equation. This equation helped us predict accuracy rates based on a coefficient (k) and an exponent (n). Additionally, we used linear models to compare mean accuracy rates across age groups at different consistency levels. Our findings indicated that: (1) learning orthographic patterns is influenced by age, suggesting the presence of a critical period; (2) there is a critical period for statistical learning between ages 4 to 6 during early childhood; and (3) there is non-linear growth in pattern acquisition from kindergarten through primary school. In addition to behavioral data, we also collected 164 children's brain activity data (ERP data). The analysis of the ERP data further confirmed the behavioural models, showing that statistical learning of orthographic regularities is age-related. Our third objective was to investigate how early brain activities related to learning patterns in Chinese characters could predict children's later understanding of characters and reading abilities. Through correlational analyses, we discovered interesting relationships among different age groups in primary school: (1) for first graders, there was a negative link between Chinese character reading scores and differences in P300 brain activity between low and moderate consistency levels in the right hemisphere of the temporal area; (2) second and third graders showed positive connections between Chinese character reading scores and differences in N170 brain activity between various consistency levels in the left hemisphere of the temporal area; and (3) interestingly, fifth graders exhibited negative associations between Chinese character reading scores and N170 brain activity differences across different consistency levels in the right occipitotemporal area. These results highlighted a significant relationship between N170 brain activity patterns during statistical learning of orthographic regularities and Chinese character reading abilities. Furthermore, we categorized our participants into poor readers, average readers, and skilled readers based on their reading performance in a character reading task. We observed that poor readers demonstrated heightened N170 responses in the left occipitotemporal area and struggled more with learning low-level positional consistency compared to children without reading difficulties. Additionally, poor readers displayed a deficiency in the left-lateralized P300 brain response compared to average and skilled readers. When it came to learning orthographic-semantic connections, both poor and average readers exhibited similar brain activation patterns, showing increased N400 brain activity for moderate- and low-consistency levels compared to high-consistency levels. These findings provide valuable insights into the neural markers and potential brain mechanisms involved in learning different types of orthographic patterns in children facing reading challenges.

28606419.label: Major findings and research outcome
28606419.value: When it comes to how our brains learn patterns of Chinese orthography, we found a few important things. First, our study revealed that there are different parts of the brain involved in learning these spelling patterns (Tong et al., 2020a,2020b, 2021). Additionally, we observed that different types of orthographic patterns are associated with both similar and unique brain signals (Duan et al., under review; Tong et al., 2020a,2020b, 2021). These results give us a better understanding of how our brains process and learn written language patterns. In terms of developmental trajectories in statistical learning of orthographic regularities, the acquisition of orthographic patterns demonstrates a sensitivity to age, implying the existence of a distinct critical period (Duan et al., under review; Tong et al., 2023). Our behavioral data showed a critical developmental phase for distributional statistical learning spanning the ages of 4 to 6 during the early stages of childhood (Duan et al., under review). A power function model analysis has revealed a non-linear growth pattern in the acquisition of regularities from the initial stages of schooling through childhood development, highlighting the complex nature of this cognitive process across different developmental stages (Duan et al., under review). Our study further revealed positive correlations between Chinese word reading ability and neural distinctions triggered by the statistical learning of different orthographic regularities. Additionally, our findings indicated that individuals with poor reading skills demonstrated lower proficiency in utilizing statistical learning mechanisms to grasp orthographic patterns in Chinese compared to those classified as average or good readers (Duan & Tong, second revision). The findings from our project have been presented at various conferences, allowing us to engage with scholars both locally and internationally. Additionally, we have published several academic papers and have submitted others to reputable journals (please refer to the list for details). Moving forward, we are excited about the prospect of generating additional research papers based on the extensive dataset we have gathered. These upcoming publications will delve deeper into our findings, contributing to the academic discourse and potentially opening up new avenues for further exploration and discovery.

28606419.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28606419.value: In an effort to further elucidate the neural mechanisms that underlie the statistical learning of Chinese orthographic regularities, which have profound implications for the advancement of theories related to language acquisition, our research team established a collaborative partnership with Dr. Lv Yating, an expert with neuroimaging research, from Hangzhou Normal University. Together, we used cutting-edge fMRI technology to explore the brain regions associated with the acquisition of Chinese orthographic patterns. Through this collaborative research initiative, we endeavored to not only expand our understanding of the neural substrates of statistical learning but also to make significant contributions to the broader field of language acquisition research. By forging synergies between our respective academic institutions and leveraging the latest advancements in neuroimaging technology, we aimed to pave the way for groundbreaking discoveries that would shape the future of cognitive neuroscience and linguistic studies. We have successfully collected fMRI data from a group of 30 participants by conducting experiments tailored specifically for our ongoing project. Once the data collection phase was completed, we analyzed the results of one of the experiments. Looking ahead, we are enthusiastic about the potential for additional publications stemming from the wealth of data we have gathered. The insights from our participants' fMRI data present a valuable opportunity to deepen our understanding of the complex neural processes involved in language acquisition and cognitive functions. As we continue to explore and interpret our dataset, we are eager to make further contributions to the field of neuroimaging and advance the collective knowledge base in brain research.

28606419.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28606419.value: It's fascinating to see how children pick up language patterns, like understanding how to learn spelling patterns in a language. This learning process includes remembering particular spelling patterns in their minds. This project explored how the brain activities linked to this learning, and how this learning process developed over time as well as the association between brain activities and their performance in spelling related task and word reading. Our study focused on exploring the importance of statistical learning (identifying patterns based on statistical information found in language, like how often words appear) and the underlying neural mechanisms in how Chinese-speaking children learn spelling patterns. Our study found that different neural activities are involved in learning spelling patterns. Children of different ages showed varying abilities in using patterns to spell words, and this skill was linked to how well they could read. Children who struggled with reading had more difficulty learning these patterns compared to those who were better readers. These results help us understand how children learn to spell in Chinese and how their brains are involved in this process. They give us valuable insights into how learning patterns and brain processes work together when acquiring language skills.

28607119.label: Realisation of objectives
28607119.value: The project has achieved four objectives listed in Section 5.1. In particular, we have examined age-related differences in the association between solitude and well-being using an experimental design in Study 1 (Objective 1), and clarified the influence of older adults’ preference on low arousal positive over high arousal positive affect (Study 2), conflict de-escalation goals (Study 3), and prioritization over close vs peripheral partners (Study 4) on age-related differences in well-being in solitude. Objective 1:After piloting materials from 20 younger adults, we recruited 207 participants (Younger sample: n = 112, Mage = 21.83 years, SDage = 2.39 years; 78% female; Older sample: n = 95, Mage = 68.28 years, SDage = 4.67 years; 71% female). Participants were recruited by sending mass mails and advertisements to universities and community centers. The older participants were required to be aged 60 years and above, and the younger participants were required to be aged 18 to 30 years. All participants were required to be able to read and write, and they did not have any self-reported psychiatric symptoms or cognitive impairment. No participants were excluded from data analyses. Using the affect valuation index, hypothesis, we found that older adults reported better affective well-being in solitude than younger adults using an experimental design. This is the first instance where the causal effects of solitude on emotional well-being have been observed among both older and younger adults. We have published these findings as Study 1 in the paper entitled “Older Adults Experience Better Affective Well-being in Solitude: The Moderating Role of Goal for Conflict De-Escalation” published in Applied Psychology: Health and Well-being. Objective 2. We conducted Study 2 to test Objective 2. This study aimed at examining whether experimentally manipulating valuing Low Arousal Positive (LAP) affect over High Arousal Positive (HAP) affect can diminish age differences in well-being in solitude. In this sample, there were 74 younger and 37 older adults; age range: 19—78 years, Mage = 37.41 years, SD = 22.24 years; 70% females). All participants were recruited by posting ad of the study on the mass mailing system of the Education University of Hong Kong. Young participants aged 19-33 years (Mage = 21.89 years, SDage = 2.50 years; 73% females). Older adults aged 61—78 years (Mage = 68.43 years, SDage = 3.80 years; 68% females). With HAP as DV, there was a significant main effect of age (F = 13.12, p < 0.01) that older adults significantly reported a higher level of HAP (M = 2.85, SD = 0.89) than did younger adults (M = 1.97, SD = 0.98). There was a significant main effect of solitude condition (F = 4.36, p = 0.42) that individuals in the solitude condition significantly reported a lower level of HAP (M = 2.16, SD = 1.00) than did those who were in the social interaction condition (M = 3.06, SD = 0.77). The two-way Solitude X Age interaction was marginally significant, (F = 3.72, p = 0.60). With LAP as DV, there was a significant main effect of age (F = 20.74, p < 0.01) that older adults significantly reported a higher level of LAP (M = 4.10, SD = 0.62) than did younger adults (M = 3.78, SD = 0.68). There was a significant main effect of solitude condition (F = 6.38, p < 0.01) that individuals in the solitude condition significantly reported a lower level of LAP (M = 3.54, SD = 0.70) than did those who were in the social interaction condition (M = 4.27, SD = 0.53). The two-way Solitude X Age interaction was not significant, (F = 0.44, p = 0.84), suggesting that age differences in LAP did not differ across solitude conditions. Contradictory to our hypothesis, ideal affect could not explain age-related differences in well-being in solitude. Objective 3. In Study 3, we experimentally manipulated conflict goals (escalation vs. de-escalation) and investigated whether this manipulation could eliminate age-related differences in links between solitude and affective well-being. We recruited 128 participants, including 64 younger adults aged 18-30 years (Mage = 22.05 years, SDage = 2.92 years; 70% female) and 64 older adults aged 60-80 years (Mage = 67.31 years, SDage = 4.44 years; 75% female). The findings supported out hypotheses, older participants reported more high arousal positive affect in the solitude condition than their younger counterparts when primed for conflict escalation. This age-related difference in HAP during solitude was not significant when participants were primed to de-escalate their conflicts. These findings suggest that older adults may have better affective well-being in solitude (relative to social interactions) than do younger adults because solitude allows them to de-escalate conflicts. When both younger and older adults are primed to de-escalate conflicts, the age differences in affective well-being in solitude (vs. social interactions) disappear. The hypothesized results have been supported in Study 3. We have published these findings as Study 2 in the paper entitled “Older Adults Experience Better Affective Well-being in Solitude: The Moderating Role of Goal for Conflict De-Escalation” published in Applied Psychology: Health and Well-being. The findings have also been presented as a keynote presentation in the annual meeting of Division of Cultural Psychology, Chinese Psychological Association in October 2024. Objective 4. Study 4 aims at testing whether age-related differences in well-being in solitude would be moderated by age-related preference for close vs. peripheral social partners. We recruited 134 participants, including 64 younger adults aged 18-30 years (Mage = 23.05 years, SDage = 2.96 years; 65% female) and 70 older adults aged 60-82 years (Mage = 68.76 years, SDage = 4.69 years; 79% female). Although the manipulation check was significant and consistent with the hypothesized direction. Similar to the previous studies, we found a robust age-related differences in well-being in solitude that older adults reported more positive affect (M = 3.85, SD = 0.79) and lower negative affect (M = 1.57, SD = 0.82) in solitude, compared to their younger counterparts (Positive affect: M = 3.17, SD = 0.62; Negative affect: M = 2.09, SD = 0.70). However, these age-related differences were not moderated by the condition of preference on social partners. Thus, we speculate that the preference on close vs peripheral social partners may not explain age-related differences in well-being in solitude. Challenges Encountered During the Project Period. The project commenced in January 2020, coinciding with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. We faced significant challenges in recruiting participants, particularly due to the requirement for interactions with unfamiliar social partners, especially for those involved in the social interaction condition. The project team made extensive efforts to recruit participants and collect data during this period. However, the difficulties in participant recruitment, coupled with the campus lockdowns during the pandemic, led to substantial delays in project progress. We would like to express our gratitude to the University and the RGC for their understanding and support in extending the project timeline. This extension has allowed us to achieve a range of valuable deliverables.

28607119.label: Major findings and research outcome
28607119.value: In this project, we developed a framework to explain age-related differences in well-being in solitude and empirically tested three proposed moderators, namely the preference for low-arousal over high-arousal positive affect, conflict de-escalation vs. escalation goals, and preferences on close vs. peripheral social partners. We found that older (vs. younger) adults reported more positive affect overall. This age-related difference was greater in the solitude (vs. social interaction) condition . Older adults reported less negative affect than younger adults in the solitude, but not the social interaction, condition. In addition, older (vs. younger) participants reported more high arousal positive affect in the solitude condition when they had been primed with the goal of conflict escalation. This difference was not significant when participants were primed to de-escalate their conflicts. The findings replicated age-related differences in affective well-being in solitude using an experimental design and provided causal evidence of the role of conflict de-escalation goals. We have delivered these findings to the public through three journal articles and two conference presentations. These findings were published in top-tier peer-refereed international journals in psychology, such as Applied Psychology: Health and Well-being and Journal of Personality. They were also presented at international and regional conferences, including the 18th European Congress of Psychology and the annual meeting of the Chinese Psychological Association (Division of Cultural Psychology). In particular, the presentation at the annual meeting of the Chinese Psychological Association (Division of Cultural Psychology) was a keynote speech.

28607119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28607119.value: Firstly, previous research on age-related differences in affective well-being in solitude has been limited to correlational designs (e.g., experience sampling) in which solitude was not manipulated. Our study addresses this gap by employing a more rigorous experimental design, which allows for direct tests of the causal relationship between solitude and affective well-being in adult lifespan samples. Future research can adopt this experimental paradigm. Secoondly, our findings highlight the importance of understanding age-related differences in affective well-being in solitude (the absence of social interaction). In Study 2, we tested the role of conflict de-escalation, an important and emotionally meaningful goal, in age-related affective well-being in solitude (vs. social interaction). These findings have the potential to be developed to interventions to improve well-being in solitude across the adult lifespan. In addition, From a practical standpoint, these findings have significant implications for care services among older adults, as they offer empirically based guidance on factors that may mitigate the adverse effects of social isolation.

28607119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28607119.value: Older adults generally reported feeling more positive emotions than younger adults, especially when they were alone rather than in social situations. In solitary settings, older adults also experienced fewer negative emotions compared to younger adults, but this difference didn’t hold true during social interactions. These findings suggest that older and younger adults have different goals when it comes to handling conflicts. Specifically, older adults felt more energetic and positive emotions when they were alone and focused on escalating conflicts. However, this difference disappeared when they were encouraged to reduce conflicts instead.

28609019.label: Realisation of objectives
28609019.value: The first objective was to assess the developmental trajectories and outcomes of critical consciousness among sexual minority youth. Over a three-year period, the team followed up with a group of sexual minority youth and conducted longitudinal assessments to track their development. They were asked to complete a questionnaire at baseline (T0), after 12 months (T1), 24 months (T2), and 36 months (T3). The use of longitudinal data can elucidate the directionality of the associations between variables and overcome limitations of previous cross-sectional studies. The prospective research design and longitudinal analysis account for the temporal ordering of variables in naturalistic conditions and provide a more precise estimation of hypothesized effects. The study design significantly contributes to understanding how early exposure to critical consciousness influences later developmental processes and outcomes in life. In 2020, a total of 1,457 sexual minority people consented to participate in the baseline survey (T0). Due to the outbreak of COVID-19 pandemic, data collection primarily took place online from May to August 2020. Participants were recruited through LGBTQ+ community organizations, listservs, and social media in Hong Kong. The eligibility criteria included (1) being 16 years or above, (2) self-identifying as gay, lesbian, bisexual, or non-heterosexual, (3) having a gender identity consistent with their sex assigned at birth, (4) residing in Hong Kong, and (5) having the ability to read and understand Chinese. Interested individuals were directed to an online survey platform where they completed a questionnaire on critical consciousness, identity-salient experiences, identity affirmation, psychological wellness, and social integration. The sample included 740 sexual minority youth aged 16-25, which has far exceeded the baseline target stated in the research proposal (n = 370). In 2021, a 12-month follow-up (T1) survey was administered to sexual minority individuals who completed the baseline survey (T0). A total of 343 sexual minority youth responded to T1 survey. The sample size exceeded the T1 target stated in research proposal (n = 315). In 2022, a 24-month follow-up (T2) survey was conducted, with 294 sexual minority youth responding. The sample size exceeded the T2 target (n = 267). In 2023, a 36-month follow-up (T3) survey was administered to the same group of participants. Approximately 255 sexual minority youth responded to T3 survey, which exceeded the T3 target (n = 227). Thus, the first project objective regarding the assessment of the longitudinal trajectories of sexual minority youth has been successfully achieved. While the project primarily focuses on critical consciousness and positive development among sexual minority youth, the COVID-19 pandemic significantly impacted the world, including the lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) community in 2020. We responded to the pandemic quickly by designing and including additional questions related to the pandemic (e.g., assessing COVID-19-related stress) in the questionnaire alongside the original measures stated in the research proposal. This provided a timely and important opportunity to understand how the experiences and mental health of sexual minority individuals were affected by the COVID-19 crisis. Due to the global research and publication priorities related to the pandemic, we prioritized analyzing this part of our research data and writing manuscripts during the initial two years of the project (2020-2021). Five research papers based on the COVID-19 findings from this data were published (see Part C #8), covering various dimensions of lived experiences of sexual minority individuals during the pandemic, such as mental health, sexual activities, access to HIV services, co-residence, and impacts of COVID-19. These findings were also reported in local news media, including South China Morning Post and Hong Kong Free Press. The second project objective aimed to examine the effects of positive and negative identity-salient experiences on the development of critical consciousness over time. Using the longitudinal data collected in this study, we investigated how different dimensions of minority stress (perceived discrimination and internalized stigma) interacted to influence participation in collective action among sexual minority individuals. Specifically, we tested the hypothesis outlined in the project proposal by analyzing the longitudinal associations between minority stress, group identification, and collective action. The results indicated that prior experiences of discrimination were positively associated with collective action at follow-up through increased levels of group identification and commitment to social justice. We also found the moderating effect of internalized stigma, whereby perceived discrimination was not significantly related to group identification and collective action among those with high levels of internalized stigma. These findings were published in Sex Roles, directly addressing the second project objective. While identity-salient experiences have been shown to impact the development of critical consciousness over time, it is crucial to understand various aspects of these experiences and their effects on the lives of LGBT individuals. For sexual minority youth, social media has become an increasingly integral part of everyday life and social routines, especially during and after the pandemic. Based on the data collected in this study, we identified both beneficial and deleterious aspects of social media use and explored how online heterosexist experiences affect the physical and mental health of sexual minority individuals. The results were published in Journal of Interpersonal Violence and Computers in Human Behavior. Sexual orientation change efforts are also recognized as critical identity-salient experiences that affect sexual minority youth. We investigated the effects of SOCE on sexual identity development and mental health, and the results were published in Sexuality Research and Social Policy. Additionally, we explored monosexism as a form of identity-salient experiences targeting bisexual and pansexual individuals. In a paper published in Journal of Sex Research, we examined how sexual identity integration moderated the effect of monosexist discrimination on the mental health of bisexual and pansexual individuals. The third objective of our project was to understand how critical consciousness contributes to identity, psychological, and social development among sexual minorities. Based on the models we hypothesized in our project proposal, we analyzed the longitudinal data to examine the mental health benefits and costs associated with critical consciousness over time. Our findings, which demonstrated both positive and negative effects of critical consciousness on mental health among sexual minority individuals, were published in Social Science & Medicine. This publication directly addresses the third objective of our project. Additionally, we focused on one aspect of critical consciousness (i.e., collective action) and developed a scale to measure collective action for LGBT rights. Our results, also published in Social Science & Medicine, revealed the moderating role of collective action in the relationship between perceived discrimination and depression symptoms.

28609019.label: Major findings and research outcome
28609019.value: The project employed a longitudinal prospective design to investigate the antecedents and developmental outcomes of critical consciousness among sexual minorities. First, we examined how experiences of minority stress contribute to collective action. The results showed that prior exposure to discrimination was associated with increased identification with sexual minorities, which in turn predicted participation in collective action for LGBT rights. Additionally, the findings revealed that the effects of perceived discrimination on group identification and collective action were moderated by internalized stigma. Notably, perceived discrimination was not significantly related to group identification and collective action among individuals with high levels of internalized stigma. These findings support the role of critical consciousness in navigating discrimination. Second, we developed a scale to measure collective action for LGBT rights and found that participation in collective action was not directly linked to mental health. This may be due to the complex emotional experiences associated with collective action, where positive and negative emotions coexist. However, collective action did moderate the relationship between perceived discrimination and mental health. Among sexual minority individuals with higher levels of collective action participation, the association between perceived discrimination and depressive symptoms was weaker. Third, we explored the longitudinal relationships between critical consciousness and mental health among sexual minority individuals. The results demonstrated a co-occurrence of positive and negative effects of critical consciousness on mental health over time. On one hand, critical consciousness was associated with improved mental health outcomes through the mediation of internalized oppression and community connectedness. Specifically, the results provided support for the liberating effect of critical consciousness, as it indirectly contributed to lower levels of emotional distress by mitigating internalized oppression. The findings also revealed the empowering effect of critical consciousness, as it indirectly led to higher levels of well-being through increased community connectedness. On the other hand, the study identified a positive association between critical consciousness and emotional distress. This association may be particularly significant in societies where systemic change is difficult and challenging. Overall, the study highlights that critical consciousness can be a pedagogical and therapeutic tool for the liberation and empowerment of sexual minority individuals. However, it is important to acknowledge the potential risks associated with critical consciousness. Striking a balance between critical consciousness and self-care is crucial to sustain meaningful engagement in the pursuit of social change.

28609019.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28609019.value: Recognizing the significant benefits of critical consciousness demonstrated in this study, it is crucial to actively involve sexual minority youth in the development of critical consciousness. In response to this need, the project team has collaborated with a local community-based organization to develop a peer advocate intervention specifically designed for sexual minority youth. The intervention involves participants undergoing a structured training program and being provided with opportunities to develop and lead community-based projects as peer advocates. The team utilizes a quasi-experimental design to evaluate the effectiveness of this intervention in enhancing critical consciousness and promoting positive identity development. Both quantitative and qualitative data will be collected to gain a comprehensive understanding of participants’ experiences and the outcomes of the intervention. Given the extensive research data collected over the past four years, the project team is dedicated to further quantitative analysis and preparing the findings for publication. This ongoing analysis will enable us to explore the data in greater depth, moving beyond the scope of critical consciousness, to uncover meaningful insights into various aspects of the lives of sexual minority youth that contribute to their resilience and long-term development.

28609019.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28609019.value: Critical consciousness is a powerful tool for individuals from marginalized groups to transcend oppressive conditions through engagement in critical reflection, motivation, and action. While previous work has conceptualized critical consciousness as an antidote to oppression, empirical studies examining its antecedents and developmental outcomes have been limited. This project employs a longitudinal design to investigate critical consciousness as a developmental asset for sexual minority youth. Participants completed a questionnaire and were followed over a three-year period. The results revealed the differential effects of minority stress on group identification and collective action. Additionally, the study demonstrated that participating in collective action can buffer the negative impacts of discrimination on mental health. Although critical consciousness can positively affect mental health by mitigating internalized oppression and strengthening community connectedness, it is important to acknowledge that the emotional disturbance resulting from critical consciousness can be detrimental to mental health. The study extends the literature by understanding critical consciousness as a form of group-level coping in the face of discrimination and providing empirical evidence of its mental health benefits and costs. The results underscore the importance of nurturing critical consciousness in educational and therapeutic settings while highlighting the need to balance critical consciousness with self-care.

28611119.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28611119.value: Student engagement in Math and Science subjects plays a critical role not only in fostering academic achievement in such academic areas but also in motivating secondary school students to choose Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) career tracks. However, studies have shown that there has been a decline in students’ motivation and engagement in Science and Math courses. It is therefore important to identify psychological factors that can promote various domains of engagement in math and science classes. The triarchic model of grit that reflects individuals’ tendency to show passion, perseverance, and adaptability for long-term goals, can lead to adaptive academic functioning such as student engagement in specific domains of academic performance. However, no longitudinal study has been carried out to examine whether triarchic model of grit dimensions predict subsequent math and science engagement as well as the psychological mechanisms underpinning the link of grit to such academic outcomes. Guided by the hierarchical model of achievement motivation, this project will test whether the triarchic model of grit dimensions (i.e., perseverance of effort, consistency of interests, and adaptability to situations) accounts for Math and Science academic engagement domains (i.e., behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and social). It will provide preliminary evidence on the mediating roles of achievement goal orientations as previous research demonstrates that motivation can operate as a psychological mechanism underscoring the link of grit to academic outcomes. As both perseverance and adaptability dimensions of grit have been linked to higher autonomous and controlled motivation in a collectivist setting, it is likely that the ability of these grit dimensions to predict mastery-approach goals and performance-approach goals may be associated with Math and Science academic engagement. This project will adopt a longitudinal structural equation modeling approach to explore: (a) the association of triarchic model of grit facets with Math and Science academic engagement; and (b) the mediating effects of achievement goal orientations on the hypothesized link of grit to engagement in such academic domains among over 2,100 secondary school students, over 700 each in HK, mainland China, and Philippines. This research will contribute to theory through identifying psychological mechanisms that can explain why grit can predict engagement in Math and Science classes. This project will provide evidence on the generalizability and benefits of grit to several Asian societies.

28611119.label: Realisation of objectives
28611119.value: The approved project entitled “Are Triarchic Model of Grit Dimensions Related to Subsequent Achievement Goals and Academic Engagement in Math and Science in Hong Kong, Mainland China, and Philippines?” examined associations of the triarchic model of grit’s (TMG) dimensions – perseverance of effort, consistency of interests, and adaptability to situations– with subsequent academic engagement in math and science via the mediating roles of all achievement goal orientation (i.e., mastery-approach goals, mastery-avoidance goals, performance-approach goals, and performance-avoidance goals). The first research objective that revolved around cross-cultural differences in the TMG’s dimensions was fulfilled by: (a) exploring whether the scores from the grit subscales were invariant across Hong Kong, mainland China, and the Philippines; and (b) assessing significant differences in all grit’s dimensions in such settings. The second research objective that focused on examining the longitudinal links of the TMG’s dimensions on subsequent achievement goal orientations and academic engagement in math and science was addressed by: (a) measuring TMG’s dimensions, achievement goal orientations, and academic engagement in math and science at three times with around six months of interval per wave of data collection; and (b) performing statistical analyses such as structural equation modelling to assess how the TMG’s dimensions predict achievement goals and engagement in math and science over time when controlling for the effects of age, gender, setting, year level, socioeconomic status, cultural variables, and conscientiousness. The third objective that revolved around the mediating roles of achievement goal orientations on the links of the TMG’s dimensions on math and science engagement after 12 months was realized by conducting statistical analyses (i.e., bias-corrected bootstrapping technique) that detect whether achievement goal orientations (e.g., mastery-approach goals and performance-approach goals) account for the associations of grit with math and science engagement.

28611119.label: Major findings and research outcome
28611119.value: This project aims to examine the longitudinal associations of the triarchic model of grit and its dimensions (i.e., perseverance of effort, consistency of interests, and adaptability to situations) with academic engagement in math and science among high school students in Hong Kong, mainland China, and the Philippines. The first research objective revolved around cross-cultural differences in triarchic model of grit in three contexts (see Datu et al., 2021 for the preliminary findings). Result showed that there were significant differences in perseverance of effort, consistency of interests, and adaptability to situations among high school students in Hong Kong, mainland China, and the Philippines, Specifically, students in the Philippines had higher scores than those in Hong Kong and mainland China. Students in mainland China had higher scores than those in Hong Kong on all grit’s dimensions. The second research objective involved assessing the links of grit’s dimensions with subsequent achievement goals and academic engagement in math and science when controlling for age, gender, GDP per capita, other cultural dimensions (e.g., individualism, power distance, and long-term orientation), and conscientiousness. Results demonstrated that adaptability was associated with higher mastery-avoidance goals and overall academic engagement in science after 12 months. Mastery-approach goals was related to greater engagement in science after 6 months. However, grit and achievement goals had different patterns of associations with subsequent academic engagement in math. Whereas perseverance was linked to greater behavioral engagement in math, adaptability was associated with emotional and overall engagement in math after 12 months. Mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, and performance-avoidance goals were related to greater behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and social engagement in math after 6 months. The third objective examined the mediating effects of achievement goal orientations on the links between grit and subsequent academic engagement in math and science. Findings showed that adaptability had positive associations with science engagement via its association with greater mastery-avoidance goals. Mastery-approach goals also mediated the indirect effects of perseverance on behavioral and cognitive engagement in math. Further, mastery-avoidance goals mediated the indirect effects of adaptability on cognitive, emotional, and social dimensions of math engagement. Taken together, this project indicates that specific dimensions of grit –such as adaptability to situations and perseverance of effort – predict either overall science engagement or several dimensions of math engagement over time in high school students in Hong Kong, mainland China, and the Philippines. Mastery-approach goals also serve as a robust predictor of succeeding engagement outcomes.

28611119.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28611119.value: This project’s findings can serve as a springboard towards future projects that may enrich our understanding of the role that grit plays in motivational processes and STEM-specific learning outcomes in young children. Although my research showed that high school students with greater adaptability to situations and perseverance of effort are likely to show higher science and math engagement, these findings may not be generalizable to younger students – such as primary school-aged children. Thus, it is critical to investigate the academic and social-emotional benefits of grit in students across developmental phases and contextual backgrounds. Future projects also need to tease out psychological processes that account for the links of grit to more objective educational outcomes (e.g., actual achievement from class records or teacher-rated engagement) in math and science. Importantly, this study points to the importance of cultivating specific dimensions (i.e., perseverance and adaptability) of grit in adolescents. Curating, implementing, and evaluating grit-based psychoeducational interventions is necessary to boost children and youth’s active involvement in academic activities in math and science. Future research can adopt more rigorous methodological approaches (e.g., randomized control trial design) to demonstrate how grit causes sustainable improvement in students’ math and science engagement.

28611119.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28611119.value: This project assessed the associations of the triarchic model of grit –characterized by perseverance of effort, consistency of interests, and adaptability to situations– with academic engagement in math and science via the mediating roles of achievement goal orientations among high school students in Hong Kong, mainland China, and the Philippines. This project has three notable findings. First, students in the Philippines had better scores than those in mainland China and Hong Kong on perseverance, consistency, and adaptability. Also, students in mainland China had higher scores on all grit’s dimensions than those in Hong Kong. Second, students with more adaptability are likely to study to avoid the risks of not mastering the content of learning materials, which in turn facilitates science engagement. This result indicates that implementing initiatives to facilitate effective adjustment of goals to situations can boost active learning involvement in science. Third, students with greater perseverance and adaptability are likely to show greater mastery-approach goals, which in turn relates to higher math engagement. This finding suggests that bolstering persistence in facing setbacks and effective adjustment of goals based environmental conditions are associated with intrinsic joy linked to studying, which in turn, relates to active involvement in math activities.
